Podcasts

Git Going with GitHub - Audio Series

Listen to the workshop as one end-to-end path. Companion lessons, Challenge Coach episodes, and reference material are interleaved so learners can hear the concept, practice it, and then keep moving through the course. Every episode includes a full transcript below the player.

Subscribe: Add the podcast RSS feed to your preferred podcast app - Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Overcast, or any RSS reader.

Transcripts: Every episode includes a complete, readable transcript. Expand the "Read Transcript" section below any episode to follow along or search the conversation.

How to Use These Episodes

  • Follow the path: Listen in order when you want the full workshop experience.
  • Practice in place: Challenge Coach episodes appear near the chapters that prepare you for that task.
  • Use references when needed: Appendix and reference episodes are placed near the moments where they help most.

1. Episode 0: Welcome to Git Going with GitHub

A tour of the workshop structure, the two-day arc, and what you will accomplish.

Based on: Course Guide

Download Episode 0 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 0: Welcome to Git Going with GitHub

Transcript

Alex: Welcome to Git Going with GitHub. I’m Alex.

Jamie: And I’m Jamie. If you’re arriving with a workshop link, a little uncertainty, or that feeling of, wait, what am I supposed to do first, this is for you.

Alex: Exactly. This opening lesson is your orientation. We’re going to make the path clear from the start: what this workshop is, how the two days fit together, how your private Learning Room works, how to get into it through GitHub Classroom, what to do when tools change, how to choose the right tool for the moment, what to listen for with a screen reader, and where to go for help.

Jamie: So this is not just a welcome message. It’s the map.

Alex: Yes. And one of the most important promises in this course is that you are not being asked to do pretend work. This workshop is built around a real contribution path in real tools: GitHub, VS Code, Git, GitHub Copilot, and accessibility-focused contribution workflows.

Alex: Let’s start with the big picture. This course guide describes the GitHub Learning Room as your workshop companion. Think of it as your base camp and table of contents for the whole experience.

Jamie: And there’s a note learners should hear early: the materials are actively refined.

Alex: Right. Content may be updated leading up to and even during the course. That’s not a warning that things are broken. It’s a reminder that this is a living curriculum built around living platforms.

Jamie: Which leads to the other big reminder: tools and websites change.

Alex: They do. GitHub.com changes. GitHub Classroom changes. VS Code changes. Copilot changes. Browser extensions change. Agent features change. Labels move, buttons get renamed, preview features appear or disappear, account policies differ, and model availability can shift.

Jamie: That can feel stressful, especially if you’re using a screen reader and following instructions carefully.

Alex: Absolutely. So the course teaches a durable strategy, not just a frozen screenshot. If the docs and your screen differ, orient yourself by the URL, the browser tab title, the page heading, landmarks, tab names, button labels, keyboard help, and in VS Code, the Command Palette.

Jamie: So instead of thinking, the page changed, I’m lost, you think, what signals tell me where I am now?

Alex: Exactly. That skill matters more than memorizing one version of a page. And if you find a mismatch, report it so the curriculum can be corrected.

Jamie: Okay, so what is the workshop structure?

Alex: It’s a two-day workshop with one central idea: you will make real contributions to a real open source project. Not simulated. Not practice in a fake interface. Real collaboration skills in real environments.

Jamie: But the live event and the written curriculum are not exactly the same size, right?

Alex: Correct. The live agenda is intentionally smaller than the full self-paced curriculum. In the live sessions, facilitators prioritize the minimum core path needed for you to make and understand a real contribution. Then the rest remains available for preparation, catch-up, remote participation, and continued work after the event.

Jamie: So there’s a live core, and then there’s asynchronous follow-up.

Alex: Yes. If something isn’t covered live, that doesn’t mean it’s optional in the sense of unimportant. It means the full chapter set, challenge flow, solutions, podcast episodes, and Slack support are there so you can keep going. Remote participants also use the same checkpoints and evidence prompts, with written instructions available before each live block.

Jamie: Walk us through the two days.

Alex: Day 1 stays in the browser. You learn GitHub’s web interface using only your keyboard and screen reader. The live Day 1 core path gets you through repository navigation, issues, branches, commits, and a first pull request.

Jamie: And then there’s more beyond the minimum live path.

Alex: Right. Review practice, merge conflicts, labels, notifications, and open source culture can be stretch goals during the live event or completed later asynchronously.

Jamie: Then Day 2 moves to the desktop.

Alex: Yes. Day 2 is Visual Studio Code plus accessibility agents. You move from the browser into VS Code, learn GitHub Copilot, and work with the Accessibility Agents ecosystem. The live core prepares you to make a real contribution, and the async continuation gives you time to improve and submit that contribution well.

Jamie: I like that there’s a progression here, not a leap.

Alex: That progression is very intentional. First you learn the skill manually in the browser. Navigate a repository. Work with an issue. Open a pull request. Review. Merge.

Jamie: Then there’s a bridge.

Alex: Exactly. On many GitHub repositories, you can press the period key to open github.dev, which is VS Code in your browser. It uses familiar keyboard patterns and a VS Code-style editor without installation.

Jamie: But it has limits.

Alex: It does. No local terminal, no debugger in the full desktop sense, only web-compatible extensions, and not the complete desktop agent workflow.

Jamie: So github.dev is a bridge, not the finish line.

Alex: Well said. Once you understand the workflow in the browser, the desktop version makes more sense. Then on Day 2 you deepen the work: VS Code basics, Copilot inline suggestions, Copilot Chat, and agent-supported workflows like daily briefings, issue tracking, pull request review, analytics, and preparing an upstream contribution.

Jamie: And there’s a principle underneath all that.

Alex: Yes. Learn the manual skill first. Then learn what automation is doing for you. Agents are helpful only if you understand the workflow they’re accelerating.

Jamie: Before learners even begin Day 1, what should already be done?

Alex: Two things matter here. First, if you want the most guided path, start with the Get Going with GitHub guide. That’s the step-by-step onboarding path from getting the assignment link to knowing where to click, what challenge to open, and how to ask for help.

Jamie: And second?

Alex: Complete the pre-workshop setup chapter before Day 1. That includes creating a GitHub account, installing Git, setting up VS Code — optional for Day 1, required for Day 2 — configuring your screen reader for GitHub, and verifying that everything works.

Jamie: How long should that setup take?

Alex: About thirty minutes, though support is available if it takes longer. And if you can’t finish every setup step before the workshop, tell a facilitator early. Setup problems are normal.

Jamie: There’s also an audio layer to the course itself, which is fitting, since we are currently in it.

Alex: Exactly. Every chapter and appendix has a companion podcast episode. You can listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after reading to reinforce them. There’s a browseable podcast page with HTML5 players, and there’s an RSS feed if you prefer a podcast app.

Jamie: And the episodes are short enough to fit into real life.

Alex: Yes, usually about eight to eighteen minutes. Good for a walk, a commute, or just a break from intensive screen reader navigation.

Jamie: Let’s make the curriculum concrete. What does Day 1 cover?

Alex: Day 1 begins with the getting-started path and pre-workshop setup, then moves into choosing your tools, understanding GitHub’s web structure, navigating repositories, understanding the Learning Room, working with issues, working with pull requests, handling merge conflicts, open source culture, labels and milestones and projects, and finally notifications and a Day 1 close.

Jamie: So by the end of Day 1, a learner should be able to use GitHub’s web interface independently.

Alex: Yes. The Day 1 self-paced total is about eight hours, but the live agenda focuses on the core path and may leave some chapters as async follow-up.

Jamie: And Day 2?

Alex: Day 2 covers the VS Code interface and setup, accessibility features in VS Code, the mental model of Git, Git in practice, code review with pull requests and diffs, GitHub Copilot, issue templates, fork-based contribution, accessibility agents, a capstone project, and next steps.

Jamie: Which is a lot.

Alex: It is. About ten hours self-paced. Live Day 2 focuses on VS Code, Git, Copilot, agent discovery, and supported contribution work, with the deeper capstone often continuing afterward.

Jamie: I also don’t want to skip the reference materials, because those are a real accessibility support feature, not an afterthought.

Alex: I agree. The appendices are there to stay open while you work. They are not part of the linear chapter sequence. They’re meant to be used at the moment you need them.

Jamie: What are the big ones learners should keep handy?

Alex: Always-open resources include the glossary and the screen reader cheat sheet. Beyond that, the guide also points you to the FAQ, troubleshooting guide, quick reference, glossary, screen reader cheat sheet, and a broader resources collection.

Jamie: So if you hit jargon, use the glossary. If you forget a command, use quick reference. If something breaks, use troubleshooting.

Alex: Exactly. And if you are still stuck, open a support issue at the Community Access support repository. Describe what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and include your screen reader and operating system.

Jamie: That detail matters because support is much easier when the context is clear.

Alex: Yes. “It doesn’t work” is hard to diagnose. “I’m using NVDA on Windows, I activated this control, I expected a repository page, and instead I heard this” is actionable.

Jamie: Before we leave the course guide, can we do a compact workshop-at-a-glance recap?

Alex: Sure. Day 1 focuses on the GitHub web interface using a browser and screen reader. The core skills are navigate, issue, pull request, review, and merge. The outcome is that you can use GitHub independently.

Jamie: And Day 2 focuses on VS Code plus accessibility agents.

Alex: Right. The tools include VS Code, Copilot, and the accessibility agent ecosystem. The core skills are Git, Copilot, agents, fork-based contribution, and the capstone path. The outcome is that you have a real contribution workflow and review process you can keep using.

Jamie: And if someone wants the official source of truth?

Alex: Use GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. The course also includes section-level source maps so learners can verify facts by topic.

Jamie: All right. Let’s shift into the guided onboarding path: getting going with GitHub.

Alex: This guide starts with a reassuring premise: if you are new, unsure, or joining from a workshop link, you do not need prior knowledge of Git, GitHub, VS Code, or the command line to begin.

Jamie: That’s important to say out loud, because many learners assume everyone else already knows the basics.

Alex: Exactly. The course is designed so you are not left guessing what comes next.

Jamie: What specifically will learners have?

Alex: You’ll have a GitHub Classroom assignment link from the facilitator, your own private Learning Room repository, challenge issues with explicit instructions, evidence prompts telling you what to post when you finish, Gandalf bot feedback on pull requests, reference solutions you can compare against after you try, and multiple tool paths so you can work in the browser, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the command line when appropriate.

Jamie: So the goal isn’t speed.

Alex: No. The goal is confidence through small, checkable steps.

Jamie: Let’s return to something you mentioned earlier, because it appears here too: what should learners do when tools or pages change?

Alex: First, do not assume that a difference means you failed. Instead, use an exploration pattern. Check the URL and browser tab title. Move by headings, landmarks, tabs, and button names instead of relying on visual order. Open keyboard shortcut help — on GitHub that’s question mark — or use the VS Code Command Palette if shortcuts differ. Read nearby labels before activating a control. And if needed, ask a facilitator or file a curriculum issue including the page link, the step that differed, and what you heard or observed.

Jamie: So the durable skill is orient, verify, continue.

Alex: Perfectly said.

Jamie: Now we get to the actual starting sequence. Step one: know your starting place.

Alex: Yes. Before Day 1, complete the pre-workshop setup chapter. That chapter helps you create or verify your GitHub account, configure accessibility settings, choose a browser, install Git and VS Code, and confirm your screen reader setup.

Jamie: And if setup is incomplete?

Alex: Tell a facilitator early. Recovery time and support are built into the workshop.

Jamie: Step two is accepting the GitHub Classroom assignment. Can you walk us through that in plain language?

Alex: Absolutely. At the start of Day 1, the facilitator gives you a GitHub Classroom assignment link. It usually begins with classroom dot github dot com slash a slash.

Jamie: And you should open it in the browser where you’re already signed in to GitHub.

Alex: Correct. Then, if GitHub asks you to authorize GitHub Classroom, activate the authorize button. If you’re asked to choose your name from a roster, select your name. If your name is missing, use the skip option and tell the facilitator. Then activate Accept this assignment.

Jamie: And then wait.

Alex: Yes. GitHub Classroom needs a moment to create your private repository. Refresh until the repository link appears, open it, and bookmark it.

Jamie: And the repository name usually follows a pattern.

Alex: Something like learning-room-your-username. That repository is your personal practice space.

Jamie: Which takes us to step three: understanding the Learning Room itself.

Alex: The Learning Room is a private repository created from a template. Everyone begins with the same materials, but your work belongs to you.

Jamie: Why is that such a useful design?

Alex: Because it gives you a safe place to practice real GitHub workflows. You have your own issues, branches, commits, and pull requests. Other students do not see your work unless pairing is intentional. Mistakes are expected and recoverable. Bot feedback is educational, not punitive. And challenge issues unlock in sequence, so you always know the next step.

Jamie: I love the phrase guided practice studio.

Alex: That’s exactly what it is. Real GitHub, but with scaffolding.

Jamie: Step four is finding Challenge 1.

Alex: Once the Learning Room is created, the Student Progression Bot opens your first challenge issue.

Jamie: So what does the learner do?

Alex: Open your Learning Room repository. Go to the Issues tab — on GitHub the shortcut is G then I. Find the issue titled Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around. Open it and read the issue body from top to bottom. Follow the checklist. Post your evidence in the requested place, either in the evidence field or as a comment. Then close the challenge issue when the instructions tell you to close it.

Jamie: And closing one challenge triggers the next.

Alex: Exactly. You do not have to hunt through the whole course wondering what comes next. The sequence is designed to reveal the next step when you finish the current one.

Jamie: Step five is tool choice, and I think this is where learners sometimes get anxious. They worry there’s one right tool.

Alex: There isn’t. The workshop teaches the workflow first, then gives you multiple tool paths.

Jamie: Can we do the plain-language version?

Alex: Yes. GitHub.com in the browser is best for Day 1, issues, pull requests, repository navigation, and reviews. github.dev is best when you want a VS Code-style editor in the browser without installing anything; on many repository pages, press period to open it. VS Code desktop is best for Day 2, local Git, Copilot, extensions, and deeper editing. GitHub Desktop is best if you want a desktop Git workflow without typing Git commands. GitHub CLI is best if you prefer terminal workflows or want automation later.

Jamie: And whichever tool you use, the important thing is understanding the contribution workflow.

Alex: Yes: issue, branch, change, commit, pull request, review, merge. Tools may differ, but that conceptual path stays consistent.

Jamie: Step six is especially for screen reader users: what to listen for.

Alex: When you feel lost, listen for structure before taking action. Useful signals include the page title, the repository name heading, landmark names like main content or repository navigation, tab names like Code, Issues, and Pull requests, the issue title, the pull request title, the branch name, button names, field labels, and bot comments or check results.

Jamie: So if I’m unsure where I am, I shouldn’t panic. I should pause and navigate by headings or landmarks.

Alex: Exactly. Re-orienting is part of the workflow. It is not evidence that you’re doing something wrong.

Jamie: Step seven is using the support built into the course.

Alex: And there’s quite a lot of it. Every challenge issue includes instructions and evidence prompts. Every chapter has an If You Get Stuck section. Every challenge has a reference solution in the solutions folder. Gandalf bot posts feedback on pull requests. The Student Progression Bot opens the next challenge when you finish the current one. Facilitators and peers are part of the support system too.

Jamie: So the advice is: don’t silently restart from scratch.

Alex: Exactly. Read the latest bot message, check the challenge issue, and ask for help with the link to the page where you got stuck.

Jamie: And then step eight is a first success check.

Alex: Yes. You are ready to continue when you can say four things: I can open my Learning Room repository. I can find the Issues tab. I can open Challenge 1. And I know where to post my evidence and how to ask for help.

Jamie: That’s such a healthy checkpoint, because it doesn’t require mastery of everything.

Alex: Exactly. You do not need to understand every GitHub feature before beginning. You just need enough orientation to take the next step.

Jamie: So where should learners go next if they want the gentlest path?

Alex: Use this order: pre-workshop setup, choose your tools, understand GitHub, navigate repositories, understand the Learning Room, and then complete your Challenge 1 issue in your own repository.

Jamie: And I think the final line of that guide is worth repeating in spirit.

Alex: Yes. You belong here. The path is meant to stay explicit, and the course keeps giving you the next step.

Jamie: Before we wrap, let’s make sure we include the administrative details learners may need later.

Alex: Good idea. For current factual reference, use GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. The course materials also include section-level source maps showing which official sources back which sections.

Jamie: And if a learner needs immediate practical backup during the workshop?

Alex: Keep the reference materials nearby: glossary, screen reader cheat sheet, troubleshooting, quick reference, FAQ, and the resources collection. If you’re still stuck, open a support issue with clear details about what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and which screen reader and operating system you’re using.

Jamie: So the through line of this whole episode is: this workshop is real, but it is also structured.

Alex: Exactly. Real tools, real workflows, real contributions, but also clear guidance, private practice space, progressive challenges, bot feedback, accessible orientation strategies, and multiple ways to continue when something changes.

Jamie: That feels like a good place to land. You do not have to know everything. You do need a starting place.

Alex: And now you have one. Open your setup chapter if you haven’t completed it yet. Accept your GitHub Classroom assignment when your facilitator provides it. Bookmark your Learning Room. Find Challenge 1. And keep moving one checkable step at a time.

Jamie: We’ll meet you in the next part.

2. Episode 18: Glossary of Terms

Comprehensive glossary: Git, GitHub, open source, and accessibility terminology.

Based on: Appendix A: Glossary of Terms

Download Episode 18 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 18: Glossary of Terms

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're doing something a little different. Instead of following one workflow from start to finish, we're building a mental map of GitHub and Git terms you'll hear over and over in open source work.

Jamie: So this is the episode people can return to when they hear a word like fork, upstream, rebase, or detached HEAD and think, wait, what exactly does that mean again?

Alex: Exactly. This glossary is meant to be a reference companion for the whole workshop, and really for all chapters. If a term feels fuzzy, this is where you come back to ground yourself.

Jamie: And because our audience includes blind and low-vision learners, let's start with the navigation tips too, not just the definitions.

Alex: Yes. If you're using a screen reader, the glossary is designed so you can move by headings. Jumping by heading level is a fast way to move term by term, especially where each term is a level-three heading. You can also open your screen reader's elements list, like NVDA plus F7 or Insert plus F6 in some screen readers, to browse all headings at once and filter by typing a few letters.

Jamie: And if you know the term but not the category, the alphabetical quick reference at the bottom is often the fastest path.

Alex: Right. For low-vision users, increasing zoom and scanning the bold term headings can make the page much easier to browse. The alphabetical table is also useful at high zoom because each row stands on its own. And for sighted users, the categories can help you narrow the search, while Control-F is still a great shortcut for everyone.

Alex: Let's start with the building blocks. First up: repository, often shortened to repo.

Jamie: This is one of those words people hear immediately, but it helps to define it carefully.

Alex: A repository is the container for an entire project. It holds the files, folders, documentation, and the full history of changes. A good analogy is a project folder with a time machine built in. You don't just have the current version of the files. You have a recorded history of how they changed over time.

Jamie: And on GitHub, a repository lives at a web address like github dot com slash owner slash repo name.

Alex: Exactly. And a few related terms matter here. A remote repository usually means the copy hosted on GitHub. A local repository is the copy on your computer. Upstream is the original project you forked from. And a fork is your own copy of someone else's repository.

Jamie: That naturally leads to organization, or org.

Alex: An organization is a shared GitHub account for groups of people. Many open source projects live under organizations rather than personal accounts. In a URL like github dot com slash microsoft slash vscode, microsoft is the organization and vscode is the repository.

Jamie: So if a learner sees a project under an org, that usually means multiple maintainers or teams may be involved.

Alex: That's often true.

Jamie: Now let's define fork, because that one can feel abstract at first.

Alex: A fork is a personal copy of someone else's repository that lives in your own GitHub account. It includes the files and the history. Changes you make in your fork do not automatically affect the original repository. If you want your changes considered by the original project, you open a pull request.

Jamie: And the reason people fork is simple: most open source repositories do not give random contributors direct write access.

Alex: Right. Forking gives you a safe place to work freely.

Jamie: Okay, then what is a remote?

Alex: A remote is a named connection from your local Git repository to a repository hosted somewhere else, usually on GitHub. Your local repository can have more than one remote. The most common two are origin and upstream.

Jamie: Origin usually points to your fork, and upstream usually points to the original repository you forked from.

Alex: Exactly. If you run a command like git push origin main, you're pushing your local main branch to the remote named origin.

Jamie: And if someone wants to inspect their remotes, the command is git remote space dash v.

Alex: Yes. That shows the remote names and URLs. And to add a remote, you might use something like git remote add upstream followed by the URL of the original repository.

Jamie: So origin is really a special case of remote.

Alex: That's a great way to say it. Origin is the default name Git gives the repository you cloned from. If you cloned your fork, then origin points to your fork on GitHub. Commands like git push and git pull often default to origin unless you specify a different remote.

Jamie: Let's talk about dot gitignore, because this one protects people from a lot of headaches.

Alex: Absolutely. A .gitignore file lives at the root of your repository and tells Git which files or folders to ignore. In other words, Git will not track or commit those files if they are untracked.

Jamie: And there are a few common categories of things people usually want to ignore.

Alex: Yes. Dependencies, like node underscore modules or vendor folders. Environment variables, like .env files that may contain secrets. Build outputs, like dist or build folders and sometimes log files. Operating system files, such as .DS underscore Store on macOS or Thumbs dot db on Windows. And IDE files, such as .vscode or .idea.

Jamie: Important accessibility note for understanding this concept: .gitignore is not just housekeeping. It's often a security and collaboration tool.

Alex: Exactly. It helps keep secrets out of Git, keeps generated files from cluttering history, and avoids editor-specific noise that doesn't belong in the project.

Jamie: And there's one important gotcha.

Alex: Yes. .gitignore only applies to untracked files. If a file was already committed, adding it to .gitignore does not magically remove it from version control. You first have to stop tracking it, often with git rm dash dash cached filename, then add it to .gitignore and commit that change.

Jamie: That's such a common beginner surprise.

Alex: It really is.

Jamie: Next term: clone.

Alex: Cloning means copying a repository from GitHub to your local computer so you can work on it in VS Code or another editor. When you clone, you get both the files and the full history.

Jamie: And this is where people mix up fork and clone.

Alex: Right. Fork is your copy on GitHub. Clone is your copy on your computer. In a typical open source workflow, you fork first on GitHub, then clone your fork locally.

Jamie: Now branch.

Alex: A branch is a separate line of development inside a repository. The main branch, often called main and in some older projects master, is usually the stable primary branch. When you want to add a feature or fix a bug, you create another branch so your work stays isolated until it's ready.

Jamie: I like the idea of branches as parallel timelines.

Alex: That's the classic mental model. They can evolve independently, then be merged later. Common names include main, develop, feature slash something, fix slash something, or docs slash something.

Jamie: So branch names often communicate purpose.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Then we have commit.

Alex: A commit is a saved snapshot of your changes at a moment in time. Each commit has a message describing what changed and why, a unique SHA hash, the author and timestamp, and the actual additions and deletions.

Jamie: And good commit messages are usually written in the imperative mood. So, Fix typo in README, not Fixed typo.

Alex: Yes. A strong commit message helps future readers understand intent. Sometimes the message also includes a longer body explaining context, and it may reference an issue number, like Fixes number 42.

Jamie: Last building-block term in this group: diff.

Alex: A diff shows the difference between two versions of a file. Added lines are typically shown in green with a plus sign. Removed lines are shown in red with a minus sign. Unchanged lines appear around them for context.

Jamie: And even if a learner can't see those colors, the conceptual point still matters.

Alex: Absolutely. Whether you're using visual diff views or screen reader-friendly text output, you're still interpreting additions, deletions, and context. Reading diffs is a core skill for code review. When you open the Files Changed tab in a pull request, you're reading a diff.

Alex: Now let's shift to collaboration workflow.

Jamie: Starting with issues.

Alex: An issue is a discussion item in a GitHub repository. Issues can report bugs, request features, ask questions, discuss ideas, or track work. Each issue gets a number, like number 42, and can include labels, assignees, milestones, and comments.

Jamie: And in many projects, issues are the starting point for contribution.

Alex: Yes. It's often best practice to find or open an issue before changing code. That helps you avoid duplicated work and align with maintainers.

Jamie: Then comes the pull request, or PR.

Alex: A pull request is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another. You're essentially saying, here is my work, please review it and consider bringing it into the target branch.

Jamie: A PR shows the source branch, the target branch, the diff, a description, and the discussion around the change.

Alex: Right. And the phrase pull request comes from the idea that you're requesting maintainers to pull your changes into their project.

Jamie: Then reviewers step in.

Alex: That process is called code review. One or more collaborators read the PR and provide feedback. They may leave comments, approve the change, or request changes before merge.

Jamie: And good reviews are not just technically correct. They're kind, specific, and constructive.

Alex: Exactly. Code review is communication as much as evaluation.

Jamie: Let's define merge.

Alex: Merging means combining changes from one branch into another. Once a PR is approved, a maintainer may merge it. Common strategies include a merge commit, which creates a new commit recording the merge; squash and merge, which combines all PR commits into one; and rebase and merge, which replays the commits on top of the target branch for a linear history.

Jamie: And then the scary phrase: merge conflict.

Alex: A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same part of the same file in different ways, and Git can't decide which version to keep. It stops and asks a human to resolve the conflict.

Jamie: That's when you may see conflict markers in the file.

Alex: Yes. You'll see markers that separate your current branch content from the incoming branch content. You resolve the conflict by editing the file so it contains the correct final version, removing the markers, and then committing the resolution.

Jamie: So a conflict is not Git failing. It's Git asking for help where ambiguity exists.

Alex: Beautifully put.

Jamie: Now upstream.

Alex: Upstream refers to the original repository you forked from. If you have a fork, your changes often go from your local clone to your fork, and then through a PR toward the original project. But updates from the original project can also move the other direction into your fork when you sync with upstream.

Jamie: So upstream is about the source project, while origin is usually your fork.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And then some organizing terms: label, milestone, and project.

Alex: A label is a colored tag used to categorize issues and pull requests. Labels might indicate bug, documentation, accessibility, good first issue, help wanted, or priority.

Jamie: A milestone groups related issues or PRs around a goal or release.

Alex: Right. And GitHub Projects is a planning tool, often board-like, used to track work across issues and PRs. Think status columns, planning views, and a shared work dashboard.

Alex: Next are people and roles.

Jamie: Maintainer is probably the most important one to define.

Alex: A maintainer is a person with responsibility for the repository. They often have write or admin access and make decisions about issues, pull requests, releases, and direction.

Jamie: A contributor is broader.

Alex: Yes. A contributor is anyone who contributes to the project. That could mean code, documentation, design, bug reports, testing, accessibility feedback, translations, discussions, and more.

Jamie: Then triage.

Alex: Triage is the work of reviewing and categorizing incoming issues or pull requests. That may include adding labels, asking clarifying questions, closing duplicates, or helping route work to the right people.

Jamie: And collaborator?

Alex: A collaborator is someone who has been granted direct access to work in a repository, usually with some level of write permission, even if they are not a full maintainer.

Jamie: The glossary also includes common abbreviations and slang. We may not have every single informal phrase spelled out in the source excerpt we saw, but let's cover the style of language learners will hear.

Alex: Good idea. You'll regularly hear repo for repository, org for organization, PR for pull request, and SHA pronounced either as individual letters or sometimes just called a hash. You'll also hear people say push, pull, fetch, merge, squash, rebase, and sync as shorthand for common Git actions.

Jamie: And it's okay if this language feels dense at first. Fluency comes from repetition.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now we move into more technical Git and GitHub concepts.

Jamie: Let's start with HEAD, because that name sounds strange.

Alex: HEAD is a pointer to your current location in Git, usually the latest commit on the branch you're currently on. If you're on a branch, HEAD generally points to that branch tip.

Jamie: So HEAD answers the question, where am I right now in the commit history?

Alex: Yes.

Jamie: Then what is detached HEAD?

Alex: Detached HEAD means HEAD is pointing directly to a commit instead of to a branch name. This often happens if you check out a specific commit, a tag, or something other than a branch tip.

Jamie: Why does that matter?

Alex: Because if you make commits while detached, those commits are not attached to a named branch. They can become hard to find later if you move away. That's the big practical meaning.

Jamie: So why it happens is usually that a person checked out a commit or tag directly.

Alex: Correct. What it means is: you're looking at a snapshot, not working on a normal branch. And how to fix it is usually to create or switch to a branch. If you want to keep work you made there, create a new branch from that point so the commits have a name and a stable reference.

Jamie: That's much less scary when explained plainly.

Alex: It really is.

Jamie: Next: stash.

Alex: A stash is a temporary shelf for uncommitted changes. If you're in the middle of work and need to switch branches or handle something urgent, stash lets you set aside your changes without making a commit yet.

Jamie: What's a common workflow?

Alex: Imagine you're working on branch A and you suddenly need to do something on main, or on another branch. You can stash your uncommitted changes, switch branches, do the urgent task, then come back and reapply the stash.

Jamie: And there are specific stash commands people should recognize.

Alex: Yes. Common ones include git stash to save changes, git stash list to see saved stashes, git stash apply to reapply one while keeping it in the stash list, and git stash pop to reapply it and remove it from the list.

Jamie: Rebase is one of the most confusing terms for beginners.

Alex: So let's frame it carefully. Merge and rebase can both integrate changes from one line of development into another, but they do it differently.

Jamie: Merge preserves the branching history and creates a merge commit.

Alex: Right. Rebase, by contrast, replays your commits on top of another base commit. The result is a cleaner, more linear history, but it rewrites commit history.

Jamie: That's the key tradeoff.

Alex: Exactly. When to use rebase? Often when you're updating your local feature branch to sit on top of the latest main before opening or updating a PR, especially in projects that prefer linear history.

Jamie: And when should you not rebase?

Alex: Do not casually rebase shared public history that other people are already building on. Because rebase changes commit identities, it can disrupt collaborators.

Jamie: What's a basic rebase workflow?

Alex: You update your knowledge of the remote branch, then rebase your current branch onto the newer target branch. If conflicts appear, you fix the conflicts, continue the rebase, and test your result.

Jamie: So that omitted heading about fixing conflicts still matters here.

Alex: Definitely. Conflicts during rebase are resolved much like merge conflicts: edit the files, remove conflict markers, then continue the process.

Jamie: Then there's cherry-pick.

Alex: Cherry-pick means taking one specific commit and applying it onto your current branch. Instead of merging a whole branch, you choose a single commit by its SHA.

Jamie: When would you use it?

Alex: When one isolated fix belongs on another branch too. For example, maybe a bug fix was made on a feature branch and you want that exact fix on a release branch without bringing over all the other work.

Jamie: Fetch versus pull is another pair that gets blurred together.

Alex: Fetch downloads new information from a remote without merging it into your current branch. Pull usually means fetch plus merge, or fetch plus rebase, depending on configuration.

Jamie: So when should learners use fetch?

Alex: Use fetch when you want to see what's changed remotely without changing your working branch yet. It's a cautious, inspect-first move.

Jamie: And pull?

Alex: Use pull when you're ready to bring remote changes directly into your local branch in one step.

Jamie: Now the term everyone approaches with caution: force push.

Alex: Force push overwrites the remote branch reference with your local branch history, even if that means discarding the remote's previous history for that branch.

Jamie: Why would anyone need that?

Alex: Most commonly after rewriting history locally, such as after a rebase or an interactive cleanup of commits. Since the commit identities changed, a normal push may be rejected.

Jamie: When is force push okay?

Alex: Usually only on your own branch, especially a personal feature branch where you understand the consequences and no one else is relying on that exact remote history.

Jamie: When is it never okay?

Alex: Never force push shared protected branches like main in a collaborative project unless there is an extraordinary, explicitly coordinated administrative reason. For ordinary work, that's off limits.

Jamie: And the safer alternative is force with lease.

Alex: Yes. Dash dash force with lease checks that the remote branch is still in the state you expect before overwriting it. It's safer because it helps prevent accidentally deleting someone else's newer work.

Jamie: Let's define SHA or hash more directly.

Alex: A SHA, often just called a hash, is the unique identifier for a commit or other Git object. Think of it like a fingerprint. Even a short abbreviated SHA is often enough to identify a commit in conversation or commands.

Jamie: Tag and release are related but not identical.

Alex: Correct. A tag is a permanent named reference to a specific commit, often used for version markers like v1 point 0 point 0. A release is a GitHub concept built around a versioned snapshot, often with release notes and downloadable assets. Releases commonly point to tags.

Jamie: Now actions, workflows, and CI slash CD.

Alex: GitHub Actions is GitHub's automation system. A workflow is an automated process defined in files in the repository, often triggered by events like pushes or pull requests. CI means continuous integration, usually automated testing and checks on new changes. CD can mean continuous delivery or deployment, where software is packaged or released automatically.

Jamie: So if a PR runs tests automatically, that's usually a workflow in Actions acting as CI.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And those results often appear as status checks.

Alex: Right. A status check is an automated pass or fail result shown on a pull request or commit. It might report that tests passed, linting failed, builds succeeded, or accessibility checks found a problem.

Jamie: Webhook sounds more infrastructure-heavy.

Alex: A webhook is a way for GitHub to send event data to another service when something happens, such as a push, issue comment, or PR update. It's part of how GitHub can integrate with outside tools.

Jamie: GitHub Discussions?

Alex: That's a dedicated discussion space for conversation that isn't necessarily an issue or a pull request. It's useful for questions, ideas, community support, and longer-form project discussion.

Jamie: Profile is simpler, but still worth naming.

Alex: Your GitHub profile is your public account presence: your repositories, contribution activity, profile README if you have one, and other information you choose to share.

Jamie: And GitHub Copilot?

Alex: GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant integrated into tools like editors and GitHub features. It can suggest code and text, but it's important to treat those suggestions as drafts to review carefully, not as unquestioned truth.

Jamie: The source also points to community files and quick reference material.

Alex: Yes. One purpose of the glossary is not just long-form explanation but also quick lookup. The alphabetical quick reference is there for flat A to Z scanning when you already know the term and just need the meaning fast.

Jamie: And that can be especially useful for screen reader users who want a simpler lookup structure, and for low-vision users at high zoom where compact self-contained rows can be easier to navigate.

Alex: Exactly. The glossary serves both learning and reference.

Jamie: There were also a few extra terms visible in the quick reference list that are useful to name briefly, even if they weren't expanded earlier in the body.

Alex: Good catch. README is usually the main documentation file introducing a repository. Review is the formal feedback process on a pull request, which we discussed under code review. Squash merge is the strategy that combines all commits in a PR into one when merging. Pull is the command that fetches remote changes and integrates them. Wiki is a multi-page documentation area some repositories use.

Jamie: And the repeated items in the table, like tag, triage, and upstream, reinforce that these terms come up a lot.

Alex: They do.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, let's include the administrative notes too.

Alex: This glossary points learners to an audio companion, which is exactly what we're creating here, and it also names an authoritative source for facts: GitHub Docs, especially the glossary and related documentation. The GitHub Changelog is also useful when details evolve over time.

Jamie: So if a learner ever finds that a feature has changed since the workshop material was written, the official docs and changelog are the place to verify current behavior.

Alex: Exactly. The section-level source map in the written material is there for that purpose: to connect major sections of the glossary with authoritative references.

Jamie: And the written appendix also points forward to the next appendix, the screen reader cheat sheet, while reminding learners that this glossary supports the GitHub fundamentals chapter and really all chapters.

Alex: That's right. If you remember nothing else, remember the structure: a repository contains the project and history, a fork is your GitHub copy, a clone is your local copy, branches isolate work, commits save snapshots, diffs show changes, issues track discussion, pull requests propose changes, reviews refine them, and merges combine them.

Jamie: Then as your confidence grows, the more advanced terms like HEAD, stash, rebase, cherry-pick, fetch, pull, and force push start fitting into that bigger map.

Alex: Well said. Keep this glossary close. Revisit it often. Fluency in Git and GitHub is not about memorizing everything at once. It's about hearing the terms repeatedly in meaningful workflows until they become familiar.

Jamie: And if you're learning with a screen reader or at high zoom, remember: good navigation strategies are part of technical fluency too.

Alex: Absolutely. Thanks for learning with us.

3. Episode 1: Pre-Workshop Setup

Creating your GitHub account, installing Git and VS Code, configuring your screen reader.

Based on: Chapter 0: Pre-Workshop Setup

Download Episode 1 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 1: Pre-Workshop Setup

Transcript

Alex: Welcome to Git Going with GitHub. Before the workshop really begins, this episode is about getting everything ready so Day 1 can start with learning, not troubleshooting.

Jamie: And that matters a lot for this audience, right? Because setup is never just setup. It can include browser quirks, screen reader settings, account security, and a bunch of little choices that affect whether GitHub feels smooth or frustrating.

Alex: Exactly. This is a Community Access workshop, and the core message is: please do this at least one day before the event. If something goes wrong, use the Community Access support repository and support discussions so help can happen before class time.

Jamie: I also noticed a big theme here: tools change.

Alex: Yes. GitHub.com, GitHub Classroom, VS Code, Copilot, browsers, extensions, and agent tools all evolve. So if a label moves or a prompt sounds different from what we describe, that does not mean you did something wrong. Explore with headings, landmarks, form fields, labels, or in VS Code use the Command Palette. And when you ask for help, describe the exact page or prompt where you got stuck.

Alex: Let’s start with what you need in practical terms. Hardware first: a Windows or macOS computer, a reliable internet connection, and headphones are recommended so your screen reader audio stays clear during group sessions.

Jamie: Software for Day 1 is pretty manageable too. You need a modern browser. Chrome or Firefox are recommended. Edge is acceptable on Windows. Safari is the recommended browser on macOS with VoiceOver.

Alex: You also need one screen reader, not all of them. Use the one you already know if possible. The workshop supports NVDA on Windows, JAWS on Windows, and VoiceOver on macOS or iOS. And you need a GitHub account. Free tier is fine.

Jamie: Then there’s the software you need before the workshop begins: Git, Visual Studio Code, and access to GitHub Copilot, either through a paid plan or Copilot Free.

Alex: Right. And one version requirement is especially important: VS Code 1.113 or later, because later in the course, accessibility agents depend on newer Copilot Chat features. There are also minimums for advanced and optional tools: latest GitHub Copilot extension, Node.js 18 if you plan to use optional CLI accessibility tools, and Git 2.20 or later for workshop Git operations.

Jamie: So if someone wants to check versions, they can run code dash dash version, node dash dash version if Node is installed, and git dash dash version.

Alex: Yes. And if Node is missing, that is okay unless you plan to do those optional Day 2 command line accessibility exercises.

Jamie: Before we move on, can we say the screen reader choices clearly one more time?

Alex: Absolutely. NVDA is free on Windows. JAWS is paid, though a trial may be available, also on Windows. VoiceOver is built into macOS and iOS and can be turned on with Command-F5 on the Mac. The workshop is designed so you are not disadvantaged by choosing one of these over another.

Alex: Next is creating your GitHub account.

Jamie: And if someone already has one, they can skip ahead in their actual setup, but they still should listen here because email verification and two-factor authentication are important.

Alex: That’s right. If you are creating a new account, go to the GitHub signup page. The form is a single page with several fields. You’ll enter your email, create a password, choose a username, answer whether you want product updates, complete a human verification step, and then activate Create account.

Jamie: Let’s slow down on the username. This is not just a technical field.

Alex: Correct. Your GitHub username appears on issues, pull requests, and comments. So choose something professional. Lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens are a good pattern. GitHub will tell you if the name is already taken.

Jamie: Now the hard part: the CAPTCHA.

Alex: Yes. For screen reader users, GitHub’s visual CAPTCHA can be an accessibility barrier. When that challenge appears, look for an Audio option or something like Try an audio challenge. If an audio alternative is available, use it. If no accessible option appears, contact the workshop organizer before the event so they can help with account verification.

Jamie: After account creation, GitHub sends a launch code to your email inbox, and you type that code back into the site. Then there may be a personalization page you can skip or answer.

Alex: And do not forget the separate email verification message. GitHub sends a dedicated verify-your-email message, and some features, including creating repositories, depend on a verified email address.

Jamie: Then we come to two-factor authentication, or 2FA.

Alex: And this is both a security issue and a workshop readiness issue. GitHub requires 2FA for accounts, so you may already have it enabled. If not, set it up now from GitHub security settings.

Jamie: What’s the recommended method?

Alex: The preferred order is GitHub Mobile app first, because push approval is often the smoothest experience for this workshop. Other methods may include authenticator apps or other verification methods GitHub offers, but the important point is to finish setup and make sure you can actually sign in successfully afterward.

Jamie: Can you give the quick version of what to do?

Alex: While signed in, open GitHub security settings, find Two-factor authentication, choose Enable, follow the prompts, pick your method, complete verification, and save what GitHub gives you for recovery.

Jamie: And the recovery piece is non-negotiable.

Alex: Absolutely. Save backup or recovery codes somewhere secure. If your phone changes, is lost, or the app stops working, those codes may be the difference between quick recovery and losing access to your account.

Jamie: The source also includes detailed setup notes and a workshop policy around this.

Alex: Yes. The policy is simple: arrive with a working GitHub account you can sign into. Because we will be using GitHub live, account access problems can block everything else.

Jamie: What about signing Git in to GitHub later on? Beginners often think they need to set up SSH keys immediately.

Alex: Good question. For this workshop, authenticating Git with GitHub can happen through browser-based sign-in using OAuth when prompted by VS Code or GitHub-related tools. That is often the most approachable path for beginners. SSH keys and personal access tokens are reference topics in the Git authentication appendix, not the required starting point here.

Alex: Once the account is ready, the next job is making GitHub easier to use with assistive tech.

Jamie: So we’re going into GitHub accessibility settings.

Alex: Yes. Navigate to your settings while signed in and find the accessibility area. There are four settings to pay attention to.

Jamie: The highest priority one is disabling hovercards.

Alex: Exactly. Hovercards can interrupt screen reader flow and clutter navigation with extra dynamic content. Turning them off usually makes GitHub calmer and more predictable.

Jamie: Next, enable link underlines.

Alex: Right. That helps low-vision users and anyone who benefits from stronger visual distinction between plain text and links.

Jamie: Then there are character key shortcuts.

Alex: Those are single-key shortcuts on GitHub. Some users like them. Others find they interfere with screen reader or browser commands. The key idea is to review that setting deliberately rather than leaving it unexplored.

Jamie: And then theme appearance settings.

Alex: Yes. Choose a theme that gives you comfortable contrast and readability. That might mean dark, light, dim, or another appearance option depending on your visual needs.

Jamie: So this step is not cosmetic. It’s about reducing friction before the real work begins.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Then there’s profile setup, which some people might think is optional.

Alex: But it matters socially and practically. In open source, maintainers are the people who review contributions, guide project direction, and help keep a project healthy. When they look at a contributor’s profile, they are often just trying to understand who is participating.

Jamie: So updating your profile helps you appear as a real person, not just a mysterious username.

Alex: That’s right. Add your name if you want, a short bio, maybe location or links if relevant. A profile picture is strongly recommended because it makes comments and pull requests easier for others to recognize.

Jamie: And the notification email setting is important too.

Alex: Very. Make sure the email GitHub uses for notifications is one you actually check. Otherwise you may miss replies, review requests, issue comments, and classroom-related updates.

Alex: After that, check GitHub feature preview settings.

Jamie: This part can sound mysterious. What is a feature preview in plain language?

Alex: It’s GitHub’s way of letting some users opt into newer interface features before they become standard. Depending on your account, there may be previews available, or there may be none listed.

Jamie: And if it says Not Listed?

Alex: That usually just means there are no available previews for your account or region at that moment. It does not mean your account is broken or missing something required.

Jamie: There was also a note specifically for NVDA or JAWS users on Windows.

Alex: Yes. If you’re checking these settings with NVDA or JAWS, use your usual form field and heading navigation, and be prepared for labels or arrangement to vary. Again, tool updates happen.

Jamie: And what do these feature previews enable?

Alex: They may unlock newer experiences or interface changes GitHub is testing. The big lesson here is not to chase every preview, but to know where to look and understand that availability varies.

Jamie: Now let’s tune the screen reader and browser themselves.

Alex: For NVDA on Windows, use a browser mode setup that supports comfortable heading, landmark, link, and form navigation on complex web pages. The guide also recommends adjusting voice settings so speech is clear and efficient during GitHub workflows.

Jamie: Not too slow, not too fast, and probably enough punctuation or formatting cues to make code and interface labels understandable.

Alex: Exactly. For JAWS on Windows, similarly configure it for efficient web browsing and review any settings that improve interaction with dynamic GitHub pages. Recommended JAWS settings for GitHub focus on reducing confusion and improving consistency when navigating dense interfaces.

Jamie: And for VoiceOver on macOS?

Alex: There are a few essentials. Make sure VoiceOver is set up for web navigation in a way you’re comfortable with. Turn on Quick Nav if that helps you move faster with arrow keys. And there’s an important note for Mac users: keyboard shortcuts can differ because macOS, VoiceOver, browsers, and VS Code all have their own command layers. So when a shortcut behaves differently, that may be a platform difference, not a mistake.

Jamie: Can we summarize browser recommendations cleanly?

Alex: Yes. Chrome or Firefox are strong choices generally. Edge is fine on Windows. Safari is the preferred browser with VoiceOver on macOS. The best browser is the one that works reliably with your screen reader and lets you navigate GitHub with the least friction.

Alex: Next, install Git and Visual Studio Code.

Jamie: Git first.

Alex: Yes, install Git before anything else. On Windows, download Git from git-scm.com and run the installer. On macOS, Git commonly comes through Xcode Command Line Tools. If macOS prompts you to install command line tools when you first use Git, follow that prompt.

Jamie: And verification matters here too.

Alex: It does. On Windows, verify installation by opening a terminal and running git dash dash version. You should hear or see a version number. There’s also a screen reader note here: terminal output can be easy to miss, so review carefully, use reading commands, and confirm you actually heard the result.

Jamie: Then install VS Code.

Alex: Right. Download and install Visual Studio Code from the official site. Once it opens, immediately turn on Screen Reader Mode.

Jamie: There are two ways to do that.

Alex: Option A is the keyboard shortcut if available in your environment. Option B is more universal: open the Command Palette, search for Screen Reader Mode, and enable it there.

Jamie: And how do you confirm it’s on?

Alex: You can check the setting through the interface or Command Palette and verify that VS Code is presenting information in a more screen-reader-friendly way. The important concept is what Screen Reader Mode changes: it adjusts editor and interface behavior to be more compatible with assistive technology, including how content is announced and navigated.

Jamie: The guide also mentions VS Code keyboard basics, though those will be taught more fully later.

Alex: Yes. For now, just know that keyboard-first work in VS Code is expected, and the workshop will teach those skills in context.

Jamie: After the tools are installed, we configure Git identity.

Alex: This is where Git records your name and email on commits. In VS Code, you can open the integrated terminal and configure Git with your user name and user email.

Jamie: What should people use for those values?

Alex: Use the name you want attached to your commits, usually your real name or the consistent professional name you use in GitHub spaces. For email, use the correct GitHub-associated email. Ideally it matches the verified email you intend GitHub to recognize for commit attribution.

Jamie: Why does this matter so much?

Alex: Because commits are historical records. If your identity is wrong, your work may not be properly attributed to your GitHub account, and your commit history can become confusing to you and to collaborators.

Jamie: So verification is part of the step, not an optional extra.

Alex: Exactly. Run Git config commands to inspect the values you set and make sure name and email are correct. And be especially careful about the email. Using the wrong email is one of the most common reasons commits fail to connect cleanly with a GitHub profile.

Alex: Then we install the VS Code extensions needed for the workshop.

Jamie: First, GitHub Copilot is built in.

Alex: Yes. Modern VS Code includes GitHub Copilot support automatically. You may still need to activate it by signing in with your GitHub account and completing any prompts.

Jamie: And then there’s the GitHub Pull Requests extension.

Alex: Right. Install the GitHub Pull Requests extension in VS Code. After installation, verify it’s working by confirming that GitHub-related panels, commands, or sign-in integration become available.

Jamie: There’s also a note about Copilot Free.

Alex: Yes. Learners do not need a paid Copilot plan to participate. Copilot Free is available to GitHub users, and that is enough for the workshop path described here.

Jamie: At this point, we’ve done a lot. So let’s talk verification checklist.

Alex: Good idea. Before Day 1, confirm all the basics: you can sign into GitHub, your email is verified, 2FA works, your accessibility settings are adjusted, your profile is updated, your screen reader and browser feel comfortable, Git is installed, VS Code is installed with Screen Reader Mode enabled, Git identity is configured, and the required VS Code integrations are available.

Jamie: This is the tool-card mindset: don’t assume. Check.

Alex: Exactly. And at the start of Day 1, the workshop will move quickly into the actual learning environment. So if setup is complete beforehand, you can focus on GitHub Classroom, repositories, editing, Git workflows, and contribution practices instead of scrambling through installation.

Alex: There are also a few access methods mentioned for reference only, not as workshop requirements.

Jamie: Those are GitHub Desktop and the GitHub CLI, usually called gh.

Alex: Yes. Both are valid tools in the wider GitHub ecosystem, but they are not the main path for this workshop. There’s also a reference mention of GitHub Copilot CLI, gh copilot, and of Git itself as the underlying version control system. Useful to know they exist, but not part of the required setup flow here.

Jamie: That distinction matters, especially for beginners who can get overwhelmed and think they need every tool.

Alex: Exactly. You do not need every tool. You need the right baseline tools.

Jamie: And if somebody still gets stuck?

Alex: They should not wait quietly. Use the support options before the event. Open a support issue in the Community Access support repository, join the support hub discussions and read the pinned Start Here guidance, or visit the GitHub Community accessibility discussions.

Jamie: I like the tone of that section. You will not be left behind.

Alex: Yes. Every setup problem solved before Day 1 creates more room for real learning during the workshop.

Jamie: Before we close, can we mention where the current source of truth lives, since tools and interfaces change?

Alex: Definitely. When in doubt, consult official GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, and core GitHub documentation on Git, GitHub flow, pull requests, issues, and contributing to projects. Those are the authoritative references behind this setup guidance.

Jamie: So the goal of this pre-work episode is simple: arrive ready, secure, and comfortable in your tools.

Alex: Exactly. Have your account working, your accessibility settings tuned, your browser and screen reader cooperating, Git and VS Code installed, your Git identity configured, and your extensions ready. Then move on to the next lesson knowing your foundation is solid.

Jamie: That’s it for this setup conversation.

Alex: And once you’re ready, continue to the next part of the course and start choosing your tools with confidence.

4. Episode 44: Choose Your Tools

A guided tour of browser GitHub, github.dev, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, and the CLI.

Based on: Chapter 1: Choose Your Tools

Download Episode 44 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 44: Choose Your Tools

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Before anyone writes code or worries about commands, we need a map of the tools. This lesson is a guided tour of five different ways to work with GitHub: the website, a browser-based editor, a desktop editor, a desktop Git app, and the command line.

Jamie: So the big idea is not, pick one forever. It’s, learn the landscape so later instructions make sense.

Alex: Exactly. And that matters because there is no single right way to use GitHub. Some people prefer the browser. Some want a visual desktop app. Some love a terminal. Many people switch tools depending on the task.

Jamie: That feels especially important for accessibility. If one path works better with your screen reader or your low vision setup, that path is valid.

Alex: Yes. In fact, this workshop is designed so exercises can be completed using any of the five paths. When later lessons say something like, open the file, create a branch, or make a commit, the meaning stays the same even if the interface changes.

Jamie: And there was an important note for screen reader users too, right?

Alex: Right. The tools are described by how they behave, not by visual appearance. If a path works well with a screen reader, we say so directly. That’s the frame for this whole lesson.

Alex: Let’s get the quick overview in place. Path one is GitHub dot com in your browser. No installation. Best for issues, pull requests, repository navigation, and code review. Path two is github dot dev, also in the browser. It feels like VS Code running in a tab. No installation. Best for editing files, making changes across multiple files, and quick commits. Path three is VS Code desktop. That does require installation. It’s best for full development: editing, extensions, a terminal, debugging, and tools like GitHub Copilot. Path four is GitHub Desktop. Also installed locally. It’s a visual Git client, good for branching, committing, and syncing changes without typing commands. Path five is GitHub CLI, the command-line tool called G H. It also requires installation and is best for scripting, automation, and learners who prefer the terminal.

Jamie: And learners do not need all five.

Alex: Not even close. A very common pattern is: start with GitHub dot com on day one, then add VS Code on day two. The other paths are available if they fit your workflow.

Alex: Let’s start with the simplest entry point: GitHub dot com in the browser.

Jamie: This is the main website. If I can sign in with a browser, I can use it.

Alex: Exactly. Every repository, issue, pull request, and setting lives there. No installation is required. What can you do on GitHub dot com? You can browse repositories, files, and folders. You can create, comment on, and close issues. You can open, review, and merge pull requests. You can edit individual files using the built-in web editor. You can manage labels, milestones, and project boards. And you can configure repository settings, including things like branch protection.

Jamie: So it handles a lot of collaboration and repository management.

Alex: It does. But there are limits. You cannot run code or tests locally there. You do not get a full-featured code editor with local extensions. And you cannot make offline changes.

Jamie: Let’s slow down for accessibility. What is the screen reader experience like?

Alex: Strong overall. GitHub dot com has solid screen reader support. Pages use ARIA landmarks. Headings are fairly consistent. Keyboard shortcuts are available for many actions. A few navigation patterns matter a lot. On many pages, pressing S can jump to the main content or search field depending on context, and slash can open search. In browse mode, D moves between landmarks. H moves between headings. In a repository, the tabs like Code, Issues, and Pull Requests sit inside the repository navigation landmark. There’s also a shortcut sequence, G then I, that jumps directly to Issues from within a repository.

Jamie: That’s the kind of thing that turns GitHub from overwhelming into navigable.

Alex: Absolutely. And if you’re new to GitHub with a screen reader, there are later lessons that go deeper into page structure.

Jamie: How about low vision users?

Alex: GitHub has several useful appearance options. You can choose light, dark, light high contrast, dark high contrast, or sync with your operating system. It also generally adapts well to browser zoom, including high zoom levels, often up to four hundred percent without horizontal scrolling on most pages. There are also practical tips. High contrast themes can make borders and text much easier to distinguish. At higher zoom levels, some layout changes happen, like sidebars collapsing into menus. And enabling link underlines can help if color alone is not enough to identify links.

Jamie: So if I’m deciding whether GitHub dot com is a reasonable starting place, the answer is yes for many learners, especially for reading, navigating, reviewing, and making small edits.

Alex: Exactly. And that last point matters: for a single-file edit, GitHub dot com is often the simplest tool.

Alex: Now let’s move to github dot dev.

Jamie: This one is easy to confuse with GitHub dot com. What’s the difference?

Alex: Think of github dot dev as a richer editor experience in the browser. It looks and behaves a lot like VS Code, but it runs entirely in a tab. You stay signed in, you don’t install anything, and you get a file explorer, tabs, diff views, staging, and commits.

Jamie: So it fills the gap between simple web edits and a full local editor.

Alex: That’s a great way to say it. In github dot dev, you can edit multiple files in a VS Code-like interface. You can view diffs, stage changes, commit directly to a branch, and use many browser-compatible VS Code extensions.

Jamie: And the limits?

Alex: You cannot truly run code, build projects, or execute terminal commands the way you can locally. Some terminal or preview elements may exist, but not as a full local runtime for Git operations and development workflows. You also cannot use extensions that depend on a local runtime, like many debuggers or compiled tools. And, like any browser-based tool, you cannot work offline.

Jamie: How do you open it?

Alex: Three easy ways. From a repository page, press the period key. Or change github dot com to github dot dev in the URL bar. Or, while viewing a file on GitHub dot com, press period to open that repository in the editor.

Jamie: And accessibility?

Alex: Because github dot dev is basically VS Code in the browser, much of the same screen reader support and keyboard navigation applies. The command palette is available with Control Shift P on Windows or Command Shift P on a Mac. Editor keybindings generally work. One practical note: some screen readers may need focus mode or application mode to interact smoothly with the editor area. If keys don’t seem to reach the editor, try Escape to settle focus, then open the command palette.

Jamie: When would you choose github dot dev over the regular GitHub website?

Alex: Use github dot dev when you need to edit more than one file in a single commit, or when you want a coding-editor experience without installing software. If you only need to fix one file, the plain GitHub dot com edit flow is often simpler.

Alex: Now the local tools begin, starting with VS Code desktop.

Jamie: This is the big one for many developers.

Alex: Yes. Visual Studio Code is a free desktop editor from Microsoft. It has built-in Git support, an integrated terminal, extensive extension support, and GitHub integration. Installation is required, and setup is covered in the workshop’s pre-work material.

Jamie: What can learners do once it’s installed?

Alex: A lot. You can edit files with syntax highlighting and IntelliSense. You can use the integrated terminal to run Git commands, scripts, and programs. You can stage, commit, push, and pull using either the Source Control panel or the terminal. You can run and debug code. You can use GitHub Copilot for code suggestions, chat, and review features. And you can work offline, with syncing happening once you reconnect.

Jamie: That sounds like the full development environment.

Alex: It is. But there’s an important limitation in the source material too: some tasks are not available by default without extensions or extra setup.

Jamie: Such as?

Alex: Depending on what you want to do, things like specialized GitHub workflows, advanced review experiences, language tooling, accessibility helpers, or debugging support may require installing extensions. So VS Code is powerful out of the box, but not every feature appears automatically.

Jamie: How is the screen reader experience?

Alex: VS Code has substantial accessibility support, but it expects a bit of setup and practice. It offers screen reader mode, keyboard-first navigation, the command palette, accessible views for certain panels, and a lot of configurability. For many blind users, it becomes a very capable environment once they learn the patterns.

Jamie: And low vision?

Alex: Also strong. VS Code supports themes, high contrast themes, zoom controls, font scaling, custom editor fonts, line height adjustments, minimap controls, panel placement, and many layout preferences. It’s one of the more adaptable environments for low vision users because you can tailor so much of the interface.

Jamie: What are the practical learning-card takeaways for VS Code?

Alex: Think in terms of a few core anchors: the Explorer for files, the editor for content, Source Control for Git changes, the integrated terminal for commands, and the command palette as the universal launcher. Once those are familiar, the environment gets much less intimidating.

Jamie: So VS Code is often the next step after learning the basics in the browser.

Alex: Yes. It’s commonly the day two tool because it opens the door to fuller development work.

Alex: Next is GitHub Desktop.

Jamie: This is for people who want Git without the command line, right?

Alex: Very often, yes. GitHub Desktop is a local application focused on Git workflows with a visual interface. It’s especially useful for cloning repositories, creating branches, committing changes, viewing diffs, and syncing with GitHub.

Jamie: So what can it do well?

Alex: It does a nice job with branch management, committing, pushing, pulling, and keeping local and remote work in sync. It can help learners understand the flow of changes without requiring terminal commands. For many people, it lowers the barrier to using Git locally.

Jamie: And what can’t it do?

Alex: It is not a full code editor. You’ll usually pair it with another editor to actually work on files. It also isn’t the best tool for every advanced Git scenario, heavy automation, or terminal-based workflows. Its strength is visual Git operations, not being an all-in-one development environment.

Jamie: How about accessibility for screen reader users?

Alex: The experience can be usable, but it’s often more mixed than GitHub dot com or the CLI. Some learners appreciate the simpler conceptual model, while others find certain controls or layouts less efficient with a screen reader than a well-structured web page or terminal output. That means it can be a good fit for some users, but not automatically the best fit for every blind learner.

Jamie: So when should someone choose GitHub Desktop?

Alex: Choose it when you want local Git workflows with less typing, especially if branching, reviewing diffs, committing, and syncing are your main needs. It’s often attractive to learners who want a visual bridge between browser-only work and more advanced local tools.

Alex: Now for path five: GitHub CLI.

Jamie: The command-line option can feel intimidating at first.

Alex: It can, so the getting-started principles matter. Learn it as a small set of repeatable actions, not as a giant wall of commands. Start with just a few goals: authenticate, view repository info, inspect issues or pull requests, and create or manage common tasks. Build confidence through patterns.

Jamie: And this is the tool called G H.

Alex: Right. GitHub CLI is the command-line tool named gh. It requires installation. Once installed, it lets you interact with GitHub from the terminal.

Jamie: What can you do there?

Alex: You can inspect repositories, issues, and pull requests. You can create issues and pull requests. You can check out PRs, review them, merge them, and automate repetitive tasks. It’s especially good for scripting, keyboard-driven workflows, and integrating GitHub actions into a broader terminal environment.

Jamie: And what can’t it do?

Alex: It is not a visual code editor. It won’t replace the experience of browsing a site visually or editing files in a full GUI editor. For people who want discoverability through menus and visible controls, the CLI can feel less approachable at first. Some tasks may also still be easier in the browser, depending on the situation.

Jamie: What about screen reader experience? I know terminal tools can actually be very efficient.

Alex: Yes, and that is a major point here. For many screen reader users, the CLI can be excellent because terminal output is linear, keyboard-driven, and avoids some of the complexity of dense graphical layouts. GitHub even has accessibility guidance specifically for the CLI. That said, the user still needs comfort with terminal navigation and command syntax.

Jamie: When should someone choose GitHub CLI?

Alex: Choose it if you already like the terminal, want automation, or want a highly efficient non-visual workflow. It’s often ideal for power users and can also become a favorite accessibility path once the basics click.

Jamie: Any learning-card mindset for the CLI?

Alex: Yes: keep a tiny starter set of commands, learn what each one returns, and reuse them often. The goal is not memorizing everything. It’s building a dependable toolkit.

Alex: So with all five paths on the table, the obvious question is: where should a learner start?

Jamie: Please say, not with all five at once.

Alex: Definitely not with all five at once. For day one, the recommendation is usually GitHub dot com. It requires no installation, it exposes core GitHub concepts clearly, and it’s enough for browsing repositories, understanding issues and pull requests, and making simple edits.

Jamie: And day two?

Alex: Usually VS Code, if local setup is ready. That’s when learners begin doing fuller editing, using Source Control, maybe trying the terminal, and getting comfortable with a local development workflow.

Jamie: Where does github dot dev fit in that progression?

Alex: It’s a great bridge. If you’re not ready to install software but you need more than single-file browser edits, github dot dev is the natural next step.

Jamie: And GitHub Desktop or the CLI are more preference-based.

Alex: Exactly. If visual Git controls make sense to you, try GitHub Desktop. If the terminal feels natural or appealing, explore GitHub CLI. Switching paths is normal. In fact, it’s expected.

Jamie: That feels worth repeating: changing tools is not failure.

Alex: Not at all. It’s good workflow design. You might review a pull request in the browser, edit files in VS Code, and use the CLI to check CI status. Or you might stay almost entirely in one tool. Both are fine.

Jamie: So the learning card here is basically: start simple, add tools when they solve a real problem, and expect your path to evolve.

Alex: Perfectly put.
