Alex: Exactly. Or "welcome.md TODO placeholder needs real content." Or "Replace TODO in welcome.md intro section with actual welcome text." Those are concrete and useful.

Alex: For the body, include enough context that another person could find and understand the problem from your description alone. A common structure for a bug-style issue includes what happened, what you expected, how to reproduce it, environment details if relevant, and any additional context.

Jamie: Let's unpack those.

Alex: What happened means the current problem. What I expected means the intended behavior or content. How to reproduce means the steps another person can follow to experience or verify the issue. Environment can include browser, screen reader, operating system, version, or other setup details. Additional context is anything else that helps, like related files, screenshots if appropriate, or impact on users.

Jamie: And for documentation issues, the environment might matter less, but location matters a lot.

Alex: Precisely. For a docs issue, file name and section are often the crucial details. If a line number is relevant, include it.

Jamie: The challenge gives a very specific task, right?

Alex: Yes. In the workshop challenge, you open docs slash welcome dot md and look for a line containing TODO. That TODO marks something needing attention. Then you go to the Issues tab, choose New issue, and file a well-structured issue about what you found.

Jamie: And the description should explain what needs to change, where the problem is, and why it matters.

Alex: Exactly. Not just "there's a TODO," but what the TODO is pointing to and why replacing it would improve the project.

Jamie: There's also an evidence step.

Alex: Yes. You're expected to paste the URL of the issue you created and explain what TODO you found and how you described it. That evidence lives in your assigned challenge issue.

Jamie: What if someone can't find the TODO?

Alex: Use Find in the browser or editor and search for the word TODO inside docs slash welcome dot md. If you're unsure what to write in the description, explain the problem as if the reader has never seen the file. If the New issue button is missing, confirm you're actually on the Issues tab, and if issues are disabled, ask the facilitator.

Jamie: There was also a peer simulation step.

Alex: Right. You may be asked to open a peer simulation issue, something like a welcome link needing context, and leave a comment about whether the title is clear and whether the needed fix is understandable from the title alone. If your facilitator provides a real buddy repository, you may review your buddy's issue instead.

Jamie: That's a smart exercise because it trains you to evaluate issue quality, not just produce one.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: The reference solution gives two valid styles. One is bug-report style. For example, a title like "TODO in welcome.md: missing workshop schedule link." The body explains that in docs slash welcome dot md, on a certain line, there's a TODO saying to add a link to the workshop schedule, and that the placeholder should be replaced with an actual link. Then it lists steps to find it: open the file, search for TODO, and locate the comment.

Jamie: That's very concrete.

Alex: It is. The second style is feature-request style. For example, "Add accessibility tips section to welcome.md." The body explains that the welcome document covers what students will do but does not mention accessibility features, and suggests adding a short section about screen reader shortcuts and keyboard navigation, perhaps after the "What you will learn" section.

Jamie: So both a bug report and a feature request can satisfy the challenge, as long as the issue is clear.

Alex: Yes. That's one of the key lessons. Alternate approaches are acceptable if a stranger could act on what you wrote.

Jamie: Can we name what makes a good issue in one quick list?

Alex: Certainly. Clear title. Enough context. Reproducible location. And I'd add actionable intent: the reader should understand what sort of fix or discussion is needed.

Jamie: That connects nicely to the chapter's agentic strategy idea.

Alex: It does. A clear issue for a human is also a strong prompt for an AI agent. If the issue describes the problem, location, and desired fix, it becomes much easier for a person or a tool to help.

Alex: Now let's bring in accessibility-specific issue writing. If you're filing an accessibility issue, be especially concrete. Describe the barrier, who it affects, how to reproduce it, and what assistive technology or browser combination you used if relevant.

Jamie: So not just "screen reader problem."

Alex: Exactly. Better would be something like: when navigating a specific page or component with a certain screen reader and browser, a button is announced ambiguously, focus order is confusing, a landmark is missing, or a heading hierarchy breaks navigation. Then include what you expected instead.

Jamie: And the same body structure still applies: what happened, what I expected, how to reproduce, environment, additional context.

Alex: Yes. Accessibility issues are strongest when they're testable and respectful. You're documenting impact, not just frustration.

Jamie: What about cross-referencing issues?

Alex: Very useful skill. You can mention another issue in a comment to connect related work. You can reference issues across repositories if needed. And in pull request descriptions or even issue comments, closing keywords can automatically close an issue when a related change is merged, depending on context.

Jamie: So issue numbers are not just labels. They're links in a work graph.

Alex: That's a great way to say it.

Alex: Sub-issues are another structural tool. If a parent issue is too broad, you can create child issues for each smaller task. The parent can then show progress as sub-issues are completed.

Jamie: When should I use a sub-issue instead of a task list?

Alex: Use a sub-issue when each step deserves its own title, description, conversation, or tracking. Use a task list when the checklist items are smaller and don't need separate issue-level management.

Jamie: And how do you create a sub-issue?

Alex: Open the parent issue, locate the Sub-issues area or related control, choose to add or create a sub-issue, give it a clear title and a short description, and create it. Then the child appears under the parent, and the child issue also shows its parent relationship.

Jamie: So you can read sub-issues from the parent, and read the parent from the child.

Alex: Exactly. That two-way context is part of what makes them useful.

Jamie: Let's shift from contributors to maintainers and triagers.

Alex: Good. Maintainers and triagers often close issues, reopen them, assign them, add or remove labels, set milestones, and sometimes transfer or delete issues. Closing can be a plain close, a close with a reason, or a close with a comment. Reopening restores discussion when the work isn't actually finished or the issue needs renewed attention.

Jamie: Assignment matters too.

Alex: Yes. You may assign yourself, assign a teammate if appropriate, add labels, remove labels, or set a milestone to group work into a release or time frame.

Jamie: And all of this metadata changes how discoverable and manageable the issue is.

Alex: Exactly. Good metadata is part of accessibility too, in a broad sense. It helps people find the right work and understand its state.

Alex: One label worth calling out for newcomers is good first issue. That label often signals a beginner-friendly entry point into a project.

Jamie: So if I'm looking for a first contribution, filtering by that label is a smart move.

Alex: Very smart. It gives you issues that maintainers have already identified as approachable.

Jamie: What about the local Git alternative mentioned in the chapter?

Alex: That reminder is important: even if you work from a local clone for code, issue work itself still lives on GitHub. You may inspect files locally to gather context, but the issue is filed and discussed in GitHub's issue system. So local Git can support issue writing, but it doesn't replace GitHub issues.

Jamie: That makes sense. Git tracks file history. GitHub issues track the conversation around work.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: For blind users, a few practical notes from the workflow. On the issues page, the first heading can confirm you've landed where you intended. Jumping by heading level can speed movement between issue titles. If a template picker appears, tabbing through and listening for link text like "Open a blank issue" can help.

Jamie: And for low-vision users?

Alex: The New issue button is typically prominent and remains visible at high zoom. The title field is wide, the body field expands as you type, and after submission your new issue page shows the title and description in a layout that's usually easy to verify. Check that the rendered content says what you meant.

Jamie: Sighted users also get visual confirmation from the green Open badge and the issue appearing in the list.

Alex: Right. And everyone should notice the auto-assigned issue number in the page title and URL, because that number becomes useful for references later.

Jamie: Let's walk through the chapter's two main challenges cleanly.

Alex: Challenge two: create your first issue. Open your Learning Room repository. Go to Issues. Choose New issue. If there's a template picker, use a fitting template or open a blank issue. Write a clear title, ideally at least a dozen characters and genuinely descriptive. Write a meaningful body, ideally with enough detail that another person can act. Include what the problem is, where it appears in the repository, and what you think the fix should be. Submit the issue. Then copy the issue URL or note the issue number.

Jamie: And how do I know I'm done?

Alex: Your issue appears in the issues list, your username is the author, the title is clear, and the description is detailed enough to understand the work.

Jamie: Challenge three?

Alex: Find another student's issue or a facilitator-provided peer simulation issue. Open it. Read the description carefully. Go to the comment box. Write a helpful comment and include an @mention of the issue author by username. Then submit it. You're done when the comment appears and the mention renders as a clickable username link.

Jamie: And the reason @mentions matter is notifications.

Alex: Exactly. They notify the specific person who should see the comment.

Jamie: Then there's the optional extension.

Alex: Yes. Add a sub-issue to a larger issue if sub-issues are enabled in your repository and you have permission. A good sub-issue title names one specific piece of the larger problem. For example, instead of one broad "Fix accessibility in welcome.md," you might create sub-issues for alt text, heading hierarchy, or link clarity.

Jamie: And after all that, there's still one administrative step.

Alex: Correct. Post evidence in your assigned challenge issue. A simple completion comment can list the issue number you created, the issue where you commented with an @mention, and optionally the sub-issue you added. Then close your assigned challenge issue if the workshop instructions tell you to do that. The facilitator reviews your activity directly.

Jamie: So completion is visible and checkable.

Alex: Yes, which makes the learning process fair and transparent.

Jamie: There was also a broader teaching point here: file, read, comment on, and triage real issues manually before relying on agents.

Alex: That's an excellent closing lesson. If you can't evaluate issue quality yourself, you can't judge whether an AI assistant is helping well. Manual skill comes first. Then tools can amplify your judgment rather than replace it.

Jamie: So today, we learn to be the triage engine.

Alex: Exactly. And once you understand issue quality, metadata, references, and communication, you're ready for more advanced workflows later.

Alex: One final note on sources. When you need the current source of truth, use GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, and GitHub's issue documentation. For accessibility-specific workflows, GitHub's accessibility guide for issues and the CLI accessibility guide are especially valuable companions.

Jamie: That's a good habit: learn the workflow here, then verify evolving details from the official docs.

Alex: Exactly. And for now, your next move is simple: find a TODO, write a clear issue, and make it easy for the next person to help.

12. Challenge 03: Join the Conversation

Comments, mentions, reactions, and constructive peer communication.

Practice focus: Day 1 foundation

Download Challenge 03 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 03: Join the Conversation

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're focusing on one of the most important open source skills that is easy to underestimate: joining a conversation in GitHub issues.

Jamie: And that sounds small, but it really is not. A lot of learners think, "I haven't written code yet, so I'm not contributing yet."

Alex: Exactly. But issues are where collaboration begins. Before code, there is noticing, describing, asking, confirming, clarifying, and coordinating. If you can do that well, you are already contributing.

Alex: This lesson draws together three things: the practical mechanics of working with GitHub issues, the specific challenge where you comment and use an @mention, and the broader culture of respectful open source communication.

Jamie: So this is both, "How do I do it?" and "How do I do it well?"

Alex: That's the idea.

Alex: First, a few setup and accessibility notes, because they matter here. GitHub issues are accessible enough to work well with keyboard and screen reader workflows, and GitHub has an official accessibility guide for issues that's worth treating as a companion reference. This workshop also assumes the newer GitHub issues experience, which has better landmark structure and announcements for screen readers.

Jamie: And if someone is using NVDA, there was also that reminder about browse mode and focus mode, right?

Alex: Yes. Browse mode is usually best for reading headings, lists, and issue content. Focus mode is what you want when typing into fields like the search box, title field, or comment box. And NVDA users can use the elements list as an orientation tool when a page feels crowded.

Jamie: So even before filing or commenting, there's a mindset here: orient yourself first.

Alex: Always. That's true in the browser, and it's true in the command line too.

Alex: Let's ground this in the workshop tasks. In this chapter, there are two core issue-based challenges and one optional extension. First, create your first issue. Second, comment on an issue and use an @mention. Third, optionally, add a sub-issue.

Jamie: And for this conversation lesson, we're really centered on that second challenge.

Alex: We are, but it helps to understand the whole environment. Chapter 5 is intentionally short and confidence-building. The pattern is claim, act, confirm. You do not need a branch. You do not need to edit files. You do not need a pull request yet. All the work happens in issue threads.

Jamie: That's a helpful relief for beginners.

Alex: It is. Your evidence is the issue activity itself: the issue you created, the comment you posted, and if applicable the sub-issue you added.

Alex: If you prefer terminal workflows, there's also a recommended sequence. First confirm your repository context, for example by checking remotes or using GitHub CLI to view the repo. Second, read before writing. View the issue before you comment on it. Third, keep comments focused, specific, and actionable. Fourth, verify each action from command output. And fifth, use documented options rather than guessing flags.

Jamie: I like "read before writing." That feels like a social rule as much as a CLI rule.

Alex: It absolutely is.

Alex: So what is a GitHub issue? At a basic level, it is a place to track a problem, request, task, question, or discussion about a repository. It might be a bug report, a feature request, a documentation fix, an accessibility problem, or a chore.

Jamie: So not every issue means, "The software crashed."

Alex: Correct. Issues are broader than bugs. They are the shared record of work and discussion.

Jamie: And if someone is brand new to GitHub, how do they even get to the issues?

Alex: Usually from a repository page by activating the Issues tab, or directly by URL if they have a link. On GitHub there are also keyboard shortcuts, and one common navigation shortcut jumps to issues. Once there, the issues list page becomes your dashboard.

Alex: On the issues list page, you'll find a page structure that includes the list itself, filter controls, and often a New issue button. Each issue entry usually announces useful information: the title, its number, whether it is open or closed, who opened it, and sometimes labels, assignees, or milestone information.

Jamie: That sounds especially important for screen reader users, because you want to know what each row tells you before you open one.

Alex: Exactly. You're building a quick mental model. Open or closed status matters. Labels matter. Recency matters. Author matters.

Jamie: And then there's searching.

Alex: Yes. Filtering and searching issues is a core skill. You can use the search or filter bar to enter queries, and GitHub supports combinations such as filtering by label, milestone, open versus closed state, assignee, or keywords. You can also use filter buttons in the interface.

Jamie: Can you give examples of why that matters for this challenge?

Alex: Certainly. If the instructions tell you to find a peer-simulation issue, filtering by a label like peer-simulation gets you there quickly. If you're looking for your own assigned work, filtering by assignee can help. If you only want active discussions, keep the list on open issues. If you remember a phrase from a title or body, use keywords.

Alex: Now, once you open an issue, there are a few things to notice. You land on the issue page, which includes the title, the issue number, the description, comments, and activity. If you're using the terminal, you can view an issue there too, and GitHub CLI can render Markdown so the structure is readable.

Jamie: And if the terminal view isn't enough?

Alex: You can open the same issue in your browser instead. Or sometimes you may want to view just the comments. The important habit is that you read the issue description before jumping in.

Jamie: Because otherwise your comment might repeat something, miss context, or answer the wrong question.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Now let's talk about the challenge itself. The assignment is to open a peer-simulation issue in the repository, or if your facilitator gave you access to a real buddy repository, use your buddy's issue from the earlier challenge. Then leave a meaningful comment, use an @mention, and add a reaction to the original issue.

Jamie: And the meaningful part is important. This isn't "Nice job" and then leave.

Alex: Right. The suggested comment types are much better: confirm that you can reproduce the problem, suggest a possible fix, or ask a clarifying question.

Jamie: And for the @mention, in the simulation you mention the bot, but in a real buddy workflow you mention the actual person.

Alex: Yes. In the simulation, use the specified bot account. In a real buddy repository, use your buddy's exact username with no space between the at sign and the username.

Alex: Let's walk through the browser steps plainly. Open the Issues tab. Find an issue created by a classmate or the peer-simulation issue. Open it. Read the description carefully. Go to the comment box near the bottom. Write a helpful comment that includes an @mention of the issue author or required account. Then submit the comment, either with the Comment button or the keyboard shortcut for submission.

Jamie: And how do you know it worked?

Alex: Your comment appears in the thread, and the @mentioned username renders as a clickable link. That means GitHub recognized it and will send a notification.

Jamie: That notification piece is the real function of the @mention.

Alex: Yes. @mentions are not decoration. They are how you direct attention in an asynchronous system.

Alex: Here's an example exchange. Suppose your buddy filed an issue about a missing link in a file called welcome dot md. A strong comment might say something like: good catch on the missing link, I found the same to-do on line 15, and then mention the person by username and ask whether they also noticed another to-do farther down, perhaps on line 28, suggesting both could be handled in the same pull request.

Jamie: That's nice because it does several things at once. It acknowledges the report, confirms the problem, adds new information, and proposes a next step.

Alex: Beautifully said. And then the reply might say, thanks for pointing that out, I had not scrolled that far, I'll update the issue description to include both items.

Jamie: So the thread moves forward.

Alex: Exactly. That is the point.

Alex: Let's make the qualities of a good comment explicit. First, specificity. Mention the file, line number, heading, step, or exact symptom you are responding to. "I found the same TODO on line 12" is much more useful than "I agree."

Jamie: Second would be tone.

Alex: Yes. Constructive tone. Add information, ask a question, or suggest an approach. Avoid dropping criticism with no path forward.

Jamie: Third is the @mention.

Alex: Right. Tag the person who needs to see the message so they are notified.

Jamie: And fourth is actionability.

Alex: Exactly. The comment should help move the work forward. Maybe it confirms reproduction. Maybe it points to where the fix belongs. Maybe it clarifies scope. Maybe it identifies a second related problem.

Jamie: What if a learner is worried there's only one "correct" kind of comment?

Alex: There isn't. There are alternate approaches. You can comment on an issue someone else filed. You can reply to a comment on your own issue. You can ask a clarifying question about someone else's proposed change. The real learning objective is participating in asynchronous collaboration.

Jamie: So one thoughtful comment with an @mention is enough evidence.

Alex: Yes. That's what matters.

Alex: Now, let's widen the lens. Open source communication has a few defining traits: it is in writing, it is asynchronous, and it is public.

Jamie: That combination changes how you write.

Alex: It does. In writing, your words have to carry tone and clarity without body language. Asynchronous means the other person may reply hours or days later, so your comment needs enough context to stand on its own. And because it is public, others may read the exchange later to understand the issue or learn from it.

Jamie: So clarity is kindness.

Alex: Very much so.

Alex: There's also a helpful structure for feedback. First, acknowledge what is working. Second, identify the specific concern. Third, explain why it matters. Fourth, when possible, suggest a path forward. Fifth, signal the weight of the concern.

Jamie: That last one is subtle. Signal the weight.

Alex: Yes. Not every comment means "This blocks merging." Some comments are optional suggestions, some are questions, some are important corrections. If you can indicate that, you reduce anxiety and confusion.

Jamie: Like the difference between "Must fix before merge" and "Small suggestion if you want."

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Language and tone matter a great deal. Prefer we language, or describe the code or content rather than the person. So instead of "You wrote this wrong," try "This link appears to point to a 404," or "We may want to update this shortcut."

Jamie: And use tentative language when you are not fully sure.

Alex: Yes. "I think," "it looks like," "I may be mistaken, but," these are appropriate when you're uncertain. That makes room for correction without sounding defensive.

Jamie: There was also a note about cultural and language diversity.

Alex: Important one. Open source communities are global. People may be writing in a second or third language. So keep sentences direct, avoid sarcasm, avoid idioms that do not travel well, and read charitably.

Jamie: And avoid fake urgency.

Alex: Exactly. Don't sprinkle "ASAP" or urgent markers unless something is genuinely urgent.

Alex: Now let's talk etiquette for comments and conversations. Keep comments focused. One comment should usually address one main thing or a small coherent set of related things. Don't leave comments unresolved if the platform supports conversation resolution and you are in a review context. Use reactions thoughtfully. Sometimes a thumbs up or eyes reaction acknowledges a point without adding noise.

Jamie: That connects directly to the challenge, because learners are asked to add a reaction too.

Alex: Yes. Reactions are part of the collaboration vocabulary. And they can be more accessible socially than repeating the same "I agree" comment over and over.

Jamie: There was also a warning not to pile on.

Alex: Right. If several people have already made the same point, adding another nearly identical comment often creates pressure without adding value. Better to react, or add only if you have new evidence or a different perspective.

Jamie: I want to ask about saved replies, because that sounds especially useful for accessibility and energy management.

Alex: It is. Saved replies let you store commonly used response templates, which is excellent for repetitive but important communication. For example, you might save a polite request for reproduction steps, a thank-you note for a first contribution, or a short accessibility-focused explanation you often need.

Jamie: So it reduces typing and reduces the risk of forgetting part of a standard response.

Alex: Exactly. And for many blind, low-vision, or fatigue-prone contributors, saved replies are a real accessibility win. The platform provides a way to create them and then insert them into comments. There is also a screen reader path for reaching that control.

Alex: Now, although today's challenge is issue comments rather than pull request review, the same etiquette carries forward. Review the work, not the person. Don't gatekeep knowledge. Ask questions instead of making demands when possible. Distinguish opinion from requirement. And if you approve something, say so explicitly.

Jamie: And for authors receiving feedback: say thank you, don't take it personally, explain your choices when needed, and surface blockers early.

Alex: Perfect. Those behaviors make later PR chapters go much more smoothly.

Alex: There's also an especially important angle here for accessibility issues. When commenting on accessibility topics, be inclusive and precise. Describe the barrier, not the user as a problem. Avoid framing accessibility as a niche extra. And when possible, include environment details and reproduction steps.

Jamie: So instead of "screen readers don't work here," say something more like "On this button, the accessible name is unclear in NVDA on this browser, so the control is difficult to identify."

Alex: Exactly. Specific, testable, respectful.

Alex: That leads naturally into issue writing more generally, because being a good commenter also means understanding what a good issue looks like. A strong issue usually has a clear title and a meaningful description. For bugs, a useful structure includes what happened, what you expected, how to reproduce, your environment, and any additional context.

Jamie: Those same categories came up in accessibility-specific issue writing too.

Alex: They did, because they are broadly useful. For accessibility issues, they are especially important. What happened? What was expected? How can someone reproduce it? What environment were you using? Browser, screen reader, operating system, zoom level, device? And what extra context might help?

Jamie: That helps other people confirm the issue instead of guessing.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: For feature requests, the structure shifts a little. You describe the need, the proposed improvement, maybe alternatives considered, and why it would help. Across both bug reports and feature requests, general principles stay the same: be specific, concise, factual, and oriented toward action.

Jamie: And there was a before-and-after idea too, right? A vague issue versus a clear issue.

Alex: Yes. "This page is bad" is vague. "The setup guide link under accessibility settings returns 404, and the expected destination appears to be the settings help page" is much clearer.

Alex: If you're filing a new issue in the browser, the path is straightforward. Go to the Issues tab, activate New issue, possibly choose a template or open a blank issue, enter a clear title, write the body, optionally assign labels if you have permission, and submit.

Jamie: And templates can shape what you write.

Alex: Yes. Some repositories have issue templates. If they do, use them. They're there to help maintainers get the information they need.

Jamie: What about the command line version?

Jamie: The interactive editor route sounds good when the comment is longer.

Alex: Exactly. And it gives you more room to format Markdown cleanly.

Alex: Speaking of Markdown, when writing comments or issues, simple formatting can help a lot. Paragraphs, bullet points, inline code for filenames or commands, and short quoted text when responding to something specific all improve readability.

Jamie: But probably don't over-format a tiny comment.

Alex: Right. Use just enough structure to make the message easier to follow.

Alex: There are also page-specific keyboard shortcuts on GitHub that can speed up issue work. On the issues list page, shortcuts help with navigation and creating new items. On an open issue, there are shortcuts related to comment actions and navigation.

Jamie: Good to know, though learners should probably focus first on clarity and orientation rather than memorizing every shortcut.

Alex: Exactly. Shortcuts are accelerators, not prerequisites.

Alex: Another useful skill is cross-referencing issues. If you mention another issue number in a comment, GitHub creates a link. In pull request descriptions and sometimes issue comments, closing keywords can automatically close linked issues when the PR is merged.

Jamie: Like "closes number 42."

Alex: Yes. And you can reference issues across repositories too, if you use the fuller repo-and-number form. These references help trace related work.

Alex: Then there are sub-issues. A parent issue can have child issues beneath it, which is useful when one problem is really several smaller tasks. For example, a parent issue about improving accessibility in one file might have separate sub-issues for alt text, heading hierarchy, and link text.

Jamie: How is that different from a task list in the body of an issue?

Alex: Good question. A task list is lightweight checklist text inside one issue. Sub-issues are independent issues with their own pages, metadata, and history. Use sub-issues when each piece deserves separate tracking.

Jamie: And the parent can show progress as sub-issues get completed.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: If you're a maintainer or triager, issues also involve management actions. You may close an issue, possibly with a reason, maybe with a comment. You can reopen closed issues. You can assign issues to yourself or others, add or remove labels, set milestones, and in some cases transfer or delete issues.

Jamie: So issue work is not just writing. It's also organizing.

Alex: That's right. And good triage is a real skill.

Alex: A common entry point for newcomers is the good first issue label. That label is meant to indicate a task appropriate for someone's first contribution.

Jamie: But it also comes with a kind of social contract, doesn't it?

Alex: Yes. If a project labels something good first issue, contributors hope the issue is reasonably scoped, explained, and welcoming. And as a contributor, you should still read carefully, ask clarifying questions, and respect existing discussion rather than assuming the label means "trivial."

Alex: Let's zoom out further into the contribution workflow that gives all of this context: GitHub Flow. Even though today's task is issue-centered, issue conversations often lead into code changes.

Jamie: Right, because eventually someone may fix the issue in a branch and open a pull request.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub Flow has six steps. Create a branch from main with a descriptive name. Make your changes and commit them in small logical units. Open a pull request, even early as a draft if needed. Discuss and review. Pass status checks. Then merge.

Jamie: And the reason this model works is that main stays deployable, branches are cheap, pull requests centralize the discussion, and small changes move faster.

Alex: Well summarized.

Jamie: And this workshop uses GitHub Flow rather than Git Flow because it's lighter weight and better suited to modern open source contribution.

Alex: Precisely. Git Flow has multiple long-lived and temporary branch types like develop, release, and hotfix branches. You may still encounter it in enterprise or legacy projects, but for this workshop and many open source repos, GitHub Flow is simpler and more practical.

Alex: One especially useful unwritten rule in that workflow is one thing per branch. Keep each branch focused on one coherent change.

Jamie: That pairs nicely with issue writing and commenting, honestly. One issue should track one coherent problem, and one branch should solve one coherent thing.

Alex: Exactly. Clear scope reduces confusion everywhere.

Alex: Another practical habit from open source culture is keeping your fork up to date. If you contribute through a fork, sync it regularly so your work starts from current main.

Jamie: There were several ways to do that.

Alex: Yes. The easiest may be GitHub's web interface if it offers a sync option. On the command line, you do a one-time setup by adding the upstream remote, then the usual sync process is: switch to your main branch, fetch upstream changes, merge upstream's main into your local main, and push that updated main back to your fork on GitHub. There's also a GitHub Desktop path.

Jamie: And when should you sync?

Alex: Before starting new work, after your PR is merged, and anytime your fork has drifted significantly from upstream.

Alex: Commit messages are another communication skill. A good commit message has a clear first line, and may optionally include a body and footer. Good commits are atomic, meaning each commit represents one coherent change.

Jamie: So even commit history is part of being understandable to other humans.

Alex: Yes. Common mistakes include vague messages, mixing unrelated changes in one commit, or writing only from your own memory without enough context for others.

Alex: Let's return to challenge logistics, because those matter too. In the workshop challenge issue for joining the conversation, you're asked to provide evidence by pasting the URL of the comment you left, along with a brief note about what you commented on and how you used a reaction.

Jamie: So the evidence itself is lightweight, but specific.

Alex: Exactly. And there's also a peer simulation check: if you had a real buddy, see whether they commented on your issue and reply. If not, reply to the bot or to your own peer-simulation comment with one follow-up thought.

Jamie: That's nice because it reinforces that conversation is not always one-and-done.

Alex: Correct.

Alex: If you get stuck, there are a few classic problems. If you can't find the peer-simulation issue, go to the Issues tab and filter by the peer-simulation label, or ask your facilitator for the link if you're using a real buddy repository. If the @mention isn't working, check that there is no space after the at sign and that the username matches exactly. If you don't know how to add a reaction, look for the Add reaction control, often represented by a smiley face, and screen readers should announce it by name.

Jamie: And if someone wants to check their work, there's a reference solution.

Alex: Yes. But remember, the exact wording of your conversation can differ. The point is the quality and function of the exchange, not copying a script.

Alex: There's also a larger learning moment here. The issue skills you practice manually now are foundational for future automation and AI-assisted workflows. Before you let a tool triage issues, search for good first issues, or draft replies, you need enough understanding to judge whether the tool is helping or hallucinating.

Jamie: I love that framing. Today, you are the triage engine.

Alex: Exactly. Then later, if you use agents or automation, you'll understand the process you are amplifying.

Jamie: Can we also touch on broader open source participation? Because commenting on issues feels like a first contribution path.

Alex: It absolutely is. Open source is not just code. Many people can contribute: writers, testers, accessibility reviewers, designers, bug reporters, maintainers, community moderators, and people who improve documentation or ask clarifying questions.

Jamie: And a good first contribution is usually small, clear, and bounded.

Alex: Yes. If a task is too large, too ambiguous, or spans too many systems, it may not be ideal as a first attempt. Good first contributions are readable, testable, and scoped.

Jamie: So part of finding something to work on is learning how to read an issue before you start.

Alex: Exactly. Read the issue, look for prior comments, understand the expected outcome, and make sure someone else is not already actively solving it.

Alex: And when you do make a contribution, the basic workflow is straightforward: fork if needed, clone if needed, create a branch, edit files, commit, push, open a pull request, and write a good PR description that explains what changed, why, and how to test it.

Jamie: Then if you need help, ask clearly.

Alex: Yes. Good help requests include the exact step where you got stuck, what you expected, what happened instead, and what you already tried. That makes it easier for maintainers and peers to respond.

Jamie: And after your contribution is merged?

Alex: Follow up, learn from the review, sync your fork, and build a habit. Small, repeated contributions are more sustainable than one giant heroic effort.

Alex: Before we close, I want to mention a few community health files because they shape the tone and process around issues and contributions. CONTRIBUTING dot md explains how the project wants contributions handled. CODEOFCONDUCT dot md explains expected behavior and what to do when interactions go wrong. SECURITY dot md explains how to report security problems. LICENSE explains the legal terms for use and contribution.

Jamie: And knowing where to find those files on GitHub can prevent a lot of confusion.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: What about difficult situations? Because public communication is not always smooth.

Alex: That's true. If you receive harsh feedback, pause before responding, separate the technical point from the emotional sting, and reply to the substance if you can. If you disagree with a decision, ask clarifying questions and state your reasoning respectfully. If someone is rude to you, follow the project's code of conduct and seek maintainer or facilitator support when needed. And if you realize you caused offense, acknowledge it, apologize plainly, and adjust.

Jamie: That's a very human part of collaboration.

Alex: It is, and it matters.

Alex: One last practical note. Different communication channels serve different purposes. Issues are for tracked work and discussion tied to repository tasks. Pull request comments are for reviewing specific proposed changes. Other channels, like discussions or chat, may be better for brainstorming or informal questions. Part of being effective is choosing the right channel.

Jamie: And when in doubt, phrases that work tend to be simple and respectful.

Alex: Exactly. "I can reproduce this in these steps." "Would this approach solve the problem?" "I may be mistaken, but I think the issue also affects this section." "Thanks for the report." "Could you share your environment details?" Those kinds of phrases do a lot of good work.

Alex: So here's the big takeaway. Joining the conversation on GitHub is not a minor side skill. It is core open source practice. You are learning how to read carefully, respond thoughtfully, notify the right people, reduce ambiguity, and help shared work move forward.

Jamie: And for this specific challenge, success is simple and meaningful: find the issue, read it, leave one thoughtful comment, include the right @mention, add a reaction, and share the comment URL as evidence.

Alex: Exactly. Specific. Encouraging. Constructive. That's enough.

Jamie: And if your buddy or the simulation replies, reply back. Because collaboration is a conversation, not a checkbox.

Alex: Well said.

Alex: For current source-of-truth details, it's always good practice to consult official GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, GitHub's docs about issues, and the open source contribution guidance referenced in the workshop materials.

Jamie: Ready to go join the conversation?

Alex: Let's do it.

14. Episode 23: GitHub Gists

Lightweight code sharing: creating, editing, forking, and embedding Gists.

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re spending time with two GitHub features that are easy to overlook at first, but incredibly useful once you understand where they fit: Discussions and Gists.

Jamie: I’m glad we’re doing both together, because they feel related without being the same. One is about conversation, the other is about sharing small chunks of content.

Alex: Exactly. Think of Discussions as GitHub’s built-in forum space for repositories and organizations. It’s where questions, brainstorming, announcements, community conversations, and polls can live without pretending to be bug reports or feature work.

Jamie: So not everything belongs in Issues.

Alex: Right. And that distinction matters to maintainers. If you open an issue, you’re signaling that there is actionable work to track. Issues imply workflow: labels, assignees, closing states, progress. A discussion, by contrast, says, “Let’s talk this through,” or “I have a question,” or “I want input before we decide what to build.”

Jamie: That sounds kinder to the project, too. A question posted as an issue can create noise.

Alex: That’s the idea. If the answer might be a conversation rather than a fix, Discussions is often the better home.

Alex: Before we go further, one administrative note for workshop alumni. If you’re using the support hub after the workshop, there are usually three places to know: the support hub home page, the Discussions area for Q and A and community conversation, and the Issues area for trackable support requests.

Jamie: So if I’m new and I need help, what are the first best steps?

Alex: Start by reading the pinned “Start Here” resources in Discussions. Then search existing discussions before opening a new thread. And if you’ve hit a setup blocker or an accessibility blocker, use the issue templates in the support repository so maintainers can triage faster.

Jamie: That’s a good open source habit generally: search first, choose the right tool second, then post.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: For learners using assistive technology, let’s ground this in navigation. In many repositories, the Discussions tab appears in the main navigation bar alongside Code, Issues, and Pull Requests. Keyboard users may use T to move through tab items in GitHub’s interface, or K to move among links and land on Discussions.

Jamie: And inside a discussion thread, replies are often exposed as article elements, right?

Alex: Yes. For many screen reader users, that’s useful because NVDA and JAWS can jump by article with A. The reply editor behaves much like the issue comment editor. You’ll usually enter focus mode to type, and Ctrl+Enter commonly submits.

Jamie: What about low-vision users?

Alex: A few important visual patterns: categories often appear in a side panel that may be on the left or right depending on viewport width. Answered Q and A threads typically show a green Answered badge. Polls display percentage bars after you vote, and those bars rely partly on color fill, so it helps to listen for labels and percentages too, not just look at the bars.

Jamie: And for sighted users, the visual organization matters: category labels, pinned items, accepted answers, and upvote controls instead of posting “plus one.”

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: Let’s make the issue-versus-discussion choice really concrete.

Alex: Sure. Use an issue when you found a bug, want a specific feature, need to track work, or expect an outcome like fixed, closed, or won’t fix. Use a discussion when you have a how-do-I question, want to brainstorm before filing a feature request, want community input, or want an open conversation that may not have one correct answer.

Jamie: So if I’m unsure whether a feature idea is mature enough, I might start in Discussions under Ideas.

Alex: Perfect example. And there are a few common categories you’ll encounter. Q and A is for support questions where one answer can be marked correct. Ideas is for feature brainstorming. Announcements is for releases, roadmaps, or breaking changes from maintainers. General catches broader conversation. And some communities use Show and Tell for sharing what members built.

Jamie: That category system helps set expectations before anyone even opens the thread.

Alex: Yes. It tells you what kind of conversation a project welcomes in that space.

Jamie: How do learners actually get to Discussions?

Alex: There are two common paths. From a repository, go to the repository page and look in the main navigation for Discussions. If it’s there, open it. If the tab is missing, that doesn’t mean you missed it. Discussions is optional. Maintainers have to enable it, and not every project uses it.

Jamie: That’s reassuring, because people often assume they’re navigating badly when a tab is simply not enabled.

Alex: Exactly. The second path is from an organization page. Larger organizations may have organization-level Discussions that aren’t tied to one repository. Those are community-wide conversations.

Jamie: So a repo discussion might be about one codebase, while an organization discussion could cover broader community questions.

Alex: That’s a useful mental model.

Alex: Once you’re on the Discussions home page, categories become the main organizing structure.

Jamie: What should a screen reader user expect there?

Alex: Each category is typically a section with its own heading. A practical pattern is to jump by heading level, then use link navigation to move among discussion titles inside a category. Many people use 3 to jump to category headings if that matches the heading structure on the page, K to move among links or discussion titles depending on browsing mode and keymap, and Enter to open the discussion.

Jamie: And the side panel?

Alex: That panel often contains all categories with item counts, pinned or announcement items near the top, most active discussions, and tags if the repository uses them. On a narrow viewport it may move to a different side or lower in the reading order, so expect layout shifts at high zoom or on smaller screens.

Jamie: So learners should think in terms of landmarks and headings, not just memorizing one exact visual location.

Alex: Yes. That’s especially important for accessibility.

Jamie: Let’s walk through creating a discussion.

Alex: From the Discussions tab, activate the New discussion button. Then choose a category, because category selection affects what options and fields appear. After that, enter a title and body, then activate Start discussion.

Jamie: And title quality matters.

Alex: Very much. A clear, searchable title helps future learners and maintainers. “How do I use the daily-briefing agent?” is far better than “Help.” If you’re posting in Q and A, phrase the title as an actual question.

Jamie: What does the screen reader path usually feel like?

Alex: Typically: tab to New discussion, press Enter, arrow through the category list, press Enter to choose one, move to the title field, then to the body editor. Enter focus mode to type or paste content, then tab to Start discussion and activate it. And often Ctrl+Enter submits, just as with issue comments.

Jamie: Before posting, search first.

Alex: Absolutely. Use the search bar in Discussions, or GitHub’s global search with a qualifier like repo:owner-slash-name in:discussions. That can save everyone time and keep knowledge in one place.

Jamie: Any low-vision details worth calling out?

Alex: Yes. The category selector may appear as labeled cards or a list with descriptions. At high zoom, take time to read the category descriptions so you choose the right space. Title and body usually stack vertically. After posting, confirmation may appear in a success banner near the top, so if you don’t immediately notice confirmation, scroll back upward.

Jamie: And for sighted users, the page often looks similar to opening a new issue, which can reduce the learning curve.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s talk about participating once a discussion exists.

Jamie: Reading first, then replying.

Alex: Good order. A discussion page is structured a lot like an issue page: original post at the top, replies below, sometimes an accepted answer pinned near the top in Q and A, and a reply editor near the bottom.

Jamie: How would you navigate it efficiently with a screen reader?

Alex: Jump by headings to move between the original post and reply headings. Some users may use heading navigation at a particular level if replies are marked that way. Then arrow through content to read details. The goal is to avoid linearly reading the entire page if you only need the accepted answer or a specific reply.

Jamie: And to reply?

Alex: Navigate to the bottom reply area, or use a Reply button on a particular comment. The text area behaves like other GitHub comment editors: enter focus mode, type, then submit with Ctrl+Enter or use the visible submit control.

Jamie: What about nested replies?

Alex: Each comment may have its own Reply button. Activating it opens a nested text area under that comment, which helps keep local back-and-forth attached to the right context.

Jamie: That’s useful, especially in long support threads.

Alex: Very. And one more etiquette point: if you agree with a post or want to signal that an answer helped, use the thumbs-up or other reactions instead of leaving a “plus one” comment. Many maintainers look at upvotes to prioritize the most useful answers.

Jamie: In Q and A, one answer can be marked correct. How does that work conceptually?

Alex: In Q and A discussions, the discussion author can mark one reply as the accepted answer. When that happens, GitHub highlights it and typically pins it near the top, with an Answered indicator on the thread.

Jamie: That’s huge for accessibility because it reduces scanning.

Alex: Exactly. Instead of reading an entire thread to discover which reply solved the problem, you can often find the accepted answer immediately. To mark an answer as the discussion author, locate the preferred reply and use the control GitHub provides to mark it as the answer. Once marked, it becomes visually and structurally distinguished from the rest of the conversation.

Jamie: And if an answer changes over time?

Alex: The author can usually update which reply is accepted if a better answer emerges. That’s one of the strengths of a living support forum.

Jamie: Now, polls. These surprise some people because they don’t realize GitHub Discussions can do that.

Alex: Yes. In communities that enable polls, they’re useful for quick preference gathering: meeting times, naming choices, roadmap priorities, and similar lightweight decisions.

Jamie: How do you create one?

Alex: You begin a new discussion in a category that supports polls, then add a poll with a question and response options. Depending on the interface and current GitHub behavior, you may also choose settings like whether voters can select one option or multiple. The key concept is that polls belong to discussion workflows, not issue workflows.

Jamie: And voting?

Alex: Open the poll discussion, review the options, select your choice or choices as allowed, and submit the vote. After voting, results are usually shown as percentages and bars.

Jamie: Important reminder for low-vision and nonvisual users: don’t rely only on bar fill color. Listen for or read the text labels and percentages.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Let’s give a focused screen reader navigation reference for Discussions.

Jamie: A kind of practical cheat sheet.

Alex: Yes. On the discussions list page, use headings to move across categories and sections, links to open individual threads, and landmarks to understand where the main content and side content live. Expect a side panel containing categories, pinned items, activity, or tags.

Jamie: And inside a discussion?

Alex: Use heading navigation to locate the title, original post, accepted answer if present, and replies. Article navigation can help move reply by reply. The editor behaves like other GitHub comment forms, so focus mode is important.

Jamie: Any reader-specific notes?

Alex: A few. In NVDA, article navigation with A is often especially handy for moving between replies. In JAWS, A can also help when articles are exposed clearly. In VoiceOver, users may lean more on the rotor for headings, landmarks, links, and form controls rather than using the exact same keystrokes as NVDA or JAWS. The deeper point is not the one perfect command. It’s understanding the page structure: headings, articles, controls, and editor regions.

Jamie: That’s a helpful framing. Learn the structure, then map your screen reader’s commands onto it.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: Tell me more about organization-level Discussions.

Alex: These are discussions attached to an organization rather than a single repo. They work well for broad community support, governance conversation, event planning, or cross-project announcements. If a repo-specific answer would be too narrow, the organization forum may be the better place.

Jamie: So learners should notice the context. A discussion at the organization level may not map to one codebase.

Alex: Correct. And that changes how you write your post. Be explicit about which repository, tool, or workflow you’re asking about if you’re in a broader community space.

Jamie: There’s also a section about accessibility agents and what’s different here. What should learners understand?

Alex: The big idea is that Discussions is less task-centric than Issues. Accessibility support tools, AI agents, or automation helpers may be less able to infer one concrete next step because the content is conversational. A thread may contain brainstorming, opinion, support, and clarification all at once.

Jamie: So if someone is using an accessibility-focused assistant or any kind of summarizing agent, they should expect ambiguity.

Alex: Yes. Ask for structure explicitly. For example: “List the accepted answer, unresolved follow-up questions, and any commands mentioned.” In Discussions, that kind of prompt can be more useful than “What should I do?” because the thread may not be about a single action.

Jamie: And because accepted answers, pinned posts, reactions, and category context all matter, an agent needs that context too.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let’s shift to GitHub Gists.

Jamie: The tiny-shareable-content side of GitHub.

Alex: That’s a good shorthand. Gists are for sharing code snippets, notes, small configuration files, examples, or short collections of files without creating a full repository workflow around them.

Jamie: So a gist is not just “a repo with a shorter name.”

Alex: Right. It has overlap with repositories, but the purpose is different. A gist is lightweight and optimized for sharing a small piece of content. It’s often used for examples, scratch notes, demos, reproducible snippets, or config sharing.

Jamie: And for accessibility learners, that can be especially practical. You may want to share one NVDA config excerpt, one Markdown note, or one short script.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What is a gist, technically and conceptually?

Alex: Conceptually, it’s a shareable code or text snippet hosted by GitHub. A gist can contain one file or multiple files. It has a page, a URL, revision history, and options like editing, commenting, forking, and cloning.

Jamie: So it’s still versioned content.

Alex: Yes. It’s lightweight, but not disposable in the sense of losing history. Git underlies it enough that you can clone a gist, edit it, and keep a revision trail.

Jamie: That makes it stronger than pasting code into a generic note tool.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: When should someone use a gist instead of a repository?

Alex: Use a gist when the content is small, self-contained, and primarily meant to be shared or referenced. A quick code example, a sample config, workshop notes, or a snippet for a Q and A answer are good candidates.

Jamie: And use a repository when the project is larger, needs structure, collaboration, issues, pull requests, documentation, or a meaningful file tree.

Alex: Exactly. If you need branching workflows, maintainers, project organization, tests, releases, or ongoing development, choose a repository. If you just need to hand someone a small, readable artifact, a gist can be ideal.

Jamie: So the question is not “Which is better?” It’s “What scale and workflow does this content need?”

Alex: Well put.

Alex: Creating a gist through the GitHub web interface is usually straightforward. Go to the gist creation page, enter an optional description, provide a filename, and add content. Then choose whether to create it as public or secret, and submit.

Jamie: Let’s pause on that filename point. That affects syntax highlighting, right?

Alex: Yes. The filename matters. If you name a file with an extension like .md, .py, .json, or .txt, GitHub can often infer the file type and render or highlight it appropriately.

Jamie: What’s the screen reader experience like?

Alex: Typically there’s a description field, then a filename field, then the editor itself. After entering content, you’ll encounter controls for creating the gist. As with other GitHub editors, focus mode may be necessary to type smoothly in the text area.

Jamie: And people can add more than one file?

Alex: Yes. A gist can contain multiple files. There’s usually an Add file option or similar control on the page. That’s useful if your example needs, say, a README plus a script, or a config file plus a sample output file.

Jamie: So even though gists are lightweight, they’re not limited to one file.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What are the practical learning-card takeaways for creating a gist?

Alex: For screen reader users: expect a filename field and code editor, enter focus mode when needed, and choose a meaningful filename for proper rendering. For low-vision users: the create page can be dense, so zoom carefully and verify whether you selected public or secret before submitting. For sighted users: don’t skip the filename, and remember that multiple files can live in one gist if your example needs context.

Jamie: Once created, can you edit a gist?

Alex: Yes. Gists can be edited, and edits create revision history. That means you can correct mistakes, improve examples, or update notes without losing the earlier state entirely.

Jamie: Useful for workshop materials that evolve over time.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: What about embedding a gist?

Alex: A gist can often be embedded in a web page using the embed script GitHub provides. That makes it useful for blogs, documentation, or course pages when you want the content to remain hosted on GitHub but displayed elsewhere.

Jamie: Any accessibility caution there?

Alex: Yes. Embedded code should still be presented in an accessible context. Don’t assume the embed alone makes the surrounding explanation accessible. If the code matters, describe what it does and provide enough narrative so users aren’t forced to parse raw code without context.

Jamie: And cloning a gist works the way many Git learners would hope?

Alex: Yes. A gist can be cloned with Git using its clone URL. That lets you pull it down locally, edit it, and push updates if it’s yours or if you have the right workflow for a forked copy.

Jamie: So for learners practicing Git commands, a gist can be a tiny sandbox.

Alex: Exactly. It’s a small target for practicing clone, edit, commit, and push.

Jamie: Forking a gist—how should people think about that?

Alex: Forking a gist creates your own copy so you can adapt or build on someone else’s snippet. That’s useful when you want to preserve the original while making your own changes. It mirrors repository forking conceptually, just at the gist scale.

Jamie: So if someone shares a config example and I tweak it for my environment, I can fork the gist rather than overwriting their version.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How do users find their own gists later?

Alex: GitHub provides a way to view your gists from your profile or gist area. Look for your gist list, where you can review public and secret gists you own. The exact path can vary with interface changes, so it helps to think in terms of profile navigation and gist listings rather than one frozen layout.

Jamie: Any screen reader guidance?

Alex: Use headings and links to scan the list, and listen carefully for filenames and descriptions. Since gist titles are often really filenames or short descriptions, good naming helps future you just as much as it helps other people.

Jamie: Can you discover public gists from other people too?

Alex: Yes. Public gists are discoverable and shareable. You can browse, search, and follow links to examples people have published openly.

Jamie: That sounds useful, but also like a reason to think carefully before publishing.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: What about gist comments?

Alex: Gists can have comments, which makes them useful for lightweight collaboration or feedback. To add a comment, open the gist, navigate to the comment area, enter your text, and submit just as you would in other GitHub comment forms.

Jamie: So a gist can become a mini conversation space around a shared snippet.

Alex: Yes, though it’s still not the same as full issue or discussion workflows.

Jamie: We need to spend real time on security and privacy here.

Alex: Absolutely. This is one of the most important parts of working with gists. Public gists are public. Anyone can access them, and they may be indexed, shared, and discovered by others.

Jamie: And secret gists?

Alex: Secret gists are not truly private in the strong sense people sometimes assume. They are unlisted, meaning they aren’t broadly discoverable in the same way, but anyone with the link can access them.

Jamie: So secret means obscure, not secured.

Alex: Exactly. Never put sensitive data in a gist. Not in a public gist, not in a secret gist. No passwords, tokens, API keys, private personal data, credentials, or confidential information.

Jamie: That warning cannot be overstated.

Alex: It really can’t. Treat gists as shareable publication surfaces. If it would be harmful for the content to leak, it does not belong there.

Jamie: Let’s ground gists in example use cases.

Alex: One good example is sharing screen reader configuration. Suppose you want to share NVDA settings for navigating GitHub’s web interface. A gist is a tidy way to publish that config snippet so others can review, copy, and discuss it.

Jamie: Another example is a quick Markdown note.

Alex: Exactly. Imagine workshop day one notes in a single Markdown file. A gist can hold that note, preserve revisions, and give you an easy URL to share with classmates.

Jamie: And a classic third example: a code snippet for answering a Stack Overflow question or similar support thread.

Alex: Yes. Instead of pasting a long block of code inline, you can link to a gist that contains the exact example.

Jamie: Can we do a quick comparison between gists and repositories?

Alex: Sure. Gists are best for small, self-contained snippets or notes, often with lightweight sharing in mind. Repositories are best for projects, collaboration, documentation, issue tracking, pull requests, and structured development.

Jamie: A gist is lightweight and fast. A repository is fuller-featured and better for sustained work.

Alex: Exactly. If your content is growing branches, documentation, tests, or contributor workflows, it’s probably time for a repository.

Jamie: And if you no longer want a gist?

Alex: You can delete it. As always, pause before deleting anything you may need later, and remember that content shared publicly may still have been copied or referenced elsewhere.

Jamie: So deletion is not a guarantee that nobody ever saw it.

Alex: Correct.

Alex: Let’s close by tying both features together. Discussions helps a community talk without overloading Issues. Gists helps people share small artifacts without building a whole repository.

Jamie: And both matter for accessible participation. Discussions gives structure to support and community Q and A. Gists gives a practical way to share reproducible snippets, notes, and configurations.

Alex: That’s the core lesson. Choose the space that matches the job. If you need conversation, especially open-ended community conversation, look for Discussions. If you need to publish a small piece of code or text, consider a gist. And in both cases, think about accessibility, naming, searchability, and privacy before you hit submit.

Jamie: And one last habit check: search first, title clearly, post in the right place, and never share secrets.

Alex: Perfect ending.

15. Episode 24: GitHub Discussions

Forum-style conversations, Q&A, polls, and navigation with screen readers.

Based on: Appendix U: GitHub Discussions

Download Episode 24 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 24: GitHub Discussions

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re exploring two GitHub features that support community learning and lightweight sharing: Discussions and Gists. These come up a lot once you move beyond just cloning a repository or opening your first issue.

Jamie: And they’re easy to confuse with other GitHub features, right? Like, a learner might think, "If I have a question, should that be an issue?" Or, "If I want to share a code snippet, do I need a whole repository?"

Alex: Exactly. And for blind and low-vision learners, there’s also a navigation question: where are these features, how do they behave with screen readers, and what should you expect from the layout? We’ll walk through all of that.

Alex: Let’s start with Discussions. GitHub Discussions is a built-in forum space for repositories and organizations. It’s meant for open-ended conversation: questions, ideas, announcements, polls, and community knowledge sharing.

Jamie: So this is different from issues and pull requests because it’s less about tracked work and more about conversation.

Alex: That’s the key distinction. Issues imply actionable work. A bug report, a feature request, something that might get assigned, labeled, closed, or linked to ongoing development. Discussions are for talking things through without automatically signaling, "A maintainer needs to take action on this right now."

Jamie: That seems important for maintainers too.

Alex: Very important. If you post a support question as an issue, it can create noise. It inflates issue counts and suggests workflow urgency. The same question in Discussions is often a much better fit because it invites conversation without pretending it’s a tracked defect or task.

Jamie: Can you give us the practical split?

Alex: Sure. Use an issue when you found a bug, want a specific feature, need progress tracking, or expect an outcome like fixed, closed, or won’t fix. Use a discussion when you have a question, want community input, want to brainstorm before filing a feature request, or you’re opening something that may not have a single correct answer.

Jamie: So if I’m wondering how a workflow works, or asking the community how they use a tool, that’s usually a discussion.

Alex: Yes. And many repositories organize Discussions into categories. Common ones include Q and A for support questions, Ideas for brainstorming, Announcements for maintainer updates, General for broad conversation, and Show and Tell for sharing what you built.

Alex: There’s also some workshop support guidance connected to this. If you’re a workshop alum looking for ongoing help, the recommended flow is to use the support hub. Start by reading pinned Start Here resources in Discussions. Search existing discussions before opening a new support thread. And if you hit a setup blocker or an accessibility blocker, use the support repository’s issue templates so maintainers can help more efficiently.

Jamie: That’s a nice example of choosing the right channel. Community conversation in Discussions, trackable blockers in Issues.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How do learners actually get to Discussions?

Alex: There are two common paths. First, from a repository. Navigate to the repo and look in the main navigation bar, where you usually find Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, and similar tabs. If Discussions is enabled, there will be a Discussions tab there.

Jamie: And if I’m using a screen reader?

Alex: You may be able to press T to move among tab items, or K to navigate links and find the Discussions link. Then press Enter to open it.

Jamie: What if the tab isn’t there?

Alex: That does not necessarily mean you’re lost. Discussions is an opt-in feature. Maintainers have to enable it in repository settings, so not every repository uses it.

Jamie: And the second path?

Alex: From an organization. Larger organizations can have organization-level Discussions that are separate from any individual repository. So you go to the organization page, look for a Discussions tab there, and those conversations are community-wide rather than tied to one repo.

Alex: Once you’re inside Discussions, categories matter a lot. The home page is organized by category, and each category acts like its own section.

Jamie: So the layout isn’t just one big flat list.

Alex: Right. For keyboard and screen reader users, category headings are useful landmarks. You may use heading navigation or a key like 3, depending on your setup, to jump among category headings. Then K may help move through discussion titles within a category, and Enter opens the discussion you want.

Jamie: And for low-vision users, there’s a sidebar too, right?

Alex: Yes. Depending on viewport width, the side panel may appear on the left or the right. It typically shows all categories with item counts, a pinned or announcements area near the top, most active discussions, and sometimes tags if the repository uses them.

Jamie: That’s helpful because zoom level can really change where that panel appears.

Alex: Exactly. It’s worth saying out loud: if something seems missing, try scanning the opposite side of the page or adjusting your viewport. The interface can reflow.

Jamie: Okay, let’s say I want to start a new discussion.

Alex: From the Discussions tab, activate the New discussion button. Then choose a category. That part matters because the category affects what kind of conversation you’re creating and sometimes what options appear.

Jamie: What comes next?

Alex: You fill in a title and body. The title should be clear and searchable. For example, "How do I use the daily-briefing agent?" is much better than just "Help." In the Q and A category, phrase the title as a question. That improves clarity and makes search results more meaningful.

Jamie: And the body uses Markdown, like issues do?

Alex: Yes. Same general editor behavior as issue comments. Then activate Start discussion to post.

Jamie: Can you give the screen reader path step by step?

Alex: Yes. Tab to the New discussion button and press Enter. In the category list, use arrow keys to select a category and press Enter. Then move to the title field and type your title. Tab to the body editor, enter Focus Mode to type or paste your content, then tab to Start discussion and press Enter. In many contexts, Ctrl+Enter can submit as well.

Jamie: And before posting, search first.

Alex: Absolutely. Search existing discussions before opening a new one. You can use the search bar on the Discussions page or GitHub’s search syntax with something like repo:owner slash name in:discussions.

Alex: A few accessibility and usability reminders here. For screen reader users, the category selector usually comes first, then the title field, then the body editor. For low-vision users, the category choices may appear as a list or grid with names and descriptions, and the form usually becomes a stacked single-column layout at higher zoom. After posting, a green success banner may appear near the top, so if you don’t hear or see confirmation where you are, scroll or navigate back upward.

Jamie: And for sighted users, this will look a lot like opening a new issue.

Alex: Very similar, yes.

Jamie: Once a discussion exists, how do I read and participate in it?

Alex: A discussion page is structured much like an issue page. You’ll usually find the original post at the top, replies in chronological order, and a reply editor at the bottom. In Q and A discussions, if an answer has been accepted, that answered reply may be pinned near the top and marked clearly.

Jamie: What about navigation?

Alex: Heading navigation is useful. You can jump between the original post heading and reply headings. Then arrow through content to read. Replies are often exposed as article elements, which is especially useful for screen reader users.

Jamie: So if I’m using NVDA or JAWS, article navigation can help me move reply by reply.

Alex: Exactly. In many cases, pressing A jumps among article elements, which often correspond to replies. That can make long threads much more manageable.

Jamie: How do I reply?

Alex: You can go to the main reply editor near the bottom of the page, enter Focus Mode, type your reply, and submit, often with Ctrl+Enter. The editor behaves like issue comments.

Jamie: And if I want to respond to one specific comment?

Alex: Use that comment’s Reply button. Tab to Reply under the specific comment, press Enter, and a nested text area opens beneath it. Then enter Focus Mode, type, and submit with Ctrl+Enter.

Jamie: Nice. That helps keep conversation context clear.

Alex: Exactly. And one etiquette point: instead of posting "+1," use the thumbs-up reaction or other reactions. Many maintainers look at upvotes to identify the most useful responses or the most requested ideas.

Jamie: Now let’s talk about accepted answers, because that’s one of the most distinctive parts of Q and A discussions.

Alex: Right. In the Q and A category, one answer can be marked as the accepted answer. That helps future readers get to the solution quickly.

Jamie: Who can mark an answer?

Alex: Typically the discussion author can do it, and repository maintainers may also have that ability depending on permissions. The basic process is to locate the correct reply and activate the control to mark it as the answer.

Jamie: And what changes once it’s marked?

Alex: You usually get a visible answered state, often a green Answered badge near the discussion title, and the accepted answer may be pinned toward the top above the rest of the reply timeline. That’s useful for everyone, and especially helpful when navigating with a screen reader because it reduces the amount of searching for the final resolution.

Jamie: So if I asked the question, I should come back and mark the reply that solved it.

Alex: Please do. It’s a kindness to the next learner.

Jamie: Discussions can also include polls, right?

Alex: Yes. Some communities use polls to gather quick input. A poll lets the author add a question and multiple answer options so people can vote.

Jamie: What should learners know about creating a poll?

Alex: First, polls depend on repository settings and category support, so they may not be available everywhere. When they are available, the creation flow usually includes fields for poll choices as part of the discussion form. You enter the discussion title and context, then add the poll options.

Jamie: And voting?

Alex: Readers choose an option and submit their vote. After voting, results are commonly displayed with percentages. For low-vision users, note that the interface may use color-filled bars to indicate proportion, so don’t rely on color alone; look or listen for percentage text when available.

Alex: Let’s pause for a more focused screen reader navigation reference for Discussions.

Jamie: Perfect. This is the kind of thing learners often want all in one place.

Alex: On the Discussions list page, look for the Discussions tab in the repository or organization navigation. Use heading navigation to move among category sections. Use link or tab navigation to find discussion titles. The sidebar with category counts, pinned content, active discussions, and tags may be placed differently depending on screen width. Inside an individual discussion, the main post is near the top, replies follow, and the editor is near the bottom. Replies are often article elements. For NVDA users, article navigation can be especially handy for moving among replies. For JAWS users, the same article quick key often works as well. For VoiceOver users, rotor navigation by headings, links, or landmarks may be more practical depending on browser and verbosity settings.

Jamie: So the exact key pattern can vary, but the underlying structure is still pretty navigable.

Alex: That’s right. The big idea is to use headings for overall structure, articles for reply-by-reply movement where supported, and Focus Mode when entering text.

Jamie: What about organization-level Discussions? We touched on them earlier, but let’s make the distinction explicit.

Alex: Good idea. Repository-level Discussions belong to one project. Organization-level Discussions belong to the broader organization community. That means the conversation may be about shared practices, support across multiple repositories, community announcements, or organization-wide Q and A.

Jamie: So if I’m in a large org with many repos, I should pay attention to whether I’m asking something repo-specific or community-wide.

Alex: Exactly. Asking in the right place improves your chances of getting useful help.

Jamie: There’s also a section here about accessibility agents and what’s different in Discussions. What should learners take from that?

Alex: A few things. Discussions often feel less rigid than issues. That can be helpful, but it also means more conversational content to skim. Accessibility tools, screen readers, and AI assistants may need stronger prompting from you: ask for the accepted answer, ask for the highest-upvoted reply, ask whether a thread is Q and A or General, and ask for the category if that context matters.

Jamie: So the challenge isn’t just navigation. It’s also interpretation.

Alex: Exactly. In issues, the status may be obvious: open, closed, assigned.
