In Discussions, you may need to infer whether a question was answered, whether a thread is still active, or whether a maintainer announcement is just informational. For blind and low-vision users working with accessibility agents or AI summarizers, it helps to ask targeted questions like, "Is there an accepted answer?" "What category is this in?" or "Are there polls or upvoted replies I should know about?"

Alex: Now let’s shift to Gists.

Jamie: These are one of those GitHub features people hear about early, but often don’t quite understand.

Alex: That’s true. A Gist is a lightweight way to share code snippets, notes, small examples, or short multi-file content on GitHub without creating a full repository in the usual sense.

Jamie: So if Discussions are for community conversation, Gists are for shareable bits of content.

Alex: Exactly. You can think of a Gist as a simple container for one or more files that you want to publish or share quickly.

Jamie: And there are learning cues here too, right?

Alex: Yes. For screen reader users, Gists are usually straightforward forms with file name and content editors, but it’s helpful to know where file controls are. For low-vision users, the page is often visually simpler than a full repository. For sighted users, it feels like a lightweight code-sharing interface rather than a project workspace.

Jamie: So what exactly is a Gist?

Alex: A Gist is a shareable collection of one or more files hosted by GitHub. It’s often used for quick code examples, Markdown notes, configuration snippets, reproducible examples, or reference text you want to link to.

Jamie: Can a Gist be versioned?

Alex: Yes. Gists do keep revision history. You can edit them, and GitHub tracks changes over time. They also support Git operations like cloning and forking.

Jamie: That surprises some people.

Alex: It does. Gists are lighter than repositories in presentation and purpose, but they still have real Git behavior behind them.

Jamie: When should someone use a Gist instead of a repository?

Alex: Use a Gist when the content is small, self-contained, and primarily meant for sharing rather than ongoing project collaboration. For example: a short code snippet for an answer, a one-page Markdown note, a sample config file, or a tiny reproducible example.

Jamie: And a repository is better when the thing has structure, issues, branches, documentation, or a life as an actual project.

Alex: Exactly. If you need project organization, multiple contributors, a README-driven home page, issue tracking, pull requests, or a longer-term development workflow, use a repository.

Jamie: So a Gist is not just "a tiny repo," even though some Git features overlap.

Alex: Right. The overlap is real, but the intended use is different.

Jamie: Walk us through creating a Gist on the web.

Alex: You go to the Gist creation interface on GitHub. Then you provide a file name, add content, and optionally a description for the Gist itself. You choose whether to create it as public or secret, then activate the create button.

Jamie: What do public and secret mean here?

Alex: Public Gists are discoverable and visible to others. Secret Gists are not shown in public listings, but anyone with the link can access them. Secret does not mean secure or private in a strong sense.

Jamie: That distinction matters a lot.

Alex: It does. Never put sensitive data in a Gist. Not passwords, tokens, private keys, personal confidential information, or anything you would regret if shared.

Jamie: Can you describe the screen reader navigation for creating a Gist?

Alex: Typically, you navigate to the description field if present, then to the first file name field, then to the editor for file contents. After that, you move to the create controls and choose either public or secret creation. As with other GitHub editors, entering Focus Mode in the code or text editor may be necessary depending on your setup.

Jamie: And if I need more than one file?

Alex: You can add multiple files to a Gist. There’s usually an Add file control. Each file gets its own file name field and content editor. That’s useful when your snippet makes sense only with a companion Markdown explanation, stylesheet, config file, or small supporting script.

Jamie: So a Gist can be more than a single paste box.

Alex: Definitely.

Alex: A few practical creation reminders. Choose descriptive file names so syntax highlighting and interpretation work correctly. If you’re sharing notes, a Markdown file can be a good choice. If you’re sharing code, use an appropriate extension. And just like with discussions, write clear descriptions when you can—they make your content easier to revisit later.

Jamie: That sounds obvious until you’re staring at ten unnamed snippets six weeks later.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about editing a Gist?

Alex: If you own the Gist, you can open it and use the Edit action. Then update the file contents, file names, description, or files themselves, and save the changes. GitHub keeps revision history, so edits become part of that record.

Jamie: Can you embed a Gist elsewhere?

Alex: Yes. Gists can often be embedded into web pages using the embed script GitHub provides. That makes them useful for blog posts, documentation pages, or demos where you want the code displayed from a maintained source.

Jamie: And cloning?

Alex: A Gist can be cloned with Git, just like a repository URL. That means you can pull it down locally, inspect it in VS Code, make changes, and push updates if it’s yours.

Jamie: And forking?

Alex: You can fork a Gist too. That’s useful if someone shared a snippet you want to adapt while preserving the original. Forking creates your own copy.

Jamie: How do I find my Gists later?

Alex: GitHub provides ways to access your own Gists from your account area and Gist pages. Once there, you can review your created Gists, starred items if supported in your workflow, and individual entries.

Jamie: Any screen reader notes?

Alex: Use heading and link navigation to move through the list. Listen for descriptions, file names, and metadata like whether the Gist is public or secret if that’s exposed in the interface. Because Gist listings are typically compact, consistent heading or link navigation works well.

Jamie: And what about discovering other people’s public Gists?

Alex: Public Gists can be browsed and discovered through GitHub’s Gist interfaces and shared links. But remember: public means public. Treat anything you publish there as openly accessible.

Jamie: Can people comment on Gists?

Alex: Yes. Gists support comments. To add a comment, open the Gist, move to the comment area, enter your text in the comment editor, and submit. The interaction is familiar if you’ve used issue or discussion comments.

Jamie: So even a quick snippet can turn into a little conversation.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s linger on security and privacy, because this is where people get into trouble.

Alex: Agreed. Public Gists are openly visible and should be treated as fully public. Secret Gists are unlisted rather than truly private. Anyone with the link can access them, and links can be shared or leaked.

Jamie: So secret is more like obscured, not protected.

Alex: That’s the right mental model. And the biggest rule is simple: never put sensitive data in a Gist. No credentials, no secrets, no internal-only information you’re not prepared to expose.

Jamie: That warning is worth repeating because people often use Gists for quick sharing and move too fast.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can we give a few example use cases?

Alex: Absolutely. One example is sharing screen reader configuration. If you wanted to share NVDA settings for GitHub web navigation, a Gist could hold a config file or a note describing recommended settings and shortcuts. That makes it easy to link in a discussion, workshop message, or support response.

Jamie: Another one was a quick Markdown note.

Alex: Yes. Imagine a "Workshop Day 1 Notes" Gist containing a Markdown file with setup reminders, command references, or links collected during training. That’s a perfect lightweight use case.

Jamie: And a third is a code snippet for answering someone on Stack Overflow or in a GitHub discussion.

Alex: Exactly. Instead of pasting a huge block inline, you can put the code in a Gist and link to it.

Jamie: Can you give us a quick comparison between Gists and repositories?

Alex: Sure. Gists are best for small, focused, easily shared files or snippets. Repositories are best for complete projects. Gists are lightweight and fast to create. Repositories support richer collaboration and project structure. Both can be versioned with Git, but repositories provide the fuller development workflow.

Jamie: So if I’m unsure, I can ask: is this a shareable snippet, or is this a project?

Alex: That’s a very good test.

Jamie: And if I no longer need a Gist?

Alex: You can delete it from the Gist’s controls if it belongs to you. As always, confirm carefully before deleting. If others rely on the link, removing the Gist may break references.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, what are the big learning cards you want listeners to remember?

Alex: For Discussions: the Discussions tab lives alongside the main repository tabs when enabled. Categories shape the kind of conversation. Q and A threads can have accepted answers. Replies often behave like article elements, so screen reader navigation can be efficient. Use reactions instead of "+1" comments. Search before posting. For Gists: use them for snippets, notes, and small multi-file shares. They can be created on the web, edited later, cloned, forked, embedded, and commented on. Public is public. Secret is unlisted, not truly private. Never store sensitive data there.

Jamie: And maybe one more theme connects both features: choose the lightest tool that fits your goal.

Alex: Exactly. If you need community conversation, use Discussions rather than forcing everything into Issues. If you need to share a small piece of code or notes, use a Gist rather than creating a whole repository.

Jamie: That makes GitHub feel less like one giant undifferentiated platform and more like a set of tools with distinct jobs.

Alex: Well said. And the more clearly you choose the right space, the easier it becomes for maintainers, classmates, and future you to understand what you meant.

Alex: For authoritative follow-up reading, GitHub Docs remains the main source for Discussions and Gists behavior, and GitHub’s changelog can help you catch interface changes over time.

Jamie: And from an accessibility perspective, remember that layouts can shift, sidebars can move, accepted answers can be pinned, and editor focus behavior matters. Slow down, use structure, and ask your tools precise questions.

Alex: Exactly. That’s it for today. Next time you’re deciding where a question belongs or how to share a useful snippet, you’ll know which GitHub feature fits the job.

Day 1: Pull Requests and Merge Day

16. Episode 6: Working with Pull Requests

Creating, reviewing, commenting on, and merging pull requests.

Based on: Chapter 6: Working with Pull Requests

Download Episode 6 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 6: Working with Pull Requests

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. This time we’re getting into pull requests, which is where individual edits turn into shared contributions.

Jamie: So this is the moment where work stops being just "my change" and starts becoming something the project can actually review and merge.

Alex: Exactly. And for blind and low-vision contributors, pull requests are also where navigation strategy matters a lot: headings, landmarks, tab choices, diff reading, comment forms, and status checks.

Jamie: And this lesson is specifically about doing that accessibly, with a screen reader, keyboard-first, and with some CLI support too.

Alex: Right. There are also a couple of companion references worth keeping nearby: the Markdown appendix and the screen reader cheat sheet. And if you want the official sources of truth, GitHub Docs and GitHub’s accessibility guidance on pull requests are the references to trust when product details change.

Alex: Before we go deeper, one important framing note: this chapter pairs well with the later material on code review, because pull requests and review overlap heavily.

Jamie: And there’s also a practical environment note here, right?

Alex: Yes. GitHub’s newer Files Changed experience is important because it improves ARIA landmarks and navigation in diffs. For many people it’s already enabled automatically. If GitHub still shows it as a feature preview in your user menu, make sure it’s enabled. If it’s not listed at all, that usually means it has already become part of the standard interface.

Jamie: So if someone is wondering why the page layout sounds different from an older tutorial, that may be why.

Alex: Exactly. And one more screen-reader-specific note for NVDA users: Browse Mode is usually best for reading PR conversations, headings, and diffs. Switch to Focus Mode only when you need to type in an edit box, search field, or comment area. Then switch back so navigation commands work normally again.

Jamie: That small mode change is one of those things that can make the difference between feeling lost and feeling in control.

Alex: Very much so.

Alex: Let’s ground this in the workshop flow. This chapter is the first one where your work is validated through a pull request. The pattern is simple: make one small branch change, open a linked pull request, then get the checks to green.

Jamie: So the evidence of success is not just "I edited a file." It’s PR metadata, issue linkage, checks, and ideally a merge.

Alex: That’s right. Three short challenges build that muscle.

Jamie: Can we state them plainly?

Alex: Sure. First, create one small change on a new branch. Second, open a pull request linked to the issue with a line like Closes number. Third, respond to feedback until required checks pass.

Jamie: And if someone wants terminal habits from the start?

Alex: There are five solid principles. Check your current branch before pushing. Keep the pull request scope small. Put the issue linkage in plain text, like Closes number. Check the PR status after each push with GitHub CLI. And prefer documented command options over guessing syntax.

Jamie: Also, branch discipline matters here.

Alex: Yes. Beginners are encouraged to use the web editor, where GitHub can create the branch automatically when you propose changes. A branch name like fix slash yourname dash issue number is the recommended pattern. If you’re working locally, create that feature branch from main. And importantly, don’t reuse a long-lived learning branch for this short exercise unless an instructor specifically wants that. The point is to experience a clean pull request loop on a short-lived branch.

Jamie: Let’s walk through that first challenge.

Alex: The goal is one small branch change in the Learning Room repository, usually using the web editor on GitHub.com. You begin from your assigned challenge issue, which tells you exactly which practice file to edit and what problem to fix.

Jamie: And those practice files are intentionally a little broken.

Alex: Right. One file may have TODO sections that need real content. Another may contain incorrect screen reader shortcut references. Another may have broken links or incomplete setup steps.

Jamie: So the teaching goal is not just editing. It’s editing with a tightly defined scope.

Alex: Exactly. Navigate to the file either through the file tree or with the Go to file shortcut. Open the file, find the Edit this file button, and activate it. Screen reader users can use button navigation or the rotor, depending on their setup.

Jamie: Then the file opens in the browser editor.

Alex: Yes. Make the exact fix the issue asks for and no more. Replace a TODO with the requested content. Correct a broken URL. Fix an incorrect shortcut value in a table. Keep it focused.

Jamie: And then comes the point where GitHub helps create the branch.

Alex: Right. Activate Commit changes. In the dialog, enter a branch name like fix slash yourname dash issue number. Then choose the option to create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request, and activate Propose changes.

Jamie: So success at this stage is seeing the open pull request page, meaning the change was saved and the branch exists.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now challenge two: opening the linked PR.

Alex: This is where contribution hygiene starts to matter. On the Open a pull request page, write a short, specific title that reflects the actual change. Something like completing a section in a file, fixing a broken accessibility link, or correcting an NVDA key reference.

Jamie: So not "update stuff."

Alex: Definitely not that. Then in the description, use the project template if one appears. Include a clear summary of what changed and why. In this workshop, the description needs enough detail to pass validation, and that includes the issue-closing line: Closes number.

Jamie: That issue link is doing real work.

Alex: Yes. When the PR is merged, GitHub can automatically close the linked issue. Also verify that the base branch is main and the compare branch is your feature branch. Then create the pull request.

Jamie: And after that, the PR should appear in the list and checks will start shortly.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Then challenge three is where the workflow becomes more real: pass required checks.

Alex: Yes. On the Conversation tab of the PR, wait a short time and then read the bot feedback carefully. It may validate issue linkage, minimum PR description detail, expected file location, and accessibility-related concerns like heading hierarchy, descriptive link text, and alt text quality.

Jamie: So this is not just syntax checking. It’s also contribution quality checking.

Alex: That’s right. If the bot reports a problem, edit the PR branch and push or commit the fix. Then return and check again. The expected result is that all required checks pass and the PR is ready for review or merge.

Jamie: I like that this teaches a healthy loop: read feedback, respond calmly, verify again.

Alex: That’s the real habit.

Jamie: There are also some support notes in this chapter that matter pedagogically, not just technically.

Alex: Yes. Expected outcomes include successfully making a branch-based change, opening a linked PR, and achieving green checks. If you get stuck, the guidance is to reduce scope, reread the assigned issue, verify your branch and base branch, and use the documented commands or page controls rather than improvising. The learning moment is that a pull request is not a test of perfection. It is a structured conversation around a change.

Jamie: And that’s part of why this can feel achievable.

Alex: Exactly. The change is small, the branch is short-lived, the checks tell you what to fix, and the issue linkage tells everyone what problem you’re solving.

Jamie: There’s also a note about learning cards in this chapter.

Alex: Yes. Think of them as compact reminders: where to navigate, what to look for, and what success sounds like in the interface.

Jamie: What if someone is not using the web editor and wants the local Git route from start to finish?

Alex: Then the full branch, edit, and PR workflow applies. Start from main, create a feature branch, make your change locally, commit it with a meaningful message, push the branch, and open the PR through GitHub CLI or the website. The conceptual sequence is the same. What changes is where the editing and committing happen.

Jamie: So the local path is not a different theory. It’s the same collaboration model with different tools.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s answer the basic question directly: what is a pull request?

Alex: A pull request is a proposal to merge a set of changes from one branch into another, usually into main. It bundles the code or content changes together with a description, conversation, review activity, status checks, and merge controls.

Jamie: So it’s part diff, part discussion, part gatekeeping mechanism.

Alex: Well put. It gives reviewers context, gives automation a place to run, and gives maintainers a decision point.

Jamie: How do you get to pull requests efficiently?

Alex: There are several paths. If GitHub sends you a PR notification, you can open it directly from there. More generally, you can go to the repository’s Pull requests tab to see open PRs.

Jamie: And for CLI users?

Alex: GitHub CLI gives you a practical toolkit. You can list open pull requests, filter by review status, inspect a specific PR in the terminal, and open a PR in your browser when the web interface is easier for a task.

Jamie: That mix matters for accessibility. Sometimes the terminal is the fastest way to orient yourself, and the browser is better for the detailed reading.

Alex: Exactly. The lesson is not to force one tool for everything. It’s to use the most accessible route for the task.

Jamie: Once you’re on the PR list page, what should a learner expect?

Alex: A list of pull requests, usually with each title as a link, plus metadata like status, author, branch, labels, and sometimes review indicators. The page is useful for triage: which PRs are open, which need your review, which are drafts, and which have active checks.

Jamie: So it’s less about reading every detail there and more about selecting the right PR to open.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And once a specific pull request opens, what is the anatomy of the page?

Alex: Think of it as a page with several major zones. There is the title and metadata near the top, including author, branch relationship, and state. There are sidebar details like reviewers, labels, assignees, projects, and development links. And there is a tab bar that switches among Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files changed.

Jamie: So learning the tab bar is essential.

Alex: Yes. Each tab answers a different question. Conversation tells you what the change is and what people are saying about it. Commits tells you how the work was built over time. Checks tells you what automation reported. Files changed tells you exactly what changed line by line.

Jamie: Let’s spend time on the Conversation tab first.

Alex: Good choice. The PR description is often the first substantial content you should read. It should explain the purpose of the change, summarize what was changed, identify related issues, describe testing, and sometimes include screenshots or recordings if visual behavior changed.

Jamie: So a good description is not decoration. It reduces reviewer effort.

Alex: Exactly. Also on the Conversation tab, pay attention to the status checks section, where GitHub summarizes whether automated checks are pending, passing, or failing.

Jamie: And review comments appear in this tab too.

Alex: Yes. You may see line-specific comments, overall review comments, and bot comments. If a conversation has been addressed, there may be a control to resolve it. Resolving conversations usually means the issue raised in that thread has been handled, and the thread can be marked as completed for organizational clarity.

Jamie: That’s helpful because unresolved conversations can act like a to-do list.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about the Commits tab?

Alex: The Commits tab shows the individual commits included in the pull request. This can help you understand whether the change was made in one clean step or many. It also helps if a reviewer says, "The fix came in the second commit," or if you need to see how the branch evolved.

Jamie: And the Checks tab?

Alex: The Checks tab is where automation details live. The summary might already be visible on Conversation, but Checks often gives more complete logs or job-level breakdowns. This is where you learn whether tests passed, formatting checks succeeded, accessibility validation ran, or deployment previews built correctly.

Jamie: So if something says failed, don’t panic. Open the check and inspect the details.

Alex: Exactly. The important literacy here is reading status, opening failures, and distinguishing between required and optional checks.

Jamie: Now the big one for many learners: Files changed.

Alex: Yes. The Files changed tab is the heart of review. In the improved experience, you typically have a file tree in the left panel and the selected file’s diff on the right. That structure is much friendlier for screen reader navigation than older layouts.

Jamie: What’s the left panel for, functionally?

Alex: The file tree lets you jump between changed files quickly. If the PR is small, that may be only one file. In larger PRs, it’s how you keep orientation and avoid scrolling through one long page of diffs.

Jamie: And the diff itself has its own reading conventions.

Alex: Exactly. Diff lines are typically read as added, removed, or unchanged context. In many interfaces, added lines correspond to plus lines and removed lines to minus lines. Context lines help you understand the surrounding code or text. A screen reader user should listen for those structural cues and not just the text content.

Jamie: That helps answer the classic beginner question: why is the same area shown with mixed line types?

Alex: Because a diff is comparative, not just descriptive. It tells you what changed against what existed before.

Jamie: What are the practical navigation techniques here with a screen reader?

Alex: Use landmarks and headings to move efficiently. Move into the pull request tabs landmark, open Files changed, then use heading navigation to jump between changed files. Within a file diff, use arrow keys or reading commands to inspect line by line. Stay in Browse Mode for reading. Only enter Focus Mode when you activate a field for commenting.

Jamie: And placing an inline comment?

Alex: Move to the diff line you want to comment on, find the comment control for that line, activate it, and then type your note. Multi-line comments are also possible. The exact keystrokes for selecting multiple lines differ by platform, so Windows and macOS users should learn the patterns their screen reader and browser expose, but the concept is the same: select a range, then open a shared comment form.

Jamie: And comments that already exist in the diff can be read right there in context.

Alex: Yes, which is one reason reviewing in Files changed can be more efficient than reading every thread only in Conversation.

Jamie: Now let’s flip to the author side again. How do you open a pull request in practice?

Alex: There are two common routes in this chapter. One is from the web editor: you edit a file on GitHub, choose to create a new branch, and GitHub takes you directly to the pull request form. The other is from an existing fork or feature branch, where GitHub presents a compare-and-pull-request flow after it detects recently pushed changes.

Jamie: Then you need to fill out the form well.

Alex: Exactly. The title field should be short and specific. The description field should tell reviewers what changed, why it changed, how it was tested, and which issue it resolves. If the repo uses a PR template, follow it.

Jamie: This chapter then breaks description writing into common sections.

Alex: Yes. Summary: what this PR does in plain language. Changes: the main edits made. Related Issues: include the linkage, especially the Closes pattern. Testing: how you verified the change. Screenshots or recordings: include these if visual UI behavior changed and they would help reviewers.

Jamie: Even in a mostly text-focused workflow, that structure signals respect for the reviewer’s time.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s talk draft pull requests, because people often hear about them but don’t know when to use them.

Alex: A draft PR is for work you want visible but not yet fully reviewable. Use a draft when you want early feedback, when checks are still being set up, when the change is incomplete, or when you want collaborators to know the work is in progress without implying it’s ready to merge.

Jamie: So what does draft status change?

Alex: It changes expectations. A draft PR is marked clearly as draft, and reviewers understand that formal review may wait. It cannot be treated the same as a ready PR for merge flow. When it becomes mature enough, you mark it ready for review.

Jamie: And there’s a screen reader path to that control.

Alex: Yes. On the PR page, find the control that marks a draft ready for review. The exact placement can vary, but it’s on the PR page rather than hidden in the diff. Similarly, an already open PR can sometimes be converted back to draft if you realize it needs more work.

Jamie: And CLI users have related abilities too: create a draft, list drafts, inspect whether a PR is draft, and mark it ready.

Alex: Exactly. That’s useful when you want a quick status check without wrestling with page layout.

Jamie: What about requesting reviewers?

Alex: On the PR page, usually in the sidebar, you can request specific reviewers. This is how you route attention intentionally instead of hoping someone notices the PR.

Jamie: And then comes submitting a review.

Alex: Yes. Reviewing usually starts in Files changed. You inspect the diff, add inline comments if needed, and then complete the review with one of three outcomes: approve, request changes, or leave comments without a verdict.

Jamie: That distinction matters.

Alex: It does. Approve means you believe the PR is ready from your perspective. Request changes means there is something that should be fixed before merging. Comment-only review is for observations, questions, or non-blocking feedback.

Jamie: And CLI helps here too.

Alex: Yes. You can view the PR diff in the terminal, approve a PR, approve with a comment, request changes, or leave a comment-only review. That can be especially efficient for experienced keyboard-first users.

Jamie: The chapter also mentions GitHub shortcuts for PR work.

Alex: Right. On the PR list page, shortcuts can help with navigation and selection. On an open pull request, other shortcuts move among page elements or actions. On Files changed specifically, shortcuts can accelerate file and diff navigation. But a key accessibility caveat is that shortcuts may interact with browser and screen reader commands, so learners should adopt them selectively and in ways that don’t conflict with their assistive tech.

Jamie: So shortcuts are optional accelerators, not prerequisites.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Suggested changes are another very GitHub-specific review feature.

Alex: Yes. As a reviewer, you can sometimes insert a suggestion directly in an inline review comment. That lets the author apply the proposed text or code with minimal friction.

Jamie: And as an author, you can apply that suggestion from the PR interface.

Alex: Exactly. Multiple suggestions can also be batched into one commit, which keeps history cleaner.

Jamie: When should someone use a suggestion instead of a plain comment?

Alex: Use a suggestion when you can express the preferred replacement concretely and it’s small enough to be applied directly. Use a comment when the issue is conceptual, ambiguous, or needs discussion rather than a literal replacement.

Jamie: So suggestions are powerful, but they’re not a substitute for explanation.

Alex: Right.

Jamie: Now let’s talk maintainers and merge options.

Alex: There are usually three common merge strategies. A regular merge commit preserves the branch history and adds a merge commit. Squash and merge combines the branch’s commits into one commit on the target branch. Rebase and merge replays the commits onto the target branch without a merge commit.

Jamie: How should a learner think about those?

Alex: Merge commit preserves more of the branch structure. Squash is often preferred for small or messy branches because it creates a clean final history. Rebase and merge keeps a linear history but still preserves individual commits. Projects choose among these based on their workflow standards.

Jamie: And there’s usually an option to delete the branch afterward.

Alex: Yes. Deleting the branch after merging is often a good cleanup step for short-lived feature branches. It reduces clutter and signals that the work is complete.

Jamie: And auto-merge?

Alex: Auto-merge lets a PR merge automatically once required conditions are satisfied, such as passing checks and required reviews. It’s useful when you don’t want to sit watching for the exact moment a PR becomes mergeable.

Jamie: So after a PR is merged, what should happen next?

Alex: Confirm that the linked issue closed if you used the closing pattern correctly. Pull or sync the updated target branch locally if needed. Clean up the feature branch if it still exists. And mentally close the loop: the contribution has moved from proposal to accepted history.

Jamie: That closure matters, especially for beginners.

Alex: It does.

Jamie: Let’s stay with auto-merge for a moment.

Alex: Good idea. To enable auto-merge on your PR, use the PR page controls once the repository and branch protections allow it. With a screen reader, locate the auto-merge option in the merge area of the PR page. After enabling it, GitHub waits for required checks and approvals, then merges when conditions are met.

Jamie: And if you change your mind?

Alex: You can cancel auto-merge before it executes. That’s useful if new information appears, a review concern arises, or you decide the branch needs more work first.

Jamie: The practical scenarios section is helpful because it turns all this into actual decision-making. Scenario one: I want to review an assigned PR.

Alex: Start by locating the PR from your notifications, assignment context, or the PR list. Read the description first to understand intent. Check status checks so you know whether automation already found problems. Open Files changed and review the diff. Add inline comments if needed. Then submit a review: approve, request changes, or comment-only.

Jamie: Scenario two: I want to respond to review feedback on my own PR.

Alex: Read each comment carefully. Distinguish blocking requests from optional suggestions. Make the requested changes on the same branch, push or commit them, and reply in the conversation where useful so reviewers know what changed. Resolve conversations when appropriate and recheck the status checks.

Jamie: Scenario three: my PR has a merge conflict.

Alex: That means your branch and the target branch now disagree in a way GitHub cannot merge automatically. You’ll need to update your branch, often by merging or rebasing the latest main into it locally, resolving the conflict, then pushing the result. The key lesson is not to panic: a conflict is a synchronization problem, not a moral failing.

Jamie: What are some common pull request mistakes to avoid?

Alex: PRs that are too large. Vague titles. Descriptions that do not explain why the change exists. Missing issue linkage. Ignoring failing checks. Mixing unrelated changes into one branch. And waiting too long to ask for review or clarification.

Jamie: So most mistakes are really about clarity and scope.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s spend a little more time on writing PR descriptions that actually get reviewed.

Alex: Yes. Reviewers usually look for purpose, scope, risk, and verification. They want to know what changed, why it changed, whether it closes or relates to an issue, and how the author tested it.

Jamie: And that Closes pattern is especially valuable.

Alex: Right. Writing Closes number in the description links the PR to the issue and closes the issue automatically when the PR merges, assuming the repository context is correct.

Jamie: The chapter also suggests a before-and-after structure.

Alex: Yes. That can be very effective. State what the problem or prior behavior was, then state what the PR changes. It helps reviewers quickly model impact.

Jamie: And there’s essentially a reusable template.

Alex: Exactly: Summary. Changes made. Related issues. Testing. Checklist. If relevant, screenshots or recordings. This kind of structure reduces reviewer guesswork.

Jamie: What are common description mistakes?

Alex: Being too short. Omitting the why. Forgetting issue linkage. Claiming testing without saying what was actually tested. Including a checklist but not updating it. Or writing something so generic that the reviewer still has to inspect the entire diff just to understand intent.

Jamie: And good versus bad examples would show that the better version is specific, linked, and testable.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: There’s also a very practical exercise here: read a real pull request.

Alex: Yes. Open a recent closed PR. Read the description and identify which file changed and what challenge it was solving. Check whether the description includes the issue-closing line. Then read the conversation and notice what the validation bot reported and how the author responded. After that, go to Files changed and inspect the actual diff.

Jamie: So the learner is tracing the full arc: intent, feedback, response, and implementation.

Alex: Exactly. And doing it through headings and landmarks reinforces accessible navigation patterns.

Jamie: That’s also a confidence builder. Once you’ve successfully followed a real PR from top to bottom, the interface feels much less mysterious.

Alex: That’s the point.

Jamie: There’s one more note near the end that feels very current: AI and agent workflows.

Alex: Yes. The chapter makes an important claim: agents shouldn’t replace your understanding of pull requests. They should come after you’ve done manual review enough times to judge their output. A tool like an automated PR review assistant can generate a draft review, change map, risk summary, or suggested comments, but you still bring the context, the project history, and the final judgment.

Jamie: In other words, the agent can document the diff, but it cannot own the decision.

Alex: Exactly. That’s why the recommendation is to review multiple pull requests manually before relying on any review agent.

Jamie: Let’s wrap this up. If a learner remembers only the essentials, what should they hold onto?

Alex: A pull request is the structured place where a branch becomes a contribution. Keep the change small. Use a clear branch name. Write a useful title and description. Link the issue with the closing pattern. Read checks and respond to feedback. Navigate with headings, landmarks, and the right screen reader mode. Review the diff, not just the summary. And understand the merge outcome, including draft state and auto-merge when available.

Jamie: And don’t skip the administrative pieces: the official docs, the accessibility guide, the appendices, the challenge hub, and the next steps into merge conflicts and code review.

Alex: Exactly. Those support materials are part of the learning workflow, not extra decoration.

Jamie: So the real win in this chapter is not merely opening a PR. It’s learning how to move through the whole cycle accessibly and confidently.

Alex: Well said.

17. Challenge 04: Branch Out

Creating a safe working branch and understanding why branches protect main.

Practice focus: Day 1 contribution

Download Challenge 04 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 04: Branch Out

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're connecting three ideas that really belong together: your personal Learning Room repository, the branch you create for your own work, and the pull request workflow that turns a private edit into a real contribution.

Jamie: So this is the moment where GitHub starts feeling less like a website full of tabs and more like an actual working environment.

Alex: Exactly. And for this workshop, that environment is your Learning Room. It is your own private practice repository, created for you by GitHub Classroom. When you accepted the class assignment, GitHub copied a template repository into the workshop organization and made a personal repo for you, usually named something like learning-room-your-username.

Jamie: Private is important there, right?

Alex: Very. You are not editing the template repository itself. You are not changing organization permissions. You are not building your own GitHub organization. Facilitators handle all of that. Your job is to work inside your own copy. You have write access there, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated feedback from the workshop bot.

Jamie: Why go through all that instead of putting everyone into one shared repo from the start?

Alex: Three reasons: safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can experiment and recover without affecting anyone else. Authenticity means you still practice the real workflow: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merges. And pace means nobody is blocked by you, and you are not blocked by anyone else while you learn.

Jamie: So it's protected practice, but still real GitHub.

Alex: That's the idea. Day 2 moves you into more public collaboration spaces, but Day 1 builds the muscle memory in a controlled environment.

Jamie: Can we walk through how someone actually gets into that repo in the first place?

Alex: Yes. First, you open the GitHub Classroom assignment link in a browser where you're already signed into GitHub. Sometimes GitHub Classroom asks for authorization the first time. If so, you activate the authorize button. Then you may get a roster page where you identify yourself. If your name is missing, there's usually a skip link, and you tell a facilitator afterward.

Jamie: Then comes the acceptance step.

Alex: Right. Activate the button to accept the assignment. GitHub Classroom then starts copying the learning-room template into the workshop organization. The page may say something like you're ready to go, but it won't necessarily announce automatically when the repo link appears.

Jamie: That sounds like one of those accessibility details people need to know ahead of time.

Alex: Absolutely. With a screen reader, it helps to refresh every so often and move through links until you find your repository link. Once it appears, open it and verify a few things: the repository name matches your username, it looks like a private workshop copy, and you see the expected folders and files such as docs, .github, and README.

Jamie: And bookmark it.

Alex: Yes. That one step saves a surprising amount of friction.

Jamie: What should be waiting for learners once the repo exists?

Alex: Usually their first challenge issue. In the Issues tab, they should find a challenge created by automation. If it does not appear after a couple of minutes, they can refresh once, then check the Actions tab for the student progression workflow. If that workflow failed or never ran, they should contact a facilitator with the repo link.

Jamie: And there's another bot we're supposed to notice early on too.

Alex: Yes, Gandalf, the PR validation bot. Before you even open a pull request, you can visit the Actions tab and confirm there is a PR validation workflow present. You do not need to run it manually. You're just confirming the automation exists so later feedback won't feel mysterious.

Jamie: So even before any coding or writing, learners are building a map: repo, issues, actions, automation.

Alex: Exactly. And the readiness checkpoint is simple. Before moving on, you should be able to find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md, explain the flow issue to branch to pull request to review to merge, and know that Gandalf feedback appears in the pull request conversation.

Jamie: The chapter also talks about two learning tracks happening at once.

Alex: It does. One track is optional GitHub Skills modules in your own account. Those are guided by GitHub's learning bot and give you extra self-paced practice. The other track is required: your Learning Room repository. That's the workshop path where you complete the actual Day 1 challenges.

Jamie: So same account, different purposes.

Alex: Yes. The Skills modules are optional skill drills. The Learning Room is the required workshop progression. They reinforce each other, but they are not the same thing.

Jamie: And there are also those learning cards and tool cards sprinkled through the material.

Alex: Right. Think of them as quick reference pieces. Some compare the two tracks. Some explain your practice branch. Some give tool-specific ways to switch branches or open pull requests. Even if we don't read them like flashcards here, their content matters.

Jamie: Let's talk about the actual content inside the repo. What are learners working on?

Alex: The Learning Room has a clear folder structure and several practice files. You'll work in files like docs slash welcome dot md, docs slash keyboard-shortcuts dot md, docs slash setup-guide dot md, and docs slash CHALLENGES dot md.

Jamie: What kinds of tasks show up in those?

Alex: In welcome dot md, there are intentional TODO sections. For example, learners may need to add content to parts like who can contribute, finding something to work on, or what happens after your contribution is merged. In keyboard-shortcuts dot md, there are screen reader shortcut references and intentional errors to fix. In setup-guide dot md, there may be broken links or incomplete steps. CHALLENGES dot md acts like the challenge menu.

Jamie: And there are bonus challenges too.

Alex: Yes. So the repo is not random. It is designed to give you authentic practice edits in accessible documentation contexts.

Jamie: Now we hit the phrase that matters for this challenge set: your practice branch.

Alex: Exactly. A separate branch is where you make changes without affecting main. That isolation is the core concept. A branch lets you experiment, edit, revise, and even make mistakes without directly changing the main line of the repository.

Jamie: So when beginners hear branch, they should not think advanced magic. They should think safe workspace.

Alex: Beautifully put. Safe workspace. In the Learning Room chapter, the practice branch is your own ongoing branch for personal work. The reason for creating it is to separate your in-progress work from main. The way you use it is straightforward: switch to that branch before you start your edits, keep your work there, and later open pull requests from branch to main when a challenge asks you to.

Jamie: And the tool cards would show how to switch to it depending on whether you're on the web, in Git, in VS Code, or elsewhere.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now let's zoom in on the specific challenge: Branch Out.

Alex: This challenge asks you to create your personal branch for Day 1 work. The required naming pattern in the challenge issue is learn slash your GitHub username. So if your username is octocat, the branch would be learn slash octocat.

Jamie: That sounds more specific than the general branch naming examples.

Alex: Good catch. In general Git practice, many branch names are valid. Common patterns include things like fix slash welcome-todo, feature slash add-schedule-link, or docs slash update-readme. Short and descriptive is usually the goal. Type slash description is common, but not required.

Jamie: But for this workshop challenge, the convention matters because automation and facilitators are looking for that exact style.

Alex: Yes. For Challenge 4, the naming convention is not just preference. It helps the workshop systems identify your work. So although the solution reference says any branch name demonstrates the idea of isolation, the challenge itself asks for learn slash username, and that's the branch learners should create.

Jamie: What if they type it wrong?

Alex: Create a new branch with the correct name. The old one usually will not cause trouble. If GitHub says the branch already exists, that probably means you already created it and you just need to switch to it and verify the name.

Jamie: Can we walk through how to create that branch on GitHub dot com first?

Alex: Yes. Go to the repository's Code tab. Find the branch dropdown. By default it often shows main. Screen reader users may hear it announced as a button labeled something like switch branches or tags. Activate it, type learn slash your username, and choose the option to create that branch from main.

Jamie: So the branch exists immediately on GitHub once you do that.

Alex: Correct. And after that, the same branch control can also switch you to it.

Jamie: That seems like the lowest-friction path for many learners.

Alex: It is. And it matches the actual challenge instructions.

Jamie: What about in VS Code with Git?

Alex: You can create a branch in the terminal with git checkout dash b and then the branch name. For example, git checkout dash b learn slash your username. In VS Code, you can also use the Source Control interface by activating the branch name in the lower status bar and selecting create new branch.

Jamie: And that's useful for learners who cloned the repo locally.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How about GitHub Desktop?

Alex: In GitHub Desktop, open the Current Branch dropdown, choose New Branch, enter the branch name, and confirm it is based on main.

Jamie: And the CLI path?

Alex: If the repository isn't cloned yet, you can clone it with GitHub CLI, move into the repo directory, and then use the same Git branch creation command. The important part is that GitHub CLI helps you get the repo locally, but the branch creation itself is still plain Git.

Jamie: So if the learner used any one of those tools successfully, they completed the branch creation idea.

Alex: Yes. The learning objective is not allegiance to a specific interface. It's understanding that branches let you work in isolation without affecting main.

Jamie: But there's a wrinkle coming, because later PR exercises recommend a different branch naming pattern.

Alex: Right, and this is an important distinction. Your personal learn slash username branch is your Day 1 personal practice branch. But in the pull request chapter, when you do a small focused change for a specific issue, you are often encouraged not to reuse that branch. Instead, use a short-lived feature branch like fix slash yourname dash issue number.

Jamie: Why not just keep piling everything onto the learn branch?

Alex: Because smaller, task-specific branches teach cleaner pull requests. One branch, one focused change, one PR. That makes review easier, keeps scope small, and mirrors good collaboration practice.

Jamie: Let's build the pull request concept from the ground up. What is a pull request?

Alex: A pull request is a structured request to merge changes from one branch into another, usually from your feature branch into main. It's where your work becomes a contribution. It holds the description, discussion, status checks, review comments, and merge controls all in one place.

Jamie: So it's not just "please copy my code over." It's a conversation and validation space.

Alex: Exactly. And the chapter is very intentional about accessibility here. It frames pull request work as something you can navigate with keyboard and screen reader, whether you're reading discussion, reviewing diffs, or checking automation.

Jamie: There's also a setup note about GitHub's improved Files Changed experience.

Alex: Yes. The material recommends using the newer Files Changed experience because it has better landmark structure and diff navigation support. Depending on your account, it may already be enabled automatically, may appear in feature preview, or may no longer be listed because it has become standard.

Jamie: And there's a Browse Mode versus Focus Mode reminder for NVDA.

Alex: Correct. Use Browse Mode for reading conversations, headings, and diffs. Switch to Focus Mode when you need to type into fields like comments or search. Then switch back. That simple habit can reduce a lot of frustration.

Jamie: Before the detailed navigation, the chapter lays out the workshop pattern for PR work.

Alex: Yes: small change, linked PR, green checks. The Chapter 6 challenge set is built around that. First, create one small branch change. Second, open a linked pull request. Third, pass required checks.

Jamie: And there's a nice CLI principles list too.

Alex: There is. Check your current branch before pushing. Keep PR scope small. Include issue linkage as plain text using Closes number. Validate check status after each push, for example with GitHub CLI. And prefer documented command options rather than guessing.

Jamie: That's a strong lesson for accessibility too: predictability beats cleverness.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: Walk us through that first small-change challenge.

Alex: You start from your assigned issue in your Learning Room. That issue tells you which practice file to edit and what to fix. You navigate to the file in the repository, open it, and choose Edit this file.

Jamie: And the source gives screen reader-specific hints there.

Alex: Yes. For button navigation, NVDA or JAWS users might use quick navigation to buttons. VoiceOver users might use the rotor to find buttons. The point is that the edit control is reachable without a mouse.

Jamie: Then you make a very small, focused edit.

Alex: Right. Replace a TODO section, correct a shortcut value, fix a broken link, complete an incomplete instruction. Only what the issue asked for. Then when you commit through the web editor, you enter a branch name, usually fix slash yourname dash issue number, select the option to create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request, and propose changes.

Jamie: So GitHub can create the branch as part of the editing flow.

Alex: Exactly, which makes it very beginner-friendly.

Jamie: Then comes opening the pull request itself.

Alex: Yes. On the Open a pull request page, you fill in the title and body. The title should briefly describe the change. The body should explain what changed and why. And critically, it should include the issue-linking line: Closes number.

Jamie: Why is that line such a big deal?

Alex: Because when the PR is merged, GitHub can automatically close the linked issue. It also helps reviewers immediately understand what problem the PR is meant to solve.

Jamie: And you also verify that the base branch is main and the compare branch is your feature branch.

Alex: Exactly. Then create the pull request.

Jamie: The materials also mention PR forms more broadly: title, description, summary, changes, related issues, testing, screenshots or recordings.

Alex: Yes. Even in simple workshop PRs, those categories matter. A reviewer wants to know what changed, why, what issue it relates to, how you checked it, and whether any visual evidence matters. Not every field is equally relevant for every doc change, but the mindset is important.

Jamie: And draft pull requests show up here too.

Alex: They do. A draft pull request is useful when you want feedback before the work is fully ready to merge. A draft is visible, but it signals "not ready for final review." Later, you can mark it ready for review. You can also convert an open PR back to draft if needed.

Jamie: So draft changes the social meaning more than the basic container.

Alex: Exactly. It's still a pull request, but with a different readiness signal.

Jamie: Once a PR exists, learners need to know how to find and read it.

Alex: Yes. You can reach pull requests from notifications, from the repository's Pull Requests tab, or with GitHub keyboard shortcuts. In browser workflows, shortcut sequences can help jump to issues or PRs. In terminal workflows, GitHub CLI can list open PRs, filter them, show a specific PR, or open one in the browser.

Jamie: So there are both web and CLI routes for navigation, not just creation.

Alex: Right. And once you're on the PR list page, you're looking at a queue of contributions. From there, you open an individual PR page.

Jamie: Which has its own anatomy.

Alex: Exactly. A pull request page includes a tab bar, typically with Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files Changed. Learning that structure is huge, because it tells you where to go depending on your question.

Jamie: For example, if I want the explanation and discussion, I use Conversation.

Alex: Yes. If you want commit history, go to Commits. If you want CI or bot results, go to Checks. If you want the actual diff, go to Files Changed.

Jamie: Let's slow down on the Conversation tab, because that's where a lot of learners first meet review as a lived thing.

Alex: The Conversation tab usually contains the PR description, the status checks summary, and any comments or reviews. You read the description to understand scope. You read the checks section to see whether validation passed or failed. And you read the review comments to understand questions, concerns, or requested changes.

Jamie: Including conversations that might later be resolved.

Alex: Yes. Resolving a conversation usually means the underlying issue has been addressed and the thread no longer needs to stay open. That can reduce clutter, but it should only be done when the concern has truly been handled.

Jamie: In this workshop, Gandalf's feedback appears in Conversation too.

Alex: Correct. And there are three broad types of feedback in the Learning Room system. Automated bot feedback arrives quickly, often around 30 seconds. Peer reviewer feedback may take longer, perhaps 15 to 60 minutes. And merge-time automation tracks your progress and can unlock the next challenge.

Jamie: What about the Commits tab?

Alex: The Commits tab shows the individual commits included in the pull request. That can help you understand the sequence of work, especially if the PR changed over time in response to feedback.

Jamie: And the Checks tab?

Alex: That's where status checks and workflow results live in more detail. If a check fails, the Checks tab often gives deeper logs or summaries than the short status snippet in Conversation. In the workshop context, this is especially useful when Gandalf or another validation workflow reports a problem.

Jamie: So if the bot says something failed, you don't just panic. You go investigate.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now the Files Changed tab. This is where many screen reader users have historically had a rougher time.

Alex: Yes, and the chapter addresses that directly. The newer interface includes a file tree panel and more navigable diffs. In Files Changed, you can move through changed files, enter a file's diff, and read line-by-line changes.

Jamie: How are those lines typically interpreted?

Alex: A plus line means added content. A minus line means removed content. Context lines show surrounding unchanged text. So when a learner hears a diff, they are not hearing a finished document; they are hearing a record of change.

Jamie: That distinction matters a lot.

Alex: It does. Especially in docs work, where a diff might contain only a few inserted lines in the middle of a paragraph or heading structure.

Jamie: And inline comments can be placed on diff lines too.

Alex: Yes. You can place comments on a specific line, or even create multi-line comments. The chapter notes that the exact interaction details differ between Windows and macOS, but conceptually you select the location in the diff, open the comment control, type the feedback, and submit it as part of a review or as a standalone comment.

Jamie: And existing comments can also appear inside the diff.

Alex: Right. Which is helpful because it keeps feedback anchored to the code or text being discussed.

Jamie: Let's come back to the workshop challenge where checks have to pass. What is the learner looking for from Gandalf?

Alex: After opening the PR, wait a short while and then read the validation comment. Gandalf checks things like whether the PR references an issue using Closes number, whether the description has enough detail, whether the changed files are in the expected place, and accessibility-oriented content checks such as heading hierarchy, descriptive link text, and valid alt text.

Jamie: So the bot is not just being fussy. It is teaching contribution quality.

Alex: Exactly. If feedback is given, you update the branch, push or commit again, and the checks rerun. This repeat cycle is normal. It is not a sign of failure. It is the pull request loop doing its job.

Jamie: The learning room chapter also explains PR sharing. Can you map that out?

Alex: Yes. First, the student opens a pull request. Then automation validates it. Then, if peer review is part of the activity, a facilitator may arrange reviewer access or pairings. The reviewer reads and comments. The author responds and updates. Finally, the PR is merged and the progression bot may post the next challenge.

Jamie: And visibility is mentioned repeatedly.

Alex: Right. Because in a private per-student repo, visibility is intentionally limited. You generally do not see everyone else's work by default. Peer review access may be granted when needed. That balance protects privacy while still allowing realistic collaboration.

Jamie: So when the FAQ asks can I see other students' PRs, the answer is basically not automatically.

Alex: Correct. And related FAQ answers matter too. If you disagree with a reviewer, respond respectfully and seek facilitator help if needed. If your PR seems buried, it generally is not lost just because many others are working at once. If your reviewer doesn't respond, ask for help. If bot feedback seems wrong, investigate and escalate rather than silently ignoring it. And no, you do not necessarily need to complete every possible challenge to learn something meaningful, though the workshop will have required paths.

Jamie: There's also practical advice on reviewing a peer's PR.

Alex: Yes. Find the PR you're assigned to. Read it carefully. Look at the description before judging the diff. Leave a review with clear, respectful feedback. And if you're the author receiving feedback, respond constructively rather than defensively.

Jamie: That's a professional skill, not just a GitHub skill.

Alex: Absolutely. The tooling is only half the lesson.

Jamie: Can we talk about submitting a review? What options do reviewers actually have?

Alex: A reviewer can start a review by adding comments on files, then complete and submit it. The final review verdict is often one of three things: approve, request changes, or comment without a formal verdict. In command-line workflows, GitHub CLI can also help view diffs and submit review outcomes.

Jamie: And there are GitHub keyboard shortcuts for PR work too.

Alex: Yes, including shortcuts on the PR list page, on an open PR, and inside Files Changed. Learners do not need to memorize every key immediately, but knowing these shortcuts exist can make review much faster and more accessible.

Jamie: What about suggested changes?

Alex: Those are especially useful in review. A reviewer can propose exact replacement text directly in the review. Then the author can apply the suggestion, often with a click, which turns the feedback into a commit. Multiple suggestions can sometimes be batched into one commit. Suggestions are best when you know the specific fix. Plain comments are better when you want to explain a concern without prescribing exact wording.

Jamie: And then eventually someone merges.

Alex: Yes. Maintainers may see different merge options. A standard merge commit preserves branch history. Squash and merge combines the branch's commits into one. Rebase and merge applies the changes without a merge commit. There may also be options to delete the branch after merging and to enable auto-merge so the PR merges automatically once required checks pass.

Jamie: That's good to know even if learners are not repository maintainers everywhere.

Alex: Exactly. Understanding the options helps you interpret what happened to your contribution after approval.

Jamie: And after a PR is merged?

Alex: The linked issue may close automatically. The branch may be deleted. In the Learning Room, merge-time automation may also record progress and unlock the next challenge.

Jamie: Auto-merge sounds worth a quick explanation too.

Alex: Auto-merge is useful when approval is done but checks are still running. You enable it on the PR, choose the merge method if allowed, and GitHub completes the merge automatically when the requirements are satisfied. You can also cancel auto-merge if circumstances change.

Jamie: So it's a convenience feature, not a different review philosophy.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: The chapter also offers practical scenarios. Can we make those concrete?

Alex: Scenario one: you want to review an assigned PR. You find the PR, read the description, inspect the diff, check the bot results, and then leave review feedback. Scenario two: you want to respond to review feedback on your own PR. You read comments carefully, update your branch, reply where helpful, and re-check status. Scenario three: your PR has a merge conflict. That means your branch and the base branch have incompatible changes that need to be reconciled before merge.

Jamie: That last one often scares beginners.

Alex: Yes, but it's a workflow problem, not a moral failing.

Jamie: What mistakes should learners try to avoid when opening PRs?

Alex: Common mistakes include making the PR too large, forgetting to link the issue, leaving the description vague, ignoring failing checks, and mixing unrelated changes into one branch. Reviewers look for clarity, scope control, and enough context to trust what they're reading.

Jamie: So a good PR description really matters.

Alex: It does. The chapter emphasizes writing descriptions that get reviewed. That means a useful summary, a clear list of changes made, related issues, testing notes, and a checklist when appropriate. The Closes number pattern is especially important. Before-and-after framing can also help reviewers understand the impact.

Jamie: And there's even a template idea.

Alex: Yes. Essentially: what changed, why it changed, which issue it closes, how it was tested, and anything else the reviewer should notice. The source even contrasts good and bad descriptions, because "fixed stuff" is not enough.

Jamie: I also noticed the chapter includes a try-it exercise where you read a real pull request.

Alex: That's a great learning move. Open a PR, read the description, inspect the conversation, and then visit Files Changed to connect the written explanation to the actual diff. For a blind or low-vision learner, this is how the interface stops being abstract. You learn where things are by traversing them in order.

Jamie: And there's a broader message there too: manual review comes before any AI-assisted review.

Alex: Yes. The material is very clear that assistive or agentic review tools can help summarize diffs or draft comments, but they do not replace your judgment. You need to know how to read a pull request yourself before delegating any part of the review process.

Jamie: Before we wrap, I want to return to the specific evidence the Branch Out challenge asks for.

Alex: Good idea. The challenge asks learners to confirm their branch name and describe how they created it. So a complete response might say, "My branch name is learn slash myusername. I created it from the branch dropdown on the Code tab," or describe doing it in VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the command line.

Jamie: And there's also a peer simulation note.

Alex: Yes. Learners are encouraged to open the peer-simulation PR and notice its branch name. And if they have a real buddy nearby, they can check whether that person created their branch and help them find the branch dropdown if they are stuck.

Jamie: Which reinforces that branch names are visible collaboration signals, not just private labels.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let's end with the big picture. What matters most here?

Alex: Your Learning Room is your private practice space. Branches give you safe isolation. Pull requests turn branch work into reviewed, validated, mergeable contributions. The workshop uses bots, issue linkage, and accessibility-aware feedback not to slow you down, but to teach you the habits of real open source work.

Jamie: And in the short term, for this challenge, the win is simple: create your personal branch, usually named learn slash your username, and understand why it exists.

Alex: Yes. Then when later exercises ask for a smaller task-specific branch and a pull request, you'll know that the branch is not just a hoop to jump through. It is the container that makes review, automation, and collaboration possible.

Jamie: So the flow becomes intuitive: issue, branch, pull request, review, merge.

Alex: Exactly. And once that sequence feels familiar, contributing becomes much less intimidating.

Alex: One final note: when you need the current source of truth, use official GitHub documentation, the GitHub changelog, and GitHub's accessibility guidance for pull requests and CLI workflows. Workshop material teaches the workflow, but official docs remain authoritative as interfaces evolve.

Jamie: That's a good habit for any tech learner.

Alex: It is. And with that, you're ready to branch out, open pull requests with purpose, and start contributing with confidence.

18. Challenge 05: Make Your Mark

Editing a file, writing a useful commit message, and connecting a change to an issue.

Practice focus: Day 1 contribution

Download Challenge 05 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 05: Make Your Mark

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're connecting three ideas that really belong together: your private Learning Room repository, the small edit-and-commit task called Make Your Mark, and the bigger pull request workflow that turns a change into a contribution.

Jamie: So this is not just, edit a file and move on. It's really, learn the whole path from assignment to branch to commit to pull request to review.

Alex: Exactly. And for blind and low-vision learners, we also want the interface and navigation model to feel predictable. Where am I? What tab am I on? What does the bot do? What can other students see? Those questions matter just as much as the Git concepts.

Alex: Let's start with the Learning Room itself. It is your own private GitHub repository for the workshop. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, GitHub makes a copy of the learning-room template repository and creates a repo named something like learning-room-your-username inside the workshop organization.

Jamie: And that means I'm not editing the shared template. I'm editing my copy.

Alex: Right. Not the template, not someone else's repo, and not a repo you had to set up yourself. Facilitators handle the organization, permissions, Classroom setup, and automation. Your job is to use your private workshop repo.

Jamie: Why give every student a separate repository instead of putting everyone into one shared practice repo?

Alex: Three big reasons. Safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can experiment and recover without damaging anyone else's work. Authenticity means you practice the real workflow: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merging. Pace means you can progress through the Day 1 challenges at your own speed.

Jamie: So the Learning Room is like a training ground before contributing in a more public shared space.

Alex: That's a great way to say it. The workshop wants you to build muscle memory in a low-risk environment first.

Jamie: Walk me through getting into that repo from the beginning.

Alex: First, you open the Classroom assignment link in the same browser where you're already signed into GitHub. The page is on classroom dot github dot com. Your screen reader should announce a heading with the assignment name. If GitHub Classroom asks for authorization, activate the authorize button. That's typically a one-time step.

Jamie: And sometimes there's a roster screen, right?

Alex: Yes. If asked to identify yourself, choose your name from the roster. You can arrow through the list or use find in page to search your name. If your name is missing, use the skip link and tell the facilitator so they can reconcile it later.

Jamie: Then comes the actual acceptance step.

Alex: Yes. Activate Accept this assignment. GitHub Classroom then copies the template repo into the workshop organization and gives you access to your private copy. This usually takes ten to thirty seconds.

Jamie: That waiting screen can be awkward with a screen reader because nothing loudly announces, hey, your repo is ready now.

Alex: Exactly. That's an important accessibility note. The page may not auto-announce readiness. In browse mode, stepping through links can help, or just refresh every fifteen seconds until the repository link appears.

Jamie: Once I open the repo, what should I confirm?

Alex: Three things. The repository name matches learning-room-your-username. The description or About area confirms it's your workshop copy. And the repo contains the expected folders and files like docs, dot github, and README. Then bookmark it, because you'll use it constantly.

Jamie: How do I know the challenges are there?

Alex: Go to the Issues tab. A quick keyboard path on GitHub is G then I. You should find Challenge 1 as an open issue, usually created by a bot account. Open it and read the body carefully because the issue tells you the task, what evidence to provide, and how completion is tracked.

Jamie: And if Challenge 1 never appears?

Alex: Refresh once. If it's still missing after a couple of minutes, check the Actions tab for the student progression workflow. If that failed or didn't run, message the facilitator with your repo link.

Jamie: And Gandalf enters the story here too.

Alex: Yes. Gandalf is the PR validation bot. Before you even open a pull request, you can confirm the workflow exists by checking the Actions tab for a workflow like pr-validation-bot or Gandalf PR Validation. You don't need to run anything yet. You're just confirming the automation is wired up.

Alex: At this point, there's a readiness checkpoint. Before moving into the issue-and-PR work, you should be able to find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md, explain the flow issue to branch to pull request to review to merge, and identify that Gandalf's feedback appears on the pull request Conversation tab.

Jamie: That flow is really the spine of the workshop.

Alex: It is. And the workshop actually runs on two reinforcing tracks.

Jamie: One is the optional GitHub Skills modules, and the other is the required Learning Room track.

Alex: Exactly. The optional self-paced track uses GitHub Skills modules on your own account, guided by Mona. Those help you practice individual skills like creating a branch, writing Markdown, or reviewing pull requests. The required track is your Learning Room repository. That's where the workshop sequence lives. Private repo, workshop-specific challenges, workshop bots, and evidence tied to your progress.

Jamie: So same GitHub account, but very different context.

Alex: Yes. One is optional skill practice. The other is the structured workshop path. They reinforce each other, but they are not interchangeable.

Jamie: What kinds of files are inside the Learning Room?

Alex: A few especially important practice files. There's docs slash welcome dot md, which introduces open source contribution and contains TODO areas to fill in. There's docs slash keyboard-shortcuts dot md, a screen reader shortcut reference with intentional errors to fix. There's docs slash setup-guide dot md, which contains getting-started instructions with broken links or incomplete steps. And docs slash CHALLENGES dot md acts like the menu of challenge work.

Jamie: And there are bonus challenges too.

Alex: Yes, for learners who want extra stretch practice.

Jamie: I want to pause on welcome dot md, because that file matters for today's challenge.

Alex: It does. The workshop describes three TODO areas in that file: one about who can contribute, one about finding something to work on, and one about what happens after your contribution is merged. So by the time you get to Make Your Mark, you're replacing a placeholder with real content in a meaningful way.

Jamie: Before we get to that challenge, we should talk about branches in the Learning Room, because there are two different branch patterns in these materials.

Alex: Good catch. Earlier Learning Room practice often uses a long-lived branch named learn slash your-username. That branch gives you a safe personal workspace separate from main.

Jamie: Why create a separate branch at all?

Alex: Because it protects main, lets you experiment, and gives you a clean place to collect your practice work. It also mirrors real collaboration, where you usually make changes on a branch and then open a pull request back to main.

Jamie: So how do you use that practice branch?

Alex: Switch to it before editing, confirm you're really on it, and keep your practice edits there rather than committing directly to main.

Jamie: But then in the pull request chapter, there's a warning not to reuse learn slash your-username for a short Chapter 6 exercise.

Alex: Right. For the dedicated pull request workflow lesson, the recommendation is a short-lived feature branch such as fix slash yourname-issueXX. That keeps one focused change per branch and makes the PR cleaner.

Jamie: So learners should notice the context. If the challenge says work on learn slash your-username, do that. If the PR chapter says create a fresh fix branch, do that instead.

Alex: Perfectly said.

Alex: Now let's talk about how pull request sharing works in the Learning Room. This is conceptually important because students often wonder, is this really private? Who sees what?

Jamie: Yes. Especially if you're new, private and peer review can sound contradictory.

Alex: Here's the sequence. First, the student opens a pull request. Second, automation validates it. A workflow file runs checks. Third, peer review may be arranged by the facilitator. Fourth, the reviewer reads and comments. Fifth, the author responds and updates the PR. Sixth, the PR is merged, and the progression bot posts the next challenge.

Jamie: And visibility changes depending on the setup.

Alex: Exactly. By default, your Learning Room is private. Other students do not automatically see your work, and you do not automatically see theirs. If a peer reviewer is intentionally paired with you, they may be given access needed for that review.

Jamie: So when the materials say peer simulation, that can mean bot-created practice inside my repo, not necessarily public student-to-student visibility.

Alex: Correct. The workshop creates realistic collaboration without requiring everyone's work to be broadly visible.

Jamie: And after merge, the next challenge can be posted automatically.

Alex: Right. That's part of the learning automation system.

Alex: That system has three kinds of feedback. Type one is automated bot feedback, usually around thirty seconds after opening a PR. Type two is peer reviewer feedback, often on the scale of fifteen to sixty minutes if a real reviewer is involved. Type three is progress tracking on merge, where the system advances your challenge sequence.

Jamie: That timing matters because it prevents a lot of panic. If checks don't appear instantly, that may be normal.

Alex: Exactly. Wait a bit, then refresh the Conversation or Checks area.

Jamie: What about study groups?

Alex: Optional. You can absolutely discuss concepts, compare approaches, and learn alongside a friend or group. But your own repository, evidence, and submissions remain yours unless the facilitator has intentionally set up shared review access.
