Jamie: What are the key differences between the GitHub Skills modules and the Learning Room, in plain language?

Alex: Skills modules are optional, self-paced, and live in your personal account with GitHub's own teaching bot. The Learning Room is required for the workshop, lives in the workshop organization, uses workshop automation, and is tailored to this curriculum.

Jamie: And if I'm reviewing a peer's PR in the workshop, what are the basic tips?

Alex: Find PRs through the Pull Requests tab, your notifications, or an assigned link. Read the PR you're assigned carefully. Look at the description, linked issue, checks, and changed files. Leave feedback that is specific and respectful. If you receive feedback, respond constructively and update your branch.

Jamie: Can you answer some of the common worries learners have?

Alex: Sure. Can I see other students' PRs? Usually no, not unless access is intentionally provided. What if I disagree with my reviewer? Ask clarifying questions, explain your reasoning, and involve a facilitator if needed. Will my PR get lost when everyone is working at once? No, GitHub tracks PRs individually. Can I comment on someone else's PR? Only if you have access. What if my reviewer doesn't respond? Check with the facilitator. Can I work with a friend? Yes for discussion, but follow the workshop's submission rules. How long does review take? Bot feedback is fast; human review varies. What if bot feedback is wrong? Treat the bot as guidance, then ask a facilitator. Do I need every challenge? Follow the workshop expectations, but the system is designed as a progression path.

Jamie: That's reassuring. And if I'm stuck more generally?

Alex: Use the issue instructions, check the Actions and PR tabs, compare against examples, and ask the facilitator. Being stuck is part of learning, not proof you're failing.

Alex: And one more emotional truth: if you've accepted the repo, made a branch, edited a file, opened a pull request, and responded to feedback, you are already contributing.

Jamie: Okay. Let's zoom into the pull request workflow itself.

Alex: A pull request is a request to merge changes from one branch into another, usually from your feature branch into main. It's not just a technical operation. It's the collaboration space where description, review, checks, comments, and merge decisions all come together.

Jamie: And this chapter is especially aimed at doing that with a screen reader.

Alex: Yes. The materials explicitly point learners to GitHub's official accessibility guide for pull requests and note the improved Files Changed experience with better landmarks and diff navigation. They also recommend staying in browse mode for reading and switching to focus mode only when you need to type in fields.

Jamie: That's a huge usability tip. If you stay in focus mode too long, the page can feel chaotic.

Alex: Exactly. Browse mode for headings, landmarks, comments, and diffs. Focus mode for text entry.

Alex: There's also a workshop recommendation for this pull request chapter: three challenges, each under ten minutes, with a simple pattern. Make one small change, open a linked PR, and pass required checks.

Jamie: And there are CLI principles too, even if a learner is mostly on GitHub dot com.

Alex: Right. Check your current branch before pushing. Keep the PR scope small. Link the issue in plain text with Closes number. Validate checks after each push, for example with GitHub CLI. And rely on documented command options.

Jamie: Now the branch naming guidance here is really specific.

Alex: Yes. For this chapter, the beginner-friendly web path is: edit on GitHub, then when proposing changes, let GitHub create a branch for you and name it something like fix slash yourname-issueXX. If you're working locally, create that branch from main yourself. And again, the chapter warns not to reuse the long-lived learn slash username branch for this short PR exercise unless a facilitator tells you to.

Jamie: Let's walk through the challenge flow. First, create one small branch change.

Alex: In your Learning Room repo, open the practice file specified in your assigned issue. That might be welcome dot md, keyboard-shortcuts dot md, or setup-guide dot md. Use the file tree or the Go to file shortcut. Open the file, activate Edit this file, and make one small focused change.

Jamie: And there are screen reader-specific navigation hints for that edit button.

Alex: Yes. For button navigation, Windows screen reader users can move by buttons to find Edit this file. VoiceOver users can use the rotor to locate buttons. The key point is that the control is typically labeled Edit this file, even if sighted users describe it as the pencil icon.

Jamie: Then after editing, you choose Commit changes.

Alex: Right. In the commit dialog, give the branch a focused name, select the option to create a new branch and start a pull request, and propose changes. That saves your edit on a new branch and takes you to the Open a pull request page.

Jamie: Then comes opening the linked PR.

Alex: Yes. Write a clear title that describes the change. For example, complete the Who Can Contribute section in welcome dot md, or fix a broken link in setup-guide dot md. In the body, summarize what changed and why, and include the issue-closing line, Closes number. Also verify base is main and compare is your feature branch before creating the PR.

Jamie: That issue linkage is not decorative. It's functional.

Alex: Exactly. When merged, GitHub can automatically close the linked issue. The curriculum emphasizes the Closes number pattern because it builds real project habits.

Jamie: And then we wait for checks.

Alex: Usually about thirty seconds. The bot reviews whether you linked an issue correctly, whether the PR description has enough detail, whether your changed files are in the expected location, and whether accessibility-related content checks pass.

Jamie: So if the bot comments that something is missing, I update the same branch, not start over.

Alex: Correct. Edit, commit, push if needed, and the PR updates automatically because the PR tracks the branch.

Jamie: Before we go deeper, how do learners even navigate to pull requests efficiently?

Alex: Several ways. From a PR notification. From the Pull Requests tab. From terminal commands if using GitHub CLI to list open PRs, filter by review status, view a specific PR, or open it in the browser. The broader lesson is that a PR is an object you can reach through multiple paths, and it helps to have both a web and CLI mental model.

Jamie: Once I'm on the PR list page, what should I expect?

Alex: A list of open or closed PRs with titles, authors, statuses, and filters. It's the staging area where you decide which PR to open.

Jamie: And once the PR is open, the page itself has anatomy.

Alex: Yes. There's a title, metadata about branches and status, a tab bar, and key tabs like Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files changed. Learning the tab bar is crucial because each tab answers a different question.

Jamie: Conversation is, what is this change and what are people saying about it?

Alex: Exactly. Commits is, how was it built over time? Checks is, what automation ran and what passed or failed? Files changed is, what actually changed line by line?

Alex: On the Conversation tab, there are four especially important things to read. First, the PR description. Second, the status checks section. Third, review comments. Fourth, any resolved or unresolved conversations.

Jamie: And resolving a conversation means, we believe this comment thread is handled.

Alex: Right. It doesn't erase history. It marks the discussion as addressed.

Jamie: What about the Commits tab?

Alex: That shows the commits included in the PR. It helps you understand whether the PR is one tidy change or a series of revisions.

Jamie: And the Checks tab?

Alex: That's where you read automation results in more detail. It can include pass or fail status, logs, and links to workflow runs. For learners, this is often where confusion turns into clarity, because instead of just seeing a red X, you can inspect what failed.

Jamie: Now the Files Changed tab is where many screen reader users have historically had the hardest time.

Alex: Yes, and the chapter tries to make that manageable. In the improved experience, there's a file tree panel and a diff area with clearer landmarks. The file tree lets you move among changed files. The diff shows removed lines, added lines, and unchanged context.

Jamie: How are lines in a diff usually read?

Alex: Conceptually: removed lines are lines that were deleted, added lines are lines that were inserted, and unchanged lines provide context around the change. Many screen readers will announce symbols or labels that distinguish these states.

Jamie: And if you want to navigate the diff efficiently?

Alex: Use headings and landmarks where available, move file by file, then line by line inside the diff. Stay in browse mode while reading. Enter focus mode only when you need to interact with a comment field.

Jamie: Can a screen reader user place an inline comment on a diff line?

Alex: Yes. The chapter covers placing inline comments and even multi-line comments on Windows and macOS. The exact commands can vary by screen reader, but the workflow is: locate the target line, activate the add-comment control, enter your text, and submit either as part of a review or as a single comment.

Jamie: And comments can also appear inside the diff itself.

Alex: Right, so when reviewing, you need to read both the changed code or text and any comments anchored to it.

Jamie: Let's return to opening a PR. Besides the web editor path, what other routes are covered?

Alex: You can open a PR after editing directly on GitHub, or from a fork or feature branch created elsewhere. Either way, you end up filling out the PR form.

Jamie: What belongs in that form?

Alex: A useful title and a useful description. The materials frame descriptions using a practical structure: summary, changes, related issues, testing, and screenshots or recordings when relevant.

Jamie: Even for non-code changes?

Alex: Yes, though screenshots may be irrelevant for text-only updates. The habit is to explain what changed, why, what issue it relates to, and how you checked it.

Jamie: And there's also the option to create a draft PR.

Alex: Yes. A draft PR says, this work is visible, but not ready for full review yet. The chapter covers when to use drafts, how they behave differently, how to mark them ready for review, how to convert an open PR back to draft, and how to check draft state in the interface or via CLI.

Jamie: So a draft is not failure. It's honest status.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about requesting reviewers?

Alex: That's the step where you explicitly ask one or more people to review your PR. In the workshop, this may be assigned or facilitated. In real projects, you often choose likely reviewers based on the code area or repository norms.

Jamie: And when you are the reviewer, what does submitting a review involve?

Alex: You can start a review, add one or more inline comments, then complete the review with one of three outcomes: approve, request changes, or leave a comment-only review with no verdict.

Jamie: And some of that can be done from the terminal too.

Alex: Yes. The chapter includes CLI actions like viewing a diff, approving a PR, approving with a comment, requesting changes, or leaving a comment-only review.

Jamie: There are also keyboard shortcuts for PR work on GitHub.

Alex: Yes, shortcuts on the PR list page, on an open PR, and on the Files Changed tab. The point is not memorizing every key today. It's knowing that keyboard navigation is a first-class path, not an afterthought.

Jamie: Let's talk suggested changes, because that's one of the most collaborative review tools.

Alex: A suggested change lets a reviewer propose an exact replacement directly in the review flow. As a reviewer, you insert the suggestion in your comment. As an author, you can apply that suggestion. GitHub can also batch multiple suggestions into one commit.

Jamie: When should I use a suggestion instead of a plain comment?

Alex: Use a suggestion when you already know the exact text or code replacement and the change is small enough to be concrete. Use a regular comment when the issue is broader, exploratory, or better solved by the author in their own words.

Jamie: Eventually the PR is ready to merge. What merge options should maintainers understand?

Alex: Three standard strategies. Merge commit preserves the branch history and creates a merge commit. Squash and merge combines the PR's commits into one commit on the target branch. Rebase and merge reapplies commits on top of the target branch without a merge commit. There are also options like deleting the branch after merge and enabling auto-merge so the PR merges automatically once checks pass.

Jamie: For a learner, what's the main idea to hold onto?

Alex: Different repositories choose different merge policies, but the practical result is the same: your approved changes become part of the target branch.

Jamie: And after merge?

Alex: The linked issue may close automatically, the branch may be deleted, progress tracking can update, and you move on to the next task.

Jamie: Tell me more about auto-merge.

Alex: Auto-merge is useful when a PR is approved but still waiting on required checks. You enable it on your PR, GitHub waits for the conditions to be satisfied, and then merges automatically. The chapter also covers the screen reader path to enable it, what happens next, and how to cancel it if needed.

Jamie: So it's a convenience feature, not a substitute for review.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: The practical scenarios in the chapter seem especially helpful.

Alex: They are. Scenario A: you want to review an assigned PR. That means navigate to it, read the description, inspect checks, review the diff, and leave clear feedback. Scenario B: you want to respond to review feedback on your own PR. Read carefully, decide what to change, update your branch, and respond so reviewers know what happened. Scenario C: your PR has a merge conflict. That means your branch can't be cleanly merged with the target branch until the conflicting changes are reconciled.

Jamie: And common PR mistakes?

Alex: PRs that are too large, vague titles, thin descriptions, missing issue links, ignoring failed checks, and mixing unrelated changes in one branch.

Jamie: Which leads nicely to writing PR descriptions that actually get reviewed.

Alex: Yes. Reviewers want to know what changed, why it changed, what issue it relates to, and how it was tested or verified. The chapter highlights the Closes pattern, before-and-after structure, and a reusable PR description template. It also calls out common description mistakes and shows good-versus-bad examples.

Jamie: Now let's bring this back to today's specific challenge: Make Your Mark.

Alex: Challenge 5 asks you to edit docs slash welcome dot md on your branch, fix the TODO you found earlier, and commit with a meaningful message.

Jamie: And in that challenge, the instructions are very concrete.

Alex: They are. Make sure you are on your learn slash your-username branch. Navigate to docs slash welcome dot md. Activate Edit this file. Find the TODO and replace it with real content. Write a meaningful commit message that explains what changed and why. Then commit directly to your branch.

Jamie: The issue even gives examples of weak versus stronger commit messages.

Alex: Yes. Instead of something vague like update welcome dot md, fix stuff, or changes, use a message that says what changed and why. For example, add workshop description to replace TODO in welcome dot md, or replace placeholder text with actual welcome message.

Jamie: And the core test is simple: can someone tell what changed just by reading the message?

Alex: Exactly. The challenge even suggests comparing your commit message with a peer simulation PR title and asking whether the change is understandable from the words alone.

Jamie: What does the reference solution show?

Alex: It shows one possible edit in welcome dot md. Before, there was a comment placeholder asking to add a link to the workshop schedule. After, that placeholder was replaced with real prose linking to the schedule file.

Jamie: So the edit is small, but meaningful.

Alex: Right. It converts a TODO into usable content.

Jamie: And the example commit message is more structured than the minimum requirement.

Alex: Yes. It uses a short summary line that begins with a type label, then a blank line, then a body explaining what changed and why. In plain terms, the pattern is: short summary, blank line, optional explanation.

Jamie: That's a common Git convention, not an absolute law.

Alex: Exactly. The solution explicitly says simpler alternatives are also fine, like fix TODO in welcome dot md or add schedule link to welcome page. Clear and descriptive beats fancy and confusing.

Jamie: So what makes a good commit message?

Alex: First line: short summary, ideally concise. A type label can help but isn't required. A blank line can separate the summary from the body. The body, if you include one, explains what changed and why. The real goal is meaning, not ceremony.

Jamie: And what matters most in this learning challenge?

Alex: Making a meaningful change and describing it clearly in the commit message. Any clear edit with any descriptive message counts as success.

Jamie: What if a learner wants to complete the edit in a different tool?

Alex: That's allowed. The solution lists alternate approaches: edit directly on GitHub dot com with the pencil button, use github dot dev by pressing period to open a browser-based editor, use VS Code locally with git add and git commit, or use GitHub Desktop.

Jamie: So the conceptual workflow matters more than the exact editor.

Alex: Yes. Different tools, same core skill.

Jamie: And if something goes wrong during Challenge 5?

Alex: There are a few common stuck points. If you're editing on main instead of your branch, switch to the correct branch first. If you can't find the edit button, look for the control labeled Edit this file. If you accidentally committed to main, ask the facilitator for help; it's fixable. If you want to check your work, compare it with the reference solution.

Jamie: I also noticed the challenge asks for evidence.

Alex: Good point. Learners are asked to paste the URL of their commit and share the commit message they used, plus a short note about what they changed. That's part of making your work inspectable and discussable.

Jamie: So even a simple commit becomes something you can point to, review, and learn from.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Before we wrap, can we connect the small Challenge 5 task to the larger pull request skill?

Alex: Absolutely. Challenge 5 is where you learn to make a small focused edit and explain it well at the commit level. Chapter 6 expands that same discipline to the pull request level: one focused branch, one understandable change, a clear title, a clear description, an issue link, successful checks, and review-ready communication.

Jamie: So the sentence-level skill in a commit message grows into the paragraph-level skill of a PR description.

Alex: Beautifully put.

Jamie: And all of this supports accessible collaboration, because descriptive commit messages, descriptive PR titles, and well-written issue links help everyone, including screen reader users.

Alex: Yes. Accessibility is not only alt text and headings. It's also clear process language, predictable navigation, and meaningful descriptions that reduce ambiguity.

Alex: Let's end with a practical mental checklist. Am I in the right repository? Am I on the right branch? Did I make one focused change? Does my commit message say what changed and why? If I open a PR, did I describe the change clearly, link the issue, and check the Conversation, Checks, and Files changed tabs? And if feedback appears, did I treat it as part of the workflow rather than as a setback?

Jamie: That's a strong checklist. Small change, clear message, visible evidence, calm review.

Alex: Exactly. That is how you make your mark.

19. Challenge 06: Open Your First Pull Request

Opening a pull request, comparing branches, and using closing keywords.

Practice focus: Day 1 contribution

Download Challenge 06 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 06: Open Your First Pull Request

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're working with pull requests, and for a lot of learners, this is the moment GitHub starts to feel real. A pull request is where a private branch change becomes a proposed contribution.

Jamie: And for some people, it's also where everything suddenly feels more complicated. There's a branch, an issue, a form, checks, comments, tabs, diffs. So can we frame this simply before we go deep?

Alex: Absolutely. Think of the workflow as a short chain. First, you make a focused change on a branch. Then you open a pull request from that branch into `main`. In the pull request description, you connect the change to the reason by linking the issue, usually with text like `Closes #12`. Then GitHub and, sometimes, repository bots run checks. Reviewers read the description, inspect the diff, maybe comment, and eventually someone merges it.

Jamie: So the pull request is not just "here's my code." It's also "here's why this exists."

Alex: Exactly. And that issue linkage matters. This chapter's challenge is specifically about opening your first PR from your branch to `main` and linking it to the issue you filed earlier. That connection is one of GitHub's most powerful workflow features.

Alex: Before the hands-on part, a few accessibility and setup notes matter. This lesson is built for keyboard and screen reader workflows. GitHub's pull request interface is usable, but it's much easier if you understand landmarks, headings, and when to switch between reading and typing modes.

Jamie: Let's make that concrete for NVDA users.

Alex: For NVDA, stay in Browse Mode for reading conversation threads, jumping by heading, moving through landmarks, and reviewing diffs. Switch to Focus Mode with `NVDA+Space` only when you need to type in an edit field, search box, or comment field. Then switch back to Browse Mode when you're done typing. Also, maximizing the browser window often makes landmark layout more consistent.

Jamie: And there was also a note about GitHub's newer Files Changed experience, right?

Alex: Yes. The improved Files Changed interface adds better ARIA structure for the file tree and diff navigation. Depending on the account, it may already be enabled automatically. If someone wants to verify, they can open the GitHub user menu, look for Feature Preview, and check whether the New Files Changed Experience is enabled. If it's missing from the preview list entirely, that usually means it has already become the standard interface.

Jamie: That matters because the diff is where many screen reader users either feel empowered or lost.

Alex: Exactly. Good structure makes the difference.

Alex: This chapter is also the first PR-validated chapter in the workshop flow. The pattern is intentionally small and repeatable: make one small change, open a linked PR, then pass required checks.

Jamie: So not a giant feature. Not ten edits. One focused change.

Alex: Right. The workshop recommendation is three short challenges, each designed to take under about ten minutes. The evidence of completion is not just that you changed a file. It's the PR metadata, the issue linkage, and the check results.

Jamie: What are the three challenge steps?

Alex: First, create one small branch change. Second, open a linked PR. Third, respond to feedback until required checks pass.

Jamie: And there was some command-line guidance here too.

Alex: Yes. If you use the CLI, keep a few principles in mind. Check your current branch before you push with `git branch --show-current`. Keep each PR small and focused. Confirm the issue linkage is present in plain text, like `Closes #number`. After each push, check status with `gh pr checks`. And when you use GitHub CLI, prefer documented command options by consulting help output rather than guessing.

Jamie: Let's talk branch naming, because beginners often get tangled there.

Alex: Good place to pause. In this workshop, beginners are encouraged to use the web editor. When you edit on GitHub and choose to propose changes, GitHub can create the branch for you automatically. A suggested naming pattern is something like `fix/yourname-issue42`.

Jamie: And there's an important warning: don't just keep piling unrelated work onto the long-lived learning branch unless the facilitator explicitly tells you to.

Alex: Exactly. For this chapter, short-lived feature branches are better because they teach the pull request loop cleanly. If you're working locally instead of in the web editor, you'd create that branch yourself from `main`, for example with `git checkout -b fix/yourname-issue42`.

Jamie: So there are two paths: web editor for the gentle on-ramp, local Git for people already comfortable working in a clone.

Alex: That's right.

Alex: Now let's walk the first challenge path in detail. The goal is to edit one practice file and save that change on a new branch.

Jamie: And the learner begins in their Learning Room repository, using GitHub.com.

Alex: Yes. They start by opening their assigned challenge issue for this step. That issue tells them which file to edit and what kind of fix to make.

Jamie: What kinds of files are they likely to see?

Alex: Three typical practice files are used. `docs/welcome.md`, which has missing content marked with TODO placeholders. `docs/keyboard-shortcuts.md`, which contains intentionally incorrect shortcut references. And `docs/setup-guide.md`, which may contain broken links or incomplete instructions.

Jamie: So the learner is not inventing a project from scratch. They're practicing realistic maintenance work.

Alex: Exactly. Very small, concrete repairs.

Jamie: What's the actual editing path?

Alex: Navigate to the specified file, either through the repository file tree or with the Go to file shortcut, `T`. Open the file. Then activate the Edit this file button, usually the pencil icon.

Jamie: And for screen reader users?

Alex: NVDA or JAWS users can move by buttons, often with `B`, until they hear Edit this file, then press Enter. VoiceOver users can use the rotor, go to buttons, find Edit this file, and activate it with `VO+Space`.

Jamie: Then they make exactly the requested change.

Alex: Yes. If the issue points to a TODO section, replace the placeholder with the requested content. If it's a broken link, correct the URL. If it's a shortcut error, fix the incorrect shortcut entry. Keep the scope small. Edit only what the issue asks for.

Alex: After editing comes the branch creation step. In the web editor, activate the Commit changes button. A dialog appears. In the branch name field, enter a short descriptive branch name, such as `fix/yourname-issueXX`.

Jamie: And then choose the option that creates a new branch and starts a pull request.

Alex: Right. Then activate Propose changes. At that point, GitHub saves the change on the new branch and usually opens the page for creating a pull request.

Jamie: So the success condition for that first part is not "I typed some words." It's "GitHub has my change on a branch and has taken me to the PR flow."

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now we're on the open pull request page. What should the learner focus on first?

Alex: Three things: the title, the body, and the branch relationship. The base branch should be `main`. The compare branch should be the feature branch they just created.

Jamie: Let's talk title first. What makes a good PR title?

Alex: A good title clearly describes the change so that someone scanning a list understands what happened without opening the PR. It should be short enough to scan, but specific enough to be meaningful.

Jamie: Can you give examples?

Alex: Sure. "Complete the Who Can Contribute section in welcome.md." Or "Fix broken accessibility settings link in setup-guide.md." Or "Correct NVDA modifier key in keyboard-shortcuts.md."

Jamie: So better than something vague like "update file" or "changes."

Alex: Much better.

Jamie: And the body?

Alex: The body should answer two basic questions: what changed, and why. A simple template works well.

Alex: ## What this changes One sentence describing the change. ## Why One sentence explaining why it matters. Closes #XX

Jamie: That's refreshingly small.

Alex: It is. And it's enough to teach the important habit: every change should be connected to a reason.

Jamie: Can we hear a full example?

Alex: Certainly. Imagine a PR titled: "Fix TODO: add workshop schedule link to welcome.md." Then the body might say: ## What this changes Replaces the TODO placeholder on line 15 of `docs/welcome.md` with an actual link to the workshop schedule. ## Why Students need a working link to find session times. The TODO was a known gap filed in issue number 3. Closes #3

Jamie: That's nice because a reviewer can immediately understand the file, the exact type of fix, and the reason.

Alex: Exactly. It's clear, scannable, and linked.

Jamie: And that `Closes #3` line is doing real work.

Alex: Yes. It creates a two-way link. The issue will show that it is referenced by the PR, and the PR will show that it closes the issue. When the PR is merged, GitHub automatically closes the issue.

Jamie: That automation is one of those small things that makes a repository feel organized instead of chaotic.

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: Are learners limited to the exact word `Closes`?

Alex: No. `Closes #3`, `Fixes #3`, and `Resolves #3` all work the same way for issue-linking in this context.

Jamie: So if someone writes `Fixes #12` instead of `Closes #12`, they're still fine.

Alex: Yes. The main learning objective is the relationship: a PR should reference the issue it resolves.

Jamie: And if they forget the line when creating the PR?

Alex: They can edit the PR description afterward. On the description block, use the edit control or the more options menu, add the line, and save.

Alex: Now, in the challenge workflow, after the learner fills out the title and body, they activate Create pull request.

Jamie: And then the checks begin.

Alex: Usually within about thirty seconds. The Conversation tab is often where the first validation feedback appears.

Jamie: What kinds of things are checked?

Alex: This workshop's validation bot checks for issue linkage, like the presence of `Closes #XX`. It checks whether the description is detailed enough, not just a one-word note. It verifies that the changed files are in the expected learning-room area. And it may check accessibility-related quality, such as heading hierarchy, descriptive link text, and valid alt text.

Jamie: So the PR is not just judged on whether it exists, but also on whether it communicates and follows accessibility expectations.

Alex: Exactly. That's an important part of contribution quality.

Jamie: And if checks fail?

Alex: Read the bot feedback carefully. Make the needed corrections on the same branch. Push or commit the fix, depending on your workflow, and GitHub reruns the checks. If the repository uses automated checks, a green checkmark appears once they pass.

Jamie: So passing checks is not a side quest. It's part of the core PR loop.

Alex: Yes. Open PR, read feedback, revise, recheck.

Jamie: Before we broaden the lesson, can we explicitly name what matters most for Challenge 6?

Alex: Certainly. If your PR has a clear title, a body that explains what changed and why, and a linked issue reference such as `Closes #number`, then you have achieved the essential learning goal. The point is connecting a change to a reason through GitHub's linking system.

Jamie: And there was also an evidence requirement.

Alex: Yes. Learners are asked to paste the URL of their pull request as evidence, and they may also note which issue the PR links to.

Jamie: Plus a peer simulation step.

Alex: Right. Find the Peer Simulation PR about improving contribution guidance and leave an encouraging comment. If you have access to a real buddy's PR, you can comment there too. The full review workflow comes later, but even now, leaving a constructive comment helps learners enter the social rhythm of pull requests.

Jamie: And if someone gets stuck during PR creation, there were a few very practical troubleshooting notes.

Alex: Yes. If you can't find the New pull request button, make sure you are on the Pull requests tab; it's usually near the top right. If GitHub says, "There isn't anything to compare," your branch may not actually contain a commit that differs from `main`, or you may have committed on the wrong branch. If you forgot `Closes #XX`, edit the description after the PR is created. And if you want to compare your work to a model, use the solution reference.

Jamie: That's reassuring. Most early PR problems are not mysterious, just workflow mismatches.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let's widen the lens. What is a pull request, in plain language?

Alex: A pull request is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another branch. It gives collaborators a place to discuss the change, inspect the diff, run checks, request revisions, and eventually merge. It is both a technical object and a conversation space.

Jamie: So it includes metadata, discussion, and code comparison.

Alex: Yes. And that's why learning to navigate it accessibly matters.

Alex: There are several ways to navigate to pull requests. You might arrive from a notification, for example if someone requested your review or commented on your PR. You can also go directly to the Pull requests tab in a repository.

Jamie: And for terminal users?

Alex: The CLI gives you several options. You can list open PRs, filter by review status, inspect a specific PR in the terminal, or open a PR in your browser. The exact subcommands can vary over time, so the safe habit is to consult `gh pr --help` and use documented flags.

Jamie: That matches the earlier principle: prefer documented command options.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: On the web, what does the PR list page offer?

Alex: A list of open, closed, or merged pull requests, each with a title, author, status indicators, and sometimes review or check summaries. Good PR titles matter here because people often decide what to open based on the list alone.

Jamie: Once a learner opens a specific PR, what should they expect on the page?

Alex: The PR page has several major areas. There's header information with the title and branch relationship. There's a tab bar, often including Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files changed. The Conversation tab contains the description, timeline events, bot comments, and review discussion. Other tabs let you inspect commits, CI details, and the diff itself.

Jamie: So if someone feels overwhelmed, a good strategy is to think: first read the description, then the status, then comments, then the actual changed files.

Alex: Exactly. That sequence works well.

Alex: Let's go tab by tab.

Jamie: Start with Conversation.

Alex: In the Conversation tab, read the PR description first. This tells you what the author believes changed and why. Then locate the status checks area, where you may hear whether checks are pending, passing, or failing. After that, review comments and timeline events.

Jamie: And comment resolution matters too.

Alex: Yes. In review conversations, some comments are part of a thread that can be marked resolved once the concern has been addressed. Resolving a conversation signals that the issue was handled, though teams differ on who should resolve it and when.

Jamie: So a learner should read not just the first comment, but the whole thread, because the answer may already be there.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: What about the Commits tab?

Alex: The Commits tab shows the individual commits included in the PR. That can be useful for understanding how the work evolved, especially if there were follow-up fixes after review.

Jamie: And the Checks tab?

Alex: The Checks tab is where you inspect automated validation results in more detail. If a status line says something failed, the Checks tab often contains the actionable information: what job ran, what step failed, and sometimes a log or annotation.

Jamie: So for accessibility learners, the principle is: don't stop at "failed." Open the area that tells you why.

Alex: Exactly. Treat failure output as guidance, not as a verdict on your ability.

Jamie: Now the big one: Files changed.

Alex: Yes, the Files changed tab is where you inspect the diff. GitHub's newer experience provides a left-side file tree and a main diff panel.

Jamie: Let's describe both.

Alex: The file tree lists changed files, helping you jump directly to a file of interest. The diff panel shows additions, deletions, and context lines for the selected file.

Jamie: How are lines in a diff read conceptually?

Alex: A removed line is read as a deletion, often marked with a minus. An added line is read as an addition, often marked with a plus. Context lines are unchanged lines shown around the edit to help you understand location.

Jamie: So a diff is not the whole file. It's a focused representation of what changed, with just enough surroundings to orient you.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What's a good screen reader strategy for this tab?

Alex: Use headings and landmarks aggressively. Jump among changed file headings. Read the file title, then move into the diff content. If your screen reader announces line-level controls, listen for whether a line is added, removed, or unchanged context. Move deliberately. Don't try to ingest the entire diff in one sweep.

Jamie: And inline comments?

Alex: You can place an inline comment on a diff line using the comment controls attached to that line. GitHub also supports multi-line comments, with slightly different keyboard interaction patterns on Windows and macOS. The key idea is that you can comment on a specific span of changed lines, not just leave a general note.

Jamie: And when reviewing an existing PR, comments may appear inside the diff too.

Alex: Yes. Part of reading the Files changed tab is noticing comments embedded near the changed code or text. Those often contain the most specific feedback.

Jamie: Let's return to opening a PR, but now as a broader skill rather than just the workshop challenge.

Alex: Good idea. A PR can begin from the web editor workflow, where you edit a file on GitHub and then propose changes. It can also begin from a fork or a feature branch created locally. In either case, the important form fields are the title and description.

Jamie: And if the repository offers a template, use it.

Alex: Absolutely. Templates reduce ambiguity and make review easier.

Jamie: What kind of sections often appear in a strong PR description?

Alex: A strong structure often includes a summary, a list of changes, related issues, testing, and, if relevant, screenshots or recordings. For accessibility or documentation work, screenshots may be less central than in UI-heavy projects, but they can still help if something visual changed.

Jamie: So the simple workshop template is the beginner version of a broader professional habit.

Alex: Exactly. Start with what and why. Add testing details and evidence as the work becomes more complex.

Jamie: Can we talk about draft pull requests?

Alex: Yes. A draft PR is useful when you want to share work early but are not yet ready for formal review or merge. It signals "please don't treat this as finished."

Jamie: When should someone use a draft?

Alex: When the implementation is incomplete, when you want early feedback on direction, when checks are still being stabilized, or when you want visibility without implying readiness.

Jamie: What does a draft PR do differently?

Alex: It changes the PR state so reviewers know it is not ready for approval in the usual way. It may limit merge actions until it is marked ready for review. It's a communication tool as much as a technical status.

Jamie: And later, the author can mark it ready for review.

Alex: Exactly. There is a control to convert draft to ready. There's also typically a path to convert an open PR back into draft if needed. In CLI-oriented workflows, you can also create a draft PR, check whether a PR is in draft state, and list only draft PRs.

Jamie: So draft is not a dead end. It's part of the lifecycle.

Alex: Right.

Jamie: What about requesting reviewers?

Alex: Requesting reviewers formally asks specific collaborators to examine the PR. It helps route work and makes expectations clearer.

Jamie: And when you're the reviewer, you need to know how to submit a review, not just a comment.

Alex: Yes. A review can contain line comments plus an overall verdict. Typically the choices are approve, request changes, or leave a comment-only review with no verdict.

Jamie: Walk us through that flow.

Alex: You usually start by reading the diff and optionally adding comments as part of a pending review. Then, when ready, you choose Submit review. From there, you can approve the PR, approve with a summary comment, request changes if something must be fixed before merge, or leave a neutral comment-only review.

Jamie: And terminal users can review too.

Alex: Yes. You can inspect a PR diff in the terminal, and GitHub CLI supports actions like approving a PR, approving with a comment, requesting changes, or leaving a comment-only review. Again, use help text for exact syntax.

Jamie: There was also a note about keyboard shortcuts on GitHub pages.

Alex: Yes. GitHub includes shortcuts that can speed navigation on the PR list page, on an open PR, and on the Files changed tab. These are useful, but for screen reader users they should be adopted carefully because some keystrokes can conflict with browser or assistive technology commands. Learn a few that fit your setup rather than trying to memorize everything.

Jamie: So landmarks and headings remain the reliable baseline.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: I'm glad this chapter also covers suggested changes, because that can seem mysterious at first.

Alex: Suggested changes are structured code or text replacements that a reviewer can propose directly in a review comment. As a reviewer, you can insert a suggestion for a specific change instead of just describing it in prose.

Jamie: And as the author?

Alex: As the author, you can often apply an accepted suggestion directly from the PR interface. Multiple suggestions can sometimes be batched into one commit, which keeps history tidy.

Jamie: When should a reviewer use a suggestion instead of a regular comment?

Alex: Use a suggestion when the fix is small, concrete, and easy to express exactly. Use a regular comment when the issue is conceptual, exploratory, or requires discussion rather than a single replacement.

Jamie: Now let's switch perspectives again. Suppose someone is a maintainer. What merge options should they understand?

Alex: Three common options are merge commit, squash and merge, and rebase and merge. A merge commit preserves the branch history as a distinct merge event. Squash and merge combines the PR's commits into one commit on the target branch. Rebase and merge reapplies commits onto the target branch without a merge commit.

Jamie: And there's also the choice to delete the branch afterward.

Alex: Yes. Deleting the branch after merging helps keep the repository tidy, especially for short-lived feature branches.

Jamie: And auto-merge?

Alex: Auto-merge lets a PR merge automatically once required conditions are met, such as approvals and passing checks. It's useful when everything is ready except a pending check and you do not want to wait around watching the page.

Jamie: How does a user enable it?

Alex: On the PR page, if the repository allows it and the necessary prerequisites are in place, there is an option to enable auto-merge. Screen reader users should navigate the action controls near merge options. Once enabled, GitHub waits for requirements to pass, then merges automatically.

Jamie: And if circumstances change?

Alex: You can cancel auto-merge before it completes.

Jamie: What happens after a PR is merged?

Alex: If the description included `Closes #number`, the linked issue closes automatically. The branch may be deleted. The PR moves from open to merged state. And the change becomes part of the target branch history.

Jamie: So merge is not just the end of the conversation. It also updates project state.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can we walk through a few practical scenarios learners may face?

Alex: Certainly. Scenario one: "I want to review an assigned PR." Start at notifications or the PR list, open the PR, read the description first, inspect checks, then review the Files changed tab. Leave inline comments where needed, then submit a review.

Jamie: Scenario two: "I want to respond to review feedback on my PR."

Alex: Open the PR conversation and diff comments. Read each thread fully. Make changes on the same branch. Reply to comments if explanation helps. Then push updates, let checks rerun, and resolve conversations when appropriate.

Jamie: Scenario three: "My PR has a merge conflict."

Alex: That means the branch can no longer merge cleanly into the base branch. The author needs to update the branch, often by bringing it up to date with `main` and resolving conflicts either locally or using GitHub's conflict tools if available. The key is to read carefully and avoid accidental content loss.

Jamie: What are some common PR mistakes to avoid?

Alex: Opening a PR with a vague title. Leaving the description blank or too thin to explain intent. Forgetting to link the related issue. Mixing unrelated changes into one PR. Ignoring failing checks. And treating reviewer comments as interruptions instead of part of the collaboration process.

Jamie: That makes sense. And the chapter also goes deeper on PR descriptions.

Alex: Yes. Writing PR descriptions that get reviewed is a genuine skill. Reviewers look for clarity, scope, reason, and confidence that the author understands the impact of the change.

Jamie: Can you name a few especially useful patterns?

Alex: One is the `Closes XX` pattern for issue linkage. Another is before-and-after structure, where you briefly explain what was true before and what is true now. And a reusable template helps authors avoid missing the essentials.

Jamie: What might such a template include?

Alex: A summary, changes made, related issues, testing, and a checklist. For example: what did you change, why, which issue does it address, how did you test it, and did you review for obvious errors before requesting review?

Jamie: And common description mistakes?

Alex: Being too vague, omitting the why, burying the issue number in a wall of text, or claiming testing that wasn't actually done.

Jamie: I want to come back to the challenge's solution reference one more time, because it's a neat model.

Alex: It is. The solution shows a complete PR with a clear title, a concise body, and linked issue syntax. The key elements are simple but powerful: a title that says what happened, a body that explains what and why, an issue link like `Closes #N`, and attention to automated checks.

Jamie: And if the checks are green, that signals the repository's automated validation agrees the PR meets the baseline expectations.

Alex: Exactly. If checks fail, read the bot's feedback and revise. That feedback loop is part of the lesson, not evidence that you failed the lesson.

Jamie: There's also a local Git alternative in this chapter, and I think it's worth making that explicit for learners who already cloned the repo.

Alex: Certainly. The full local workflow is: start from `main`, create a feature branch, make the small edit locally, commit it, push the branch to GitHub, and then open a pull request from that branch into `main`. After that, the rest of the workflow is the same: fill out the PR form, link the issue, watch checks, respond to feedback.

Jamie: So whether the branch was born in the web editor or from `git checkout -b`, the conceptual model is unchanged.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: There's also a nice exercise in this chapter: reading a real pull request.

Alex: Yes, and it's excellent practice. Open a recent PR. Read the description first and identify which file changed and what challenge it was solving. Check whether the description references `Closes #XX`. Then read the conversation and bot feedback. Finally, open Files changed and inspect the actual additions and deletions.

Jamie: That sequence teaches people to follow a PR from intention to discussion to implementation.

Alex: Exactly. And for screen reader users, it reinforces that headings and landmarks are enough to navigate a full review path without sighted scanning.

Jamie: Before we wrap, I want to mention one philosophical thread I noticed. This chapter frames pull requests as preparation not just for human collaboration, but for reviewing AI-generated changes too.

Alex: Yes. That's an important idea. AI systems may generate code or documentation, but responsible workflows still route those changes through pull requests. The PR is where humans inspect, question, verify, and judge. An agent can draft. A human supplies context and final judgment.

Jamie: So learning to edit Markdown cleanly, link issues correctly, read diffs, and respond to checks is future-proof.

Alex: Very much so.

Alex: Let's close with a compact review. A pull request proposes merging a branch into another branch, usually into `main`. For this chapter's challenge, you make one small change, open a PR, and include a linked issue reference like `Closes #XX`. Your title should clearly describe the change. Your body should explain what changed and why. GitHub and repository checks may then validate the PR. If something fails, read the feedback, revise, and rerun.

Jamie: When navigating PRs, start with the list page, then the PR page itself. Read the Conversation tab for the description, checks, and comments. Use the Commits and Checks tabs when you need deeper detail. Use the Files changed tab to inspect the diff, relying on headings, landmarks, and line status cues.

Alex: And remember the practical habits: keep PRs small, use short-lived feature branches, request or submit reviews thoughtfully, use draft PRs when work is not ready, and choose merge options intentionally.

Jamie: Most of all, connect the change to the reason.

Alex: Exactly. That's what turns editing into contribution.

Alex: If you want the current source of truth after this lesson, check GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, and GitHub's official pull request documentation and accessibility guidance. Those references change over time, and they're the authoritative place to verify details.

Jamie: And if today's challenge is in front of you right now: go to Pull requests, choose New pull request if needed, make sure base is `main`, compare is your feature branch, write a descriptive title, add what changed, why, and `Closes #XX`, then create the PR.

Alex: You've got this.

20. Episode 7: Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary

Why conflicts happen, how to read conflict markers, and resolving them confidently.

Based on: Chapter 7: Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary

Download Episode 7 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 7: Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re talking about merge conflicts, and I want to start by lowering the temperature right away. Merge conflicts are normal. They are not proof that you broke Git, and they are not a sign that you are bad at collaboration.

Jamie: That helps, because the phrase merge conflict sounds dramatic.

Alex: It does. But in practice, a merge conflict just means Git found two overlapping changes and needs a human decision. This lesson is about understanding what that means, how to prevent conflicts when you can, and how to resolve them calmly when they show up.

Alex: A quick orientation before we dig in. This chapter pairs well with a short companion episode called Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary, and there are also related appendices on advanced Git and a VS Code reference. The authoritative references behind this lesson are GitHub Docs on resolving merge conflicts and the Git book’s section on basic merge conflicts.

Jamie: So this is one of those topics where the course teaches the workflow, but learners can also cross-check with official documentation.

Alex: Exactly. And that matters, especially if you’re contributing in open source or working across GitHub, Git, and VS Code.

Alex: The core idea is simple. A merge conflict happens when two people changed the same part of the same file in different ways, and Git cannot safely choose which version should win.

Jamie: So Git can merge some things automatically, just not all things.

Alex: Right. If I edit line 5 and you edit line 80, Git can usually combine those changes without trouble. But if we both change the same sentence, the same table row, the same function body, or one person deletes something while another person edits it, Git stops and asks for help.

Jamie: Can you give a tiny example?

Alex: Sure. Suppose one person changes a button label to say Submit form, and another changes that exact same line to say Send message. Git sees two different truths for one location. That is the conflict.

Alex: This chapter uses a controlled practice exercise, which is a smart teaching choice. Instead of waiting for a stressful real-world conflict, learners get one small challenge designed just for practice.

Jamie: What does that challenge look like?

Alex: There is one challenge in this chapter, designed to take under ten minutes. The evidence for completion is an issue-linked pull request and a completion comment. The learning pattern is observe, resolve, verify.

Jamie: That’s nice and concrete.

Alex: Very. The challenge is to resolve conflict markers in a practice file, then open the linked pull request. Learners are told to use a short-lived branch named in the same style as the previous chapter, something like fix slash your-name dash issue-number.

Jamie: Let’s walk through that challenge slowly, because I think that’s where many learners need the most reassurance.

Alex: Absolutely. The goal is to identify the three conflict markers in a practice file, decide which content to keep, remove the markers, and submit a clean pull request. There is also an important learning point here about AI. Sometimes an AI tool confidently generates code or text that conflicts with human-written work. Resolving merge conflicts is not only a human teamwork skill. It is also part of supervising and correcting AI-generated changes safely.

Jamie: That’s a great framing. Conflict resolution is really decision-making.

Alex: Exactly. In the exercise, learners work either in their Learning Room repository on GitHub.com using the web editor, or in VS Code if they cloned the repository locally. Before starting, they open their assigned challenge issue. The issue tells them which practice file contains the conflict markers. Then the steps are very specific. First, open the practice file named in the issue. Second, search the file for less-than signs repeated seven times, the marker that begins with left angle brackets. That start marker shows where the conflict begins. Third, read the text between the opening marker and the line of equals signs. That block is your version, meaning the current branch version. Fourth, read the text between the equals signs and the closing marker made of greater-than signs. That block is their version, meaning the incoming branch version. Fifth, decide what to keep. You might keep only your version, only their version, or combine the two into one cleaner result. Sixth, delete all three marker lines. That includes the opening marker line, the middle separator line, and the closing marker line. Seventh, review the file and confirm that no conflict markers remain. Search again for the opening marker. You should get zero results. Eighth, commit the changes on your fix branch. Ninth, open a pull request. The suggested title is fix: resolve conflict markers in filename. In the body, include Closes issue-number and one or two sentences explaining what you kept and why.

Jamie: I love that the instructions don’t just say remove the markers. They also ask learners to explain their content decision.

Alex: Yes, because randomly deleting text is not conflict resolution. Intentional selection is.

Jamie: What about accessibility support in that challenge?

Alex: There is a specific screen reader tip. Use your find command to jump directly to the markers. In a browser, that’s typically Control F. In VS Code, learners may also use find. The key point is that the markers are plain text, so they are fully readable to screen readers.

Jamie: That’s reassuring. No hidden visual trick, just text.

Alex: Exactly. And the done condition is also concrete: the pull request passes bot validation checks and contains no remaining conflict markers.

Jamie: Once the PR is open, what evidence do learners submit?

Alex: They return to their assigned challenge issue and post a completion comment. The format is straightforward: Chapter 7 completed, then a bullet noting the PR number and file, and another bullet stating the content decision they made and why.

Jamie: So the issue, branch, PR, and comment all connect together.

Alex: Right. That linkage is part of good contribution workflow.

Alex: The expected outcomes for the chapter are also worth naming plainly. By the end, a learner should be able to recognize the three conflict marker lines immediately, read both sides of a conflict, make an intentional decision, remove all markers, and submit a clean issue-linked PR.

Jamie: And if they get stuck?

Alex: The course gives very practical guidance. If you can’t find the markers, search for the opening marker string. They always appear in sets. If you’re unsure which side to keep, read both versions aloud and pick the clearer one, or combine them. If you deleted too much, undo and try that section again. If a PR bot says the content is wrong, search again for all three marker patterns to make sure none remain. And it is completely appropriate to ask a facilitator to sanity-check your final content before you open the PR.

Jamie: There’s also a reference solution, right?

Alex: Yes. If a learner finishes but still feels unsure, they can compare their work to the chapter’s reference solution.

Alex: Now let’s zoom out to the bigger lesson. Merge conflicts are not failures. They are a normal checkpoint in collaboration. In real open source work, they happen whenever people edit near the same lines. The skill is not to magically avoid every conflict forever. The skill is to resolve them clearly and calmly.

Jamie: And the chapter’s learning pattern supports that confidence.

Alex: It does. Start with a safe, controlled conflict. Learn the structure. Make a deliberate decision. Submit evidence through the normal pull request workflow. Build confidence for future real-world conflicts.

Jamie: There’s also a note about learning cards in this chapter.

Alex: Yes, and we should include that because it’s part of the learner support design. This chapter uses expandable learning cards tailored to different ways of working. Not every card appears at every step, so learners are encouraged to open the ones that match their setup. The five card types are: visual or mouse guidance for sighted users; low vision guidance for magnification, zoom, and high contrast workflows; NVDA and JAWS guidance for Windows screen reader users; VoiceOver guidance for macOS users; and CLI guidance for terminal users.

Jamie: So accessibility here is not an afterthought. It is built into the chapter structure.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Before we get into prevention strategies, can we cover the local Git alternative?

Alex: Definitely. The main teaching path in this chapter uses the GitHub web conflict editor, but there is a local Git option for learners who cloned the repository earlier and prefer terminal workflows. The steps are: go into the repository folder, check out main, pull the latest main from origin, switch back to your branch, and merge main into your branch. If there is a conflict, Git reports the affected files and stops the merge. Then open the conflicted file in your editor, maybe with VS Code. Inside the file you will see the conflict markers showing your version, the separator, and the incoming version from main. Edit the file. Keep the version you want, or combine both. Delete all three marker lines. Save the file. Then mark the file resolved with git add, create a commit such as Resolve merge conflict in filename, and push. Your pull request on GitHub updates automatically.

Jamie: And the same checks and review still apply.

Alex: Exactly. Different workspace, same collaboration rules.

Alex: Let’s talk about why conflicts happen in the first place. The most common causes are pretty predictable. Two people edit the same line. One person deletes a file while another edits it. Two people restructure the same section in different ways. Or a pull request stays open for a long time and drifts farther and farther away from main.

Jamie: That last one feels especially common.

Alex: It is. Long-running branches tend to collect conflict risk.

Jamie: Okay, so how do we prevent conflicts without becoming afraid to collaborate?

Alex: Great question. The chapter emphasizes that prevention is easier than resolution, and it gives a practical list. First, keep branches short-lived. Small, focused work merged quickly usually produces fewer conflicts than branches that linger for weeks. A useful target is roughly one to three days from branch creation to merge. If the work is larger, break it into smaller pull requests. Second, sync with main frequently. If main keeps moving and your branch never checks in, you increase the chance of painful surprises later. From your feature branch, fetch the latest changes and merge origin slash main into your branch. If you are comfortable with rebasing, rebasing onto origin slash main is another option, but that assumes you understand rebase and its tradeoffs.

Jamie: So the idea is not just pull once at the beginning and hope for the best.

Alex: Exactly. Stay current. Third, communicate with your team. If you know you’ll be editing a shared file, say so. A quick message can prevent duplicated work and awkward overlap. Fourth, avoid mass reformatting unless it is planned. Huge whitespace-only changes, big reorganizations, or style rewrites make conflicts much more likely for everyone else. Fifth, pull before you push. Make sure you are integrating recent remote changes instead of trying to land outdated work. Sixth, work on separate files when possible. Sometimes work can be divided in ways that reduce overlap. Seventh, keep pull requests small. Smaller PRs are easier to review, easier to merge, and less likely to drift. Eighth, use draft pull requests for early visibility. Even before the work is done, a draft PR helps others see what area you are touching.

Jamie: That’s such a useful social signal. It says, I’m working here.

Alex: Exactly. Conflict prevention is partly technical and partly communicative.

Jamie: There’s also an advanced prevention concept in the chapter: fast-forward merges. Can you unpack that without going too deep into Git theory?

Alex: Sure. A fast-forward merge happens when the target branch has not moved ahead independently, so Git can simply move the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is needed, and there is no competing history to combine at that moment.

Jamie: So in a sense, the cleanest merge is one where there was never a divergence to reconcile.

Alex: Exactly. Understanding fast-forward merges helps learners see why staying up to date and merging quickly can reduce complexity.

Jamie: I noticed a section called when conflicts are actually good. That sounds counterintuitive.

Alex: It does, but it’s important. Sometimes a conflict is a useful safety signal. It means Git refused to make a silent guess about overlapping edits. Instead, it asked a human to choose intentionally.

Jamie: So a conflict can protect meaning.

Alex: Precisely. If two people changed the same accessibility instruction, keyboard shortcut, or critical sentence in different ways, you want that pause. It gives you a chance to combine the best ideas or choose the clearer wording instead of letting one overwrite the other without review.

Jamie: Let’s move to the very practical question: how do you spot a conflict on GitHub?

Alex: On a pull request, GitHub may indicate that the branch has conflicts that must be resolved before merging. In other words, the PR is not merge-ready yet. That status message is your cue to inspect the conflicting files.

Jamie: And the tool card idea here is basically: resolve a merge conflict by editing the file and removing the markers.

Alex: Exactly. The heart of the task is always the same. Open the conflicting file. Remove the marker lines. Keep the content you actually want.

Alex: Now let’s spend real time on conflict markers, because once learners understand the markers, a lot of fear disappears. A conflicted file contains three special marker lines. The opening marker, made of left angle brackets, marks the start of the conflict region. The middle line of equals signs separates the two versions. The closing marker, made of right angle brackets, marks the end of the conflict region and often names the incoming branch.

Jamie: And between those markers, one block is your version and one block is their version.

Alex: Right. Usually the top block, between the opening marker and the equals line, is the current branch version. The bottom block, between the equals line and the closing marker, is the incoming version.

Jamie: Could we do a plain-language example?

Alex: Yes. Imagine a markdown table in a file about keyboard shortcuts. Before the conflict, there was one existing row. Then two students both edited that same row area to add different shortcut information. When Git tries to combine them, the file may end up showing both edits wrapped in conflict markers. One resolution option is to keep the first student’s row. Another is to keep the second student’s row. A better option in many cases is to combine both additions into one clean, correctly formatted table so no information is lost.

Jamie: That’s the key idea: the resolution isn’t always choosing sides. Sometimes it’s synthesizing.

Alex: Exactly. And after that decision, all the marker lines must be removed. If any marker remains, the file is still unresolved.

Jamie: How does conflict resolution work in the GitHub web editor?

Alex: The chapter teaches the web editor as the primary method. The step-by-step flow is roughly this: open the pull request or conflict prompt, choose the option to resolve conflicts, move through each conflicted file, edit the content directly in the browser, remove the markers, keep the final clean text, mark the conflict resolved, and complete the commit that updates the branch.

Jamie: What does it look like in the editor?

Alex: Visually, GitHub may show the conflicted region clearly, but the important point for blind and low-vision learners is that the underlying content is text. Screen reader users can navigate by line, search for the marker strings, and read both versions directly. Low-vision users can increase zoom, use high contrast themes, and rely on the strong textual markers rather than color alone.

Jamie: So even if the interface has visual cues, the lesson still works text-first.

Alex: Exactly. That’s why the learning cards matter. A visual learner might use click targets and color-coded regions. A low-vision learner might enlarge text and inspect marker visibility. NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver users may rely on find, line navigation, and careful reading of the plain-text markers.

Jamie: What about VS Code on day two?

Alex: In VS Code, conflicts are often shown with special indicators and action choices. You may see labels for current change and incoming change, and quick actions such as accept current, accept incoming, accept both, or compare changes.

Jamie: That sounds convenient, but also potentially dangerous if someone clicks too quickly.

Alex: Exactly right. Those commands are helpful, but they should support your thinking, not replace it. Learners should still read both sides carefully. Sometimes accept both is correct. Sometimes it creates duplicated or awkward content. Sometimes neither version should be kept exactly as written, and you need to edit manually.

Jamie: So VS Code gives you tools, but your judgment still matters.

Alex: Always.

Jamie: Let’s talk directly to the learner who feels frozen when they see a conflict.

Alex: Yes. If you feel stuck, first remember that asking for help is normal. Conflicts happen to experienced developers too. A teammate or facilitator can often confirm your interpretation in a minute or two. Second, there is a nuclear option: abandon the attempt and start fresh. If your branch became messy and you are no longer confident, it may be faster to back out, recreate a clean branch from updated main, and reapply the intended change carefully.

Jamie: That’s important. Starting over is not defeat.

Alex: Not at all. Sometimes it is the most professional choice.

Jamie: Can we cover what a conflict message looks like from the Git command line?

Alex: Absolutely. This is a useful reference workflow. Step one: start the merge that causes the conflict. For example, while on your branch, merge main into it. Step two: Git tells you there was a conflict and lists files with conflict status. You are especially looking for entries that say both modified. Step three: open each conflicted file in your editor. Inside the file, edit the content. Remove the opening markers, separator, and closing markers. Keep the content you want. Step four: after editing, mark each resolved file with git add. Step five: complete the merge with a commit. Git usually auto-fills the merge commit message for you. Then check the result. View the pull request status. Confirm the merge state is now healthy. Check all PR checks and merge readiness. And review the diff so you understand exactly what changed.

Jamie: I like that final step. Don’t just trust that it worked. Inspect the result.

Alex: Yes. Verification matters.

Alex: Let’s do a quick summary checklist in plain language. Know what a merge conflict is: overlapping edits Git cannot decide between. Know why conflicts happen: same-line edits, delete-versus-edit situations, structural overlap, and long-diverged branches. Prevent them when possible: short-lived branches, frequent sync with main, communication, smaller PRs, separate files when possible, and early visibility through draft PRs. Recognize the three conflict markers immediately. Read both sides before making any decision. Keep one side, the other side, or combine both intentionally. Delete all marker lines. Commit, push, and verify the pull request is clean and passing checks.

Jamie: And emotionally, read a conflict without fear.

Alex: Exactly. That is one of the chapter’s quiet goals. A conflict message should become something you can inspect, decode, and solve, not something that makes you panic.

Jamie: Before we close, can you say a word about sources and trust?

Alex: Yes. This lesson is grounded in the official GitHub documentation, the Git documentation, GitHub flow guidance, and pull request guidance. That matters because merge conflict workflows can vary a little across tools, but the underlying principles remain stable.

Jamie: So if a learner remembers only one sentence?

Alex: A merge conflict is just Git asking for a human decision about overlapping changes.

Jamie: And if they remember two?

Alex: The second is this: read both sides, keep what belongs, remove the markers, and verify the result.

Alex: You’ve got this. Conflicts are part of real collaboration, including accessible and open source workflows. The more calmly you practice them, the more confident you become.

Jamie: And that confidence carries across GitHub, VS Code, and the terminal.

Alex: Exactly. See you next time.

Reading conflict markers, choosing content, deleting markers, and committing a resolution.

Alex: Let's define the core idea. A merge conflict happens when two people change the same part of the same file in different ways, and Git cannot automatically decide which version to keep.

Jamie: So if I edit line twelve and you edit line two hundred, Git usually handles that fine.

Alex: Usually, yes. But if we both edit the same line, or nearby lines in a way that overlaps, Git may stop and ask for help.
