Jamie: That last one feels especially realistic in open source.

Alex: Very realistic. Long-running branches invite conflicts.

Alex: Before we resolve conflicts, let's make them less likely. Prevention is easier than resolution.

Jamie: Give us the practical list.

Alex: Keep branches short-lived. Aim for small, focused work that merges in a few days, not a few weeks. Sync with main frequently. From your feature branch, you may merge origin slash main into your branch. And if you're comfortable with rebasing, rebasing onto origin slash main is another option. Communicate with your team. If you know you'll be editing a heavily used file, say so. Avoid mass reformatting unless it's coordinated, because changing lots of lines creates unnecessary overlap. Pull before you push, so you're not building on stale history. Work on separate files when possible. Keep pull requests small. And use draft pull requests for early visibility, so other contributors can see what area you're touching before things collide.

Jamie: That's a strong pattern: short branches, frequent sync, small PRs, visible work.

Alex: Exactly. Those habits reduce stress.

Jamie: And there was also an advanced prevention idea about fast-forward merges.

Alex: Yes. The important concept is that simpler branch histories can reduce complexity. You don't need to master fast-forward behavior today, but it helps to know that the shape of history affects how cleanly changes integrate.

Jamie: Okay. Now let's talk about the thing learners actually see: conflict markers.

Alex: Yes. When Git can't merge automatically, it inserts plain-text markers directly into the file. Here is the classic shape: Less-than signs repeated seven times, then HEAD. Then one version of the content. Then a separator line made of equals signs. Then the other version of the content. Then greater-than signs repeated seven times, followed by a branch name.

Jamie: And because this is an audio lesson, let's label the sections clearly.

Alex: Good idea. There are three important parts. First, the section between the start marker and the separator. Second, the section between the separator and the end marker. Third, the marker lines themselves. In the solution reference, the section between the start marker and the separator is described as the version on the branch you are merging into, usually main. The section between the separator and the end marker is the version on your branch.

Jamie: But in the practice chapter instructions, the wording says the first block is your version, the current branch, and the second block is their version, the incoming branch.

Alex: Right, and that's why context matters. Different tools and workflows describe the sides a little differently depending on where the merge is happening. The safe habit is this: do not rely only on labels like "yours" and "theirs." Read the actual text on both sides and decide what final content should remain.

Jamie: That's helpful, especially for learners who worry about memorizing the wrong mapping.

Alex: Exactly. The universally safe truth is: the marker lines are not content, and the final file must contain only the text you actually want to keep.

Alex: Let's make that concrete with the example resolution from the reference solution. Suppose one side says, "Welcome to the Learning Room. This is the main branch version." The other side says, "Welcome to the Learning Room. This is my improved version with more detail." Your options are threefold. Keep yours: delete the other section and all marker lines. Keep theirs: delete your section and all marker lines. Or combine both: write one clean final version that incorporates the best parts of each.

Jamie: So there is not always one magic correct answer.

Alex: Correct. The decision depends on what is better for the project. Two valid resolutions may use different wording.

Jamie: That fits the peer simulation note too. It's okay if your final wording differs from someone else's, as long as it's a valid resolution.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Now let's walk through the challenge flow step by step. First, wait for your facilitator to trigger the conflict. If you don't see a conflict yet, it may simply not be ready. Second, open your assigned challenge issue. It tells you which practice file contains the conflict markers. Third, open that file and search for the start marker. In a browser you can use Control F. In VS Code you can also search directly. Screen reader users can search for the literal characters, since the markers are plain text and fully readable. Fourth, read both sides carefully. Fifth, decide: keep one side or combine them. Sixth, delete all three types of marker lines: the start line, the equals separator, and the end line with the branch name. Seventh, review the file and search again so there are zero remaining markers. Eighth, commit your changes on your short-lived feature branch. The recommended naming pattern is fix slash your name dash issue number. Ninth, open or update your pull request. The suggested title pattern is fix: resolve conflict markers in filename. In the body, include Closes number, with your issue number, and a brief sentence or two explaining what content you kept and why.

Jamie: And when everything is open and passing checks, there's one more administrative step.

Alex: Yes. Post a completion comment on your assigned challenge issue. The example format is: Chapter 7 completed, then the PR number, the filename, and your content decision with a short reason.

Jamie: That matters because this course wants issue-linked evidence, not just a private sense that "I think I fixed it."

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let's stay with accessibility for a moment. What should blind or low-vision learners know about navigating this?

Alex: A few key points. The conflict markers themselves are just text, so screen readers can read them directly. Search is your friend. Searching for the start marker is often the fastest way to jump into the conflict area. If you're on GitHub and can't find the Resolve conflicts button, look on the PR conversation tab near the merge section toward the bottom. Screen reader users may want to search the page for the phrase "Resolve conflicts" button. For low-vision users, high contrast themes and zoom can make the conflict regions easier to parse, especially in editors that highlight current and incoming changes. And this chapter also includes learning card guidance for different working styles: visual and mouse users, low vision users, NVDA or JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS, and CLI users.

Jamie: So the chapter is intentionally not one-size-fits-all.

Alex: Right. Open the guidance that matches how you work.

Alex: Let's talk about spotting a conflict on GitHub. On a pull request, GitHub may show a message that the branch has conflicts that must be resolved before merging.

Jamie: And that's your cue that GitHub needs human help.

Alex: Yes. If the web editor is available, choose Resolve conflicts. GitHub's conflict editor will show the conflicting sections, and your task is to edit the file into one clean final version. Step by step on GitHub: click Resolve conflicts, edit the file so the markers are removed and the final content is what you want, choose Mark as resolved, and then Commit merge.

Jamie: What does the editor generally feel like?

Alex: It highlights the conflict region and places you right where the disagreement is. But the same rule applies: don't just click through. Read both sides. Decide intentionally.

Jamie: Now compare that with VS Code.

Alex: In VS Code, conflicts are often shown with highlighted regions and helpful actions above each conflict. Common actions include Accept Current Change, Accept Incoming Change, and Accept Both Changes.

Jamie: And we should translate those a little.

Alex: Yes. "Current" usually means the version currently checked out in your workspace. "Incoming" usually means the version being merged in. "Accept Both" keeps both chunks, after which you may still need to edit for clarity and formatting.

Jamie: So even when the tool gives you buttons, you still need judgment.

Alex: Always. Tooling helps, but it doesn't replace understanding.

Alex: If you cloned the repository and prefer local work, there is a terminal-based alternative. You update main, switch back to your branch, and merge main into your branch. If a conflict happens, Git pauses the merge and reports the affected files. Then you open each conflicted file in your editor, look for the markers, remove the markers while keeping the content you want, save the file, mark it resolved with git add, complete the merge with git commit, and push. Your pull request updates automatically.

Jamie: Can we also walk through the command-line conflict reading pattern more explicitly?

Alex: Definitely. Start the merge that causes the conflict. Then check which files have conflicts. Look for lines like "both modified" in Git's output. Open each conflicted file in your editor. Edit the file: remove the marker lines, keep the content you want. After editing, mark the file as resolved with git add. Then complete the merge with git commit. Git often auto-fills the merge commit message. After that, check the result. Review the diff so you understand what changed. On the PR, review merge state, checks, and overall readiness.

Jamie: That sequence really matters: detect, edit, add, commit, verify.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: There was also a real-file style example in the chapter, where two students both add content to the same table row.

Alex: Yes, and that example is useful because it shows that conflicts aren't always huge. Sometimes two people just edited the same small region, like one row in a Markdown table. The resolution options remain the same: keep one edit, keep the other, or combine them into one clean row that preserves the useful information.

Jamie: So the skill scales from tiny wording changes to larger sections.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now, something important philosophically: conflicts are not always bad.

Jamie: That sounds surprising.

Alex: A conflict can be evidence that two contributors both cared about the same important area. The conflict forces a deliberate review. In that sense, it can improve quality, because someone must consciously choose the final wording or logic rather than letting one change silently overwrite the other.

Jamie: And the chapter also frames this as relevant to AI-assisted work.

Alex: Yes. Sometimes an AI tool confidently produces changes that overlap with human-written changes. Conflict resolution becomes part of supervising AI safely. You are not just merging text. You are evaluating which content deserves to survive.

Jamie: Let's cover the most common stuck moments, because learners definitely hit these.

Alex: Absolutely. If you do not see a conflict, your facilitator may not have triggered it yet. Wait for the signal. If you cannot find the Resolve conflicts button, check the PR conversation area near the merge section, or search the page for that button label. If you are not sure what to keep, read both versions aloud. If both are useful, combine them. There is often no single correct answer. If the autograder still reports conflict markers, search the file for all three marker types. Every one of them must be completely removed. If you accidentally deleted too much, undo and redo that section carefully. And if you want a sanity check, ask your facilitator before opening the PR.

Jamie: What about the nuclear option?

Alex: Also valid. If you feel tangled up, you can abandon the attempt and start fresh from a clean copy of the branch or file. Sometimes restarting is faster than untangling confused edits.

Jamie: That's reassuring. Starting over is not cheating.

Alex: Not at all.

Alex: Let's do a compact checklist. A merge conflict means overlapping edits need a human decision. Conflict markers are plain text and come in three parts: start marker, separator, end marker. Read both sides. Choose one side or combine them. Delete all marker lines. Search again to confirm none remain. Commit the resolution. Verify the PR status, checks, and diff. Submit your issue-linked evidence.

Jamie: And emotionally?

Alex: Conflicts are normal. They are manageable. The skill is calm reading and intentional editing.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, what are the expected outcomes for this chapter?

Alex: You should be able to identify the three marker lines immediately, read both sides of a conflict, make an intentional content decision, remove all markers, and submit a clean pull request linked to the issue.

Jamie: And that's the learning moment, really. Not "avoid all conflicts forever," but "recognize them without panic and resolve them clearly."

Alex: Exactly. That is the point.

Alex: If you want to check current official guidance beyond the course material, the authoritative sources named for this chapter are GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, GitHub documentation about Git and pull requests, GitHub Flow guidance, and the Git SCM book's discussion of basic merge conflicts.

Jamie: So the course teaches the workflow, and those references are your source of truth when interfaces change.

Alex: Well said.

Alex: One final reminder for the challenge: your job is not to preserve the markers. Your job is to produce a clean file that says what the project should actually say.

Jamie: Delete the markers, keep the meaning.

Alex: Perfect. And once you can do that, merge conflicts stop feeling scary.

Jamie: They start feeling like editing.

Alex: Exactly.

22. Episode 8: Open Source Culture and Etiquette

Communication norms, code review etiquette, inclusive language, and asking questions.

Based on: Chapter 8: Open Source Culture and Etiquette

Download Episode 8 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 8: Open Source Culture and Etiquette

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. This time we’re focusing on the part of open source that isn’t just about commands or files. It’s about people. Technical skill can help you make a contribution, but communication skill is what helps you work with a community, get reviews, ask for help, and keep contributing.

Jamie: I’m glad we’re doing this one. A lot of learners can follow steps, but then freeze when it’s time to comment on an issue, open a pull request, or respond to feedback in public.

Alex: Exactly. And this chapter also includes workshop logistics, so let’s make those clear. There’s one Chapter 8 challenge, and it’s a guided reflection, not a bot-graded task. There’s no automation check because communication quality is too subjective for fair automatic scoring.

Jamie: So what do learners actually submit?

Alex: A reflection comment on their assigned Chapter 8 challenge issue in their Learning Room repository on GitHub. That comment is the evidence. No extra file, no screenshot, no separate upload. When the comment is posted, the facilitator reviews it for specificity, and then the learner closes the issue.

Jamie: And the reflection isn’t just, “I’ll try to be respectful,” right?

Alex: Right. It needs three specific, actionable behaviors. The format is: Chapter 8 reflection. One respectful review habit I will use. One way I will ask for help clearly. One way I will respond to feedback constructively. Each answer should be a real behavior you can do today.

Jamie: Like, “I will start review comments by naming something that works before suggesting a change,” instead of “I will be nice.”

Alex: Perfect example. Or, “I will explain the exact step where I got stuck and what I already tried,” instead of “I will ask better questions.”

Alex: The step-by-step process is simple. Read the chapter, think about a real communication moment from earlier work, open your assigned issue, go to the comment box, write the reflection using the required prompts, and activate the Comment button, or use Control+Enter if that works better for you.

Jamie: And if someone gets stuck writing the reflection?

Alex: Keep it simple. One sentence per prompt is enough. Draft in a text editor first if that’s more accessible or less stressful. Revisit the sections on feedback and asking for help for examples. And if needed, ask a facilitator for a sample response, then adapt it in your own words.

Jamie: So the learning goal here is really behavior change.

Alex: Yes. The expected outcomes are that learners can name respectful collaboration behaviors, prepare for constructive review work later, and feel safer asking for help in public threads. The deeper lesson is that technical quality and communication quality reinforce each other. Clear, respectful communication helps good work move faster.

Jamie: And the pattern of learning here is also deliberate.

Alex: It is. First, absorb community norms and the reasons behind them. Second, reflect on your own experience. Third, commit to behaviors in writing. Fourth, apply those behaviors later in reviews, comments, and pull requests.

Alex: Now, before we talk about etiquette, we need the workflow that those conversations sit inside: GitHub Flow.

Jamie: Because comments and reviews make more sense when you understand what a branch and a pull request are doing socially, not just technically.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub Flow is the standard lightweight contribution workflow. It works well in open source because it stays simple. The six steps are: create a branch from main, make changes and commit them, open a pull request, discuss and review, pass status checks, and merge.

Jamie: Let me try to say that back in everyday language. Start a branch for one task, do the work in small logical commits, open a PR even before everything is perfect if you need early feedback, respond to comments, make sure tests and checks pass, and then a maintainer merges it.

Alex: That’s it. And there are a few ideas behind why this works. First, main stays deployable. You don’t commit directly to main in a healthy collaborative project. Changes go through pull requests and review. Second, branches are cheap. You make one for a task and delete it after merge. Third, the pull request becomes the unit of conversation. The why, the tradeoffs, the test notes, the feedback, the approval, all in one place. And fourth, small changes move faster.

Jamie: That last one matters a lot. A tiny pull request is easier to review, easier to understand, and usually less emotionally intimidating.

Alex: Exactly. A focused PR also supports accessibility. It reduces cognitive load for reviewers, including blind and low-vision contributors using screen readers who may need to navigate comment by comment and file by file.

Jamie: Now I know some learners will hear “Git Flow” somewhere else and wonder if it’s the same thing.

Alex: Good distinction. Git Flow is a different branching model, older and more complex. It uses multiple branch types: a permanent main branch for production releases, a permanent develop branch for upcoming work, temporary feature branches, release branches, and hotfix branches.

Jamie: So instead of branching from main and coming back to main, feature work usually branches from develop and merges back into develop.

Alex: Right. Then when enough work is ready, a release branch is created for final testing and version updates. That release merges into main and back into develop. If a production bug appears, a hotfix branch starts from main and then merges to both main and develop.

Jamie: That sounds useful in some environments, but heavy for a workshop.

Alex: That’s the key point. GitHub Flow differs by having only one long-lived branch, main. Feature work branches off main and returns to main through a PR. Releases are continuous instead of centered on release branches. Hotfixes are handled as normal PR work. So GitHub Flow is lower complexity and is especially good for open source, web projects, and continuous deployment.

Jamie: Where might learners still encounter Git Flow?

Alex: In enterprise software with scheduled releases, mobile apps with app store review, embedded or firmware work, or older legacy teams that adopted it before continuous deployment became common.

Jamie: And this workshop uses GitHub Flow because it maps well to how open source contribution usually works.

Alex: Yes. It’s easier to learn, easier to practice, and easier to collaborate with across many contributors.

Jamie: There’s also an unwritten rule that people often learn the hard way: one thing per branch.

Alex: Yes. A branch should represent one coherent change. If you are fixing alt text, don’t also refactor unrelated code and update dependency versions in the same branch. One thing per branch leads to clearer commits, smaller pull requests, easier reviews, and fewer merge conflicts.

Jamie: So even if I notice three unrelated problems, I shouldn’t treat one branch as my personal cleanup spree.

Alex: Exactly. Separate branches create separate conversations.

Alex: Another practical skill in open source is keeping your fork up to date.

Jamie: Because if your fork drifts behind the original repository, your future work starts from stale code.

Alex: Right. You sync your fork so your copy of main matches the upstream project. That reduces conflicts, helps you branch from current code, and prevents confusing pull requests based on outdated history.

Jamie: What’s the easiest way?

Alex: On GitHub’s web interface, many forks show a Sync fork control. That’s often the easiest method. Activate it, review what will sync, and update your fork.

Jamie: And if someone is using Git in the VS Code terminal?

Alex: Then there’s a one-time setup step: add the upstream remote, meaning the original repository, not your fork. Typically that means a command like git remote add upstream followed by the original repository URL.

Jamie: So origin is your fork, upstream is the project you forked from.

Alex: Exactly. After that, the sync process is four steps. First, switch to your main branch. Second, fetch upstream changes. Third, merge upstream’s main into your own main. Fourth, push your updated main back to your fork on GitHub.

Jamie: And only after your main is current do you create a new feature branch.

Alex: Yes. That’s a healthy rhythm. Sync before starting new work, and sync again if a lot has changed while you were away. You may also sync before opening a PR if the project moved quickly and you want to reduce surprises.

Jamie: There’s also GitHub Desktop for people who prefer a graphical app.

Alex: Right. That can be a comfortable option for some learners. The principle is the same: update your fork from upstream so your main branch stays current.

Alex: Let’s move to commit messages, because they are a form of communication too.

Jamie: This is where people often type “stuff” or “updates” and regret it later.

Alex: Exactly. A good commit message tells future readers what changed and why. The common structure has three parts: a first line, which is required; an optional body; and an optional footer.

Jamie: The first line is the headline.

Alex: Yes. It should be short, clear, and specific. Something like, “Add alt text to workshop screenshots,” or, “Fix broken README link.” The body is optional, but useful when context matters. It can explain why the change was needed, what tradeoff you made, or any detail a reviewer would want later. The footer is also optional and often used for issue references or structured metadata.

Jamie: So for many small changes, a strong first line might be enough.

Alex: Correct. But whatever you write, avoid vague messages like “fixes,” “more changes,” or “final version.” Those don’t help reviewers, maintainers, or your future self.

Jamie: And this ties into atomic commits.

Alex: It does. An atomic commit is one coherent, complete change. Not half a fix. Not three unrelated fixes. One logical unit. Atomic commits are easier to review, revert, understand, and explain.

Jamie: So common mistakes would include mixing unrelated work in one commit, making giant catch-all commits, or writing messages that don’t describe the actual change.

Alex: Exactly. Good commit messages in practice are specific, action-oriented, and aligned with the actual contents of the commit.

Alex: Now let’s widen the lens. Open source communication has three characteristics that shape everything else.

Jamie: In writing, asynchronously, and in public.

Alex: Exactly. In writing means your words persist. People may reread them later, quote them, or interpret tone without hearing your voice. Asynchronously means the other person might not reply for hours or days, and silence doesn’t automatically mean rejection. In public means many conversations happen where others can see them, learn from them, and join them.

Jamie: That changes how we should phrase things. You can’t rely on facial expression or instant clarification.

Alex: Right. Clarity matters more. Specificity matters more. And kindness matters more because text strips away a lot of context.

Jamie: Let’s talk about feedback. What makes feedback actually helpful?

Alex: There’s a strong five-part pattern. First, acknowledge what’s working. That shows respect and gives the author a stable point to build from. Second, identify the specific concern. Not “this is confusing,” but “the installation step assumes Node is already installed.” Third, explain why it matters. Maybe it affects accessibility, maintainability, accuracy, or user success. Fourth, suggest a path forward when you can. And fifth, signal the weight of the concern.

Jamie: That last part is really useful. Not every comment has the same force.

Alex: Exactly. A reviewer should indicate whether something is required, recommended, or just a personal preference. That prevents authors from treating every sentence as a blocker.

Jamie: Can we model the difference?

Alex: Sure. Less helpful: “Change this.” More helpful: “Nice clarification in this section. I think the image also needs alt text so screen reader users receive the same information. Could we add a brief description here? I’d treat this as important before merge.”

Jamie: That gives praise, names the issue, explains why, offers a fix, and signals the concern level.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Language and tone also matter. A strong default is to prefer “we,” or describe the code or document, not the person.

Jamie: So instead of “You did this wrong,” say, “This function may fail when the input is empty,” or, “We may want to handle the empty state here.”

Alex: Yes. That lowers defensiveness and keeps the focus on improving the work. Another good habit is using tentative language when you’re uncertain. Phrases like, “I think,” “I may be missing context,” “Could we,” or, “Would it make sense to…” can signal openness.

Jamie: Especially when you’re not a maintainer or you’re still learning.

Alex: Right. Also remember cultural and language diversity. Not every contributor reads or writes English the same way. So avoid sarcasm, idioms, and overly compressed shorthand if clarity matters. Write plainly.

Jamie: And avoid fake urgency.

Alex: Exactly. Don’t mark something urgent unless it truly is. Urgency markers can create stress, especially in volunteer communities. If something is genuinely urgent, say why.

Jamie: Now for commenting etiquette, because even people with good intentions can make review threads messy.

Alex: Absolutely. First, keep comments focused. One comment should usually address one concern. That makes it easier to reply, resolve, and track. Second, don’t leave comments unresolved if the issue is actually settled. If the author changed the code and the concern is handled, resolve the conversation.

Jamie: And resolving conversations is not just tidying up. It’s communication.

Alex: Yes. It tells everyone, including future readers, that this point has been addressed. Third, do not pile on. If another reviewer already raised the same issue, add value only if you have new information. Repeating the same criticism can feel overwhelming.

Jamie: What about reactions?

Alex: They’re useful. A thumbs up or similar reaction can signal agreement without creating noise. That’s often better than posting “same” or “agree.”

Jamie: There’s also a really practical accessibility tip here: saved replies.

Alex: Yes. Saved replies are a major accessibility and efficiency win. If you often write similar comments, like requesting tests, asking for reproduction steps, thanking contributors, or pointing to contribution guidelines, you can store a reusable response. That reduces repetitive typing, lowers fatigue, and helps keep tone consistent.

Jamie: What are common uses?

Alex: Welcoming first-time contributors, asking for more detail in a bug report, explaining review timelines, requesting screenshots or test notes, or giving a standard accessibility reminder in respectful language.

Jamie: And how do you create one?

Alex: In GitHub settings, there’s a Saved replies area where you can create and name a reusable reply. Then, when writing a comment, you can insert that saved reply into the comment box.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, the important part is that there is a navigable path to the saved replies controls and insertion options, so this can support efficient commenting without copy-paste hunting.

Alex: Exactly. The details of the interface may shift over time, but the concept remains: use saved replies to reduce effort and improve consistency.

Alex: Let’s split code review etiquette into two sides: reviewers and authors.

Jamie: Start with reviewers.

Alex: Review the code, not the person. Don’t gatekeep knowledge by acting like unfamiliarity is a flaw. Ask questions instead of making demands when there’s room for discussion. Distinguish opinion from requirement. And when the work is ready, approve explicitly.

Jamie: That “don’t gatekeep knowledge” point is important. A review should not say, “You should already know this.”

Alex: Exactly. Better to explain briefly, link to a resource, or name the convention being applied. Reviews should help the project and help people grow.

Jamie: And distinguishing opinion from requirement could sound like, “Required: this needs alt text for accessibility,” versus, “Optional: I personally prefer this variable name.”

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: What about for authors?

Alex: Say thank you. Don’t take feedback personally. Explain your choices when context matters. And surface blockers early.

Jamie: So if I can’t reproduce a suggested fix, or I’m confused by a review comment, I shouldn’t silently stall.

Alex: Correct. Respond clearly. Say what you tried, what you’re uncertain about, and where you’re blocked. That makes collaboration easier and keeps momentum.

Jamie: This chapter also calls out inclusive commenting for accessibility issues.

Alex: Yes, and that matters a lot in this course. When raising accessibility concerns, focus on the user impact and the fix, not on blame. For example, instead of, “You forgot accessibility again,” try, “This image appears to be missing alt text, which means screen reader users may miss the information here. Could we add a short description?”

Jamie: So accessibility feedback should be firm when needed, but still respectful and explanatory.

Alex: Exactly. Accessibility is not a cosmetic preference. It often belongs in the required category. But the tone can still be inclusive and collaborative.

Alex: There’s also something called the social contract around “good first issue.”

Jamie: Meaning that label creates expectations.

Alex: Yes. If a maintainer labels something “good first issue,” the issue should be reasonably scoped, documented clearly enough for a newcomer to attempt, and not hide major unstated complexity. And if you’re a contributor picking one up, you should still read carefully, ask clarifying questions when needed, and respect that someone else may already be working on it.

Jamie: So the label is an invitation, not a guarantee of zero difficulty.

Alex: Exactly. But it should be a sincere invitation.

Jamie: What about difficult situations? Because eventually everyone runs into one.

Alex: Yes. If you receive harsh feedback, pause before replying. Separate the technical point from the tone. Respond to the substance calmly, and if needed, ask for clarification. If you disagree with a decision, state your reasoning respectfully, ask if there are project constraints you may not see, and accept that maintainers make final calls in their projects.

Jamie: And when someone is rude to you?

Alex: Don’t escalate in the heat of the moment. Point back to the issue at hand, stay factual, and use the project’s code of conduct or moderation channels if needed. You do not have to absorb mistreatment as a price of participation.

Jamie: And if you accidentally caused offense?

Alex: Acknowledge it plainly. Don’t get defensive. Apologize, restate your intent if helpful, and then adjust your behavior. In open source, repair matters more than perfection.

Alex: Let’s switch to documentation, starting with your first README.

Jamie: Because a README is often the first conversation a project has with a newcomer.

Alex: Exactly. A good README helps someone understand what the project is, how to install it, how to use it, how to contribute, and what license applies.

Jamie: So the basic skeleton is: Project Name, Installation, Usage, Contributing, and License.

Alex: Yes. Project Name identifies the project clearly. Installation explains how to get it running. Usage shows how to actually use it. Contributing tells people how to participate. License explains the legal terms.

Jamie: What belongs in each section in practice?

Alex: For Project Name, usually a short explanation of what the project does. For Installation, prerequisites and commands or steps. For Usage, examples, expected behavior, maybe screenshots if they’re accessible. For Contributing, branch workflow, issue or PR expectations, testing steps, and links to CONTRIBUTING.md if there’s a fuller guide. For License, the license name and ideally a link to the license text.

Jamie: And accessibility in READMEs?

Alex: Very important. Use meaningful headings, descriptive link text, accessible image alt text, and plain language. Avoid giant unstructured walls of text. If you include screenshots, don’t let the screenshot carry essential information without a text equivalent.

Jamie: So a bad README might be vague, missing setup steps, full of unexplained jargon, and inaccessible in structure.

Alex: Exactly. A good README helps a stranger succeed.

Jamie: That connects to community health files too.

Alex: It does. Community health files tell contributors how the project works. CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to contribute. CODEOFCONDUCT.md defines behavior expectations and reporting paths. SECURITY.md explains how to report vulnerabilities safely. LICENSE states the legal permissions and restrictions.

Jamie: And finding these files on GitHub is a practical skill.

Alex: Yes. Learners should know to look in the repository root, in a .github folder, or in GitHub’s community standards surfaces where these files may be highlighted. Reading them before contributing saves time and helps avoid social mistakes.

Alex: Another important topic is choosing the right communication channel.

Jamie: Because not every question belongs in the same place.

Alex: Right. Use issues for bugs, feature requests, and trackable discussions. Use pull request comments for feedback tied to a specific change. Use discussions, if enabled, for broader questions or ideas. Use security channels for vulnerabilities, not public issues. And use synchronous channels like chat sparingly and with awareness that important decisions should usually be summarized back in a public, durable place.

Jamie: That “durable place” idea matters in open source. If the answer only happens in a private message, future contributors can’t benefit.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: The chapter also gives quick phrases that work well.

Alex: Yes, and they’re worth practicing. Phrases like, “I may be missing context, but…”, “Could we…”, “One thing that’s working well here is…”, “I’m blocked at this step…”, “Here’s what I tried…”, “Would you prefer A or B?”, or, “I think this may need alt text because…” These phrases keep communication specific, calm, and collaborative.

Jamie: And there’s a practical exercise: rewrite one comment.

Alex: Right. Take a blunt or vague comment and turn it into one that is specific, respectful, and actionable. That’s excellent practice because tone is a skill, not just a personality trait.

Alex: Now let’s zoom out to contributing to open source more generally, especially for first-time contributors.

Jamie: Starting with the most basic question: what is open source?

Alex: Open source means the source code is publicly available under a license that allows people to inspect, use, modify, and share it under defined terms. It’s not just code posted online. The license matters.

Jamie: And who can contribute?

Alex: Anyone who follows the project’s rules and norms. Contributions aren’t limited to code. Documentation, issue triage, testing, accessibility improvements, design, examples, bug reports, and review are all valuable.

Jamie: What makes a good first contribution?

Alex: Something small, clear, and realistically finishable. Good first contributions often improve docs, fix typos, add missing alt text, improve labels, clarify setup steps, or resolve a well-scoped bug.

Jamie: And signs a first contribution is too large?

Alex: If it spans many files, changes architecture, requires deep project knowledge, has unclear requirements, or depends on unresolved design decisions, it may be too large for a first attempt.

Jamie: How do you find something to work on?

Alex: Look for labels like good first issue, help wanted, documentation, accessibility, or bug. Read recent issues and pull requests. Check whether the project is active and whether maintainers respond. Start where the path is visible.

Jamie: Then before starting, read the issue carefully.

Alex: Yes. Make sure the problem is still relevant, see whether anyone has claimed it, read linked discussion, and understand any constraints. If needed, leave a brief comment saying you’d like to work on it.

Jamie: Then comes making the contribution itself.

Alex: Right. The tool sequence is familiar: fork the repository if you don’t have write access, clone your fork locally if you’re working on your machine, create a branch, edit files, commit your changes, push the branch, and open a pull request.

Jamie: And the basic workflow should align with GitHub Flow.

Alex: Exactly. One task, one branch, clear commits, then a PR.

Jamie: What makes a good PR description?

Alex: Explain what changed, why it changed, how to test it, and any context reviewers need. Link the related issue when appropriate. If there are limitations or open questions, say so. A good PR description reduces back-and-forth and helps reviewers review efficiently.

Jamie: Then there’s getting help.

Alex: Yes. Ask in the most appropriate public place when possible. Be specific. Include the exact step where you got stuck, error messages if any, what you expected, and what you already tried. Good help requests make it easier for others to help you.

Jamie: And after the contribution is merged?

Alex: Say thank you, delete the merged branch if appropriate, sync your fork again, and stay open to follow-up learning. Your first merged contribution is not the end. It’s the start of familiarity.

Jamie: Which leads to building a contribution habit.

Alex: Exactly. Practical habits include keeping contributions small, reading project docs first, syncing your fork regularly, asking clear questions, responding graciously to review, and coming back consistently rather than waiting for a “perfect” giant contribution.

Jamie: Before we close, let’s circle back to the workshop task one more time.

Alex: Good idea. For Chapter 8, your assignment is to post a reflection comment on your assigned challenge issue. Include three specific behaviors: one respectful review habit, one way you’ll ask for help clearly, and one way you’ll respond to feedback constructively. The comment itself is your evidence. No bot check. No extra submission. Once it’s posted and reviewed, close the issue.

Jamie: And if writing in GitHub’s comment box feels awkward, draft somewhere else first, then paste it in.

Alex: Exactly. Use whatever workflow supports clear thinking and accessible writing.

Jamie: One more administrative note: this chapter points learners toward related appendices on accessibility standards, Git security, branch protection, and GitHub Pages, and it also points to authoritative sources like GitHub Docs and Open Source Guides.

Alex: Right. Those are valuable references if you want the official documentation behind these practices.

Alex: Here’s the big takeaway. Open source isn’t only a place where code is evaluated. It’s a place where people coordinate in writing, often in public, often asynchronously. If you can make focused branches, write useful commits, open clear pull requests, give respectful feedback, receive review without panic, and ask for help clearly, you become much easier to collaborate with.

Jamie: And that’s not a soft extra. That’s core contributor skill.

Alex: Exactly. Clear, respectful communication is infrastructure.

Jamie: Thanks for learning with us.

Alex: See you next time.

23. Challenge 08: The Culture Layer

Reflection, community norms, issue triage, labels, and respectful communication.

Practice focus: Day 1 stretch

Download Challenge 08 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 08: The Culture Layer

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're working on two layers of open source that beginners often underestimate: culture and organization. In other words, how people work together, and how work gets sorted so collaboration stays manageable.

Jamie: So this is not just about writing code.

Alex: Exactly. Technical skill matters, but open source is also a social system. Communication quality affects whether people can participate, whether reviews feel safe, and whether issues and pull requests move forward.

Jamie: And for our learners, that includes accessible participation too.

Alex: Absolutely. Accessibility is not only about the final app or website. It also includes whether issues are readable, whether labels are understandable, whether saved replies reduce typing burden, whether a screen reader user can find the right controls, and whether people describe their reasoning clearly in public threads.

Alex: A quick workshop note before we go deeper. In this chapter, the challenge is a guided reflection. There's no bot grading because communication quality is too subjective for fair automation.

Jamie: That's refreshing.

Alex: It is. The evidence is your reflection comment on your assigned challenge issue. The pattern is simple: read, reflect, and commit to one or more specific behaviors.

Jamie: What are learners actually asked to do?

Alex: They reflect on questions like: what made you feel welcome, what would make the learning room more accessible or inclusive, or what they learned from a peer simulation issue, pull request, or classmate. Then they practice triage by finding an open issue, adding at least one label, and optionally tagging a specific person if the issue needs that person's attention.

Jamie: So it blends reflection with action.

Alex: Right. And the guided reflection version asks for concrete behaviors, not vague intentions. For example: one respectful review habit you will use, one way you will ask for help clearly, and one way you will respond to feedback constructively.

Jamie: Not "I'll be nice," but something observable.

Alex: Exactly. Better examples sound like: "I'll start review comments by acknowledging something that works," or "I'll describe the exact step where I got stuck and what I already tried."

Jamie: And if someone gets stuck writing the reflection?

Alex: Use one simple sentence per prompt. Draft in a text editor first if that feels easier. Focus on one real behavior you can start now. Ask a facilitator for an example if needed. And if you finish but feel unsure, compare against the reference solution.

Alex: That reference solution matters because it shows what counts as success.

Jamie: What does it emphasize?

Alex: That open source projects are communities, not just code repositories. Reading files like CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and CONTRIBUTING.md can change how you see participation. A good reflection notices that filing a clear issue, structuring docs well, or communicating access needs are real contributions.

Jamie: I like that. It expands the idea of contribution.

Alex: It also points out that accessibility affects the development process itself. The way we write issues, name branches, structure documentation, and discuss changes can either include or exclude people.

Jamie: And the solution includes triage too, right?

Alex: Yes. For example, if an issue says a welcome page loads slowly on mobile, a strong recommendation is the label bug, because the behavior is not working as expected. An additional label might be accessibility, because slow reloads can disproportionately burden users of assistive technology.

Jamie: So good triage includes justification, not just a guess.

Alex: Exactly. The point is thoughtful reasoning. Alternate approaches are also valid: reflecting on the code of conduct, the contributing guide, or comparing one project's norms to another. What matters is understanding that open source has cultural norms, not just technical rules.

Alex: Now let's put those conversations in workflow context. Most open source contribution in this workshop follows GitHub Flow.

Jamie: That's the lightweight model centered on pull requests, right?

Alex: Yes. Six steps. Create a branch from main with a descriptive name. Make your changes and commit in small logical units. Open a pull request early, even as a draft if needed. Discuss and review collaboratively. Pass status checks like tests or linting. Then a maintainer merges into main.

Jamie: Why is this model so common?

Alex: Because it keeps main deployable, treats branches as cheap and temporary, makes pull requests the unit of conversation, and encourages small changes that are easier to review.

Jamie: That "pull requests are the unit of conversation" idea feels important.

Alex: It is. The why, the tradeoffs, the linked issue, the feedback, and the approval all live together. That's especially helpful when work is asynchronous and public.

Jamie: You mentioned GitHub Flow. Some learners will also hear about Git Flow. What's the difference?

Alex: Git Flow is older and more complex. It usually has long-lived main and develop branches, plus temporary feature, release, and hotfix branches. Feature work branches off develop, release branches collect work for scheduled releases, and hotfixes branch from main for urgent production fixes.

Jamie: So Git Flow fits projects with planned release cycles.

Alex: Exactly. Enterprise products, mobile apps with app store review, embedded systems, or older projects with versioned releases. GitHub Flow is simpler: usually just main plus short-lived branches, with each merge to main expected to be deployable.

Jamie: And this workshop uses GitHub Flow because it's better for open source contribution and fast-moving web work.

Alex: Right. Lower complexity, easier onboarding, and fewer branching rules to memorize.

Jamie: There's also an unwritten rule here, isn't there?

Alex: Yes: one thing per branch. One fix, one feature, one documentation change. That makes commit history cleaner, reviews narrower, and rework less painful. If a branch tries to solve three unrelated problems, reviewers struggle and authors get tangled.

Alex: Another practical habit is keeping your fork up to date.

Jamie: Because if your fork drifts too far from upstream, you inherit old problems and more merge conflicts.

Alex: Exactly. Syncing reduces conflicts, keeps you working from current code, and avoids opening pull requests based on stale main.

Jamie: What are the main ways to sync?

Alex: Three common ones. First, the GitHub web interface, which is often the easiest. If GitHub shows a sync option on your fork's main branch, you can update from the browser. Second, the command line in a terminal, including the VS Code terminal. One-time setup: add the upstream remote, usually the original repository. After that, the sync process is: switch to your own main branch, fetch upstream changes, merge upstream main into your main, then push the updated main to your fork on GitHub.

Jamie: Can you say those steps cleanly one more time?

Alex: Sure. One: switch to main. Two: fetch upstream. Three: merge upstream's main into your local main. Four: push your updated main to origin, meaning your fork.

Jamie: And the third method?

Alex: GitHub Desktop, if that's your preferred interface.

Jamie: When should people sync?

Alex: Before starting new work, before creating a new branch, if your pull request shows conflicts, and any time the upstream repo has moved significantly since your last update.

Alex: Next: commit messages. These are tiny pieces of communication, but they carry a lot of weight.

Jamie: What makes a commit message good?

Alex: A clear first line is required. It should briefly state what changed. The body is optional and can explain why, context, or tradeoffs. A footer is also optional for references like issue numbers or special notes.

Jamie: So the first line is the must-have.

Alex: Yes. Keep it specific and meaningful. "Fix broken README link" is useful. "Stuff" is not.

Jamie: And atomic commits?

Alex: That means each commit should represent one coherent, complete change. Not half a fix, not an unrelated bundle. Atomic commits make review easier, make rollback safer, and help future readers understand the history.

Jamie: Common mistakes?

Alex: Messages that are too vague, too long, or trying to describe multiple unrelated changes at once. Another common mistake is using commits as a dumping ground instead of making deliberate checkpoints.

Jamie: So a good commit message is part clarity, part respect for your future collaborators.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let's zoom out to the nature of open source communication. It is usually in writing, asynchronous, and public.

Jamie: Each of those changes how we should communicate.

Alex: They do. In writing means your words may be read without tone of voice or facial cues, so clarity matters. Asynchronously means people respond later, possibly in different time zones, so your message should stand on its own. In public means others may learn from the thread later, so context and professionalism matter even when you are talking to one person.

Jamie: That explains why vague comments feel extra costly online.

Alex: Yes. The reader cannot interrupt in real time to ask what you meant.

Alex: A very useful structure for feedback has five parts. First, acknowledge what's working.

Jamie: That lowers defensiveness and shows you actually read the work.

Alex: Exactly. Second, identify the specific concern. Be precise. Third, explain why it matters. Fourth, suggest a path forward when you can. And fifth, signal the weight of the concern.

Jamie: Meaning say whether it's required, optional, blocking, or just an idea.

Alex: Right. Not every comment has equal importance. If you don't signal weight, authors may treat preferences like hard requirements or ignore serious issues by mistake.

Jamie: Could that sound like, "Non-blocking suggestion," versus, "Required before merge because this breaks keyboard navigation"?

Alex: Perfect example.

Alex: Language and tone matter too. Prefer "we" language or describe the code rather than the person.

Jamie: So instead of "You wrote this wrong," say something like, "This function may fail when the input is empty," or "Could we handle the empty case here?"

Alex: Exactly. Use tentative language when you're uncertain: "I think," "It looks like," "Could this be." Acknowledge cultural and language diversity, because not everyone shares the same idioms, confidence norms, or first language. And avoid urgency markers unless something is truly urgent.

Jamie: Because "ASAP!!!" creates stress and often hides weak reasoning.

Alex: Yes. If it is genuinely urgent, say why.

Alex: Let's talk commenting etiquette. Keep comments focused.

Jamie: One comment per concern when possible?

Alex: Yes. Focused comments are easier to resolve and discuss. Also, don't leave comments unresolved without intention. Use conversation resolution thoughtfully.

Jamie: Meaning if a concern was addressed, resolve it. If not, don't quietly move on.

Alex: Right. And do not pile on. If someone already made the same point, you usually don't need to repeat it. Add a reaction or briefly note agreement if useful.

Jamie: That helps reduce noise.

Alex: It does. Reactions are part of etiquette too. A thumbs up can acknowledge agreement without forcing the author to read five duplicate comments.

Jamie: There's also a really practical accessibility trick here: saved replies.

Alex: Yes, and it's one of my favorite workflow improvements. Saved replies let you reuse common comment text. That reduces repetitive typing, supports consistency, and can lower cognitive and physical effort.

Jamie: Common uses?

Alex: Thank-you notes, review templates, requests for missing information, accessibility reminders, testing instructions, and standard explanations like "Please link the related issue" or "Could you add reproduction steps?"

Jamie: How do you create one?

Alex: In GitHub settings, create a saved reply with a name and body. Then when writing a comment, insert it from the comment box tools.

Jamie: And using it in a comment is basically choosing the saved reply and then customizing as needed.

Alex: Exactly. Never let templates make you sound robotic. Use them as a starting point.

Jamie: Any screen reader guidance?

Alex: Yes. Learn the path to the saved replies control in the comment editor and practice it once when you're not under time pressure. That turns it into a reliable accessibility win later.

Alex: Now, code review etiquette for reviewers. Review the code, not the person. Don't gatekeep knowledge. Ask questions instead of making demands when appropriate. Distinguish opinion from requirement. And when the work is ready, approve explicitly.

Jamie: Let's unpack "don't gatekeep knowledge."

Alex: If a contributor didn't know something, explain it or point to the resource. Don't act as though the lack of knowledge disqualifies them from participating.

Jamie: And "distinguish opinion from requirement" means separating style preferences from actual project policy or correctness issues.

Alex: Exactly. "I prefer this variable name" is different from "This violates the documented API contract."

Jamie: What about authors receiving review?

Alex: Say thank you. Don't take feedback personally. Explain your choices when needed. And surface blockers early.

Jamie: So if you're stuck applying requested changes, don't disappear.

Alex: Right. Say what is blocking you: a merge conflict, uncertainty about the request, lack of permissions, failed tests, or needing clarification.

Alex: There's also a specific topic here: inclusive commenting around accessibility issues.

Jamie: Meaning don't frame accessibility as a niche preference or optional extra.

Alex: Exactly. Describe the barrier and its impact. Focus on users and outcomes. Avoid language that minimizes the issue. And when possible, connect the feedback to standards, keyboard access, screen reader behavior, color contrast, focus order, meaningful alt text, or whatever concrete concern applies.

Jamie: So accessible feedback is precise, respectful, and grounded.

Alex: Yes.

Alex: Another subtle idea is the social contract behind the label "good first issue."

Jamie: That label is more than decoration.

Alex: Exactly. It suggests the issue is scoped appropriately for a newcomer, the problem is reasonably described, and maintainers will be responsive enough that a beginner is not abandoned.

Jamie: So if a project labels something "good first issue" but it actually needs deep architecture knowledge, that breaks trust.

Alex: Well said.

Alex: Open source also includes difficult moments. If you receive harsh feedback, pause before replying, extract the technical point if there is one, and respond calmly or seek help. If you disagree with a decision, ask for clarification and reasoning instead of escalating immediately.

Jamie: And if someone is rude to you?

Alex: Document what happened, disengage if needed, and use the project's code of conduct or moderation channels. You do not have to tolerate abuse to be a "good contributor."

Jamie: What if you realize you caused offense?

Alex: Acknowledge it directly, apologize without defensiveness, and change the behavior. Don't turn the conversation into a debate about your intentions.

Alex: Let's shift to documentation. Writing your first README is one of the most beginner-friendly and high-value contributions.

Jamie: What belongs in a README?

Alex: At minimum: project name, a short explanation of what the project is, installation steps if relevant, usage, contribution guidance, and license information.

Jamie: So a simple skeleton might be project name, installation, usage, contributing, and license.

Alex: Exactly. That skeleton is a strong starting point. A good README helps new users and contributors understand what the project does, how to run it, how to help, and what rules apply.

Jamie: What makes a README accessible?

Alex: Clear headings, meaningful link text, readable structure, alt text for images when appropriate, not relying on screenshots alone for essential instructions, and keeping prose concise and scannable.

Jamie: And good versus bad?

Alex: A good README answers basic newcomer questions quickly. A bad README is vague, outdated, missing setup steps, or visually flashy but structurally weak for screen reader users.

Alex: Related to that are community health files. These are the governance and guidance files that help people participate responsibly.

Jamie: Let's name them.

Alex: CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to contribute. CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md describes expected behavior and reporting paths. SECURITY.md tells people how to report security vulnerabilities safely. LICENSE defines legal reuse rights. And you should know how to find these files on GitHub, because they often answer questions before you need to ask them.

Jamie: So before contributing, reading these files is both polite and strategic.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Another important skill is choosing the right communication channel.

Jamie: Public issue, pull request comment, discussion, direct contact, security report"”those aren't interchangeable.

Alex: Right. Use issues for trackable work and bugs, pull requests for code-specific review, discussions when a repository enables broader conversation, and private security channels for vulnerabilities. Match the channel to the purpose and privacy needs.

Jamie: There was also a quick-reference idea in the chapter: phrases that work.

Alex: Yes. Practical phrases like: "I may be missing context, but"¦", "Could we clarify"¦", "Non-blocking suggestion: "¦", "Thanks, this part is especially clear," and "I'm stuck at step three; I tried A and B." These are small wording choices that make collaboration easier.

Jamie: And learners are encouraged to rewrite one comment as practice.

Alex: Exactly. Turning a blunt or vague comment into one that is specific, respectful, and actionable is a great exercise.

Alex: Now let's widen the lens to first-time contribution in general. Open source means source code and project materials are available for people to inspect, use, and often modify under a license.

Jamie: Who can contribute?

Alex: Anyone. Not only expert programmers. Documentation writers, testers, designers, translators, accessibility reviewers, issue triagers, and people who improve examples or reporting all contribute.

Jamie: What makes a good first contribution?

Alex: Something small, clear, and contained. Maybe a documentation fix, typo, broken link, simple bug reproduction clarification, or a focused accessibility improvement.

Jamie: And signs it's too large for a first attempt?

Alex: The issue is vague, touches many files, requires architecture decisions, has unclear acceptance criteria, or depends on unfinished background work.

Jamie: How do people find something to work on?

Alex: Look for labels like good first issue, documentation, help wanted, or accessibility. Read the repository's README and contribution guide. Search issues with clear scope. And notice whether maintainers seem active and responsive.

Jamie: Then read the issue carefully before starting.

Alex: Yes. Understand the problem, expected behavior, current discussion, linked files, and whether someone is already working on it.

Alex: The basic contribution workflow is often: fork the repository, clone your fork locally if you're working locally, create a branch, edit files, commit your changes, push, and open a pull request.

Jamie: That connects back to GitHub Flow.

Alex: Exactly. And your pull request description matters. Explain what changed, why, how to test it, and link the related issue when appropriate.

Jamie: Such as using a closing keyword if the PR should close an issue when merged.

Alex: Right. We'll come back to that in the cross-reference section.

Jamie: What about getting help?

Alex: Ask clear questions. Include what you expected, what happened instead, what step you were on, and what you already tried. That's more helpful than "It doesn't work."

Jamie: And after your contribution is merged?

Alex: Celebrate, but also keep learning. Read feedback, note what reviewers focused on, maybe thank maintainers, and consider a second contribution while the workflow is still fresh.

Jamie: That's how you build a contribution habit.

Alex: Yes. Practical habits include making small contributions regularly, reading project docs before asking, keeping branches focused, and leaving the project slightly clearer than you found it.

Alex: Now we move into the organizational layer: labels, milestones, projects, and cross-references.

Jamie: This is the part that turns a messy issue list into something navigable.

Alex: Exactly. And there's a workshop challenge here too. Learners read an open issue and post a structured triage recommendation that a maintainer could act on immediately.

Jamie: What's in that recommendation?

Alex: Four fields: suggested labels, suggested milestone, suggested project board column, and a one-sentence reason. If the learner has write access, they can apply the labels and milestone directly.

Jamie: And if they don't have permissions?

Alex: They can still do valuable triage. Triage is about clarity, not authority.

Jamie: I love that line.

Alex: It's true. A clear recommendation saves maintainers time even if you cannot click the controls yourself.

Jamie: There's also an agentic angle mentioned in the material.

Alex: Yes. Labels and issue states can drive automation or agents. For example, an agent might only activate when an issue gets a specific label like needs-review or accessibility-check.

Alex: So, labels. They are colored tags on issues and pull requests that communicate category, priority, status, or other metadata at a glance.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, those labels are announced with the issue title.

Alex: Right. You may hear "Label: bug" or "Labels: accessibility, good first issue." That auditory context helps scanning.

Jamie: What standard labels should beginners recognize?

Alex: Common ones include bug, enhancement, documentation, good first issue, help wanted, question, invalid, wontfix, duplicate, accessibility, and needs triage.

Jamie: How do you get to the labels page?

Alex: From a repository, go to the Issues tab and find the Labels link near Milestones in the toolbar. For screen reader users, that may mean navigating to the Issues tab and using link navigation to find Labels. On macOS with VoiceOver, quick nav or rotor navigation can help. On Windows with NVDA or JAWS, heading or link shortcuts can help.

Jamie: And in the terminal?

Alex: Using GitHub CLI, you can list all labels with descriptions using gh label list, or output structured data with JSON fields like name and description.

Alex: Applying labels can happen in several environments. In the browser, open the issue or PR, find the Labels control in the right sidebar, activate it, and select one or more labels. In VS Code with the GitHub Pull Requests extension, you can manage labels from the GitHub panel. GitHub Desktop doesn't directly manage labels, so you usually bounce to the browser. In GitHub CLI, you can edit an issue or PR and add labels from the command line.

Jamie: What should screen reader users expect when using the browser control?

Alex: Usually a button or gear next to Labels in the sidebar. Activating it opens a dropdown where labels can be navigated, filtered by typing, selected or deselected, and then closed with Escape. Selections save automatically.

Jamie: Can you add multiple labels at once?

Alex: Yes. You can add more than one, remove labels, and apply labels to either issues or pull requests.

Jamie: And filtering by label is where labels really become useful.

Alex: Exactly. You can list issues with a specific label, combine multiple labels, combine label filters with state like open or closed, and search across labels to find patterns.

Jamie: Can repos create custom labels too?

Alex: Yes. A maintainer can create a new label, give it a name, description, and color. Color can be meaningful visually, but the text name and description matter most for accessibility.

Alex: Next are milestones. A milestone groups issues or pull requests toward a larger target, often a release, sprint, phase, or event.

Jamie: So if labels classify the type of work, milestones group work by shared destination.

Alex: Exactly. You can navigate to Milestones from the Issues area. Reading a milestone typically tells you its title, due date if any, description, and progress, such as how many items are open or closed.

Jamie: What does opening a milestone mean here?

Alex: Creating or viewing an active milestone for current work. Then individual issues can be assigned to that milestone or removed from it.

Jamie: And with GitHub CLI or the web, you can list issues in a milestone too.

Alex: Right. That helps you see what belongs to a shared goal.

Alex: Cross-references are another small but powerful feature.

Jamie: Meaning linking issues and pull requests to each other?

Alex: Yes. Types of cross-references include mentioning an issue number, linking from a pull request to an issue, or using closing keywords like "Closes #42."

Jamie: And when does the closing keyword actually fire?

Alex: When the pull request is merged into the relevant branch. Merely opening the PR does not close the issue. The merge triggers the close.

Jamie: That's an important nuance.

Alex: It is. Good cross-references make work traceable. They connect the problem discussion to the proposed fix.

Alex: Then there are GitHub Projects, which are planning and tracking spaces that can show work in table or board views.

Jamie: What should a blind or low-vision learner know about navigating them?

Alex: First, know where to find a project from the repository or organization. In table view, think in rows and fields. A screen reader may announce the item title plus row-related details depending on focus. In board view, think in columns and cards, similar to To Do, In Progress, Done, or Needs Triage.

Jamie: So table view may be more structured for some users, while board view may mirror workflow stages.

Alex: Exactly. And issues can be added to a project so they appear in that planning system alongside metadata.

Alex: For the hackathon, the materials suggest a practical organization strategy.

Jamie: Let me guess: create a small useful label set, maybe a milestone, and follow a simple workflow.

Alex: That's it. Labels to create might include documentation, bug, accessibility, enhancement, and good first issue. A milestone could represent the hackathon or a workshop phase. The workflow is to inspect new issues, label them, decide whether they belong in the milestone, and place them in the right project column such as Needs Triage, To Do, or In Progress.

Jamie: So not overengineering. Just enough structure to make the work visible.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let's tie this back to the triage challenge. A strong triage recommendation might sound like this: issue number, suggested labels documentation and accessibility, suggested milestone hackathon day one, suggested project column Needs Triage, one-sentence reason explaining that the issue is a docs fix affecting access and should be reviewed before active implementation.

Jamie: And if milestone or project placement is unclear?

Alex: Say none and explain why, or use Needs Triage as the safe default. Uncertainty stated clearly is better than pretending confidence.

Jamie: That's a nice general rule for open source communication too.

Alex: It is.

Alex: Before we close, let's revisit the challenge logistics from both chapters in one place. For the culture challenge, you may be asked to share a reflection in the peer simulation issue or with a buddy. Different perspectives enrich the community. If you don't see labels, you may need to create them or ask a facilitator to set up defaults. If you can't label someone else's issue, that may be a permissions issue, not a personal mistake.

Jamie: And if you don't know what to reflect on, start simple: what is one thing you learned today?

Alex: Exactly. There are no wrong answers if the reflection is thoughtful. For the organization challenge, if you're unsure which label to pick, start with one of documentation, bug, or accessibility. If the milestone is unclear, say none with a reason. If the board column is unknown, Needs Triage is a valid default.

Jamie: And both challenges use a similar philosophy: explain your reasoning clearly.

Alex: Yes. Reflection and triage are both forms of visible thinking.

Jamie: Can we end with a few behaviors learners can carry into every repository they touch?

Alex: Absolutely. Keep branches focused: one thing per branch. Sync your fork before starting new work. Write clear commit messages. Read the README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, and LICENSE files. In review, acknowledge what works, be specific about concerns, explain why they matter, and signal whether they're blocking. Use respectful, low-assumption language. Don't pile on duplicate comments. Use reactions and saved replies wisely. Label and link issues so work is easier to find. And remember that accessibility includes the collaboration process, not just the shipped product.

Jamie: That last point really changes how you see open source.

Alex: It does. The best projects do not only welcome contributions in theory. They make participation understandable, navigable, and humane.

Jamie: And that's good culture and good engineering.

Alex: Exactly.

Read Transcript - Episode 9: Labels, Milestones, and Projects

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're focusing on how GitHub stops being just a pile of issues and pull requests and starts becoming an organized workspace. The big tools are labels, milestones, projects, and cross-references.

Jamie: So this is the part where GitHub becomes less of a list and more of a system?

Alex: Exactly. These are the organizational layer. They help people categorize work, set priorities, group related items, and connect conversations across issues and pull requests.

Jamie: And for our learners, especially people using screen readers, that organization matters a lot.

Alex: It really does. Good organization reduces hunting. Instead of opening issue after issue, you can filter, sort, and listen for useful metadata like labels, milestone names, and project status.

Alex: A quick administrative note before we teach the tools. This lesson pairs with the chapter's audio episode, and there are also related appendices, including a projects deep dive and a glossary. The authoritative references behind this lesson are GitHub Docs on labels, milestones, and projects.

Jamie: And there's also a workshop task in this chapter, right?

Alex: Yes. This chapter's workshop recommendation is a guided triage activity. You are asked to read an issue and post a structured triage recommendation that a maintainer could act on immediately.

Jamie: So not just, "I think this is important," but a usable recommendation.

Alex: Right. The challenge count is one guided challenge. There's no automation check by default. Your evidence is a structured comment in your assigned challenge issue. And the learning pattern is inspect, classify, explain.

Jamie: That pattern sounds simple, but also very real-world.

Alex: It is. In open source, triage is often the difference between chaos and momentum.

Jamie: Walk us through the actual challenge.

Alex: Your goal is to read the details of a Learning Room issue and post a structured triage recommendation. You're working in your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com. You'll use your assigned Chapter 9 challenge issue plus one other open issue that you inspect. First, open the Issues tab in your repository. Second, find an open issue that doesn't already have labels, or use one assigned by a facilitator. Third, read the title and full description carefully.

Jamie: And what are learners looking for while reading?

Alex: A few things. What type of work is this? Documentation fix, bug report, accessibility improvement, new content, something else? How urgent does it seem? Is it blocking other work, is it nice-to-have, or is the urgency unclear? And what file or area of the repository does it affect?

Jamie: So before touching labels, you're forming a mental model.

Alex: Exactly. Then you open your assigned challenge issue, the one titled something like Chapter 9.1 with your name, and in the comment box you post a recommendation in a four-part format. You name the issue number. You suggest labels, usually one to three, from examples like documentation, bug, accessibility, enhancement, or good first issue. You suggest a milestone, or say none and give a reason. You suggest a project board column such as To Do, In Progress, or Needs Triage. And then you give a one-sentence reason explaining the choice.

Jamie: That's nicely constrained. It forces clear thinking.

Alex: Yes. And if you happen to have write access, you can go beyond recommending and directly apply the labels and milestone on the issue itself. Then activate the Comment button to submit your recommendation.

Jamie: There was also an important accessibility tip here.

Alex: Yes. If you're browsing available labels with a screen reader, open the repository's Labels page using the slash labels path. That page presents label names and descriptions together, which is often easier to review than a compact dropdown.

Jamie: And when are you done?

Alex: When your triage recommendation comment appears in your assigned challenge issue with all four fields filled in.

Jamie: What counts as evidence for completing the chapter?

Alex: That comment is your evidence. After you're done, close your Chapter 9 challenge issue. If you also applied labels directly, mention that in your comment.

Jamie: And the expected outcomes?

Alex: You should be able to read an issue and recommend appropriate labels, a milestone, and project placement. You should understand triage reasoning even if you don't have maintainer permissions. And you should be able to leave a clear note that a maintainer could act on immediately.

Jamie: Let's also normalize getting stuck.

Alex: Absolutely. If you're unsure which label to choose, start with one basic label like documentation, bug, or accessibility. If the milestone is unclear, writing none with a reason is valid triage. If you don't know the project board placement, Needs Triage is the correct default. If the issue itself is unclear, say that. "Issue description is unclear, needs more detail" is useful triage feedback. And you can always ask a facilitator to review your one-sentence reason before you post.

Jamie: I love the chapter's core idea here: triage is about clarity, not authority.

Alex: Yes. You do not need maintainer permissions to be helpful. A clear recommendation saves maintainers time and speeds collaboration. This is a daily open-source skill.

Jamie: And for continued learning, there was a GitHub Skills course mentioned.

Alex: Right. The Introduction to Repository Management course is a good follow-up for labels, milestones, and contributor settings.

Jamie: Let's move into labels. What are they, in plain language?

Alex: Labels are colored tags applied to issues and pull requests. They communicate category, priority, or status at a glance.

Jamie: And from an audio or screen reader perspective?

Alex: When you scan an issue list, labels are announced alongside the issue title. A screen reader might say, "Label: bug," or "Labels: accessibility, good first issue." That makes labels more than visual decoration. They're spoken metadata.

Jamie: What are the standard labels learners will commonly encounter?

Alex: A typical set includes bug for something not working as expected, enhancement for a new feature or improvement, documentation for docs-only work, good first issue for beginner-friendly tasks, help wanted when maintainers want community help, question when more information is needed, invalid when an issue doesn't meet project criteria, wontfix when the project won't address it, duplicate when another issue already covers it, accessibility for accessibility-related work, and needs triage for items not yet reviewed by a maintainer.

Jamie: That list already teaches a vocabulary for participation.

Alex: Exactly. A consistent label vocabulary makes collaboration faster.

Jamie: How do you get to the Labels page in a repository?

Alex: From the repository, go to the Issues tab, then find the Labels link or button in the toolbar near Milestones. The Labels page lists every label with its color, name, and description. For Windows screen reader users with NVDA or JAWS, you can navigate to the Issues tab, press K to move through links until you find the Labels link, then press Enter. For VoiceOver on macOS, go to the Issues tab, use Quick Nav K to find the Labels link, and activate it with VO+Space.

Jamie: And there's also a terminal option.

Alex: Yes. With GitHub CLI, you can list all labels with descriptions using gh label list. If you want structured output, you can use gh label list with JSON fields such as name and description.

Jamie: That can be especially helpful if someone prefers terminal output they can pipe, search, or reformat.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now let's actually apply labels. How does that work on an issue or PR?

Alex: In the browser on GitHub.com, open the issue or pull request. In the right sidebar, find Labels and activate the gear or edit button. A dropdown opens with available labels. Select one or more labels, then click outside or press Escape. The selections save automatically.

Jamie: And that same idea applies to pull requests, not just issues?

Alex: Yes. Labels can be applied to both.

Jamie: What about other tools?
