Alex: In github.dev, label management isn't available in the code editor itself, so you use the issue or PR page. In VS Code Desktop with the GitHub Pull Requests extension, you can open the issue in the GitHub sidebar and use the label area to add or remove labels. In GitHub Desktop, labels aren't directly supported, so you'd use View on GitHub in the browser.

Jamie: And on the command line?

Alex: With GitHub CLI, you can edit an issue and add a label, or add multiple labels at once by passing a comma-separated list. You can do the same for a pull request.

Jamie: Let's make the accessibility steps concrete.

Alex: For NVDA or JAWS, navigate to the Labels heading in the sidebar, activate the Labels button, use arrow keys in the dropdown, press Enter to select or deselect a label, and type to filter, like typing access to jump toward accessibility. Press Escape to close. For VoiceOver, find the Labels heading, activate the button with VO+Space, navigate the dropdown with VO+Down or arrow keys, select with VO+Space, and use typing to filter.

Jamie: So the key actions are open the control, navigate, select, filter if needed, and close.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let's name the common tasks explicitly: add a label to an issue, add multiple labels at once, remove a label, and add a label to a PR.

Alex: Right. Those are the core operations learners should expect.

Jamie: Once labels exist, filtering is where they really become useful.

Alex: That's right. You can filter issues by label to narrow a long list. For example, show only issues with a specific label like accessibility. You can also combine multiple labels to find issues that meet several conditions at once.

Jamie: Like issues that are both documentation and good first issue?

Alex: Exactly. You can also combine label filters with state, such as open issues with a particular label. And you can search across labels more generally when you're exploring patterns in the repository.

Jamie: So labels aren't just tags. They're handles for finding work.

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: What if the label you need doesn't exist yet?

Alex: Then you create a new label, assuming you have permission. On the Labels page, there's an option to create a label by giving it a name, description, and color. You can create a basic new label, or create one with a specific color to support a consistent visual system.

Jamie: Does the description matter much?

Alex: Yes. The description is especially important for accessibility and clarity. A good label description tells contributors when the label should be used. That's useful for everyone and especially helpful on the Labels page where screen readers announce both name and description.

Jamie: Any learning summary for labels?

Alex: Yes. Think of labels as reusable categories. Keep them meaningful. Use a stable vocabulary. Apply only what helps. And remember that labels support both quick scanning and powerful filtering.

Jamie: Next up: milestones. How are milestones different from labels?

Alex: A milestone groups issues and pull requests toward a shared target, often a release, phase, or deadline. Labels answer, "What kind of work is this?" Milestones answer, "What larger goal or time-bound effort is this part of?"

Jamie: So labels classify, milestones group.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How do you navigate to milestones?

Alex: From the Issues area of a repository, find the Milestones link near Labels. The milestones page lists available milestones. When you open one, you're reading a summary of that target: its title, optional description, due date if there is one, and progress based on open and closed items.

Jamie: That progress view is helpful. It's not just a bucket; it's a tracking tool.

Alex: Right. Reading a milestone means noticing what it represents and how much work remains.

Jamie: How do you open a milestone from an issue workflow?

Alex: You can go directly from the Milestones page and activate the milestone title. Or from an issue, if a milestone is already assigned, you can follow that reference to inspect the milestone's details.

Jamie: And how do you add an issue to a milestone?

Alex: Open the issue, go to the right sidebar, find the Milestone control, and assign one. If you're using GitHub CLI, you can edit the issue and set or change the milestone there as well.

Jamie: And the chapter specifically expects learners to understand three milestone operations: assign an issue to a milestone, remove it from a milestone, and list issues in a milestone.

Alex: Exactly. Assigning places the issue into that tracked target. Removing detaches it if it was misclassified or deprioritized. Listing issues in a milestone lets you review everything contributing to that goal.

Jamie: What about creating a milestone?

Alex: If you have permission, go to the Milestones page and create one with a title, description, and optionally a due date. A good milestone name is specific enough to communicate a concrete target, like a release, a sprint, or a hackathon phase.

Jamie: What's the main learning card for milestones?

Alex: Use milestones for grouped outcomes, not tiny categories. If labels are descriptive tags, milestones are shared destinations.

Jamie: Now cross-references. This is one of those GitHub features people use constantly without always naming it.

Alex: Very true. A cross-reference is when one GitHub item mentions another in a way GitHub understands and links. Common types include referencing an issue from another issue, referencing an issue from a pull request, and using special closing keywords in a pull request to connect code changes to issues.

Jamie: Let's start with the basic typing pattern.

Alex: The most common form is the number reference, like hash 42, inside the same repository. GitHub turns that into a link to issue or pull request number 42. You can also reference items across repositories using owner slash repo, then hash number.

Jamie: And when you do that, GitHub often creates a visible backlink, right?

Alex: Yes. That's one of the most useful effects. The referenced issue often shows that it was mentioned elsewhere, which helps people trace related work and discussion.

Jamie: Now the special case: the closes keyword.

Alex: Important one. If a pull request description or a merged commit message uses a closing keyword like closes, fixes, or resolves followed by an issue reference, GitHub can automatically close the linked issue when the pull request is merged into the right branch.

Jamie: So not when the PR is opened.

Alex: Correct. The keyword fires on merge, not merely on mention. That's crucial. A plain reference links discussion. A closing keyword links discussion plus intended completion.

Jamie: That's a subtle but important distinction.

Alex: It is. And it's part of writing responsibly on GitHub. If you're not sure the PR fully solves the issue, use a plain reference rather than a closing keyword.

Jamie: What's the compact learning summary here?

Alex: Cross-references connect context. Plain references say, "these items are related." Closing keywords say, "merging this should complete that issue." Use them intentionally.

Jamie: Let's talk about GitHub Projects. People sometimes confuse projects with milestones.

Alex: That's common. A GitHub Project is a broader planning and tracking space. It can include issues, pull requests, and draft items, arranged in views like tables or boards. Projects are useful for workflow management across a repository, or even across multiple repositories.

Jamie: So if milestones are targets, projects are like planning dashboards.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How do you find a project?

Alex: You may find one from a repository, an organization, or a user profile, depending on how it's set up. Look for a Projects tab or project links associated with the repository or organization.

Jamie: Once inside a project, what does table view look like conceptually?

Alex: Table view presents each item as a row with fields in columns. Those fields might include title, status, assignee, labels, milestone, repository, and other custom properties.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, what matters per row?

Alex: What is announced per row is usually the item title plus the current values for the visible fields. So you want to understand that each row is not just the issue title; it's a bundle of metadata. Moving row by row lets you hear status, owner, and category in sequence.

Jamie: That's a great mental model.

Alex: In board view, items are grouped into columns, often by status. Think of columns like To Do, In Progress, and Done or Needs Triage. You move across columns to understand workflow stage, and within a column to review the items at that stage.

Jamie: So table view is dense metadata. Board view is stage-oriented.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: How do you add an issue to a project?

Alex: There are a few common ways. From the issue page, use the sidebar control to add the issue to a project. Or within the project itself, add an existing item by selecting the issue. Once added, the project can track fields like status and priority separately from the issue's own labels and milestone.

Jamie: That "separately" matters. Projects don't replace labels and milestones.

Alex: Right. They complement them. Labels describe. Milestones group toward goals. Projects manage workflow and planning.

Jamie: And the learning summary for projects?

Alex: Use projects when you need a live workspace for planning, prioritizing, and moving work through stages.

Jamie: Let's make this practical. The chapter includes an organization strategy for a hackathon.

Alex: Yes. This is where all the pieces come together. For a hackathon or workshop repo, create a small, purposeful set of labels. For example, documentation, bug, accessibility, enhancement, good first issue, and needs triage. You might also include help wanted if community pickup is encouraged.

Jamie: So not dozens of labels just because you can.

Alex: Exactly. Keep the set teachable and useful.

Jamie: What milestone should be created?

Alex: A milestone representing the hackathon target. That might be the event name, a release goal, or a chapter completion target. The key is that all related issues can be grouped under that shared outcome.

Jamie: And what's the workflow?

Alex: New issues start in Needs Triage. After review, apply one to three meaningful labels. If the work belongs to the event goal, assign the milestone. Add it to the project and place it in the appropriate column, such as To Do or In Progress. As implementation proceeds, use cross-references to link issues and pull requests. If a pull request truly completes an issue, use a closing keyword so the issue closes on merge.

Jamie: That sounds like a clean repeatable process.

Alex: It is. And it's scalable.

Jamie: There's also a hands-on prompt here: label and link.

Alex: Yes. The idea is to practice both organization and connection. Pick an issue, apply or recommend an appropriate label, and create a useful cross-reference to related work. That reinforces that GitHub organization is not just tagging; it's building navigable context.

Jamie: Before we wrap, I want to return to one line from earlier about agents waking up when labels or states change.

Alex: That's an excellent detail. Labels and issue states aren't only for humans. They're also signals for automation and agentic workflows. In a future capstone, you might design an agent that activates only when an issue gets a label like needs-review or accessibility-check. So good triage can trigger the right follow-up work automatically.

Jamie: Which means classification can become action.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can you give us a final compact comparison of the four tools?

Alex: Sure. Labels tell you what kind of work something is. Milestones tell you what larger target it's part of. Projects tell you where it sits in a workflow or planning system. Cross-references tell you what other conversations or changes it's connected to.

Jamie: And the habit behind all of them?

Alex: Inspect carefully, classify consistently, explain your reasoning, and leave the repository easier to navigate than you found it.

Jamie: That's a strong open-source habit.

Alex: It is. And one final administrative note: the chapter includes authoritative sources and a section-level source map pointing back to GitHub Docs, the GitHub changelog, and the GitHub Projects, labels, and milestones documentation. Those references are there so you can verify details and keep learning from the primary sources.

Jamie: So if you finish this lesson, your next move is simple: open an issue, read it carefully, recommend or apply a label, consider the milestone and project placement, and connect it to related work if needed.

Alex: Exactly. Clear triage is real contribution.

25. Episode 26: GitHub Projects Deep Dive

Project boards, table and roadmap views, custom fields, cross-repo management.

Based on: Appendix R: GitHub Projects Deep Dive

Download Episode 26 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 26: GitHub Projects Deep Dive

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re doing a deep dive into GitHub Projects, especially the modern Projects experience sometimes called Projects v2. Think of this as GitHub’s built-in project management system for issues, pull requests, and draft work items, all in one place.

Jamie: So this is for people who already know GitHub issues and maybe milestones, but want the bigger planning picture?

Alex: Exactly. And it’s especially helpful if you want one living workspace that can pull work from one repository or many repositories, then show it as a table, a board, or a roadmap. We’ll also keep accessibility front and center: keyboard use, screen reader behavior, and low-vision navigation.

Alex: One quick framing note. This appendix is a companion to the earlier material on labels, milestones, and projects. Here we’re going beyond the basics.

Jamie: And before we get into the how, what changed with the newer Projects system?

Alex: A lot. GitHub had an older generation sometimes called classic projects. That older system was mostly Kanban only. The newer Projects version gives you three layouts: Board, Table, and Roadmap.

Jamie: So not just sticky notes in columns anymore.

Alex: Right. You also get custom fields now, which is a huge shift. Instead of just title and labels and assignees, you can add your own fields like text notes, numeric estimates, dates, single-select choices like priority, and iteration fields for sprint-style planning.

Jamie: What about automation?

Alex: Also improved. Classic projects had very limited built-in behavior. Projects v2 supports built-in workflows and integrates with GitHub Actions. Filtering is much stronger too. You can query by labels, assignees, statuses, and custom field values. Cross-repository tracking is supported, and the API story is more powerful through GraphQL.

Jamie: And if someone sees old references to Projects Beta?

Alex: That was the earlier rollout period for this newer system. Today, Projects v2 is the standard one people mean.

Jamie: Okay, I want to create one. Where can a project live?

Alex: Two common places. At the organization level, which makes sense when a team wants shared planning across multiple repositories. Or at the repository level, which is narrower and centered on one repo.

Jamie: Let’s start with organization-level creation.

Alex: You navigate to the organization page, open the Projects tab, activate the New project button, choose a template or start blank, give the project a name, and activate Create project.

Jamie: What kinds of templates are we talking about?

Alex: Things like a blank table, blank board, or a more opinionated setup like a feature release template. Templates can save time if you already know the workflow pattern you want.

Jamie: And from a repository?

Alex: Very similar. Go to the repository, open its Projects tab, then use Link a project or New project, depending on what GitHub shows there. If you create a new one, the template and naming flow is basically the same.

Jamie: Can we pause on the screen reader flow? Because this is one of those spots where sighted walkthroughs can hide important interaction details.

Alex: Absolutely. A typical screen reader path is: go to the org or repo Projects tab, tab to the green New project button, press Enter. The template dialog opens. Use arrow keys to move among template cards, each announcing its name and description. Press Enter on the one you want. Then type the project name in the name field, tab to Create project, press Enter, and you’ll land in the new empty project.

Jamie: And after creation, what should users expect?

Alex: Usually an empty project in Table view. There’s often a plus Add item control near the bottom. For screen reader users, tabbing to that control is a reliable way to start adding work. For low-vision users, one practical note: at high zoom, that add-item row may be off-screen, so scrolling down matters.

Jamie: And visually, the New project button tends to be easy to spot?

Alex: Yes, typically a green high-contrast button on the Projects tab.

Jamie: Now let’s talk about the three layouts, because this seems like the heart of the system.

Alex: It is. The default is usually Table view. Think spreadsheet. Each row is an issue, a pull request, or a draft item. Each column is a field: title, status, assignee, labels, priority, dates, repository, or any custom fields you create.

Jamie: What is Table view best at?

Alex: Bulk editing, sorting, filtering, and scanning lots of structured information quickly. If you want the most information density, this is usually the winner.

Jamie: And accessibility-wise?

Alex: It’s generally the most accessible layout. Keyboard movement is strong. Common shortcuts and navigation patterns include jumping to the table, moving up and down between rows, left and right between columns, pressing Enter to open the item detail panel in the right sidebar, Escape to close that panel, Space on a cell to edit the value, and F2 on the title cell for inline title editing.

Jamie: What does a row sound like in a screen reader?

Alex: Something like: title first, then field-value pairs. For example, “Fix keyboard trap in modal dialog, Status: In Progress, Assignee: alice, Priority: High, Labels: bug, accessibility.” That row-style verbal summary is one reason Table view works so well nonvisually.

Jamie: So if someone is blind and choosing a default working view, Table is probably the safest choice.

Alex: Yes. Table first, especially for editing.

Jamie: What about Board view?

Alex: Board view is the Kanban-style layout. Columns represent status values, and cards sit inside those columns. It’s excellent for workflow tracking, work-in-progress conversations, and quick standup-style reviews.

Jamie: But I know there’s an accessibility catch here.

Alex: There is. Drag-and-drop is not keyboard accessible in the way many users need. So the accessible method for changing a card’s column is not dragging. Instead, open the card, find the Status field in the right-side detail panel, activate the status dropdown, choose the new value, and then close the panel.

Jamie: That’s such an important pattern: don’t imitate the visual gesture if the underlying field can be edited directly.

Alex: Exactly. The column is just a visual expression of the Status field. Change the field, and the card moves.

Jamie: Keyboard-wise, how do people move around the board?

Alex: Tab commonly moves among columns and cards. Enter on a card opens the detail panel. In some contexts, heading or region navigation can help jump among board areas. And within a card context, Space may toggle selection for bulk actions.

Jamie: For low-vision users, any practical warning?

Alex: Yes. Board columns can overflow horizontally, so at high zoom you may need to scroll sideways. Card details like label badges or avatars can become small and crowded, so zooming in on a single card or switching to Table view can be easier.

Jamie: And Roadmap view?

Alex: Roadmap is a horizontal timeline. Items appear as bars spanning dates, often start dates and due dates, or iteration windows. It’s useful for release planning, sprint capacity planning, and communicating timing to stakeholders.

Jamie: This sounds visually rich, but maybe less accessible directly.

Alex: That’s the right instinct. Roadmap is chart-like, so for screen reader users it’s best treated as a visual summary rather than the primary editing surface. The underlying data is still accessible in Table view. So the recommended workflow is: edit and verify in Table, then switch to Roadmap if you want the big timeline picture.

Jamie: How do items get onto the roadmap timeline?

Alex: They need date information. You can add Date custom fields like Start Date and Due Date, or sometimes use milestone-related timing depending on your setup. Items without dates usually sit outside the timeline grouping.

Jamie: And low-vision users may need more zoom because those bars can be narrow.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s move into custom fields, because this is where Projects starts feeling like a real planning database.

Alex: That’s a great way to say it. Projects includes default fields like Title, Assignee, Labels, Milestone, and Repository, but its real power comes from adding your own structured fields.

Jamie: Walk us through the major field types.

Alex: Text fields are free-form notes, useful for links, criteria, or reminders. Number fields are for numeric values like estimates or story points. Date fields store deadlines or start dates. Single select gives you a dropdown of predefined choices, great for priority, size, risk, or type. And Iteration fields support sprint or cycle planning.

Jamie: How do you create one?

Alex: From Table view, you usually move to the far end of the header row and activate the plus button that adds a field. Then you choose the field type, provide the field name, and configure options if needed. For single-select, for example, you define the allowed values such as P0, P1, and P2.

Jamie: What about the screen reader path for that?

Alex: The important pieces are: get into Table view, move across the header row until you reach the add-field control, activate it, select the field type from the menu or dialog, then fill in the naming and option fields. Because this interaction can involve horizontal movement across many columns, it may take some patience, especially in a busy project.

Jamie: And once the field exists, how do you edit a value on an item?

Alex: Usually two ways. In Table view, navigate to the cell and activate it, often with Space, then choose or type the value. Or open the item detail panel and edit the field there in the sidebar. The panel method is often clearer for screen reader users because it exposes labeled controls in a more linear form.

Jamie: So if a learner finds the grid editing model awkward, the sidebar is a good fallback.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: Now let’s add work items. What exactly can live inside a project?

Alex: Three main categories: existing issues, existing pull requests, and draft issues. Drafts are especially handy when you want to capture work before a formal issue exists in a repository.

Jamie: How do you add an existing issue or pull request?

Alex: Use the add-item control in the project, then search for the issue or PR you want. Depending on the project’s scope and permissions, you can pull in items from linked repositories or other repos in a cross-repository setup.

Jamie: And a draft issue?

Alex: A draft issue is created directly in the project without immediately creating a repository issue. It’s useful for planning, brainstorming, backlog triage, or work that isn’t ready to be assigned to a repo yet.

Jamie: Then later you can promote it?

Alex: Yes. Promoting a draft turns it into a real GitHub issue in a repository. That’s a nice bridge between planning and execution.

Jamie: So a team can start fuzzy, then formalize later.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about bulk editing?

Alex: That’s one of Table view’s strengths. You can select multiple items and update shared properties together, such as status, iteration, assignee, or other field values. In practice, this is useful when moving a batch of tasks into a sprint, closing out a release phase, or assigning a common label or priority pattern.

Jamie: Accessibility tip there?

Alex: Know how selection is announced, and confirm the set of selected items before applying the bulk change. In any bulk operation, the risk isn’t understanding one item; it’s accidentally changing many.

Jamie: Let’s get to automations. What can Projects do on its own?

Alex: GitHub Projects includes built-in workflows and can also work with GitHub Actions. The idea is to reduce repetitive project maintenance.

Jamie: Where do people access automations?

Alex: Typically through project settings or a workflows area associated with the project. The exact UI can shift over time, but conceptually you’re looking for automation or workflow configuration within the project’s controls.

Jamie: And what kinds of built-in workflows are we talking about?

Alex: Common examples include automatically adding items to a project when they meet certain conditions, or updating fields based on status changes and project events. The source emphasizes native workflows and GitHub Actions integration rather than treating the project as a totally manual tool.

Jamie: I noticed auto-add was specifically called out.

Alex: Yes. Auto-add is especially useful when you want matching issues or pull requests to appear in a project automatically. For example, perhaps all issues with a certain label, or work from a specific repository, should flow into a tracking project without someone manually adding them every time.

Jamie: That sounds powerful, but also like something you’d want to test carefully.

Alex: Absolutely. Start with a narrow rule, verify the results, then expand. Automation should reduce work, not create surprise clutter.

Jamie: And GitHub Actions integration means you can go beyond built-in toggles?

Alex: Right. Actions can update project fields, move work through states, or synchronize project data with repository events in more advanced workflows. If your team already uses Actions, Projects becomes another place where automation can keep planning data current.

Jamie: Now the sprint story: iterations.

Alex: Iterations are GitHub’s sprint-like field type. Instead of storing just a random date, an iteration field defines repeating cycles, such as two-week sprints.

Jamie: How do you create one?

Alex: Create a custom field and choose Iteration as the type. Then configure the cadence, such as duration and start date. GitHub generates the repeating iteration values from that setup.

Jamie: And using iterations means assigning each item to one of those sprint buckets?

Alex: Exactly. Once the field exists, items can be assigned to a specific iteration, making it easy to filter by current sprint, next sprint, or backlog. This is often clearer than manually typing sprint names in a text field because the values are structured and date-aware.

Jamie: What are iteration insights?

Alex: They’re the planning benefits you get from that structure: seeing which items are in the current cycle, comparing upcoming cycles, and using roadmap or filtered views to understand sprint load and timing. In other words, the insight comes from consistent structured data.

Jamie: So it’s not just labeling work “Sprint 4.” It’s giving GitHub enough semantics to reason about time.

Alex: Perfectly put.

Jamie: Views and filters feel like another big productivity layer.

Alex: They are. A project can have multiple saved views, each showing the same underlying items differently.

Jamie: So one project, many perspectives.

Alex: Exactly. You might have a Table view for backlog grooming, a Board view for daily status, and a Roadmap view for release timing. You can also create specialized views like “My open work,” “Current sprint,” or “Only accessibility bugs.”

Jamie: How do you create a view?

Alex: You usually start from the current layout, apply filters, grouping, sorting, and visible fields the way you want, then save that configuration as a named view.

Jamie: Let’s unpack filter syntax a bit.

Alex: Projects supports query-style filtering using fields and common GitHub metadata. The exact syntax can include things like status values, labels, assignees, repository names, and custom fields. The important conceptual point is that filtering is expressive. You are not limited to one simple dropdown; you can build meaningful queries.

Jamie: So for example, I might isolate items assigned to me, with a certain label, in a particular status.

Alex: Exactly. Or only items from one repository inside a cross-repo project. Or only the current iteration. Filters become much more valuable once your project has structured fields.

Jamie: And grouping?

Alex: Grouping changes how items are clustered visually. In Table view, you might group by Status, Assignee, Priority, or Iteration. That lets you treat one project almost like several logical sections without creating separate projects.

Jamie: Sorting is more straightforward, I assume.

Alex: Yes. Sorting orders items by one or more fields. Useful examples include due date ascending, priority descending, or recently updated work first. Combined with grouping, sorting can make a large project much easier to read.

Jamie: Cross-repository projects feel especially important for open source maintainers and org-level planning.

Alex: Definitely. One of the biggest advantages of Projects v2 is that it can track work from multiple repositories together.

Jamie: How do you add a repository to a project?

Alex: At a high level, you configure the project so it can include items from that repository, then add or auto-add issues and PRs from it. The exact UI wording can vary, but the concept is: this project is not limited to one repo. It can aggregate work across several.

Jamie: And then the Repository field becomes important.

Alex: Very. Once you’re mixing repos, the Repository field tells you where each item came from. It’s useful in Table view for filtering, sorting, and basic orientation. If two repositories both have an issue named something vague like “Update docs,” the Repository field keeps those items distinguishable.

Jamie: So cross-repo planning without the Repository field visible can get confusing fast.

Alex: Exactly. In a multi-repo view, showing repository is often a best practice.

Jamie: Let’s do the dedicated screen reader navigation reference, because a lot of learners need a reliable mental map.

Alex: Great idea. Start from the project home page, meaning the list of projects for an organization or repository. Expect a list or grid of project entries. Use standard navigation keys to move through links and buttons, and activate the project you want.

Jamie: Once you’re inside a project, what’s the general model?

Alex: There are a few recurring regions: view selectors or tabs near the top, the main content area showing Table, Board, or Roadmap, filtering controls, and often a detail panel that opens on the right when you activate an item.

Jamie: So learners should think in regions, not just individual controls.

Alex: Yes. Region awareness matters. In general, it helps to locate the current view, then the filter bar, then the content area. When you open an item, understand that focus may move into a right sidebar panel with editable fields.

Jamie: Give us the Table view mental map.

Alex: Header row of fields across the top. Rows of items below. Arrow navigation can move within the grid. Enter opens details. Space may edit a cell. Because it’s grid-like, listen carefully for row and column context so you always know which field you’re on.

Jamie: And Board view?

Alex: Think columns, then cards within columns. Tab often moves through cards and related controls. Enter opens the selected card in the detail panel. Remember: if you need to move a card between columns accessibly, edit its Status field in the panel instead of trying to drag.

Jamie: Tell us about the detail panel.

Alex: This right sidebar appears from any view after opening an item. It’s often the most linear and therefore accessible place to review and edit title, status, assignees, labels, custom fields, and other metadata. Escape commonly closes it.

Jamie: And the filter bar?

Alex: The filter bar is where you type or refine project queries. For screen reader users, that’s a powerful control because it can quickly reduce noise. If a project feels overwhelming, filtering down to one assignee, one status, one repo, or one iteration can make the experience much more manageable.

Jamie: I’m intrigued by the accessibility agent command mentioned here: slash project-status. What is that for?

Alex: The idea is an accessibility-oriented helper that summarizes the state of a project in a compact, textual way. Instead of navigating every visual element to answer basic status questions, you ask for a project-status style summary.

Jamie: What kind of information would it show?

Alex: Typically things like counts by status, notable items, upcoming dates or sprint context, and a plain-language snapshot of project health or progress. It’s meant to surface the information someone might otherwise gather by visually scanning a board or roadmap.

Jamie: So it’s a translation layer from visual project dashboard to text summary.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Was there an example output conceptually?

Alex: Yes, the chapter points to example output to show what a concise project snapshot can look like: a summary of where work sits, what’s active, what’s blocked or upcoming, and what deserves attention next.

Jamie: When should someone use a tool like that?

Alex: When the project is large, when a quick orientation is needed, when Roadmap or Board would take too long to parse nonvisually, or when you want a status check before drilling into details. It’s not a replacement for direct project access, but it can be an excellent first pass.

Jamie: Before we wrap, let’s turn the chapter’s exercises into practical listening prompts.

Alex: Exercise one is to create a personal tracking project. That means making a project, giving it a clear name, and adding a few items that represent your own work. The learning goal is simply getting comfortable with creation, layout switching, and item entry.

Jamie: Exercise two is automation.

Alex: Right. Set up a basic automation, especially auto-add, so that matching work flows into the project without manual effort. Then verify that the rule behaves as expected.

Jamie: Exercise three is a sprint view.

Alex: Create an iteration field, assign some items to iterations, and save a filtered view that shows the current sprint or a chosen cycle. This reinforces field creation, filtering, and saved views all together.

Jamie: And exercise four goes advanced with cross-repo work.

Alex: Yes. Build or modify a project so it includes multiple repositories. Then make sure the Repository field is visible and useful in your layout. Try filtering by repo and compare how one shared project can coordinate work across codebases.

Jamie: Can we end with a few key takeaways, especially for blind and low-vision learners?

Alex: Absolutely. First, Table view is usually the best primary workspace for accessibility and precision. Second, Board view is useful conceptually, but move cards by editing Status rather than dragging. Third, Roadmap is best treated as visual summary; use Table for the real data work. Fourth, custom fields are what transform Projects from a simple task list into a structured planning tool. Fifth, saved views, filters, grouping, and sorting let one project serve many different needs.

Jamie: And for cross-repo planning?

Alex: Show the Repository field. Always. It reduces ambiguity.

Jamie: And one final administrative note: where should learners go for the most current behavior if GitHub’s interface changes?

Alex: Use GitHub Docs as the authoritative source, especially the Projects documentation, and keep an eye on the GitHub changelog. Labels and milestones docs also matter because those objects often appear inside project workflows.

Jamie: That’s a great place to stop. GitHub Projects is much more than a board. It’s a flexible planning system, and with the right habits, it can be highly workable for accessible contribution workflows too.

Alex: Exactly. See you next time.

26. Episode 27: Advanced Search

GitHub search query language, qualifiers, and filtering for issues, PRs, and code.

Based on: Appendix N: Advanced Search

Download Episode 27 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 27: Advanced Search

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re working on one of the most useful GitHub skills that people often skip: advanced search. And for blind and low-vision learners especially, this is not just a power-user trick. It can be a faster, cleaner, more accessible way to move through GitHub than opening a pile of filters, dropdowns, and side panels.

Jamie: I’m glad you said that up front, because search can sound optional, like a nice extra. But this chapter really treats it like a core workflow skill, right?

Alex: Exactly. If you can type a precise query, you can often find issues, pull requests, code, commits, repositories, users, and organizations more efficiently than by browsing. This appendix is a reference companion to issue workflows and also connects naturally to labels, milestones, and project organization. And the authoritative reference behind what we’re teaching is GitHub Docs on searching on GitHub.

Alex: Here’s the big idea: GitHub’s search engine is powerful and underused. And because query syntax works directly from the keyboard, it can reduce the need to hunt through visual controls.

Jamie: So instead of thinking, “Where is that filter menu again,” I can think, “What do I want,” and type it.

Alex: That’s the mindset.

Alex: Let’s start with how you reach search. GitHub gives you a few entry points. There’s the global search bar at the top of nearly every GitHub page. There are repository-specific search bars inside issues and pull requests views. And there’s also an Advanced Search page at github dot com slash search slash advanced.

Jamie: And that Advanced Search page is the form version, right? Separate fields instead of one compact query?

Alex: Yes. It’s accessible, but it can feel verbose. For many learners, especially keyboard and screen reader users, typing the query directly is often faster.

Jamie: What’s the quickest way to get to the global search bar?

Alex: Press the forward slash key. On most GitHub pages, slash focuses the global search field. Then type your query, press Enter, and GitHub opens a results page grouped by result type, like Code, Issues, Pull Requests, and Repositories.

Jamie: That’s a wonderful shortcut because it removes the whole “Tab until you find the top navigation” problem.

Alex: Exactly. And that leads into the accessibility guidance from the learning cards. For screen reader users: pressing slash is often the fastest way to jump to search. After you run the query, results are grouped under headings, so heading navigation can move you between result types efficiently. And again, direct query syntax is often easier than filling out the Advanced Search form.

Jamie: What about low-vision users?

Alex: A few practical notes. If the top bar is hard to relocate at high zoom, slash brings focus back to the search box instantly. Search results highlight matching terms, so browser zoom can help make those highlights easier to spot. And if you prefer large labeled fields on some days, bookmarking the Advanced Search page is a smart option.

Jamie: And for sighted users?

Alex: Look for the search bar in the top navigation with the slash hint inside it. After searching, the left sidebar can narrow by result type visually. And GitHub highlights matched terms, often in yellow, which helps you scan results quickly.

Jamie: Once I can get to search, the next question is scope. Am I searching all of GitHub, one repo, one organization, titles only, comments only?

Alex: Right. By default, GitHub searches broadly. Scope modifiers let you narrow that. Some of the most important are repo colon owner slash name for one repository, org colon orgname for all repositories in an organization, and user colon username for repositories owned by a particular user.

Jamie: And then there are field-specific scopes too.

Alex: Yes. In colon title searches only titles. In colon body searches only the body text. In colon comments searches comments.

Jamie: Can you give a concrete example?

Alex: Sure. If you type repo colon community-access slash accessibility-agents in colon title keyboard, you’re asking GitHub to find issues or pull requests in that specific repository whose titles mention the word keyboard.

Jamie: That’s nice because it avoids noisy matches in long discussions.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s build the core query language. Think of GitHub search like a compact sentence made of words and qualifiers.

Jamie: Start with Boolean logic?

Alex: Yes. If you type two words with a space between them, GitHub usually treats that like an implicit AND. So word one, space, word two means results should include both ideas. If you use OR in capital letters, GitHub matches either term. Quotation marks create an exact phrase match. And a minus sign excludes terms.

Jamie: So minus word excludes the word, and minus label colon bug excludes items with the bug label.

Alex: Exactly. Then come common qualifiers. Is colon open means open items only. Is colon closed means closed items. Is colon merged means merged pull requests only. Is colon unmerged means pull requests that were not merged. Is colon issue limits to issues. Is colon pr limits to pull requests. Is colon draft finds draft pull requests.

Jamie: And labels and assignments matter a lot in workflow searches.

Alex: They do. Label colon name filters by label. No colon label finds items with no labels. Assignee colon at me means assigned to you. Assignee colon username means assigned to a specific person. Author colon at me means created by you. Author colon username means created by that user. Mentions colon username finds items that mention someone. Involves colon at me is broader: you are author, assignee, mentioned, or a commenter.

Jamie: That one sounds especially useful when you just want “everything I’m tied to.”

Alex: It is. Then there are milestone filters like milestone colon quoted milestone name and no colon milestone. There’s no colon assignee for unassigned items. Comments colon greater than 5 filters by discussion volume. Reactions colon greater than 10 filters by reaction count.

Jamie: And dates?

Alex: GitHub supports date qualifiers too. Created colon greater than a date means created after that date. Created colon less than a date means before. You can specify a range with two dates separated by two periods. Updated colon greater than a date filters by recent activity. Closed colon greater than a date filters by close date.

Jamie: So once you understand words, quotes, minus, OR, and qualifiers, you can express a lot.

Alex: That’s the foundation.

Alex: Now let’s apply that to issues and pull requests, because this is where many learners first feel the payoff.

Jamie: Where do you go if you want issue or PR search directly rather than global search?

Alex: Github dot com slash issues gives you your issues view, and github dot com slash pulls gives you your pull requests view. Those pages are pre-scoped to repositories you have access to and items involving you, which makes them a great starting point for personal workflow.

Jamie: Let’s walk through the practical queries one by one.

Alex: First: find all unassigned, open accessibility issues across an organization. The query is org colon community-access is colon issue is colon open label colon accessibility no colon assignee.

Jamie: That says organization-wide, issues only, open only, must have the accessibility label, and nobody owns them yet.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Next: good first issues in any language.

Alex: That query is is colon issue is colon open label colon quote good first issue quote no colon assignee.

Jamie: And to narrow to a specific programming language?

Alex: Add language colon python, or another language you care about. So: is colon issue is colon open label colon quote good first issue quote language colon python no colon assignee.

Jamie: That’s a neat bridge between beginner-friendly and skill-relevant.

Alex: Right. Next: all pull requests you need to review. Use is colon pr is colon open review-requested colon at me.

Jamie: That feels like a daily dashboard query.

Alex: It is. Another daily-use query is all open pull requests where you were mentioned: is colon pr is colon open mentions colon at me.

Jamie: How about finding your own open issues across all repositories?

Alex: Is colon issue is colon open author colon at me.

Jamie: And stale issues?

Alex: For stale open issues in a repository, use something like is colon issue is colon open repo colon owner slash name updated colon less than 2024-08-01. The exact date will depend on what you mean by stale, but the pattern is open issues in a repo with no updates since before a given date.

Jamie: The learning cards for this section had some especially practical accessibility advice.

Alex: They did. For screen reader users, the review-requested query is a strong daily default because it gives a clean list of PRs waiting on you without browsing tabs. Combining assignee colon at me with is colon open creates a simple task list. And using in colon title or in colon body can reduce noisy results from long comment threads.

Jamie: For low-vision users, I remember the reminder that the URL itself becomes useful.

Alex: Yes. After you run a search, bookmark the page. The query is encoded in the URL, so you can reuse it later. The github dot com slash issues page is often easier to scan at high zoom because it is more focused than a broad global search layout. And labels appear as badges next to results, so zooming in or hovering can help if color alone is not enough.

Jamie: And sighted users get quick visual triage with the state icons.

Alex: Exactly: green for open, purple for merged, red for closed. And saving a good-first-issue query is an easy way to keep contribution opportunities close at hand.

Jamie: Let’s switch to code search, because this behaves a little differently.

Alex: Yes. Code search uses a specialized engine, and GitHub’s improved code search has better indexing than older versions. It’s designed for searching inside files, symbols, paths, and language-specific content.

Jamie: What’s a basic example?

Alex: Repo colon owner slash name language colon javascript aria-label. That means search within one repository, in JavaScript files, for the text aria-label.

Jamie: So if I’m investigating accessibility support in a project, that could quickly show where labels are being set.

Alex: Exactly. Another useful pattern is symbol search. For example, repo colon owner slash name symbol colon handleKeyDown. That asks GitHub to find a specific symbol or function name across the repository.

Jamie: Very useful when you know the function name but not where it lives.

Alex: Right. And to find a pattern across all repositories in an organization, you could use org colon community-access aria-hidden equals quote true quote.

Jamie: Let’s list the core code search qualifiers too.

Alex: Language colon python filters by language. Path colon src slash restricts to files under a folder. Filename colon config dot yml narrows to files with that exact name. Extension colon md narrows by extension. Symbol colon functionName searches a symbol. Content colon quote exact string quote searches for an exact string in file content.

Jamie: That’s powerful because it lets you be precise about where the match should happen.

Alex: Yes. If you’re auditing documentation, extension colon md helps. If you’re looking for a config setting, filename or path helps. If you’re investigating source usage, symbol or content can be the right tool.

Jamie: What about commit search?

Alex: Commit search lets you inspect project history without cloning the repo first. One example is finding commits with a keyword in the commit message. The source gives repo colon owner slash name fix keyboard navigation.

Jamie: That one is interesting because it reads almost like plain language.

Alex: It does. For commits by a specific author, use repo colon owner slash name author colon username. For commits in a date range, use repo colon owner slash name committer-date colon 2025-01-01 two dots 2025-03-31. And to find commits that touched a specific file, use repo colon owner slash name path colon docs slash README dot md.

Jamie: So you can answer questions like, “Who changed this file,” or “What happened to keyboard navigation earlier this year?”

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Repository search is the next major category. This helps you discover projects to study or contribute to.

Jamie: Such as finding accessibility-focused repositories.

Alex: Yes. One example is topic colon accessibility stars colon greater than 50 is colon public. That finds public repositories tagged with the accessibility topic and more than 50 stars.

Jamie: And if I want a language and topic combination, sorted by popularity?

Alex: You might use language colon typescript topic colon screen-reader sort colon stars-desc.

Jamie: What repository qualifiers do we have explicitly from the source?

Alex: Stars colon greater than 100 means more than 100 stars. Forks colon greater than 10 means more than 10 forks. Is colon public filters to public repositories.

Jamie: The source we received was truncated in that table, but those examples still show the pattern: repository search can filter by popularity, fork count, visibility, language, and topic.

Alex: Exactly. Even with partial table content, the conceptual workflow is clear.

Jamie: We also need to cover searching users and organizations.

Alex: Yes. Even though the provided excerpt doesn’t include the example lines under that section, the heading matters conceptually. GitHub search can target people and orgs as result types, and you can use user-related terms to discover maintainers, contributors, or organizations relevant to a topic.

Jamie: So the lesson for learners is: search is not only for issues and code. It also helps you find who is doing the work and what organizations are hosting it.

Alex: Exactly. If you’re looking for a maintainer, a contributor profile, or an organization focused on accessibility or open source education, search can be your entry point.

Alex: Now let’s bring this back to the workshop with practical queries you might really use.

Jamie: The first one is finding open contributions you can make right now in the accessibility-agents project.

Alex: A strong pattern would combine the project scope with issue state and beginner-friendly or accessibility labels. For example, repo colon community-access slash accessibility-agents is colon issue is colon open no colon assignee. Then you might add label colon accessibility or label colon quote good first issue quote depending on what you want.

Jamie: So the teaching point is to compose from building blocks rather than memorize one sacred query.

Alex: Exactly. Another workshop use case is checking whether your issue is already filed. For that, search within the repository before opening a new issue. Use repo colon owner slash name plus keywords, and consider in colon title for concise matching or exact phrases in quotes if you know likely wording.

Jamie: That helps avoid duplicates and saves maintainers time.

Alex: Right. Another common need is finding all accessibility-related issues in a project. That might look like repo colon owner slash name is colon issue is colon open label colon accessibility, or if labels are inconsistent, keywords like keyboard OR screen reader OR aria.

Jamie: What about proof of contribution?

Alex: To see your merged pull requests, use is colon pr is colon merged author colon at me. If needed, add repo colon owner slash name to limit it to one repository. That gives you a concrete record of merged work.

Jamie: And recent discussions about a topic?

Alex: That’s where keywords plus date filters help. Use terms for the topic and add updated colon greater than a recent date. Depending on what you want, you might search issues, pull requests, discussions if available, or even commits and code. The key idea is combining subject keywords with freshness.

Jamie: Let’s talk about saving and reusing searches, because if a query is helpful once, it’s probably helpful again.

Alex: Absolutely. One of the simplest tricks in GitHub is that your search is reflected in the URL. That means the page itself can be bookmarked. You do not need a separate export or saved-search feature just to reuse a query.

Jamie: So if I build a query for open review requests, good first issues in Python, or all my merged PRs, I can save that URL in bookmarks.

Alex: Yes. You can even organize a small personal library of GitHub searches: daily review queue, issues assigned to me, stale issues in one repo, accessibility bugs across an organization, and so on.

Jamie: And the source explicitly mentions an example bookmarkable URL, even though the exact URL text wasn’t included in the excerpt we received.

Alex: Right. But the principle is clear and important: search URLs are reusable workflow tools.

Alex: Before we close, let’s not skip the administrative and reference material. This appendix points learners to GitHub Docs on searching on GitHub as the authoritative source. It also includes a section-level source map connecting the search interface, scopes, core syntax, issue and PR search, code search, commit search, repository search, user and organization search, practical workshop queries, and saving searches back to GitHub Docs, GitHub code search syntax documentation, the GitHub changelog, and in some sections, About Git.

Jamie: That’s worth emphasizing. Search behavior evolves, especially code search, so the docs matter.

Alex: Exactly. Use this lesson to understand the concepts and workflows, and check the official docs when syntax changes or new qualifiers appear.

Jamie: Can we end with a compact mental model?

Alex: Yes. Think in layers. First, choose the thing you want: issues, pull requests, code, commits, repositories, users, or organizations. Second, choose the scope: all of GitHub, one organization, one user, or one repository. Third, add qualifiers for state, labels, authorship, assignment, language, path, date, or visibility. Fourth, save the URL if it’s useful.

Jamie: And accessibility-wise: start from the keyboard, use slash to focus search, prefer direct syntax when forms feel slow, and bookmark the searches you rely on.

Alex: Exactly. Advanced search is not just about finding things. It’s about building accessible, repeatable workflows on GitHub.

Jamie: That’s a great place to stop.

Alex: See you next time.

27. Episode 10: Notifications and Mentions

Managing your notification inbox, @mentions, and strategies for avoiding overload.

Based on: Chapter 10: Notifications and Mentions

Download Episode 10 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 10: Notifications and Mentions

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re talking about GitHub notifications, which sounds administrative, but it’s really about protecting your attention.

Jamie: I’m glad you said that, because notifications can feel like the moment GitHub stops being helpful and starts becoming noisy.

Alex: Exactly. The goal is not to see everything. The goal is to notice the things that truly need you: a review request, an assignment, an @mention, maybe activity in a thread you’re already part of.

Jamie: So this is less about inbox perfection and more about building a workflow.

Alex: Yes. A useful workflow, ideally one you can manage with just a keyboard and screen reader. And if you want a related reference later, there are also appendices on community and social features, discussions and gists, and the GitHub mobile app. For the core concepts today, GitHub’s own documentation on notifications is the main authoritative source.

Alex: Let’s start with the practical framing for this workshop. This part is guided practice, not a graded automation check.

Jamie: Meaning there isn’t a bot verifying your notification settings.

Alex: Right. Notification settings are account-level, so the Learning Room pull request bot can’t validate them. Instead, you’ll do one guided walkthrough, then leave structured evidence in your assigned challenge issue.

Jamie: What’s the pattern learners should listen for?

Alex: Configure, filter, act.

Jamie: That is pleasingly compact.

Alex: It’s also realistic. First, configure your watch level so GitHub doesn’t flood you. Second, filter your inbox so you can find the important items quickly. Third, act on what you find by responding, marking done, or muting.

Jamie: Can you walk us through the actual challenge flow?

Alex: Absolutely. The single challenge here is to configure notifications and practice inbox management. First, open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com. Second, find the Watch button near the top right of the repository page, close to Star and Fork. Third, open that Watch menu and choose Participating and @mentions.

Jamie: And that setting means what, exactly?

Alex: It means GitHub mainly notifies you when you are directly involved. If you comment on a thread, get assigned, or someone mentions your username, you’ll hear about it. But you won’t get every single issue and comment in the repository.

Jamie: Which is probably the right choice for most learners.

Alex: Very much so. After that, open the notifications inbox. You can go directly to github.com slash notifications, or use the bell icon in the GitHub header. Then test two filters. Turn on Review requested, which shows notifications where someone asked you to review a pull request. Then clear that filter and turn on Assigned, which shows issues and pull requests assigned to you.

Jamie: So we are practicing finding two common categories of work.

Alex: Exactly. After that, open one notification by activating its title link, read it briefly, then go back to the inbox. Finally, perform one inbox action on a non-critical thread. You can mute it, or mark it done.

Jamie: And the difference matters, right?

Alex: It does. Mark done removes it from your current inbox, but you can still get future updates on that thread. Mute means you’re saying, I do not want future updates from this thread.

Jamie: That sounds like a good distinction to memorize.

Alex: It is. And here’s the simple screen reader framing: the notification list behaves like a standard list of links. Each item usually announces the title, the repository, and the reason, such as mention, review request, or assignment. Move through notifications with arrow keys, and press Enter to open one.

Jamie: What counts as done for the challenge?

Alex: Three things. You changed the watch level, you tested two different filters, and you performed one inbox action, either mute or mark done.

Jamie: And then you need to submit evidence.

Alex: Yes. In your assigned Chapter 10 challenge issue, post a completion comment with three details: your watch level, the filters you tested, and which inbox action you performed on which thread. Then close the challenge issue when you’re done.

Jamie: And the expected outcomes are pretty straightforward: reduce noise, find review and assigned work quickly, and clean up notifications intentionally.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Before we get deeper, what if things don’t line up the way the instructions suggest?

Alex: Good question. If you can’t find the Watch button, look near the top right of the repository page, in the same row as Star and Fork. If your notification inbox is empty, that’s okay. You may simply not have any active notifications yet. You can switch to the Done tab and practice with an older item.

Jamie: What if keyboard shortcuts don’t work?

Alex: Sometimes the screen reader intercepts the key. If that happens, click or focus the notification row first, then try again. Also, apply filters one at a time. If results seem strange, clear existing filters before adding a new one.

Jamie: And if someone is still unsure?

Alex: Ask a facilitator to model one inbox action live, then repeat it yourself. The point is to build confidence, not to guess silently.

Alex: Now let’s look at what actually generates a notification.

Jamie: Because a lot of anxiety comes from not knowing why GitHub is talking to you.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub may notify you when someone @mentions your username in an issue, pull request, or discussion. You may be notified when you’re requested as a reviewer on a pull request. You may be notified when an issue or pull request is assigned to you.

Jamie: Those all feel personal and direct.

Alex: They are. You can also get notifications from threads you’re subscribed to, maybe because you commented there, were mentioned there, or explicitly chose to subscribe. If a CI check fails on your pull request, GitHub Actions may generate a failure notification. And if you’re watching a repository for all activity, even things like published releases can trigger notifications.

Jamie: So there are really two big buckets: things involving me directly, and things I subscribed to broadly.

Alex: That’s a great mental model.

Jamie: Let’s unpack subscription levels, because this is where people often either miss important things or get buried.

Alex: For each repository, you choose how much activity you want. Participating and @mentions gives you notifications only when you’re part of the conversation or specifically addressed. That’s the recommended setting for most repositories. All Activity gives you essentially everything: issues opened, comments, pull requests, updates. Useful for your own repository, maybe, or for a situation where you truly need a broad pulse. But often it’s too noisy. Ignore means no notifications from that repository at all. And Custom gives you finer control, such as issues only, pull requests only, releases, and similar options.

Jamie: So the workshop recommendation is clear: Participating and @mentions for most repos.

Alex: Yes. It keeps you in the loop without punishing you for joining a project.

Jamie: How do you change it accessibly?

Alex: On any repository page, find the Watch button in the header area. Mouse users can click it and choose from the dropdown. Screen reader users on Windows can jump through buttons, find Watch or Unwatch, press Enter, move up and down through the menu, and press Enter again to choose a level. On macOS with VoiceOver, use Quick Nav or VoiceOver navigation to the Watch button, open it with VO+Space, move through the choices, and select with VO+Space.

Jamie: And the button label updates afterward?

Alex: Yes, that change is your confirmation.

Jamie: Now let’s go to the inbox itself.

Alex: Your notifications inbox lives at github.com slash notifications. There’s also a keyboard shortcut on GitHub: press G, then N.

Jamie: Sequentially, not together.

Alex: Exactly. Press G, release it, then press N. That matters, especially in browse mode with a screen reader.

Jamie: What can you do once you’re there?

Alex: In the browser, the key actions include marking an item done, toggling read or unread, and muting a thread. The source material specifically calls out E to mark done, I to mark read or unread, and Shift+M to mute a thread.

Jamie: Interesting, because the challenge directions mention M for mute.

Alex: Right, and that’s a useful teaching note: interface shortcuts can vary over time or by context, so if a key doesn’t do what you expect, rely on focused controls in the page and the visible commands in the web interface. The important concepts are the actions themselves: done, read state, and mute.

Jamie: What about outside the browser?

Alex: In VS Code, if you use the GitHub Pull Requests extension, there’s a Notifications view in the GitHub sidebar. You can open a related issue or pull request directly from there. GitHub Desktop does not manage notifications, so use the browser or command line instead.

Jamie: And the command line options?

Alex: GitHub CLI is useful for checking related work, even though it does not have a first-class dedicated notifications command for full inbox management. For example, you can list pull requests requesting your review with a search command for review-requested at me. You can open the notifications page in your browser with gh browse notifications. You can also call the notifications API to inspect recent notification subjects, list issues assigned to you, or view a particular pull request if a notification references it.

Jamie: So CLI is good for triage and context, but not the full mute-archive-manage experience.

Alex: Exactly. For complete inbox management, the web interface is still the main tool.

Jamie: Let’s make the inbox concrete. What is the page structure like?

Alex: Think of it as a page with navigation controls, filters, and then a list of notifications. Each notification row typically includes the title of the issue or pull request, the repository name, and a reason label telling you why it reached your inbox.

Jamie: Like review requested, assigned, or mention.

Alex: Exactly. That reason is often the quickest clue about urgency. A review request usually means someone is waiting on you. Assigned means you own follow-up. Mention means someone explicitly pulled you into a conversation.

Jamie: How should a screen reader user move through the list?

Alex: Usually as a list of links or interactive rows. Use arrow keys or normal reading navigation to move item by item. Listen for the title, repository, and reason. Open the title link with Enter when you want the full context. Then return to the inbox and continue.

Jamie: And what gets announced per notification is important because it determines whether you can triage quickly.

Alex: Exactly. You don’t want to open every item just to know whether it matters.

Jamie: What are the most useful inbox actions and shortcuts to remember?

Alex: Conceptually, remember three things. First, mark done when you’ve processed something and want it out of your current inbox view. Second, mute when a thread is noisy and no longer relevant to you. Third, read or unread state can help you keep track of what still needs attention.

Jamie: So this is really about making the inbox reflect reality.

Alex: Yes. If everything stays in the inbox forever, the inbox stops meaning anything.

Jamie: How about filtering? Because that’s often the difference between panic and clarity.

Alex: Filtering is one of the most powerful habits here. You can filter by reason, like review requested or assigned. You can also filter by repository or organization.

Jamie: That would help if you contribute to multiple places.

Alex: Exactly. Instead of scanning a mixed stream of everything, you narrow the list to one repo, one org, or one kind of task. In practice, that means if you’re sitting down to do review work, filter to review requests. If you’re planning your own tasks, filter to assigned items. If you only want to think about one workshop repository, filter to that repository.

Jamie: And if filters seem broken?

Alex: Clear the active filters first, then apply one at a time. Stacking filters can be useful, but it can also hide results in ways that feel mysterious if you forget what’s already active.

Jamie: Now let’s talk about scale. Suppose the inbox is no longer tiny.

Alex: Then you need deliberate habits. One important workflow is mark all as done.

Jamie: That sounds a little dangerous.

Alex: It can be, if used carelessly. But it’s helpful when you’ve reviewed a batch of low-priority notifications and want to reset the inbox to only current, active work. The principle is not to preserve clutter for sentimental reasons.

Jamie: And muting a noisy thread?

Alex: Very useful. If a conversation keeps updating but no longer needs your involvement, mute it. That prevents future updates from continuing to consume your attention.

Jamie: What about unexpected @mentions? Those can feel socially awkward.

Alex: They can. Sometimes you’re mentioned because someone thinks you can help. Sometimes they used your name broadly. The healthy response is to assess whether action is actually needed. If yes, respond or redirect. If no, and the thread keeps producing noise, mark it done or mute it. Being mentioned does not obligate you to live inside the thread forever.

Jamie: That is a surprisingly freeing sentence.

Alex: Good notification management at scale means not every ping becomes a commitment.

Jamie: The source also points to account-level notification settings. What should learners know there?

Alex: Some notification preferences apply across your account, not just one repository. That can include delivery methods and broader subscription behavior. The key practical idea is that repository watch settings are only one layer. Your account settings also shape how and where notifications reach you.

Jamie: So if someone says, I changed the repo watch level but I’m still getting more than expected, account settings might be part of the explanation.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: I definitely want to cover starring versus watching, because people mix those up constantly.

Alex: They do. Starring a repository is mostly a bookmarking or appreciation signal. It says, I want to remember this repo, or I think it’s interesting. Watching a repository affects notifications.

Jamie: So star is social and organizational. Watch is operational.

Alex: Perfectly said. If you star a repo, you are not necessarily signing up for updates. If you watch it, you are.

Jamie: Let’s do the two sides clearly. What does starring involve?

Alex: Starring is a lightweight way to save or endorse a repository. It helps you find it later and can signal interest publicly.

Jamie: And watching?

Alex: Watching subscribes you to notifications according to the level you choose: participating only, all activity, custom, or ignore.

Jamie: What’s the common mistake?

Alex: Accidental watching. Someone means to star a repo, or they click around the Watch controls without realizing they’ve subscribed to far more updates than they wanted.

Jamie: How do they fix it?

Alex: Go back to the repository’s Watch menu and lower the subscription level. In many cases, set it to Participating and @mentions. If you truly want silence, choose Ignore.

Jamie: And for this workshop, the recommendation stays the same.

Alex: Yes. Use Participating and @mentions unless you have a specific reason to broaden it.

Jamie: Let’s give some screen reader-specific tips, because the inbox can be busy.

Alex: For NVDA users, browse mode is often useful for reading the page structure and hearing the list of notifications, but you may need focus mode or direct interaction when using keyboard shortcuts on specific rows. If a shortcut seems swallowed, move focus deliberately to the notification item first.

Jamie: And JAWS?

Alex: Similar principle. Use quick navigation to move through links, buttons, and regions, and be aware that some single-letter keys may be intercepted by screen reader commands depending on mode. If GitHub shortcuts don’t respond, switch interaction approach and focus the item directly.

Jamie: What about VoiceOver on macOS?

Alex: Use the rotor or normal web navigation to move through links, buttons, and lists. When working with menu buttons like Watch, VO+Space is your friend. In the inbox, listen for the reason label as part of each item so you can triage without opening everything.

Jamie: So across all three screen readers, the strategy is: understand the page landmarks, focus the right control, and don’t assume a shortcut failing means you did something wrong.

Alex: Exactly. Sometimes it’s just a mode issue.

Jamie: There’s also a note about the GitHub mobile app.

Alex: Yes. Think of mobile as a reference option, not the primary workflow for this lesson. You can manage notifications on your phone, but for learning the inbox structure, filters, and actions clearly, the browser is the best place to practice.

Jamie: Especially when you’re trying to understand watch settings and keyboard flows.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s turn this into a quick practical exercise. If someone wants to tame their inbox today, what should they actually do?

Alex: Do a short routine. Set your Learning Room repository to Participating and @mentions. Open github.com slash notifications. Filter to Review requested and see whether anything needs your attention. Clear that and filter to Assigned. Open one item. Then choose one action on a non-critical thread: mark it done, or mute it.

Jamie: That’s small enough to repeat daily.

Alex: And that is the point. Notification management works best as a light recurring habit, not a dramatic cleanup every three weeks.

Jamie: I want to end the day with a sense of progress. What did learners accomplish today, beyond just learning a new page?

Alex: A lot, actually. You practiced controlling noise instead of just enduring it. You learned what kinds of events generate notifications. You learned the difference between broad subscriptions and direct involvement. You practiced finding review requests and assigned work. And you learned actions that keep your inbox meaningful.

Jamie: If this was someone’s first time managing GitHub notifications, that’s a big shift.

Alex: It is. And if this was your first time, remember: an empty inbox is not failure, and a noisy inbox is not a personal flaw. Both are normal states while learning. What matters is that you now know how to shape the system.

Jamie: Let’s do a quick confidence check.

Alex: Ask yourself: can I explain what Participating and @mentions means? Can I find review requests? Can I find assigned issues or pull requests? Do I know when to use mark done versus mute? If yes, you’re on solid ground.

Jamie: And your challenge progress for this chapter is simply whether you completed the walkthrough and posted the evidence comment.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: So what happens next, after today?

Alex: Day 2 builds on this foundation. The more comfortable you are with notifications, the easier it is to stay responsive during collaboration. Between days, a good habit is to check filtered notifications once or twice a day rather than constantly.

Jamie: That feels healthier than living inside the bell menu.

Alex: Much healthier. And one final encouragement: you already know more than you think. If you can set a watch level, filter for review requests, and decide whether to mark something done or mute it, you are already practicing a real open source contribution skill.

Jamie: Not glamorous, but deeply practical.

Alex: And practical is powerful. Good contributors are not the people who read every notification. They’re the people who know how to notice the right things.

Jamie: Before we close, can you restate the core learning pattern one more time?

Alex: Gladly. Configure settings proactively before the noise starts. Use filters to find signal in the noise. Take a clear action on each notification: respond, mark done, or mute. Then build a daily routine that keeps the inbox manageable.

Jamie: That’s the whole lesson in four moves.

Alex: It is. And with that, you’ve finished today’s work: set your notification flow, submit your completion comment on the assigned challenge issue, and close that issue when done.

Jamie: Nice work, everyone.

Alex: See you next time.

Alex: What You Accomplished Today: Day 1 is complete -- and you did a lot. That gives the learner a foothold: here is every skill you practiced, mapped to the chapter where you learned it and the evidence you created along the way.

Alex: Keep the teaching thread moving. Here is the learner-facing version. If today was your first time using GitHub -- or your first time using it with a screen reader -- you have already done something most developers take weeks to piece together on their own. The next useful detail is concrete: You navigated a complex platform, created real contributions, and collaborated with other people in a shared codebase. A good GitHub workflow is like a well-run meeting: everyone knows the topic, the next action, and who has the floor.

Each step should leave a trace you can name.

Alex: Keep the teaching thread moving. Anchor this part on Your Challenge Progress. Look at how many challenge issues you completed today. That matters in practice: Each one represents a skill you did not just read about -- you practiced it, posted evidence, and moved on.

Alex: Here is the part to remember. You navigated GitHub entirely by keyboard: headings (H), landmarks (D), buttons (B), links (K), and form fields (F or E) became your primary navigation tools. You created issues, opened PRs, resolved conflicts, and managed notifications -- all skills that transfer to any repository on GitHub. Revisit any chapter by pressing Ctrl+L in your browser and typing the URL, or by navigating to the docs folder in the Learning Room repository. Everything you did today at your current zoom level and contrast settings will work the same way tomorrow; GitHub's layout adapts consistently to browser zoom up to 400%. If you found certain pages hard to read, revisit Settings, Accessibility on GitHub to try a different theme or motion preference before Day 2. Your profile page at github.com/your-username now shows contribution activity from today; zoom in on the contribution graph to see your green squares.

Alex: Keep the teaching thread moving. Do not treat What Day 2 Adds as decoration. See also: Chapter 11: VS Code Interface is where Day 2 begins -- have VS Code installed and ready. The listener should be able to check this: On Day 1, you worked entirely on GitHub.com. The workshop is closer to rehearsal than lecture. You hear the move, try the move, and then check what changed.

Alex: If the interface shifts, Between Days is still useful because if your workshop has a gap between Day 1 and Day 2, here are three optional things you can do to stay sharp. That is not trivia. GitHub Skills courses use bot-driven feedback inside pull requests.

There is no wrong configuration -- just find what feels manageable. Then: Read issues in a project you care about. Pick any open source project on GitHub and browse its issue tracker. You now know enough to understand labels, milestones, and comment threads. Notice how maintainers communicate -- you will recognize the patterns from. Next: Try a GitHub Skills course. GitHub Skills offers free, self-paced courses that run inside real repositories. "Introduction to GitHub" is a good one if you want to reinforce what you learned today. See Appendix Z for the full list of recommended courses. The sequence works because every action has a confirmation.

29. Challenge bonus-d: Notifications

Notification hygiene, mentions, subscriptions, and avoiding overload.

Practice focus: Bonus

Download Challenge bonus-d (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge bonus-d: Notifications

Transcript
