Alex: Very much. Do not paste the token into an unencrypted document that syncs to cloud storage. Do not email it to yourself. Do not save it in a public GitHub file. Treat it like a password.

Jamie: Then step three is using it when Git asks for credentials.

Alex: Yes. The next time Git prompts you over HTTPS, you enter your GitHub username in the username field, and paste the Personal Access Token into the password field.

Jamie: Not your regular GitHub account password.

Alex: Correct. The token goes where Git says password.

Jamie: And the operating system may help remember it.

Alex: On Windows, Git Credential Manager often stores it automatically after first use. On macOS, Keychain may offer to save it; the guidance here is to allow that, often by selecting Always Allow. On Linux, you may want to configure credential caching with a Git command so you’re not prompted every single time.

Alex: The command is: git config double-dash global credential dot helper cache.

Jamie: So that’s the recommended workshop path: generate, store securely, then use the token in place of a password when Git asks.

Jamie: Now let’s cover the alternative, because some learners will prefer SSH.

Alex: Definitely. The first step in SSH setup is checking whether you already have a key. In a terminal, run the command to list files in your .ssh directory.

Alex: You’re looking for names like id underscore rsa dot pub or id underscore ed25519 dot pub. If you see a matching private key and public key pair, you may already have a usable key.

Jamie: If not, generate a new one.

Alex: Right. The command shown here uses the modern ed25519 algorithm with your email as a label. When prompted, press Enter to accept the default file location, and optionally set a passphrase. Optional in the sense that the command allows it, but recommended for security.

Jamie: And Git creates two files.

Alex: Yes. The private key, usually named id underscore ed25519, must stay private. The public key, usually id underscore ed25519 dot pub, is the one you can share with GitHub.

Jamie: That private-versus-public distinction is one of the most important concepts in this whole lesson.

Alex: Absolutely. Never share the private key. Only upload the public key.

Jamie: Next comes copying the public key, and the commands vary by operating system.

Alex: On Windows PowerShell, there’s a command that reads the public key file and sends it to the clipboard. On macOS, pbcopy can copy the public key file directly into the clipboard. On Linux, the reference shows a command to print the file contents, then manually select and copy the output.

Jamie: That manual-copy note deserves to be said out loud because it appears as a separate heading in the source.

Alex: Good catch. On Linux in particular, if your setup doesn’t provide a simple clipboard command, you may need to run the command that displays the key, then manually select and copy the full output yourself.

Jamie: Once you’ve copied the public key, you add it to GitHub.

Alex: Yes. Go to github dot com slash settings slash keys. Choose New SSH key. Give it a descriptive title, like Workshop Laptop SSH Key. For key type, choose Authentication Key. Then paste the public key into the key field. It should begin with something like ssh dash ed25519 or ssh dash rsa. Then select Add SSH key and confirm with your password or two-factor authentication if prompted.

Jamie: After that, test the connection.

Alex: Exactly. Use the SSH test command to connect to GitHub. If everything is set up correctly, GitHub responds with a greeting like, “Hi username, you’ve successfully authenticated.”

Jamie: And from then on, you need to use SSH-style repository URLs, not HTTPS ones.

Alex: That’s crucial. The SSH format looks like git at github dot com, colon, owner slash repo dot git. The HTTPS format starts with https colon slash slash github dot com slash owner slash repo dot git. If you set up SSH but keep using an HTTPS remote, Git won’t suddenly switch methods on its own.

Jamie: That leads perfectly into switching between HTTPS and SSH.

Alex: Yes. First, check your current remote with git remote dash v. That shows the fetch and push URLs currently configured for origin.

Jamie: If you want SSH, set the origin URL to the SSH form.

Alex: Right. Use git remote set-url origin followed by the SSH URL, like git at github dot com colon your-username slash repo dot git.

Jamie: And if you want to go back to HTTPS, do the same with the HTTPS URL.

Alex: Exactly. Same command pattern, different URL. This is useful if you started one way and later decided the other method fits your workflow better.

Jamie: There’s also accessibility guidance for troubleshooting here.

Alex: Yes. For screen reader users, each troubleshooting entry starts with the error message itself, so jumping by heading is effective. The commands are in code blocks, so using a focused reading mode can help when copying. For low vision users, the error messages are intended to be easy to scan, and if terminal output is hard to read, it may help to paste commands into VS Code’s integrated terminal where your own color theme and zoom settings apply. For sighted users, the practical advice is to locate the exact error heading and try the most common fix first.

Jamie: Let’s go through the common failures.

Alex: First: “Authentication failed” when pushing. If you’re using HTTPS and a Personal Access Token, this usually means the token is expired, incorrect, or an old cached credential is interfering.

Jamie: What should the learner do?

Alex: Generate a new PAT if needed. Then clear the cached credentials. On Windows that often means checking Credential Manager. On macOS, Keychain. On Linux, the command shown is git credential-cache exit. Then try pushing again so Git prompts you for fresh credentials.

Jamie: Second: “Permission denied, publickey.”

Alex: That usually points to SSH. It means GitHub didn’t accept the SSH key being offered, or no appropriate key was offered.

Jamie: So the fixes are?

Alex: First, verify that your public key is actually added to your GitHub account at the SSH keys settings page. Then check whether the SSH agent is running and knows about your key. The reference suggests using ssh-add dash l to list loaded keys, and if necessary, adding your key with ssh-add followed by the path to your private key file.

Jamie: And third: “Host key verification failed.”

Alex: That one means your computer doesn’t yet trust GitHub’s host key, or the known-hosts record needs attention. The provided fix is to use ssh-keyscan github dot com and append the result to your known_hosts file.

Jamie: So the theme in troubleshooting is: identify whether the problem is token-related, key-related, or host-trust-related.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now let’s zoom out to security best practices, because authentication setup can accidentally turn into security mistakes if people rush.

Alex: Well said. First, never share your private key or your Personal Access Token. Treat both like passwords. Second, use scoped PATs, meaning give them only the permissions you need. Third, set expiration dates on PATs so they don’t live forever. Fourth, use a passphrase on SSH keys for an extra layer of protection. Fifth, revoke old tokens when you’re finished with a project or stop using a device. And sixth, never commit tokens or keys into Git repositories. If a config file might contain secrets, make sure it’s excluded appropriately, often with .gitignore.

Jamie: That point about not committing secrets is huge in open source.

Alex: It really is. Accidental secret exposure is one of the easiest mistakes for new contributors to make.

Jamie: The appendix also introduces commit signing, verified badges, and something called vigilant mode. Even though the source excerpt is shortened, we should teach the concepts that are clearly signposted there.

Alex: Agreed. Commit signing is related to authentication but serves a different purpose. Authentication proves you can access GitHub for operations like push. Commit signing proves that a particular commit was cryptographically signed by a key associated with you. On GitHub, signed commits may show a Verified badge, while unsigned or improperly configured commits may show as unverified.

Jamie: So why does that matter?

Alex: It adds trust and traceability. Maintainers and collaborators can see stronger evidence that a commit genuinely came from the claimed authoring identity and was not altered in transit. In some projects, especially security-conscious ones, signed commits are encouraged or even expected.

Jamie: The source mentions two methods for signing commits: SSH signing and GPG signing.

Alex: Right. SSH signing is often the simpler option because it can reuse an SSH key you already have. GPG signing is the traditional method and has been common for years, but it usually involves more setup steps.

Jamie: The source specifically highlights SSH signing as simpler because it reuses your existing SSH key.

Alex: Yes, and that’s a practical recommendation for many learners. If you already set up SSH successfully, SSH signing may be the lowest-friction path to getting verified commit signatures.

Jamie: But the material also includes a GPG path with some very specific prompts.

Alex: It does. If using GPG signing, one instruction is to choose RSA and RSA, 4096 bits, and never expires, and to enter your GitHub email address when prompted. Those details matter because the email on the key needs to align with your GitHub identity for GitHub to recognize the signature properly.

Jamie: Then there’s a step to find the key ID.

Alex: Yes. The output from GPG includes a line with something like sec rsa4096 slash followed by a long identifier. That identifier is the key ID. The source explicitly calls out that the Xs in that pattern stand in for your actual key ID.

Jamie: After that, export the public key.

Alex: Correct. You export the public portion of the GPG key and copy the block that begins with the line BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK. That public key block is what you add to GitHub.

Jamie: Then add it to GitHub, and configure Git to sign all commits.

Alex: Exactly. Once GitHub has the corresponding public signing key, you can configure Git so new commits are signed automatically.

Jamie: Now let’s explain vigilant mode, because that term can sound intimidating.

Alex: Vigilant mode is a GitHub feature some maintainers enable to emphasize commit signature verification more strongly. The reason some maintainers use it is simple: they want clearer security signals in repositories, especially for collaborative or sensitive projects.

Jamie: What does a contributor experience when vigilant mode is in play?

Alex: You may notice that commit verification states become more noticeable, and unsigned commits may stand out more clearly. In practice, it means verification badges matter more in the social and review workflow. If you contribute to a repository with vigilant mode expectations, signing your commits can help avoid confusion and make your work easier to trust.

Jamie: And there’s an accessibility point here too: how to read verification badges with a screen reader.

Alex: Yes. The key idea is not to rely only on the visual badge. Screen reader users should inspect the accessible text associated with the verification state on the commit page or in commit details. In other words, listen for whether GitHub reports the commit as Verified or Unverified rather than assuming that a badge color or icon communicates enough.

Jamie: So for this workshop, what’s the practical recommendation?

Alex: For authentication, the recommended approach is a Personal Access Token, because it’s the most accessible and least disruptive setup path for many learners using HTTPS with Git. SSH remains a solid alternative if you’re comfortable in the terminal and want a smoother long-term workflow. And for commit signing, if you decide to pursue verified commits later, SSH signing is often the simplest next step if you already use SSH, while GPG remains a traditional option with more setup overhead.

Jamie: And the appendix also points learners back to the bigger learning path.

Alex: Yes. This material is a reference companion to pre-workshop setup and also connects to later practical Git work. It’s not meant to be memorized all at once. It’s a just-in-time guide for the moment authentication becomes necessary.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, can we give learners one short mental model to carry forward?

Alex: Definitely. Here it is: if you use HTTPS, Git will usually ask for your username and a token. If you use SSH, Git will use your key pair. If something breaks, first identify which method you’re using, then troubleshoot that method specifically.

Jamie: That’s clean. And the final reminder?

Alex: Use official GitHub documentation as the authority when details change. Authentication interfaces evolve. Token pages move. Security defaults get updated. So use this lesson to understand the concepts and workflow, and use GitHub Docs to confirm the latest exact steps.

Jamie: Thanks for listening. If authentication has ever felt mysterious, hopefully now it feels more like a set of clear choices.

Alex: And more importantly, choices you can make accessibly and securely.

33. Episode 46: How Git Works: The Mental Model

Commits, branches, staging, local versus remote, push, pull, fetch, and why conflicts happen.

Based on: Chapter 13: How Git Works: The Mental Model

Download Episode 46 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 46: How Git Works: The Mental Model

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Before we get into Git commands, we need the picture in our heads that makes those commands make sense. Today is all about that mental model: what Git is storing, where your changes live, what a commit really is, what a branch really is, how your computer relates to GitHub, and why conflicts happen.

Jamie: I like that framing, because a lot of learners can follow a recipe right up until something unexpected happens. Then suddenly every word in the terminal feels mysterious.

Alex: Exactly. And this lesson is designed to prevent that. On GitHub's website, you may have edited files without thinking about Git underneath. The site handled the commit creation, branch management, and history tracking for you. Locally, you do those operations yourself. The commands are learnable, but the real goal is understanding what each one changes.

Jamie: So this is not really a memorization lesson. It's a how-to-think lesson.

Alex: That's right. And one practical note: later Git practice depends on this model. If you understand the three areas, branches, and the difference between local and remote, Day 2 Git work becomes much more predictable. There's also a learning principle here that matters for accessibility and confidence: first understand local Git mechanics, then connect them to GitHub workflows and tools like the GitHub CLI. That order makes terminal work easier to recover from.

Jamie: And if someone wants deeper documentation after this episode?

Alex: The core ideas here line up with the Pro Git book, Git SCM documentation, GitHub Docs, and the GitHub Accessibility Lab CLI guide. There are also related appendices on advanced Git, authentication, and Git security for later.

Alex: Let's start with the most important concept in this whole lesson: Git has three main areas.

Jamie: This is the part people hear about, but often only vaguely. Working tree, staging, repository, something like that?

Alex: Yes, and we want it to be concrete. First, the working directory. That's the folder on your computer where the files actually live. If you open a project in VS Code and browse files in the Explorer, you're looking at the working directory. These are ordinary files on disk. You can edit them, rename them, delete them, create new ones.

Jamie: So if I type in a Markdown file and save it, I've changed the working directory.

Alex: Exactly. Git notices that change, but Git does not automatically preserve it in history. Noticing is not the same as recording.

Jamie: And that's where the staging area comes in.

Alex: Right. The staging area, also called the index, is a holding zone. When you decide a particular change belongs in your next save point, you stage it. You're telling Git, include this in the next commit.

Jamie: So staging is like selecting what counts.

Alex: Perfect phrasing. You can stage one file and leave another unstaged. You can group related changes together. That's one of Git's big strengths: your commit can reflect a meaningful unit of work instead of every edit you've made that afternoon.

Jamie: And then the repository is the permanent record.

Alex: Yes. The repository is where Git stores committed history. Inside your project is a hidden folder named dot git, written as .git. That's where Git keeps its metadata and history. When you commit, Git takes the staged content and stores it in the repository as a snapshot.

Jamie: Let's connect the flow clearly.

Alex: Always: edit in the working directory, stage the changes you want, then commit the staged changes into the repository.

Jamie: Edit, stage, commit.

Alex: Yes. In command terms, that often looks like: edit a file, run git add on the file, then run git commit with a message. But focus on the idea, not just the syntax.

Jamie: And I want to call out something accessibility-related from the source material. A lot of visual Git tutorials use arrows and diagrams. But the actual information is just that three-step flow.

Alex: Exactly. You do not need a diagram to understand it. The text sequence is the same content. Edit in the working directory. Stage into the index. Commit into the repository.

Jamie: Can we use the packing analogy?

Alex: Definitely. Imagine your desk is covered with papers and objects. That's the working directory. An open box on the floor is the staging area. You choose what goes into that box. When you're satisfied, you seal the box, label it, and put it on the shelf. That's the commit. The sealed, stored box is now part of the permanent record.

Jamie: And before sealing it, I can add things or remove things from the box.

Alex: Yes. You can stage and unstage as much as needed before committing.

Jamie: Let's make this practical for different learners in VS Code and the terminal.

Alex: For screen reader users, git status is extremely helpful. Run it in the terminal and Git tells you which files are changed, which are staged, and which are untracked. In VS Code Source Control, usually opened with Control Shift G, files are grouped into Changes and Staged Changes, and you can move through them with arrow keys. Press Enter on a file to hear the diff, with added and removed lines announced.

Jamie: And for low vision learners?

Alex: In Source Control, staged files appear in a separate Staged Changes group, often with a green plus icon. Unstaged files appear under Changes, often with an orange modified indicator. If the panel is hard to read, increase zoom or font size. In the editor gutter, added lines and modified lines are also marked by color.

Jamie: And for sighted users, the Source Control badge count and the file status letters like M, U, A, and D give a fast visual summary.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let's talk about commits.

Jamie: People often say a commit is a save point. That's helpful, but a little incomplete.

Alex: Agreed. A commit is a snapshot of your project at a moment in time. Importantly, it's not just a loose note saying what changed. Git records the state of the staged files as they are at commit time.

Jamie: So a commit contains more than a message.

Alex: Much more. Four key parts matter here. First, the snapshot: the recorded state of the staged files. Second, the message: a human-readable description, like fix broken link in setup guide. Third, the author information: who made the commit, typically name and email. Fourth, a parent pointer: a reference to the commit that came before it.

Jamie: That parent pointer is what turns separate save points into a timeline.

Alex: Exactly. Each commit knows what came before, so Git can follow history backward.

Jamie: And every commit gets an ID.

Alex: Yes. A unique identifier called a hash, specifically a SHA hash. The full form is a 40-character string. In practice, you'll often see just the first seven characters because that short form is usually enough to identify the commit in a given repository.

Jamie: So learners do not need to memorize long strings of random-looking characters.

Alex: Not at all. You usually copy, tab-complete, or use the short form.

Jamie: What about permanence? People hear that Git never forgets, then later hear about rewriting history and get confused.

Alex: A good way to phrase it is: commits are permanent, mostly. Once a commit is part of the repository history, it exists in that timeline. You can create later commits that reverse its effects, but the original commit is still part of history. That stability is one reason Git feels safe. You can usually get back to earlier states. There are advanced history-rewriting tools, but for this mental model, think of commits as durable recorded points.

Jamie: And this connects directly back to Day 1 on GitHub.com.

Alex: Yes. When you clicked Commit changes in the web editor, GitHub handled staging and committing in one web action. Locally, those steps are separated. That separation gives you more control.

Jamie: Accessibility tips here too?

Alex: For screen reader users, after committing, git log dash dash oneline dash 5 is a great command to hear the last five commits as short hashes and messages. In VS Code Source Control, move to the commit message box, type your message, then use the commit shortcut, often Control Enter. And remember, the short hash is enough for most commands.

Jamie: For low vision users, widening the Source Control panel can make the message field easier to read, and after a successful commit the Source Control badge count usually drops to zero.

Alex: Right. And the Timeline view in VS Code can also help learners inspect file history.

Alex: Next up: branches.

Jamie: This is another word people use constantly, and beginners sometimes imagine branches as separate folders or duplicate repositories.

Alex: That's a very common misconception. A branch is best understood as a movable pointer to a commit. It marks the tip of a line of development. When you make a new commit on that branch, the branch label moves forward to point to the new commit.

Jamie: So the branch name is not the work itself. It's a label pointing to the latest commit in that line.

Alex: Exactly. And the default branch in many repositories is called main. That's usually the primary line of development.

Jamie: What happens when I create a new branch?

Alex: Git creates a new pointer that starts at your current commit. At first, the new branch and the old branch point to the same place. Then, once you make commits on the new branch, that branch moves forward while the other stays where it was.

Jamie: So branches let timelines diverge without interfering with each other.

Alex: Precisely. That's why they're so useful for features, fixes, experiments, and pull request workflows.

Jamie: Let's define HEAD, because learners see it everywhere.

Alex: HEAD tells you what you're currently on. More precisely, it identifies the current checked-out branch or commit. In everyday use, think of HEAD as Git's answer to the question, where am I right now? If HEAD is on your feature branch, new commits go there.

Jamie: And when you switch branches, your working directory updates to reflect that branch's files, as much as Git can safely do.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: Can we turn that into a simple mental card?

Alex: Sure. Main is the usual default branch. Creating a branch does not duplicate the whole project in a clumsy way; it creates a new pointer from the current commit. Commits made while HEAD is on that branch advance that branch. HEAD tells you your current position.

Jamie: And in tools, learners can often check the current branch in the VS Code status bar or with git branch or git status in the terminal.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let's widen the picture from one computer to two locations: local and remote.

Jamie: This is where Git and GitHub get tangled in people's minds.

Alex: Right. Git is the version control system on your machine. GitHub is a hosting service for remote repositories. Your local repository is the Git history stored on your computer, inside that hidden .git folder in the project. The remote repository is a copy hosted somewhere else, often on GitHub.

Jamie: So when people say, I committed my work, that might only mean locally.

Alex: Exactly. A local commit records history on your computer. It does not automatically publish anything to GitHub.

Jamie: That is such an important distinction.

Alex: It really is. Think in terms of a two-copy model. You usually have one repository copy on your computer and another on the remote host. They are related, but they are not magically identical every second. You must intentionally sync them.

Jamie: And sync goes in both directions.

Alex: Yes. You push local commits to share them with the remote. You fetch or pull remote changes to bring them to your local environment.

Jamie: So local is where I work and experiment. Remote is where I share and collaborate.

Alex: That's a solid basic model. Also, the remote is especially important in open source because it becomes the shared reference point for collaborators, issues, pull requests, code review, and CI workflows.

Jamie: Any learning card version of this?

Alex: Sure. Local repository: on your computer. Remote repository: hosted elsewhere, often GitHub. They start related but can drift apart. Syncing them requires explicit operations. And a commit is not the same thing as a push.

Alex: That brings us directly to push, pull, and fetch.

Jamie: These three get mashed together in beginners' minds.

Alex: Let's separate them clearly. Push means send your local commits to the remote repository. It's how you share work you've already committed locally.

Jamie: So if I edit a file and push without committing, nothing meaningful happens because the change never became a local commit.

Alex: Exactly. Push shares commits, not loose unstaged edits in your working directory.

Jamie: What about pull?

Alex: Pull means get changes from the remote and integrate them into your local branch. In everyday usage, pull is often thought of as fetch plus merge, or fetch plus rebase depending on configuration, but for this mental model the key point is that pull brings remote work down and combines it with your local state.

Jamie: And fetch is the quieter one.

Alex: Yes. Fetch checks the remote for updates and downloads information about new commits, but it does not merge them into your current branch. It's a safe way to see what's changed before integrating anything.

Jamie: So if I want awareness without immediate change to my current branch, fetch is the cautious choice.

Alex: Exactly. Push shares your work. Pull gets others' work and updates your branch. Fetch gets the information first without merging.

Jamie: That distinction is great for learners who want to stay oriented.

Alex: Now, one of the most emotionally charged Git topics: merge conflicts.

Jamie: Because people often read the word conflict as failure.

Alex: Right, but conflicts are normal. A merge conflict usually happens when Git cannot automatically decide how to combine competing changes. The classic case is two different edits to the same part of the same file.

Jamie: So if I changed line 20 one way and someone else changed line 20 another way, Git may need a human decision.

Alex: Exactly. Git is very good at auto-merging non-overlapping changes. But when the same region was changed in incompatible ways, Git stops and asks you to resolve it.

Jamie: What does that look like?

Alex: In a conflicted file, Git inserts conflict markers that show the competing versions. One section represents your current branch's content, another represents the incoming change, and markers divide them. Your job is to edit the file into the final correct version, removing the markers and choosing or combining the content as needed.

Jamie: So the goal is not to pick a side automatically. The goal is to produce the right final text.

Alex: Exactly. Sometimes you keep your version. Sometimes the other version. Sometimes a blend of both. After editing the file so it's correct, you stage the resolved file and complete the merge process with a commit if needed.

Jamie: And the important emotional lesson is that conflicts are not evidence you've broken Git.

Alex: Yes. They are a normal consequence of collaborative editing. In fact, a conflict is Git being careful. Instead of guessing and possibly damaging content, Git pauses for your decision.

Jamie: Any accessibility note here?

Alex: Very much so. Screen reader users may find conflict markers easier to understand in a plain text editor or VS Code diff view because the markers are literal text in the file. Listening carefully to marker boundaries and surrounding lines can make the structure clear. Low vision and sighted users may benefit from VS Code's merge editor, but the underlying plain-text markers are the essential concept for everyone.

Jamie: Let's make the learning card version concise.

Alex: Conflicts happen when Git cannot safely combine changes by itself. A conflicted file contains markers showing the competing edits. You resolve by editing the file into the correct final form, removing markers, then staging the resolution. And conflicts are normal.

Alex: Let's zoom out to the Git timeline.

Jamie: This is where the parent pointers and branches start to feel like a map.

Alex: Exactly. Because each commit points back to its parent, Git history forms a timeline. Reading the timeline means understanding that commits are connected in sequence. If you look at a log, you're seeing points in that history, usually newest first.

Jamie: And branching creates parallel timelines.

Alex: Right. If you create a branch and commit on it, you now have a line of development that moves separately from main. Both lines share earlier history, then diverge.

Jamie: And merging reconnects those timelines.

Alex: Yes. When you merge, Git creates a commit that brings the lines back together, preserving the fact that parallel work existed. So the history is not just one straight line forever. It can branch and reconnect.

Jamie: That helps explain why Git feels more like a graph than a stack of files.

Alex: Exactly, though for beginners it's often enough to picture a timeline with occasional side paths that later rejoin.

Alex: So let's put the whole model together.

Jamie: A checklist would help.

Alex: Here's a compact one. Your files live in the working directory. You choose what belongs in the next snapshot by staging it. A commit records the staged state in the repository with a message, author, and link to previous history. A branch is a movable pointer to the latest commit in one line of work. HEAD tells you your current position. Your local repository on your computer and the remote repository on GitHub are separate copies that must be synced intentionally. Push sends your commits up. Pull brings remote changes down and integrates them. Fetch checks for updates without merging. Conflicts happen when Git needs human help combining overlapping changes. And the overall history is a timeline that can branch and merge.

Jamie: That is the kind of checklist a learner can rehearse before typing commands.

Alex: Exactly. If a command seems confusing, ask: which area am I changing, which copy am I changing, and which branch am I on?

Jamie: That's a great recovery framework.

Alex: And if you do get stuck, here's the reassuring part. Most Git confusion becomes manageable when you slow down and inspect your state.

Jamie: Meaning, don't panic and start pasting random commands from the internet.

Alex: Please don't. Instead, check where you are and what Git thinks is happening. Commands like git status are often the best first step. Look at the current branch. Look at which files are changed, staged, or untracked. Check whether your commits are only local or also pushed. Think in terms of the mental model you built today.

Jamie: And if the issue involves authentication, advanced history editing, or security concerns, that's where those related appendices come in.

Alex: Yes. Use the right source for the right problem. For trusted references, lean on Git SCM docs, GitHub Docs, the Pro Git book, GitHub flow guidance, pull request documentation, and accessibility-focused CLI guidance from GitHub's Accessibility Lab.

Jamie: So the big takeaway is not just Git stores history. It's that Git has a structure: areas, snapshots, pointers, copies, and sync actions.

Alex: Exactly. Once you understand that structure, Git stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like a system you can reason about.

Jamie: And that's when commands become less scary, because they each have a place in the model.

Alex: Well said. In the next practice-oriented work, you'll use this model directly while cloning, staging, committing, branching, and syncing with GitHub. Keep the mental picture active while you work, and every command will have a why behind it.

Jamie: That's it for this lesson. Take a breath, maybe repeat the flow out loud: edit, stage, commit; local and remote; push, pull, fetch.

Alex: And remember: confusion usually means you need to inspect state, not that you've failed. We'll see you next time.

34. Episode 12: Git and Source Control in VS Code

Cloning, branching, staging, committing, pushing, and pulling from VS Code.

Based on: Chapter 14: Git and Source Control in VS Code

Download Episode 12 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 12: Git and Source Control in VS Code

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re working in that very practical space where Git, GitHub, and VS Code all meet. This lesson is about using source control accessibly on your own machine: cloning repositories, checking branches, staging changes, committing, pushing, pulling, reviewing history, handling conflicts, and recovering when things go sideways.

Jamie: And this is a big milestone, right? Because up to this point, learners may have done plenty in the browser, but local Git is where things start to feel more real.

Alex: Exactly. This is the first hands-on local Git workflow chapter, and it supports a challenge built around a repeatable pattern: clone, branch, edit, commit, push, and open a pull request. The expectation is not perfection. It’s building a reliable workflow you can repeat with confidence.

Jamie: Before we get into the mechanics, what should learners already know?

Alex: You’ll have a much easier time if you already know the VS Code interface and accessibility basics, how pull requests work, and the general idea of merge conflicts. And one quick accessibility note: when the material says Control on Windows or Linux, Mac users should usually think Command. Alt usually maps to Option. So shortcuts like Control Shift G become Command Shift G on Mac.

Alex: Let’s anchor this in the workshop challenge. There are three short practices. First, clone your private Learning Room repository to your machine. Second, create or switch to your learn slash username branch, make a small meaningful edit, stage it, and commit it. Third, push that branch and open a pull request that links back to the relevant issue.

Jamie: I like that it’s evidence-based. Not just “I think I did it,” but branch names, commit history, and PR metadata.

Alex: Right. Your evidence is in the actual workflow artifacts: the branch, the commit, the push, and the linked PR.

Jamie: And even though the work is happening in VS Code, the chapter recommends some CLI habits too.

Alex: Yes, and they’re excellent habits. Before doing anything, run git status so you know your current state. Keep branch context explicit with git branch dash dash show-current. Before pushing, fetch and then check status so you understand whether your local branch is aligned with the remote. And if you’re creating or updating a pull request tied to an issue, include plain-text linkage like Closes number. Also, avoid mystery convenience flags you don’t understand. Use stable commands with clear output.

Alex: Let’s walk through the first practice: cloning your Learning Room repository.

Jamie: And this is an important distinction: not the template repository.

Alex: Correct. You want your own private Learning Room repo, the one created for you, not the facilitator-maintained template. The URL should look like a workshop organization followed by learning-room-your-username. If GitHub says you don’t have access, double-check that URL first. Often the problem is simply cloning the wrong repository.

Jamie: So how do we do it in VS Code in the most accessible way?

Alex: The recommended method, especially for screen reader users, is the Command Palette. Open VS Code. If no folder is open, you may land on the Welcome tab. Press Control Shift P, or Command Shift P on Mac, type Git: Clone, and select it. Then paste the repository URL and press Enter. VS Code will ask where to save the clone. Choose a location you can find again easily, like Documents or Desktop, then confirm the destination. When cloning finishes, VS Code asks whether you want to open the cloned repository. Activate Open.

Jamie: And then verify, don’t assume.

Alex: Always verify. Open Explorer with Control Shift E. Your screen reader should announce the file tree. In the Learning Room repository, you should hear familiar items like README dot md and the docs folder.

Jamie: What if the learner hears nothing while the clone is happening and starts wondering whether VS Code froze?

Alex: There’s a good accessibility tip here. After choosing the destination, VS Code shows a progress notification. NVDA often reads this automatically. If you hear nothing for a while, you can use the Command Palette and run Notifications: Focus Notification Toast to check the current status.

Jamie: Once the clone is done, there’s one subtle thing learners may miss: they only have the default branch checked out locally.

Alex: Yes. A fresh clone usually checks out only main. But the remote repository may already contain other branches you made earlier, such as learn slash yourname. Open the integrated terminal and run git branch -a. That shows local and remote-tracking branches. The starred branch is your current one. Entries starting with remotes slash origin slash are on GitHub. If you see remotes slash origin slash learn slash yourname, you can check it out locally with git checkout learn slash yourname or git switch learn slash yourname.

Jamie: The chapter also teaches more than one way to clone, right?

Alex: It does, and that matters because different situations call for different methods. In VS Code, there are three broad ways. First, the Command Palette, which is the recommended route for screen reader users because it gives predictable keyboard access. Second, the Start Page clone button if you’re on the welcome experience and want a more visual starting point. Third, initiating from GitHub dot com, often through the Code button, copying the URL, and then completing the clone in VS Code or the terminal.

Jamie: And on the CLI side, there are several clone patterns learners should recognize.

Alex: Yes. Standard Git clone uses the full repository URL. GitHub CLI offers a shorter syntax like gh repo clone owner slash name, and it often handles authentication more smoothly once you’re signed in. You can clone into a specific folder by adding a target directory name. For large repositories, a single-branch clone can be faster if you only need the default branch initially. And after cloning, always verify. That can mean opening the folder in VS Code, listing files, or checking git status.

Jamie: There was also a concrete practice repo mentioned.

Alex: Yes, a sci-fi themes repository used as a try-it exercise. The point isn’t the theme itself. It’s that learners practice the flow: clone using owner slash name instead of a full URL when using GitHub CLI, change into the cloned folder, and open that repo in VS Code. It builds muscle memory.

Alex: Now let’s move into the Source Control panel in VS Code, because this is where many learners spend most of their time once a repo is open.

Jamie: Can you describe what opens when someone presses Control Shift G?

Alex: When you open Source Control, VS Code focuses the source control view. From top to bottom, you’ll typically find a commit message input, action buttons like Commit or more actions, then grouped lists for changes. Depending on state, you may hear sections such as Changes, Staged Changes, and sometimes merge-related groups. If the repository is clean, you may hear that there are no changes.

Jamie: And screen reader navigation differs a little by platform.

Alex: It does. For NVDA and JAWS, users often move through the panel with Tab to reach major controls, then arrow keys to navigate within file lists. For VoiceOver, interacting with groups and lists may require VoiceOver navigation patterns, but the core idea is the same: move to the Source Control area, then navigate the tree or list of changed files and controls.

Jamie: What does each file item actually tell you?

Alex: A changed file generally announces its name and status. That status might be modified, added, deleted, or untracked. If you open the file’s diff, you can review what changed. And if the file has been staged, it moves into the staged section, which is a very important conceptual cue: staged means ready for the next commit; unstaged means changed but not yet included.

Jamie: There’s also a context menu learners should know about.

Alex: Absolutely. Right-click, or Shift F10 on many keyboards, opens file actions. That can include stage, unstage, discard changes, open changes, reveal in explorer, and sometimes compare options. For keyboard users, that context menu can be more discoverable than trying to hunt for tiny inline buttons.

Jamie: How does this map to the CLI?

Alex: Very directly. If you want to see all modified, staged, and untracked files in a compact way, use git status with the short format. If you want to see only what is staged, use git diff dash dash cached. If you want to see modified but unstaged changes, use plain git diff. And if you want both the staged and unstaged picture with actual content differences, you combine those diff views intentionally.

Alex: Branch management is next, and it’s one of those skills that prevents a lot of confusion later.

Jamie: First question learners often ask: how do I know what branch I’m on right now?

Alex: In VS Code, look to the status bar at the bottom. The current branch is shown there. Keyboard users can move focus to the status bar and have the screen reader announce it. In the terminal, git branch dash dash show-current is a clean way to hear just the current branch name.

Jamie: And if you want a new branch?

Alex: The recommended accessible method in VS Code is again the Command Palette. Use Git: Create Branch. Enter the branch name, such as feature slash something, fix slash issue-number, or in the workshop context, learn slash username. Good branch names are descriptive, short, and consistent.

Jamie: CLI equivalents?

Alex: To create and switch in one step, you can use git checkout -b branch-name or the newer syntax git switch -c branch-name. To list local branches, git branch. To list local and remote-tracking branches, git branch -a. To switch to an existing branch, git checkout branch-name or git switch branch-name.

Jamie: What about deleting branches?

Alex: After a PR is merged, it’s often good housekeeping to delete the branch you no longer need. Locally, git branch -d branch-name performs a safe delete and refuses if the branch isn’t merged. A force delete uses uppercase D, but that’s riskier. You can also rename the current branch with git branch -m new-name. And if you need to push a new branch to GitHub the first time, you’ll typically use git push -u origin branch-name so the upstream tracking is set.

Jamie: The chapter also mentioned deleting a remote branch and even creating a branch linked to an issue.

Alex: Yes. Remote branch deletion is possible and useful after merge cleanup. And GitHub tooling can create an issue-linked branch, sometimes auto-naming it from the issue title. The exact interface can vary, but the important concept is that issue context and branch context can be connected.

Jamie: When you switch branches in VS Code, what should learners expect?

Alex: Files in the working directory may change to match the target branch. That can feel surprising if you’re new to Git. So before switching, check whether you have uncommitted work. If you do, commit it, stash it, or consciously discard it. Otherwise Git may block the switch, or you may create confusion for yourself.

Alex: Now let’s make the branch idea concrete with the second practice: create a branch and commit.

Jamie: Walk us through it.

Alex: Open the Command Palette. If your learn slash username branch already exists on the remote, use Git: Checkout to and select that branch. If it doesn’t exist yet, use Git: Create Branch and enter learn slash your-username. Then confirm your branch by checking the status bar. Next, open Explorer, go into the docs folder, and open the file your challenge refers to, such as docs slash welcome dot md. Make one small, meaningful change. Save with Control S. Then open Source Control with Control Shift G. Your changed file appears under Changes. Navigate to the file and either press Enter to open the diff or activate the Stage Changes control, often announced as a plus button. Once staged, the file moves to Staged Changes. Move to the commit message box, type a clear message like docs: improve welcome.md introduction, then press Control Enter to commit. When the staged changes disappear, that’s your success signal.

Jamie: That step where the file moves from Changes to Staged Changes is really important for understanding Git’s three areas.

Alex: It is. You edit in the working directory, stage in the index, and commit into repository history. That separation is what gives Git precision.

Jamie: So let’s talk staging in more detail, because this chapter goes beyond whole-file staging.

Alex: Yes. You can stage an entire file, multiple files at once, or just individual lines or chunks. In VS Code, staging a whole file is usually as simple as activating the plus button next to that file or using the file’s context menu. There may also be a keyboard shortcut depending on focus and platform.

Jamie: And staging multiple files?

Alex: You can often stage all changes from the group header, or select multiple files using list interaction patterns if your setup supports it. On the CLI, git add filename stages a specific file, and git add dot or git add -A stages broadly depending on what you intend.

Jamie: What about partial staging, which can feel a little more advanced?

Alex: Partial staging is incredibly useful. Suppose you fixed a typo and also made an unrelated formatting change. Rather than bundling them together, you can stage just the relevant hunk. In terminal Git, git add -p launches interactive patch staging. Git shows each hunk and asks whether to stage it, with choices like yes, no, split, or edit. In VS Code, chunk-level staging may be available from the diff or context actions.

Jamie: That seems especially helpful in a workshop where you want one clean commit for one clear improvement.

Alex: Exactly. One commit, one idea is a very strong habit.

Jamie: And unstaging is just the reverse?

Alex: Yes. In VS Code, use the minus button or context menu on a staged file. In terminal Git, git restore --staged filename is the modern form for unstaging a file. And to check what is staged versus unstaged, compare git diff with git diff --cached.

Alex: Once changes are staged, it’s time to commit, and the chapter gives special attention to screen reader workflows here.

Jamie: What’s the standard process?

Alex: Open Source Control, review the staged items, move to the message input, type a meaningful commit message, and trigger commit with Control Enter. Screen reader users should listen for focus changes carefully, because it’s easy to land on action buttons before the message field. The panel structure matters.

Jamie: Any differences for NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver?

Alex: The experience differs mainly in how each screen reader announces grouped controls and text inputs. NVDA and JAWS users often navigate with Tab and arrows. VoiceOver users may need to interact with the source control region and move deliberately into the message field. But the key goal is the same: confirm you’re in the message box before typing.

Jamie: Let’s spend a moment on commit messages, because learners often overthink them.

Alex: A good commit message is short, specific, and tells future-you what changed. Many teams like a format such as type colon description, for example docs: clarify setup steps, fix: correct broken link, feat: add keyboard shortcut notes. The quick reference is: use imperative mood, keep it descriptive, and tie it to the actual change.

Jamie: And CLI commit options?

Alex: Git commit -m lets you commit staged changes with a one-line message. Git commit without dash m opens your editor for a multi-line message. And git commit -am can stage tracked files and commit in one step, but note the limitation: it does not include new untracked files, so beginners should use it carefully.

Jamie: What happens after a commit?

Alex: The changes are saved in local history on your current branch. They are not on GitHub yet until you push. In VS Code, the source control lists usually clear if there are no remaining modifications. Your branch indicator remains, and history tools can now show the new commit.

Alex: That brings us to push and pull operations.

Jamie: Let’s start with pushing.

Alex: After committing locally, open the Command Palette and run Git: Push, or use the sync and push controls in the interface. If the branch has never been pushed before, VS Code may prompt you to publish the branch. Accept that. After the push completes, the sync indicator should show that local and remote are aligned.

Jamie: The CLI versions learners should know?

Alex: Git push sends commits to GitHub. For a brand-new branch, git push -u origin branch-name both pushes and sets upstream tracking. Pulling changes from GitHub is git pull. If you want to see updates first without merging them into your files, use git fetch.

Jamie: When should learners pull?

Alex: Before starting work for the day, before pushing if others may have changed shared branches, and any time you know the remote may have advanced. Some tools also auto-fetch in the background, which can be helpful, but you should still understand what fetch means: it updates your knowledge of remote branches without changing your working files.

Jamie: What if push fails?

Alex: Don’t panic. Read the error. Common causes include authentication problems, trying to push to a branch you don’t have permission to modify, or a non-fast-forward situation where the remote has commits you don’t have locally. In that last case, fetch or pull, inspect what changed, resolve any conflicts if necessary, then push again.

Jamie: Now let’s tie this to the third workshop practice: push and open a linked PR.

Alex: After your local commit, run Git: Push. If asked to publish the branch, confirm. Wait for the push to finish. Then open your Learning Room repository on GitHub. Often you’ll see a banner saying you recently pushed to your branch, with a Compare and pull request button. Activate it. If not, go to Pull requests, choose New pull request, set base to main and compare to your learn slash username branch. Then write a descriptive PR title, usually close to your commit theme. In the PR description, include plain text linking to the issue, such as Closes number. Submit the pull request.

Jamie: And that plain-text linkage matters because it creates traceability.

Alex: Exactly. It helps reviewers, and when merged it can automatically close the linked issue depending on repository settings.

Jamie: The chapter also covers syncing a fork with upstream, which learners may encounter in open source contribution workflows.

Alex: Yes, and there are two main patterns. The quickest on GitHub is often the Sync fork button on the web interface. For screen reader users, the path is generally to open your fork on GitHub, find the sync control near branch information, and activate it.

Jamie: And if you’re doing it with Git remotes?

Alex: That’s the classic one-time setup plus recurring sync workflow. First, add the upstream remote once, pointing to the original repository. Then fetch updates from upstream. Next, make sure you’re on your default branch, usually main. Merge upstream slash main into your local main. Finally, push your updated main back to your fork on GitHub.

Jamie: So conceptually: upstream is the source project, origin is your fork.

Alex: Precisely. And in VS Code, some of these operations may be available through the Command Palette, but it’s helpful to know the underlying Git model. If conflicts occur during sync, you resolve them just like other merge conflicts: inspect, choose or combine changes, stage, and complete the merge.

Alex: Sometimes, though, the right move is not to keep a change but to discard it.

Jamie: This is one of those areas where wording matters, because discard is permanent in many cases.

Alex: Yes. Discard only when you truly want to restore content to the last committed state. In VS Code, you can discard a single file from its context menu, or discard broader groups of changes from group actions. The CLI equivalents are worth knowing too. For a specific file, you can restore it to the last commit. For all unstaged changes, you can restore the working tree more broadly. If changes are staged, unstage first, then restore. And there is a nuclear option that throws away staged and unstaged work together. That one should be treated with extreme caution.

Jamie: Is there a safer way to preview before discarding?

Alex: Absolutely. Review the diff first. In terminal Git, inspect with git diff for unstaged changes and git diff --cached for staged changes. In VS Code, open the diff view and listen carefully to what changed before taking destructive action.

Jamie: And the chapter explicitly recommends stash as a safer alternative in many cases.

Alex: It does. If you’re not sure whether you’ll need the changes later, stash instead of discard.

Jamie: There’s also a section on deleting files from a repository, which is slightly different from simply removing them in your file explorer.

Alex: Correct. Git-aware deletion means Git records the removal. Git rm removes a file and stages that deletion in one step. If you want Git to stop tracking a file but keep it on your machine, use the cached form. You can remove an entire directory recursively as well. Then commit the deletion and verify the file is no longer tracked.

Jamie: So the main distinction is whether you want the file gone everywhere or just no longer version-controlled.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Now let’s talk history, because Git isn’t just about changing files. It’s also about understanding what happened.

Jamie: That’s where Timeline view comes in.

Alex: Yes. In VS Code, you can open Timeline from the Explorer sidebar when a file is selected, or use the Command Palette to access history-related views. Timeline shows events associated with the selected file, including commits. You can browse backward through changes, open a particular commit entry, and inspect what changed.

Jamie: And then there’s blame, which has a dramatic name but a practical purpose.

Alex: Very practical. Git blame shows who last changed each line and in which commit. In some setups it appears inline or in an extension-provided view. For screen reader users, the most important thing is whether the information is exposed accessibly. Sometimes the terminal or a text-based history command is easier to read than a dense visual annotation.

Jamie: The chapter also includes CLI history commands learners should recognize.

Alex: Yes. You can view commit history for the whole repository with git log. For a specific file, git log double-dash path-to-file. To see what changed in each commit, use patch output. For line-level history, blame commands show authorship. You can show a specific commit’s changes with git show commit-sha. You can compare two commits, filter commits by author, limit to recent days, inspect recent commits on the web, and review PR history on GitHub.

Jamie: And there’s an accessibility point here too: structured diff review often beats visually scanning for changes.

Alex: Exactly. A diff viewer that lets you move hunk by hunk is often more efficient than searching manually through a changed file.

Jamie: Which leads naturally to merge conflicts.

Alex: Yes. Conflicts happen when Git can’t automatically reconcile competing changes. VS Code displays conflict regions in the editor and often provides actions such as accepting the current change, the incoming change, both changes, or manually editing the result.

Jamie: What does a good screen reader workflow look like for resolving conflicts?

Alex: First, identify which file has the conflict. Open it and navigate carefully through the conflict regions. If your setup exposes structured conflict actions accessibly, use them. If not, reading the conflict markers and editing manually may be necessary. Review the surrounding context so you understand what each version is trying to do.

Jamie: The chapter emphasizes accessible diff tools here.

Alex: Yes, because accessible diff navigation gives you structured, hunk-by-hunk movement instead of forcing you to hunt for markers in a long file. After choosing or combining content, save the file, stage it, and complete the merge commit. If the merge is not worth continuing, you can abort the merge and return to the pre-merge state.

Jamie: So an aborted merge is not failure. It’s a controlled retreat.

Alex: Exactly. Sometimes stepping back is the best troubleshooting move.

Alex: Stash management is another skill that helps when your work is in-between states.

Jamie: When should someone use stash?

Alex: Use stash when you have uncommitted changes but need to switch tasks, change branches, pull updates safely, or test something without committing half-finished work. Think of it as temporarily setting your changes aside.

Jamie: How do you create a stash?

Alex: In VS Code, the Command Palette may offer stash commands. In the terminal, you can stash all uncommitted changes with a message, which is especially helpful because named stashes are easier to identify later. If you also want to include untracked new files, use the include-untracked option.

Jamie: How do you see what stashes exist?

Alex: Either through the Command Palette if your interface exposes them, or in terminal with git stash list. To inspect a specific stash, use a show command that reveals its contents.

Jamie: And restoring?

Alex: Applying a stash restores the changes but keeps the stash entry. Popping a stash restores the changes and removes that stash entry in one step. You can apply the most recent stash or a specific stash by reference. That difference between apply and pop is important: apply is safer when you’re unsure.

Jamie: And cleanup?

Alex: You can drop a specific stash or clear all stashes, but clearing all should be done very carefully.

Jamie: Then there’s the emergency recovery section, which I think comforts a lot of learners.

Alex: It should. Git reflog is one of the best safety nets in Git. It records where your HEAD and branch references have been locally, even when commits seem lost after resets, rebases, or branch deletions.

Jamie: Local is the key word there.

Alex: Exactly. Reflog is local-only. It’s your machine’s memory of reference movements. It is not a shared remote history.

Jamie: So if you think you lost a commit, what’s the recovery pattern?

Alex: First, open the VS Code terminal and read the reflog to find the last good commit SHA. Second, preview that commit with a show command so you know it’s the right one. Third, take the safer recovery route whenever possible: create a new branch at that commit. That preserves the current state while giving you access to the lost work. The riskier option is resetting your current branch back to that point.

Jamie: And if you deleted a branch entirely?

Alex: Use reflog to find the commit that branch pointed to, then recreate the branch at that SHA. This is one reason experienced Git users seem calm in situations that feel catastrophic to beginners.

Jamie: Because they know the history is often still recoverable.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: The chapter also acknowledges that VS Code is not the only interface.

Jamie: Right. There are alternatives depending on accessibility preferences and task type.

Alex: Yes. GitHub Desktop can be appealing for a more guided visual workflow. GitHub CLI, the gh tool, is excellent for repository and pull request tasks and often works very well with screen readers when you like structured terminal output. And the core Git CLI remains the most universal interface, with common commands for status, add, commit, branch, switch, push, pull, fetch, stash, log, show, diff, and reflog.

Jamie: So the real goal is not loyalty to one interface. It’s fluency across concepts.

Alex: Beautifully said. Tools differ. The model stays the same.

Jamie: Before we wrap, can we give learners a quick practical recap they can actually use the next time they sit down to work?

Alex: Absolutely. Start by checking your state: git status. Confirm your branch: git branch --show-current. If you need the repo locally, clone it and verify it opened correctly in Explorer. Create or switch to the correct branch before editing. Make one meaningful change. Stage intentionally, either whole file or selected chunks. Write a clear commit message. Commit locally. Push to GitHub, publishing the branch if needed. Open a pull request and include issue linkage like Closes number. If you need updates first, fetch or pull. If something feels risky, stash instead of discarding. If something seems lost, reflog may save you.

Jamie: And for accessibility specifically?

Alex: Prefer predictable keyboard-first workflows. The Command Palette is often the most screen-reader-friendly route in VS Code. Use the Source Control panel deliberately: know where the message field is, know where the file groups are, and use context menus when inline buttons are awkward. Verify feedback through notifications, status bar announcements, diffs, and terminal commands. Never rely on visual assumptions alone.

Jamie: One more thing: the chapter includes a try-it prompt to practice clone, branch, and commit. That’s worth doing even if you think you understood the lesson.

Alex: Absolutely. Git becomes clear through repetition. Practice the sequence until it feels boring. That’s when it becomes dependable.

Jamie: And if someone gets stuck?

Alex: Pause, check status, check branch, read the exact message Git or VS Code is giving you, and ask for help with those details. “It didn’t work” is hard to debug. “Git says non-fast-forward on branch learn slash jamie after push” is very debug-friendly.

Jamie: That is such a good learning habit.

Alex: It is. And one final note: this chapter points learners toward authoritative sources too, especially the VS Code source control docs, GitHub’s Git documentation, and the GitHub Accessibility Lab CLI guide. Those are excellent references as you keep practicing.

Jamie: So the big takeaway is that accessible Git is absolutely possible, and a careful workflow beats a fast, fuzzy one.

Alex: Exactly. Clear state, explicit branches, deliberate staging, meaningful commits, and accessible review habits. That’s a professional workflow.

Alex: Thanks for learning with us.

Jamie: We’ll see you next time.

35. Challenge 10: Go Local

Cloning, local branches, commits, pushing, and understanding local versus remote.

Practice focus: Day 2 local workflow

Download Challenge 10 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 10: Go Local

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're doing something important: taking Git from the browser to your own computer. That means cloning a repository, creating a branch, editing locally, staging, committing, and pushing back to GitHub.

Jamie: So this is the point where Git stops being kind of magical and starts being real?

Alex: Exactly. On GitHub.com, the website quietly handled a lot for you. Locally, you do those steps yourself. The good news is the workflow is very consistent, and once you understand the model behind it, Git gets much less mysterious.

Alex: Let's start with the goal for this challenge. You are working in your own Learning Room repository, not the shared template repository. Your task is to clone that private repo to your machine, create a non-default branch, make at least one edit, commit locally, and push the branch to GitHub from a local tool.

Jamie: And local tool here could be VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the command line?

Alex: Yes. VS Code is recommended for this day, but all three count. The autograder is looking for evidence that at least one commit exists on a pushed non-default branch created from a local workflow.

Jamie: So the exact content of the edit is not the big thing.

Alex: Right. The workflow matters most. Fix a typo, improve a sentence, add a helpful comment in the docs folder. Small and meaningful is perfect.

Alex: Before we walk the tools, let's build the mental model. Git makes more sense when you know its three areas: the working directory, the staging area, and the repository.

Jamie: I hear those terms a lot, especially staging area, and I think that's where many people start nodding politely instead of actually understanding.

Alex: Fair. So let's make it concrete. The working directory is the actual project folder on your computer. In VS Code, it's the files you open in Explorer. If you edit a file there, you've changed the working directory.

Jamie: But changing a file does not automatically become a commit.

Alex: Exactly. Git notices the change, but it does not save it to history yet. The staging area, also called the index, is the holding zone for the next commit. When you stage a file, you're telling Git, yes, include this version in my next snapshot.

Jamie: And then the repository is where committed history lives.

Alex: Yes. The repository is Git's database, stored in the hidden .git folder. Once you commit, Git records a snapshot of what was staged. So the flow is: edit in the working directory, stage what belongs together, then commit that staged snapshot into the repository.

Jamie: So edit, stage, commit. Working directory, staging area, repository.

Alex: Perfect. One useful analogy is packing a box. Your desk is the working directory. The open shipping box is the staging area. Sealing and labeling the box is the commit. You can add or remove items from the box before sealing it.

Jamie: That actually helps. Especially because it explains why unstaging is not the same as deleting.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: A few accessibility notes go with this mental model. If you use a screen reader, `git status` is one of the clearest tools you have because it reports what is changed, staged, and untracked in plain language. In VS Code Source Control, files are grouped under headings like Changes and Staged Changes, which mirrors the model directly.

Jamie: So the interface is different, but the structure is the same.

Alex: Yes. And pressing Enter on a changed file in Source Control can open a diff. Screen readers can read added and removed lines with change indicators. For low vision users, the separate headings, status letters, and gutter colors can help distinguish modified, added, or deleted content.

Jamie: Okay, now what exactly is a commit?

Alex: A commit is a snapshot of your project at a moment in time. It includes the staged content, a human-readable message, the author identity, and a pointer to the previous commit.

Jamie: So it's more than "here are the lines that changed."

Alex: Right. Git can show differences between commits, but a commit itself records a full project state for the tracked files involved in that snapshot. Each commit also gets a unique ID called a hash, often shortened to a seven-character form when you're reading logs.

Jamie: And commits are mostly permanent.

Alex: That's the big safety feature. You can add more commits to fix mistakes, revert changes, or move around in history, but the original commit becomes part of the timeline. That permanence is what makes Git such a reliable record.

Jamie: For screen reader users, is there a good way to confirm a commit happened?

Alex: Yes. In the terminal, `git log --oneline -5` reads out recent commit hashes and messages. In VS Code, after a successful commit, Source Control usually clears out because there are no staged or unstaged changes left. The badge count drops, and your branch name remains in the status bar.

Jamie: And branches?

Alex: A branch is simply a movable label pointing to a series of commits. The default branch is usually `main`. When you create a new branch, you create a safe place to work without changing `main` directly.

Jamie: So a branch is not a full copy of the repository in the everyday sense.

Alex: Correct. It's lightweight. You create the branch, then as you make commits on it, that branch advances. `HEAD` tells Git which branch, or more precisely which current checkout, you are on right now.

Jamie: And in practical terms, the status bar in VS Code or `git branch --show-current` in the terminal tells you where you are.

Alex: Exactly. And that matters a lot. One of the best habits you can build is checking your current branch before you edit or commit.

Alex: Now let's connect local and remote. Your local repository lives on your computer. The remote repository lives on GitHub. After you clone, you have a local copy to work in, but GitHub still has its own copy.

Jamie: So this is the two-copy model.

Alex: Yes. Local and remote are related, but they are not automatically synced every second. You make changes and commits locally. Then you push to send your commits to GitHub. If other people have changed the remote, you pull to bring those changes into your local repo. And fetch lets you check for updates without merging them yet.

Jamie: Push shares your work. Pull gets other people's work. Fetch checks what changed first.

Alex: Beautifully said.

Jamie: Before the step-by-step, can we talk about merge conflicts? People get nervous the moment that phrase appears.

Alex: Absolutely. A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically combine competing changes, usually because two versions modified the same part of the same file. Conflict markers may appear in the file, or VS Code may show conflict resolution controls.

Jamie: And the important emotional message is that conflicts are normal, not proof that you broke Git.

Alex: Exactly. Conflicts are a routine collaboration event. You resolve them by deciding what the final content should be, removing the conflict markers, testing the result mentally or practically, then staging and committing the resolution. In VS Code, accessible diff and structured conflict navigation can help review hunks more safely than hunting manually through a file.

Jamie: And if a merge is going badly, you can abort it.

Alex: Yes. That is an important recovery move.

Alex: One last piece of the mental model: the Git timeline. Think of history as a sequence of commits. Branching creates parallel timelines. Merging reconnects them. Reading the timeline helps you understand where your work sits, what came before, and how branches relate.

Jamie: So when we say "make a commit on your branch and push it," we're really saying "add a new point to your branch's timeline, then publish that timeline to GitHub."

Alex: Exactly. If you remember the checklist"”working directory, staging area, repository; branch context; local versus remote; push and pull"”you can predict most Git behavior.

Alex: Now let's do the challenge workflow itself. The professional local workflow is five verbs: clone, branch, edit, commit, push.

Jamie: Simple list, but each word hides a lot.

Alex: True, which is why we'll unpack each one clearly.

Alex: First: clone. Cloning copies the remote repository from GitHub onto your machine and sets up the connection back to the remote, usually named `origin`.

Jamie: And for this challenge, the correct URL is your private Learning Room repository, something like `https://github.com/workshop-org/learning-room-your-username.git`.

Alex: Right. Not the shared template. Your own private repo. If GitHub says you do not have access, first confirm you copied your own Learning Room URL. If authentication fails, that usually points to Git setup or credentials.

Jamie: Which is why the challenge troubleshooting mentions authentication help and facilitator support.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let's begin with the terminal or CLI approach because it maps very clearly to the mental model.

Jamie: Great. Walk us through it slowly.

Alex: You run `git clone` followed by your repository URL. Then you change into the cloned folder. Often that folder is named `learning-room` locally, though the repository name may include your username on GitHub.

Jamie: After cloning, are you automatically on `main`?

Alex: Usually yes, the default branch. That's why the next step is to create a new branch. You can use `git checkout -b fix/local-edit` or another name that fits the instructions, such as `fix/YOUR-USERNAME`. That command creates the branch and switches to it in one step.

Jamie: And there's a newer style too, right?

Alex: Yes, `git switch -c branch-name`. Both ideas matter: create and switch. The branch name should be descriptive and non-default.

Alex: Then make an edit in any text editor. The challenge suggests editing something in the `docs/` folder. A good example is fixing a typo or improving `docs/welcome.md`.

Jamie: Then stage the specific file.

Alex: Yes. For a targeted change, use `git add docs/welcome.md`. You can also stage all current changes with `git add .`, but especially for beginners, staging the specific file helps reinforce intention.

Jamie: Then commit with a descriptive message, like `docs: fix typo in welcome page`.

Alex: Exactly. Descriptive commit messages help both you and collaborators. Then push the branch to GitHub with `git push -u origin fix/local-edit` or whatever branch name you chose. The `-u` sets the upstream so future pushes and pulls can be shorter.

Jamie: That's the whole local loop in plain text.

Alex: Yes: clone, branch, edit, add, commit, push.

Jamie: Now let's do the VS Code version, since that's the recommended route.

Alex: Open VS Code. If no folder is open, you may be on the Welcome tab. Open the Command Palette with Control+Shift+P, or Command+Shift+P on Mac, then run Git: Clone.

Jamie: And this method is especially recommended for screen reader users.

Alex: Yes. The Command Palette is often the most predictable and keyboard-friendly path. Paste the repository URL, press Enter, then choose a folder location like Documents or Desktop when VS Code asks where to save the clone.

Jamie: Then wait for the progress notification and choose Open when VS Code asks whether to open the cloned repository.

Alex: Exactly. If you use a screen reader and don't hear progress, you can focus notification toasts to check status. Once open, go to Explorer with Control+Shift+E and verify you can access files like README.md and the `docs/` folder.

Jamie: So that's how you verify the clone worked inside VS Code.

Alex: Yes. You can also verify in the terminal with commands like `git status` or list branches with `git branch -a`.

Alex: After cloning, branch management matters. A fresh clone usually checks out only the default branch locally, but the remote may already have branches you created earlier on GitHub, such as `learn/yourname`.

Jamie: So `git branch -a` is useful because it shows both local and remote-tracking branches.

Alex: Exactly. In VS Code, you can create a branch from the status bar branch name or from the Command Palette with Git: Create Branch. The Command Palette method is often recommended for accessible workflows. Name the branch something like `fix/YOUR-USERNAME` or, in some exercises, `learn/YOUR-USERNAME`, depending on the instruction set.

Jamie: And if the branch already exists remotely, you may use Git: Checkout to and select it.

Alex: Right. You can also list local branches, switch to an existing branch, rename the current branch, or delete a branch after it has been merged. In the CLI, common actions include creating and switching to a new branch, listing local branches, listing all branches including remote-tracking ones, switching to an existing branch with either `checkout` or `switch`, deleting safely after merge, force deleting if absolutely necessary, and pushing a new branch to GitHub for the first time.

Jamie: There's also remote branch deletion and issue-linked branch creation in some workflows.

Alex: Yes, and those become more relevant as your collaboration grows.

Alex: Once you're on the right branch, edit a file in the `docs/` folder. Save it. Then open Source Control with Control+Shift+G.

Jamie: Can we pause on the Source Control panel itself? Because if someone has never used it with a screen reader, that panel can feel a bit busy.

Alex: Absolutely. When you open Source Control, you typically get a commit message input near the top, action buttons, and file groups below such as Changes and Staged Changes. For screen reader navigation, arrow keys are often best inside the file lists. NVDA and JAWS users may hear group headings and file status. VoiceOver users may prefer interacting carefully with groups and using rotor or navigation commands depending on setup.

Jamie: And if a file is modified, untracked, staged, or deleted, that status is announced or shown with a short indicator.

Alex: Exactly. In CLI terms, `git status` gives a compact but readable snapshot. You can view all modified, staged, and untracked files, see what is staged and what is not, and inspect diffs for both staged and unstaged changes.

Alex: For staging in VS Code, navigate to your changed file and activate the plus button, or use the context menu. The file moves from Changes to Staged Changes.

Jamie: And this matches the mental model perfectly: it moved from working directory change to staging area.

Alex: Exactly. You can stage an entire file, multiple files at once, or even individual lines and chunks. That last option is very powerful.

Jamie: Why would someone stage only part of a file?

Alex: Because one file might contain two unrelated edits. Maybe you fixed a typo and also rewrote a paragraph for a different reason. Partial staging lets you build cleaner commits. In CLI, interactive staging presents hunks and asks whether to stage each one, often with choices like yes, no, split, or edit.

Jamie: And unstaging is just reversing that decision.
