Alex: Correct. You can unstage a file if you staged too much. It's a great safety valve.

Alex: Now commit. In VS Code, move to the Message input box in Source Control, type a clear message like `docs: improve welcome.md introduction`, then press Control+Enter, or Command+Enter on Mac.

Jamie: What makes a good commit message here?

Alex: Short, specific, and meaningful. A quick reference pattern is a scope or category plus a concise description, like `docs: fix typo in welcome page`. You can also create multi-line messages in the CLI if you need more detail. And there's a convenience pattern to stage tracked files and commit in one step, though for learning I prefer keeping staging and commit as separate actions so the model stays visible.

Jamie: And after commit, the changes disappear from the staged and unstaged lists.

Alex: Exactly. That's a useful confirmation. In terminal, `git log --oneline` gives another confirmation.

Alex: Next comes pushing. In VS Code, open the Command Palette and run Git: Push, or use Publish Branch or sync controls when they appear.

Jamie: And if it's the first push of a new branch, VS Code may ask you to publish the branch.

Alex: Right. Confirm it. In CLI, you'd use `git push` for an existing tracked branch or `git push -u origin branch-name` for the first push. Push sends your local commits to GitHub.

Jamie: How is that different from pull again?

Alex: Push is you sharing outward. Pull is bringing remote changes into your local branch. Fetch is the cautious middle step: get the latest remote information without merging it into your files yet.

Jamie: And that's why one best practice is fetch first, then status, before pushing.

Alex: Yes. A few solid CLI habits were recommended: run `git status` before acting, keep branch context explicit with `git branch --show-current`, verify remote alignment with `git fetch` and `git status`, and write plain text PR linkage like `Closes #number` before opening or updating a pull request.

Jamie: What if push fails?

Alex: A few common causes. If you get an authentication error during clone or push, check your Git authentication setup. If you get permission denied, confirm you actually have write access to that repository and that you're using your own Learning Room repo. If the remote has changes you don't have, you may need to fetch and pull first.

Jamie: So a failed push is not a dead end. It's a clue.

Alex: Exactly. Git's error messages are often trying to tell you what relationship is out of sync: identity, permission, or branch history.

Alex: Now let's talk about verifying success, because the challenge is not complete until you know the result landed on GitHub.

Jamie: What should learners look for?

Alex: After pushing, go to GitHub.com and open your repository. You should see your branch in the branch dropdown. You may also see a banner saying that your branch had recent pushes, with a Compare and pull request button. And if you open the branch's commit history, your commit should be there.

Jamie: So the success signal is not just "VS Code said done." It's "GitHub now shows my branch and my commit."

Alex: Exactly. If your branch appeared on GitHub with your commit, you succeeded.

Jamie: Can we cover the GitHub Desktop path too?

Alex: Definitely. In GitHub Desktop, use File, Clone Repository, paste the URL, and clone. Then use the Current Branch dropdown or Branch menu to create a new branch. Open the repo folder in your editor or file manager, make your change, return to GitHub Desktop, review the diff it shows, write a commit message in the lower-left area, commit, then select Publish Branch.

Jamie: That's nice because the app exposes the same workflow with fewer typed commands.

Alex: Yes. Same concepts, different interface: clone, branch, edit, commit, publish.

Jamie: The challenge instructions also ask learners to submit evidence. What should that include?

Alex: Describe what tool you used, what you edited, your branch name, and your commit message. For example: tool used, VS Code; branch name, `fix/myusername`; edited file, maybe `docs/welcome.md`; commit message, something like `docs: improve welcome introduction`.

Jamie: There's also a peer simulation reflection.

Alex: Yes. Compare your local tool choice with a peer simulation PR workflow or a buddy's workflow. What was different? Maybe they used the browser before and you used VS Code now. Maybe one of you relied on visual buttons while the other used keyboard commands or CLI output. That comparison helps you notice workflow structure rather than just memorizing clicks.

Alex: Now, because this chapter also teaches broader practice, let's briefly cover the rest of the VS Code Git toolkit so learners have a usable map, not just one narrow recipe.

Jamie: Good, because once someone completes one clone-and-push cycle, the next questions come fast.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Cloning can happen three common ways in VS Code: through the Command Palette, which is often best for screen readers; from the Start page Clone button; or by starting on GitHub.com and opening the repository into your local tools. In CLI, you also have variations: standard `git clone`, GitHub CLI clone with shorter owner-slash-name syntax and automatic authentication handling in many setups, cloning into a specific folder, and cloning only the default branch for speed in large repositories.

Jamie: And after clone, verify it either in Explorer, with `git status`, or by opening the folder in VS Code.

Alex: Exactly. There was even a practice example about cloning a sample repo, entering the folder, and opening it in VS Code.

Alex: The Source Control panel deserves a full mental map. It lets you see all modified, staged, and untracked files; view short status indicators; check what is staged versus unstaged; and inspect diffs with content. Right-click or Shift+F10 opens context menu actions. The panel structure matters for screen reader users, because predictable navigation reduces guesswork.

Jamie: So learning the panel once pays off across every Git task.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: More on branches: you can view the current branch in the status bar, access it with the keyboard, create a new branch, switch between branches, view all branches, delete a branch after merge, force delete if necessary, rename the current branch, list remote branches, and create issue-linked branches in some GitHub-aware workflows.

Jamie: And branch naming conventions help keep work understandable.

Alex: Yes. Names like `fix/username`, `docs/update-intro`, or `learn/username` communicate intent.

Alex: Staging also has depth. You can stage a specific file, stage all changes, stage specific lines interactively, unstage a file, and compare staged versus unstaged differences. This is especially useful when one editing session produced several logically separate changes.

Jamie: So "stage everything" is not always the best choice.

Alex: Right. It's convenient, but selective staging creates cleaner history.

Alex: Committing with screen readers has a few practical considerations. Know where the message box is. Listen for the control labeled Message. Use the keyboard shortcut to commit. On Windows and Linux that's usually Control+Enter; on Mac, Command+Enter. If nothing happens, first confirm you actually staged something, because some interfaces warn you or require confirmation before committing unstaged changes.

Jamie: And after commit, no pending changes is the happy silence.

Alex: Well put.

Alex: Push and pull operations also include sync awareness. You can push commits to GitHub, publish a new branch for the first time, pull changes from GitHub, and fetch without merging to review the situation first. Some tools auto-fetch in the background. That can be helpful, but it's still worth understanding what happened conceptually.

Jamie: And if someone is working with a fork, there's another layer: upstream.

Alex: Exactly. If you have your own fork of a project, the original project is often added as `upstream`. Then a common sync sequence is: fetch updates from upstream, make sure you're on your default branch, merge or rebase upstream changes into your local branch, then push the updated branch back to your fork on GitHub. GitHub also offers a Sync fork button on the website for a quicker route.

Jamie: And if conflicts happen during sync, you resolve them the same general way as any merge conflict.

Alex: Correct.

Alex: Sometimes you do not want to keep a change. That's where discarding and stashing come in, and the difference matters.

Jamie: Discard means throw away. Stash means set aside.

Alex: Exactly. You can discard changes to a specific file and restore it to the last commit, discard all unstaged changes, unstage then restore if changes were already staged, or in extreme cases discard everything staged and unstaged. But always preview what would be discarded first when possible.

Jamie: And the safer alternative is often stash.

Alex: Yes. Stash saves your uncommitted changes temporarily so you can switch tasks without losing work. You can create a stash with a message, include untracked files if needed, list stashes, inspect what a stash contains, apply the most recent stash while keeping it, pop it to apply and remove it, apply a specific stash, drop one stash, or clear all stashes very carefully.

Jamie: That feels like a great tool for "I need to switch branches right now but I'm not ready to commit this half-finished thought."

Alex: That's exactly the use case.

Alex: There's also deleting tracked files properly. Using Git-aware deletion such as `git rm` removes the file and stages the deletion in one step. You can also stop tracking a file while keeping it locally, or remove an entire directory. Then commit the deletion and verify the file is no longer tracked.

Jamie: So deleting a file in Git is not just about the filesystem; it's also about recording that deletion in version history.

Alex: Precisely.

Alex: History tools matter too. In VS Code, Timeline view can show a file's history. You can open it from Explorer or Command Palette. It helps you inspect what changed over time for a file. Git blame shows who last changed each line.

Jamie: Which can sound accusatory, but it's really traceability.

Alex: Exactly. It helps answer: when did this line appear, and in what commit? In CLI, you can view history for the whole repo, history for a specific file, history with patches, blame with short hashes and author, specific commit changes, differences between two commits, commits by a particular author, recent commits in a time window, PR history on the web, and more.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, an accessible diff viewer can make these reviews much more structured.

Alex: Yes. Structured, hunk-by-hunk review is often much easier than visually oriented diff layouts.

Alex: If you run into a merge conflict in VS Code, the editor can display conflict regions, and you may use accessible diff tools or direct text editing to resolve them. Read carefully, decide the final content, remove conflict markers, save, stage, and commit. If the merge attempt was premature, aborting the merge is a valid recovery path.

Jamie: Again: normal event, not failure.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: And then there is emergency recovery: reflog.

Jamie: The "I thought I lost my work" command.

Alex: Yes. `git reflog` is a local record of where HEAD and branches have pointed recently. If you lost a commit through reset, branch deletion, or another accident, reflog can help you find the last good commit SHA. Then you can preview that commit, create a new branch at that point"”which is the safest method"”or reset the current branch back to it if you know what you're doing.

Jamie: And if you deleted a branch, you can often recreate it at the commit you find in reflog.

Alex: Exactly. Important note: reflog is local-only. It reflects your machine's recent reference history, not GitHub's.

Jamie: Before we wrap, can we name the alternative interfaces clearly?

Alex: Of course. Three major interfaces here are GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI `gh`, and the Git CLI in the terminal. GitHub Desktop gives a friendly visual workflow. GitHub CLI adds GitHub-aware commands, often with smoother authentication and pull request actions. The Git CLI is the foundational command set and works everywhere.

Jamie: So learners don't need loyalty to one interface. They need a strong underlying model.

Alex: Exactly. Interfaces change. Concepts persist.

Alex: Let's land the challenge very concretely. If you want the shortest successful path, here it is.

Jamie: I love a checklist.

Alex: Use your own Learning Room repo URL. Clone it locally. Open the cloned folder. Create and switch to a non-default branch such as `fix/YOUR-USERNAME`. Edit one file in `docs/`. Save it. Stage that change. Write a descriptive commit message. Commit locally. Push the branch to GitHub. Then confirm on GitHub.com that your branch and commit appear.

Jamie: And if you're using VS Code, the key shortcuts are Command Palette with Control+Shift+P, Explorer with Control+Shift+E, Source Control with Control+Shift+G, and commit with Control+Enter. Mac users swap Control commands here for Command where the chapter notes that convention.

Alex: Exactly. And if VS Code doesn't show Source Control, make sure the cloned folder is actually open as your workspace.

Jamie: If you're unsure what to edit, fix any typo or improve any sentence. The workflow matters more than the size of the edit.

Alex: If clone fails with auth, check authentication. If push fails with permission denied, confirm you have write access and the right repo. If you want to compare approaches, notice how the same five-step workflow appears in CLI, VS Code, and GitHub Desktop.

Jamie: So the deep lesson is not "memorize these buttons." It's "understand the movement of work."

Alex: Yes. Work begins in your working directory, gets selected in the staging area, becomes history in a commit, advances on a branch, and gets shared to a remote with push.

Jamie: That is a lovely summary.

Alex: And once that model clicks, Git becomes much less intimidating. You're no longer performing rituals. You're making deliberate snapshots and sharing them safely.

Jamie: That's the point where local Git starts feeling professional instead of scary.

Alex: Exactly. And today's challenge is your proof. Clone, branch, edit, commit, push. Then verify it on GitHub and submit your evidence.

Jamie: We'll see you next time.

36. Challenge bonus-e: Git History

Reading history, understanding commits over time, and using history as a learning tool.

Practice focus: Bonus

Download Challenge bonus-e (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge bonus-e: Git History

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're doing something really useful for Git confidence: connecting the picture of Git history to the mechanics underneath it.

Jamie: I like that, because a lot of learners can use Git commands one by one, but the history can still feel mysterious.

Alex: Exactly. And for blind and low-vision learners, we want to say this clearly: Git history is not only a picture. Visual graphs are helpful, but the underlying ideas are completely available in text, in screen-reader-friendly command output, and in structured views in tools like VS Code and GitHub Desktop.

Alex: Let's start with the practical bonus activity. The goal is to explore repository history visually, or at least history-first, using a tool that helps you inspect commits over time.

Jamie: And the tools here are GitHub Desktop, GitHub.com, and a little bit of VS Code, right?

Alex: Right. The bonus specifically invites learners to use GitHub Desktop, or GitHub.com as an alternative. In GitHub Desktop, you open the learning-room repository and go to the History tab. There, you explore the commit timeline and notice a few things: branches can appear as parallel lines, merges can bring those lines back together, and you can often distinguish your own commits from seeded peer-simulation commits by author name and commit message.

Jamie: So this is not just "look at a graph because graphs are cool." It's more like: use the history view to answer real questions.

Alex: Yes. Questions like: how many branches exist right now? Can you find your commit from an earlier challenge? Where does your personal branch diverge from main? Can you locate the merge commit from your pull request? And what's the oldest commit in the repository?

Jamie: That's a really good checklist because it forces you to read history as a story.

Alex: Exactly. And if GitHub Desktop doesn't show all branches, fetch from the remote first. In plain language, ask Git to check in with GitHub and bring down the latest branch information.

Jamie: And if somebody's using GitHub.com instead?

Alex: They can open the repository on GitHub.com, choose the commits link near the top of the repository page to see the linear commit history, or use Insights and then Network to inspect branch relationships. The commit list is usually easier to read. The network graph can be powerful, but it can also get crowded.

Jamie: Especially in a repository with lots of contributors.

Alex: Right. If the graph feels overwhelming, zoom in mentally on a smaller slice of time, or switch to a commit list and use author names, dates, messages, and SHAs to orient yourself.

Jamie: Before we go deeper into history views, can we build the mental model underneath all of this? Because if someone sees a branch line but doesn't know what a branch actually is, the picture won't help much.

Alex: Perfect transition. Git gets much easier when you understand its basic model. The key idea is that Git is tracking states of files over time, and most day-to-day operations make sense once you understand three areas: the working directory, the staging area, and the repository.

Jamie: Let's do those one at a time.

Alex: The working directory is the actual folder on your computer. In VS Code, it's the files you can open, edit, rename, or delete. If you change a file there, Git notices that something changed, but it does not automatically save that change into history.

Jamie: So editing is not the same as committing.

Alex: Exactly. Next is the staging area, also called the index. Think of it as a holding zone for the next commit. You decide which changes belong in the next snapshot. That means you can edit five files, stage two of them, and commit only those two if that tells a cleaner story.

Jamie: And then the repository?

Alex: That's Git's stored history, usually inside the hidden .git folder in the project. When you commit, Git takes what's staged and records it as a snapshot in that repository.

Jamie: So the flow is edit, stage, commit.

Alex: Yes. Working directory, then staging area, then repository. Edit a file. Add it. Commit it.

Jamie: Can you give the analogy?

Alex: Sure. Your desk is the working directory. An open box on the floor is the staging area. When you choose which items go into the box, you're staging. When you seal the box and label it, that's the commit. Before sealing, you can add or remove items as much as you want.

Jamie: That makes staging feel less mysterious.

Alex: That's the idea.

Alex: Now, an important accessibility note here. Many Git tutorials show this as a diagram with arrows. But the arrow diagram is not the concept. The concept is the sequence: edit in the working directory, stage the changes you want, commit them to the repository.

Jamie: So if someone can't access the diagram, they're not missing the actual lesson.

Alex: Correct. And there are tool-specific ways to inspect these areas nonvisually. In the terminal, git status tells you what's changed, what's staged, and what's untracked in labeled text. In VS Code Source Control, files are grouped under headings like Changes and Staged Changes. Screen readers can navigate those groups with arrow keys, and pressing Enter on a file can open the diff. For low-vision learners, separate headings, file badges, and zoom controls help make the same information readable.

Jamie: So the mental model lives in the text as much as in the visuals.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What exactly is a commit, then? People often say it's a save point.

Alex: That's a good beginner description. More precisely, a commit is a snapshot of your project at a moment in time. It includes the state of the staged files, a commit message, author information, and a pointer to its parent commit, meaning the commit that came before it.

Jamie: And each commit gets that long ID.

Alex: Yes. A SHA hash. Usually forty characters, though you often use a shorter form, like the first seven characters, when it's unique in the repository.

Jamie: Do learners need to memorize SHAs?

Alex: Not at all. Just recognize what they are and that Git accepts short hashes in many situations.

Jamie: And commits are permanent"¦ mostly?

Alex: Mostly. Once a commit exists, it becomes part of history. You can add new commits that undo or replace it, and there are advanced ways to rewrite local history, which we'll discuss later. But the default mental model is that a commit is a durable record, which is one reason Git is so safe.

Jamie: And this connects to earlier web editing too, right?

Alex: Yes. When learners edited on GitHub.com and clicked Commit changes, GitHub was doing staging and committing behind the scenes. Locally, you perform those steps more explicitly.

Jamie: Any accessibility support for understanding commits?

Alex: Definitely. In the terminal, git log --oneline reads out recent commit hashes and messages clearly. In VS Code Source Control, there's a commit message input box announced by screen readers, and a keyboard shortcut to commit. For low-vision users, panel width and zoom matter because long messages can get truncated.

Jamie: Okay, now branches. This is where many people start to imagine tangled spaghetti.

Alex: Which is fair, but the underlying idea is simple. A branch is just a movable pointer to a line of commits. The default branch is often called main. When you create a new branch, you're creating another pointer that starts at your current commit.

Jamie: So a branch isn't a separate universe.

Alex: Right. It begins from some existing commit. Then when you make commits on that branch, that branch pointer moves forward. If you switch back to main, main stays where it was unless you merge or rebase changes.

Jamie: And HEAD?

Alex: HEAD tells Git what you currently have checked out. Usually it means "the branch I'm on right now." If HEAD points to your feature branch, new commits advance that branch.

Jamie: So when people say "what branch am I on," they're really asking where HEAD is attached.

Alex: Exactly. In most beginner workflows, HEAD is attached to a branch name. Later we'll talk about detached HEAD, which is when that's no longer true.

Jamie: How does this connect to local and remote?

Alex: Another foundational idea: there are usually two copies in play. Your local repository on your machine, and a remote repository, often on GitHub. Your local copy is where you edit, stage, and commit. The remote is where you share, back up, collaborate, and open pull requests.

Jamie: So GitHub is not "the repository" in the singular sense. It's one repository location, usually the remote.

Alex: Exactly. Your local repository is fully real and fully capable. Git is designed around that distributed model. Local and remote stay in sync through explicit actions. You push your commits up. You fetch and pull other people's commits down.

Jamie: What's the easiest distinction between fetch and pull?

Alex: Fetch checks for updates and downloads remote information without merging it into your current branch. Pull usually means fetch plus merge, or fetch plus rebase, depending on configuration. Push sends your local commits to the remote.

Jamie: So if I want to inspect safely before changing my branch, fetch is gentler.

Alex: Exactly. Fetch is often the least surprising step.

Alex: Now let's talk about merge conflicts, because they sound scary but they're actually a normal consequence of collaboration.

Jamie: When do they happen?

Alex: Usually when Git tries to combine changes and can't decide automatically which version should win. Most often, two branches changed the same part of the same file in incompatible ways.

Jamie: And what does that look like?

Alex: In a text file, Git can insert conflict markers like less-than signs, equal signs, and greater-than signs around competing sections. Your job is to edit that area into the final desired result, remove the markers, stage the resolved file, and continue the merge, rebase, or cherry-pick.

Jamie: So a conflict is a request for human judgment.

Alex: Beautifully said. It's not Git failing in a dramatic way. It's Git pausing because it needs you to choose. And that's why conflicts are normal.

Jamie: Any accessibility angle here?

Alex: Yes. Conflict markers are plain text, which is good for screen readers. And git status is your friend because it names the files needing attention. VS Code also has conflict tools, but even without visual editors, the file itself contains all the needed information.

Jamie: Now we can come back to the timeline idea, because branches and merges are really about time.

Alex: Yes. The Git timeline is the history of commits and how they connect. Reading the timeline means noticing order, parent relationships, branch divergence, and merge points. A branch creates a parallel line of development. A merge reconnects lines by creating a commit that has more than one parent.

Jamie: That explains why merge commits are special in history views.

Alex: Exactly. They represent a moment when two lines came together.

Jamie: And this is what the bonus wants learners to observe in GitHub Desktop and on GitHub.com.

Alex: Right. In GitHub Desktop, the History tab presents commits as a timeline, and when available, the branch visualization helps you see where lines split and reconnect. Clicking a commit reveals its diff. On GitHub.com, the commit list gives chronological history with author, date, message, and SHA, and clicking into a commit shows added and removed lines.

Jamie: And in VS Code?

Alex: VS Code's Timeline view is file-specific. That's important. It shows the history of the currently selected file, not necessarily the whole repository graph. That makes it excellent for answering questions like, "How did this README evolve?" or "Which commit changed this config file?"

Jamie: So if I want the history of one file, VS Code Timeline is great. If I want the project story, GitHub Desktop or GitHub.com may be better.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: A few practical observations from exploring history: merge commits show where branches came together and usually have two parents. The first commit in a repository is often something like an initial commit that creates the project structure. And commit frequency naturally varies. Some days have many commits, some none.

Jamie: That's useful because learners sometimes assume a "healthy" repo should have a perfectly even cadence.

Alex: Not at all. Real work is uneven.

Jamie: What matters most in this visual exploration bonus?

Alex: The real learning objective is understanding that Git history is navigable. It's not just an archive. You can inspect a commit, read its message, identify its author, view its SHA, open its diff, see how branches diverged, and understand how work came together.

Jamie: So if a learner explored the history, opened at least one commit diff, and can describe what that history says about the project, they've done the important part.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can we do a quick all-together summary before we enter the advanced section?

Alex: Absolutely. Here's the compact checklist. You edit files in the working directory. You stage the changes you want in the staging area. You commit those staged changes into the repository. A branch is a pointer to a line of commits. HEAD says where you currently are. Your local repository lives on your machine. The remote repository often lives on GitHub. Push sends your work up. Fetch checks for updates without merging. Pull brings remote work into your current branch. Conflicts happen when Git needs human help combining changes. And the timeline is the connected story of all those commits.

Jamie: That really does make the commands feel less magical.

Alex: That's the whole point of the mental model.

Jamie: What if someone still gets stuck, though?

Alex: Then slow down and ask: which area am I changing, which branch am I on, and am I dealing with local history or remote history? Those three questions solve a surprising number of Git mysteries. Also, use official docs as your source of truth. Git SCM, GitHub Docs, and GitHub's accessibility guidance are all strong references.

Jamie: Okay. Let's go deeper. Advanced Git operations often sound intimidating, but they're really specific tools for specific situations.

Alex: Exactly. You don't need them all every day. But understanding what they're for helps you recognize the right tool when a real workflow problem appears.

Jamie: And this appendix is designed for people who already know the basics: clone, branch, commit, push, pull.

Alex: Right. It also offers multiple paths: VS Code, GitHub CLI, and plain Git CLI. Different tools, same Git concepts.

Jamie: Any navigation note for accessibility?

Alex: Yes. The reference is structured consistently by operation, then tool-specific paths. For screen reader users, heading navigation is especially effective. For low-vision users, the repeated structure and code blocks help scanning. And there's also a quick reference table later for fast lookup.

Jamie: First advanced tool: cherry-pick. What is it really?

Alex: Cherry-pick lets you take a specific commit from one branch and apply it onto your current branch. Think of it as copying one change without merging the entire branch that contains it.

Jamie: So if I fixed a bug on one branch, but main urgently needs that exact fix, I can cherry-pick just that commit.

Alex: Exactly. Or if a teammate has one useful commit among many unfinished ones, you can bring over only that one. Or if you committed to the wrong branch, cherry-pick can help move the change where it belongs.

Jamie: How do I find the commit I want?

Alex: You need its SHA. In VS Code, you can inspect timeline details on the branch containing it. In Git CLI, you can use git log with a branch name and oneline formatting to inspect commits on another branch without switching to it. GitHub CLI doesn't directly cherry-pick, because cherry-pick is a local Git operation, but it can help list commits through the API so you can grab the SHA.

Jamie: And then the application step?

Alex: In VS Code, the Command Palette has a Git: Cherry Pick action. In Git CLI, git cherry-pick followed by the SHA applies a single commit. You can also cherry-pick a range of commits, and there's a no-commit option if you want to apply changes but review before creating the commit.

Jamie: What if cherry-pick hits a conflict?

Alex: Then it behaves a lot like a merge conflict. Git pauses, marks the files, and waits for you to resolve them. After resolving and staging, continue the cherry-pick. Or abort to return to the starting state.

Jamie: Good to know that abort exists.

Alex: Very good to know.

Jamie: Next up: interactive rebase. This is the one people whisper about.

Alex: It sounds dramatic, but it's really a history cleanup tool. Interactive rebase lets you reorder commits, combine them, edit commit messages, drop unwanted commits, or pause to amend a commit.

Jamie: So this is for polishing your story before a pull request.

Alex: Exactly. Maybe you made eight tiny "work in progress" commits and want one clean commit. Maybe a commit message is vague and needs rewording. Maybe you accidentally committed a debug file and want that commit removed.

Jamie: What's the big warning?

Alex: Only rewrite history that is not already shared on a branch other people are using, unless you truly understand the consequences. Rewriting public history means others may have based work on commits you're about to replace.

Jamie: How does interactive rebase start?

Alex: Usually in the terminal with git rebase -i and then a commit range, like the last three commits or everything since branching from main. VS Code can help, and using VS Code as the editor for the rebase todo list is often more accessible than letting it open in vim. If your default editor is hard to use, configuring core.editor to code --wait can make rebasing much more approachable.

Jamie: And then you get a list of commits with action words.

Alex: Right. Pick keeps a commit. Squash combines it with the one above. Fixup also combines it but discards its message. Reword lets you change the message. Drop removes it. Edit pauses the rebase so you can amend that commit.

Jamie: So if I want to turn three messy commits into one, I keep the first as pick and mark the next two as squash.

Alex: Exactly. Save, close, then Git asks for the combined message. If something goes wrong, you can abort the rebase. And if you hit a conflict mid-rebase, resolve it, stage the result, and continue.

Jamie: Now let's talk about reset, because this word scares beginners.

Alex: Understandably. Reset changes where your branch pointer points, and depending on mode, it may also affect staging and your working directory. The three classic modes are soft, mixed, and hard.

Jamie: Can you translate those into plain English?

Alex: Soft reset moves the branch back but keeps your changes staged. Mixed reset, which is the default, moves the branch back and unstages the changes while keeping them in your working directory. Hard reset moves the branch back and discards the changes from both staging and working directory.

Jamie: So hard reset is the dangerous one.

Alex: Yes. Use it only when you mean to throw changes away, and understand recovery may require reflog knowledge.

Jamie: What about simple undo in VS Code?

Alex: VS Code can help undo the last commit through Source Control or the Command Palette. But conceptually it's still a reset-like action under the hood. In Git CLI, you can undo the last commit while keeping changes staged, keep them unstaged, undo multiple commits while preserving changes, or reset to a specific SHA.

Jamie: And unstaging a file without undoing the commit?

Alex: That's another useful distinction. Unstaging means "remove this from the next commit," not "erase the edit." In VS Code you can unstage from Source Control. In Git CLI you can unstage one file or everything.

Jamie: If reset can be risky, what's the safer undo for shared branches?

Alex: That's git revert. Revert creates a new commit that reverses the effect of an earlier commit. It does not erase history. That's why it's the preferred undo when the original commit is already on a shared branch.

Jamie: So reset rewrites branch history, but revert adds a new corrective commit.

Alex: Exactly. In VS Code and Git CLI, you can revert a specific commit, use the default message or edit it, and even stage the revert without auto-committing if you want to customize the result first. Reverting a merge commit is a special case because Git needs to know which parent to treat as the main line.

Jamie: So when in doubt on a shared branch, revert is usually the safer instinct.

Alex: Yes.

Jamie: Tags next. These feel simple, but they matter a lot in real projects.

Alex: A tag marks an important point in history, often a release. There are lightweight tags, which are basically named pointers, and annotated tags, which carry extra metadata and are usually preferred for releases.

Jamie: How do people create them?

Alex: In VS Code, there are Command Palette paths depending on extensions and built-in support. With GitHub CLI, you can create a release through GitHub's API or release tooling, which also creates the underlying tag. In Git CLI, you can create a lightweight tag at the current commit, create an annotated tag, tag a specific older commit, list tags, filter them, and inspect details.

Jamie: And tags don't magically appear on GitHub unless pushed.

Alex: Exactly. You can push a specific tag or all local tags. And deletion also has two sides: delete local, and if needed, delete the remote tag as well.

Jamie: Now the mysterious detached HEAD.

Alex: Detached HEAD means HEAD is pointing directly at a commit instead of at a branch name. This often happens when you check out a specific commit or tag.

Jamie: Why is that a problem?

Alex: It's not automatically a problem. It's fine for inspecting history. The risk is making commits there and then navigating away, because those commits won't belong to a named branch unless you create one.

Jamie: So how do you get out?

Alex: If you just want to go back, switch back to a branch like main or whatever branch you were on. If you made commits in detached HEAD and want to keep them, create a new branch at that current position. Then those commits are anchored safely to a branch.

Jamie: And VS Code can help reveal this state too.

Alex: Yes, often through the branch status area and checkout actions.

Jamie: Let's talk about force pushing safely, because that phrase contains both "force" and "safely," which seems suspicious.

Alex: Fair reaction. Force push is needed after rewriting history on a branch that already exists on the remote, for example after an interactive rebase. But there's a safer version: force-with-lease.

Jamie: What does that extra protection do?

Alex: It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else has pushed changes you haven't seen yet. Plain force will overwrite regardless. So force-with-lease is the recommended option in almost all cases where force pushing is necessary.

Jamie: When would you use it?

Alex: Typically after rebasing your own feature branch to clean history or update it onto main, then pushing the rewritten branch back to origin. GitHub CLI doesn't replace the underlying Git push for this; you still use Git directly for force pushing. And it's wise to check what will happen before pushing.

Jamie: Can you outline the common workflow?

Alex: Sure. You're on your feature branch. You rebase onto the latest main. If conflicts appear, resolve and continue. Then because your branch history changed, you push with force-with-lease so the remote branch matches your cleaned-up local branch.

Jamie: Next: git bisect. This one feels like detective work.

Alex: It absolutely is. Bisect helps you find the commit that introduced a bug by using binary search through history. You mark a known bad commit and a known good commit. Git checks out a midpoint. You test it and say whether it's good or bad. Git keeps narrowing the range until it identifies the likely culprit.

Jamie: That's brilliant.

Alex: It is. You start bisect mode, mark the broken state as bad, mark an earlier working state as good, then repeat the testing cycle. You can use SHAs, tags, or branch names to identify known points in history.

Jamie: And when you're done?

Alex: End the bisect session and Git returns you to your original branch. You can also automate the testing step by giving Git a test script. Then Git runs the script at each midpoint and uses the exit status to continue automatically.

Jamie: That sounds especially useful when the bug condition is easy to script.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now a cleanup tool: git clean.

Alex: Yes. Git clean removes untracked files, and optionally directories and ignored files too. That can be useful when your working directory has accumulated clutter, build artifacts, or experimental files.

Jamie: But the warning here is huge.

Alex: Huge. Always dry-run first. Ask Git what it would delete before actually deleting anything. The option names matter: dry run, force, directories, ignored files. Those switches change the scope dramatically.

Jamie: So remove untracked files only is one thing. Remove untracked directories too is broader. Remove ignored files too is broader still.

Alex: Exactly. And interactive mode can let you confirm item by item. In VS Code, some cleanup can happen through file explorer actions, but the Git CLI is the clearest place to understand what clean will do.

Jamie: Let's move to branch protection, because this often confuses learners when a push or merge gets blocked.

Alex: Branch protection is a repository policy layer, usually on important branches like main. It can require pull requests, reviews, passing status checks, up-to-date branches, or restrict direct pushes.

Jamie: So if someone tries to push directly to main and gets blocked, that's not Git being broken. That's policy doing its job.

Alex: Exactly. The correct flow for protected branches is: don't work directly on main. Create a branch. Make commits there. Push that branch. Open a pull request. Then wait for reviews and automated checks, and merge through the PR process.

Jamie: What if the branch is out of date?

Alex: Then update it. In VS Code or Git CLI, you can merge main into your branch, which creates a merge commit, or rebase your branch onto main for a cleaner history. If you rebase a branch that already exists remotely, you'll need a force push afterward. GitHub CLI can also help interact with pull requests and some update flows from GitHub's side.

Jamie: Can you inspect protection rules directly?

Alex: Yes. On GitHub.com, repository settings expose branch rules if you have permission. GitHub CLI can also query protection rules for a branch like main.

Jamie: So the big lesson is: protection rules shape workflow, not just access.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: Before we wrap, let's cover GitHub Copilot for Git operations. Not as a replacement for understanding, but as support.

Alex: That's the right framing. Copilot can help explain confusing Git output, suggest the right command for a goal, draft clearer commit messages, help reason through merge conflicts, troubleshoot bisect sessions, and decode branch protection errors.

Jamie: So if I paste terminal output and ask, "What does this mean?" that can be a reasonable use.

Alex: Yes, especially when the output is dense. It can also help compare options like reset versus revert, or suggest prompts for resolving conflicts. In the terminal, Copilot can suggest commands. In chat, it can explain concepts and output more conversationally.

Jamie: But learners still need judgment.

Alex: Always. AI can suggest; you decide. Especially with history-rewriting commands, verify before pressing Enter.

Jamie: This has been a lot, but I think it hangs together around one central idea: Git history is readable.

Alex: Yes. Readable, navigable, and recoverable. Whether you inspect it in GitHub Desktop, GitHub.com, VS Code Timeline, or the terminal, you are learning to read the project's past and make informed choices about its future.

Jamie: And that includes the accessible workflows too. Screen-reader-friendly status output. Structured Source Control headings. Plain-text conflict markers. Keyboard-first command access. File timeline views.

Alex: Exactly. None of that is secondary. Accessibility is part of the workflow design.

Jamie: Last thing: where should learners go for the most authoritative source of truth?

Alex: For core Git behavior, the Pro Git book and Git SCM documentation are excellent. For GitHub-specific workflows, GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog are strong references. For GitHub Copilot, use the official Copilot docs. And for accessible command-line practices, GitHub Accessibility Lab guidance is valuable.

Jamie: So explore the history, click into commits, inspect diffs, and practice connecting what you see to working directory, staging area, repository, branches, and remotes.

Alex: That's the path. Once the history stops feeling like a mystery, Git becomes much more understandable.

37. Episode 13: The GitHub Pull Requests Extension

Viewing, creating, reviewing, and merging PRs from inside VS Code.

Based on: Chapter 15: The GitHub Pull Requests Extension

Download Episode 13 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 13: The GitHub Pull Requests Extension

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're getting practical about code review: how to work with pull requests in VS Code, how to read diffs accessibly, how to leave comments that actually help, and how to decide whether to approve, request changes, or just comment.

Jamie: So this is not only, "What is a pull request?" It's also, "How do I manage one, review one, and respond like a good collaborator?"

Alex: Exactly. And for our blind and low-vision learners, there's a second thread running through everything: how to do this with a screen reader in a way that is efficient, not exhausting.

Jamie: I appreciate that. A visual diff can be overwhelming fast.

Alex: It can. So we'll keep returning to the workflows that reduce noise, especially the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension in VS Code, GitHub's web review tools, and the Accessible Diff Viewer in VS Code.

Alex: A quick setup note before we dive in. This material assumes you've already practiced basic pull request workflows and Git in VS Code. Also, whenever we mention Windows-style shortcuts like Control, Mac users should translate them: Control becomes Command, Alt becomes Option, and Shift+F10 context menu behavior is typically Control+Return on Mac.

Jamie: And there are some related references in the background too, right?

Alex: Yes. If you need them, a VS Code reference appendix and a Markdown reference appendix support this lesson. And the main source guidance behind today's material comes from GitHub Docs on reviewing pull requests and GitHub's accessibility guidance for pull request reviews.

Jamie: Nice. So what's the big picture for the day?

Alex: Three parts. First, using the GitHub Pull Requests extension in VS Code. Second, accessible code review in both the browser and VS Code. Third, the reviewer's craft: what to look for, how to write constructive feedback, and how to use judgment.

Jamie: And there were workshop tasks tied to this too.

Alex: Right. Two guided practice items for the extension portion: install the extension and sign in, then check out a classmate's pull request and post one constructive comment. No automation check for those, because extension state and review state live on your local machine and your account. Evidence is usually a comment confirming what you completed.

Jamie: Let's start with the extension itself.

Alex: The GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension brings GitHub workflow directly into VS Code. Instead of constantly switching to a browser tab, you can see open pull requests, inspect changes, check out a PR branch, comment, create PRs, and sometimes merge, all from the editor.

Jamie: That sounds convenient, but I want the concrete steps. If I'm starting from zero, how do I install it?

Alex: You have two main methods. The first is through the Extensions sidebar. Press Control+Shift+X. The search box in the Marketplace usually gets focus. Type GitHub Pull Requests, press Enter, move through the results, choose the extension published by GitHub, and activate Install.

Jamie: And if someone prefers the Command Palette?

Alex: That's method two. Open the Command Palette with Control+Shift+P, search for extension-related commands or directly search for the GitHub Pull Requests extension, then install it from there. The sidebar method is usually simpler for most learners, but both are valid.

Jamie: What happens after install?

Alex: Often VS Code prompts you to sign in to GitHub. Activate Sign in to GitHub, which opens a browser window for OAuth authorization. Complete the approval in the browser, then return to VS Code.

Jamie: How do I know it worked?

Alex: Verify sign-in by going to the Explorer sidebar with Control+Shift+E. You should find a GitHub section that includes pull requests and issues. That's one of the clearest signs the extension is active and authenticated.

Jamie: And if a notification appeared and disappeared too fast for the screen reader?

Alex: Great accessibility detail. Open the Command Palette and run Notifications: Focus Notification Toast. That brings the latest toast into focus so you can read what happened.

Jamie: So the extension adds a GitHub area in the interface, commands for PR work, and tighter connection between local Git and GitHub's review system.

Alex: Exactly. It adds views, commands, PR trees, changed file access, comment features, checkout options, PR creation tools, and integration points with review and merge workflows.

Jamie: Let's say the extension is installed. How do I actually view pull requests?

Alex: There are two common entry points. One is the GitHub Pull Requests panel from the Activity Bar. The other is a GitHub section in Explorer. In practice, many screen reader users like using the Command Palette to jump directly into the Pull Requests view by running GitHub Pull Requests: Focus on Pull Requests View.

Jamie: Once I'm there, what can I do?

Alex: You can list open pull requests, move through them, open one to inspect its details, open it in your browser if needed, and filter the list so you only hear the PRs that matter to you, like items awaiting your review.

Jamie: Let's slow down on filtering. Why is that important?

Alex: Because long PR lists are noisy. Filtering by status helps you narrow to open, closed, or review-requested items. Filtering by repository matters if you're connected to multiple repos. And a specific filter for PRs waiting for your review is especially useful when you're acting as reviewer rather than author.

Jamie: What does the PR list sound like for a screen reader user?

Alex: Typically you're navigating a tree or list structure. A pull request entry may announce the PR title, number, repository context, branch information, and status indicators. Inside a specific PR tree, you may find sections like description and changed files. The key idea is orientation: understand what level of the tree you're on and what object currently has focus.

Jamie: So description, changed files, and maybe actions are all nested under that PR.

Alex: Right. And a good screen reader announcement example might sound like a tree item with the PR title and state, then child items underneath for description or files. The exact wording varies by VS Code version and screen reader, but the structural pattern matters.

Jamie: If I want full details for one PR, what should I expect?

Alex: You should be able to open a detail view that includes the title, author, status, branch relationship, description, and the list of changed files. For many users, that's enough to decide whether to inspect the diff in VS Code or jump to the browser for a more familiar review form.

Jamie: Now the next big skill: checking out a PR branch. Why would I do that instead of just reading the pull request online?

Alex: Because checking out a PR makes the proposed changes local. That means you can test them, run the project, inspect files with your normal editor setup, and review the diff in context. It's especially useful if you need more than a surface-level read.

Jamie: So it's not just reading. It's validating.

Alex: Exactly. You might want to verify the change actually works, that it only changes what it claims, or that it doesn't break something nearby.

Jamie: How do I check out a PR?

Alex: Three common methods. First, from the PR detail view, activate Checkout. Second, from the PR tree itself, use the context menu on the PR item and choose checkout. Third, use the Command Palette and search for a GitHub Pull Requests checkout command.

Jamie: And once I do that, VS Code switches me to that PR's branch?

Alex: Yes. Your local workspace now reflects that pull request branch. It's smart to notice the branch indicator in the status bar or Source Control area so you know you're no longer on your original branch.

Jamie: That brings up an anxious question learners often have: how do I get back?

Alex: Important question. Return to your original branch using the branch switcher in VS Code, the Source Control UI, or Git commands if you're comfortable with them. After a review, many people switch back to main or to their own feature branch. The key is situational awareness: always know what branch you're on before editing or committing.

Jamie: That sounds like one of those small habits that prevents big mistakes.

Alex: It absolutely is.

Jamie: Now let's get to the heart of review: reading changed files and understanding the diff.

Alex: When you open a pull request for review, one of the main things you'll inspect is the files changed list. In the PR detail view, you can usually move through the changed files and open one in the Diff Editor.

Jamie: What does the Diff Editor look like conceptually?

Alex: By default, it's often a split view. Old content on the left, new content on the right. Removed lines appear on the old side, added lines on the new side. That's visually useful, but with a screen reader, raw side-by-side navigation can be tiring.

Jamie: Is there another display mode?

Alex: Yes. Inline view puts the diff into a single flow instead of two side-by-side panes. Some learners prefer that because it reduces lateral complexity. You can toggle between split and inline views in the editor controls.

Jamie: But the big recommendation here is still the Accessible Diff Viewer, right?

Alex: Yes. For screen reader users, the Accessible Diff Viewer is usually the best way to read changes. Press F7 to move to the next change and Shift+F7 to move to the previous one. Instead of making you navigate every visual artifact in the editor, it announces the change as structured information.

Jamie: Can you give an example of what that means?

Alex: Imagine the screen reader telling you something like: line changed, one line removed, two lines added, then reading the old and new text in a logical sequence. That is far superior to manually crawling through split columns, where context can be easy to lose.

Jamie: So instead of deciphering a picture, I'm getting a concise explanation of the edit.

Alex: Exactly. That's why the chapter emphasizes that structured reading is much better than navigating the visual diff manually.

Jamie: What should I be listening for during review?

Alex: Ask questions like: what changed, why did it change, and does it improve the file? Also: is anything missing, misleading, inaccessible, or inconsistent? If you're reviewing documentation, you might listen for heading hierarchy, clear link text, missing steps, grammar, or formatting problems. If you're reviewing code, the questions shift toward correctness, clarity, safety, tests, and maintainability.

Jamie: And if I notice an issue?

Alex: Flag it. But flagging doesn't always mean blocking. Some issues are must-fix, some are optional improvements, and some are questions. That distinction matters a lot when you write comments.

Jamie: Before we leave the extension workflow, there's a part many learners really want: creating a pull request from VS Code.

Alex: Yes. The extension can help you create a pull request from your editor. Before you do that, make sure you have a branch with commits pushed to GitHub. The extension can't create a meaningful PR if your work isn't available on the remote.

Jamie: What are the ways to create it?

Alex: Method one, and generally the recommended one, is from the Command Palette. Search for a GitHub Pull Requests create command. Method two is from the Source Control panel, where VS Code may offer a Create Pull Request action when your branch is pushed and differs from the base branch. Method three is from the GitHub panel itself.

Jamie: When the PR form opens, what fields matter most?

Alex: Title is required. Description is optional in a technical sense, but strongly recommended. Then you choose the base branch, which is the target you're merging into, usually main. The compare branch is your source branch. You may also be able to add reviewers, labels, a milestone, and mark the PR as draft.

Jamie: Let's unpack draft for a second.

Alex: A draft pull request says, in effect, "Please look if you want, but this isn't ready for final decision yet." That's useful when you want early feedback without implying the work is finished.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, any advice on the form itself?

Alex: Move steadily through the fields, confirm which branch is base and which is compare, and don't rush through the controls because they're easy to invert mentally. Title first, description next, then metadata like reviewers and labels.

Jamie: How is submission handled?

Alex: Some flows are interactive and prompt you step by step for title, body, and base branch. Other flows are more inline, where you fill details directly in a form. You may get an option to create as draft, or to open the form in your browser if you prefer or need more stable accessibility for complex fields.

Jamie: So if the in-editor form gets awkward, opening in the browser is a perfectly acceptable move.

Alex: Absolutely. The goal is a correct, clear PR, not loyalty to a single interface.

Jamie: That leads naturally to pull request description templates. Why do they matter?

Alex: Templates reduce ambiguity. They remind authors to include the information reviewers need: what changed, why it changed, related issues, testing performed, and any checklist items.

Jamie: Where are those templates usually stored?

Alex: They're typically stored in the repository, often in a .github directory as a pull request template file. A repo may also offer multiple templates depending on the kind of change.

Jamie: And a typical template might ask for what?

Alex: A short description, a related issue reference, the type of change, testing notes, a checklist, and screenshots if applicable.

Jamie: For a screen reader user, what's the best workflow when a template opens?

Alex: Read the prompts first. Then move section by section and replace placeholder text with real content. Don't leave headings like Description or Testing blank if the project expects them. Templates are there to help reviewers, so filling them out thoughtfully is part of accessibility too.

Jamie: All right. Now let's get into comments and formal reviews.

Alex: You can add an inline comment directly on a changed line. In VS Code, position your cursor on the relevant line and run GitHub Pull Requests: Add Comment from the Command Palette. Then type your comment and submit it.

Jamie: What makes a good inline comment?

Alex: Be specific. Mention the exact problem or praise. If possible, explain why it matters. And if you're asking for change, make the next step clear.

Jamie: Can you give some formats?

Alex: Sure. A blocking comment might say, "Blocking: this heading skips from level two to level four, which breaks document structure for screen reader navigation. Please change this to a level three heading." A non-blocking note might say, "Nit: consider shortening this sentence for clarity." A question might say, "Question: should this setup step mention logging in first?"

Jamie: So we are not dumping vague reactions like, "This seems off."

Alex: Exactly. Review comments should be actionable whenever possible.

Jamie: What if I have several comments to make across the PR?

Alex: Then use Start Review rather than posting each comment immediately. That lets you batch multiple comments and submit them together with a final verdict.

Jamie: And the verdict options are approve, request changes, or comment only.

Alex: Right. Approve means the PR is acceptable to merge. Request changes means there are issues that should be fixed before merge. Comment-only means you're adding feedback without a merge verdict.

Jamie: What happens after submission?

Alex: Your comments and verdict are attached to the PR. The author gets notified. They may reply, push updates, or ask for clarification. If they revise the PR, reviewers often come back to inspect what changed since the last round.

Jamie: There's also a note that some review actions can happen from other environments too, correct?

Alex: Yes. You can view a PR diff in your terminal with Git tools if that's part of your workflow, though today's focus is browser and VS Code. And the three formal outcomes still map across environments: approve, request changes, or comment without verdict.

Jamie: What about merging pull requests from VS Code?

Alex: You can sometimes merge directly from the extension, assuming prerequisites are met. Typically that means the PR is in a mergeable state, required reviews are satisfied, required checks have passed, and you have permission to merge.

Jamie: How do you do it?

Alex: Either from the PR detail view, where a merge action may be available, or via a Command Palette command for merging the current PR.

Jamie: And merge type matters here.

Alex: It does. Common merge types are the default merge commit, squash and merge, and sometimes rebase merge depending on repository settings. Which one to use depends on the team's conventions. Squash is often used to keep history cleaner for small feature branches. The default merge strategy preserves the branch history more explicitly.

Jamie: There's also auto-merge sometimes.

Alex: Yes. If the repository allows it, you may be able to enable auto-merge so the PR merges automatically once required checks pass.

Jamie: After merging, what's the housekeeping?

Alex: Switch back to main and pull the latest changes so your local repo reflects the merged work. Then consider deleting the feature branch if it's no longer needed. Some workflows even combine squash and merge with branch deletion as a standard cleanup step.

Jamie: Let's make room for troubleshooting, because these workflows rarely go perfectly the first time.

Alex: Agreed. If you see "No pull requests found," first check whether you're signed in, in the correct repository, and looking at the right filter, such as All Open instead of a narrower view.

Jamie: What if you get "Could not create pull request"?

Alex: Usually that points to branch state or permissions. Confirm your changes are committed and pushed, make sure the compare branch exists on GitHub, and check that you have rights to create PRs in that repository.

Jamie: And "Authentication failed"?

Alex: Verify that your GitHub browser session is active, then retry sign-in. Sometimes closing and reopening VS Code helps. If the extension seems stuck, reloading the window from the Command Palette can reset the interface.

Jamie: What about checkout problems?

Alex: If checkout fails because of permissions or repository restrictions, you can still review read-only on GitHub.com. That's an explicit fallback in the practice guidance. And if the Diff Editor itself feels too hard to navigate, go straight to F7 and use the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Alex: Let's pause and walk through the first guided practice in plain language.

Jamie: Good. This is the install-and-sign-in one.

Alex: Yes. Open Extensions with Control+Shift+X. Search for GitHub Pull Requests. Choose the extension published by GitHub. Install it. If prompted, sign in to GitHub through the browser OAuth flow. Return to VS Code. Then verify success by checking Explorer for a GitHub section showing pull requests and issues.

Jamie: And the learner is done when that GitHub section appears and is populated for the repository they're working in.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: Then comes the second practice: check out a PR and leave a comment.

Alex: Right. Open the Command Palette. Run GitHub Pull Requests: Focus on Pull Requests View. Find an open PR that is not your own. Check it out if permissions allow. Open the changed files. Open a changed file in the Diff Editor. Use F7 and Shift+F7 to navigate changes accessibly. Find one specific item to comment on, such as a typo, unclear sentence, missing step, or a genuinely good improvement. Then add a comment with the Add Comment command.

Jamie: And if checkout is blocked?

Alex: Skip local checkout and review in the browser instead. Use the Files changed tab on GitHub.com and post your comment there.

Jamie: What counts as completion evidence for this part?

Alex: A completion comment stating whether the extension was installed, whether you signed in, which PR you reviewed, whether you posted the comment inline or on GitHub.com, and a one-sentence summary of what your comment was about.

Jamie: Expected outcomes are practical, not theoretical.

Alex: Exactly. Install and authenticate the extension. Check out or view a PR. Navigate diffs with F7. Post constructive, specific feedback.

Jamie: And if someone gets stuck, the recovery steps are very concrete: reload window, retry OAuth, switch to All Open, use browser fallback, use F7, search directly for Add Comment, and ask a facilitator for help verifying the panel.

Alex: Yes. And the deeper lesson here is worth naming: PR tooling multiplies your impact. Reviewing others' work sharpens your own standards and builds trust in a community.

Jamie: Now let's move from tool use to accessible code review more broadly. Not just extension mechanics, but how to review well with a screen reader.

Alex: Good shift. There are really two environments for code review: GitHub.com in the browser and VS Code with the extension. You should be able to work in both, because sometimes one is more accessible or more efficient than the other for a given task.

Jamie: Before starting that, what prerequisites should a learner mentally check off?

Alex: You should already know the basics of pull requests, branches, and diff concepts. You should be signed in to GitHub, have access to the repo, and know how to navigate either the GitHub web UI or VS Code at a basic level.

Jamie: And there were learning cards in this part too.

Alex: Yes. Conceptually, those cards reinforce a few repeatable tasks: view the full PR diff in your terminal if needed, inspect PR details like description and checks, check out the PR branch locally for testing, and choose one of the three review actions: approve, request changes, or leave a comment-only review.

Jamie: Let's start in the browser. How do I review on GitHub.com accessibly?

Alex: The good news is that the modern interface is now the default. Step one is to reach the Files changed tab of the pull request. That's where the actual diff review happens.

Jamie: Step two?

Alex: Use the file tree to orient yourself. Listen for the list of changed files, which tells you scope. Ask: how many files changed, and which ones are likely high value to inspect first?

Jamie: So before reading the lines, I should understand the map.

Alex: Exactly. Step three is navigating between file diffs. Move file by file rather than wandering line by line through the entire page without context.

Jamie: Then step four: read a diff.

Alex: Right. Pay attention to what each line announces or shows: whether it's context, a removal, or an addition. The goal is to reconstruct the author's change, not just hear isolated lines.

Jamie: And then comes placing a comment.

Alex: Yes. Step five is placing an inline comment on a specific line. In web review, GitHub provides comment controls adjacent to changed lines. You can also place a multi-line comment when the issue spans several lines.

Jamie: That seems important for accessibility issues that are structural rather than line-local.

Alex: Very much so. A heading hierarchy problem, for example, may need you to reference surrounding lines, not just a single word.

Jamie: What's next after commenting?

Alex: Step six is reading existing comments and threads. Reviews are conversations. Before adding a duplicate comment, check whether another reviewer already raised the same issue and whether the author has responded.

Jamie: Then step seven is submitting the review.

Alex: Correct. Choose approve, request changes, or comment. Understand the meaning of each. Request changes should be used for issues that must be resolved before merge. Approve means you're satisfied. Comment-only is for feedback that doesn't need to block progress.

Jamie: And step eight?

Alex: Re-request review for authors when appropriate, especially after updates. In some workflows the author or maintainer handles that, but knowing the concept matters: review is iterative.

Jamie: Now mirror that in VS Code with the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Alex: In VS Code, first open the PR for review through the GitHub extension. Then open a changed file. From there, use the Accessible Diff Viewer with F7.

Jamie: What's the navigation model there?

Alex: F7 moves to the next change, Shift+F7 moves back. The viewer presents the change in a structured way so you can understand additions and deletions without wrestling with split panes.

Jamie: And what makes that better than the raw diff editor?

Alex: Less visual clutter, stronger structure, and more reliable screen reader announcements. Instead of scanning for color and alignment you can't use, you're handed the semantic change.

Jamie: Can you place comments in VS Code too?

Alex: Yes. Once you identify the relevant changed line, use the extension's Add Comment command. So the workflow becomes: open PR, inspect changed files, use Accessible Diff Viewer to understand the edit, then attach a comment at the right location.

Jamie: That feels more controlled than browser review for some learners.

Alex: Often it is, especially if VS Code is already your primary workspace.

Jamie: Let's talk about the content of review comments, because tooling alone doesn't make feedback helpful.

Alex: Exactly. A useful review comment usually has three parts: what you noticed, why it matters, and what action or suggestion follows.

Jamie: Can we do examples?

Alex: Definitely. A blocking example for a documentation PR might be: "Blocking: this keyboard shortcuts page lists a command without indicating the Mac equivalent. That makes the instructions incomplete for Mac users. Please add the Command or Option version here."

Jamie: Clear, specific, and tied to the learner's experience.

Alex: A non-blocking nit might be: "Nit: this welcome paragraph could be shortened into two sentences for easier reading." Helpful, but not a merge blocker.

Jamie: And a question example?

Alex: "Question: should this setup guide mention that the user must be signed into GitHub before running this command?" That's not asserting an error as fact. It's inviting clarification.

Jamie: The chapter also mentions prefixes that set expectations.

Alex: Yes. Prefixes like Blocking, Nit, Question, Suggestion, or Praise help the author quickly understand the weight of your comment. That reduces social ambiguity.

Jamie: How many comments is too many?

Alex: There's no fixed number. Too many is when you're overwhelming the author with low-value noise or repeating the same point. If you have lots of small issues, look for patterns and combine where appropriate. Prioritize clarity and signal over volume.

Jamie: What about keyboard reference? I know we won't read a giant list, but what should learners remember?

Alex: A few anchor keys matter a lot. In VS Code: Control+Shift+P for Command Palette, Control+Shift+X for Extensions, Control+Shift+E for Explorer, F7 and Shift+F7 for Accessible Diff navigation, and Control+Shift+G for Source Control. On Mac, substitute Command for Control and Option for Alt-based shortcuts.

Jamie: And in the browser?

Alex: The exact keys depend more on your screen reader and browser, but the principle is to use heading, button, link, and region navigation to move efficiently, especially within the Files changed tab and comment controls.

Jamie: Now let's handle some common review scenarios, because that's where learners often hesitate.

Alex: Great idea.

Jamie: Scenario one: "I want to verify the PR only changes what it claims."

Alex: Start with the PR description. Then inspect the changed file list. If the PR says it updates one setup document but also changes unrelated files, that's a signal to investigate. You're checking scope alignment.

Jamie: Scenario two: "I want to find all changes to one specific section."

Alex: Use the file tree and search strategically. In VS Code, once the branch is checked out locally, normal editor search can help you find a heading or phrase across files. In the browser, navigate by file and scan for the relevant area.

Jamie: Scenario three: "I agreed, but then the author made more changes. Did anything new appear?"

Alex: Return to the updated diff and focus on changes since your last review if the interface offers that view. At minimum, reread the changed files and comment threads so you understand what was added or revised after your earlier approval.

Jamie: Scenario four: "A reviewer left a comment I don't understand."

Alex: Read the surrounding diff, check whether the comment is blocking or optional, and ask for clarification if needed. Review comments are part of collaboration, not judgment from a mountaintop.

Jamie: There were also structured exercises around this. Can we turn those into an audio walkthrough?

Alex: Absolutely. Exercise A is a complete web review. First, navigate to the pull request. Second, read the PR description. Third, go to Files changed. Fourth, if available, activate focus mode or whatever reading mode improves diff clarity for you. Fifth, find a heading hierarchy issue. Sixth, place a blocking review comment on that heading. Seventh, find a link text issue. Eighth, place a comment on the link. Ninth, submit your review.

Jamie: And then reflect.

Alex: Yes. Ask yourself what was easy, what was difficult, and what clues helped you orient inside the diff.

Jamie: Exercise B shifts to VS Code.

Alex: Right. Make sure the extension is installed. Open the GitHub Pull Requests extension. Open the Pull Requests sidebar. View the changed files for a PR. Access the Accessible Diff Viewer with F7. Listen to the first change carefully. Find the heading hierarchy issue. Locate the heading line and add an inline comment. Write your accessible diff comment. Then create the GitHub PR comment through the extension.

Jamie: And again, reflect on the experience.

Alex: Yes. Especially compare how much context you retained in VS Code versus the web interface.

Jamie: Then Exercise C is the comparison exercise.

Alex: Exactly. Gather your data from both review environments. Navigate to the PR or designated place to leave a reflection comment. Write your comparison of browser versus VS Code. Then review your comment, submit it, and validate your learning at the checkpoint.

Jamie: Let's do that reflection out loud. Browser versus VS Code: how should learners think about preference?

Alex: Ask which environment made orientation easier, which made comment placement easier, and which made the diff itself easier to understand.

Jamie: So, specific strengths.

Alex: Yes. Maybe the browser made overall PR context easier because the discussion, checks, and review form are native there. Maybe VS Code made the actual code or document changes easier because the Accessible Diff Viewer reduced clutter.

Jamie: And the real-world impact?

Alex: In real collaborative work, you don't need a single perfect tool. You need the judgment to choose the environment that best supports the task and your access needs.

Jamie: The chapter also introduces GitHub Copilot during code review. This is one of those areas where people can either overtrust it or ignore it completely.

Alex: Well said. Copilot can help you understand code changes, summarize a diff, explain an unfamiliar pattern, or suggest questions to investigate. In VS Code, that might happen with an open diff. On GitHub.com, it may assist through integrated features depending on your setup.

Jamie: Can you give an example exchange?

Alex: Sure. You might ask Copilot, "Explain what changed in this diff and what risk areas I should inspect." Or, "Summarize the functional impact of these additions." That can give you a starting frame.

Jamie: But not a final verdict.

Alex: Exactly. Copilot has limitations that are critical to know. It can misread intent, miss context outside the diff, sound confident when uncertain, and overlook project-specific requirements. Best practice is to use it as a helper for understanding, not as a substitute for reviewing.

Jamie: So skill first, assistant second.

Alex: Always.

Jamie: That phrase actually connects to the final part: the reviewer's craft.

Alex: It does. Good reviewing is not just clicking buttons. It's noticing important things, weighing their impact, and communicating clearly.

Jamie: What should a reviewer look for?

Alex: Start with purpose. Does the change do what the PR says it does? Then clarity. Is the code or documentation understandable? Then correctness. Then accessibility. Then consistency with project style. Then testing or evidence. And finally scope: are there unrelated changes that should be split out?

Jamie: And the three review actions fit into that judgment.

Alex: Yes. Approve when the work is ready. Request changes when there are blockers. Comment-only when you want to contribute feedback without stopping progress.

Jamie: How do you write constructive feedback instead of demoralizing feedback?

Alex: Focus on the work, not the person. Be specific. Explain why. Offer a path forward. Use respectful language. And include positive observations when they're real, not performative.

Jamie: So something like, "This section is strong because the steps are explicit, but one accessibility issue remains: the link text 'click here' doesn't describe the destination. Please revise it to the page name."

Alex: Perfect example. Clear praise, clear issue, clear next step.

Jamie: Is there a reviewer checklist we can leave listeners with?

Alex: Yes. Before submitting a review, ask: Did I understand the PR description? Did I inspect the changed files rather than guessing? Did I verify the scope matches the claim? Did I note any accessibility, correctness, or clarity issues? Are my comments actionable? Did I choose the right verdict? And if I used Copilot or another aid, did I independently verify its suggestions?

Jamie: I like that. Reviewing becomes a learning tool too, doesn't it?

Alex: Absolutely. Reviewing teaches you to recognize quality. You start noticing patterns in structure, clarity, tests, accessibility, and collaboration. That makes you a stronger author as well as a stronger reviewer.

Jamie: There's also a teaser about a larger accessibility agents review ecosystem.

Alex: Yes. The idea is that more tools and agents can assist with code review, perhaps by surfacing patterns, checking policies, or helping summarize changes. But the guiding principle remains the same: skill first, agent second.

Jamie: So agents help, but they do not replace human judgment.

Alex: Exactly. A real review flow might include you reading the PR, using accessibility tools to inspect the diff, optionally asking an assistant for a summary or risk checklist, then making your own decision and writing your own review comment.

Jamie: Before we close, can we restate the practical takeaways from the whole lesson?

Alex: Of course. Install and sign in to the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension. Use it to view pull requests, filter them, and open details. Check out a PR branch when local testing or deeper inspection will help. Review changed files in VS Code, and for screen reader users, strongly prefer the Accessible Diff Viewer with F7 and Shift+F7.
