Create pull requests from VS Code when convenient, but don't hesitate to open the form in the browser if accessibility is better there. Use PR templates fully and thoughtfully. Add inline comments that are specific, respectful, and actionable. Batch comments into a review when needed, then choose approve, request changes, or comment-only. Merge only when prerequisites are satisfied, and clean up afterward by returning to main, pulling, and deleting old branches when appropriate.

Jamie: And on the craft side: understand the change, evaluate its impact, set expectation with comment prefixes, avoid noisy review behavior, and remember that reviewing is part of learning.

Alex: Exactly. Also remember your fallback paths. If the extension gives you trouble, reload the window. If authentication fails, re-establish browser sign-in. If checkout isn't allowed, review on GitHub.com. If the visual diff is too chaotic, use the accessible tools designed for this job.

Jamie: I think that's the reassuring note many learners need: there is almost always another route.

Alex: There is. Good collaboration isn't about forcing yourself through one interface. It's about using the tools that let you understand the change and communicate effectively.

Jamie: And if you're doing the practice work tied to this lesson, your evidence comment should say whether the extension was installed, whether you signed in, which PR you reviewed, whether your comment was inline or on GitHub.com, and what your comment was about.

Alex: Exactly. Then close out any related challenge issues if your course setup uses them.

Jamie: All right. Today's lesson was a big one, but the through-line is simple: make pull requests manageable, make diffs readable, and make feedback constructive.

Alex: Beautifully said. We'll stop there.

38. Episode 15: Accessible Code Review

Navigating diffs with a screen reader, reviewing PRs in browser and VS Code.

Based on: Chapter 15: Accessible Code Review

Download Episode 15 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 15: Accessible Code Review

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re working on code review in a way that is practical, accessible, and very real to how teams actually collaborate. We’re going to talk about pull requests, diffs, review comments, approvals, requested changes, and how to do all of that both in VS Code and on GitHub.com.

Jamie: And importantly, for our learners using screen readers, we’re not treating accessibility as an extra feature tagged on at the end.

Alex: Exactly. Accessibility is part of the workflow itself. We’ll cover the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension in VS Code, the Accessible Diff Viewer, browser-based review on GitHub.com, and the craft of writing useful feedback.

Jamie: Before we jump in, are there prerequisites?

Alex: Yes. This lesson assumes you already know the basics of pull requests and Git in VS Code. It also assumes you have a repository open in VS Code. And a quick keyboard note: when we say Control shortcuts on Windows, use Command on Mac. When we say Alt on Windows, use Option on Mac. And if we mention a context menu with Shift+F10 on Windows, Mac users will often use Control+Return.

Jamie: Good. So this is one of those chapters where setup matters.

Alex: Very much. The pattern here is: install and configure first, practice reviewing someone else’s work, use the accessibility tools that make the review process efficient, and write specific constructive feedback instead of vague praise.

Alex: Let’s start with the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension in VS Code. This extension brings GitHub pull request workflows into your editor so you can browse PRs, check out branches, read changed files, comment, create pull requests, and in some cases merge, all without bouncing constantly to a browser tab.

Jamie: That sounds convenient, but also potentially overwhelming. What does installation actually look like?

Alex: You have two common methods. Method one is the Extensions sidebar. Open it with Control+Shift+X. The search box usually gets focus. Type GitHub Pull Requests, find the extension published by GitHub, and activate Install.

Jamie: And method two?

Alex: The Command Palette. Open it with Control+Shift+P, then search for extension-related commands or for the extension itself, and install from there. The sidebar method is usually more straightforward for first-time setup, but both are valid.

Jamie: What happens after installation?

Alex: Usually VS Code prompts you to sign in to GitHub. Activate the sign-in action, which opens your browser for OAuth authorization. Approve access, return to VS Code, and then verify you’re signed in.

Jamie: How do you verify?

Alex: Open the Explorer with Control+Shift+E and look for a GitHub section. If the extension is active and authentication worked, that section should show pull requests and issues for your current context.

Jamie: Any screen reader-specific advice there?

Alex: Yes. Sometimes install or sign-in notifications disappear before you can review them. If that happens, open the Command Palette and run Notifications: Focus Notification Toast. That can bring focus back to the latest notification so you can hear it clearly.

Jamie: What new capabilities does the extension add once it’s installed?

Alex: It adds GitHub-aware panels and commands. You can view open pull requests, inspect descriptions, list changed files, check out a PR branch locally, add comments, start reviews, submit verdicts, and create pull requests from within VS Code. Think of it as making GitHub collaboration available from your editor instead of only through the web interface.

Jamie: So the learning card version would be: install it, sign in, confirm the GitHub section appears, and understand that it expands VS Code into a pull request workspace.

Alex: That’s a perfect summary.

Alex: Now let’s talk about viewing pull requests.

Jamie: This is where many learners think, “I installed the extension, but where did the pull requests actually go?”

Alex: Yes, and that confusion is normal. There are two common entry points. One is the Activity Bar, where the GitHub Pull Requests view may have its own icon depending on your setup. The other is the Explorer, where the extension can add a GitHub section.

Jamie: Once you’re there, what should you expect?

Alex: A list or tree of open pull requests. You can list open PRs, choose a specific PR to inspect, open the PR in your browser, and filter to things like PRs waiting for your review.

Jamie: Filtering sounds especially helpful.

Alex: It is. You may filter by status, such as open or closed depending on the view, and sometimes by repository if you work across more than one. That matters because “No pull requests found” may simply mean you’re in the wrong repo context or the current filter is too narrow.

Jamie: What does the PR tree usually contain?

Alex: Typically the PR title, number, author, status, and child items like description or changed files. A screen reader user may hear something like a tree item that announces the PR title and metadata, then expandable content beneath it.

Jamie: And viewing details means what, specifically?

Alex: Reading the PR description, checking status checks, seeing branch information, seeing changed files, and identifying whether the PR is ready for review, draft, assigned to you, or blocked by checks. For a screen reader user, it helps to think of this as a structured information panel rather than a visual card.

Jamie: So the main task here is orientation: where is the PR list, how do I filter it, and how do I open the details that actually tell me what changed.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Once you’ve found a pull request, the next skill is checking out its branch.

Jamie: Why would I do that instead of just reading the PR online?

Alex: Several reasons. Local checkout lets you test the changes in your own editor, inspect files with your own tools, navigate diffs more accessibly, and run the project if needed. It’s especially useful when you want deeper verification than a quick browser review.

Jamie: How do you check out a PR branch?

Alex: There are several methods. From the PR detail view, there’s often a Checkout action. From the PR tree, you may open the context menu and choose Checkout. Or from the Command Palette, you can run GitHub Pull Requests commands to check out the current or selected pull request.

Jamie: What happens after checkout?

Alex: VS Code switches your repository to the pull request’s source branch. That means your working copy now reflects the proposed changes from that PR.

Jamie: That sounds powerful, but also like something people could forget they did.

Alex: Exactly right. One important follow-up is returning to your original branch when you’re done. Usually that means using the branch picker in VS Code or Git commands to go back to main or to your own feature branch.

Jamie: So there’s a mental model here: checking out a PR is temporary context switching.

Alex: Yes. Review there, test there, then switch back deliberately.

Alex: Now we get to one of the most important sections: reviewing pull requests in VS Code.

Jamie: This is where diffs stop being abstract and start becoming something you can actually read.

Alex: Exactly. A review begins with the files changed list. In the PR detail view, you can open the list of modified files. A screen reader may announce each file along with whether it was added, modified, or deleted.

Jamie: And then opening one gives you the diff editor.

Alex: Right. By default, VS Code often opens diffs in split view mode, with the old version on the left and the new version on the right.

Jamie: Which is visually common, but not always ideal for a screen reader user.

Alex: Correct. There’s also an inline view mode that places changes in a more linear flow. Some users prefer that. You can toggle between split and inline views depending on the task and your access needs.

Jamie: But the big accessibility feature here is the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Alex: Yes. For many screen reader users, the most reliable review workflow in VS Code is to use the Accessible Diff Viewer. Press F7 to move to the next change and Shift+F7 to move to the previous change. Instead of wandering through a visually structured editor line by line, you hear a structured announcement of the change itself.

Jamie: Can you describe the benefit in plain language?

Alex: Absolutely. The raw visual diff can be noisy. The Accessible Diff Viewer condenses a change into something like: line removed, line added, maybe line numbers or a short context. That means you spend your attention on what changed, not on fighting layout.

Jamie: So if a learner has ever thought, “I can technically open the diff, but I can’t efficiently understand it,” this is the answer.

Alex: Often, yes. It’s far superior to manually navigating the visual diff when you’re using a screen reader.

Jamie: What kinds of issues should a reviewer flag?

Alex: Look for typos, unclear instructions, missing steps, inaccessible wording, incorrect structure, broken logic, or even strong choices worth praising. Good review isn’t just catching problems. It’s helping the author understand what works and what needs attention.

Jamie: And the learning card version here would be: read changed files, understand split versus inline diff, prefer the Accessible Diff Viewer for screen reader efficiency, and note issues worth commenting on.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can we make this concrete with the practice workflow?

Alex: Yes. A practical exercise is: install the extension, sign in, open the pull requests view, choose a PR that is not your own, check it out if permissions allow, open changed files, navigate with F7, and leave one constructive comment.

Jamie: And if checkout is blocked?

Alex: Use the fallback. Open the PR on GitHub.com and review it there. The goal is the review skill, not proving that branch checkout worked on your account.

Jamie: What counts as finishing the exercise?

Alex: Posting at least one constructive review comment on someone else’s pull request.

Jamie: And the evidence submission matters too, right?

Alex: Yes. Learners should post a completion comment on the assigned practice issue indicating whether the extension was installed, whether sign-in succeeded, which PR they reviewed, whether the comment was inline or on GitHub.com, and a one-sentence summary of what their comment addressed. Also, close the earlier challenge issues when directed.

Jamie: Expected outcomes?

Alex: You can install and authenticate the extension, check out or at least view a PR, navigate diffs with F7, and post specific feedback.

Jamie: If someone gets stuck?

Alex: Try reloading VS Code with Developer: Reload Window if installation feels incomplete. If OAuth sign-in fails, confirm you’re already signed into GitHub in the browser and retry. If the PR list is empty, switch to a broader filter like all open. If checkout fails, verify repository permissions and use the read-only browser fallback if needed. If the diff editor feels hard to navigate, use F7. If the Add Comment command seems missing, search for GitHub Pull Requests: Add Comment in the Command Palette. And of course, ask a facilitator to model one review if needed.

Jamie: I like the learning moment embedded here.

Alex: Me too. Reviewing other people’s work strengthens your own standards. Explaining why something is clear or unclear is a learning tool in itself.

Alex: Now let’s turn to creating a pull request from VS Code.

Jamie: So far we’ve been the reviewer. Now we become the author.

Alex: Exactly. The extension can help you open a pull request directly from your editor after you’ve committed work and pushed your branch.

Jamie: What are the prerequisites?

Alex: You generally need a branch with committed changes pushed to GitHub, and you need the extension installed and authenticated.

Jamie: What are the main ways to create the PR?

Alex: Three common methods. Method one, and usually the recommended one, is through the Command Palette. Method two is from the Source Control panel. Method three is from the GitHub panel itself.

Jamie: And then comes the PR form.

Alex: Right. The form usually includes a required title, an optional but strongly recommended description, a base branch target like main, a compare branch source which is your feature branch, and optional fields like reviewers, labels, milestone, and a draft PR checkbox.

Jamie: Why is the description “optional but recommended” instead of just optional?

Alex: Because reviewers need context. A good description explains what changed, why it changed, how to test it, whether there’s a related issue, and anything the reviewer should pay special attention to. Technically optional does not mean socially optional.

Jamie: That’s an important distinction.

Alex: Very. For accessibility and screen reader navigation, move through the form deliberately. Confirm focus as you tab through fields, verify the target branch and source branch, and listen carefully before submitting.

Jamie: What submission styles are available?

Alex: Sometimes the extension guides you interactively, prompting for title, body, and base branch one piece at a time. Other times it offers a fuller inline form where you can provide details directly. You may also create the PR as a draft, or open the form in your browser if that interface works better for you.

Jamie: So the tool card version is: use your editor to create the PR, but choose the exact interaction pattern that best matches your access needs.

Alex: Precisely.

Alex: A closely related concept is the pull request description template.

Jamie: Those are the pre-filled structures some repos give you, right?

Alex: Yes. Repositories can store PR templates so when you open a new pull request, the description starts with a checklist or prompts. Common sections include a plain-language description, related issue, type of change, testing performed, a checklist, and screenshots if applicable.

Jamie: Why do teams use these?

Alex: Because templates improve consistency. They remind authors to include context reviewers need. They also reduce back-and-forth like “What issue does this fix?” or “How should I test this?”

Jamie: How should a screen reader user work through a template?

Alex: Treat it as a form you complete carefully. Move section by section, replace placeholder text with real answers, and confirm that you haven’t left generic prompts in place. A template is helpful only if it gets filled out meaningfully.

Jamie: So don’t submit a PR that still says something like “Describe your changes here.”

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s focus on commenting and requesting changes.

Jamie: This is where review quality really shows.

Alex: Yes. You can add an inline comment on a specific line or hunk of code or text. In VS Code, position the cursor on the relevant line and use the command to add a comment. On GitHub.com, use the add-comment controls in the Files changed view.

Jamie: What makes an inline comment useful?

Alex: It should identify the issue clearly, explain why it matters, and, when possible, suggest a fix or ask a focused question. A helpful format is something like: what I noticed, why it matters, and what I recommend.

Jamie: And if you have multiple comments?

Alex: Use Start Review rather than submitting each one individually. That lets you collect several comments and then submit them together with an overall verdict.

Jamie: What are the verdict options?

Alex: Approve, Request changes, or Comment-only. Approve means the PR is acceptable from your perspective. Request changes means there’s a blocking issue that should be addressed before merging. Comment-only means you have feedback, but you’re not issuing a formal approval or blocking verdict.

Jamie: And what happens after submission?

Alex: The author gets notified. Your comments become part of the PR conversation. If changes are requested, the author may push updates and ask for another review. You can also view PR details and sometimes even inspect diffs in your terminal depending on your workflow, but the main idea is that review is an iterative conversation, not a one-time pronouncement.

Jamie: That leads nicely into etiquette.

Alex: Yes. Comments should be constructive, specific, and proportionate. Don’t leave “Looks good” on a serious accessibility issue. Don’t write a novel for a tiny nit unless the repo culture expects exhaustive review. Match the comment to the importance of the issue.

Alex: Next, merging pull requests.

Jamie: Which many learners think is just pressing a button.

Alex: Sometimes it is. But there are prerequisites. The PR may need required approvals, passing status checks, conflict-free branches, or repository permissions. You should not merge just because you can see the button.

Jamie: How do you merge from VS Code?

Alex: Often from the PR detail view, or through a command in the Command Palette. The exact actions depend on repository settings and extension support.

Jamie: And then we have merge types.

Alex: Right. The common ones are merge commit, squash and merge, and rebase and merge. Merge commit preserves the full branch history as a distinct merge. Squash and merge combines the branch’s commits into one before merging. Rebase and merge reapplies commits onto the base branch for a linear history.

Jamie: How should learners choose?

Alex: Follow the repository’s conventions. Many teams prefer squash and merge for small feature branches because it keeps history tidy. Some repos prefer merge commits for preserving context. Use the project norm rather than personal habit.

Jamie: What happens after merging?

Alex: Switch back to main and pull the latest changes so your local repository matches the remote state. If appropriate, delete the feature branch locally and remotely. Some workflows also allow auto-merge, where the PR is set to merge automatically once checks pass.

Jamie: So a realistic sequence is: merge with the default strategy or squash and merge, optionally delete the branch, then return to main and pull.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: We should talk shortcuts and troubleshooting too, because those are part of actual usability.

Alex: Absolutely. A few high-value shortcuts include Control+Shift+P for the Command Palette, Control+Shift+X for Extensions, Control+Shift+E for Explorer, Control+Shift+G for Source Control, and F7 or Shift+F7 for navigating changes in the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Jamie: And the common problems?

Alex: If you hear “No pull requests found,” check the repository, check your filters, and confirm you’re signed in. If you get “Could not create pull request,” make sure your branch is pushed, your base and compare branches are correct, and your authentication is still valid. If authentication fails, sign into GitHub in your browser first, then retry VS Code authorization.

Jamie: There’s also a practical invitation here.

Alex: Yes. Try reviewing a PR from VS Code. Don’t just read about it. Open the panel, inspect a PR, use F7, and leave one thoughtful comment.

Alex: Now we move into accessible code review more broadly.

Jamie: So this is bigger than just the extension.

Alex: Exactly. This section is about how to conduct pull request reviews with a screen reader in two environments: GitHub.com and VS Code. It also includes the formal review actions of approve, request changes, and comment-only review, plus local checkout and even terminal-based inspection as supporting tools.

Jamie: Before starting, what should learners verify?

Alex: That they’ve completed the earlier prerequisite work: basic pull requests, Git in VS Code, and ideally the extension setup. Also understand that this chapter uses learning cards to reinforce specific, repeatable actions in both the browser and the editor.

Jamie: Two environments, two strengths.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub.com is strong for the full review conversation and threaded comments. VS Code is strong for local file context and accessible diff reading.

Alex: Let’s walk through browser-based review first.

Jamie: On GitHub.com, where does a screen reader user begin?

Alex: Start by opening the pull request and reaching the Files changed tab. The modern interface is the default now, which is helpful because the current review experience is more consistent than older legacy patterns.

Jamie: Once you’re in Files changed, what’s next?

Alex: Use the file tree to orient yourself. Listen for file names, whether sections are expanded, and your current position in the list. This helps you build a mental map of the PR before diving into individual diffs.

Jamie: Then navigate between file diffs.

Alex: Right. Move through the files methodically. Don’t just arrow endlessly and hope meaning appears. Treat each file as a unit: what file is this, why was it changed, what kind of change do I expect here?

Jamie: How should a learner read a diff on GitHub.com?

Alex: Understand what each line represents. You may encounter removed lines, added lines, unchanged context lines, and controls for adding comments. Listen for line numbers and change indicators. The goal is to understand the before and after, not merely hear a stream of text.

Jamie: And placing an inline comment?

Alex: Find the relevant line, activate the add-comment control, and type a focused comment. For a multi-line comment, select a range where the platform allows it, then attach one comment to that whole section instead of leaving scattered fragments.

Jamie: What about existing discussions?

Alex: Read existing comments and threads before repeating feedback someone else already gave. This avoids duplication and teaches you how other reviewers frame issues.

Jamie: And then submit your review.

Alex: Yes. Choose the correct verdict. Approve if the PR is ready. Request changes if there’s a blocking issue. Comment-only if you have feedback without a formal decision. Then, if the author updates the PR, they may re-request review from you later.

Jamie: That whole workflow is a skill: orient, inspect, comment, read discussion, submit verdict, and potentially review again.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s compare that to reviewing in VS Code with the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Jamie: What’s the opening sequence there?

Alex: Open the GitHub Pull Requests extension, open the pull requests sidebar, choose the PR, and inspect the changed files. Then open a diff for a specific file.

Jamie: And from there, use F7.

Alex: Yes. Press F7 to move change by change through the file. This accessible diff mode provides structured navigation that is often much better than wandering through the raw diff editor. It highlights the essence of each change.

Jamie: Why exactly is it better than the raw diff editor?

Alex: Because raw visual diffs encode meaning through side-by-side layout, color, and spacing. Screen reader users can access pieces of that, but it’s cognitively expensive. The Accessible Diff Viewer turns that visual structure into a more linear, semantic reading experience.

Jamie: Can you still place comments in VS Code?

Alex: Yes. Once you identify the line or hunk you want to discuss, use the GitHub Pull Requests extension command to add a comment. The extension then posts that review comment back to the pull request conversation.

Jamie: So the learning cards here would emphasize opening the PR, using the Accessible Diff Viewer, and then placing a comment tied to a meaningful change.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s talk about review structure and content, because access to the tool is only half the story. The other half is judgment.

Jamie: What makes a useful review comment?

Alex: A useful comment has a clear purpose. It tells the author what the reviewer noticed, why it matters, and whether it blocks merging. There are at least three common kinds.

Jamie: Blocking, non-blocking nit, and question?

Alex: Exactly. A blocking example might say that a heading hierarchy in a documentation file skips levels and needs correction for accessibility before merge. A non-blocking nit might suggest cleaner wording in a welcome document but explicitly signal that it’s minor. A question might ask whether an instruction in a setup guide assumes a tool the learner hasn’t installed yet.

Jamie: So prefixes can help set expectations.

Alex: Yes. Prefixes like “blocking,” “nit,” or “question” are helpful because they tell the author how to prioritize the comment. They reduce anxiety and ambiguity.

Jamie: How many comments is too many?

Alex: There isn’t a fixed number. Too many comments is when the volume stops helping. Ten precise comments on ten real issues may be excellent. Three vague comments may be worse. Group related feedback when possible, avoid repetitive phrasing, and make sure each comment adds distinct value.

Jamie: That’s a very professor answer.

Alex: I’ll take that as a compliment.

Jamie: What about a keyboard reference? Learners often need a compact mental list.

Alex: For web review, focus on the browser’s standard navigation plus the controls in the Files changed tab for adding comments and submitting a review. For VS Code, remember the GitHub PR commands, opening the pull requests view, and especially F7 and Shift+F7 for the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Jamie: So not an encyclopedia of shortcuts. Just the ones that support the actual review flow.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let’s ground this with common review scenarios.

Jamie: I love scenarios.

Alex: Scenario one: you want to verify the PR only changes what it claims. Read the PR description first, then compare it to the changed files list. If the PR claims to update one guide but also modifies unrelated files, that deserves attention.

Jamie: Scenario two: you want to find all changes to one specific section.

Alex: Use file names, heading text, search where available, and structured navigation in either the browser or editor. The idea is to review thematically instead of linearly.

Jamie: Scenario three: you already agreed, but then the author made more changes.

Alex: Revisit the PR and identify what’s new since your last review. Don’t assume your earlier approval still covers the current state. Re-review the updated diff.

Jamie: And scenario four: a reviewer left a comment you don’t understand.

Alex: Read the surrounding code or text, read the full thread, and if needed ask a clarifying question rather than guessing. Review is collaborative, not a test of mind reading.

Alex: The chapter also includes exercises, and those matter.

Jamie: Walk us through them.

Alex: Exercise A is a complete web review. Navigate to the pull request, read the description, go to Files changed, use focus mode or a similarly simplified reading mode if available, locate a heading hierarchy issue, place a blocking comment on that heading, find a link text issue, place another comment, and then submit the review. Afterward, reflect on the experience.

Jamie: So that exercise combines navigation, accessibility judgment, and actual submission.

Alex: Yes. Exercise B uses the VS Code Accessible Diff Viewer. Open the GitHub Pull Requests extension, open the pull requests sidebar, inspect file changes, access the Accessible Diff Viewer, listen to the first change, identify the heading hierarchy problem, locate the heading line, add an inline comment, write the comment clearly, and create the GitHub PR comment from VS Code. Then reflect on that experience too.

Jamie: And Exercise C compares the two environments.

Alex: Exactly. Gather your observations, navigate to the PR, leave a reflection comment, and write a comparison of browser versus VS Code review.

Jamie: What should that reflection include?

Alex: Your environment preference, specific strengths of each environment, real-world impact, and a checkpoint that validates what you learned. For example: the browser may make threaded conversation easier, while VS Code may make reading diffs more efficient with a screen reader.

Jamie: That kind of reflection helps learners choose tools intentionally, not just by habit.

Alex: Precisely.

Alex: There’s also a section on using GitHub Copilot to understand code changes.

Jamie: This is an area where people can either get real support or be misled.

Alex: Very true. Copilot can help you summarize a diff, explain a block of code, or answer questions about what a change appears to do. You can use it in VS Code with an open diff, or sometimes in GitHub’s web interface where available.

Jamie: Can you give the safe framing?

Alex: Use Copilot to support understanding, not to replace judgment. Ask it to explain a change, identify possible impacts, or help interpret unfamiliar code. But verify against the actual diff.

Jamie: And the limitations?

Alex: Critical ones: Copilot can be wrong, overly confident, incomplete, or unaware of project-specific conventions. It may miss accessibility implications, repository policies, or nuanced author intent. Never approve or reject solely because Copilot suggested it.

Jamie: Best practices?

Alex: Use narrow questions, keep the diff visible, verify claims, and treat Copilot as a study partner rather than an authority.

Jamie: And what comes next after that?

Alex: You fold that AI-assisted understanding back into human review craft.

Alex: Which brings us to the reviewer’s craft.

Jamie: My favorite part.

Alex: Mine too. A good reviewer looks for correctness, clarity, accessibility, completeness, consistency with project norms, and whether the change matches the stated goal.

Jamie: And the three review actions are the formal expression of that judgment.

Alex: Yes. Approve, request changes, or comment without a verdict. Choosing among them is part of professional review skill.

Jamie: What makes feedback constructive?

Alex: Constructive feedback is specific, respectful, and actionable. It addresses the work rather than the person. It explains impact. It suggests a path forward when appropriate. And it distinguishes blocking issues from suggestions.

Jamie: Can we turn that into a checklist?

Alex: Absolutely. Ask yourself: Did I read the PR description? Did I verify the changes align with the claim? Did I check for accessibility implications? Did I focus on important issues first? Did I read existing comments? Did I choose the right verdict? Did I phrase my comments so the author can act on them?

Jamie: And reviewing is also a learning tool.

Alex: Deeply so. When you review, you internalize quality standards. You notice patterns. You learn what maintainers care about. And you improve your own future pull requests because you begin to write with the reviewer in mind.

Jamie: Before we close, there’s a teaser about a broader accessibility review ecosystem.

Alex: Yes. The idea is that code review can be supported by multiple agents and tools, but the principle is skill first, agent second. Learn how to review with your own judgment, your own screen reader workflow, your own understanding of diffs and feedback. Then let tools assist.

Jamie: So the tools help, but they don’t replace fluency.

Alex: Exactly. In a mature workflow, different agents may help summarize, test, lint, flag accessibility risks, or explain changes. But the reviewer still decides what matters and how to communicate it.

Jamie: That “real example: the flow” idea is basically: human reviewer leads, tools support, conversation refines.

Alex: Beautifully put.

Alex: Let’s end with a practical recap. Install the GitHub Pull Requests extension. Sign in and verify the GitHub section appears. Open pull requests from VS Code. Filter and inspect them. Check out a PR branch locally when useful. Read changed files. Use the Accessible Diff Viewer with F7 and Shift+F7. Add inline comments. Start a review when you have multiple comments. Submit the correct verdict: approve, request changes, or comment-only. Create pull requests from VS Code when you’re the author. Fill out templates thoughtfully. Merge only when prerequisites are satisfied. Troubleshoot filters, authentication, and branch setup when things go wrong.

Jamie: And on the craft side: orient yourself, read the description, review with purpose, write comments that are specific and respectful, use prefixes to signal priority, and reflect on whether browser or VS Code better serves the task and your access needs.

Alex: Exactly. And remember: a good review is not performative criticism. It is collaborative problem-solving.

Jamie: That’s a lovely note to end on.

Alex: It is. See you next time.

39. Challenge 11: Open a Day 2 PR

Opening a pull request from a locally pushed branch and reading it in VS Code.

Practice focus: Day 2 local workflow

Download Challenge 11 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 11: Open a Day 2 PR

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're connecting the local Git workflow you practiced in VS Code with the pull request workflow on GitHub. The big idea is simple: a pull request is still the destination. What changes on Day 2 is how your edits get there.

Jamie: So if I edited in VS Code instead of directly on GitHub, I'm not learning a totally different process?

Alex: Exactly. You're learning the same collaboration pattern with one extra transport step. On Day 1, the edits were made on GitHub.com, so the commit already lived on GitHub. On Day 2, you edit locally, commit locally, then push those commits up to GitHub, and only then open the pull request.

Alex: Let's anchor this in the actual challenge. Your task is to open a pull request from the branch you pushed locally in the earlier local workflow practice. On GitHub.com, you go to your learning-room repository. If GitHub shows the recent-push banner, you can use the Compare and pull request button. If not, you go to Pull requests, choose New pull request, set the base branch to main, and set the compare branch to your branch, often something like fix slash your username.

Jamie: And then write the title and description the same way I would have before?

Alex: Yes. Clear title. Clear description. And if the pull request addresses an issue, include plain text like Closes number-something so GitHub can link and close that issue when the PR merges.

Jamie: So the challenge is not really about fancy wording. It's about recognizing the workflow pattern.

Alex: Right. The evidence asks for two things: the PR URL and the pattern you noticed. That pattern is the learning objective.

Alex: Here's the contrast the course wants you to notice. Day 1: edit on GitHub.com, commit, open PR. Day 2: edit locally, commit, push, open PR. The pull request step is identical. The difference is where the commits came from and how they reached GitHub.

Jamie: That makes the PR feel less mysterious. It's not a different object. It's just pointing at a branch that now contains my proposed changes.

Alex: Perfectly said.

Alex: Before we stay at the PR layer, we need to revisit the local Git workflow in VS Code, because that's what feeds this challenge. This chapter covers managing repositories, branches, and changes accessibly. It assumes you already know the VS Code basics, and it keeps calling out screen reader-friendly paths, especially through the Command Palette and structured panels.

Jamie: And there was also some admin guidance around this local workflow chapter, right?

Alex: Yes. This local workflow unit supports the earlier hands-on challenge where you cloned your learning room repository, created a branch, made a commit, pushed it, and opened a PR. The recommended practice pattern was: clone, branch, edit, commit, push, PR. The expected evidence included PR metadata, branch names, and committed changes.

Jamie: So even the workshop recommendation is really teaching a repeatable sequence.

Alex: Exactly. And there are CLI habits that the material treats as best practices even if you prefer VS Code. Check your current state before acting with git status. Keep branch context explicit with git branch dash dash show-current. Fetch before pushing if you want to verify alignment. Confirm your PR-closing text like Closes number-something in plain text. And avoid obscure convenience flags if they make output harder to understand or verify.

Alex: Start with cloning. For screen reader users, the most recommended method in VS Code is the Command Palette. Open it with Control Shift P, or Command Shift P on Mac, type Git: Clone, paste the repository URL, choose a destination folder, and then open the cloned repository when prompted.

Jamie: Why is the Command Palette preferred?

Alex: Because it gives a stable searchable command surface. Screen reader users often get more predictable announcements there than on start pages or visually arranged buttons. There are other methods too. You can use a clone button from the start page, or begin from GitHub.com and send the repo into VS Code. But Command Palette tends to be the cleanest path.

Jamie: And after cloning, I shouldn't just assume everything is ready.

Alex: Correct. Verify the clone. Open Explorer and confirm the file tree. If the course repo has files like README and a docs folder, you should hear those in the Explorer. If a progress notification was silent, there's a notification focus command you can run to check status.

Jamie: What about branch visibility after a fresh clone?

Alex: Very important. A fresh clone checks out only the default branch locally, usually main, even if remote branches already exist. So run git branch dash a to list local and remote-tracking branches. You may see main locally and origin slash learn slash yourname remotely. That tells you the branch exists on GitHub and can be checked out locally.

Alex: There are several useful clone commands the material teaches as learning cards. Standard git clone with the full repository URL. GitHub CLI clone using owner slash name, which is shorter and can handle authentication automatically. Clone into a specific folder by supplying a destination. Clone only the default branch for faster work on large repositories using a single-branch style option. And always verify the result.

Jamie: There was also a quick practice repo mentioned, right?

Alex: Yes, a sci-fi themes repo example to practice cloning. The point wasn't the content of the repo. It was building comfort with clone commands like gh repo clone owner slash repo, then changing into the folder, then opening that repo in VS Code.

Alex: Once the repo is open, the Source Control panel becomes your day-to-day dashboard. Open it with Control Shift G. It includes the commit message box near the top, action buttons, and grouped lists for staged and unstaged changes.

Jamie: Can we slow down there? For a new learner, what does that panel actually tell me?

Alex: It tells you what Git currently sees. Modified files, untracked files, staged files, and actions you can take. Screen reader navigation matters here. NVDA and JAWS users often move through the panel with standard arrow and tab patterns. VoiceOver users may need to interact with groups and be mindful of nested controls. The course emphasizes learning the panel structure from top to bottom so the announcements make sense.

Jamie: And if I'm not in VS Code, what are the CLI equivalents?

Alex: Good question. git status shows all modified, staged, and untracked files in a readable summary. git status dash s gives the short format with compact one-letter markers. git diff dash dash cached shows what is staged and ready to commit. git diff shows what is modified but not staged. And git diff HEAD shows both staged and unstaged differences compared to the last commit.

Jamie: So if I ever feel lost in the panel, I can cross-check in the terminal.

Alex: Absolutely. That's often the most accessible confidence check.

Alex: Branch management comes next. You always want to know what branch you're on. In VS Code, the current branch is shown in the status bar. You can focus the status bar and have your screen reader announce it. In the terminal, git branch dash dash show-current says it plainly.

Jamie: And creating a branch is also best done through the Command Palette?

Alex: For many learners, yes. Use Git: Create Branch, type a meaningful name, and switch to it. Naming conventions matter. In this workshop you've seen names like learn slash username or fix slash something-descriptive. The name should hint at purpose.

Jamie: What are the core commands I should know?

Alex: Create and switch to a new branch with git checkout dash b branchname, or the newer style git switch dash c branchname. List local branches with git branch. List all including remote-tracking with git branch dash a. Switch to an existing branch with git switch branchname or git checkout branchname. Delete a branch after it's merged with git branch dash d branchname. Force delete with dash capital D only if you truly mean it. Rename the current branch with git branch dash m newname. Push a new branch for the first time with git push dash u origin branchname. Delete a remote branch with git push origin dash dash delete branchname. And if you work with issues, GitHub CLI can even create a branch linked to an issue and auto-name it.

Jamie: What happens when I switch branches in VS Code?

Alex: Your working tree changes to match that branch. Files may appear, disappear, or revert depending on what that branch contains. That's normal, but it's exactly why branch awareness matters.

Alex: Now staging. This is where many people blur together saving, staging, and committing. They're different. Saving writes your file to disk. Staging tells Git which changes you want included in the next commit. Committing records that staged snapshot.

Jamie: So I can save lots of things, but stage only some of them.

Alex: Exactly. In VS Code, you can stage an entire file from the Source Control panel using the plus button, a shortcut, or the context menu. You can also stage multiple files at once. And for more precise work, you can stage individual lines or chunks from a diff.

Jamie: That feels advanced, but useful.

Alex: Very useful for keeping commits focused. In CLI terms, git add filename stages one file. git add dot stages many changes. git add dash p lets you stage interactively, one hunk at a time. Git will ask whether to stage each hunk, with prompts like yes, no, split, or edit. That's powerful when a file contains two unrelated edits and you only want one in the next commit.

Jamie: And if I staged the wrong thing?

Alex: Unstage it. In VS Code, reverse the process from the staged area. In CLI, git restore dash dash staged filename will unstage without discarding the file content. Then check staged versus unstaged state again with git diff and git diff dash dash cached.

Alex: Committing comes after staging. The standard workflow is: make changes, save, stage, write a commit message, commit. The chapter spends time on how this feels with screen readers because the message box and panel state are part of the feedback loop.

Jamie: What does a good commit message look like here?

Alex: Short, specific, and meaningful. A common format is a brief prefix and description, like docs: improve welcome page introduction. The quick reference idea is: say what changed, not your emotional state while changing it.

Jamie: And the commands?

Alex: Commit staged changes with git commit dash m quoted message. For a multi-line message, use git commit without dash m and let your editor open. If you intend to stage all tracked modified files and commit in one step, git commit dash a dash m quoted message can do that, but remember it won't include untracked new files unless you add them first.

Jamie: What's the feedback after a successful commit?

Alex: In VS Code, staged and unstaged entries disappear if everything was included. In Git, the commit gets a hash and becomes part of local history. But it is still only local until you push.

Alex: Push and pull operations are the bridge between local work and GitHub. After a local commit, pushing sends your commits to the remote repository. In VS Code, you can do this from the sync controls or Command Palette. If it's a new branch, VS Code may ask to publish it.

Jamie: What are the core terminal commands?

Alex: git push sends commits to GitHub. For a new branch the first time, git push dash u origin branchname sets the upstream so future pushes are simpler. git pull brings changes down and merges them. git fetch downloads remote updates without merging, which is often safer when you want to inspect first.

Jamie: When should I pull?

Alex: Before starting work if the remote may have changed. Before pushing if others may have updated the same branch. And any time your local view may be stale. Some tools auto-fetch in the background, but it's still worth understanding the difference: fetch updates your knowledge; pull updates your branch.

Jamie: What if push fails?

Alex: Usually one of a few reasons: authentication trouble, no upstream set for a new branch, or remote changes require you to pull first. The fix depends on the message, but a safe pattern is read the error, run git status, possibly run git fetch, confirm your branch, and then either authenticate, set upstream, or reconcile remote changes.

Alex: The chapter also covers syncing a fork with an upstream repository. That may not be central to your classroom repo, but it's essential in open source. The quickest route on GitHub.com is often the Sync fork button. There's also a more explicit Git workflow: add an upstream remote once, fetch from upstream, switch to your default branch, merge upstream changes, then push the updated branch back to your fork.

Jamie: Can you say that as commands?

Alex: Sure. First add upstream one time with something like git remote add upstream repository-URL. Then git fetch upstream. Then make sure you are on main or your default branch. Then merge, often with git merge upstream slash main. Then push to origin. VS Code can help through Command Palette too. And if conflicts occur during sync, you resolve them before pushing.

Alex: Sometimes you don't want to keep changes. The course addresses discarding carefully because it can be destructive. Discard a single file to restore it to the last committed state. Discard all unstaged changes if you really mean to abandon your current edits. If changes are staged, unstage first, then restore. There's also the nuclear option that discards everything, staged and unstaged, but you should preview first whenever possible.

Jamie: What would previewing look like?

Alex: Check git diff for unstaged changes and git diff dash dash cached for staged ones. Know what you're about to lose. The chapter also teaches a safer alternative: stash instead of discard.

Jamie: And file deletion has its own Git-aware form too.

Alex: Yes. git rm removes a file and stages the deletion in one step. git rm dash dash cached removes it from tracking but keeps the local file. You can remove directories too. Then commit the deletion and verify the file is no longer tracked.

Alex: For history and accountability, VS Code has Timeline view and Git blame. Timeline can be opened from the Explorer sidebar or the Command Palette. It shows file history, including commits that affected the file.

Jamie: And blame is the line-by-line history, right?

Alex: Right. It tells you who last changed each line and often links to a commit hash. For screen reader users, this can be much more useful than trying to infer history visually. In terminal form, you can view repo history with git log, a specific file's history with git log dash dash filename, history plus patch content with git log dash p, blame with git blame filename, concise blame with author and short hashes, a single commit with git show commitSHA, changes between commits with git diff sha1 sha2, commits by a specific author, or recent commits in the last seven days.

Jamie: So this is where I answer questions like who changed this, when, and why.

Alex: Exactly. Also PR history can often be viewed on the web when you want the review context, not just the raw commit history.

Alex: The material also covers merge conflicts in VS Code. When conflicting changes touch the same area, VS Code displays conflict regions and offers resolution controls. But for screen reader users, the best workflow is often to use structured navigation and the Accessible Diff tools rather than hunting manually for conflict markers.

Jamie: And if the merge is going badly?

Alex: You can abort it. That's an important safety valve. Stop, return to the pre-merge state, and approach again more deliberately.

Alex: Now stash management. A stash is a temporary shelf for uncommitted work. Use it when you need to switch branches, pull updates, or test something without committing half-finished work.

Jamie: What are the key stash commands?

Alex: Stash all uncommitted changes with a message using git stash push dash m quoted message. Include untracked files with an include-untracked style flag. List stashes with git stash list. Show what one stash contains with git stash show dash p stash at brace zero brace. Apply the most recent stash but keep it with git stash apply. Apply and remove it with git stash pop. Apply a specific stash by name. Drop a specific stash with git stash drop. And clear them all with git stash clear, carefully.

Jamie: So Apply keeps the stash, Pop applies and deletes it.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: There's even an emergency recovery section on git reflog. This matters when you think you lost a commit, reset too far, or deleted a branch and regret it.

Jamie: Reflog is like Git's memory of where HEAD has been?

Alex: That's a great way to think about it. Read the reflog in the terminal, find the last good commit or branch tip, preview it with a show command, then recover safely either by creating a new branch at that point or by resetting the current branch back there. If a branch was deleted, find the SHA from reflog and recreate the branch at that commit. And remember: reflog is local-only. It is not a shared team history.

Alex: The chapter briefly acknowledges alternative Git interfaces too: GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI, and the raw Git CLI. The point is not that one is morally superior. It's that you should understand the workflow deeply enough to transfer across tools.

Jamie: And I remember there were keyboard shortcuts and try-it activities too.

Alex: Yes. There's a quick reference for Git operations in VS Code, plus a practical exercise around clone, branch, and commit. The learning cards throughout the chapter reinforce the same few moves in different forms so they become habits.

Alex: Now let's move from local Git to code review and PR management in VS Code. This chapter brings together the GitHub Pull Requests extension, accessible diff reading, and the craft of giving useful feedback.

Jamie: And there was another workshop recommendation here too.

Alex: Yes. For the first part, the recommended practice was: install the extension, authenticate, check out a pull request, review it, and comment. The evidence was a confirmation comment describing whether you installed the extension, signed in, which PR you reviewed, whether your comment was inline or on GitHub.com, and what your comment was about.

Jamie: That's nice because it makes the invisible setup work visible.

Alex: Exactly. The expected outcomes were practical: install and authenticate the extension, check out a PR branch in VS Code or use a browser fallback, navigate diffs using F7 and the Accessible Diff Viewer, and post one specific constructive comment.

Alex: Installing the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension is straightforward. Open the Extensions sidebar with Control Shift X, search for GitHub Pull Requests, choose the GitHub-published extension, install it, and sign in through the browser OAuth flow.

Jamie: How do I verify it really worked?

Alex: Return to VS Code and look for the GitHub section in the Explorer or related PR views. It should show pull requests and issues from the repository context you're in.

Jamie: And if install or sign-in fails?

Alex: Reload the window. Make sure your browser is already signed into the correct GitHub account. Close and reopen VS Code if needed. These setup issues are common enough that the course treats them as normal troubleshooting, not user failure.

Alex: Once installed, you can view pull requests inside VS Code. You can open the PR panel from the Activity Bar or through Explorer sections. It can list open PRs, show specific PRs, open them in the browser, and filter to items waiting for your review.

Jamie: What does the PR list look like for a screen reader?

Alex: Think of it as a tree with repositories, PR items, and details you can expand. The course even gives examples of what a screen reader might announce, so you can orient to title, status, and repo association. Filtering can narrow by status or repository if the list is noisy.

Jamie: And viewing details gives me description, checks, metadata, all that?

Alex: Exactly. You can inspect the title, body, changed files, review status, and related metadata without leaving the editor.

Alex: Checking out a PR branch is the next key move. Why do it? Because some reviews need local testing, richer navigation, or terminal inspection. You can check out from the PR detail view, from the PR tree, or by Command Palette.

Jamie: And after that, I can return to my original branch normally.

Alex: Right. That return step matters. Reviews should not strand you on someone else's branch.

Alex: Now reviewing pull requests in VS Code. The changed files list tells you what files were touched. Open one and you'll get a diff editor. By default it may be split view, old on the left and new on the right. Some people prefer inline view. You can toggle between them.

Jamie: But for screen reader users, the star of the show is the Accessible Diff Viewer.

Alex: Yes. Press F7 to move through changes in a structured way, Shift F7 to move backward. Instead of fighting a visual side-by-side layout, you get hunk-by-hunk announcements: what was removed, what was added, and where. The material is very clear that this is far better for screen reader users than trying to navigate the raw visual diff manually.

Jamie: So review becomes about understanding change blocks, not wrestling the interface.

Alex: Exactly. And as you review, flag issues, ask questions, or note strengths. Good reviewing isn't only about finding mistakes.

Alex: You can also create a pull request directly from VS Code. There are a few methods: Command Palette, Source Control panel, or the GitHub panel. Before creating one, you need the basics in place: local commits on a branch, that branch pushed to GitHub, and a sensible base branch target.

Jamie: What do I fill out in the PR form?

Alex: A title is required. A description is optional but strongly recommended. You choose the base branch the changes should merge into, and the compare branch they're coming from. You may also set reviewers, labels, milestones, and whether it should be a draft PR. Some workflows prompt you interactively for title, body, and base branch. Others let you provide details inline. And if the in-editor form feels awkward, you can open it in the browser.

Jamie: So for this Day 2 challenge, that means I could open the PR from VS Code or from GitHub.com, as long as the result is the same.

Alex: Exactly. The workflow concept matters more than the exact button path.

Alex: The chapter also covers pull request description templates. These usually live in repository-defined locations and can pre-fill sections like description, related issue, type of change, testing, checklist items, and screenshots if applicable.

Jamie: That seems especially helpful for learners who don't know what to write.

Alex: Yes. Templates reduce guesswork. They also support accessibility by making expectations consistent. A screen reader workflow here is mostly about moving field by field and replacing placeholder text with specific content.

Alex: Then we get to commenting and formal review actions. You can add an inline comment on a specific line, or start a review and collect multiple comments before submitting them together.

Jamie: That "start review" option is useful when I don't want to interrupt the author with a bunch of isolated notifications.

Alex: Exactly. And when you submit your review, you usually choose one of three verdicts: approve, request changes, or comment-only. Approve means you think it's ready. Request changes means there's something blocking that should be fixed before merging. Comment-only means feedback without a merge verdict.

Jamie: The chapter also mentions terminal support for PR review, right?

Alex: Yes. You can view PR diffs in the terminal too, which some learners may find more linear and readable. And GitHub CLI can help with approving, requesting changes, or leaving a comment-only review depending on repository permissions and setup.

Alex: Merging pull requests is its own skill. First check prerequisites: reviews, passing checks, permissions, and whether the branch is up to date. In VS Code you may merge from the PR detail view or through commands. Merge types matter too.

Jamie: Can you summarize those merge types?

Alex: Default merge preserves the branch history as a merge commit. Squash and merge compresses the branch's commits into one before merging, which many teams prefer for a tidy main branch. Some repositories enable auto-merge so the PR merges automatically once required checks pass.

Jamie: And after merging?

Alex: Switch back to main and pull the latest changes. Then delete the feature branch if it's no longer needed, locally and sometimes remotely.

Alex: There's also a troubleshooting section worth keeping. If you see no pull requests found, check your filters and repository context. If VS Code says it could not create a pull request, confirm the branch is pushed, the repo is recognized, and authentication is valid. If authentication fails, re-sign in and verify your browser session.

Jamie: That kind of troubleshooting matters because PR work spans local Git, GitHub auth, and editor integration all at once.

Alex: Exactly. Problems are often at the boundaries between tools.

Alex: The chapter then broadens from tool use to accessible code review in general. It asks you to verify prerequisites first, then reminds you there are really two review environments: GitHub.com and VS Code. Both matter. Learning cards help you compare them rather than treating one as universally better.

Jamie: So if a learner asks, "Do I have to review in VS Code?" the answer is no, but they should understand both.

Alex: Yes. On GitHub.com, modern review interfaces support a file tree, structured navigation, inline comments, review threads, and final review submission. In VS Code, the Accessible Diff Viewer often gives a better reading experience for change hunks. Each environment has strengths.

Alex: A GitHub.com review usually goes like this: open the PR, read the description, move to the Files changed tab, use the file tree to orient yourself, move between file diffs, read the additions and deletions, place inline comments, read existing threads, and finally submit a review with approve, request changes, or comment-only.

Jamie: And there was also a re-request review step for authors after updates.

Alex: Right. After the author makes changes, they can re-request review so reviewers know to revisit the PR.

Alex: In VS Code review, the flow is similar but the tools differ. Open the PR for review, open changed files, use F7 for the Accessible Diff Viewer, navigate change by change, and place comments through the GitHub PR extension. The course emphasizes that structured diff reading is superior to trying to decode the raw split editor by ear.

Jamie: This is where accessibility and code review intersect directly.

Alex: Exactly. Accessibility is not an afterthought here. It shapes which workflows are realistic and sustainable.

Alex: Then we get into review quality. A useful review comment should be specific, actionable, and clear about whether it blocks merging. The course gives examples of blocking comments, non-blocking nits, and questions.

Jamie: Can you model the difference?

Alex: Sure. A blocking comment might say, "Blocking: this heading level skips from H1 to H3, which breaks document structure for screen reader navigation. Please change it to H2." A non-blocking nit might say, "Nit: consider tightening this sentence for clarity." A question might say, "Question: was this link text intentionally shortened? I'm wondering whether a more descriptive label would help users."

Jamie: So tone and labeling matter.

Alex: Very much. Prefixes like Blocking, Nit, and Question set expectations and reduce ambiguity. The chapter also asks, how many comments is too many? The answer is usually: enough to be helpful, not so many that you overwhelm the author with fragmented noise. Group comments when possible, and focus on impact.

Alex: There's a keyboard reference too, for both GitHub web review and VS Code accessible diff navigation. For learners who rely on keyboard access, that reference isn't optional background. It's part of fluency.

Jamie: And the common review scenarios were practical.

Alex: Yes. For example: I want to verify the PR only changes what it claims. Check the description, then compare it against the changed files and diff hunks. I want to find all changes to one section. Use file search, structured navigation, or history tools. I approved, but then the author pushed more changes. Revisit the diff and look for what's new. A reviewer left a comment I don't understand. Read the thread, inspect the local context, and ask for clarification rather than guessing.

Alex: The exercises make these skills concrete. One exercise walks through a full web review: navigate to the PR, read the description, go to Files changed, use focus-friendly reading strategies, identify issues like heading hierarchy or link text, place comments, and submit the review. Another exercise does the same in VS Code with the Accessible Diff Viewer. A third asks you to compare the two environments and reflect.

Jamie: I like that the course doesn't force one "correct" environment. It asks for evidence-based reflection.

Alex: Exactly. You might conclude the browser made threaded discussion easier, while VS Code made diff reading easier. That's useful professional knowledge.

Alex: There's also a section on using GitHub Copilot to understand code changes. The recommendation is cautious. Copilot can help summarize or explain a diff in VS Code or on GitHub.com, but it is not a substitute for your judgment.

Jamie: So it can support review, but not replace it.

Alex: Right. The course stresses limitations and best practices. Use it to ask clarifying questions, not to outsource the final decision. Skill first, assistant second.

Alex: That idea continues in the reviewer's craft section. Good reviewers look for correctness, clarity, accessibility, scope, and alignment with the PR's stated purpose. They understand the three main review actions. They write constructive feedback. They use a checklist. And they treat reviewing as a learning tool, not just a gatekeeping role.

Jamie: That feels especially important in an accessibility-centered course.

Alex: Yes. A review is not just "I found a problem." It's "I can explain the problem in a way that helps someone improve."

Alex: There's also a teaser about a fuller accessibility agents review ecosystem. The principle is explicit: skill first, agent second. Tools can assist, but you need to understand the workflow and standards yourself.

Jamie: That's a nice guardrail. Learn the craft before leaning on automation.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let's return now to the Day 2 pull request solution reference, because it ties everything together. The example PR title is a concise docs-style summary, something like improving formatting and fixing a broken link. The body has a changes section listing what was fixed or added, a short explanation of how the changes were made locally in a clone using VS Code, a Closes issue reference, and a pattern recognition section comparing the Day 2 PR to the Day 1 PR.

Jamie: So the solution isn't only saying what to type. It's modeling how to explain your workflow.

Alex: Exactly. And the comparison table is worth memorizing in spirit. Day 1 edits happened on GitHub.com or github.dev. Day 2 edits happened locally in VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the terminal. Day 1 often meant a single web-created commit. Day 2 could involve one or more commits created with git commit. Day 1 branches might be created on GitHub. Day 2 branches are often created locally with checkout or switch. Day 1 needed no push because the commit was already on GitHub. Day 2 required git push. And the PR could be created from the web prompt or a command like gh pr create.

Jamie: And the "what matters" section keeps the focus narrow.

Alex: Yes. If you created a PR from a locally pushed branch and recognized how that workflow differed from Day 1 while still ending the same way, you met the objective.

Jamie: What about the challenge's "peer simulation check"?

Alex: Good catch. The learner is asked to review the peer-simulation PR title and description and ask whether it clearly communicates what changed. If they have real buddy access, they can review a real peer's PR too. That's an administrative instruction, but it also teaches that PR quality begins before review comments. A readable title and description reduce reviewer burden.

Jamie: And the stuck points?

Alex: Also important. If you do not see your branch, make sure it was pushed, for example with git push dash u origin fix slash your-username. If GitHub says there is nothing to compare, your branch may not contain any new commits relative to main. If you don't know what to write in the description, reuse the earlier PR template pattern: what changed and why. And if you want to check your work, compare with the reference solution.

Jamie: Before we close, can we give learners a compact mental model for the whole lesson?

Alex: Absolutely. Here it is. Local work happens in your clone. You make edits, save files, stage intentionally, and commit with a clear message. Your branch is local until you push. Once pushed, GitHub can compare that branch against main and create a pull request. The pull request is where collaboration becomes visible: description, diffs, comments, review verdicts, and merge decisions. Accessibility matters at every layer, from using the Command Palette and Source Control panel accessibly, to reading diffs with F7, to writing review comments that clearly identify blocking issues versus suggestions.

Jamie: And the recurring pattern is clone, branch, edit, stage, commit, push, PR, review, merge.

Alex: Yes. And if you remember only one comparison from today, remember this: Day 1 and Day 2 are not rival workflows. They are two paths into the same pull request-centered collaboration model.

Alex: One final note on source quality. The materials point learners back to authoritative documentation, especially GitHub Docs, the GitHub changelog, VS Code source control documentation, and GitHub accessibility guidance for CLI and pull request reviews. That means your workshop notes teach the workflow, but official docs remain the source of truth when interfaces change.

Jamie: Which is a great habit in tech generally.

Alex: Exactly. Practice the pattern, use accessible tools, verify with authoritative sources, and keep your pull requests clear enough that another human can understand them without guessing.

Jamie: That's a strong place to end.

Alex: It is. Next time, keep noticing not just what button you pressed, but what collaboration step you completed. That's how Git starts to feel coherent.

40. Challenge 12: Review Like a Pro

Reviewing a classmate PR, leaving specific feedback, and owning review tone.

Practice focus: Day 2 local workflow

Download Challenge 12 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 12: Review Like a Pro

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're focusing on a skill that sits right at the center of healthy collaboration: reviewing pull requests well.

Jamie: And not just technically well, right? Also accessibly, respectfully, and in a way that actually helps the author.

Alex: Exactly. We're going to bring together three threads: how to work with pull requests in VS Code, how to review diffs accessibly on GitHub and in VS Code, and how to write feedback that is constructive instead of vague, harsh, or unhelpful.

Jamie: I like that combination, because learners often get split advice. One lesson shows the buttons. Another talks about etiquette. Another talks about GitHub Flow. But in real life, those all happen at once.

Alex: That's the goal here. And one practical note: if you're on Mac, whenever you hear Control in a shortcut, think Command instead. And if you hear Alt, think Option. Context menus that use Shift+F10 on Windows are often Control+Return on Mac.

Jamie: Before we touch the tools, can we ground this in the bigger open source workflow?

Alex: Yes. Most of what we're doing here lives inside GitHub Flow. That means: create a branch from main, make your changes in small logical commits, open a pull request, discuss and review, pass checks, and merge.

Jamie: So the pull request is not just a delivery envelope. It's the conversation space.

Alex: Perfectly said. The PR holds the description, the changed files, the review comments, the approvals, the requested changes, and often the connection to an issue. It's the unit of conversation.

Jamie: And that explains why one branch should usually do one thing.

Alex: Right. One thing per branch keeps review understandable. Small, focused pull requests are easier to read, easier to test, and easier to merge. Reviewers can tell whether the change actually does what the description claims.

Jamie: Which is one of the first review questions we should ask.

Alex: Yes: does this PR do what it says it does? That sounds simple, but it's a powerful habit.

Jamie: Okay, now let's get practical. Suppose I want to manage pull requests from VS Code instead of constantly jumping to the browser.

Alex: Then the first step is installing the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension. It brings pull request workflows directly into VS Code.

Jamie: What does it add once it's installed?

Alex: It adds a GitHub section in the Explorer or a Pull Requests view, depending on layout. From there you can list open PRs, open one in detail, check out its branch locally, inspect changed files, add comments, create pull requests, and in some cases merge.

Jamie: So it turns VS Code into a review workstation, not just an editor.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Walk us through installation in a screen-reader-friendly way.

Alex: Method one is through the Extensions sidebar. Open it with Control+Shift+X. The search field usually gets focus and a screen reader may announce something like Extensions, Marketplace. Search for GitHub Pull Requests. Move through results, choose the extension published by GitHub, then activate Install.

Jamie: And then comes sign-in.

Alex: Yes. After installation, VS Code may prompt you to sign in to GitHub. Activate that, complete the browser-based authorization, and return to VS Code. If a notification vanishes too quickly, open the Command Palette and run Notifications: Focus Notification Toast.

Jamie: Nice accessibility tip.

Alex: A second installation path is through the Command Palette: open it with Control+Shift+P, search for extension install commands, and find the GitHub Pull Requests extension that way.

Jamie: How do I verify I'm signed in successfully?

Alex: Open Explorer with Control+Shift+E and look for the GitHub section. If it appears and shows pull requests or issues for the repo you're in, that's a good sign. You can also check Accounts in VS Code if needed.

Jamie: And if authentication fails?

Alex: Make sure you're already signed into GitHub in the browser, close and reopen VS Code, and retry. OAuth hiccups are common enough that it's worth trying a fresh window.

Jamie: Once the extension is installed, how do I find pull requests?

Alex: You can open the GitHub Pull Requests panel from the Activity Bar or by using the Command Palette and running GitHub Pull Requests: Focus on Pull Requests View.

Jamie: And then I'll get a list of open PRs?

Alex: Yes, often grouped in a tree. You may hear repositories, then categories, then pull request items underneath. The exact wording depends on VS Code and the extension version, but the structure typically includes PR title, number, author, and status.

Jamie: That tree structure matters for orientation, especially with a screen reader.

Alex: It does. Knowing whether you're on the repository node, the open PRs list, or a specific PR keeps navigation much less confusing.

Jamie: Can I filter the list?

Alex: Yes. You can filter by status, such as all open or waiting for review, and sometimes by repository. Filtering is especially useful when a repo has many pull requests and you want the ones assigned to you or pending your review.

Jamie: And if I want to open a specific PR in the browser?

Alex: That option is usually available from the PR item's context menu or detail view. That's helpful when the web interface is better for the task you're doing, like certain comment workflows or checking thread context.

Jamie: What if the PR panel says no pull requests found?

Alex: First, confirm you're signed in. Second, switch to a broader filter like All Open. Third, make sure you're in the expected repository. That solves a surprising number of cases.

Jamie: Now let's say I want to review a PR more deeply. Why would I check it out locally instead of only reading it on GitHub.com?

Alex: Three reasons. One, you can test the branch locally. Two, you can use VS Code's editor and accessibility features, including the Accessible Diff Viewer. Three, sometimes it's easier to inspect surrounding files and project context in your editor than in a browser.

Jamie: How do I check out a PR branch?

Alex: Several ways. From the PR detail view there's often a Checkout action. From the PR tree, the context menu may offer Checkout. And from the Command Palette you can use GitHub Pull Requests commands to open or check out a pull request.

Jamie: If checkout works, VS Code switches me to that branch?

Alex: Yes. You're effectively moving onto the PR's branch so you can inspect it locally.

Jamie: And how do I get back to my own branch afterward?

Alex: Use normal Git branch switching in VS Code or the terminal. Go back to your original branch, often main or your own feature branch. That step matters, because people sometimes forget they're still on someone else's PR branch.

Jamie: What if checkout is blocked by permissions?

Alex: Then use the read-only fallback: review the PR on GitHub.com. You can still complete the review work without local checkout.

Jamie: Now we're at the heart of it: reading the diff.

Alex: Yes. In VS Code, once a PR is open, you can read the Files Changed list. In the PR detail view you'll find the changed files, open one, and VS Code launches the Diff Editor.

Jamie: Usually split view by default, right?

Alex: Correct. Old content on the left, new content on the right. Some people prefer inline mode, where changes are shown in one combined flow. You can toggle between split and inline view.

Jamie: For a screen reader user, the raw visual diff can be pretty painful.

Alex: That's why the Accessible Diff Viewer is so important. Press F7 to move to the next change and Shift+F7 to move to the previous change. Instead of forcing you to hunt visually, it reads changes in a structured way.

Jamie: What kind of structure does it announce?

Alex: Typically the file, the changed region, and whether lines were added or removed. That's much better than arrowing through a visually optimized editor that was not designed for spoken understanding first.

Jamie: So for screen reader users, the recommended workflow is not "open diff and wander around." It's "open diff and use F7 navigation."

Alex: Exactly. Open the changed file, enter the diff, and use the Accessible Diff Viewer to move hunk by hunk. This structured reading is far superior to manually navigating the visual diff line by line.

Jamie: Can we make that concrete? What might a change sound like?

Alex: Something like: removed line, heading level two, getting started; added line, heading level two, Getting Started. The exact announcement varies, but the key is that you hear both what changed and where.

Jamie: That makes review much more intentional.

Alex: Yes, and it supports common review goals: verify that the PR only changes what it claims, find all changes in a specific section, or check what changed after the author pushed more commits.

Jamie: And if I'm reviewing on GitHub.com instead of in VS Code, what's the accessible path there?

Alex: Go to the pull request and open the Files changed tab. For screen reader users, those top tabs are tab links inside the PR page: Conversation, Commits, Files changed.

Jamie: Then what?

Alex: Use the file tree to orient yourself. Listen for file names and expand or move among them as needed. Then navigate between file diffs and read the changes. You want to understand what each changed line is doing: was a line added, removed, or modified? Which heading, link, code line, or paragraph changed?

Jamie: And on the web, placing a comment usually starts by focusing a line.
