Alex: The YAML challenge also includes a peer simulation check.

Jamie: Meaning compare your Copilot-improved result with a peer-simulation pull request or a real buddy, if available, and ask whether the AI suggestion genuinely improved the document.

Alex: Exactly. That comparison step is pedagogically strong, because AI output can feel persuasive in isolation. Comparison restores perspective.

Alex: Let's cover "if you get stuck," because administrative and troubleshooting guidance matters.

Jamie: Yes, especially in workshops.

Alex: If Copilot controls are missing, update VS Code and reload the window. If OAuth sign-in fails, verify you're signed into GitHub in the browser, then retry. If the chat panel doesn't open, use the Command Palette and confirm AI features are enabled. If Copilot seems unresponsive, check the model selector or account state.

Jamie: And in the challenge YAML, if Copilot is not available at all, the note says you may need Copilot access, including possible student access via GitHub Education, or ask a facilitator for alternatives.

Alex: Right. If you don't know what to ask, start simple: "Improve the clarity of this paragraph" or "Suggest a better heading for this section." If everything seems good, raise the difficulty: ask for a rewrite for a screen reader user, then evaluate whether it actually helps.

Jamie: And if you finish but want to compare, there's a reference solution.

Alex: Yes.

Alex: There's also a "learning moment" embedded in this chapter, even if not always labeled aloud. The bigger lesson is that Copilot is not just autocomplete.

Jamie: It can explain, draft, propose, and customize, but the human still defines success.

Alex: Exactly. And the learning pattern used here is intentional: sign in, prompt, apply, reflect. It builds both technical confidence and editorial judgment.

Jamie: What about the learning cards mentioned throughout the chapter?

Alex: Those sections reinforce the main concepts in compact form: inline suggestions, chat, edits, agent mode, Copilot on GitHub dot com, effective prompting, Accessible View, and critical evaluation. They're not extra topics so much as reinforcement points.

Jamie: And the "about learning cards" note basically tells learners how to use those as quick-reference study aids.

Alex: Yes.

Alex: Before we wrap up, let's touch on a few advanced and newer features mentioned later in the chapter: Smart Actions, Browser Agent, Plan Agent and Copilot Spaces, and pricing updates.

Jamie: Do beginners need to master those now?

Alex: No. The takeaway is awareness. Copilot is expanding beyond simple suggestion and chat experiences. Some features are experimental. Some may depend on version, plan, region, or policy. And pricing is evolving, including usage-based billing for some AI-powered actions, while code completions and next edit suggestions may be treated differently on paid plans.

Jamie: So learners should avoid assuming every Copilot feature is universally available or billed the same way.

Alex: Exactly. Check current docs when it matters.

Jamie: Can we do a concise checklist for the challenge mindset?

Alex: Yes. Ask Copilot for a specific documentation improvement. Read the response in a way that works for you, ideally with Accessible View if needed. Compare the suggestion to the original. Check accuracy, clarity, tone, audience fit, and accessibility. Accept, modify, or reject. Then document what happened in your evidence comment.

Jamie: And if the suggestion feels polished but suspicious, slow down.

Alex: Always.

Jamie: And if it gives you a link, command, setting, policy statement, or accessibility claim?

Alex: Verify it.

Jamie: And if it rewrites something in a way that erases meaning or makes it harder for the intended audience?

Alex: Reject or revise it.

Jamie: And if it genuinely helps, but needs trimming?

Alex: Then collaborate. Keep the good part, improve the rest.

Alex: One last note on sources. This chapter and the solution both point learners to authoritative references: GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, GitHub Copilot docs, VS Code Copilot documentation, the custom instructions support matrix, guidance on custom agents and agent skills, auto model selection information, the Copilot changelog feed, and GitHub accessibility documentation.

Jamie: So even in a lesson about AI assistance, the real source of truth is still the official documentation.

Alex: Exactly. Copilot can help you navigate, draft, and explore. Official docs and your own review confirm what is correct.

Jamie: That feels like the perfect closing idea.

Alex: GitHub Copilot is most useful when you treat it as a collaborator with speed, not as a collaborator with judgment. The judgment is still yours.

Jamie: And that is what makes "AI as your copilot" better than "AI as your autopilot."

Alex: Well said.

45. Episode 16: Issue Templates

Creating YAML-based issue templates for bug reports, features, and custom forms.

Based on: Chapter 17: Issue Templates

Download Episode 16 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 16: Issue Templates

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re talking about issue templates, and this is one of those topics that sounds administrative until you realize it can completely change how accessible and useful contribution workflows feel.

Jamie: Yes. A blank issue box can feel like someone saying, "Tell me everything," with no structure, no prompts, and no clue what matters.

Alex: Exactly. Templates turn that blank box into guidance. They help contributors include the right details, help maintainers spend less time asking follow-up questions, and help projects get to action faster. And for accessibility work, structure matters even more, because missing environment details, assistive technology details, or reproduction steps can make a report much harder to use.

Alex: A quick orientation before we go deeper. This lesson connects to a few other parts of your learning path. You should already know how to work with GitHub issues, and it helps if you have a repository where you have write access, like a fork or personal repo. You’ll also want an editor that highlights YAML syntax, such as VS Code. Optional but helpful background includes GitHub Copilot, notifications, and basic terminal comfort, though you can do a lot in the browser if needed.

Jamie: And there’s a really practical hook here. Learners in this workshop already filled out a workshop registration template, right?

Alex: Right. That registration form is not just paperwork. It is the teaching example for this lesson. You’ve already experienced what a polished GitHub form template feels like from the user side. Now you’re going to analyze it, remix it, and potentially create your own.

Jamie: And there’s also a forward-looking note here. Later, in the Accessibility Agents material, there’s a template builder agent that can help automate some of this. But the idea is: learn the manual structure first, then use the automation.

Alex: Exactly. Learn the craft before you delegate it.

Alex: Here’s the overall learning path for this chapter. First, understand what templates are and why they matter. Second, learn how GitHub handles them. Third, navigate the template picker accessibly. Fourth, read a real template file. Fifth, create your own template step by step. Sixth, compare Markdown templates with YAML form templates. Seventh, build an accessibility bug report template. Eighth, look at pull request templates. Ninth, do hands-on exercises. And finally, see how the template builder agent fits in.

Jamie: And there’s also a challenge structure wrapped around all of that.

Alex: Yes. The recommended workshop challenge for this chapter is a design-and-implementation challenge focused on template remixing. The pattern is analyze, remix, create, and test. Evidence can be an issue comment or a pull request showing what you remixed or created. There isn’t an automation check here; quality is judged more by structure and thoughtfulness.

Jamie: So what are the challenge pieces?

Alex: There are four. Analyze the registration template. Remix it for a different use case. Optionally create a Markdown template from scratch. And optionally test your template in the GitHub chooser.

Jamie: Let’s start at the beginning. What is an issue template?

Alex: An issue template is a reusable structure that appears when someone creates a new issue in a repository. Instead of giving people only an empty text area, GitHub can offer prepared templates that guide them through what information to provide.

Jamie: So, in practice, that might mean prompts like describe the bug, list steps to reproduce, explain expected behavior, and so on.

Alex: Exactly. Or for a feature request, it might ask what problem you’re trying to solve, who benefits, and what alternatives you considered. The big idea is that templates create consistent, higher-quality reports.

Jamie: Why does that especially matter for accessibility projects?

Alex: Because accessibility issues often depend on context. A report may need the component affected, the screen reader or magnifier involved, the browser, the operating system, the keyboard steps used, what was expected, what actually happened, and maybe even a relevant WCAG success criterion if known. Without prompts, contributors may leave out critical information, not because they’re careless, but because they don’t know what maintainers need.

Jamie: So the template is doing both instructional and organizational work.

Alex: Yes. It teaches contributors what counts as a useful report while also collecting that information in a predictable format.

Jamie: How do templates work on GitHub at a practical level?

Alex: GitHub supports issue templates and pull request templates. For issues, repositories typically store them inside a special folder, usually .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. Templates can be either Markdown files or YAML form files. GitHub reads those files and uses them to populate the issue creation experience.

Jamie: And there’s also a configuration file sometimes, right?

Alex: Yes. A config file, commonly called config.yml in that templates area, can control behavior like whether blank issues are allowed and whether contact links appear. That means maintainers can shape the overall issue intake process, not just individual templates.

Jamie: So one repo might offer several choices like bug report, feature request, accessibility issue, workshop registration, and maybe a support link.

Alex: Exactly. The chooser becomes a little intake desk.

Jamie: Can you give the high-level difference between Markdown templates and YAML forms right now, before we get deeper?

Alex: Sure. Markdown templates are simpler text-based issue starters. They include frontmatter and then a Markdown body, often with headings and HTML comments. YAML form templates are more structured. They render actual form fields like text inputs, dropdowns, textareas, and checkboxes. YAML forms generally provide a more guided and accessible experience because each field has a clear label, description, and validation rules.

Jamie: Let’s talk about the template picker itself, because learners will encounter that first on GitHub.com.

Alex: When a repository has templates configured, selecting New Issue typically opens a chooser. You’ll hear or encounter template names, short descriptions, and usually a button like Get started for each template. For screen reader users, the important strategy is to move methodically: identify the template name, listen for its description, then activate the control to start with that template.

Jamie: And if there are multiple templates, those descriptions matter a lot.

Alex: They do. A good description helps someone decide, "Is this for a bug, a feature idea, an accessibility problem, or something else?" Clear naming and description are accessibility features in their own right.

Jamie: What about bypassing the chooser?

Alex: Sometimes GitHub allows direct links that preselect templates or a blank issue option if maintainers have enabled that. But as a learner, the important thing is to understand both experiences: the chooser helps route people properly, and bypassing it may exist for advanced or direct workflows. Still, maintainers often want the chooser used because it improves consistency.

Jamie: Now let’s ground this in the real example: the Accessibility Agents issue templates and especially the workshop registration template.

Alex: Yes. This is a great exercise because it’s a real production file, not a toy example. The first challenge is to open that template file on GitHub.com and analyze it.

Jamie: What exactly should learners look for first?

Alex: Start with the frontmatter at the top. In a YAML issue form, key items include name, description, title, and labels. Name is what appears in the template chooser. Description is the helper text shown there. Title can prefill the issue title or at least provide a prefix. Labels let GitHub automatically tag issues created from that template.

Jamie: So right away, the template is doing organizational work before the user even fills anything out.

Alex: That’s right. Then look at the body section. That’s where the form fields live. In the workshop registration template, you’ll find field types like markdown for instructions, input for single-line entries, dropdown for fixed options, and textarea for longer responses.

Jamie: And each field has metadata.

Alex: Yes. This is crucial. Each field can include an id, which is the internal identifier and not typically what the user sees; a label, which is the visible field name; a description, which gives helpful guidance; a placeholder, which offers example text inside the field; and validations such as required true, which tells GitHub that the field must be completed.

Jamie: That pairing of visible guidance plus required-optional clarity is really powerful.

Alex: It is. And the challenge specifically asks learners to search the file for the word accessible, noticing that the template description explicitly considers screen reader usability. That models professional thinking: not just collecting data, but collecting it in a way people can successfully provide.

Jamie: And then there’s the comparison with a blank issue.

Alex: Exactly. A blank issue is one giant invitation to guess. A template replaces guessing with structure.

Jamie: Let’s turn that into the remix challenge. Suppose a learner understands the registration template. What do they do next?

Alex: They adapt it for a new context while preserving the underlying structure. This is a fantastic exercise because it teaches that good template design is partly architecture and partly content design.

Jamie: What stays the same?

Alex: The YAML skeleton stays the same: name, description, title, labels, body. The field structure also stays recognizable: type, id, attributes, validations.

Jamie: And what changes?

Alex: The context-specific parts. Change the template name and description to match the new purpose. Change the title prefix. Change labels. Rewrite each field’s label, description, placeholder, and dropdown options so they fit the new workflow. And reconsider which fields should be required.

Jamie: So if I remix a registration template into a bug report template, I might replace attendee details with component name, browser, screen reader, steps to reproduce, expected behavior, and actual behavior.

Alex: Perfect example. And after editing, validate the YAML syntax. The lesson recommends pasting the contents into a YAML linter like yamllint.com. That catches indentation mistakes and formatting errors, which are common in YAML.

Jamie: YAML is very unforgiving about spacing.

Alex: It is. Small indentation errors can break a whole template.

Jamie: There’s also an optional challenge to create a Markdown template. Why include that if YAML forms are more structured?

Alex: Because understanding both formats gives you flexibility. A Markdown template is simpler to create and easier to support in repositories where you want a lightweight starter rather than a full form. It also helps learners understand the evolution from freeform guidance to structured input.

Jamie: What does a Markdown template look like?

Alex: At the top, it has frontmatter between triple-dashed lines. Typical keys are name, about, title, and labels. One detail matters a lot here: Markdown templates use about, while YAML forms use description. That difference is easy to forget.

Jamie: Good catch.

Alex: Below the frontmatter comes the Markdown body. Usually that means headings like Problem, Context, and Solution Ideas, with HTML comments underneath to guide the writer without leaving visible instructional clutter in the rendered issue.

Jamie: So something like a heading for Problem and then an HTML comment saying, describe the problem you encountered.

Alex: Exactly. It’s guidance embedded in plain text structure.

Jamie: Can we spend a moment on those example Markdown sections, because the source calls them out very specifically?

Alex: Absolutely. A classic bug-style Markdown template might include sections for Describe the Bug, Steps to Reproduce, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Environment, and Additional Context.

Jamie: That sequence matters, doesn’t it?

Alex: It does. Describe the Bug gives the summary. Steps to Reproduce makes the issue testable. Expected Behavior clarifies what should have happened. Actual Behavior records what did happen. Environment provides context like browser, operating system, app version, or assistive technology. Additional Context gives space for screenshots, logs, workarounds, or anything else.

Jamie: And for accessibility-specific reporting, the source adds more focused sections.

Alex: Right. You might include Component Affected, Your Assistive Technology Setup, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Steps to Reproduce, WCAG Success Criterion if known, Additional Context, and Before Submitting.

Jamie: That “Before Submitting” part is interesting.

Alex: It reminds contributors to do a final quality check. For example: have you reproduced the issue, provided enough detail, checked for duplicates, and included your environment? It reduces incomplete submissions.

Jamie: When would you use this Markdown version instead of YAML?

Alex: Use Markdown when you need a quick, portable template, when a project prefers simple text, or when the issue type benefits from freer narrative. Use YAML when you want stronger structure, clearer labels, required fields, and a more guided experience.

Jamie: And there are accessibility considerations for Markdown templates too.

Alex: Yes. Keep headings clear and logical. Use plain language. Don’t overload the page with dense instructions. Make placeholders and comments specific but brief. And remember that Markdown templates still rely more on the contributor to interpret and follow the structure, so they are usually less constrained than YAML forms.

Jamie: What are the practical workflows for creating Markdown templates?

Alex: There are two main ones described. The manual browser workflow and the VS Code workflow. In the browser, you can create the file directly in GitHub’s web editor inside .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. In VS Code, you create the same file locally, edit it with syntax support, then commit and push.

Jamie: And file naming conventions matter.

Alex: They do. Give the template a clear descriptive filename, like bug-report.md or accessibility-bug-report.yml. Good names help maintainers and collaborators understand what each file is for.

Jamie: Now let’s go deeper into YAML form templates, because that seems to be the star of this chapter.

Alex: I agree. YAML forms are often better for accessibility because they create explicit form controls. Users encounter labeled fields rather than a giant blank editing area. The template author can provide descriptions, placeholders, dropdown choices, and required-field validation. That reduces ambiguity and makes the reporting process more predictable.

Jamie: So the accessibility benefit is not just that the content is better, but that the interaction model is clearer.

Alex: Exactly. A clear form with good labels is often easier to navigate and understand than a freeform page of instructions.

Jamie: What is the structure of a YAML form template?

Alex: At the top level, you usually see keys like name, description, title, labels, and body. The body is a list of items, and each item has a type. Depending on the type, it may also have an id, attributes, and validations.

Jamie: Can we walk through the field types one by one?

Alex: Yes. First, markdown. This is instructional text only. It’s used for context, reminders, or directions. It does not collect user input.

Jamie: So that’s good for a short introduction or a note about checking for duplicate issues first.

Alex: Exactly. Second, input. That’s a single-line text field. Use it for concise information like component names, email addresses, version numbers, or short summaries.

Jamie: Third is textarea.

Alex: Right. Textarea is for multi-line responses. Use it when contributors need room to explain steps to reproduce, describe actual behavior, or add contextual details.

Jamie: Fourth is dropdown.

Alex: A dropdown gives a select menu of predefined options. It’s great when you want consistent values, such as browser names, severity levels, proficiency levels, or screen reader choices.

Jamie: And fifth is checkboxes.

Alex: Checkboxes allow one or more confirmation items or option selections. They’re useful for acknowledgments like “I searched existing issues” or “I can reproduce this in the latest version,” and sometimes for multiple-choice-style selections where multiple values may apply.

Jamie: How should learners choose the right field type?

Alex: Ask what kind of answer you need. If you want instructions only, use markdown. If the response should be short and open-ended, use input. If it needs detail, use textarea. If the answer should come from a controlled list, use dropdown. If the user needs to confirm or select multiple items, use checkboxes.

Jamie: Now let’s build the accessibility bug report template conceptually.

Alex: This is one of the most important parts of the chapter. A strong accessibility bug report template should gather the information maintainers actually need without overwhelming contributors.

Jamie: What fields make that work?

Alex: A good set might include Component Affected, so maintainers know where the problem lives. Your Assistive Technology Setup, so they know the screen reader, magnifier, browser, operating system, or other tools involved. Expected Behavior and Actual Behavior, so the gap is clear. Steps to Reproduce, so someone else can verify the issue. WCAG Success Criterion if known, which is optional but valuable for teams working against standards. Additional Context for anything else. And possibly a Before Submitting checklist.

Jamie: What makes that template accessible, beyond just collecting accessibility-related information?

Alex: Several things. Clear labels. Brief descriptions that explain why information is needed. Sensible required fields so users aren’t blocked by nonessential details. Predictable field order. Controlled choices where helpful. And language that respects varying levels of expertise. For example, “WCAG Success Criterion if known” is much better than implying the reporter must be a standards expert.

Jamie: That phrase “if known” is doing a lot of inclusive work.

Alex: It is. It invites useful information without turning knowledge gaps into barriers.

Jamie: The chapter also mentions a second template: a feature request form.

Alex: Yes. That reinforces the idea that templates should fit the workflow. A feature request form might ask what problem the feature solves, who it helps, why current behavior is insufficient, possible approaches, and any accessibility considerations. The exact fields differ because the task differs.

Jamie: And that leads into designing templates for your own projects.

Alex: Right. Don’t copy blindly. Look at issue patterns in your project. What information do maintainers repeatedly ask for? What information do contributors often forget? Which details help triage or reproduce? Your template should reflect those realities.

Jamie: Before we leave templates, we also need to cover pull request templates.

Alex: Absolutely. Pull request templates guide contributors when proposing changes, not just when reporting issues. A PR template might include sections for Description, Type of Change, How to Test, Accessibility Considerations, and Related Issues.

Jamie: Let’s unpack those.

Alex: Description explains what the PR does. Type of Change categorizes the work, such as bug fix, documentation update, new feature, or refactor. How to Test gives reviewers concrete steps to verify the change. Accessibility Considerations asks the author to think explicitly about keyboard support, screen reader impact, semantic structure, contrast, motion, or anything else relevant. Related Issues links the PR back to the issues it resolves or supports.

Jamie: That accessibility section in a PR template is really important, because it nudges people to think about impact before merging.

Alex: Yes. Good templates don’t just collect text. They shape contributor behavior.

Jamie: Let’s move into the hands-on activities. First, using an existing template.

Alex: In the first exercise, learners go to the Accessibility Agents repository’s issues area. Then they open the New Issue flow and inspect the template chooser with a screen reader or other assistive technology.

Jamie: What should they pay attention to there?

Alex: Template names, descriptions, and whether the controls are understandable and easy to navigate. Then they select a template, move through the form fields, and notice how labels, descriptions, and required indicators are presented.

Jamie: Then fill in the form.

Alex: Yes, with realistic sample content. After that, preview the issue before submitting. That’s a valuable step because it lets you catch missing details, formatting problems, or unclear wording. Then submit the issue and reflect: Did the template help? Were any fields confusing? Did the structure make the task easier?

Jamie: That reflection step matters because we’re not just consuming templates. We’re learning to evaluate them.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: The next exercise is adding the accessibility bug report template to your own fork. Walk us through that workflow.

Alex: First, clone your fork to your machine. Second, open it in VS Code. Third, navigate to the templates folder, usually .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. Fourth, create a new template file with a descriptive name.

Jamie: Then paste in the YAML template.

Alex: Right. Copy in the accessibility template YAML. Then verify the syntax carefully. YAML errors often come from indentation, misplaced dashes, or inconsistent spacing. After that, create a branch, commit your changes, and push.

Jamie: And then test it on GitHub web.

Alex: Yes. Open the repository on GitHub.com, activate New Issue, and make sure your template appears in the chooser. Launch it, inspect the fields, and confirm the rendered form matches your expectations.

Jamie: Then comes a particularly important step for this audience: test with your screen reader.

Alex: Absolutely. Don’t stop at “it loads.” Check whether labels are understandable, whether descriptions are discoverable, whether required fields are clear, and whether the order makes sense in real navigation. If you can merge your branch afterward, that’s optional depending on your workflow. The key checkpoint is that the template is present, valid, and usable.

Jamie: And then there’s the upstream contribution exercise.

Alex: Yes. Once your template is ready, create a pull request. Write a clear PR title and description. The source suggests organizing the PR body around questions like: What does this PR do? Why is this useful? How was this tested? And what related issue connects to it?

Jamie: That mirrors the idea of a PR template, even if you’re writing manually.

Alex: Exactly. Then review your PR before submitting, submit it, respond to feedback from maintainers, and celebrate your contribution.

Jamie: That last part is not fluff.

Alex: No, it’s not. Shipping contribution infrastructure is real open source work.

Jamie: There’s one more design exercise: creating a template for your own project from scratch.

Alex: This is where the chapter shifts from imitation to authorship. First, choose a project. Second, identify recurring issue patterns. What kinds of reports show up repeatedly? Third, decide which fields are required. Ask yourself what maintainers truly need every time.

Jamie: And then optional fields.

Alex: Yes. Optional fields are for useful but nonessential information. Then write strong placeholders and help text. Good help text reduces confusion without overwhelming the contributor.

Jamie: Then test locally.

Alex: Right. Review the file, lint the YAML if needed, and inspect it carefully. Optionally deploy it to GitHub and ask a friend to try it, especially with assistive technology if possible. Finally, reflect on the design. Did your fields collect what matters? Did they avoid jargon? Did they reduce unnecessary effort?

Jamie: So template design is really a user experience task.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: Let’s circle back to the challenge evidence and completion process, because that’s easy to skip over.

Alex: Good point. After completing the challenge work, learners are supposed to open their assigned challenge issue and post a completion comment. The comment should indicate whether they analyzed the registration template, what context they remixed it for, whether the YAML validates, which repository contains the template, and whether they also created a Markdown version or tested in the chooser. Then they close the challenge issue.

Jamie: That’s useful evidence because it documents both the work and the quality checks.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What outcomes should learners expect by the end?

Alex: They should understand template structure, including YAML frontmatter, field types, and validation. They should be able to analyze and remix professional templates. They should be able to create both YAML form and Markdown templates. They should understand why templates improve contribution quality. And they should appreciate how thoughtful templates reduce maintainer effort while helping contributors succeed.

Jamie: And if someone gets stuck?

Alex: A few likely sticking points are worth naming. If you can’t find the registration template, double-check the repository path under .github slash ISSUE_TEMPLATE. If your YAML fails, inspect indentation first. If the template doesn’t appear in GitHub, confirm the filename and folder location, then push the branch and refresh the web view. If the form feels confusing with a screen reader, simplify labels and descriptions and retest.

Jamie: And more broadly, compare your work to a known-good template rather than debugging in the abstract.

Alex: Yes. Working from a professional example is one of the strongest learning patterns in this chapter.

Jamie: Speaking of learning patterns, what’s the deeper learning moment here?

Alex: The learning moment is that contribution quality often depends less on contributor talent and more on workflow design. If you give people an accessible, well-structured form, you raise the floor for everyone. Templates are not bureaucracy. They are support.

Jamie: And the learning pattern used here really is analyze, remix, create, test.

Alex: Exactly. First read a real example closely. Then adapt it. Then create your own. Then test it in the actual environment. That sequence builds both confidence and judgment.

Jamie: Before we end, let’s talk about the Day 2 amplifier: the template builder agent.

Alex: Yes. Later in the course, there’s an agent called at-template-builder that helps generate templates in VS Code. Conceptually, it works by turning your description of a workflow into a draft issue or pull request template.

Jamie: But this chapter makes sure you understand what good output should look like before using that tool.

Alex: Right. Otherwise you’d get automation without judgment. In VS Code, the agent can help you draft, revise, and iterate faster. But it matters because it saves time only when you can review the result critically.

Jamie: So the tool is an amplifier, not a substitute for understanding.

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: Any final notes on sources or where learners should look when they want the official word?

Alex: Yes. The authoritative references are GitHub’s documentation about issue and pull request templates and GitHub’s documentation on configuring issue templates for a repository. If behavior changes over time, those docs are the place to verify details. The chapter also points learners to related appendices like Markdown reference material and GitHub Actions context.

Jamie: So the practical takeaway is: use the chapter to learn the workflow, and use the official docs to confirm implementation details.

Alex: Exactly. And if you remember just one thing from today, let it be this: a good template is an accessibility tool, a communication tool, and a maintenance tool all at once.

Jamie: Which is a pretty strong payoff for something that starts as “just a form.”

Alex: It really is. See you next time.

46. Challenge 14: Template Remix

YAML issue forms, accessible labels, required fields, and useful maintainer intake.

Practice focus: Day 2 capstone

Download Challenge 14 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Challenge 14: Template Remix

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

Jamie: And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

Alex: Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

Jamie: So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

Alex: Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

Jamie: Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

Alex: A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

Jamie: And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

Alex: Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

Jamie: I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

Alex: Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

Jamie: And time-wise?

Alex: Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

Alex: The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

Jamie: That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

Alex: That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

Jamie: Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

Alex: Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository's `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` folder and that it contains a valid `name` field. But pedagogically, the real goal is broader: understanding how structured templates guide contributions.

Jamie: Let's define the basic concept clearly. What is an issue template?

Alex: An issue template is a reusable structure GitHub offers when someone clicks New Issue. It can be a Markdown template or a YAML form-based template. Both help contributors provide the right information. The difference is in how structured and interactive they are.

Jamie: So a Markdown template is more like a prewritten document with headings and instructions.

Alex: Yes. It usually opens a text area containing sections like Problem, Context, Steps to Reproduce, or Additional Context. A YAML form template is more interactive. It creates actual fields like text inputs, dropdowns, textareas, and checkboxes.

Jamie: And for accessibility, the YAML form often wins.

Alex: Often, yes. A good YAML form can make navigation more predictable, clearly indicate required fields, constrain answers when appropriate, and reduce cognitive load. It gives contributors helpful labels and descriptions instead of asking them to infer the structure.

Jamie: How do templates work on GitHub at the repository level?

Alex: GitHub looks in a special folder: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`. Files there can appear in the issue template chooser. If they're YAML form templates, they typically use the `.yml` extension. Markdown templates use `.md` and include frontmatter.

Jamie: And when someone clicks New Issue, GitHub may show a template picker.

Alex: Right. In that chooser, the template's name appears as the visible option, and the description appears below it as helper text. Once the user selects it, GitHub generates the issue form or prefilled issue body.

Jamie: And there's also repository-level configuration, like `config.yml`, though this lesson seems more focused on individual template files.

Alex: Yes. The chapter mentions configuration and the chooser behavior, including that some setups can change how templates are presented. It also notes there are ways users may bypass the chooser in some situations, so maintainers should think of templates as guidance, not a magical enforcement system.

Jamie: That's useful. Templates improve the default path, even if they don't control every path.

Alex: Now let's ground this in the challenge. The challenge issue itself is actually built from a YAML template. That's a teaching move.

Jamie: So the assignment is also an example of the thing you're learning.

Alex: Exactly. In the challenge template, the top-level keys are doing important work. There's a `name`, which is shown in the chooser. There's a `description`, which tells the user what the template is for. There's a `title`, which pre-fills the issue title using a pattern. In the challenge it includes the username token so the issue title can identify the learner. There are `labels`, which are automatically applied to issues created from that template. And there's a `body`, which defines the form fields themselves.

Jamie: That mirrors the solution reference too.

Alex: It does. The solution file gives a complete example: an accessibility report template. The comments in that example are especially instructive because they annotate each part.

Jamie: Let's unpack those top-level keys one by one, because these are must-know.

Alex: First, `name`. This is what someone sees in the template chooser after clicking New Issue. It should be short, clear, and specific enough that a contributor knows when to use it.

Jamie: Like "Accessibility Report."

Alex: Exactly. Second, `description`. This appears below the name in the chooser and gives one sentence of context, like "Report an accessibility barrier in workshop materials."

Jamie: Third, `labels`.

Alex: Those are automatically applied to the issue. In the example, labels like `accessibility` and `bug` categorize the issue immediately. That helps triage.

Jamie: Fourth, `title`.

Alex: That pre-fills the issue title with a pattern, such as `[A11y]: `. The contributor then finishes the title rather than starting from scratch.

Jamie: And fifth, the big one: `body`.

Alex: Yes. The body is the definition of the form fields. This is where you choose input types and specify labels, descriptions, placeholders, and validation rules.

Jamie: Now I want to zoom in on the anatomy of a field, because that's where YAML can feel intimidating.

Alex: A field usually starts with a `type`. Then it often includes an `id`, which is an internal identifier not typically shown to the user. Inside `attributes`, you define what the user experiences: the visible label, the description, placeholder text, and sometimes options. Then under `validations`, you can declare whether the field is required.

Jamie: So `id` is for the template structure, while `label` is for the human filling it out.

Alex: Exactly. And that distinction is important. Good labels should be plain language and user-centered. Good IDs should be stable, concise, and meaningful to the template author.

Jamie: Let's cover the field types. The source is very explicit here.

Alex: There are five primary field types highlighted. First, `markdown`. This is display-only text. It's not an input field. You use it for instructions, context, reminders, or notices. In the example template, a markdown block thanks the reporter and explains why their feedback matters. Second, `input`. That's a single-line text field. Use it for short answers like file names, URLs, versions, or a specific location where a problem occurred. Third, `textarea`. That's a multi-line text area for longer responses, such as describing the barrier, outlining steps to reproduce, or adding context. Fourth, `dropdown`. This presents predefined options, like assistive technology type or severity. It reduces ambiguity and makes responses easier to sort and compare. Fifth, `checkboxes`. These allow multiple selections and are good for acknowledgments, checklists, or multi-select categories.

Jamie: And the key design question is not just what fields exist, but when to use each one.

Alex: Exactly. If the answer should be brief and unique, use `input`. If it requires explanation, use `textarea`. If the answer should come from a controlled set, use `dropdown`. If users may need to select several items, use `checkboxes`. And if you want to communicate without collecting data, use `markdown`.

Jamie: Can we walk through the accessibility report example from the solution?

Alex: Absolutely. It begins with a markdown block that sets a respectful tone and explains why reporting accessibility barriers matters. That kind of context can make reporting feel safer and more purposeful. Then there's an input field asking where the barrier occurred. The label is clear. The description explains what kinds of answers are acceptable, like a file name, URL, or description of the location. A placeholder gives an example. Next comes a required textarea: describe the barrier. The prompt combines what happened with what the user expected to happen. That encourages useful, comparative reporting. Then there's a dropdown for assistive technology, with options like NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, screen magnifier, voice control, switch access, keyboard only, Other, or Not applicable.

Jamie: That option list is a subtle accessibility win, because it acknowledges different toolchains and avoids assuming everyone uses the same setup.

Alex: Exactly. And then another dropdown captures severity: blocked, difficult but workable, or minor. That helps maintainers prioritize.

Jamie: So the structure is not just neat. It captures information maintainers actually need.

Alex: Right. That's why templates matter.

Jamie: The chapter also compares Markdown templates and YAML templates. Let's make that concrete.

Alex: A Markdown template is simpler and more manual. It uses YAML frontmatter at the top, then plain Markdown sections below. One important detail: in Markdown templates, the frontmatter uses `about`, not `description`.

Jamie: That's a small syntax difference that could trip people up.

Alex: Definitely. A Markdown template might start with frontmatter like name, about, title, and labels, wrapped in triple-dash lines. Then the body might include sections such as Problem, Context, and Solution Ideas, often with HTML comments giving instructions.

Jamie: So the user sees headings and writes under them, but there are no typed controls like dropdown menus.

Alex: Correct. Markdown templates are useful when you want flexibility, when the structure is lightweight, or when a form would be overkill. YAML forms are better when you want consistency, stronger guidance, built-in required fields, and a more structured reporting experience.

Jamie: The chapter also calls out when to choose each.

Alex: Yes. Use Markdown when a looser format is acceptable or when you want maximum compatibility and simplicity. Use YAML forms when you want better structure, clearer required input, and a more accessible guided workflow for frequent issue patterns.

Jamie: There's also a very practical list of common Markdown bug-report sections in the source. Can we include those?

Alex: We should. Typical bug-report sections include Describe the Bug, Steps to Reproduce, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Environment, and Additional Context.

Jamie: And for accessibility-focused reporting, there are even more specific fields.

Alex: Yes: Component Affected, Your Assistive Technology Setup, Expected Behavior, Actual Behavior, Steps to Reproduce, WCAG Success Criterion if known, Additional Context, and Before Submitting.

Jamie: That "if known" phrasing matters.

Alex: It does. It invites expert detail without making novices feel excluded. Good accessibility templates welcome useful specificity without requiring people to speak in standards language.

Jamie: And the chapter also emphasizes accessibility considerations for Markdown templates.

Alex: Right. Because Markdown templates are more manual, instructions must be especially clear. Use meaningful headings, concise prompts, and plain language. Avoid burying essential instructions in large blocks of text. Think about screen reader navigation and cognitive load.

Jamie: What about actually creating files? The chapter includes both browser and VS Code workflows.

Alex: Yes. For Markdown templates, you can create them manually in the repository browser or in VS Code. File naming conventions matter because the file must live in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, and the extension determines the kind of template GitHub recognizes. YAML form templates should use `.yml`. Markdown templates use `.md`.

Jamie: And indentation matters a lot in YAML.

Alex: It does. YAML is sensitive to indentation. Use spaces, typically two spaces per level, and do not use tabs. Also make sure colons are followed by a space where appropriate. These tiny syntax details are often the difference between a working template and a broken one.

Jamie: Let's go through the guided challenge sequence, because it's a big part of the chapter.

Alex: Challenge 14.1 is analysis. You open the existing workshop registration template on GitHub and study it. The goal is to identify the frontmatter fields: `name`, `description`, `title`, and `labels`. Then you inspect the body and notice the field types used there: markdown, input, dropdown, and textarea.

Jamie: And you also inspect field metadata.

Alex: Yes. For each field, identify the `id`, the visible `label`, the explanatory `description`, any `placeholder`, and whether the field is required. One specific prompt in the chapter is to search the registration template for the word "accessible" and notice that the template explicitly mentions screen reader compatibility. That models professional accessibility thinking.

Jamie: And the final reflection is to compare this with a blank issue.

Alex: Exactly. A blank issue gives you one giant text box. A template gives structure, guidance, and clarity about what matters.

Alex: Challenge 14.2 is the remix. You take the structure of the registration template and adapt it for a new purpose.

Jamie: The chapter gives some example contexts: bug report, event attendance, product research, accessibility audit request.

Alex: Right. The instruction is to keep the YAML skeleton. That means keep the overall structure: `name`, `description`, `title`, `labels`, and `body`. Keep the internal field pattern too: `type`, `id`, `attributes`, and `validations`.

Jamie: But change the content.

Alex: Exactly. Change the context-specific parts: labels, visible field names, descriptions, placeholders, and dropdown options. And rethink which fields should be required.

Jamie: Then validate the YAML.

Alex: Yes. The chapter explicitly suggests using a YAML validator like yamllint.com. Fix any errors, then commit and push the template file.

Jamie: And the "done" condition is a committed remixed template that validates.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: Challenge 14.3 is optional and switches formats.

Alex: Yes. You create a Markdown-based issue template from scratch. The instructions say to create a new file in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` with an `.md` extension, add YAML frontmatter, and then add a few sections with HTML comment guidance.

Jamie: And again, the frontmatter detail matters: Markdown templates use `about` instead of `description`.

Alex: Exactly. That distinction is easy to miss.

Alex: Challenge 14.4 is also optional: test your template in the template chooser. Go to your repository on GitHub, activate New Issue, make sure your template appears, then open it and file a test issue.

Jamie: That test is important because syntax can be valid but the overall behavior can still be wrong if the file is misplaced or named incorrectly.

Alex: Exactly. Testing verifies the real user experience.

Jamie: The challenge issue file itself includes a minimum YAML structure. Can we restate that as a checklist?

Alex: Yes. At minimum, your challenge template should include: - a `name` field, - a `description` field, - a `title` field using a prefix pattern, - and at least one `textarea` or `input` field in the `body`.

Jamie: And the topic is flexible.

Alex: Very flexible. The challenge explicitly suggests possibilities such as an accessibility feedback form, workshop improvement suggestion, bug report for a specific tool, or a structured feature request. The solution reference reinforces that almost any topic works: bug report, feature request, session evaluation, help request, and so on.

Jamie: So the point is not to copy one exact template. It's to show you understand the pattern.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let's make the "what matters" part explicit, because learners often worry they need the exact same fields as the example.

Alex: The solution says the learning objective is understanding structured issue templates as a way to guide contributors. If your YAML file has a `name`, a `description`, and at least one `body` field, you've met the essential learning target for the challenge.

Jamie: That's reassuring.

Alex: Yes. Precision matters, but creativity is allowed. Alternate valid templates are expected.

Jamie: The chapter also spends time on navigating the template picker. What should audio learners understand there?

Alex: When you activate New Issue in a repository with templates, GitHub may present a list of template choices. Screen reader users should expect to navigate through each template option, hear the template name and usually its descriptive text, and then activate the associated action such as Get started.

Jamie: And the chapter specifically includes a screen reader-oriented hands-on exercise.

Alex: It does. In Exercise A, learners are told to go to the Accessibility Agents repository issues section, open the template chooser, inspect it with their screen reader, select a template, navigate the form fields, fill in the form, preview before submitting, submit the issue, and then reflect on the experience.

Jamie: That reflection step matters for accessibility learning.

Alex: Very much. You're not just clicking through. You're evaluating whether the structure supports efficient, understandable input.

Jamie: Can we cover the broader hands-on activities too, even if the challenge focus is issue templates?

Alex: Yes, because the source explicitly includes them and we shouldn't omit that administrative and workflow context. Exercise B has learners add the accessibility bug report template to their own fork. The steps are: clone your fork, open it in VS Code, navigate to the templates folder, create a new template file, paste in the accessibility template YAML, verify syntax, create a branch and commit, test the template on GitHub web, test again with your screen reader, and optionally merge your branch.

Jamie: That's a complete local-to-web workflow.

Alex: Exactly. Then Exercise C is about submitting the work upstream as a pull request. You verify the template is ready, create the PR, write a strong title and description, review before submitting, submit it, respond to feedback, and celebrate the contribution.

Jamie: And the PR description itself is structured too.

Alex: Yes. The source gives prompts like: What does this PR do? Why is this useful? How was this tested? Related issue. That mirrors the general principle we've been teaching: structure helps reviewers too, not just issue reporters.

Jamie: That connects nicely to the chapter's section on pull request templates.

Alex: It does. The chapter includes pull request templates as a parallel concept. PR templates can ask for Description, Type of Change, How to Test, Accessibility Considerations, and Related Issues.

Jamie: So templates are part of a larger idea: guiding contribution quality across the workflow.

Alex: Exactly. Issue templates improve incoming reports. PR templates improve proposed changes. Both reduce ambiguity and make collaboration easier.

Jamie: There's also a section on building an accessibility bug report template. We've touched that, but what makes that template accessible according to the chapter?

Alex: Several things. It asks for concrete, relevant information without overwhelming the user. It uses clear labels and descriptions. It includes assistive technology setup, which is crucial context in accessibility debugging. It gives structured severity choices to support prioritization. And it balances required and optional fields so users can provide enough detail without facing an exhausting form.

Jamie: And there's a second example too, a feature request form.

Alex: Yes. That signals that the same design principles apply beyond bug reporting. Once you understand the field types and the top-level structure, you can design templates for many recurring contribution patterns in your own projects.

Jamie: Let's talk about designing your own project template, because that's one of the final exercises.

Alex: The chapter breaks that into practical parts: choose your project, identify recurring issue patterns, decide which fields are required, decide which are optional, write placeholders and help text, test locally, optionally deploy to GitHub and test with another person, then reflect on the design.

Jamie: That reflection step is interesting again.

Alex: Yes. Template design is user experience design. After testing, ask: Did contributors know what to enter? Were the field labels understandable? Did the required fields collect enough information without creating friction? Was the flow comfortable with a screen reader?

Jamie: We should also cover common problems and troubleshooting, because the challenge template includes a specific "If you get stuck" table.

Alex: Good point. Common problem one: YAML syntax error. The recommended fix is to check indentation carefully, use two spaces rather than tabs, and make sure colons are followed by spaces. Problem two: the template does not appear in the issue chooser. Check that the file is in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, has a `.yml` extension if it's a YAML form template, and includes a `name` field. Problem three: you don't know what topic to choose. The advice is simple: any structured form works. You can build a feedback form, recipe, book review, help request, accessibility feedback form, or bug report. Problem four: you finished but want to verify your approach. Use the reference solution.

Jamie: So the troubleshooting advice is both technical and motivational.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What are the expected overall outcomes for this chapter?

Alex: Learners should understand template structure, including YAML frontmatter concepts, field types, and validation. They should be able to analyze and remix professional templates. They should be able to create both YAML form and Markdown templates. They should understand why templates improve contribution quality. And they should see how templates reduce maintainer effort by guiding contributors toward complete, actionable reports.

Jamie: That's a strong payoff for what initially looks like just a formatting lesson.

Alex: It is. This is contribution design.

Jamie: Let's return to the specific challenge evidence, because learners often need that exact administrative step.

Alex: To complete Challenge 14, you open your assigned challenge issue and post a completion comment. The chapter gives a sample format including whether you analyzed the registration template, what context you remixed it for, whether the YAML validates, where the template was committed, whether you created the optional Markdown template, and whether you tested it in the chooser. Then you close the challenge issue when done.

Jamie: So there are two outputs: the actual template file in your repository, and the evidence comment in the assigned challenge issue.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Before we wrap, can you give a compact mental model learners can carry into VS Code right now?

Alex: Sure. Think of a YAML issue template as having two layers. Layer one is chooser metadata: - `name` is what the contributor sees. - `description` explains when to use it. - `title` gives a starting pattern. - `labels` classify the issue automatically. Layer two is the form itself: - `body` contains fields. - Each field has a `type`. - Many fields also have an `id`, visible `label`, supportive `description`, optional `placeholder`, and `validations` such as `required: true`. Then ask yourself three design questions: - What information do maintainers need? - What structure will make that information easier to provide? - How can I make the form clear and accessible for someone using assistive technology?

Jamie: That's excellent.

Alex: One final note on sources. The chapter points learners to official GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog as the authoritative references for current template behavior. That matters because GitHub's interface and features can evolve.

Jamie: So if a label changes in the UI or a docs example shifts, trust the official docs for the latest details.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: All right. Your next move is simple: inspect a real template, remix one for your own purpose, validate the YAML, test it in GitHub, and submit your evidence.

Alex: And as you do, remember what you're really learning: not just how to write YAML, but how to design a contribution path that is clear, respectful, and accessible.

Jamie: See you next time.

47. Episode 17: Accessibility Agents

55 agents across 3 teams and 5 platforms, 54+ slash commands, custom agents, and agentic accessibility workflows.

Based on: Chapter 19: Accessibility Agents

Download Episode 17 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 17: Accessibility Agents

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re exploring accessibility agents: what they are, where they run, how to decide whether you’re actually ready to use one, and how to contribute to an open ecosystem of agents without treating automation like magic.

Jamie: And I’m glad we’re starting there, because a lot of learners hear “AI agents” and think, great, now the tool will just do accessibility for me.

Alex: Right, and this chapter pushes back on that. The core idea is simple: skill first, agent second. An agent multiplies a skill you already have. It does not create that skill for you.

Alex: A quick orientation note before we go deeper. There’s an audio companion for this material, related appendices for agents and Copilot reference material, and a set of authoritative sources from GitHub Docs and VS Code Docs. If you want the official product behavior, those docs are the source of truth.

Jamie: So this lesson is teaching practice and workflow, but not replacing the official documentation.

Alex: Exactly. Also, there’s an important product note: newer VS Code versions include an Agents window in stable as a preview feature. That does not replace custom accessibility agents. It gives you a dedicated place to run and organize agent sessions, review changed files, and manage work across projects.

Jamie: So learners should think, custom agents are still the substance, and the Agents window is one interface for working with them.

Alex: Perfectly said.

Alex: Let’s frame the landscape. The repository highlighted in this chapter is a growing open source ecosystem of AI-powered agents organized into three teams and deployable across five platforms.

Jamie: I noticed one number early on says fifty-five agents, and another later says eighty. How should learners hear that?

Alex: As a living project. The exact count can change as the ecosystem grows. The important ideas are the structure and the breadth: three teams, multiple platforms, and a wide range of workflows. You are not expected to use every agent. You’re expected to find the agents that match skills you already built manually.

Jamie: And the platforms matter too, right?

Alex: Yes. These agents aren’t trapped in one editor. The chapter positions them across GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, and Codex CLI. So the lesson isn’t “use this one exact interface.” It’s “understand the pattern, then choose the platform that fits your workflow and access needs.”

Jamie: Before anyone starts, what’s the checklist?

Alex: There’s a real prerequisites checklist, and it matters. First, learners should already have workshop setup completed: Git, VS Code, and a GitHub account. Second, GitHub Copilot should already be enabled and working in VS Code. Third, Copilot access is required, but the free tier is enough for this workshop. Fourth, your repository should include a .github slash agents folder, or you should be prepared to create custom agents.

Jamie: And then there’s the deeper prerequisite: not just software, but skill.

Alex: Yes. The chapter explicitly maps agent categories to manual experience. For GitHub workflow agents like daily briefings, issue tracking, pull request review, and analytics, you should already know how to navigate repositories, file issues, review pull requests, and explore repository insights.

Jamie: So if I’ve never reviewed a pull request by hand, I should not ask an agent to review one and assume I understand the result.

Alex: Correct. For accessibility monitoring agents, you should already know how to file an accessibility bug, apply accessibility labels, and inspect things like heading hierarchy. For template creation agents, you should already have designed and tested templates manually. For web accessibility auditing agents, you should already understand WCAG success criteria and have tested pages with assistive technology.

Jamie: And the document-specific agents have their own manual prerequisites too.

Alex: They do. If you want help with Word, Excel, PDF, or EPUB accessibility, you should already know something about document structure and manual accessibility review. If you want remediation agents, you should understand tagging, alternative text, bookmarks, or the relevant toolchain. Python or wxPython agents assume Python knowledge and GUI accessibility basics. Developer tool agents assume CI or testing experience.

Jamie: So the self-check question is: could I do this manually right now?

Alex: Exactly. If the answer is no, learn the manual skill first.

Jamie: This chapter also includes a workshop recommendation and a challenge set, right?

Alex: Yes. This is an exploration and validation chapter. The challenge sequence asks learners to discover agents, validate one against their own manual understanding, inspect an agent’s instructions, and optionally improve an existing agent or propose a new one.

Jamie: Let’s walk that in plain language.

Alex: Challenge 15.1 is agent discovery mapping. The goal is to identify three to five agents that match skills you already have from earlier workshop work. The recommended starting set, especially if the ecosystem feels large, is daily briefing, issue tracker, and pull request review.

Jamie: And the workflow is practical.

Alex: Very practical. Fork the accessibility-agents repository on GitHub. Open the repository. Review the list of agents. For each one, ask yourself whether you’ve performed that task manually. Then post a comment on your assigned challenge issue that maps each chosen agent to the manual skill that makes you ready.

Jamie: So not just “I want to use this,” but “I am ready because I already did this work myself.”

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Then comes validation.

Alex: Challenge 15.2 asks you to clone your fork into VS Code or open it in github.dev, open Copilot Chat, choose one agent from your discovery list, run a simple prompt, and then evaluate the output against your manual expectations.

Jamie: That evaluation step feels important.

Alex: It’s essential. The automation check for this chapter is explicitly none. Agent output always requires human judgment. You’re expected to read the output carefully and say whether it looks accurate, helpful, incomplete, or questionable.

Jamie: And Challenge 15.3 goes inside the agent itself.

Alex: Yes. Agent instructions deep dive. You read one agent source file and assess what it can and cannot do. That helps learners move from “AI said a thing” to “I understand how this tool is framed, constrained, and prompted.”

Jamie: Then there are optional hackathon-style extensions.

Alex: Right. Improve an existing agent by finding a gap in its instructions and opening a pull request, or propose a new agent for a workflow the ecosystem doesn’t yet cover.

Jamie: And when learners finish?

Alex: They submit evidence. The expected evidence is usually an issue comment showing agent output and your evaluation. The expected outcomes are that you can match agents to your current skills, test them critically, inspect their instructions, and begin thinking like a contributor rather than just a user.

Jamie: What if someone gets stuck?

Alex: The chapter explicitly normalizes that. If you get stuck, narrow the scope. Start with the simplest agents. Use one short prompt. Compare results to something you already know how to do manually. The learning moment is not “the agent was perfect.” The learning moment is “I can judge what the agent did.”

Jamie: And there’s even a teaching pattern behind this.

Alex: Yes: explore, validate, read internals, optionally contribute. That’s the learning pattern of the chapter.

Jamie: There’s also a capstone note that sounds unusually direct.

Alex: It does, and we should keep it. One of the most important tasks in the chapter is to share workshop feedback. Not busywork—feedback that helps improve the curriculum, tooling, and accessibility of the learning experience.

Jamie: So submitting workshop feedback is framed as a genuine contribution.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: I saw a table of contents in the source, but for listeners, maybe we should turn that into a road map.

Then multi-platform deployment beyond VS Code. Then detailed hands-on reference for specific agents. Then slash commands and prompts. Then contributing your own agents or improving existing ones. Then the bigger orchestration picture. Then GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI, and Copilot CLI. And finally, accessibility shortcuts, troubleshooting, and the official source trail.

Alex: Let’s come back to the principle, because it is the foundation for everything else. Every agent has a manual prerequisite. If you have not done the corresponding skill by hand, the agent is not ready for you yet, and you are not ready for it.

Jamie: Now setup. If someone wants to begin using these agents, what does that look like?

Jamie: Now the ecosystem section. We mentioned three teams earlier. Let’s unpack them.

Jamie: Team two is GitHub Workflow.

For example, hook-based enforcement in tools like Claude Code can apply checks or automation rules at the right moment in a development workflow.

Jamie: So an agent isn’t always a chat personality. Sometimes it’s part of a workflow system.
