Alex: Correct. That structure also improves readability for users consuming the notes with screen readers, magnification, or quick visual scanning.

Jamie: We should also cover draft and pre-release states, because those badges change how people interpret a release.

Alex: Absolutely. A draft release is not publicly finalized. It lets maintainers prepare the version, edit notes, and attach assets before publishing. A pre-release is published, but it is explicitly marked as an early or not-yet-stable version, often for alpha, beta, or release candidate testing.

Jamie: So draft means private preparation stage, pre-release means publicly visible but not the stable recommendation.

Alex: That’s the distinction. And as a learner or contributor, if you see pre-release, interpret it as test-oriented or not fully final. If you’re guiding others, don’t confuse the Latest stable badge with the existence of a newer pre-release.

Alex: Now let’s pivot to repository insights.

Jamie: This is the part that can feel mysterious. What exactly is the Insights tab?

Alex: It’s a set of repository analytics and summary views that help you understand activity: recent work, contribution patterns, traffic, dependency relationships, community documentation, and more.

Jamie: Who can see it?

Alex: That can vary by repository visibility, permissions, and specific insight type. In many public repositories, at least some insights are visible broadly. In private repositories, access is often more restricted to people with repository permissions.

Jamie: And what does Insights not show?

Alex: It does not magically reveal everything about a project’s quality or team dynamics. Metrics don’t fully capture collaboration quality, accessibility quality, maintainer responsiveness, or whether contributors feel welcome. They’re clues, not complete truth.

Jamie: That’s such an important warning. Numbers can be useful without becoming the whole story.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How do I get to Insights?

Alex: Usually from the repository tab bar. Activate the Insights tab if it’s present. Once there, you’ll often encounter a secondary navigation for specific views such as Pulse, Contributors, Traffic, Dependency Graph, Network, Forks, and Community Standards.

Jamie: What’s the screen reader strategy?

Alex: First locate the main repository tab bar and activate Insights. Then look for the sub-navigation within the Insights area. That secondary nav is important because Insights is not one page but a family of views.

Jamie: So don’t assume landing on Insights means you’ve seen all of it.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: Let’s start with Pulse.

Alex: Pulse is a recent activity summary. It gives a quick overview of what’s happened in the repository over a recent window of time, often including merged pull requests, open issues, closed issues, and general momentum.

Jamie: Why does that matter to a contributor?

Alex: Because it answers practical questions. Is this project actively merging work? Are issues being closed? Does the repository look maintained? If the Pulse view shows recent activity, that can be encouraging. If activity is sparse, that may shape your expectations about review timing.

Jamie: And navigation?

Alex: For screen reader users, after opening Pulse, use headings and lists to move through activity summaries. Read the recent counts and then drill into linked issues or PRs if needed. The aim is to understand the rhythm, not necessarily inspect every item in one pass.

Jamie: So Pulse is like the repository heartbeat.

Alex: That’s a nice way to put it.

Jamie: Next up: Contributors.

Alex: The Contributors view shows who has been contributing to the project, often with counts or graphical summaries over time.

Jamie: Why does this matter to a new contributor?

Alex: Several reasons. It helps you see whether one person does nearly everything or whether the project has a broader contributor base. It can suggest whether the project is healthy, collaborative, or bottlenecked. It may also help you identify maintainers or regular contributors whose names you’ll recognize in issues and pull requests.

Jamie: The source emphasized table accessibility here.

Alex: Yes. When contributor data is presented in table form, that’s good news for accessibility because tables can often be navigated cell by cell or row by row by screen readers more reliably than purely visual charts. If there is a chart, it may still require interpretation support, but tabular data is usually more accessible.

Jamie: And what’s the screen reader advice?

Alex: Use table navigation when available. If the view includes headings plus contributor names and commit counts, move systematically. Listen for patterns rather than trying to memorize every row. You’re trying to understand who builds the project and at what scale.

Jamie: Traffic sounds more external-facing.

Alex: It is. Traffic shows who visits the repository and how people discover or use it, often including metrics such as views, visitors, clones, and referrers, depending on what GitHub exposes.

Jamie: Why should a contributor care?

Alex: Because it helps contextualize impact. A project with substantial traffic may have many users relying on it. A project with modest traffic may still be important, but the audience shape is different. Traffic can also help maintainers understand documentation needs, onboarding priorities, and visibility.

Jamie: Any caution here?

Alex: Yes. Traffic is interesting, but it is not a direct measure of project quality or community health. Also, some traffic views are more limited in who can access them.

Jamie: What about commits and code frequency?

Alex: Those views show development activity over time. Commit histories can suggest cadence. Code frequency visualizations may show additions and deletions over time. Together, they can hint at whether development is steady, bursty, or quiet.

Jamie: But charts can be hard for screen reader users.

Alex: Absolutely. This is where general strategy matters. If a chart is not accessible in a rich textual way, look for summaries, axes labels, adjacent tables, or alternate views that communicate the same information. Don’t assume the graph alone is the only source of truth.

Jamie: So for inaccessible graphs, we fall back to nearby text, commit lists, release cadence, Pulse, and contributor summaries.

Alex: Exactly. Build an evidence picture from multiple accessible clues.

Jamie: Dependency graph.

Alex: The dependency graph shows relationships between the repository and the packages it depends on, and often packages that depend on it, depending on the project setup and GitHub features enabled.

Jamie: Why does this matter?

Alex: It can reveal security and maintenance implications. Dependencies are part of a project’s supply chain. Seeing them helps maintainers and contributors understand what external components matter and where updates may be needed.

Jamie: And there was a note about enabling or viewing.

Alex: Yes. In some repositories, dependency graph features may need to be enabled or may only appear when GitHub can detect supported dependency manifests. So if you don’t see it, that doesn’t always mean the project has no dependencies.

Jamie: Network and forks feel related but not identical.

Alex: Right. Network helps visualize the relationship among branches and forks over time. Forks indicate how many copies of the repository people have created under their own accounts or organizations.

Jamie: Why should a learner care?

Alex: Fork counts can suggest interest and reuse, though again not perfect quality. Network views can help you understand branching and divergence patterns, especially in active open source ecosystems. But visually dense network graphs may be challenging for assistive tech users, so use them carefully and rely on supplementary information where possible.

Jamie: Community Standards sounds less numeric and more policy-oriented.

Alex: Exactly. Community Standards surfaces whether the repository has key project health files and practices, like a README, contributing guidelines, code of conduct, issue templates, pull request templates, and often a license.

Jamie: That seems incredibly useful for a new contributor.

Alex: It is. It tells you whether the project has documented how people should contribute and interact. Strong community standards usually reduce ambiguity and make contribution more approachable.

Jamie: Screen reader advice?

Alex: Treat it like a checklist view. Move item by item. Listen for which standards are present and which are missing. If contributing guidelines are available, open them before making your first contribution.

Jamie: We should gather the screen reader navigation reference into one practical bundle.

Alex: Good idea. For releases pages, start on the repository home page and locate the Releases area, often in the right sidebar. Use heading navigation to find it. Open either the latest release or the full releases list. On the releases list page, jump between release headings, navigate links for assets and compare views, and read notes linearly. On an individual release page, use the same strategy: heading first, then metadata like badge, date, and tag, then note sections, then assets and source links.

Jamie: And comparing two releases?

Alex: The changelog or compare view between tags is where you inspect every merged pull request between versions. Navigate by headings and lists, and expect a denser page because it’s more of a full comparison than a polished summary.

Jamie: Now the Insights side.

Alex: Within Insights, first identify the sub-navigation. That’s essential. Then for charts and graphs in general, look for textual summaries, table forms, labels, and alternate linked views. For Pulse, use headings and linked items to assess recent activity quickly. For contributor and traffic views, prefer tables or summaries when available over trying to infer everything from a graph alone.

Jamie: That “general strategy” point feels like one of the most useful accessibility lessons in the whole appendix.

Alex: I agree. Accessible navigation isn’t just about keystrokes. It’s also about deciding where the most reliable information is.

Jamie: And finally, there were accessibility agents for personal and team metrics too.

Alex: Yes: slash my-stats and slash team-dashboard. The idea is to turn repository activity into summaries that are easier to consume than raw charts.

Jamie: What would slash my-stats be for?

Alex: A personal contribution summary. Think of it as surfacing information like your pull requests, reviews, commits, or other activity in a more direct format that you can read without mining multiple GitHub views.

Jamie: And slash team-dashboard?

Alex: That’s a higher-level team summary. It can help maintainers or coordinators understand overall project activity, patterns, and participation without relying exclusively on graphical insight pages.

Jamie: So just like slash draft-release helps turn history into readable release notes, these commands help turn activity data into readable status summaries.

Alex: Exactly. They are accessibility-minded shortcuts to understanding.

Jamie: Let me see if I can tie this together. A release is an official published snapshot built on a tag. A tag is fixed, a branch moves. Version numbers often follow semantic versioning, so they communicate the scale of change. Release notes tell the story of what changed, and the full changelog comparison shows every merged PR between versions.

Alex: Yes.

Jamie: Maintainers can create releases in the GitHub UI, save them as drafts, mark them as pre-releases, and use tools like slash draft-release to generate structured notes. Then on the repository side, Insights gives activity views like Pulse, Contributors, Traffic, commit and code frequency trends, dependency information, network and forks, and community standards.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: And the accessibility throughline is: use headings, sub-navigation, tables, and text summaries intentionally; don’t rely on charts alone; and use agent-generated summaries when they reduce friction.

Alex: That’s the heart of it. Releases tell you where the project has been published. Insights help you understand how the project lives between releases.

Jamie: And as a contributor, both matter. One tells me when my work becomes part of a version users can point to. The other helps me understand the project’s rhythm and health.

Alex: Beautifully put.

Alex: If you want one practical next step after listening, open a repository you know, find its releases page, read the latest notes, activate the full changelog, then visit Insights and inspect Pulse and Community Standards. That one short workflow will make today’s concepts concrete.

Jamie: And if you’re using a screen reader or magnification, do it slowly enough to notice the navigation landmarks we discussed. That’s part of the skill.

Alex: Exactly. We’ll leave it there.

58. Episode 28: Branch Protection and Rulesets

Required reviews, status checks, rulesets, and diagnosing blocked merges.

Based on: Appendix O: Branch Protection and Rulesets

Download Episode 28 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 28: Branch Protection and Rulesets

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re unpacking one of the most common GitHub mysteries: you open a pull request, everything looks fine, and yet the merge button is disabled.

Jamie: That moment where GitHub seems to be saying, no, but not in a very friendly tone.

Alex: Exactly. And the good news is that it usually is telling you why. This lesson is for contributors trying to understand why a PR is blocked, and for workshop facilitators or maintainers who need to configure these rules in practice repositories.

Jamie: And since this series is built for blind and low-vision learners too, we’re also going to cover how those merge requirements show up with a screen reader, what to listen for, and where the important controls live.

Alex: At a high level, branch protection is a quality gate for important branches, usually `main`. A branch protection rule is a set of requirements that must be satisfied before a pull request can be merged.

Jamie: So this is not Git being difficult for fun. It’s there to protect the project.

Alex: Right. Branch protection can require code review before changes enter the default branch. It can require automated tests to pass. It can prevent direct pushes to `main` so work has to come through pull requests. It can require your branch to be current with the latest `main`. And in some repositories, it can require commits to be signed.

Jamie: So when a learner says, my PR won’t merge, one likely answer is: the repository is enforcing standards, not rejecting you personally.

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: Can we make this concrete for navigation? If someone is on a pull request page, where do these rules actually surface?

Alex: Usually in the merge box near the bottom of the PR conversation view. For screen reader users, one practical strategy is to press End to jump to the bottom, then navigate by heading to find the merge area. The status lines just above the merge button explain what’s missing. You might hear things like, one review required, some checks haven’t completed yet, or this branch is out of date.

Jamie: And if the merge button is disabled or announced as unavailable, don’t stop there. The explanation is usually right above it.

Alex: Exactly. For low-vision users, the merge area also uses color and small status icons: green for ready, yellow for pending, red for blocked. Zooming in can help a lot, especially because buttons like Update branch or links like Show all checks can be easy to miss at high magnification if you’re scanning quickly.

Jamie: And for sighted users, same idea: bottom of the PR conversation tab, look above the merge button, read the checklist, expand checks if needed.

Alex: Let’s talk through the most common branch protection rules.

Jamie: First up: reviews.

Alex: Required reviews are probably the most common rule. A maintainer can say that a pull request needs one or more approving reviews before it can be merged.

Jamie: So if the repository says require one approving review, the merge box might literally tell me one review required.

Alex: Yes. And there are a couple of details learners often miss. If a reviewer requests changes, that does not count as approval. Also, if you push new commits after approval, some repositories dismiss stale reviews automatically. That means previous approvals are withdrawn and you need a fresh approval after the latest changes.

Jamie: That prevents a bad pattern where someone gets approval and then sneaks in extra changes after the review.

Alex: Exactly. And if you do push a fix, it’s good practice to re-request review from the original reviewer.

Jamie: What about automated checks?

Alex: That’s the next big category: required status checks. These are automated workflows, often GitHub Actions, but they can also come from third-party services. The repository can require those checks to succeed before merging is allowed.

Jamie: What are some example check names a learner might encounter?

Alex: Things like `ci / build`, which compiles the code. `ci / test`, which runs tests. `lint`, which checks formatting or code style. `accessibility-check`, for automated accessibility scanning. `CodeQL`, for security analysis. Or something like `netlify/deploy-preview`, where a preview site has to build successfully.

Jamie: And required means not optional. If a required check is failing or still running, merge is blocked.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: Another one people see a lot is being out of date with the base branch.

Alex: Yes. Some repositories require your branch to be up to date before merge. If new commits landed on `main` after you created your branch, the merge box may say this branch is out of date with the base branch.

Jamie: And then there may be an Update branch button.

Alex: Right. Clicking Update branch tells GitHub to merge current `main` into your branch. Some teams may prefer a rebase workflow instead, but that depends on project policy and your comfort level.

Jamie: Then we have signed commits.

Alex: If a repository requires signed commits, every commit in the PR must show as verified. That usually means GPG or SSH signing is configured correctly. If commits are unverified, the PR cannot be merged until you create signed commits instead.

Jamie: And linear history?

Alex: That rule means the repository wants a clean, non-branchy history. No merge commits into the protected branch. So maintainers may only allow squash merges or rebase merges.

Jamie: So if I see a message that the repository requires a linear history, it usually means the eventual merge strategy must avoid a merge commit.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And lock branch sounds even stricter.

Alex: It is. A locked branch is effectively read-only. No merges go in. Maintainers might do this for archived repositories or temporary release freezes.

Jamie: Now, there’s a newer concept here too: rulesets.

Alex: Yes. Repository rulesets are the modern evolution of branch protection. Classic branch protection still exists and is still very common, but rulesets are more flexible.

Jamie: What do they add?

Alex: They can apply rules at the organization level across many repositories, not just one repo and one branch. They support bypass lists, so specific users, roles, or automation accounts can be exempted. They can target branch patterns like `release/*` or `v*`. They provide violation insights, which help admins audit when rules were bypassed. And they support enforcement modes such as active, evaluate, and disabled.

Jamie: Evaluate is interesting. That means log violations without actually blocking people yet.

Alex: Exactly. It’s useful when an organization wants to test a policy before enforcing it.

Jamie: Can you compare classic branch protection and rulesets in plain language?

Alex: Classic branch protection is narrower: typically one branch in one repository, no real bypass list, active enforcement only. Rulesets are broader and more modern: multiple branches, patterns, organization-wide use, configurable bypass, and multiple enforcement modes.

Jamie: But for most learners contributing to public repositories, they’ll still often encounter classic branch protection.

Alex: Yes. Many repos still use it. And importantly, contributors usually do not need admin access to understand what’s happening. The merge box messages usually tell you enough.

Jamie: If someone does have access and wants to inspect rulesets, where would they look?

Alex: Typically in a repository’s Insights tab under Rulesets, if visible to them, or in Settings, then Rules, then Rulesets, which is generally admin-only.

Alex: Let’s move into diagnosis mode. Suppose your PR cannot be merged. How do you read the message and decide what to do?

Jamie: Let’s do the common messages one by one.

Alex: If the merge area says something like one review required or two reviews required, the meaning is straightforward: you do not yet have the required number of approvals.

Jamie: So what should the contributor do?

Alex: Request review from the right people, often a maintainer or code owner. Check whether someone requested changes, because that can block approval. Wait for the reviewer to submit their review. If you respond by pushing new commits, re-request review afterward.

Jamie: Next: some checks haven’t completed yet, or some checks were not successful.

Alex: That means at least one required status check is pending or failing. The next step is to expand the checks list, often through a Show all checks control, identify the failing check, and open its Details link to read the full log.

Jamie: And then fix the actual problem, not the symptom.

Alex: Exactly. Maybe a test failed. Maybe linting found formatting issues. Maybe the build broke. Maybe an accessibility scan found a violation. Push a new commit with the fix, and the checks usually re-run automatically.

Jamie: How long should someone expect to wait?

Alex: Often one to five minutes, though it varies. If checks pass on `main` but fail on your PR, that strongly suggests the issue is specific to your changes. And if a check has been stuck in progress for a long time, say over thirty minutes, the workflow runner or service may have a problem. At that point, contact the maintainer.

Jamie: Next message: this branch is out of date with the base branch.

Alex: That means new commits reached `main` and your branch no longer includes them. The easiest fix may be the Update branch button in the merge box. Or, if you’re comfortable and the project permits it, you can update locally with fetch and rebase, then force-push carefully.

Jamie: And the signed commits message?

Alex: If the message says commits must have verified signatures, your commits are not signed in the required way. The fix is not usually a button on the PR page. You need to configure commit signing properly, then re-create or amend the commits so GitHub recognizes them as verified.

Jamie: And then there’s the more generic message: merging is blocked.

Alex: That one often means there are multiple unmet rules or a broader ruleset restriction. Read every status line in the merge box. Don’t assume there is only one problem. There may be a missing review and a failing check, for example.

Jamie: So the general method is: read the exact text, identify whether the blocker is people, automation, branch freshness, commit verification, or repository policy, then take the next action that matches that category.

Alex: Perfect summary.

Jamie: Let’s spend real time on accessibility and the merge box, because this is where a lot of frustration happens.

Alex: Absolutely. If you’re using a screen reader, start by getting to the lower part of the pull request page. Pressing End is often the fastest route. Then navigate by headings or landmarks until you reach the merge area.

Jamie: What should the learner listen for once they’re there?

Alex: Listen for status text before the button itself. The merge box is not just a button area. It is an explanation area. You may hear whether the PR is ready to merge, blocked, waiting on checks, or waiting on review.

Jamie: Can we mention specific screen reader workflows?

Alex: Yes, while keeping in mind that GitHub’s interface evolves. For NVDA users, browse mode with heading navigation is often effective. Jump to the bottom, then use H to move through headings near the merge section, and arrow through the status text and controls like Show all checks, Details, Update branch, or the merge button.

Jamie: And for JAWS?

Alex: A similar strategy works: move to the bottom, use heading navigation or the links list and buttons list as needed, then read line by line around the merge controls. If the button is unavailable, keep reading nearby text because the explanation is usually adjacent.

Jamie: So regardless of screen reader, the principle is: don’t just tab until you hit a disabled button and stop. Explore the surrounding text.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: How do status checks fit into that navigation?

Alex: Look for controls that expand the checks summary, often labeled Show all checks. Once expanded, each check may have a name, a state, and a Details link. The state might indicate passing, failing, pending, or cancelled.

Jamie: And reading check details means opening the detailed log for the failing job.

Alex: Yes. That’s where you learn whether the issue is a failed test, a dependency install problem, a style violation, a deployment error, or something else.

Jamie: Let’s broaden from merge box mechanics to the concept of status checks themselves.

Alex: A status check is a reported result attached to your commit or pull request. It tells GitHub whether some automated process succeeded, failed, is still running, or did not run successfully enough for the repository’s rules.

Jamie: And many of these come from GitHub Actions.

Alex: Right. GitHub Actions is GitHub’s built-in automation system. A repository can include workflow files under `.github/workflows`, and one common example is a file like `ci.yml`.

Jamie: Which usually means continuous integration.

Alex: Exactly. A CI workflow might run when you push commits or open a pull request. It may check out the code, install dependencies, build the project, run tests, run linters, maybe run accessibility or security checks, and then report the result back to GitHub as status checks.

Jamie: So when a learner sees something like `ci / test`, that’s probably one job inside a workflow file, not some mysterious separate system.

Alex: Correct. Though not all checks come from GitHub Actions. Some come from third-party services, like external CI platforms, deployment previews, security scanners, or code quality services.

Jamie: What are the main states a learner should recognize?

Alex: Passing or successful, which usually shows a green indicator. Pending or in progress, often a spinner or waiting state. Failing or unsuccessful, usually marked in red. You may also encounter cancelled, skipped, or neutral states, though whether those block merge depends on repository configuration and whether the check is required.

Jamie: So the key question is not just did a check run, but is it required, and what state is it in.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Who can actually configure all this?

Alex: Usually repository administrators, maintainers with the right permissions, or organization owners for org-level rulesets. Regular contributors generally cannot change branch protection. They can only comply with it.

Jamie: Which is useful emotionally too. If you’re blocked by a rule, it does not mean you’re expected to fix the repository settings yourself.

Alex: Right. Your job is to understand the rule, satisfy it if you can, and ask a maintainer when the blocker is infrastructural or administrative.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, can we give a practical workshop-oriented reference setup? What might a training repository enforce?

Alex: A workshop repository often enables a simple but realistic set of protections on `main`: require at least one approving review, require key status checks like build or test to pass, prevent direct pushes to `main`, and sometimes require the branch to be up to date before merging.

Jamie: Usually not every advanced rule all at once.

Alex: Right. For teaching, you want enough realism to show the workflow, but not so many restrictions that learners spend the whole session debugging policy instead of learning GitHub.

Jamie: And that also helps facilitators explain why a pull request may be blocked in a controlled, understandable way.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let me try a compact recap. Branch protection is the repository’s quality gate for important branches. Common blockers are missing reviews, failing or pending checks, an out-of-date branch, unsigned commits, linear-history rules, or a locked branch. Modern repositories may use rulesets, which are more flexible than classic branch protection. And for accessibility, the merge box is the key area to inspect, especially the status text above the button.

Alex: That’s it. And one final note: if you want the most authoritative details, GitHub’s documentation on protected branches and rulesets is the source to trust, because exact UI wording and available options can change over time.

Jamie: So when your merge button is greyed out, treat it like feedback, not failure.

Alex: Well said. Read the message, identify the category of blocker, take the matching next step, and you’ll usually get unstuck quickly.

Jamie: And if not, you’ll at least know what question to ask a maintainer.

Alex: Exactly. That’s a strong open source skill.

59. Episode 29: GitHub Security Features

Dependabot, secret scanning, code scanning, and private security advisories.

Based on: Appendix P: GitHub Security Features

Download Episode 29 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 29: GitHub Security Features

Transcript

Alex: Today we're walking through GitHub security features in a way that's practical for contributors, especially if you're navigating with a screen reader or low vision workflow. This is a companion to open source contribution skills, and it's especially relevant when you're working in public repositories and want to understand what security alerts mean, what actions are appropriate, and how to report problems responsibly.

Jamie: So this is not just for maintainers doing advanced security work.

Alex: Exactly. If you contribute to open source at all, you should know four big ideas: dependency alerts, secret leaks, code scanning findings, and private vulnerability reporting. And we also need to cover how the Security and quality area works in GitHub, how to find a repository's security policy, how SBOM export fits in, and how to navigate all of this accessibly.

Alex: A quick orienting note: GitHub's documentation on code security is the authoritative source here. And if you're studying alongside broader course material, this connects closely with open source culture and responsible contribution practices.

Jamie: And there was also a quick navigation list in the source, right?

Alex: Yes, and instead of reading that list aloud, we'll simply move through the same sequence naturally: first the Security and quality tab, then Dependabot, secret scanning, code scanning, private reporting, SECURITY dot MD, SBOM, screen reader navigation, and finally a real-world style security dashboard example for an accessibility-focused project.

Alex: Let's start with the Security and quality tab itself. Every GitHub repository has this area in its navigation, but what you can actually see depends on your access level.

Jamie: That's one of those details that confuses learners. Two people can open the same repo and get different results.

Alex: Right. If you're just a public viewer, you'll typically see the repository's security policy if it has a SECURITY.md file, and you may also see a private vulnerability reporting form if the maintainer has enabled that feature.

Jamie: So public viewers do not necessarily see the full alert dashboards.

Alex: Correct. Contributors with write or admin access see much more: Dependabot alerts, secret scanning alerts, code scanning alerts, security advisories, and security settings management options.

Jamie: That explains why a learner might hear someone say, "Go check Security," and then not find the same links.

Alex: Yes. The interface is role-sensitive.

Jamie: How do you get there efficiently with a screen reader?

Alex: On any repository page, you can Tab through the secondary navigation region until you reach the Security link and press Enter. If GitHub keyboard shortcuts are enabled and Focus Mode is on, G then S can jump directly there. That's much faster than tabbing across the whole page.

Jamie: And once you're inside that area?

Alex: The alert categories are separate links, so moving by link or using keyboard navigation like K, depending on your setup, can help you move among Dependabot, Secret scanning, and Code scanning.

Jamie: Can we pause on accessibility cues for different learners?

Alex: Absolutely. For screen reader users: the fastest mental model is that Security and quality is a container, and the specific alert systems are separate pages inside it. For low vision users: the tab lives alongside Code, Issues, Pull requests, and Actions, and alert severity badges include text labels like Critical or High, not just color. For sighted users: a shield icon and sometimes a count badge visually signal security status, and a green shield or no alert count generally means no open alerts.

Alex: Now let's move to Dependabot. Dependabot is GitHub's automated system for monitoring dependencies and helping keep them updated.

Jamie: And it really does two related but distinct jobs.

Alex: Exactly. First, Dependabot alerts tell you when a package your project depends on has a known vulnerability. Second, Dependabot can open pull requests to fix those problems, and it can also open routine version update PRs even when the change isn't specifically security-related.

Jamie: Let's unpack the alerts first. What triggers one?

Alex: If a vulnerability is discovered in a dependency used by your project, GitHub can create a Dependabot alert. You'll usually see details like the package name, ecosystem such as npm, the vulnerable version range, the fixed version, an advisory identifier such as a GHSA code, and a short description of the risk.

Jamie: So the alert is not just saying, "Something is bad." It gives actionable specifics.

Alex: Exactly. And severity matters. The source laid out the common levels using CVSS ranges. Critical, roughly 9.0 to 10.0, means very serious and likely needing immediate attention. High, around 7.0 to 8.9, is significant risk and usually should be fixed within the current sprint or very soon. Medium, 4.0 to 6.9, still matters but may require specific conditions to exploit. Low, 0.1 to 3.9, is lower urgency but should still be addressed when practical.

Jamie: That's helpful, because learners often see severity labels without understanding the difference between "drop everything" and "plan this responsibly."

Alex: Right. And when you see a dependency alert as a contributor, a good process is: first, read the advisory so you understand scope. Second, check whether the project actually uses the vulnerable code path. Third, the fix is usually to update the dependency to the patched version. Fourth, look in Pull Requests, because Dependabot Security Updates may already have opened a PR for you.

Jamie: I like that middle step. Sometimes the vulnerable package is present, but the exact dangerous feature isn't used.

Alex: Yes, though you still generally want to patch it. Understanding actual exposure helps prioritize and communicate clearly.

Jamie: What does a Dependabot security update PR typically look like?

Alex: Usually a title like, "Bump lodash from version A to version B," authored by dependabot bot. The PR description often includes release notes, changelog links, and commit references.

Jamie: And reviewing those is a good contribution path.

Alex: A very good one. For contributors with access, reviewing and merging Dependabot PRs is often high-value and relatively low-risk, provided tests pass and the change is understood.

Jamie: And then there are version updates, not just security updates.

Alex: Correct. Dependabot can also be configured to keep dependencies generally current. That's controlled in a file named .github slash dependabot.yml. The example in the source showed version 2 syntax, npm as the package ecosystem, the root directory slash, a weekly schedule, and a limit on open PRs. In plain language, that means GitHub checks for dependency updates each week and opens at most a set number of update pull requests at a time.

Jamie: So if a learner sees a dependabot.yml file, that is not application code. It's repository automation configuration.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Next is secret scanning, and this one is urgent by nature. Secret scanning looks for accidentally committed credentials such as API keys, tokens, and passwords.

Jamie: This is the one that can stop your push before it lands, right?

Alex: Yes. Push Protection is the real-time prevention layer. If GitHub detects a known secret pattern during a git push, it can block the push and return an error. The example in the source showed a GH013 repository rule violation, followed by lines identifying the commit, file, secret type, and line location.

Jamie: Which is actually pretty useful if you slow down and read it.

Alex: Exactly. If your push is blocked, do three things. First, remove the secret from the file immediately. Second, rotate the exposed credential. GitHub may automatically revoke detected GitHub tokens, but you should still treat the credential as compromised. Third, if you suspect a false positive, a bypass may be possible with justification, but only after careful investigation.

Jamie: And the best practice is to avoid hardcoding secrets in the first place.

Alex: Always. The source gave a very clear bad-versus-good example. Bad: assigning a token string directly in code. Good: reading it from an environment variable like process dot env dot GITHUB underscore TOKEN.

Jamie: That distinction matters for accessibility too, because if you're reviewing code by speech or braille, variable names are easier to reason about than a long credential string buried in a file.

Alex: Well said. And for public repositories, GitHub can also scan existing commits and create secret scanning alerts for already-exposed secrets. Those alerts appear under Security and quality, then Secret scanning.

Jamie: What's the right response if you find one?

Alex: Treat it as urgent. Especially if it's a token or API key, assume the credential may have been exposed for a long time. The immediate priorities are revocation or rotation, removing the secret from the codebase, and following project procedures for cleanup and disclosure.

Jamie: Let's do the accessibility layer here too.

Alex: For screen reader users, the terminal output from Push Protection is valuable because it names the exact file, line, and secret type. Read those error lines carefully. In the GitHub interface, go to Secret scanning and navigate to the alerts table; jumping to tables can help, then use row and cell navigation. For low vision users, terminal errors may appear in red, so increase font size and contrast if needed, and in the alert table zoom in on columns like secret type and location. For sighted users, visual banners and icons can help, but the key lesson is the same for everyone: never hardcode tokens.

Alex: Now to code scanning and CodeQL. This is different from dependency scanning. Dependabot is about packages you use. Code scanning is about vulnerabilities in your actual code.

Jamie: So this is static analysis.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub's built-in system commonly uses CodeQL, which analyzes code patterns and logic. The source explicitly mentioned risks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and this category also generally includes other dangerous data flow or unsafe coding patterns.

Jamie: How should a learner think about a code scanning alert when they open one?

Alex: Read it as a structured explanation. A code scanning alert usually tells you what type of vulnerability was found, where it appears in the code, how severe it is, and often a path of reasoning from source to sink, meaning how untrusted input could reach a dangerous operation.

Jamie: And that's the part people sometimes find intimidating.

Alex: Yes, but you can break it down. Ask: what is the risky behavior, where in the file is it, what data is involved, and what safer pattern should replace it? For example, if the issue is SQL injection, the fix may involve parameterized queries rather than string concatenation. If it's XSS, the remedy may involve proper escaping, sanitization, or avoiding unsafe rendering patterns.

Jamie: Where do contributors find these alerts?

Alex: In the Security and quality area, under Code scanning. If you have the necessary access, you'll see a list of open findings. Opening one gives you alert details and links back into the relevant code locations.

Jamie: And if you don't have write access?

Alex: You may not see the internal alert list, which is another reason to understand access-dependent behavior in this area.

Alex: Next is private vulnerability reporting, which is a major open source professionalism topic.

Jamie: Meaning: if you find a serious bug, do not immediately open a public issue describing exactly how to exploit it.

Alex: Exactly. If the repository has private vulnerability reporting enabled, you should use that pathway to submit the report confidentially.

Jamie: How does that usually work from the contributor side?

Alex: You go to the repository's Security and quality area and look for the private vulnerability reporting form. Then you submit the details privately: what the vulnerability is, how to reproduce it, what impact it has, and any suggested mitigation if you have one.

Jamie: And then comes responsible disclosure.

Alex: Right. Responsible disclosure means giving maintainers time to validate the report, prepare a fix, coordinate any advisory publication, and reduce harm before broad public disclosure. The goal is not secrecy for its own sake. The goal is protecting users while giving the project a fair chance to respond.

Jamie: What if the maintainer doesn't respond?

Alex: Then you move carefully. The source included that question explicitly, and the guiding principle is still responsibility. Follow the project's stated policy if it has one. If there is no response after a reasonable period, you may need to consider escalation paths that reduce harm, such as using broader security reporting norms rather than dropping exploit details publicly. The exact timing and method depend on context, but the key is to act ethically and document your attempts to contact the maintainers.

Jamie: So the main lesson is: private first, thoughtful process, minimize risk to users.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Closely related is the SECURITY.md file. This is the repository's security policy file.

Jamie: What should learners expect to find in it?

Alex: Usually reporting instructions, supported versions, contact guidance, and expectations around vulnerability disclosure. In practice, it answers the question, "If I discover a security problem here, what does this project want me to do?"

Jamie: How do you navigate to it?

Alex: Often through the Security and quality area if GitHub exposes the security policy there, or directly in the repository files if you know the project includes SECURITY.md. Once open, read it carefully before reporting anything. It may say not to use public issues, may specify an email address or form, and may list response expectations.

Jamie: That sounds administrative, but it's actually critical.

Alex: Very much so. Following SECURITY.md is part of being a responsible contributor.

Alex: Now let's talk about SBOM, the Software Bill of Materials.

Jamie: That's a phrase people hear more and more, but it can sound abstract.

Alex: An SBOM is essentially an inventory of software components used by a project. Think of it as a structured list of ingredients. For security work, that matters because you want to know what dependencies are present, what versions are involved, and what could be affected by newly discovered vulnerabilities.

Jamie: And GitHub can export one?

Alex: Yes, in repositories and plans where the feature is available, GitHub can export an SBOM. The important conceptual point is not memorizing a button path here, but understanding why you would do it: to inspect component inventories, support audits, aid compliance, or respond quickly when a package ecosystem issue appears.

Jamie: So SBOM is less about fixing one alert and more about seeing the whole supply-chain picture.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let's now gather the screen reader navigation guidance into one place, because the source had a dedicated section for that.

Jamie: Good, because scattered keyboard hints are easy to forget.

Alex: To reach the Security and quality tab, use the repository navigation. Tabbing to the secondary nav region works, and G then S can be faster if GitHub keyboard shortcuts and focus mode are enabled.

Jamie: Once there, how do you handle Dependabot alerts accessibly?

Alex: Treat the alert list like a structured page. Move by headings, links, or tables depending on your screen reader commands. Open an alert and listen for core fields: package, severity, affected versions, fixed version, advisory identifier, and description. If a related Dependabot PR exists, switch to the Pull Requests tab and review the bot-authored update.

Jamie: And code scanning alerts?

Alex: Similar principle, but the content is more code-centric. Navigate to the Code scanning area, open an alert, then work through the explanation and linked code. Read both the alert summary and the code snippet context. If your tooling supports it, opening the file locally in VS Code can make the analysis easier than staying only in the browser.

Jamie: What about the private vulnerability reporting form itself?

Alex: Expect a form with fields for summary, details, reproduction, and impact. For screen reader users, forms mode or structured form navigation is useful. Move field by field, verify required fields, and review before submitting. Because these reports can be sensitive, clarity matters. Keep the report concise but complete.

Jamie: So the accessibility message is not just "you can get there." It's also "here is how to reason through the information once you arrive."

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: The source also included a section on security and accessibility agents, plus a security dashboard example for the community-access slash accessibility-agents repository.

Jamie: That's interesting because it ties security practice directly to accessibility-focused development.

Alex: Yes. The broader lesson is that accessible projects still need the same security hygiene as any other software project: dependency monitoring, secret leak prevention, code scanning, and clear vulnerability reporting. Accessibility and security are not competing concerns. Mature projects do both.

Jamie: What should learners notice in a sample security dashboard?

Alex: You'd look for categories like Dependabot alerts, Secret scanning, Code scanning, and the number of open Dependabot PRs. Then you'd ask practical questions. Are there known vulnerable packages? Are any secrets exposed? Are there code scanning findings that need review? Are there already automated PRs waiting for maintainers to merge?

Jamie: And then the recommendation piece is basically prioritization.

Alex: Exactly. A sensible recommendation framework would be: urgent first for exposed secrets, then critical and high dependency vulnerabilities, then serious code scanning findings, then routine dependency maintenance through open Dependabot PRs. For contributors, reviewing existing bot PRs is often one of the safest ways to help. For maintainers, enabling and monitoring these systems reduces risk over time.

Jamie: Can you say more about what "sample output" implies in this section?

Alex: It implies that learners should be able to interpret a dashboard-like summary, not just read definitions. If an agent or report says there are zero secret scanning alerts but several open Dependabot PRs, that means credential exposure is not the immediate crisis, but dependency maintenance is pending. If code scanning is clear and secret scanning is clear, that's reassuring, but it doesn't mean you stop monitoring. Security posture is ongoing.

Jamie: Before we wrap, I want to make sure we don't lose the administrative content from the source. There was an explicit note that this appendix is for anyone contributing to open source repositories, because you need to understand how GitHub protects code and what these alerts mean.

Alex: Yes, and that framing matters. These features are not just for security specialists. They're part of normal contribution literacy. Also, the source pointed to GitHub Docs code security materials as the authoritative foundation, and included a section-level source map pointing back to GitHub Docs, the GitHub changelog, GitHub security features docs, Dependabot docs, and secret scanning docs.

Jamie: So if a learner wants the official reference after listening, the place to start is GitHub Docs on code security, then the specific documentation for Dependabot and secret scanning.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can we do a final compact checklist?

Alex: Certainly. In any repository, know how to reach Security and quality. Remember that public viewers and contributors see different things. Read Dependabot alerts for package, versions, advisory, and severity. Check for auto-opened Dependabot PRs. Never commit secrets; if Push Protection blocks a push, remove and rotate immediately. Use environment variables instead of hardcoded credentials. Understand that code scanning looks at your code logic, not just dependencies. Report vulnerabilities privately when that option exists, and follow responsible disclosure. Read SECURITY.md before reporting. Understand SBOM as a component inventory. And for accessible workflows, use keyboard shortcuts, table navigation, and form navigation strategically.

Jamie: That's a solid toolkit.

Alex: It is. And it makes you not only a better GitHub user, but a safer and more responsible open source collaborator.

60. Episode 30: VS Code Accessibility Reference

Complete accessibility settings, audio signals, diff viewer, and screen reader configs.

Based on: Appendix G: VS Code Accessibility Reference

Download Episode 30 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 30: VS Code Accessibility Reference

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. This time we’re doing something a little different. Think of this as your technical field guide for making Visual Studio Code work well if you use a screen reader, have low vision, or just want a more accessible setup for coding, reviewing diffs, using Git, and working with Copilot.

Jamie: So not just a beginner tour.

Alex: Right. More like a reference lesson in conversation form. The appendix behind this episode is meant to be a lookup manual. It even recommends practical ways to jump around it: Go to Line with Control+G, Go to Symbol with Control+Shift+O, and bookmarking the file in VS Code with Control+K, then Control+K so you can reopen it fast later.

Jamie: That’s helpful because reference files can be long, and long can feel intimidating.

Alex: Exactly. And the appendix is explicit about different access strategies. For screen reader users, it treats the file as something you navigate structurally. For low vision users, it suggests bumping font size with Control+Equals before scanning long tables, using orientation aids like breadcrumbs or the minimap if that helps, and using high contrast themes so tables and inline code are easier to distinguish. For sighted users, it points to the table of contents links and the outline view with Control+Shift+O.

Jamie: I like that it doesn’t assume one kind of learner.

Alex: And one more administrative note: this appendix is a companion reference to the main VS Code setup and accessibility chapters, and it points to the official VS Code accessibility docs as the authoritative source.

Alex: Let’s start with the main settings you’ll actually tune. In VS Code, accessibility settings can be changed in the Settings interface with Control+Comma, or directly in settings dot json through the Command Palette by opening User Settings JSON.

Jamie: Can we separate the settings into categories that matter in practice?

Alex: Yes. Core editor behavior, diff and merge behavior, terminal behavior, and announcement or notification behavior.

Jamie: Let’s do core editor behavior first.

Alex: The most important setting is editor dot accessibilitySupport. Its values are auto, on, and off. Auto tries to detect screen readers like NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver. On forces screen reader optimizations. Off disables them.

Jamie: And if detection is flaky?

Alex: Then forcing it to on is often the right move.

Jamie: What else matters right away?

Alex: Editor dot accessibilityPageSize controls how many lines are read with page navigation in screen reader mode. Default is ten. That sounds minor, but it changes how much content you hear at a time.

Jamie: So it’s part comfort, part efficiency.

Alex: Exactly. Then there are several visual guide settings, like bracket pair guides, horizontal bracket guides, active bracket highlighting, indentation highlighting, and indentation guides. These are mainly visual. The appendix’s message is clear: for screen reader users, many of these aren’t useful and may just add visual complexity for mixed workflows.

Jamie: So if I’m blind and not using that visual information, I can simplify.

Alex: Yes. Similarly, editor dot minimap dot enabled is visual only, and the recommendation is to turn it off for screen reader users. Editor dot renderWhitespace is also important. The recommended value for screen readers is none, because hearing code is hard enough without trying to manage a UI designed to show whitespace visually.

Jamie: What about line wrapping?

Alex: Editor dot wordWrap is recommended on for screen reader users, especially with long lines. It can reduce horizontal navigation friction. And workbench dot editor dot enablePreview is worth considering too. If preview mode stays on, opening files can reuse one tab. Turning it off means files open in persistent tabs, which many users find easier to track.

Jamie: And hover popups?

Alex: Editor dot hover dot enabled can stay on, but the key point is this: for accessible reading of hover content, use Accessible View with Alt+F2.

Jamie: Now diffs. This matters a lot for GitHub learners.

Alex: It really does. A few settings make a huge difference. DiffEditor dot diffAlgorithm should generally be advanced. The appendix specifically says it tends to produce better hunks for screen reader users.

Jamie: Meaning more sensible blocks of changes.

Alex: Right. DiffEditor dot ignoreTrimWhitespace should usually stay true. That reduces noise from whitespace-only changes. DiffEditor dot renderSideBySide is a major one: the visual default is true, but for screen readers the recommendation is false, which gives you inline diffs.

Jamie: Why is inline better?

Alex: Because you hear one stream of content with change markers, instead of trying to mentally coordinate two columns. DiffEditor dot wordWrap can also be turned on for long lines. And merge conflict decorators are visual helpers, but the appendix nudges screen reader users toward the Accessible Diff workflow instead.

Jamie: So if I remember only one thing: inline diffs, advanced algorithm, ignore trim whitespace.

Alex: That’s an excellent practical summary.

Alex: The terminal has its own accessibility settings. Terminal dot integrated dot screenReaderMode can be auto, on, or off, parallel to editor accessibility support. Terminal dot integrated dot enableBell is recommended on if you want audio feedback. Terminal dot integrated dot accessibleViewFocusesTerminal controls whether focus returns to the terminal after closing Accessible View, and by default it does. Terminal dot integrated dot accessibleViewPreserveCursorPosition controls whether your cursor position is preserved when opening Accessible View.

Jamie: That’s subtle, but I can imagine it matters if you’re reading command output and then want to continue right where you left off.

Alex: Exactly. Small settings, big effect on rhythm.

Jamie: And then there’s the verbosity layer.

Alex: Yes. A whole group of accessibility dot verbosity settings controls whether VS Code announces context in particular parts of the interface. The appendix lists comments, the diff editor, the main editor, hover, inline chat, inline completions, the keybindings editor, notebooks, panel chat, the settings editor, and the terminal.

Jamie: So if something feels too chatty, or too quiet, this is where I tune it.

Alex: Exactly. And that leads naturally into audio cues, because accessible feedback in VS Code isn’t just speech.

Alex: Audio cues provide nonverbal feedback through sound. You can get to those settings by opening Settings with Control+Comma and searching for audio cue, or by editing settings dot json directly.

Jamie: And each cue has the same value choices, right?

Alex: Yes: auto, on, and off. Auto means play the sound only in screen reader mode. On means always play it. Off means never.

Jamie: What kinds of events can have sounds attached?

Alex: A lot. The appendix lists a broad set of accessibility signals. Some are about terminal or output actions, like clear. Some are tied to Copilot chat, including when a request is sent, while a response is pending, and when a response is received. Some are about debugging, like hitting a breakpoint or landing on a line with a breakpoint. Several are specific to diff navigation, including sounds for deleted, inserted, and modified lines. Others signal formatting completion, errors, warnings, folded areas, inline suggestions, unavailable inlay hints, and notebook events.

Jamie: So this is really a sensory feedback system, not just a convenience feature.

Alex: Exactly. And the recommendations in the appendix are practical. Important state changes, like a line with an error or a completed chat response, are often recommended on. Some lower-priority cues are auto, and a few are off if they tend to add little value.

Jamie: Can users change the sounds themselves?

Alex: Yes, the appendix includes customization of signal sounds, including sound file requirements. The big idea is that if you do customize, use supported audio files and keep them short, distinct, and easy to recognize. You want cues that clarify, not cues that become a second source of clutter.

Jamie: Let’s get into the Accessible Diff Viewer, because that’s probably one of the most important workflows for Git and pull request review.

Alex: I agree. The appendix gives a complete guide. First, when should you use it? Any time the standard visual diff is hard to interpret with a screen reader, when you want a text-forward representation of changes, or when navigating code review changes line by line would be easier than trying to understand two-pane layout.

Jamie: How do you open it?

Alex: The appendix emphasizes the accessible diff workflow and points to function-key navigation, especially F7, as part of moving through changes. In practice, you use the diff tools built into VS Code and then switch to the accessible representation designed for screen reader reading.

Jamie: And once it opens, what is its structure like?

Alex: At the top level, it’s organized to present changed content as understandable text rather than as a visual comparison grid. One concept the appendix calls out is line prefixes. Those prefixes indicate what kind of change you’re hearing or reading: added, deleted, modified, or context. That labeling is essential because it replaces the color and spatial layout sighted users rely on.

Jamie: So the prefixes are the semantic anchors.

Alex: Exactly. Then there are hunks. A hunk is a block of related changes. That’s the unit you navigate. Instead of thinking, I’m moving through the entire file visually, think, I’m moving through meaningful clusters of edits.

Jamie: That sounds more cognitively manageable.

Alex: It usually is. The appendix also talks about navigating hunks and about screen reader-specific navigation differences. For NVDA and JAWS, the workflow often depends on browse mode versus focus mode and using heading or structural navigation appropriately. For VoiceOver on macOS, navigation conventions differ, so users rely on VoiceOver’s own reading and interaction commands.

Jamie: And what are context lines in this setup?

Alex: Context lines are unchanged lines included around the edits to help you understand where a change happened. They answer the question, what was around this edit before and after? The appendix even gives an example to reinforce that changed lines without surrounding context can be hard to interpret.

Jamie: So context is not noise. It’s orientation.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: And then the big comparison: inline versus side by side.

Alex: Yes. The appendix is explicit. Inline diff view is recommended for screen readers. Side by side is the default visual presentation and works well if you can compare columns visually, but it’s much harder in speech output. So to switch to inline view, set diffEditor dot renderSideBySide to false.

Jamie: That one setting keeps coming up for good reason.

Alex: It really does. And the appendix includes learning-card style reminders for the accessible diff viewer, reinforcing when to use it, how to think in hunks, and why inline structure is friendlier for nonvisual review.

Alex: Next, the appendix gets very specific about screen reader configurations.

Jamie: Which I appreciate, because “it supports screen readers” is not the same as “here’s how to make your screen reader and editor cooperate.”

Alex: Exactly. For NVDA, it includes recommended NVDA settings, mentions NVDA add-ons that may help with VS Code, and highlights VS Code-specific NVDA commands.

Jamie: Without assuming everyone uses the same add-ons.

Alex: Right. The point is not that every user must install extras, but that VS Code users often benefit from checking whether speech modes, punctuation levels, browse-versus-focus behavior, and any editor-friendly add-ons align with coding work.

Jamie: And JAWS?

Alex: Similarly, it covers recommended JAWS settings, JAWS scripts for VS Code, and VS Code-specific JAWS commands. That matters because JAWS users may depend more heavily on custom scripts in some environments, and because verbosity and cursor behavior can shape the coding experience dramatically.

Jamie: Then VoiceOver on macOS gets its own configuration section.

Alex: Yes. The appendix includes recommended VoiceOver Utility settings, VS Code-specific VoiceOver commands, and Quick Nav navigation when Quick Nav is enabled. That last part matters because Quick Nav changes how arrow keys behave, and in a code editor that can significantly affect movement and interaction.

Jamie: So the general lesson is: don’t just tweak VS Code. Tune the screen reader and the editor together.

Alex: Exactly. Accessibility is an ecosystem, not a single checkbox.

Jamie: Now for the part many learners want as a cheat sheet: keyboard shortcuts.

Alex: The appendix organizes them by task. Let’s walk through the categories rather than pretending one giant list is memorable all at once.

Jamie: Please.

Alex: Global navigation includes the commands that help you move around VS Code itself: Command Palette, settings, quick open, outline and symbol navigation, and panel focus changes. These are the shortcuts that reduce hunting.

Jamie: Then sidebar panels.

Alex: Right. Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run and Debug, Extensions, and related panel focus commands. For accessibility, knowing how to jump directly to a panel is better than tabbing through unpredictable interface layers.

Jamie: What about file work in the editor?

Alex: Editor file operations include opening files, saving, saving all, closing, reopening, and managing tabs. Combined with turning preview tabs off, these shortcuts make file handling more stable.

Jamie: And navigation inside files?

Alex: That’s its own category: go to line, go to symbol, move by word, move by line, page movement, and other cursor travel commands. If you’re reading code nonvisually, navigation fluency is everything.

Jamie: Editing is separate from navigation.

Alex: Yes. Editor editing includes line manipulation, indentation, commenting, duplicating, deleting, and formatting. Then there’s find and replace, which is especially important in large files and long markdown documents.

Jamie: And multi-cursor?

Alex: Included too. Powerful, but not always the first tool a screen reader user reaches for. Still, the appendix treats it as part of complete coverage.

Jamie: Terminal shortcuts must be in there.

Alex: Yes, along with Source Control and Git shortcuts, diff viewer shortcuts, Copilot shortcuts, accessibility feature shortcuts, Problems panel shortcuts, and Markdown preview shortcuts.

Jamie: That’s a lot of ground.

Alex: It is, but the categories matter because they mirror real workflows. For example, a Git review flow might involve Explorer, editor navigation, Source Control, diff viewer movement, and Problems panel checks. A writing flow might lean on editor commands, markdown preview, and find and replace. A Copilot-heavy flow adds inline completions and panel chat navigation.

Jamie: So the appendix is not just listing keys. It’s mapping the terrain.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Then there’s a deeper section on accessibility signals types and customization.

Jamie: How is that different from the earlier audio cues list?

Alex: Earlier, we talked about what cues exist. Here, the appendix expands into how signals behave as a system: announcement verbosity settings, custom announcement timing, and signal priorities.

Jamie: Let’s unpack that.

Alex: Announcement verbosity means deciding how much spoken context VS Code gives in different parts of the interface. If you’re overwhelmed, reduce verbosity in the places where you already know the pattern. If you miss important context, increase it.

Jamie: And timing?

Alex: Custom announcement timing is about when feedback occurs and whether it arrives at moments that interrupt you or moments that support you. Some users want immediate cues. Others want fewer interruptions and more manual access through Accessible View.

Jamie: Signal priorities sounds like triage.

Alex: That’s a good way to think about it. Not every event deserves equal prominence. Errors, completed responses, and change-type indicators in diffs may be high priority. Less important status information can be downgraded to auto or off. The appendix’s learning cards on accessibility signals reinforce that the goal is usable feedback, not maximum feedback.

Jamie: That sets us up for the settings dot json profiles.

Alex: Yes, and these are very practical. The appendix offers example configurations for different working styles.

Jamie: Let’s go one by one.

Alex: First is a minimal screen reader profile. This is for users who prefer fewer announcements and who open Accessible View manually when needed. The philosophy is low noise, deliberate reading.

Jamie: So maybe a strong fit for experienced users who don’t want constant narration.

Alex: Exactly. Second is a maximum feedback profile for users who want all audio and verbal announcements. That’s especially helpful when you’re learning the interface or want confirmation for many actions.

Jamie: Then there’s a Copilot-optimized profile.

Alex: Right. That one emphasizes settings useful for GitHub Copilot workflows, like announcing inline completions and chat activity, and making AI interactions easier to track nonvisually.

Jamie: And a Git or diff-optimized profile.

Alex: Yes. That profile is for heavy pull request review and diff work. It would center the accessible diff experience: inline diffs, strong diff signals, and settings that reduce review noise, such as ignoring trim whitespace.

Jamie: Then performance-optimized.

Alex: For slower machines or very large repositories. The idea there is that accessibility also includes responsiveness. Turning off visually rich or nonessential features can make the editor lighter and easier to use.

Jamie: And then there’s a quick-copy balanced setup.

Alex: Yes. The appendix includes a complete recommended settings block that you can paste into settings dot json for a balanced screen reader profile. The intent is not “one true setup,” but a solid baseline you can customize.

Jamie: Which is reassuring, because people sometimes think accessibility settings are pass or fail.

Alex: Exactly. Better to think in profiles and tradeoffs.

Alex: The appendix also includes an update section for VS Code 1.120, focused on chat, the Agents window, and markdown diff updates.

Jamie: So this is where the reference acknowledges that the tool keeps changing.

Alex: Right. It covers what changed, then breaks the implications into three workflows: screen reader, low vision, and sighted.

Jamie: What’s the practical takeaway?

Alex: For screen reader users, the takeaway is to reevaluate chat and agent workflows whenever VS Code adds new panes or interaction models. You may need to check focus movement, verbosity settings, and whether Accessible View gives you a better way to read generated content.

Jamie: And for low vision users?

Alex: Consider how the newer chat and agent surfaces present dense information, whether scaling, contrast, or layout adjustments are needed, and whether markdown diff improvements make review easier. If markdown diffs become more readable, that can matter a lot in documentation-heavy repositories.

Jamie: And sighted workflows are included too, even though this appendix centers accessibility.

Alex: Yes, because accessibility references still need to explain the visual defaults that many teams assume. The section also includes settings references tied to those newer features, so learners know where to look when behavior changes after an update.

Jamie: Before we close, I want to ask about the table of contents and source map material. People often skip those.

Alex: They shouldn’t. The table of contents is part of accessibility because navigation is accessibility. It tells you the reference is organized into settings, audio cues, accessible diff viewer, screen reader configurations, keyboard shortcuts, accessibility signals, configuration examples, and the newer 1.120 updates. That mental map lowers cognitive load.

Jamie: And the authoritative sources?

Alex: Also important. The appendix points to the official VS Code accessibility documentation as the primary authority, and then includes a section-level source map. Even if the extracted list in our source snapshot is messy, the purpose is clear: this reference is meant to be traceable and maintainable, so learners can verify details against official documentation when VS Code evolves.

Jamie: So the document is both a learning tool and a maintenance-minded reference.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can you give us a practical closing setup recommendation? Not a giant JSON block, just the decision points.

Alex: Absolutely. If you use a screen reader in VS Code, start by forcing accessibility support on if auto detection is unreliable. Turn minimap off. Set word wrap on. Set whitespace rendering to none. Turn preview tabs off if you want steadier file tracking. For diffs, use the advanced diff algorithm, ignore trim whitespace, and switch to inline diff view. In the terminal, keep screen reader mode on or auto, and consider enabling the bell. Then tune verbosity and audio cues based on whether you prefer minimal interruption or rich feedback.

Jamie: And if I’m doing a lot of Git review?

Alex: Build around the Accessible Diff Viewer. Think in hunks, rely on line prefixes, keep context lines, and use inline rather than side-by-side comparison. That one workflow can make pull request review dramatically more usable.

Jamie: And if I’m still learning?

Alex: Choose the maximum-feedback end of the spectrum first, then reduce noise gradually as you build confidence.

Jamie: That’s a great rule.

Alex: And maybe the most important one. Accessible setup is iterative. You’re not trying to discover the perfect editor in one session. You’re trying to build a working environment that tells you what matters, stays quiet about what doesn’t, and supports the way you actually code.

Jamie: That’s it for this reference conversation. Keep the appendix handy, treat it like a manual, and come back to it when your workflow changes.

Alex: And when VS Code updates, check your assumptions. Accessibility features are improving, but the best setup is still the one you verify in practice.

61. Episode 31: GitHub Codespaces

Cloud dev environments, accessibility setup, and screen reader usage.

Based on: Appendix J: GitHub Codespaces

Download Episode 31 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 31: GitHub Codespaces

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're exploring GitHub Codespaces, which is one of the most practical ways to get a full development environment without doing a bunch of local setup first.

Jamie: So if a learner has heard the phrase but never used it, what is it, exactly?

Alex: A Codespace is a cloud-hosted development environment. GitHub provisions a virtual machine for you, clones your repository into it, and then gives you a VS Code interface connected to that machine. You can use that interface right in your browser, or connect the Codespace to your local VS Code desktop app.

Jamie: So the code editor feels like VS Code, but the machine doing the work is somewhere else.

Alex: Exactly. And that matters a lot for accessibility and teaching. You don't have to install compilers, runtimes, or project dependencies on your own computer just to participate. Your screen reader, keyboard preferences, operating system settings, and browser setup stay on your machine, while the development environment lives in the cloud.

Jamie: That sounds especially helpful in workshops.

Alex: It is. Everyone can use the same environment, which means instructors can reproduce problems more reliably. If one learner says, "I opened the repository and this command failed," the facilitator is much more likely to see the same thing in the same environment.

Jamie: And for cost, is this something learners should worry about right away?

Alex: Usually no. GitHub offers a monthly free allowance of Codespaces hours for personal accounts, and for typical workshop use, that usually fits within the free tier.

Alex: A quick orientation point: this topic connects closely to choosing your tools and understanding the VS Code interface. If you already know basic VS Code navigation, Codespaces will feel familiar very quickly.

Jamie: And before we go deeper, can we make a simple distinction between cloud editors in general?

Alex: Sure. Think of Codespaces as a full cloud development machine with a terminal. That's different from lighter browser editors that let you edit files but don't give you the same runtime environment.

Jamie: Let's make that concrete for different learners.

Alex: For screen reader users: Codespaces gives you a full VS Code interface and terminal access, while your screen reader stays local on your own device. In the browser version, screen reader optimized behavior can activate automatically when the operating system signals that a screen reader is running. And if you want the most familiar experience, you can connect the Codespace to local VS Code desktop. For low vision users: your VS Code settings sync can carry over font size, theme, and zoom preferences. Browser zoom shortcuts like Control plus equals and Control plus minus work as expected, and high-contrast themes apply in the cloud editor just like they do locally. For sighted users: if you press period on a GitHub repository page, GitHub can open a lightweight browser editor quickly, but that is not the same as a full Codespace. Use a Codespace when you need to run code, use a terminal, or work in a complete development environment. And for most workshop exercises, the default two-core machine is enough.

Jamie: Okay, let's say I'm ready to make one. What's the easiest path?

Alex: There are two common ways. First, from a repository page. You navigate to the repository on GitHub, tab to the Code button, activate it, move to the Codespaces tab in the panel that opens, and choose Create codespace on main, or on whatever branch you want. GitHub then provisions it, and after a short wait, often around thirty to sixty seconds, it opens in a new browser tab.

Jamie: So that path is tied to a specific repository.

Alex: Right. The second path is from the Codespaces dashboard at github dot com slash codespaces. There, you activate New codespace, search for your repository, choose a branch, machine type, and region, then activate Create codespace.

Jamie: When would the dashboard path be better?

Alex: It's useful when you manage several repositories, want to resume older environments, or want a more deliberate creation flow with branch and machine choices surfaced up front.

Jamie: Let's talk machine types, because that can sound intimidating.

Alex: It really doesn't need to be. GitHub offers sizes like two-core with eight gigabytes of RAM, four-core with sixteen gigabytes, and eight-core with thirty-two gigabytes. A two-core machine is usually fine for documentation, general development, and workshop exercises. Move up only when you're doing heavier builds, running larger test suites, or multiple services.

Jamie: So learners should not assume bigger is always necessary.

Alex: Correct. Bigger can cost more and is often unnecessary for getting started.

Jamie: Once a Codespace exists, what environments can I actually use it in?

Alex: Two main ones. The first is the browser experience, basically VS Code for the web. The Codespace opens directly in your browser as a full editor interface.

Jamie: And what should accessibility-minded learners know there?

Alex: It works in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari, but screen reader support is most consistent in Chrome and Edge, especially with NVDA and JAWS. The big advantage is no installation. The tradeoff is that some extensions available in desktop VS Code may not be available in the browser version.

Jamie: And the second option is local VS Code desktop connected to the cloud machine.

Alex: Exactly. To do that, install the GitHub Codespaces extension in VS Code, sign in to GitHub inside VS Code, open the Command Palette with Control Shift P or Command Shift P on Mac, run the command Codespaces: Connect to Codespace, and then choose an existing Codespace or create a new one.

Jamie: Why do some learners prefer that setup?
