Alex: Because then your screen reader is interacting with your local VS Code installation, with your familiar settings, local extensions, and established workflow. The code still runs in the cloud environment, but the interface feels more like home.

Jamie: Now let's get into accessibility features directly. If someone is using Codespaces, what should they check first?

Alex: First, screen reader optimized mode. When VS Code detects a screen reader, it can turn on Screen Reader Optimized mode automatically. But it's worth knowing how to verify it manually. Open the Command Palette, search for Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode, and press Enter.

Jamie: And what changes when that mode is on?

Alex: A few important things. The editor presents content in a way that's more readable with screen readers, often emphasizing line-by-line reading rather than a noisier character-by-character experience. Diff views become accessible text comparisons instead of more visual-only presentations. And inline suggestions, such as from Copilot, are announced on a keypress rather than constantly interrupting you.

Jamie: That last part matters a lot, because surprise announcements can be exhausting.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about audio cues?

Alex: Codespaces supports the same VS Code audio cues as desktop. You can get tones or chimes for events like an error on the current line, a warning on the current line, a breakpoint being hit, a task completing, or a Copilot suggestion becoming available.

Jamie: How do you enable or review those?

Alex: You can go into Settings and search for audio cues, or use the Command Palette command Help: List Audio Cues.

Jamie: And for low vision users, those cues aren't just a screen reader feature.

Alex: Right. They also supplement visual indicators you might miss at high zoom, with magnification, or when multiple interface elements are competing for attention.

Jamie: Now the terminal. This is where many learners get nervous.

Alex: Understandably. The integrated terminal in a Codespace behaves like a standard terminal. With NVDA and JAWS, screen readers typically read output after it arrives. In NVDA, a common pattern is to switch to Browse Mode to review static terminal output, then switch back to Focus Mode to type commands.

Jamie: So reading mode for reviewing, focus mode for input.

Alex: Exactly. And VS Code also offers Accessible View. When the cursor is in the terminal, Alt F2 can open terminal output in a navigable buffer, which can be much easier to review with a screen reader.

Jamie: That sounds like one of those features people are thrilled to discover after struggling for a while.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: Can we do a quick learner-specific recap here?

Alex: Yes. For screen reader users: verify screen reader optimized mode with the Command Palette if needed, use audio cues to supplement what you hear from the editor, and use the same NVDA terminal pattern you would locally, browse to read and focus to type. For low vision users: browser-based Codespaces respects zoom and theme choices, Control plus equals can enlarge the editor, and Chrome and Edge often provide the most consistent rendering at high zoom and magnification. For sighted users: the browser Codespace looks a lot like desktop VS Code, you can confirm you're connected to a cloud environment by looking for the Codespaces indicator in the lower left, and if a browser extension limitation gets in your way, connect through local VS Code desktop instead.

Jamie: Let's go screen reader by screen reader. Starting with NVDA.

Alex: For NVDA, there is no special profile required just for Codespaces. The same good practices apply as elsewhere. Use Browse Mode for reading and Focus Mode for typing. If you have access to NVDA settings, setting maximum line length to ten thousand in Browse Mode can help with reading long lines of code or output more smoothly. And Chrome or Edge generally gives the most reliable Browse Mode behavior.

Jamie: How about JAWS?

Alex: With JAWS, use Virtual Cursor for reading general page content, then switch to PC Cursor when you're in the editor and writing code. The common shortcut mentioned is Insert plus Z or the numpad plus key, depending on layout and configuration. And again, Chrome or Edge tends to work best.

Jamie: And VoiceOver on macOS?

Alex: Use Quick Nav, often with left and right arrows, to move through the VS Code interface efficiently. The Rotor, with VO plus U, can help surface landmark regions. And if the editor text is not reading fluidly, check whether screen reader optimized mode is active.

Jamie: So across all three, the pattern is: learn the mode changes, use the browser that behaves most consistently, and verify accessibility mode if things feel off.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: Now let's cover keyboard shortcuts, because this is one of those topics where people often memorize too many at once.

Alex: Yes. Start with the ones that matter every day. Codespaces uses standard VS Code shortcuts. For navigation: Control Shift P opens the Command Palette. Control P opens Quick Open so you can search files by name. Control backtick toggles the integrated terminal. Control Shift E opens Explorer. Control Shift G opens Source Control. Control Shift X opens Extensions. And Control B toggles the sidebar.

Jamie: That's already a solid survival kit.

Alex: It is. For editing: Control Shift K deletes the current line. Alt Up Arrow or Alt Down Arrow moves a line up or down. Control slash toggles a line comment. Control G jumps to a line number. And F8 moves to the next error or issue.

Jamie: Even from the partial source, that one is important enough to say plainly: F8 helps you move through problems.

Alex: Exactly. It's a very useful shortcut during debugging or when fixing linter errors.

Jamie: What about source control shortcuts in the Codespaces context?

Alex: The key idea is that the Source Control panel works the same way it does in VS Code generally. Learners should know how to open it with Control Shift G, review changed files, stage changes, write a commit message, and commit. Even if you rely on menu navigation rather than memorizing every shortcut, the workflow is consistent.

Jamie: So if someone already learned source control in VS Code, they can transfer that knowledge directly.

Alex: Yes. Codespaces is meant to reduce surprises, not add them.

Jamie: Let's talk maintenance. Once you've created a Codespace, what does it mean to manage it?

Alex: Three common actions are stopping it, deleting it, and resuming it. Stopping a Codespace means shutting down the running cloud machine without necessarily destroying the environment. That's useful when you're done for now and want to preserve the workspace while not continuing to use compute time. Deleting a Codespace removes that Codespace environment entirely. That's a much bigger action. Resuming a Codespace means reopening one you've used before and continuing where you left off.

Jamie: This sounds like a place where beginners can make an expensive mistake, conceptually or literally.

Alex: Yes, especially confusing stop with delete. Stopping is like putting the workspace to sleep. Deleting is more final. Before deleting, make sure you've pushed important commits to GitHub.

Jamie: And where do learners usually do these actions?

Alex: Often from the Codespaces dashboard or related GitHub interface controls. The important conceptual model is that a Codespace is a managed cloud environment you can reopen later, not just a one-time browser tab.

Jamie: Now, dotfiles and persistent configuration. This is one of those topics that sounds advanced, but it matters a lot for accessibility.

Alex: Absolutely. Dotfiles are your personal shell and environment configuration files, and in the Codespaces world they let you carry forward custom setup from one Codespace to another. That can include shell aliases, prompt customization, scripts, and settings that make your environment more usable.

Jamie: So if a learner has accessibility-friendly terminal preferences, useful aliases, or startup scripts, those can become part of a repeatable environment.

Alex: Exactly. Persistent configuration matters because the more predictable your environment is, the less cognitive load you spend re-learning where things are or re-enabling tools every time.

Jamie: And paired with VS Code settings sync, that can make the cloud environment feel much closer to your own machine.

Alex: Yes. Your editor settings and your shell environment can work together to make Codespaces feel stable and personalized.

Jamie: Earlier you hinted at the difference between Codespaces and github dot dev. Let's really unpack that.

Alex: Great idea. GitHub dot dev is a lightweight browser editor experience. It's fast and convenient for quick edits, browsing files, and making simple changes. Codespaces, by contrast, provisions a full virtual machine with terminal access and the ability to run code.

Jamie: So the practical question is not which one is better, but which one matches the task.

Alex: Exactly. If you just need to inspect files or make a quick edit, github dot dev may be enough. If you need to run tests, install dependencies, use a terminal, or work in a complete reproducible development environment, use Codespaces.

Jamie: Can we do another quick chooser for different learners?

Alex: Sure. If you need the simplest no-setup editing experience and don't need a terminal, github dot dev can be a good quick option. If you need full accessibility features in a complete VS Code environment, want consistency across learners, or need to execute code, Codespaces is the stronger choice. For screen reader users in particular, local VS Code connected to Codespaces is often the most familiar path when browser limitations or extension availability become frustrating.

Jamie: Let's finish with troubleshooting, because that's where learners often need the most reassurance.

Alex: Absolutely.

Jamie: What if the Codespace takes a long time to open?

Alex: Provisioning can take a little time, especially the first time or when demand is higher. If it feels unusually slow, wait a bit, then refresh carefully or check the Codespaces dashboard. Also remember that larger machine types or more complex repository setup can add time. Slow opening does not necessarily mean failure.

Jamie: What if the screen reader stops reading after switching to the terminal?

Alex: That's a common mode issue. In NVDA, switch to Browse Mode to review terminal output, then back to Focus Mode to type. If the terminal itself is awkward, use Accessible View with Alt F2 while the terminal has focus. The problem is often not that reading is impossible, but that the current mode is wrong for the task.

Jamie: What if audio cues are not working in the browser?

Alex: Check VS Code settings for audio cues, and remember that browser permissions and audio behavior can differ from desktop apps. Try listing audio cues from the Command Palette, verify they're enabled, and consider using Chrome or Edge if your current browser is inconsistent.

Jamie: What if extensions I rely on locally are not available?

Alex: That's one of the main reasons to connect the Codespace to local VS Code desktop instead of relying only on the browser interface. The cloud machine can stay the same while the local desktop app gives you broader extension support.

Jamie: Now the painful one: I accidentally deleted my Codespace before pushing.

Alex: If changes were never committed and pushed, recovery may be difficult or impossible. That's why a good habit is to commit and push regularly, especially before deleting or making major environment changes. Stopping a Codespace is safer when you're unsure. Deleting should be deliberate.

Jamie: And finally, my changes are not showing in GitHub after committing.

Alex: A local commit inside the Codespace is not the same as pushing to GitHub. Check whether you actually pushed the branch. Also verify which branch you're on and whether the commit happened in the repository you expected. Many "missing changes" problems are really "committed locally but not pushed" or "pushed to a different branch."

Jamie: Before we close, can you give listeners the big picture?

Alex: Yes. GitHub Codespaces gives you a full VS Code development environment running in the cloud, with strong accessibility benefits: less local setup, more consistent workshop environments, support for screen reader optimized mode, audio cues, terminal accessibility features, and the option to connect through local VS Code for an even more familiar experience. Choose the browser version when convenience matters, choose local VS Code connection when you want your established desktop workflow, use the default machine size unless you truly need more power, and treat stop, resume, and delete as different actions with different consequences.

Jamie: And if you're deciding between quick editing and full development, remember: github dot dev is the quick editor, Codespaces is the full environment.

Alex: Exactly. And if you want the most trustworthy information as these tools evolve, GitHub Docs on Codespaces is the authoritative source, with GitHub Changelog and VS Code documentation also useful for updates and related accessibility behavior.

Jamie: That's a great place to end. Thanks, everyone.

62. Episode 32: GitHub Mobile

VoiceOver and TalkBack guide for iOS and Android GitHub apps.

Based on: Appendix V: GitHub Mobile

Download Episode 32 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 32: GitHub Mobile

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're focusing on GitHub Mobile: what it is, how to get around it, and how to use it accessibly on iOS and Android.

Jamie: And this feels especially useful for people who don't always want to open a laptop just to check a review request or respond to an issue.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub Mobile is best understood as a companion workflow. It brings issues, pull requests, notifications, and code review to iPhone, iPad, and Android devices. For many learners, especially blind and low-vision contributors, it can be a very practical way to stay engaged when away from the desktop.

Jamie: So this isn't, "replace your whole Git workflow with a phone."

Alex: Right. It is not your full desktop environment. You are not doing heavy branch management, conflict resolution, or large-scale coding comfortably in the app. But for triage, quick reviews, comments, issue management, and keeping up with team activity, it can be excellent.

Jamie: Before we go farther, can we do a fast mental map of the app for different kinds of users?

Alex: Yes. For screen reader users, GitHub Mobile supports VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android natively. A common pattern is swipe right to move to the next element, swipe left to move back, and double tap to activate. The app is organized around five bottom tabs, and that tab bar is one of the main navigation landmarks. For low-vision users, the app respects system text sizing, supports dark mode, and generally presents information in simpler mobile layouts. One especially important example is pull request diffs: on mobile they appear in a simplified single-column form rather than the more visually dense desktop diff table. For sighted users, the same structure applies: bottom tabs, notification badges, quick actions by swiping notifications, and a mobile-optimized PR diff view.

Jamie: So even though our audience here is blind and low vision, it's helpful to know the visual model too, because people collaborate across different access preferences.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: A quick administrative note. This appendix is a reference companion to the material on working with issues, and it's also closely connected to notifications workflows. And if you ever need the current source of truth, use GitHub Docs and the GitHub changelog, because mobile apps change over time.

Jamie: That's a really important reminder. A button name or gesture support detail may shift as the app evolves.

Alex: Yes. So learn the concepts, then verify the latest details in the official documentation.

Alex: Let's start with setup. Installing GitHub Mobile is straightforward. On iOS, you download GitHub from the App Store. On Android, you download it from Google Play.

Jamie: Then sign in with your GitHub account.

Alex: Right. And when the app asks whether to enable notifications, say yes if you want mobile to be genuinely useful. Notifications are central to the whole experience. They let you know about review requests, mentions, issue updates, and other activity without repeatedly checking the website.

Jamie: So if someone installs the app but disables notifications, they may miss the app's biggest advantage.

Alex: That's exactly it.

Alex: Once you're in, the app is organized around five tabs at the bottom of the screen.

Jamie: Let's name them slowly, because this is the core map.

Alex: Home, Notifications, Explore, Pull Requests, and Profile. Home is your personalized activity feed across repositories. Notifications is where mentions, review requests, and issue updates appear. Explore helps you discover repositories and trending projects. Pull Requests collects PRs assigned to you, created by you, or waiting for your review. And Profile contains your own profile information, repositories, stars, and settings.

Jamie: For a screen reader user, that tab bar becomes a repeated anchor point.

Alex: Yes. On iOS with VoiceOver, you might swipe across the bottom to move between tabs, then double tap to activate. Sighted users may single tap directly. The important idea is that these five tabs define the app's main structure.

Jamie: And if someone gets lost, returning to the tab bar can re-orient them.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Now let's turn to iOS and VoiceOver.

Jamie: Starting with the basics: how do you turn VoiceOver on?

Alex: Two common ways. You can triple-click the side button on newer iPhones, or the Home button on older devices, if that accessibility shortcut is configured. Or you can go through Settings, then Accessibility, then VoiceOver, and toggle it on.

Jamie: Once VoiceOver is running, what gestures matter most inside GitHub Mobile?

Alex: The essential set is: swipe right for next element, swipe left for previous element, double tap to activate the focused item, two-finger swipe up to read from the top, two-finger tap to pause or resume speech, three-finger swipe left or right to move between screens, and the two-finger scrub, that Z-shaped gesture, to go back.

Jamie: That last one is especially nice on iOS because it gives you a quick escape route.

Alex: Yes. If you've gone into a notification or opened a pull request and want to return, scrub can be very efficient.

Jamie: What about the rotor? Because that's one of the most powerful VoiceOver tools, and many learners underuse it.

Alex: Absolutely. In GitHub Mobile, the rotor can make navigation much faster. You open it by rotating two fingers on the screen as though turning a dial. Useful rotor settings here include Headings, Links, Form Controls, and Actions. Headings helps you jump between sections in an issue or pull request description. Links helps you move through linked issues, commits, or external URLs. Form Controls can take you directly to interactive fields, such as a comment box. And Actions can expose operations related to the focused element, such as assign, label, or close, when those actions are available.

Jamie: So if a learner is swiping endlessly through a long PR description, the advice is: stop, use the rotor, switch to Headings.

Alex: Exactly. That's one of the highest-value accessibility habits in the app.

Jamie: And if they want to comment?

Alex: A typical VoiceOver workflow is: navigate to the comment field, either by swiping or by using the rotor set to Form Controls. Double tap to activate the field and bring up the keyboard. Type the comment, with VoiceOver announcing characters as you enter them. Then swipe until you reach the Comment button and double tap to submit.

Jamie: That sounds simple, but it's worth stating because forms on mobile can feel disorienting.

Alex: Yes, especially when focus shifts unexpectedly or the keyboard changes the layout. A deliberate pattern helps.

Alex: Now let's look at Android with TalkBack.

Jamie: How do you enable it?

Alex: You can go to Settings, then Accessibility, then TalkBack, and toggle it on. Many Android devices also support a shortcut by holding both volume keys for three seconds, if that shortcut has been enabled.

Jamie: And the core gestures?

Alex: Much like VoiceOver in spirit, though not identical in detail. Swipe right for the next element, swipe left for the previous one, double tap to activate. Swipe up then down to scroll down. Swipe down then up to scroll up. Swipe right then left to go back. And two-finger swipe down to read from the top.

Jamie: One thing that helps learners is remembering that screen readers often share a navigation philosophy even when the exact gestures differ.

Alex: Well said. Learn the pattern: move, activate, read continuously, go back, adjust granularity.

Jamie: That brings us to the TalkBack menu.

Alex: Yes. You can open the TalkBack menu with a three-finger tap, or on some setups by swiping down then right. In that menu, you can do things like change reading granularity to character, word, line, or paragraph; access reading controls; and copy text.

Jamie: Why does granularity matter in GitHub Mobile?

Alex: Because technical text can be dense. If you're reviewing a pull request, reading an issue description, or trying to inspect a changed line, the ability to move by character or word can be essential. It gives you finer control than simply swiping element by element.

Jamie: And writing a comment with TalkBack?

Alex: The common pattern is: locate the comment field, which TalkBack may announce as something like "Edit text, double tap to edit." Double tap to enter the field. Type using the on-screen keyboard or dictation. Then locate the Comment button and double tap to submit.

Jamie: So the iOS and Android workflows are parallel, even though the screen reader mechanics differ.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now to one of the strongest parts of GitHub Mobile: notifications.

Jamie: This is where mobile can actually be better than the website for some accessibility users, right?

Alex: Very often, yes. The Notifications tab presents activity in a clean, linear list. For assistive technology users, especially screen reader users, that can be much easier to navigate than a more crowded web page.

Jamie: Let's paint the picture.

Alex: Each notification appears as an item in a chronological list. Unread items typically have an unread indicator. For sighted users, that may be a blue dot on the left. The row also includes useful context like repository name, notification type, and title. For screen reader users, swiping through the list one item at a time can make triage very manageable.

Jamie: And there are quick actions too.

Alex: Yes. Swipe left on a notification to reveal actions such as Mark as read, Archive, and Unsubscribe. In some contexts, swiping right can mark a notification as done. Tapping the notification opens the underlying issue or pull request.

Jamie: How does this translate for VoiceOver users, since swipe gestures can mean navigation rather than app-specific actions?

Alex: Great question. On iOS, custom actions may be available through the VoiceOver Actions rotor item on each notification. So instead of relying purely on sighted-style swipe gestures, a VoiceOver user can focus the notification, switch the rotor to Actions, and then perform the available action.

Jamie: That's a very helpful clarification.

Alex: Filtering is another important feature. At the top right of the Notifications tab, there is a filter control, often represented visually by a funnel icon. You can filter by type, such as issues, pull requests, or releases; by repository; and by reason, such as being mentioned, assigned, or asked to review.

Jamie: And with a screen reader?

Alex: Those filters should appear as accessible form elements. Open the filter panel, navigate through the available controls, and toggle the criteria you want. This lets you narrow a busy inbox to the most relevant activity.

Jamie: So if someone says, "My notifications are overwhelming," the answer is not just archive more. It's also filter intelligently.

Alex: Exactly. Filter by reason, filter by repository, and use quick actions aggressively.

Alex: Let's move into pull requests. Mobile is well suited to quick PR review: checking status, reading the description, scanning changed files, and leaving an approval or short comment.

Jamie: But maybe not a forty-file architectural review on a phone.

Alex: Correct. Use the right tool for the task. When you open a pull request in GitHub Mobile, you'll generally encounter a few main sections: the Description, the Commits list, Files changed, and Checks for CI or other status information.

Jamie: And these are often announced as headings.

Alex: Yes. That's important. VoiceOver users can use the rotor set to Headings to jump among those sections. TalkBack users can use heading navigation or reading granularity methods available on their device. That means you don't have to swipe through every single element in sequence.

Jamie: Let's walk through leaving a review.

Alex: A typical flow is: find the Review changes button, activate it, choose whether you want to Approve, Request changes, or Comment, optionally add text in the review comment field, and then activate Submit review.

Jamie: So the review is not just a comment; it's a structured decision.

Alex: Exactly. Approve means the changes look good. Request changes signals that the author should revise something before merge. Comment lets you leave feedback without explicitly approving or blocking.

Jamie: And viewing diffs on mobile has a distinct accessibility advantage.

Alex: It often does. In the Files Changed area, GitHub Mobile uses a simplified diff. Additions and removals are shown as text rather than forcing you through a two-column desktop-style table. Changed lines may be announced in a direct way, such as "Added" followed by content, or "Removed" followed by content.

Jamie: That can be easier to understand with a screen reader than a dense side-by-side layout.

Alex: Yes. On a small screen, the simpler structure can actually improve access.

Alex: Now let's talk about issues.

Jamie: This is one of the most practical mobile tasks: filing something when you notice it, instead of telling yourself you'll remember later.

Alex: Exactly. To file an issue, you generally navigate to the repository, choose Issues, then find the plus button or New Issue. Enter the title and body. Optionally set labels, assignees, and a milestone if those are part of the workflow. Then submit the issue.

Jamie: Even if the source text was truncated there, the workflow is clear: repository, issues, new issue, fill in fields, optionally set metadata, submit.

Alex: Right. And those optional fields matter in team workflows. Labels classify the issue, assignees indicate responsibility, and milestones connect the issue to a broader goal or release.

Jamie: What about finding issues that matter to you?

Alex: In mobile, you can use your notifications, repository issue lists, and your personal areas in the app to return to issues you've opened, been assigned, or been mentioned in. The core idea is to combine repository navigation with notification-driven access, rather than hunting manually every time.

Jamie: So for many learners, notifications become the front door to issue work too.

Alex: Very much so.

Alex: At this point it's worth stepping back and asking: what does mobile do well, and what should remain a desktop task?

Jamie: Let's make that explicit.

Alex: GitHub Mobile does well at staying current. Notifications, quick triage, lightweight issue filing, short comments, straightforward PR reviews, and checking checks or CI status are all good mobile tasks. The interface is linear, compact, and often easier for assistive technology users than a more cluttered desktop page.

Jamie: And desktop still wins for deep work.

Alex: Yes. If you need to read a very large pull request, compare lots of files, manage complicated issue templates, perform substantial code editing, resolve merge conflicts, or do anything that depends on a full Git client and development environment, desktop is the better choice.

Jamie: So mobile is not lesser. It's specialized.

Alex: Exactly. Think of it as the right tool for quick response and continuous awareness.

Alex: Let's finish with common issues and workarounds, because these practical frustrations matter.

Jamie: First: VoiceOver skips some pull request descriptions.

Alex: A good workaround is to switch the rotor to Headings or Links and navigate by structure instead of plain sequential swiping. If the description contains complex formatting, try moving by headings, then by links, and explore the content in smaller pieces. If necessary, reopen the item or use another navigation mode rather than assuming the content is absent.

Jamie: Second: TalkBack does not announce the new notifications badge.

Alex: In that case, don't rely only on the badge. Open the Notifications tab directly and review the list. Mobile badges can be inconsistent across apps and devices, so the reliable method is to check the tab itself.

Jamie: Third: the keyboard covers the comment field.

Alex: This is a common mobile problem. After activating the comment field, you may need to scroll slightly, dismiss and reopen the keyboard, rotate the device if your setup allows, or move focus carefully until the submit control comes back into view. On either platform, patience and incremental navigation help.

Jamie: Fourth: after writing a review, you can't find the Submit button.

Alex: This often means focus is still trapped near the keyboard or text field. Try navigating past the editing area deliberately. On iOS, rotor settings like Form Controls can help jump among interactive elements. On Android, move through controls methodically or adjust granularity if needed. If the button still doesn't appear, dismiss the keyboard and continue exploring the screen.

Jamie: And fifth: the app crashes or freezes.

Alex: The practical steps are the usual ones: force close and reopen the app, make sure it's updated, and if the problem persists, sign out and sign back in through Profile and Settings. If you still cannot complete the task, switch to the web or desktop workflow so your work is not blocked.

Jamie: That's an important accessibility principle in itself: have a fallback path.

Alex: Absolutely. Accessibility isn't only about one perfect interface. It's also about knowing alternate routes when a tool becomes unreliable.

Jamie: Can we close with a compact recap?

Alex: Certainly. GitHub Mobile gives you five main tabs for navigation: Home, Notifications, Explore, Pull Requests, and Profile. On iOS, VoiceOver users rely on familiar gestures and especially the rotor, with Headings, Form Controls, Links, and Actions being especially valuable. On Android, TalkBack users use core swipe and activation gestures, plus the TalkBack menu for reading granularity and controls. Notifications are one of the strongest mobile features, because they provide a clean linear inbox with filtering and quick actions. Pull request review works well for lightweight review, comments, and approvals, with a simplified diff view that can be more accessible than desktop on a small screen. Issues can be filed and managed on mobile, especially for quick capture and response. And throughout all of this, mobile is best seen as a companion to desktop rather than a full replacement.

Jamie: And if learners want the latest details, they should check GitHub Docs, the GitHub Mobile docs specifically, and the GitHub changelog.

Alex: Exactly. Official references matter, because apps evolve.

Jamie: That was a practical one.

Alex: It was. And for many contributors, mastering mobile means staying connected to open source and team workflows in the moments between full desktop sessions.

63. Episode 33: Publishing with GitHub Pages

Free static site hosting, custom domains, HTTPS, and accessibility.

Based on: Appendix W: Publishing with GitHub Pages

Download Episode 33 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 33: Publishing with GitHub Pages

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re talking about publishing a static website with GitHub Pages, which is one of the simplest ways to take files from a repository and make them available on the web.

Jamie: And this is especially useful for documentation, workshop materials, portfolios, project home pages, and other sites that don’t need a back-end server, right?

Alex: Exactly. GitHub Pages is built into GitHub. For a simple site, you don’t need to rent a server or build a complicated deployment pipeline. You can publish directly from a repository.

Jamie: Before we go deeper, I want to make sure we frame it for our learners. This appendix is a reference companion to earlier material on open source culture and also connects to later next-step work. And the main authoritative source behind the material is GitHub’s Pages documentation.

Alex: Right. So think of this lesson as practical, but also grounded in the official docs.

Alex: Here’s the basic idea. GitHub Pages hosts static files. That means files are served as they already exist: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, PDFs, and similar assets.

Jamie: So when people hear website, they might imagine a full web app. But GitHub Pages is not running server-side code for you.

Alex: That’s the key distinction. No PHP, no Python app server, no Node request handlers, no database-backed logic running on the server. If your project needs dynamic server behavior, GitHub Pages is not the right host by itself.

Jamie: But for static content, it’s great.

Alex: Very often, yes. It’s good for documentation sites, workshop materials like this project, project landing pages, personal portfolios, and simple blogs, including some Jekyll-based workflows.

Jamie: And the URL pattern matters too. Usually the published address looks like username dot github dot io, slash repository name, slash.

Alex: Yes. In the common case, it’s: username dot github dot io slash repository-name slash. For a user site or an organization profile repository named username slash username dot github dot io, the published site becomes just username dot github dot io.

Jamie: Let’s talk setup. If I’m on GitHub dot com and I want to enable Pages for a repository, what do I do?

Alex: Go to the repository. Open Settings. In the left sidebar, find Pages under the Code and automation group. Then under Build and deployment, choose how the site will be published.

Jamie: And there are two major choices.

Alex: Right. One is Deploy from a branch. The other is GitHub Actions.

Jamie: If I choose deploy from a branch, I then choose a branch like main or master, and a folder source.

Alex: Yes. The folder choices are the repository root, shown as slash, or the docs folder, shown as slash docs. Then you select the combination and choose Save.

Jamie: And after that, GitHub usually builds and deploys within a minute or two, and once the first deployment succeeds, the site URL appears near the top of the Pages settings.

Alex: That’s the typical flow.

Jamie: Let’s do the accessibility walk-through too, because that matters here.

Alex: Absolutely. For screen reader users, the Settings control is a link in the repository’s top navigation and has the accessible name Settings. Inside repository settings, the Pages link is in the left sidebar under the Code and automation grouping. The branch and folder controls are standard select elements, so you can navigate them with arrow keys.

Jamie: And for low-vision users, the Pages screen follows the same general settings layout GitHub uses elsewhere. You click Settings, then look in the left sidebar for Pages. The deployment status uses familiar visual signals like a green check for success and a red X for failure.

Alex: Also important: the published website does not inherit accessibility styling from GitHub itself. Your site’s own CSS has to provide readable font sizing, adequate contrast, visible focus indicators, and so on.

Jamie: And for sighted mouse users, it’s still just Settings, then Pages, then choose the branch and folder source, then Save. After success, there’s generally a green banner with the site URL.

Alex: Now let’s compare publishing sources a little more carefully. Deploying from a branch is the simplest model. GitHub reads files directly from the branch.

Jamie: And the two folder modes behave differently.

Alex: They do. If you choose root, GitHub serves the repository root. If you choose docs, it serves only the docs folder. Using docs is often the better practice because it isolates published content from source code and other repository files.

Jamie: Especially when a project has a build pipeline and the built site lives in a specific output folder.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: So when do we reach for GitHub Actions instead?

Alex: When the site needs a build step before publishing. For example, if your source is Markdown and you generate HTML, or if you use a static site generator such as Jekyll, Hugo, or Eleventy, or if you want automated tests to run before deployment, including accessibility checks.

Jamie: And in this project, there is a build step.

Alex: Yes. A representative workflow here would check out the repository, run the Node script that builds the HTML, then upload the html folder as the Pages artifact.

Jamie: That brings us to the project-specific part: the html folder.

Alex: Right. This project already has a prebuilt HTML mirror of the Markdown content in an html folder, created by scripts slash build-html dot js.

Jamie: But GitHub Pages, when you use branch deployment, only supports the root folder or docs as the source folder.

Alex: That’s the constraint. So if your output is in html, you need to adapt.

Jamie: Let’s start with the manual approach.

Alex: Option A is manual publishing from the html folder. Since html is not an allowed branch-based Pages source folder, one safe approach is to copy the contents of html into docs.

Jamie: So conceptually, generate the site into html, copy those built files into docs, commit docs, push, then configure Pages to use the branch and the docs folder.

Alex: Yes. The example commands are essentially: copy recursively from html into docs, add docs to Git, commit with a message noting that HTML output was published to docs for GitHub Pages, and push.

Jamie: Then in Pages settings, set the source to the branch, here given as master, and the folder to slash docs.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: There’s also a rename option, but with an important warning.

Alex: Option A2 is renaming html to docs after first changing the build script output path. That could work in a project where docs is free to use for generated output.

Jamie: But not in this project.

Alex: Right. This project already uses docs for Markdown source files, so renaming html to docs would create a conflict. That’s why copying into docs, or better yet using GitHub Actions, is safer here.

Jamie: Let’s unpack the GitHub Actions approach, because a lot of learners hear workflow YAML and tense up.

Alex: Fair. The purpose of the workflow is straightforward: on each push to the chosen branch, GitHub runs a series of steps to rebuild the site and deploy it.

Jamie: In the example workflow, the trigger is a push to master.

Alex: Yes. The workflow requests permissions needed for Pages deployment, including reading contents, writing Pages data, and using an ID token. It also sets a concurrency group for pages so deployments are managed predictably.

Jamie: Then there are two jobs: build and deploy.

Alex: The build job runs on Ubuntu, checks out the repository, sets up Node version 20, installs dependencies with npm install, runs node scripts slash build-html dot js, and uploads the html folder as the Pages artifact.

Jamie: And the deploy job waits for build, then deploys that artifact using the official deploy-pages action.

Alex: Exactly. That means you don’t have to copy files manually into docs. The workflow turns html into the deployed site automatically.

Jamie: Which is cleaner and less error-prone once you’re comfortable with Actions.

Alex: Usually, yes.

Jamie: Now custom domains. A lot of people don’t want the default github dot io address forever.

Alex: GitHub Pages supports custom domains, so instead of something like community-access dot github dot io slash Learning-Room, you can use a domain you control, like a subdomain or apex domain.

Jamie: What’s the setup sequence?

Alex: In repository Settings, then Pages, enter the domain in the Custom domain field and save. GitHub creates a CNAME file in the repository root containing that domain name. Then you configure DNS with your domain provider.

Jamie: And the DNS record type depends on whether it’s a subdomain or an apex domain.

Alex: Right. For a subdomain like learning dot community-access dot org, you typically create a CNAME pointing to the GitHub Pages host, here illustrated as community-access dot github dot io. For an apex domain like community-access dot org, you use A records.

Jamie: And the current A record IPs listed here are four addresses: 185 point 199 point 108 point 153, then 109 point 153, 110 point 153, and 111 point 153.

Alex: Correct. And DNS changes may take up to 48 hours to propagate, so this is one of those places where patience matters.

Jamie: Then GitHub checks and verifies the domain once DNS is configured.

Alex: Yes, and there’s another security step learners should know: domain verification.

Jamie: That’s to reduce domain takeover risk?

Alex: Exactly. GitHub recommends verifying your custom domain in your account or organization settings under Pages. That way, if the domain is ever temporarily removed from one repo, another party has a harder time claiming it for their own GitHub Pages site.

Jamie: Let’s move into HTTPS and security more broadly.

Alex: For github dot io subdomains, HTTPS is enforced automatically. For custom domains, once DNS has propagated, you should enable Enforce HTTPS in Pages settings.

Jamie: And GitHub Pages uses Let’s Encrypt to provision the certificate automatically.

Alex: Yes. When HTTPS is enforced, HTTP traffic is redirected to HTTPS.

Jamie: And there’s a big security reminder here: do not put secrets into a GitHub Pages repository.

Alex: Exactly. No API keys, no private credentials, no confidential data. A GitHub Pages site serves public content. Treat everything in the published site and its repository as potentially public unless the hosting model and repo settings clearly guarantee otherwise.

Jamie: Now to one of the most important parts for this audience: accessibility of the published site itself.

Alex: Yes. Publishing accessible source material is not enough if the resulting website becomes harder to navigate after deployment. The published site should meet the same accessibility expectations as the source.

Jamie: So let’s go point by point.

Alex: First, navigation and landmarks. Use meaningful landmark regions and semantic structure so screen reader users can move efficiently among major areas of the page. That usually means a clear header, navigation region, main content, and footer where appropriate.

Jamie: And headings should reflect the content hierarchy, not just visual styling.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Next: skip navigation.

Alex: Provide a skip link so keyboard and screen reader users can move past repeated navigation and get to the main content quickly. It should be keyboard reachable and visible on focus.

Jamie: Then focus management, especially if the site behaves like a single-page app or has in-page navigation.

Alex: Right. If navigation changes the visible content without a full page reload, manage focus intentionally so users understand that context has changed. Don’t leave keyboard focus stranded in an old control while the page appears to have moved somewhere else.

Jamie: Images are another big one.

Alex: Every meaningful image needs appropriate alt text. Decorative images should not create noise for assistive technology. The rule is not just add alt text everywhere. It’s use the right text alternative for the function and meaning of the image.

Jamie: Color contrast comes up a lot with static sites because people may assume a simple site is automatically accessible.

Alex: It is not automatic. Your CSS needs sufficient color contrast, readable text sizing, and visible interactive states. GitHub Pages does not fix poor contrast for you.

Jamie: And testing has to happen after deployment, not just before.

Alex: Absolutely. Test the published site itself. Sometimes the generated HTML, asset paths, deployment context, or production CSS changes what users experience.

Jamie: What are some good post-deployment checks?

Alex: At minimum: verify page titles are correct and unique enough to orient users, confirm landmarks and heading structure still make sense, tab through navigation and interactive controls, test the skip link, check focus visibility, inspect image alt behavior, confirm color contrast in the real published theme, and try the site with a screen reader on the actual deployed URL.

Jamie: So the accessibility learning cards here really boil down to this: the hosted site is its own user experience, and it has to be evaluated as such.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: How does this connect back to GitHub Actions and continuous deployment?

Alex: Continuous deployment means every push can rebuild and republish the site automatically. That’s efficient, but it also means mistakes can go live quickly.

Jamie: Which is why accessibility checks in the workflow are valuable.

Alex: Yes. You can add automated accessibility checks to the workflow so common issues are caught in CI before or during deployment. Automation won’t replace human testing, but it can flag missing alt text, obvious structural problems, and some color contrast or labeling issues depending on the tooling.

Jamie: So a mature workflow might build the site, run accessibility checks, and only then deploy if everything passes.

Alex: That’s the idea.

Jamie: What limitations should learners keep in mind with GitHub Pages?

Alex: The biggest one is the static-only model. No server-side processing, no custom back-end logic. Also, if your source folder arrangement doesn’t match Pages’ branch deployment options, you may need a docs copy step or an Actions-based workflow. And custom domains and HTTPS can involve DNS timing and certificate delays that aren’t under your direct control.

Jamie: So it’s wonderfully convenient, but it’s not universal hosting.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Let’s finish with troubleshooting, because that’s usually where stress spikes.

Alex: Good idea.

Jamie: First: the site is not updating after a push.

Alex: Check whether you pushed to the correct branch, whether Pages is configured for the branch and folder you intended, and whether the deployment actually succeeded. In a branch-based setup, make sure the changed files are in the published folder, not just somewhere else in the repo. In an Actions-based setup, inspect the workflow run for build or deploy failures.

Jamie: Also remember that deployments may take a minute or two, and browsers can cache aggressively.

Alex: Yes. Give it a little time, then refresh carefully or test in a private window.

Jamie: Next: 404 on all pages except index.

Alex: That often points to path issues. Internal links, asset paths, or route assumptions may work locally but break when the site is hosted under a repository subpath. Remember that many project Pages sites live under slash repository-name slash, not the domain root.

Jamie: So absolute paths can be dangerous if they assume the site lives at slash.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about HTTPS certificate not provisioning?

Alex: Usually check the custom domain DNS first. If DNS isn’t correct or hasn’t fully propagated, certificate provisioning can stall. Wait for propagation, confirm records, then try enforcing HTTPS again. This is especially common right after initial domain setup.

Jamie: And the accessibility-specific troubleshooting item: a screen reader announces the wrong page title.

Alex: That usually means the built HTML has incorrect title elements, duplicated templates, or client-side navigation isn’t updating document titles when the visible content changes. The fix is to inspect the deployed page source and the actual browser title behavior, not just the local authoring files.

Jamie: So again, test the deployed experience.

Alex: Always.

Jamie: Before we wrap, I want to mention the source trail because that matters for technical learners.

Alex: Yes. The key authoritative references here are GitHub Docs broadly, the GitHub Changelog, the GitHub Pages docs, the Pages quickstart, and where relevant related Git and security documentation. For accessibility expectations, WCAG overview material is part of the factual grounding.

Jamie: And that section-level source map is useful as a verification tool. It tells you where to confirm each major section if GitHub changes interfaces or workflow details over time.

Alex: Exactly. That’s a strong habit for open source learners: learn the concept, then know where the living documentation lives.

Jamie: So the big picture is: GitHub Pages gives you a low-friction path from repository to public static site. You can publish from a branch or through Actions, adapt build outputs like html when needed, add a custom domain, enable HTTPS, and keep accessibility central from source through deployment.

Alex: Well said. And if you remember just one thing, let it be this: publishing is not the end of accessibility work. The deployed site is the product users actually experience.

Jamie: That’s it for today.

Alex: See you next time.

64. Episode 34: GitHub Actions and Workflows

Workflow YAML structure, CI/CD, automation, and the Actions marketplace.

Based on: Appendix Q: GitHub Actions and Workflows

Download Episode 34 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 34: GitHub Actions and Workflows

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're talking about GitHub Actions and workflows, which sounds technical, but for most contributors the practical question is much simpler: when GitHub runs automated checks on your pull request, what are those checks doing, what do the results mean, and what should you do next?

Jamie: And that really matters in open source, because a person can make a perfectly good contribution and still feel stuck when a red X appears.

Alex: Exactly. Automation is everywhere in real repositories. Tests run, linters run, docs builds run, accessibility scans run, and sometimes deployment previews run too. You do not need to become a workflow author to contribute well. But you do need to become comfortable reading the signals.

Jamie: Before we get into the mechanics, I want to call out a few practical notes. This lesson has an audio companion role in the course, and it's also connected to earlier material on issue templates and related material on accessibility agents. And if you want the official reference for the platform itself, GitHub's documentation on understanding Actions is the authority.

Alex: Well said. Also, if you're a blind or low-vision learner, this topic has a lot of interface reading in it, so we'll keep surfacing navigation strategies, not just definitions.

Alex: Let's start with the core idea. GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation system. A repository can define automated processes that run when certain events happen. For example, someone pushes commits, opens or updates a pull request, submits a review, posts a comment, or publishes a release.

Jamie: So when people say, the checks are running, that's usually GitHub Actions behind the scenes?

Alex: Often yes. Think of it as a configurable robot assistant for a repository. Maintainers tell that assistant what events to watch for and what jobs to run in response. Those jobs might test code, check formatting, scan for accessibility problems, check spelling, build documentation, or publish a preview version of a site.

Jamie: And the key reassurance here is that contributors usually do not need to write the automation.

Alex: Right. Most contributors are readers of workflow results, not authors of workflow files. Your everyday skill is understanding what ran, whether it passed, and what to fix if it did not.

Jamie: Can we make that concrete for different learners?

Alex: Yes. If you're using a screen reader, workflow files live in a folder named dot github, inside a subfolder named workflows. On GitHub, the T shortcut for go to file can help you search for files ending in dot yml there. The Actions tab sits in the repository navigation landmark, so in NVDA or JAWS you can jump by landmarks with D to find it quickly. And again, you do not need to write YAML just to contribute. If you're a low-vision learner, it helps to know that the Actions tab uses a play-button style icon in the top navigation. Zooming in can make the label easier to catch. Workflow files use indentation-sensitive syntax, so in VS Code, larger font size and visible whitespace can make the structure much easier to read. On pull requests, the check results are paired with small colored icons, so zoom to a comfortable level and read the text beside the icons rather than relying on color alone. And for sighted learners, the Actions tab is in the top repository navigation, and the quickest way to understand a workflow file is usually to open one in the Code tab and look for its trigger section and its job steps.

Jamie: Let's build the vocabulary, because this topic gets confusing fast if all the words blur together.

Alex: Good idea. A workflow is the complete automated process described in one YAML file. A repository can have many workflows. A job is one major unit inside a workflow. Jobs usually run on their own machine environment. A step is one task inside a job, like running a shell command or calling a reusable action. An action is a reusable unit of automation, almost like a plugin. Many public actions are shared through GitHub Marketplace. A runner is the machine that executes the job. Often it's a GitHub-hosted virtual server. A trigger, or event, is what starts the workflow. Push, pull request, schedule, and manual launch are common examples. A status check is the pass or fail result that appears on a pull request. An artifact is a file produced by a workflow, like a report, build output, or downloadable package. A secret is an encrypted value stored in repository settings so workflows can use sensitive data without exposing it directly. And YAML is the format used to write workflow files. Indentation matters a lot.

Jamie: There are also two little YAML keys that people see constantly: on and runs-on.

Alex: Exactly. The key called on defines the trigger. The key called runs-on tells GitHub what operating system or runner environment to use, like ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, or macos-latest.

Jamie: Now where do these files actually live?

Alex: In a very specific location: a folder named .github, and inside that, a folder named workflows. So the full path is .github slash workflows slash some-file-name dot yml.

Jamie: And that location is not optional.

Alex: Correct. GitHub expects workflow files there. Example names might include ci dot yml for tests, lint dot yml for style checks, a11y-scan dot yml for accessibility scanning, or deploy dot yml for deployment after merge.

Jamie: That dot at the start of dot github matters too.

Alex: It does. It means the folder is hidden by convention. On GitHub.com, you can still navigate to it in the file browser, or use the T shortcut to search for files. In VS Code, it appears in the Explorer, though some setups may require hidden files to be shown. For screen reader users, it's useful to hear the folder name as dot github, then workflows inside it. And when you hear filenames ending in dot yml, those are workflow definitions written in YAML.

Jamie: Can we walk through what a workflow file looks like without turning this into a YAML programming lesson?

Alex: Absolutely. Imagine a file named ci dot yml. At the top, it might say name: CI. That's the display name you'll often see in the Actions tab. Then it has on, the trigger section. Maybe it runs on push to the main branch and also on pull_request targeting main. Then it has jobs. Inside jobs, perhaps there is one job called test. That job says runs-on: ubuntu-latest, meaning it uses a Linux runner. Then under steps, you might see a sequence like: check out the code, set up Node.js, install dependencies, and run tests.

Jamie: So the logic is basically: when this event happens, run this job, and inside the job run these steps.

Alex: Exactly. And reading a workflow file is usually easier if you ask three questions. First, what triggers it? Second, what jobs does it define? Third, what steps run inside those jobs?

Jamie: And if the step that runs tests returns an error, the job fails, and that failure shows up on the pull request.

Alex: That's the practical consequence. You do not need to memorize the syntax. You need to recognize the structure well enough to interpret what the automation is trying to do.

Alex: Now let's talk triggers, because they explain why something ran when it did. Common triggers include push, which means any commit pushed to a branch; pull_request, which covers a pull request being opened, updated, synchronized, or reopened; pull_request_review, when someone submits a review; issue_comment, when someone comments on an issue or PR; schedule, which is a recurring timer; workflow_dispatch, which allows a manual run from the Actions tab; release, when a release is published; and merge_group, which is used with merge queues.

Jamie: If I'm contributing, the most important one is pull_request.

Alex: Yes. That's usually what causes checks to appear on your PR. Sometimes push also matters, especially if the repository runs checks on every branch update, but pull_request is the one most contributors experience directly.

Jamie: Okay, now the part learners really care about: the status checks on a pull request.

Alex: When you open a PR in a repository that uses GitHub Actions, you'll usually find a checks or status checks section on the Conversation tab, often near the merge area. A spinning yellow or orange indicator means checks are still running. Wait. A green checkmark means the relevant checks passed. A red X means one or more checks failed, and you should read the failure before trying to merge. A gray slashed circle usually means a check was skipped, often intentionally. And sometimes you'll encounter a warning state that is not a hard blocker. It still deserves review, but it may not prevent merging.

Jamie: That distinction matters, because learners often see anything that's not green and assume disaster.

Alex: Right. Not every non-green state means you broke the project.

Jamie: What about navigating this with a screen reader?

Alex: For NVDA or JAWS in browse mode, open the pull request Conversation tab, jump by headings with H or by heading level if that works well in your setup, find the checks section, then move through the individual check items. Each result is typically announced as a link or button with its name and status. Activate a failed check with Enter to reveal or open more detail. For VoiceOver on macOS in Safari, open the Rotor with VO+U, move to Headings, locate the checks section, then read through the listed results with VO navigation. Activate a selected check with VO+Space.

Jamie: And then there's the idea of required versus non-required checks.

Alex: Yes. Required checks must pass before a PR can be merged. Non-required checks are informative. They may still point to a real problem, but they are not configured as merge blockers.

Jamie: So if I see a failed non-required check, I shouldn't ignore it automatically, but I also shouldn't assume the merge button is permanently blocked.

Alex: Exactly. The right question is, is this required, and what is it telling me? A useful mental model here is: status checks are automated reviewers. They do not replace human review, but they often catch predictable problems quickly.

Jamie: Let's move to the Actions tab itself, because sometimes the pull request only shows the summary and you need to inspect the run.

Alex: That's right. The Actions tab is where you can browse workflow runs across the repository. On GitHub, it's in the repository's main navigation. For screen reader users, a reliable way to reach it is to jump through landmarks or tab through the repository navigation until you hear Actions. Once there, you'll find a list of workflow runs, often with the workflow name, branch, triggering event, commit message, time, and status.

Jamie: How would someone navigate that list efficiently in NVDA or JAWS?

Alex: In browse mode, use heading navigation and links navigation to move among workflow names and run entries. The page is often structured with headings, links, and status text. Open the run you want, then explore the jobs and steps. If the page feels busy, switching between browse mode reading and focused interaction can help.

Jamie: And in VoiceOver on macOS?

Alex: Use the Rotor to jump among headings, links, and landmarks. Once inside a run page, VO navigation can move through job names and step entries. The key is to identify the status summary first, then the failing job, then the failing step.

Jamie: What details should a learner expect inside one run?

Alex: Usually you'll find the overall result, then one or more jobs, and within each job a sequence of steps. Expanding a failed step reveals log output. That log is often the most important evidence: it tells you what command ran and what error it produced. Sometimes the run also includes artifacts, such as generated reports or preview outputs, which can be downloaded.

Jamie: Now let's name the kinds of workflows learners are likely to encounter over and over.

Alex: First, continuous integration, or CI. This is the general category for automatically building and testing the project whenever code changes. Second, linting or code style checks. These look for formatting problems, style violations, or patterns the project considers incorrect. Third, spelling and documentation checks. These catch typos, broken docs builds, malformed markdown, or documentation rules. Fourth, accessibility scanning. These workflows try to detect common accessibility issues, often in web content. Fifth, security scanning. These look for known vulnerable dependencies, insecure patterns, or other security concerns. Sixth, deployment or preview builds. These create a temporary preview of a site or publish a new version after changes are merged.

Jamie: I like that list because it helps learners interpret a check name. If the workflow is called CI, it probably runs tests. If it's called lint, it's probably style. If it's called preview, it may be building something you can inspect.

Alex: Exactly. The workflow name is a clue about the kind of feedback you're getting.

Jamie: Let's tackle the emotional side and the practical side together: what should you do when a check fails?

Alex: Step one: don't panic. A failed check is information, not a judgment about your worth or your ability. Step two: navigate to the failed check. From the PR checks section or the Actions tab, open the failed run. Step three: find the failing step. Don't stop at the workflow name. You need the exact job and exact step that failed. Step four: read the error message carefully. Look for the command that ran, the file involved, the line number if one is given, and whether the issue is a test failure, formatting issue, missing dependency, syntax error, or something else. Step five: fix the issue locally or in the web editor, depending on the kind of change and the repository's workflow. Some problems are quick text edits. Others are best fixed in VS Code where you can run tools locally. Step six: commit and push the fix. That usually retriggers the relevant checks automatically. Step seven: if you're stuck, ask for help. Leave a comment on the PR or issue, explain what check failed, what you already tried, and what part you don't understand.

Jamie: Let's slow that down with a realistic example. Suppose the lint check fails.

Alex: Then the failing step might say something like run linter, and the log may point to a file with a formatting problem. Maybe a line is too long, indentation is off, or a style rule was violated. You fix the file, commit, push, and the lint workflow runs again.

Jamie: And if the CI test fails?

Alex: The log may show a test name, expected versus actual output, or a missing setup step. In a beginner-friendly repository, this may still be something you can fix. In a more complex project, you may need maintainer guidance. The important skill is locating and naming the failure clearly.

Jamie: So a useful learning card here would be: failed check, open it; failing workflow is not enough, find the failing step; read the message; make a fix; push again; ask for help if needed.

Alex: Perfect summary.

Jamie: Now security and permissions. This is the part where learners can accidentally click through prompts without understanding the risk.

Alex: Yes, and that is worth taking seriously. Some workflows need approval before they can run, especially in contexts involving pull requests from forks or contributors who do not yet have trusted status in the repository. The reason is security. Workflows can execute code, and maintainers need to protect secrets, infrastructure, and deployment systems.

Jamie: So if a workflow says it is waiting for approval, that is not a personal rejection.

Alex: Not at all. It's a guardrail.

Jamie: What should contributors never do?

Alex: Never paste secrets, tokens, passwords, API keys, or private credentials into workflow files, issue comments, pull request comments, logs, or screenshots. Never approve or modify automation you do not understand just because you're trying to make a red message disappear. And never assume that because something is automated, it is automatically safe.

Jamie: What about Dependabot?

Alex: Dependabot is GitHub's tool for automated dependency updates and some security-related pull requests. You may see PRs created by it, and repositories may have workflows that respond to those updates. The key contributor takeaway is that automated dependency PRs are normal, but they are still subject to checks, review, and security awareness.

Jamie: Let's spend real time on accessibility-focused workflows, since this course cares about accessible contribution practices.

Alex: Absolutely. Some repositories run accessibility-specific workflows. GitHub has its own accessibility-related scanning action offerings, and many projects use other common tools in a11y workflows as well.

Jamie: What kinds of tools are we talking about?

Alex: Often browser-based or static analysis tools that catch issues like missing alt text, insufficient form labels, color contrast concerns detectable from code, missing ARIA attributes in certain contexts, heading structure problems, or landmark-related issues. Commonly used tooling in the broader ecosystem includes automated accessibility checkers integrated into CI pipelines.

Jamie: But we should be careful not to oversell them.

Alex: Exactly. Automated tools catch some problems, not all problems. They are very good at repeatable rule-based checks. They are not good at judging whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order makes sense in a complex interaction, whether instructions are understandable, or whether the overall user experience works well with assistive technology.

Jamie: So if an accessibility workflow passes, that does not prove the experience is fully accessible.

Alex: Correct. It means the automated checks did not detect certain known issues. That's useful, but incomplete.

Jamie: The source also mentions preparing the environment for GitHub-hosted agents.

Alex: Yes. In accessibility workflows, the runner often needs the right environment before scans can succeed. That may include installing dependencies, setting up a browser, building the site, launching a local server, or ensuring the app is reachable to the scanning tool. In other words, accessibility scanning in Actions usually depends on ordinary setup steps being correct first.

Jamie: So a failed a11y scan may actually mean the site never built or the test environment never started.

Alex: Exactly. Always read the failing step before assuming the accessibility findings themselves are the problem.

Jamie: Let's make this hands-on. If a learner wants to explore a workflow in a repository, what should they do?

Alex: Here's a good activity. Go to the repository's Code area and look for the .github slash workflows folder. Open a workflow file, perhaps ci dot yml or something similarly named. Then identify these pieces: the workflow name, the trigger or triggers under on, the jobs that are defined, the runner listed under runs-on, and the steps inside a job. Next, visit the Actions tab and locate a recent run of that workflow. Open it and answer a few questions for yourself: what event triggered this run, did it pass or fail, which job ran, and what steps were included? If there is a failed run available, try to find the exact failing step and read its log message.

Jamie: And if this is being used as a class or self-study discussion?

Alex: Good discussion questions include: what is this workflow trying to protect or verify? Which trigger matters most for contributors? If it failed, would the likely fix be in code, documentation, configuration, or infrastructure? And how easy was it to navigate the run details with your current accessibility tools?

Jamie: I really like that last one, because it treats accessibility as part of the workflow experience, not as an afterthought.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: We should also be honest about what we're not covering.

Alex: Yes. We are not teaching full workflow authoring, advanced YAML design, matrix builds, custom composite actions, caching strategies, reusable workflows, self-hosted runners, deployment architecture, or deep GitHub Actions security engineering. Those are real topics, just beyond the scope of a contributor-focused introduction.

Jamie: So where should learners go next?

Alex: Start with GitHub Docs for workflow syntax and understanding Actions. Check GitHub's changelog for evolving features. Review GitHub's security guidance for secure use and hardening of Actions. And if your goal is contribution rather than automation engineering, stay grounded in the basics we've covered today: know where workflows live, know what triggers them, know how to read checks, and know how to respond when something fails.

Alex: Let's wrap it up. GitHub Actions is the automation system many repositories use to run tests, checks, scans, and builds. Workflows live in .github slash workflows and are written in YAML. They are triggered by events like push or pull request. On your PR, their results appear as status checks.

Jamie: Your job as a contributor is usually not to write the automation. It's to interpret it.

Alex: Exactly. Learn the vocabulary: workflow, job, step, action, runner, trigger, status check, artifact, secret. Learn the common statuses: running, passed, failed, skipped, warning. Learn how to navigate the checks section and the Actions tab with your screen reader or visual setup. And when a check fails, don't panic. Open the run, find the failing step, read the error, fix what you can, push again, and ask for help when needed.

Jamie: And for accessibility work especially, remember that automated a11y checks are useful but partial. They support human judgment; they do not replace it.

Alex: Well said. The more comfortable you become reading automation, the more confident you'll feel contributing to real projects.

Jamie: And the next time a red X appears, you'll know it's not the end of the story. It's the start of an investigation.

65. Episode 35: Profile, Sponsors, and Wikis

Profile README, GitHub Sponsors, and repository Wikis.

Based on: Appendix T: Profile, Sponsors, and Wikis

Download Episode 35 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 35: Profile, Sponsors, and Wikis

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're exploring a side of GitHub that matters just as much as commits and pull requests: how people present themselves, support each other, organize communities, and discover projects. GitHub is not only a code host. It's also a social and collaborative space.

Jamie: I like that framing, because a lot of learners think, I need to master Git commands first, and only then maybe worry about profile pages or stars or organizations.

Alex: Right, but these features are part of real contribution workflows. They affect how you find projects, how maintainers communicate, how documentation is shared, and how other people understand who you are.

Alex: Let's start with three community-facing features: your profile README, GitHub Sponsors, and repository wikis. Think of them as three different kinds of presence. Your profile README is how people meet you. Sponsors is how people financially support open source work. Wikis are one way projects share extra documentation.

Jamie: And there are accessibility details built into all three, which is especially important for this audience.

Alex: Exactly. For screen reader users, a profile README is read like regular page content on your profile, so heading structure matters. The Sponsor control is a standard button, so button navigation can help you find it quickly. And wiki pages behave like other GitHub Markdown pages, so heading navigation is useful there too.

Jamie: What about low vision learners?

Alex: A few practical notes. Profile READMEs respect GitHub's light and dark themes, so test readability in both. The Sponsor button uses a heart icon with a pink or magenta accent, usually near the profile photo or repository header. And wiki navigation often appears in a sidebar area with links to pages.

Jamie: And for sighted users, the profile README is basically right below your avatar and bio, the Sponsor button sits near Star and Watch, and wiki pages usually show a page list in the sidebar.

Alex: That's it.

Alex: Now, profile customization. GitHub has a special feature: if you create a public repository whose name exactly matches your username, and the owner is you, then that repository's README appears on your profile page.

Jamie: So if my username were jamie-prof, I'd create a repository also named jamie-prof?

Alex: Yes. Same spelling, same case, owned by your account. That README becomes your profile README.

Jamie: That's such a wonderfully GitHub-ish trick.

Alex: It is. To create it, you make a new repository, name it exactly as your username, make it public, initialize it with a README, and then edit that README with the introduction you want visitors to see.

Jamie: What should actually go in it?

Alex: A simple structure works well. Start with an introduction: who you are and what you work on. Then your current focus, like technologies or projects you're learning. You can add skills if that's helpful, though it is optional. Include ways to reach you, such as email, LinkedIn, or a personal site. And if you want, a fun fact or human detail.

Jamie: So not a giant résumé. More like a welcoming front door.

Alex: Exactly. For example, someone might say they are an accessibility advocate and open source contributor, then list a current focus like NVDA documentation, accessible React components, or learning TypeScript. Then they might mention skills such as JavaScript, Python, HTML and CSS, screen reader testing, Git, GitHub, and Actions. Then a contact section, then perhaps a small personal note.

Jamie: That example works because it tells me what kind of work they care about, not just what tools they've touched.

Alex: Yes, and that's part of the best-practice advice. Keep it concise because visitors skim. Update it occasionally so it does not feel abandoned. Be authentic instead of stuffing it with buzzwords. Include links so people can continue the conversation.

Jamie: And also, please, maybe don't turn it into a carnival of badges.

Alex: Please don't. Excessive badges create visual clutter and screen reader noise. Auto-generated stats widgets can also be inaccessible or distracting. A short, thoughtful README is usually better than an elaborate one.

Jamie: Let's slow down on accessibility here, because this is one of those places where people accidentally make their profile less usable.

Alex: Absolutely. Use headings like level two headings for major sections. Provide alt text for images. Avoid ASCII art, because screen readers read it character by character, which is tedious. And if possible, test your profile README with a screen reader before publishing.

Jamie: So if someone wants flair, they should choose flair that still respects navigation and readability.

Alex: Precisely.

Alex: There are also other profile customizations worth knowing. You can pin up to six repositories on your profile. That's useful for highlighting your best work, beginner-friendly projects, or things that represent your interests.

Jamie: And that's through the profile interface where you customize your pins?

Alex: Yes. You choose which repositories appear first. Then there's the contribution graph, which shows activity over the past year. Commits, pull requests, issues, and related activity can all contribute to that graph.

Jamie: Important note: you can't manually redesign the graph.

Alex: Correct. It reflects activity rather than being something you style. And you can also set a temporary status message from your profile, like being away, focusing, or available for collaboration.

Jamie: That sounds small, but status messages can be helpful socially. They tell people whether now is a good time to expect a reply.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let's move to GitHub Sponsors. GitHub Sponsors is a way to financially support developers and projects you depend on.

Jamie: So if I rely on an open source maintainer's work every week, Sponsors gives me a built-in way to support them?

Alex: Yes. A developer or project can create a Sponsors profile, define tiers, and receive recurring support. The learner-friendly way to think about it is: Patreon-style support for open source, integrated into GitHub.

Jamie: How does it work at a high level?

Alex: Maintainers create a Sponsors profile. You choose a monthly tier, maybe five dollars, ten dollars, twenty-five dollars, or a custom amount. Payment goes to the developer, and the platform is designed so GitHub does not take fees from that sponsorship flow.

Jamie: Why should someone sponsor instead of just starring a repository and saying thank you?

Alex: Because stars are appreciation and visibility, but sponsorship supports sustainability. Many maintainers are doing critical work in their free time. Sponsorship can help them keep a project alive. It's also a direct form of gratitude. And sometimes maintainers offer sponsor benefits like private chats, early releases, or priority support.
