Jamie: How do you actually sponsor someone?

Alex: Go to a user or repository page, find the Sponsor button with the heart icon, choose a tier or amount, select a payment method such as card or PayPal, and complete the process. GitHub sends a receipt, and your sponsorship may appear publicly on your profile if you choose that visibility.

Jamie: Accessibility tip: for screen reader users, that Sponsor control is a button, so pressing the shortcut to move through buttons can help you locate it.

Alex: Yes. It's often near the profile photo area or near the repository title and action buttons.

Jamie: And can learners receive sponsorships too, or is that only for famous maintainers?

Alex: You can absolutely apply to receive sponsorships if you maintain projects or contribute regularly. The basic setup is to go to the Sponsors page, join or set up your profile, connect a payment method like Stripe or a bank account, create sponsorship tiers with descriptions, and then share that page with your audience.

Jamie: I appreciate that the source specifically notes accessibility advocates often use Sponsors to fund work on assistive technology and inclusive design.

Alex: Yes. That's an important reminder that accessibility work is real technical labor and worth supporting.

Alex: Now, GitHub Wikis. A wiki is a documentation space attached to a repository but separate from the main code tree.

Jamie: So not the README, and not GitHub Pages either.

Alex: Right. It's a lightweight, Markdown-based place for multi-page documentation.

Jamie: When is a wiki a good fit?

Alex: When you need multi-page docs such as tutorials, guides, FAQs, or community notes, especially if the material is too long or too specific for the README. It's also useful when you want a more community-editable documentation area.

Jamie: And when is it not a good fit?

Alex: If your project already has a full docs site, like GitHub Pages or an external documentation platform. Also if documentation must be version-controlled tightly with the source code, because the wiki is actually a separate Git repository. And if you need deep customization, the wiki is more limited than a full site.

Jamie: That separate repository detail matters.

Alex: Very much. To access a wiki, you go to the repository and open the Wiki tab. If none exists, you may be offered a way to create the first page.

Jamie: And making pages is pretty straightforward?

Alex: Yes. Open the Wiki tab, choose New page, add a title and Markdown content, then save. The wiki automatically includes navigation, usually through a sidebar listing pages.

Jamie: What should learners know about wiki accessibility?

Alex: The editor is similar to the issue and pull request comment editor, so familiar Markdown features work: headings, lists, links, code blocks. Use a proper heading hierarchy for navigation. You can link between wiki pages using wiki link syntax with double brackets around a page title.

Jamie: And there's an especially important caveat here.

Alex: Yes. Because the wiki is a separate Git repository, changes pushed directly to the wiki remote are not governed by the main repository's branch protection rules. That means the normal pull request review safeguards may not apply. So treat wikis as supplementary, community-editable docs, not your primary source for critical reviewed documentation.

Jamie: That is one of those details contributors really need to understand before assuming every GitHub surface has the same review workflow.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: From there, let's widen out to organizations, templates, and repository settings. These are structural features. They shape how projects are owned, duplicated, and presented to contributors.

Jamie: So now we're talking less about your personal profile and more about the architecture around repositories.

Alex: That's right. Start with repository templates. A template repository is a starter repository intended to be used as the basis for new repositories.

Jamie: How is that different from a fork?

Alex: A fork preserves a relationship to the original repository. It's meant for contributing back or maintaining your own related copy. A template creates a new repository from the starting files without creating that fork relationship. So if you're bootstrapping a fresh project, template. If you're building on someone else's project history and likely collaborating upstream, fork.

Jamie: That distinction helps. Template for starting point, fork for lineage.

Alex: Exactly. Creating a template repository usually means marking an existing repository as a template in repository settings. Using a template typically means choosing the option to create a new repository from that template, then deciding things like the new name, owner, and whether to include all branches or only the default branch depending on the interface.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, the path matters.

Alex: Yes. Usually you're on the template repository page and activate the control to use this template, then follow the repository creation form. The exact wording may vary over time, but conceptually that's the path.

Alex: Now organizations. A GitHub organization is an account type used by teams, companies, nonprofits, and many open source communities.

Jamie: So instead of repositories belonging to one individual, they belong to a shared organization account.

Alex: Correct. That's why many mature projects live under organization names. Organizations support multiple owners, repositories, teams, permissions, and policies.

Jamie: What does joining an organization usually look like from a contributor's perspective?

Alex: You may be invited by email or through GitHub. Once you accept, you become a member. Depending on the organization, your membership might be public or private.

Jamie: Let's unpack membership visibility.

Alex: Public membership means other people can see on your profile that you belong to that organization. Private membership hides that relationship from public view, though of course the organization itself still knows you're a member.

Jamie: And teams inside organizations?

Alex: Teams are subgroups used to manage permissions and communication. For example, docs team, accessibility team, maintainers team, release team. Contributors may interact with teams through mentions, access controls, and code ownership workflows.

Jamie: If I'm navigating an organization profile page, what should I expect?

Alex: Usually an overview of the organization, repository listings, pinned repositories, people, sometimes packages or projects, and possibly links to teams if you have permission. For learners, the key idea is that the organization page is often the front door to a whole ecosystem rather than a single project.

Alex: Next, repository settings that contributors should understand even if they cannot change them. First, visibility.

Jamie: Public versus private?

Alex: Yes. Public repositories are visible to anyone. Private repositories are restricted. As a contributor, this affects discoverability, access, and whether your work is visible publicly.

Jamie: Archived repositories are another important signal.

Alex: Exactly. An archived repository is generally read-only and no longer actively maintained. If you find one, treat it as historical unless the maintainers clearly indicate otherwise.

Jamie: Topics are also part of repository settings, and they matter more than people realize.

Alex: They do. Topics are descriptive tags attached to repositories. They improve discoverability and help people find projects by category, such as accessibility, screen-reader, docs, education, python, or beginner-friendly themes.

Jamie: And then there's the default branch name.

Alex: Right. Contributors need to know which branch is the main starting point, because it affects where pull requests target and what branch you compare against. Not every repository uses the same default branch name.

Alex: Now let's dive into social features more broadly. Stars, watching, following, your home feed, Explore, Trending, topics, lists, and strategies for finding accessible and inclusive projects. These are not fluff. They are practical discovery and community tools.

Jamie: Let's start with stars, because almost everyone sees that button early on.

Alex: A star is basically a bookmark plus a public signal of appreciation. It lets you save a repository to your starred list, and it also contributes to visible interest around that project.

Jamie: Why does star count matter to projects?

Alex: It's not a perfect measure of quality, but it can indicate interest, trust, momentum, or discoverability. More stars can help a project show up in searches and encourage others to take a look.

Jamie: How do you star a repository?

Alex: On GitHub.com, go to the repository page and activate the Star button. If you use keyboard navigation, there may be a shortcut depending on context, though buttons and headings are usually more reliable navigation anchors. For screen reader users, button navigation works well to find the Star control.

Jamie: And there are CLI options too.

Alex: Yes. With GitHub CLI, you can star a repository, unstar it, list your starred repositories, and check whether you've starred a repo. The exact command syntax depends on the CLI version, but conceptually those actions are available.

Jamie: So stars are manageable from both the web and command line.

Alex: Exactly. And viewing your stars on the website gives you a personal collection of interesting repositories.

Alex: Watching a repository is different. Watching is about notifications.

Jamie: So starring says, I care about this project, while watching says, keep me updated.

Alex: Perfect distinction. Watching determines whether you receive notifications about activity in that repository.

Jamie: And there are multiple watch levels, right?

Alex: Yes. Depending on GitHub's interface, you may watch all activity, watch only certain kinds of events like releases, or ignore the repository entirely. The web interface offers the most granular control.

Jamie: Important technical note: some of those granular watch levels are really web-interface features, not something you fully manage through the API alone.

Alex: Correct. Through CLI, you can do core actions like watch all activity, ignore a repository, list watched repositories, or stop watching. But if you want a very specific notification mode, the web UI may be required.

Jamie: That's a good example of not assuming the CLI exposes every nuance.

Alex: Yes. As a learner, use watching deliberately. Watching too many active repositories can flood your notifications.

Jamie: So star broadly, watch selectively.

Alex: That's often wise.

Alex: Following people is the social equivalent for users. When you follow someone, their public activity can influence what you see and helps you keep track of their work.

Jamie: Who should learners consider following?

Alex: Maintainers you learn from, accessibility advocates, tool builders, educators, organizations, and contributors whose issue discussions or pull requests teach you something.

Jamie: How do you follow someone?

Alex: Open their profile and activate Follow. Screen reader users can navigate by buttons to find that control. In CLI, you can also follow a user, unfollow a user, list who you're following, list your followers, check whether you follow a specific person, and inspect who another user follows.

Jamie: That last one is a powerful discovery trick. Looking at who thoughtful people follow can lead you to more thoughtful people.

Alex: Exactly. And when viewing someone's profile, pay attention not just to follower counts but to pinned repositories, README content, organizations, recent activity, and whether their work aligns with your interests.

Alex: Your home feed is what you see when you log in. It includes activity from repositories and people you follow or interact with, plus recommendations and discovery items.

Jamie: So it is not just a dashboard. It's a discovery tool.

Alex: Yes. It helps you notice trends in your own circles. You may see releases, stars, discussions, pull requests, and repository activity. Over time, your feed reflects your interests and connections.

Jamie: Can you customize it?

Alex: To a degree, yes, mostly indirectly by what you follow, what you star, what you watch, and what organizations or repositories you engage with. The main lesson is that you can shape your feed by shaping your network.

Alex: Explore is GitHub's broader discovery area. It shows repositories, collections, events, and recommendations beyond your immediate network.

Jamie: How should a screen reader user approach Explore?

Alex: Use heading navigation to move through sections, and landmarks or lists where available. Explore pages can be content-dense, so structured navigation matters. Move by headings, then open items of interest rather than trying to read linearly through everything.

Jamie: That sounds like good advice for most complex web pages.

Alex: It is.

Alex: Trending is related but more time-sensitive. It highlights projects or developers that are popular right now.

Jamie: And you can filter trending results?

Alex: Yes, often by language and time period. There is also a view for trending developers.

Jamie: What about CLI here?

Alex: Trending repositories are not really exposed as a first-class official API feature in the same way some other data is. But you can approximate trending by searching for recently starred popular repositories, including within a specific language.

Jamie: So if someone wants trending Rust accessibility tools, they may need a mix of web exploration and clever search.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Topics are another discovery tool. Topics are category labels for repositories.

Jamie: So if I browse a topic like accessibility or screen-reader, I can discover related repositories quickly.

Alex: Yes. Browsing topics helps you move from one relevant project to many. Useful topics for this learning community might include accessibility, a11y, screen-reader, docs, education, open-source, python, javascript, vscode, assistive-technology, and beginner-friendly labels depending on the repo metadata.

Jamie: And from the CLI side?

Alex: You can search for repositories with a given topic, and if it's your own repository, you can add topics to improve discoverability.

Jamie: That means topics are both a search tool and a contribution to the ecosystem.

Alex: Well said.

Alex: GitHub Lists are for organizing your stars into collections.

Jamie: So stars are the raw pile, and lists are the shelves.

Alex: Exactly. You can create a list, add repositories to it, then view or share that list. It's useful when you want separate collections like accessibility tools, learning repositories, documentation examples, or projects to contribute to later.

Jamie: Can you manage lists from the CLI?

Alex: Not in the same way. Lists are managed through the web interface. The CLI can help you view stars, but list management is web-based.

Alex: One especially valuable part of this material is how to find accessible and inclusive projects.

Jamie: Yes, because discovery is not neutral. If you know what to search for, you find healthier places to contribute.

Alex: Exactly. Use search strategies that combine subject matter and contribution signals. Search for accessibility-focused repositories. Search for repositories with good first issues related to accessibility. Search for issues tagged both accessibility and help wanted.

Jamie: So instead of searching only by language, you search by values and workflow readiness.

Alex: Yes. Also follow organizations known for accessibility work, inclusive design, assistive technology, open education, and good documentation practices. And one smart social trick is to look at who trusted people in your community follow. That's often a better discovery path than trending alone.

Jamie: Because it gives you a human-curated network instead of just popularity.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let's connect all of this to building your own presence. Your contribution graph, pinned repositories, and profile README all help people understand your work. But the goal is not to perform productivity.

Jamie: I'm glad you said that.

Alex: The real goal is clarity. Show what you care about. Pin repositories that represent your interests or contributions. Use your README to introduce yourself. Contribute steadily if you can, but don't treat the graph like a moral scorecard.

Jamie: And activity tips?

Alex: Small consistent contributions count. Issues, pull requests, discussions, documentation edits, and review participation all help you become visible in a healthy way. Focus on meaningful engagement, not gaming metrics.

Alex: Before we close, let's gather the CLI angle on social features, because many of our learners like working from the terminal.

Jamie: A quick tour then.

Alex: For following: you can follow or unfollow users, list who you follow, list followers, and check follow relationships. For stars: you can star and unstar repositories, list your starred repositories, and check whether you've starred a particular repo. For discovery: some searching can be done through CLI, including repository search by topic or other qualifiers, though Explore and Lists are still mainly web experiences. For watching: core actions like watch, unwatch, ignore, and list watched repositories are available, but very granular watch settings may still require GitHub.com.

Jamie: So the CLI is strong for direct actions, but weaker for highly visual discovery surfaces.

Alex: That's a fair rule of thumb.

Alex: Let's end with a practical screen reader navigation recap across these social features. To follow a user, go to the profile and navigate by buttons until you reach Follow. To star a repository, use heading or landmark navigation to get to the repository header, then move to the Star button. To browse your stars, go to your profile or stars page and navigate through repository lists and headings. To explore topics, move by headings and links on the topics or search pages. And for Explore and Trending, don't try to consume the whole page linearly—use structure to jump between sections.

Jamie: That's a really important meta-skill: on GitHub, navigation strategy is part of technical literacy.

Alex: It absolutely is.

Jamie: So if we put the whole episode into one thought, maybe it's this: GitHub has social and structural features that shape how you discover projects, support maintainers, present your work, and participate in communities. Learning them makes you a more effective contributor.

Alex: Beautifully said. And one final note: the authoritative details for these features can evolve, so GitHub Docs and the GitHub changelog remain your best reference points for up-to-date behavior.

Jamie: Thanks for learning with us.

Alex: See you next time.

66. Episode 36: Organizations and Templates

GitHub Organizations, repository templates, visibility, and archiving.

Based on: Appendix T: Organizations and Templates

Download Episode 36 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 36: Organizations and Templates

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re exploring the parts of GitHub that make it feel less like a pile of repositories and more like a real community. That includes how you present yourself, how people support open source work, how projects organize documentation, how organizations structure collaboration, how repository templates help people start new work, and the social signals that help you discover people and projects.

Jamie: So this is not just about code files and pull requests.

Alex: Exactly. It’s also about visibility, trust, discovery, and participation. And for our audience, we also need to talk about how these features behave with screen readers, keyboard navigation, and low-vision workflows.

Alex: Let’s start with your public presence. GitHub has a special profile customization feature that surprises a lot of people. If you create a public repository whose name exactly matches your username, with the same capitalization, the README from that repository is shown right on your GitHub profile.

Jamie: That’s the special profile README.

Alex: Right. It’s basically your introduction page on GitHub. When someone visits your profile, they don’t just see your avatar and a short bio. They can also see the content of that README as regular page content.

Jamie: And that matters because a profile is often the first thing someone checks before deciding whether to follow you, collaborate with you, or trust your contributions.

Alex: Yes. It helps answer simple human questions. Who are you? What are you working on? What are you learning? How can someone reach you?

Jamie: Walk me through creating one.

Alex: Create a new repository. Name it exactly the same as your GitHub username. Make it public. Initialize it with a README. Then edit that README with the information you want visitors to see on your profile.

Jamie: What should go in it?

Alex: A short introduction is a great start. Then maybe your current focus, like technologies you’re learning or projects you’re contributing to. You can include skills, though that part is optional. You can add contact information such as email, LinkedIn, or a personal site. And if you want, a fun fact or two. That last piece can make you feel like a real person instead of a résumé in Markdown.

Jamie: So something like: Hi, I’m Jane Smith. I care about accessibility. I’m learning TypeScript. I contribute to NVDA docs. Here’s how to contact me.

Alex: Exactly. The source gave an example like that, with sections for current focus, skills, contact information, and a fun fact. The bigger lesson is structure. Keep it scannable and honest.

Jamie: What makes a good profile README instead of an overwhelming one?

Alex: A few best practices. Keep it concise, because most visitors skim. Update it occasionally so it doesn’t look abandoned. Be authentic rather than stuffing it with buzzwords. Include useful links so people can learn more.

Jamie: And what should people avoid?

Alex: Excessive badges. A wall of fifty technology badges can create visual clutter and a lot of screen reader noise. Also be cautious with auto-generated stats widgets. Those commit charts and flashy profile cards are often inaccessible, sometimes poorly labeled, and not always very meaningful.

Jamie: So a simple profile is better than a noisy one.

Alex: Very often, yes.

Jamie: Let’s make the accessibility part explicit.

Alex: Definitely. Use headings, especially level-two headings, so screen reader users can jump by heading with a key like H. If you include images, provide alt text. Avoid ASCII art, because screen readers read it character by character and it becomes frustrating fast. And test your README with a screen reader before you publish it.

Jamie: What about low-vision considerations?

Alex: Profile READMEs respect GitHub’s dark and light themes, so test in both. Make sure contrast stays readable and that decorative elements don’t become distracting.

Jamie: Your profile has more than just the README, right?

Alex: Yes. You can pin up to six repositories, which is a great way to highlight your best work or the projects you want people to notice first. There’s also your contribution graph, which shows activity over the past year. You can’t really customize that, but it does reflect consistent activity like commits, pull requests, and issues. And you can set a temporary status message, like saying you’re away until a certain date.

Jamie: That’s useful for expectation-setting.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s shift from self-presentation to supporting others: GitHub Sponsors.

Jamie: This is GitHub’s way of letting people financially support open source maintainers and projects.

Alex: Yes. Think of it as a funding layer for open source work. A developer or project can create a Sponsors profile. Then supporters choose a monthly tier or sometimes a custom amount. The important point in the source is that GitHub sends the money directly to the developer and does not take a cut.

Jamie: Why would someone sponsor a project?

Alex: Three main reasons were highlighted. Sustainability, because many maintainers are volunteers and funding helps them continue. Gratitude, because a tool may have saved you hours of effort. And sometimes sponsor benefits, like priority support, early access, or special community channels.

Jamie: How do you sponsor someone?

Alex: Go to their profile or repository page. Look for the Sponsor button, usually with a heart icon near the top, close to the profile photo area or near the repository controls. Choose a tier or amount, pick a payment method like credit card or PayPal, and complete the process. GitHub sends a receipt, and your sponsorship can appear publicly on your profile if you choose.

Jamie: And for screen reader users?

Alex: The source specifically notes that the Sponsor control is a standard button. On a page, you can move through buttons with the B key in many screen readers until you hear Sponsor.

Jamie: Can regular contributors apply to receive sponsorships too?

Alex: Yes. If you maintain a project or contribute consistently, you can go to the GitHub Sponsors area, join the waitlist or set up sponsors, connect a payout method such as Stripe or a bank account, create sponsorship tiers, and promote that page. The text specifically notes that many accessibility advocates use Sponsors to support work on assistive technology and inclusive design.

Jamie: Next up: wikis. These can be a little confusing because some projects use them heavily and others ignore them.

Alex: That’s because a GitHub wiki is one documentation option, not the only one. A wiki is a separate Markdown-based documentation space attached to a repository. It’s useful when you want multi-page docs, tutorials, FAQs, or information that doesn’t belong in the main README.

Jamie: So if a README is getting too long, a wiki might make sense.

Alex: Exactly. Also if you want community-editable documentation. Wikis can be a lightweight place for shared knowledge.

Jamie: When should you not use a wiki?

Alex: If the project already uses GitHub Pages or another docs site, a wiki may be redundant. If you need documentation changes to be version-controlled right alongside code, a wiki may be a poor fit because it is a separate Git repository. And if you want strong customization or tighter review control, a wiki is more limited.

Jamie: How do you access one?

Alex: Go to the repository and open the Wiki tab. If the project has no wiki yet, GitHub may show an option to create the first page.

Jamie: And creating pages?

Alex: Open the Wiki tab, choose New page, add a title and Markdown content, then save. Pages automatically appear in the wiki sidebar for navigation.

Jamie: Anything special for accessibility?

Alex: Yes. The wiki editor is basically the same kind of editor used for issues and pull request comments, so standard Markdown works well. Use headings and lists for structure. Link between wiki pages with double bracket syntax like page title references. And there’s one important caveat: because the wiki is its own Git repository, changes pushed directly to the wiki are not governed by the main repository’s branch protection rules. In practice that means wiki edits may bypass the review process you expect for code. So treat wikis as supplementary, community-editable docs rather than the place for your most critical, tightly controlled documentation.

Alex: Now let’s pivot into structural features that shape how repositories are organized: templates, organizations, and settings.

Jamie: This is the part that helps contributors understand how projects are set up behind the scenes.

Alex: Exactly. As a contributor, you won’t always manage these features, but you’ll run into them constantly.

Jamie: Let’s start with repository templates. What problem do they solve?

Alex: A template repository is a starter repository. Instead of copying files manually or forking a project when you don’t want shared history, you can create a new repository from the template. It gives you the structure, files, and often default workflows you need to begin.

Jamie: So how is that different from a fork?

Alex: That distinction matters a lot. A fork keeps a relationship to the original repository. It preserves history and signals that your repository is derived from that upstream project, often because you may contribute back. A template gives you a starting snapshot to build your own independent repository. Usually there is no ongoing fork relationship.

Jamie: So if I’m building my own course project from a starter kit, use a template. If I’m planning to contribute changes back to someone else’s codebase, fork.

Alex: Precisely.

Jamie: How does a repository become a template?

Alex: A maintainer enables the template setting in repository settings. Once it’s marked as a template, GitHub can offer a Use this template button.

Jamie: And to use it?

Alex: Open the template repository, choose Use this template, then create a new repository from it. Depending on the interface, you may choose whether to include all branches or just the default branch, though many learners will mainly use the default branch option.

Jamie: Is there an accessibility note here?

Alex: Yes. The source explicitly calls for a screen reader path, so the key practical idea is that the Use this template control is on the repository page and can be reached through standard heading, button, and landmark navigation. For blind users, it’s helpful to navigate to the main repository controls area and listen for Use this template.

Jamie: Now organizations. A lot of major open source projects live under organization accounts instead of personal accounts.

Alex: Right. An organization is a shared account structure used by companies, teams, nonprofits, and open source communities. Instead of one person owning everything, the organization owns repositories and manages access through membership and teams.

Jamie: From a contributor’s point of view, why does that matter?

Alex: Because the org structure explains who maintains the project, who has permissions, and how collaboration is grouped. You might be invited to join an organization, or you may just contribute to repositories it owns. Either way, understanding the model helps.

Jamie: How does joining work?

Alex: Usually an owner invites you. You accept the invitation, and then you become a member. Your membership may have certain permissions or team assignments depending on the organization’s setup.

Jamie: And the visibility of that membership can vary, right?

Alex: Yes. Membership visibility can be public or private. Public membership means people can see on your profile that you belong to the organization. Private membership hides that affiliation from public view.

Jamie: That has privacy implications.

Alex: It does. Some people want their affiliations visible for networking or credibility. Others prefer not to list every organization publicly.

Jamie: What about teams inside organizations?

Alex: Teams are subgroups within an organization. They can represent maintainers, documentation writers, accessibility reviewers, release managers, or any other functional grouping. Teams help control access and make notifications more targeted.

Jamie: And if I’m just browsing an organization page, what should I expect?

Alex: You’ll typically find the organization profile, repositories, perhaps pinned projects, member information if visible, and sometimes teams or package info depending on your permissions. For contributors, this page is a helpful map of a project ecosystem.

Jamie: Repository settings may sound administrative, but contributors still need to understand them.

Alex: Absolutely. A few settings shape your experience directly. First, repository visibility. A repository can be public, private, or in some cases internal within enterprise contexts. Public means anyone can view it. Private means access is restricted.

Jamie: Second, archived repositories.

Alex: Yes. An archived repository is effectively read-only. You can still inspect the code and issues, but active development has stopped. As a contributor, seeing that a repo is archived tells you not to expect merges or ongoing maintenance.

Jamie: What about repository topics?

Alex: Topics are labels attached to repositories that help with discovery. They might say things like accessibility, screen-reader, docs, python, good-first-issue themes, or framework names. Topics make repositories easier to find via search and topic browsing.

Jamie: And the default branch name?

Alex: That matters because many instructions assume a branch name like main. The default branch is the branch GitHub treats as primary. Pull requests often target it, cloned repositories often check it out first, and some workflows depend on it.

Alex: Now for the broader social layer: stars, watching, following, feeds, discovery tools, lists, and searching for inclusive projects.

Jamie: This is where GitHub starts to feel a bit like a professional social network, but for code and contribution.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub is more than code hosting. It’s a community system.

Jamie: Let’s start with stars.

Alex: A star is basically a bookmark plus a public signal of appreciation. When you star a repository, you’re saying this project matters to me, or I want to come back to it.

Jamie: Why does star count matter to projects?

Alex: Stars are an imperfect metric, but they can still indicate visibility, interest, and community recognition. A high star count can attract more contributors or users. But it does not prove quality by itself.

Jamie: How do you star a repo?

Alex: On GitHub.com, open the repository and activate the Star button near the top. Keyboard users can tab to it. Screen reader users can navigate by buttons or landmarks until they hear Star. There may also be a keyboard shortcut in some contexts. And with GitHub CLI, you can star a repository from the command line.

Jamie: The source also expects specific CLI coverage.

Alex: Right. Conceptually, the CLI supports starring a repository, unstarring it, listing your starred repositories, and checking whether you’ve starred a particular repository. Even if learners don’t memorize command syntax here, they should know those actions exist.

Jamie: And viewing your stars on the web?

Alex: That gives you a bookmark list of projects you care about. It becomes more useful over time if you’re intentional.

Jamie: How is watching different from starring?

Alex: Watching controls notifications. Starring is mostly bookmarking and signaling. Watching says, keep me informed about activity in this repository.

Jamie: So if I want updates, I watch. If I just want to save it, I star.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What watch levels should people know about?

Alex: There are different notification levels, such as all activity, custom levels in the web interface, releases only, and ignore. The key idea is that watching is granular. You can choose to be highly informed, lightly informed, or explicitly ignore activity.

Jamie: Can all of that be done from the CLI?

Alex: Not equally. The source points out that some granular watch levels, like releases only, require the GitHub web interface and are not available via API alone. The web UI is where you’ll typically choose nuanced watch behavior. The CLI still supports actions like watching a repository for activity, ignoring a repository, listing watched repositories, and stopping watching.

Jamie: That’s a good example of a place where the website still matters.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: Next is following people.

Alex: Following is about people rather than repositories. When you follow someone, GitHub may surface their public activity in your experience. It helps you build a network around maintainers, educators, accessibility advocates, or contributors whose work you respect.

Jamie: Who should learners consider following?

Alex: People whose work you learn from, projects you contribute to, communities aligned with your goals, and individuals active in accessibility or inclusive open source. Following can become a discovery path.

Jamie: How do you follow someone?

Alex: Visit their profile and activate the Follow button. Screen reader users can use button navigation to find it. The CLI also supports following a user, unfollowing, listing who you follow, listing your followers, checking whether you follow a specific person, and seeing who another user follows.

Jamie: That last one is underrated.

Alex: It really is. Looking at who respected contributors follow can help you discover more of the community.

Jamie: Then there’s the home feed.

Alex: Your home feed is what you see when you log in. It may contain activity from repositories you watch, people you follow, recommendation signals, and other discovery content. Think of it as a personalized activity stream.

Jamie: So it’s not just noise. It can actually help you discover opportunities.

Alex: Exactly. Your feed can show new repositories, releases, issues, or people that matter to your interests. And over time, you can shape it by deciding who to follow and what to watch.

Jamie: Customizing your feed is really customizing your inputs.

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: What about Explore?

Alex: GitHub Explore is a discovery area for finding new repositories, topics, collections, and developers. It helps you move beyond the projects you already know.

Jamie: Any accessibility guidance?

Alex: Yes. When using Explore with a screen reader, rely on headings, landmarks, and structured navigation because Explore pages can be visually dense. Move section by section rather than linearly scanning everything.

Jamie: And Trending?

Alex: Trending shows what’s popular right now, often with filters by language and time period. There’s also a developers view in some interfaces, so you can discover active people as well as repositories.

Jamie: Can the CLI show official trending data?

Alex: Not directly through an official API endpoint. The source notes that trending repositories are not in the official API, but you can approximate them by searching for recently starred popular repositories, including within a specific language. That’s a useful reminder that CLI and API access sometimes lag behind the full web experience.

Jamie: Topics are another big discovery tool.

Alex: Definitely. Topics let you browse repositories by category. If you care about accessibility, screen readers, docs, educational resources, or beginner-friendly projects, topics can quickly narrow your search.

Jamie: The source also calls out useful topics for this community.

Alex: Right. Learners in this audience should watch for topics like accessibility, a11y, screen-reader, inclusive-design, documentation, open-source, good-first-issue, and language-specific topics relevant to their stack.

Jamie: And with the CLI?

Alex: You can search for repositories with a specific topic, and if it’s your own repo, you can add a topic so others can discover it.

Jamie: GitHub Lists are newer for some learners. What do they do?

Alex: Lists let you organize starred repositories into named collections. So instead of one giant pile of stars, you can group repositories by purpose, such as accessibility tools, learning resources, projects to contribute to, or examples to revisit.

Jamie: Can you manage lists from the CLI?

Alex: The source says lists are managed through the web interface only. The CLI can still help you view stars, but list management itself is a web feature.

Jamie: That’s another case where the browser remains important.

Alex: Yes.

Jamie: I’m glad this appendix includes a section on finding accessible and inclusive projects, because that’s especially relevant for our audience.

Alex: Absolutely. Search intentionally. Look for repositories focused on accessibility. Search for good first issues in accessibility-related projects. Search for issues labeled both accessibility and help wanted. Combine topic filters and issue filters when possible.

Jamie: And beyond raw search?

Alex: Follow organizations known for accessibility work. Pay attention to who your community follows. If a trusted accessibility advocate follows certain projects or maintainers, that’s often a strong signal.

Jamie: So social discovery and technical search work best together.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: There’s also a section about building your own presence, which kind of brings us full circle.

Alex: It does. Your contribution graph tells part of your story, though it should not become a source of anxiety. Pin repositories that represent the kind of work you want people to notice. Keep your profile README current enough to reflect who you are now. And make activity choices intentionally.

Jamie: Meaning?

Alex: Meaning consistent, meaningful contribution beats performative busyness. Open issues thoughtfully. Improve docs. Review pull requests when appropriate. Make small contributions regularly instead of obsessing over streaks or vanity metrics.

Jamie: Before we wrap, let’s call out the CLI angle one more time, because the appendix bundles a lot of social actions with GitHub CLI.

Alex: Good idea. Learners should know the CLI can help with following and unfollowing users, listing followers and following relationships, starring and unstarring repositories, listing stars, and some discovery searches. It can also help with some watch-related actions, though not every granular notification preference is exposed there. The general rule is this: if you prefer the command line, GitHub CLI supports a meaningful chunk of social and discovery workflows, but the web interface still matters for rich navigation, Explore, Lists, and certain watch settings.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, the appendix also included practical navigation guidance.

Alex: Yes. For following a user, navigate to the user profile and find the Follow button using button or landmark navigation. For starring a repository, find the Star button near the top controls. For browsing your stars, use heading and list navigation to move through saved repositories. For exploring topics, jump by headings and links. And for Explore and Trending, expect dense pages and navigate by sections rather than trying to read everything in sequence.

Jamie: That’s a great reminder that accessibility strategy is not just about whether something is technically labeled. It’s also about how to move through complex interfaces efficiently.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: So if we zoom out, what’s the big takeaway?

Alex: GitHub is not only where code lives. It’s where people introduce themselves, support maintainers, document projects, structure communities, discover opportunities, and build long-term professional relationships. Understanding profiles, sponsors, wikis, templates, organizations, repository settings, and social features helps you contribute more effectively and participate more confidently.

Jamie: And if you care about accessible contribution, these features are not side details. They’re part of how people find your work, understand your project, and decide whether your space is welcoming.

Alex: Well said. Build a profile that’s readable. Support the work you depend on if you can. Use wikis carefully. Learn the difference between templates and forks. Understand how organizations shape collaboration. Use stars, watches, topics, follows, and lists intentionally. And always keep accessibility in view.

Jamie: That’s our lesson for today.

Alex: Thanks for listening.

67. Episode 37: Contributing to Open Source

Finding issues, scoping contributions, the fork-to-PR workflow, and building habits.

Based on: Chapter 8: Contributing to Open Source

Download Episode 37 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 37: Contributing to Open Source

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re focusing on the human side of open source: culture, etiquette, community standards, and the workflows that make collaboration work.

Jamie: I’m glad we’re doing this, because people often think open source is mainly about code quality.

Alex: Right, and code quality matters. But technical skill helps you make a contribution. Communication skill helps that contribution get understood, reviewed, merged, and welcomed. That is the real lesson here.

Alex: Before we get into the details, a couple of learning notes. This chapter pairs well with accessibility standards, Git security, branch protection, and GitHub Pages materials. And if you want official references, GitHub Docs on contributing to open source and the Open Source Guides are strong sources to keep bookmarked.

Jamie: And there’s also a workshop task attached to this chapter, right?

Alex: Yes. This chapter’s workshop activity is a guided reflection, not an auto-graded coding task. That matters. Communication quality is subjective, so the evidence is a structured reflection comment posted on your assigned Chapter 8 challenge issue in your Learning Room repository.

Jamie: So instead of proving you can run a command, you’re proving you can think clearly about how you’ll collaborate.

Alex: Exactly. The pattern is: read, reflect, and commit to one set of behaviors in writing.

Jamie: What does the learner actually do?

Alex: They read the chapter, think about a real situation where communication helped or could have helped, open the assigned issue titled with their Chapter 8 reflection prompt, and post a short comment in a specific format. The format is essentially three commitments: one respectful review habit, one clear way they’ll ask for help, and one constructive way they’ll respond to feedback.

Jamie: And the important part is specificity.

Alex: Yes. Not “I will be nice.” Instead, “I will begin review comments by naming something that works before suggesting a change.” Not “I’ll ask good questions.” Instead, “I will include the exact step where I got stuck and what I already tried.”

Jamie: That’s much easier for a facilitator to evaluate, and honestly easier for the learner to remember.

Alex: Right. The learner is done when that comment appears on the issue with three specific, actionable behaviors. That comment is the evidence. No extra upload is needed, and then they can close the challenge issue.

Jamie: What outcomes are expected here?

Alex: That the learner can name respectful collaboration behaviors, can prepare for future review work, and feels safer asking for help in public threads.

Jamie: If someone gets stuck writing the reflection?

Alex: Keep it simple. One sentence per prompt. Draft bullets in a text editor first if that’s easier. Look back at the examples on feedback and asking for help. Or ask a facilitator for a model response and rewrite it in your own words.

Jamie: So the point is not perfection. It’s building a communication habit.

Alex: Exactly. Technical quality and communication quality reinforce each other. Good communication helps good code move faster.

Alex: Now let’s ground all of this in the standard workflow you’ll see in many open source projects: GitHub Flow.

Jamie: Because etiquette makes more sense when you know where the conversations happen.

Alex: Exactly. GitHub Flow is a lightweight contribution model. It works whether you’re fixing one typo or building a substantial feature.

Jamie: Walk us through the steps.

Alex: Step one: create a branch from main, and give it a descriptive name like fix slash missing-alt-text or docs slash update-contributing-guide. Step two: make your changes and commit them in small, logical pieces, with clear messages. Step three: open a pull request. You can do that early, even as a draft. Explain what changed, why it changed, how to test it, and link the related issue if there is one. Step four: discuss and review. Reviewers comment, you revise, and ideally everyone treats that exchange as collaboration rather than conflict. Step five: pass status checks. Tests, linting, and other automated checks exist to protect the project. Step six: merge. A maintainer merges the pull request into main, and if the PR closes an issue, that issue can close automatically.

Jamie: That’s straightforward. Why does this model work so well?

Alex: A few reasons. Main stays deployable. Branches are cheap and disposable. Pull requests become the central place for context and discussion. And small changes move faster than huge ones.

Jamie: That last point is huge. A small pull request is easier to review, easier to test, and easier to trust.

Alex: Exactly. In practice, a focused five-file PR may get quick attention, while a sprawling fifty-file PR often waits.

Jamie: Now, learners may hear about Git Flow too. How is that different?

Alex: Git Flow is an older, more structured branching model designed for scheduled releases. It usually includes permanent main and develop branches, plus temporary feature, release, and hotfix branches.

Jamie: So instead of branching from main and coming back to main, feature work typically branches from develop and returns to develop.

Alex: Right. Then when enough features accumulate, a release branch gets created for final testing, version bumps, and release prep. Critical production bugs may go through a hotfix branch from main, then merge back into both main and develop.

Jamie: That sounds more complex.

Alex: It is. GitHub Flow has one long-lived branch, main, and a simple rule: main should always be deployable. Git Flow has multiple branch types and stricter merge paths.

Jamie: So when might you still see Git Flow?

Alex: In enterprise products with planned release cycles, mobile apps that depend on app store review, embedded systems, firmware, or older legacy projects.

Jamie: And why teach GitHub Flow here?

Alex: Because for open source contributions, workshops, web projects, and fast collaborative work, GitHub Flow is simpler and maps well to how GitHub pull requests are actually used.

Jamie: There’s also an unwritten rule here, right?

Alex: Yes: one thing per branch. One fix, one feature, one focused purpose. If you mix unrelated changes in one branch, review becomes harder, testing becomes harder, and the conversation becomes muddled.

Jamie: That rule also helps accessibility reviewers and documentation reviewers, because they can focus on the actual topic of the PR.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s talk about forks, because many open source contributions begin in your own fork of someone else’s repository.

Jamie: And forks can drift out of date if the original project keeps moving.

Alex: Correct. So you need to keep your fork synchronized. The reason is simple: if your fork is behind, your branches may start from stale code, your pull requests may show unrelated changes, and merge conflicts become more likely.

Jamie: What’s the easiest way?

Alex: Method one is the GitHub web interface. On your fork on GitHub, there is usually a sync option to bring your fork’s main branch up to date with the upstream repository. It’s often the simplest path.

Jamie: And if someone is working in VS Code with the terminal?

Alex: Then there’s a command-line method. First, one-time setup: add the upstream remote, meaning the original repository, not your fork. Typically that means your fork remains origin, and the original project is added as upstream.

Jamie: Then the sync process?

Alex: Switch to your main branch. Fetch upstream changes. Merge upstream’s main into your local main. Then push the updated main back to your fork on GitHub.

Jamie: So in plain language: make sure you’re on main, bring down new information from the original repo, combine it into your local copy, then upload your refreshed main branch to your fork.

Alex: Exactly. And there’s also a desktop option using GitHub Desktop for people who prefer a graphical workflow.

Jamie: When should you sync?

Alex: Before starting new work, before opening a pull request, after a long break, and anytime you notice your fork is behind. Frequent syncing keeps surprises small.

Alex: Next: commit messages. This sounds small, but it’s part of professional communication.

Jamie: Because a commit is a message to future reviewers, future maintainers, and your future self.

Alex: Exactly. A good commit message usually has a first line, optionally a body, and optionally a footer.

Jamie: What’s special about the first line?

Alex: It’s required. It should be short, clear, and describe what the commit does. Think of it as the headline. For example: fix broken heading structure in README, or add alt text to homepage screenshots.

Jamie: And the body?

Alex: Optional, but useful when the change needs explanation. The body can explain why the change was needed, what tradeoffs were made, or anything a reviewer might not infer from the diff alone.

Jamie: The footer is optional too?

Alex: Yes. It might reference issues or other metadata, depending on project conventions.

Jamie: The chapter also emphasizes atomic commits.

Alex: Right. An atomic commit is one complete, coherent change. Not half of a fix. Not three unrelated edits bundled together. Atomic commits make history cleaner, make review easier, and make rollback safer.

Jamie: What mistakes should people avoid?

Alex: Vague messages like update stuff. Commits that mix unrelated changes. Overly long subject lines that bury the point. And messages that describe effort instead of outcome.

Jamie: So “worked on README” is weak, but “clarify installation steps for Windows users” is strong.

Alex: Exactly. Good commit messages tell the story of the codebase.

Alex: Now we reach a big idea: the nature of open source communication.

Jamie: Which is different from chatting with a teammate sitting next to you.

Alex: Very different. Open source communication is largely written, asynchronous, and public.

Jamie: Let’s unpack that.

Alex: Written means your wording matters. People cannot hear your tone of voice, so clarity and care matter more. Asynchronous means replies may take hours or days. So good messages must contain enough context to stand on their own. Public means your issue comments, pull request discussions, and review threads may be read by many people, including future contributors. You are not just solving today’s problem. You are leaving a trail others may learn from.

Jamie: That public aspect can feel intimidating.

Alex: It can. But it also means a clear question or respectful review comment can help many readers, not just one.

Jamie: So what does helpful feedback actually look like?

Alex: A useful pattern has five parts. First, acknowledge what’s working. That lowers defensiveness and shows you read the contribution carefully. Second, identify the specific concern. Not “this feels off,” but “this heading skips from level two to level four,” or “this function name doesn’t match the project’s naming pattern.” Third, explain why it matters. Maybe it affects accessibility, maintainability, consistency, or user understanding. Fourth, suggest a path forward when you can. That might be a proposed wording, an example, a question, or a reference. Fifth, signal the weight of the concern. Is this required before merge, a strong recommendation, or just a possible improvement?

Jamie: That last one is really helpful. Otherwise every comment can feel equally urgent.

Alex: Exactly. If you say whether something is blocking or optional, you reduce ambiguity.

Alex: Tone matters too. A strong guideline is to prefer “we” language or describe the code, not the person.

Jamie: So instead of “you wrote this wrong,” say “we may want to rename this for consistency,” or “this code path may fail when the input is empty.”

Alex: Perfect. Also use tentative language when you’re uncertain. Phrases like “I think,” “it looks like,” or “would it make sense to” can be respectful when you are exploring rather than declaring.

Jamie: But not so tentative that you hide required issues.

Alex: Right. If something truly must change, be clear. Another important point is to acknowledge cultural and language diversity. Many contributors are communicating in a second or third language. So favor plain language, avoid idioms, and interpret awkward phrasing generously.

Jamie: And avoid fake urgency.

Alex: Exactly. Don’t use urgency markers like “ASAP” or “urgent” unless the situation is genuinely urgent. Otherwise you create stress and noise.

Jamie: Let’s talk about commenting etiquette inside pull requests and issues.

Alex: Keep comments focused. One thread should address one concern when possible. That makes it easier to respond clearly and to resolve the conversation later.

Jamie: And don’t leave comments unresolved forever.

Alex: Right. If the issue is addressed, mark the conversation resolved. If it is not addressed, explain what still needs attention. Lingering unresolved comments create confusion.

Jamie: What about piling on?

Alex: Don’t do it. If someone has already raised a point, add a reaction or a brief note if necessary, but avoid repeating the same criticism in multiple voices. That can feel overwhelming, especially to new contributors.

Jamie: So reactions have a real purpose.

Alex: They do. A thumbs up or similar reaction can signal agreement without adding noise.

Jamie: The chapter also highlights Saved Replies as an accessibility win.

Alex: Yes, and this is a very practical tool. Saved Replies let you store common comment templates in GitHub. They reduce typing, improve consistency, and can be especially helpful for screen reader users or anyone who wants to lower writing fatigue.

Jamie: What are common uses?

Alex: Welcoming a contributor, asking for more information, requesting tests, reminding someone about contribution guidelines, or sharing a respectful accessibility review pattern.

Jamie: How do you create one?

Alex: In GitHub settings, there is a Saved Replies area where you can add a name and the reply text.

Jamie: And when using it in a comment?

Alex: You start typing the shortcut that invokes saved replies in the comment box, then select the one you want and edit it as needed before posting.

Jamie: Anything specific for screen reader users?

Alex: Yes. Learn the path to the comment field, invoke the saved reply chooser, and review the inserted text carefully before submitting. The benefit is that repeated, structured responses become faster and less fatiguing.

Alex: Now, etiquette differs slightly depending on whether you are reviewing or authoring.

Jamie: Let’s start with reviewers.

Alex: Review the code, not the person. Don’t gatekeep knowledge by acting as though unfamiliarity is a moral failing. Ask questions instead of issuing demands when appropriate. Distinguish opinion from requirement. And if the work is ready, approve explicitly rather than leaving the author guessing.

Jamie: That distinction between opinion and requirement is so important.

Alex: It is. “Required: this needs alt text for accessibility” is different from “Optional: I prefer a different variable name.”

Jamie: What about authors receiving review?

Alex: Say thank you. Don’t take feedback personally. Explain your choices when context matters. And surface blockers early.

Jamie: Meaning if you disagree, or if you can’t complete a requested change, say so clearly instead of going silent.

Alex: Exactly. Silence creates uncertainty. A short update is better than none.

Jamie: The chapter also calls out inclusive commenting for accessibility issues.

Alex: Yes. Accessibility comments should be specific, respectful, and framed around user impact. Instead of shaming language, describe the barrier and the improvement. For example: “This image needs alt text so screen reader users can access the same information.” That keeps the focus on access, not blame.

Jamie: So accessibility feedback is part of quality, not an optional afterthought.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And what’s the “good first issue” social contract?

Alex: If a project labels something as a good first issue, there’s an implied promise: the task should be reasonably scoped, documented enough to start, and welcoming to a newcomer. On the contributor side, the social contract means reading carefully, asking clarifying questions respectfully, and not assuming the label means no effort is required.

Jamie: What about difficult situations? Open source is human, so sometimes things go wrong.

Alex: They do. If you receive harsh feedback, pause before responding. Extract the technical point, if there is one, and reply calmly. If needed, ask for clarification on the concrete change being requested. If you disagree with a decision, state your reasoning respectfully, accept that maintainers set direction, and avoid turning disagreement into a personal contest. If someone is rude to you, document the behavior, disengage from escalation, and use the project’s code of conduct or moderator channels when appropriate. And if you accidentally caused offense, acknowledge it directly, apologize without defensiveness, and adjust your language moving forward.

Jamie: That’s a good reminder that repair matters.

Alex: It does.

Alex: Now let’s shift to project documentation, starting with your first README.

Jamie: A README is often the first thing a newcomer experiences.

Alex: Exactly. A useful README usually includes what the project is, how to install it, how to use it, how to contribute, and what license applies.

Jamie: So if we think in terms of a simple skeleton, it starts with the project name, then installation, usage, contributing, and license.

Alex: Yes. That structure gives readers a quick map.

Jamie: What belongs in each part?

Alex: Project name and a short description tell people what they’re looking at. Installation explains setup steps. Usage gives examples or basic instructions. Contributing tells potential collaborators how to participate and where to look for guidelines. License states the legal terms.

Jamie: And accessibility in READMEs?

Alex: Very important. Use meaningful heading structure. Prefer descriptive link text over “click here.” Keep language clear. Provide alt text or accessible descriptions for images. Don’t rely only on screenshots to convey essential instructions.

Jamie: So a bad README is vague, incomplete, and inaccessible. A good README is clear, structured, and helpful to both users and contributors.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Related to that, there are community health files people should know how to find.

Alex: Yes. These files set expectations for participation and maintenance. CONTRIBUTING dot md explains how to contribute. CODEOFCONDUCT dot md describes behavior expectations and reporting processes. SECURITY dot md tells people how to report vulnerabilities responsibly. LICENSE explains legal reuse rights.

Jamie: And where do learners find these on GitHub?

Alex: Usually in the repository root, sometimes in a dot github folder, and GitHub may also surface them in repository sidebars or insights areas depending on the project setup.

Jamie: So before contributing, it’s smart to look for these files and read them.

Alex: Absolutely. They answer questions before you have to ask them.

Alex: Another practical topic is choosing the right communication channel.

Jamie: Because not every message belongs in the same place.

Alex: Right. Use issues for trackable problems and feature discussions. Use pull request comments for feedback tied to a specific change. Use discussion forums, chat, or community spaces when the project provides them for broader questions. Use security channels, not public issues, for vulnerabilities. And use documentation when the information should persist for future readers.

Jamie: So a good rule is: choose the channel that matches the audience, sensitivity, and need for long-term visibility.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: The chapter also gives quick phrase patterns that work well.

Alex: Yes. Phrases like “Nice improvement here; I have one suggestion,” “Could we clarify this for new users?” “I’m blocked at this step; here’s what I tried,” or “I think this may affect screen reader users because…” These patterns are clear, respectful, and actionable.

Jamie: And there’s a rewrite exercise too.

Alex: Right. Take one comment that sounds blunt or vague and rewrite it into something specific, respectful, and useful. That exercise helps you practice tone, not just understand it intellectually.

Alex: Now let’s widen the frame to contributing to open source more generally, especially for first-time contributors.

Jamie: A lot of people still wonder what open source actually means.

Alex: At the core, open source means the source code is publicly available under a license that permits use, study, modification, and sharing under defined terms.

Jamie: And who can contribute?

Alex: Almost anyone. Contributions are not limited to code. Documentation, bug reports, design ideas, accessibility fixes, testing, issue triage, translation, examples, and community support all matter.

Jamie: What makes a good first contribution?

Alex: Something small enough to finish, clear enough to understand, and valuable enough to matter. Documentation fixes, accessibility improvements, typo corrections, test additions, or small bug fixes are often strong starting points.

Jamie: What are signs a first contribution is too large?

Alex: If it spans many unrelated files, requires deep architectural knowledge, changes many systems at once, or depends on unresolved product debates, it may be too large for a first attempt.

Jamie: How do you find something to work on?

Alex: Look for issues labeled good first issue, help wanted, documentation, accessibility, bug, or similar onboarding labels. Read the README and contribution guide. Explore the issue tracker. Start with projects you already use or care about.

Jamie: That emotional connection helps motivation.

Alex: It does. And once you find an issue, read it carefully before you start. Check whether someone is already assigned or has claimed it. Read the full thread. Understand the expected outcome. If anything is unclear, ask before investing major time.

Jamie: That can save a lot of duplicated effort.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Then comes making the contribution.

Jamie: This is where the tools and workflow come together.

Alex: Right. In a fork-and-clone model, you fork the repository, clone your fork locally, create a branch, edit files, test your changes if appropriate, commit with clear messages, push your branch, and open a pull request.

Jamie: So even the simple phrase “edit files” sits inside a larger contribution system.

Alex: Exactly. The basic workflow is not just typing changes. It’s preparing a clean branch, making focused edits, reviewing your work, and then explaining it well in the PR.

Jamie: What belongs in a good pull request description?

Alex: What changed, why it changed, how it was tested, any screenshots or text examples if relevant, and links to related issues. If there are limitations or unfinished parts, say so.

Jamie: So the PR description is another communication artifact, not just a formality.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: And if you need help during all this?

Alex: Ask clearly. Include the exact step where you’re stuck, what you expected, what happened instead, and what you already tried. That makes it easier for others to help without guessing.

Jamie: What happens after your contribution is merged?

Alex: Celebrate a little. Then sync your fork, delete the merged branch if appropriate, thank the reviewers, and stay open to follow-up work. One merged PR is often the beginning of a relationship with a project.

Jamie: And how do you build a contribution habit?

Alex: Start small and repeat. Keep a shortlist of projects you care about. Look for modest issues regularly. Improve docs when you notice confusion. Respond to feedback calmly. Save useful reply templates. And treat contribution as a practice, not a one-time performance.

Jamie: Practical habits beat grand intentions.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let’s close by returning to the core idea. Open source is technical, but it is also social. Branches, commits, forks, pull requests, README files, and community health files all create structure. Your communication gives that structure life.

Jamie: So being a strong contributor means more than writing working code. It means asking clear questions, making focused changes, writing useful commit messages, giving respectful reviews, receiving feedback well, and helping create an environment where more people can participate.

Alex: Beautifully said. And for this chapter’s task, your next step is simple: write that reflection comment with three specific behaviors you will actually practice.

Jamie: One respectful review habit.

Alex: One clear way to ask for help.

Jamie: And one constructive way to respond to feedback.

Alex: That commitment is small, but it can change every contribution you make after this.
