70. Episode 42: Accessing Workshop Materials

Downloading the repository, reading offline, keeping updated, audio format.

Based on: Appendix Y: Accessing Workshop Materials

Download Episode 42 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 42: Accessing Workshop Materials

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're focusing on a very practical question: how do you actually access these workshop materials, read them in the format that works best for you, download them, and keep your copy current over time?

Jamie: I like that this is practical, because learners may be wondering, is there one official way to read all this?

Alex: No, and that's the point. The materials are available in multiple formats. There are Markdown source files, pre-built HTML pages, and, when enabled by the facilitator, a live GitHub Pages website. This appendix exists to explain how to use each option, including offline access and updates.

Jamie: And we should mention the administrative context too, right?

Alex: Exactly. There is an audio companion episode for this material, this appendix is a reference companion to the pre-workshop setup chapter, and the authoritative source for the materials is the Community-Access GitHub repository for Git Going with GitHub.

Alex: Before we walk through the options, here are some quick access tips tailored to different users.

Jamie: Let's start with screen reader users.

Alex: If you're using a screen reader, the GitHub Pages site includes skip-to-content links and ARIA landmarks. On those pages, you can press D in NVDA or R in JAWS to move to the main landmark. On GitHub.com, if you're on the repository main page, press T to open the file finder so you can type a filename and jump straight to it without working through the full file tree. And after cloning the repository, opening it in VS Code gives you the Explorer panel with Control+Shift+E, where you can browse the tree with arrow keys.

Jamie: What about low vision learners?

Alex: The HTML version in the html folder usually provides the most polished reading experience. It's styled, navigable, and works offline in a browser. If you're reading Markdown source files, VS Code's built-in preview with Control+Shift+V can render headings, links, and code blocks in a cleaner way than raw text alone. And if you're downloading a ZIP from GitHub, remember that the Code button is the green button near the top of the repository page.

Jamie: And for sighted users more generally?

Alex: There are three main access paths: the GitHub Pages site, which is online and styled; GitHub.com, where Markdown is rendered in the browser; and a local clone, which works offline and is editable. The docs folder holds the Markdown source, the html folder holds pre-built HTML, and cloning with Git gives you a full copy that you can later update with git pull. A ZIP download is just a snapshot and does not update by itself.

Alex: A simple way to think about the flow is this: you can browse online, read on GitHub.com, download everything, download just one file, learn what each folder contains, read offline, update your local copy, and then decide which format best matches your needs.

Jamie: So let's take those one at a time. Suppose I just want to browse online in the easiest possible way.

Alex: If the facilitator has enabled GitHub Pages for the repository, the workshop materials may be available as a website at a GitHub Pages URL, something like an organization dot github dot io address followed by the site name. Your facilitator should provide the exact URL.

Jamie: And once I have it?

Alex: Open it in your browser. The landing page, usually index dot html, functions as the workshop homepage and is effectively the website counterpart to the README. From there, you can navigate within a page by headings, using the H key in browse mode for NVDA or JAWS. Internal links between chapters and appendices should work, so cross-references take you directly where you need to go. And it's worth bookmarking that URL so you can get back to it quickly during the workshop.

Jamie: This sounds especially good for accessibility.

Alex: Yes. The HTML pages include skip links, breadcrumb navigation, and ARIA landmarks. So for screen reader users, jumping to the main landmark with D in NVDA or R in JAWS can make navigation much faster. And if you want the deeper technical background on how GitHub Pages publishing works, there's a separate appendix dedicated to GitHub Pages.

Jamie: Now let's say I don't want a separate website. I just want to read directly on GitHub.com.

Alex: You can do that too. Go to the repository page your facilitator shares. On GitHub.com, the README renders automatically on the main repository page, so you begin with a formatted overview. Then click into the docs folder to find all the chapters and appendices. When you open any Markdown file ending in dot md, GitHub renders it as formatted text with headings, links, and code blocks.

Jamie: That sounds straightforward visually, but what about screen reader navigation inside the repository?

Alex: A few important details. The repository file listing behaves like a grid or table. You can use T to jump to the file table, then move through rows with arrow keys. Once you're inside a file, GitHub renders the Markdown, so heading navigation with H works well. At the top of a file view, breadcrumb links show the path, for example repository, then docs, then a specific file. Those breadcrumbs help you move back up a level. And again, on the repository main page, T opens the Go to File finder so you can type the filename directly.

Jamie: That's one of those shortcuts that can save a lot of effort.

Alex: Absolutely.

Jamie: What if I want everything on my own machine?

Alex: Then you're in the downloading section, and there are two main approaches. Option A is cloning with Git, which is the recommended method. Option B is downloading a ZIP if you don't want to use Git.

Jamie: Let's do the Git option first.

Alex: Cloning gives you a full copy of the repository and lets you update later with git pull. The commands are straightforward: first run git clone with the repository URL, then change into the folder with cd Learning-Room.

Jamie: And after that, what do I actually have?

Alex: You have the whole repository on your computer: Markdown source, HTML output, scripts, and learning-room materials. If you're using a screen reader, it's a good moment to open the folder in VS Code, for example with code dot, then use Control+Shift+E for the Explorer panel. From there, arrow through files and press Enter to open one in the editor.

Jamie: So clone is best if I want a living copy, not just a one-time download.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now the no-Git route: ZIP download.

Alex: If Git isn't installed, or you simply prefer not to use the command line, go to the repository page on GitHub.com. Find the green Code button near the top of the file listing. Activate it to open the dropdown menu, then choose Download ZIP. Save the file and extract it on your computer.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, that Code button can be annoying to find if you don't know where it lives.

Alex: Right, so the appendix gives very specific guidance. The Code button is near the repository description and after the branch selector. In NVDA or JAWS browse mode, press B to jump between buttons until you hear Code. Activate it with Enter or Space. Then arrow down in the dropdown until you reach Download ZIP.

Jamie: Important caveat?

Alex: A ZIP download is a snapshot. It does not update automatically. If the repository changes, your ZIP copy does not know that. You'll need to download a fresh ZIP later if you want a newer version.

Jamie: Sometimes people don't need everything. What if I only want one chapter or one cheat sheet?

Alex: Then download an individual file. From GitHub.com, navigate to the file, activate the Raw button above the file content, and the browser will show the raw text of the file. Then save it with Control+S on Windows or Linux, or Command+S on macOS.

Jamie: And if it's an HTML file instead of Markdown?

Alex: Go to the html folder, find the corresponding dot html file, and use the same Raw then Save approach.

Jamie: What if I've already cloned the repository?

Alex: Then you already have every file locally. Just open the folder and copy out the specific files you need.

Jamie: Let's talk about folder structure, because that can be confusing when learners first open a repository.

Alex: Definitely. The docs folder contains all 17 numbered chapters, from 00 through 16, plus 31 appendices labeled A through Z and then AA through AE. Those are Markdown files.

Jamie: So docs is the source reading material in Markdown.

Alex: Correct. The html folder contains pre-built HTML versions of every Markdown file. Within that, html slash docs contains HTML versions of all chapters and appendices specifically. The learning-room folder contains practice repository files, challenges, group exercises, and setup guides, again mainly in Markdown. The html slash learning-room folder contains HTML versions of those learning-room documents.

Jamie: And then there are the project-maintenance folders.

Alex: Yes. The dot github folder includes issue templates, a pull request template, Copilot agents, and slash commands, usually in YAML and Markdown. The scripts folder contains the build script that converts Markdown to HTML, using JavaScript. And the repository root contains items like the README, agendas, facilitator guide, contributing guide, and other project files.

Jamie: That's useful, because it tells learners not just where to read, but where different kinds of work happen.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: Now suppose I'm offline. Can I still use all this effectively?

Alex: Yes. Once you've downloaded or cloned the repository, you can read everything offline.

Jamie: Let's separate Markdown and HTML.

Alex: For Markdown files, open the dot md files in any text editor. They are plain text with lightweight markup. In VS Code, Control+Shift+V opens a rendered Markdown preview, which many learners find easier to read than raw syntax.

Jamie: And the HTML path?

Alex: Open html slash index dot html in any web browser. From there, internal links between pages should work locally, so you can move through the material without internet access. You can navigate among chapters using the links on the pages themselves, including bottom navigation.

Jamie: Accessibility still works offline?

Alex: Yes. The HTML files work offline the same way they do online. The ARIA landmarks, heading structure, and skip links are built into each file.

Jamie: If someone asks for the best offline setup, what would you recommend?

Alex: Two strong options. One is VS Code with the Markdown files: open the repository folder, browse with the Explorer, and read source files directly, using the preview when needed. The other is a browser with the local HTML site: open html slash index dot html and navigate from there. That gives the most polished reading experience.

Jamie: Okay, now the maintenance question. How do I keep my copy updated?

Alex: If you cloned with Git, navigate to your local copy, typically with cd Learning-Room, and run git pull.

Jamie: And if I haven't changed anything locally, that should just update cleanly?

Alex: Yes. If you have not made local changes, git pull should update your copy cleanly. If you have made local edits, Git will attempt to merge those changes with the incoming updates. And if that creates conflicts, you'll need merge conflict skills from the chapter on merge conflicts.

Jamie: There's also one more step mentioned here after pulling.

Alex: Right. After pulling, rebuild the HTML so your local generated site matches the latest Markdown source. The command given is npm run build:html.

Jamie: And if I used a ZIP instead of a clone?

Alex: Then there is no incremental update mechanism. You simply download a fresh ZIP from the repository and replace your local copy.

Jamie: This brings us to the big decision question: which format should I use?

Alex: If you're reading during the workshop, GitHub Pages, meaning the online HTML site, is usually the best choice. It requires no setup, stays current, and is designed to be fully accessible.

Jamie: For offline reference?

Alex: Local HTML from the html folder. It works in any browser, doesn't require internet, and gives you the styled reading experience.

Jamie: For editing and contributing?

Alex: Use the Markdown source files in docs. Those are the canonical source files you edit, and then the HTML is rebuilt from them.

Jamie: For a quick lookup of one section while I'm already in a browser?

Alex: GitHub.com is great for that. You can jump straight to a file without downloading everything.

Jamie: For archiving a copy?

Alex: Either a ZIP download or a Git clone gives you a full snapshot. But for staying updated long-term, a Git clone is better because you can use one command, git pull.

Jamie: Let's revisit the learning-card guidance by audience, because it's full of useful detail.

Alex: For screen reader users, the GitHub Pages HTML site is usually the most accessible choice during the workshop because every page includes skip links, landmarks, and consistent heading structure. For offline reference, the local HTML files in the html folder work essentially the same way. For contributing edits, work in the Markdown source in docs using VS Code, because that's the canonical source that generates everything else.

Jamie: And low vision guidance?

Alex: GitHub Pages and local HTML both support browser zoom to 200 percent or more without layout breakage, so choose whichever gives you the better reading experience. VS Code's Markdown preview inherits your editor theme, which is helpful if you use a high-contrast theme. And if you're reading on GitHub.com, GitHub's dark theme can reduce eye strain during long sessions.

Jamie: And for sighted users broadly?

Alex: Use the GitHub Pages site during the workshop for the cleanest hyperlinked reading experience with no setup. Clone the repository if you want a permanent offline copy, and remember that html slash index dot html acts as a local homepage. And if you want to improve the materials, edit the Markdown in docs; those changes are what get rebuilt into HTML, typically through the project's build process and automation.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we keep the source-of-truth piece in view. Where should learners verify current facts if GitHub changes something?

Alex: Use the official references: GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. Those are the authoritative external sources listed for this appendix. The appendix also provides a section-level source map, pointing each major part of this topic back to those official references.

Jamie: So the practical takeaway is: choose the format that matches your goal.

Alex: Exactly. If you want easiest reading during the workshop, use GitHub Pages. If you want quick browser access, use GitHub.com. If you want a full offline, updateable copy, clone the repository. If you want a one-time snapshot with no Git required, download a ZIP. And if you're contributing, edit the Markdown source.

Jamie: That's a helpful framework, especially for learners who may have assumed there was only one correct way to access the materials.

Alex: There isn't one single correct way. There is a best-fit way for your task, your device, and your accessibility needs.

Alex: And from here, learners can continue on to the appendix about GitHub Skills, revisit the resources appendix, or return to the pre-workshop setup material that this appendix supports.

Jamie: See you next time.

71. Episode 43: GitHub Skills - Complete Course Catalog

All 36 GitHub Skills modules organized into six learning paths.

Based on: Appendix Z: GitHub Skills - Complete Course Catalog

Download Episode 43 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 43: GitHub Skills - Complete Course Catalog

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. This time we’re doing something a little different: a guided tour of GitHub Skills, which is GitHub’s free, self-paced interactive learning platform.

Jamie: So this is not a separate learning website with quizzes and videos?

Alex: Exactly. And that’s an important point. Every course runs inside GitHub itself. No external classroom, no extra login, no video player to manage. You start from a GitHub Skills module, copy the repository to your own account, and then an automated bot named Mona teaches you through real GitHub issues and pull requests.

Jamie: That sounds especially useful for learners who just spent time getting comfortable with GitHub navigation, because they don’t have to learn a whole second interface.

Alex: Right. The same skills you’ve practiced already apply directly: moving by headings, jumping by landmarks, reading issues, opening pull requests, reviewing comments, tracking state changes, and working inside normal repository pages.

Jamie: And this appendix is basically the roadmap for what to do after the workshop?

Alex: Yes. It catalogs the available GitHub Skills modules and groups them into learning paths so you can keep building after Day 2. It also connects back to pre-workshop setup and to the chapter on next steps, so think of this as a bridge between the workshop and your independent practice.

Alex: Let’s make the accessibility details explicit, because they matter here. For screen reader users, every course appears in a standard GitHub repository. After you copy a course with Use this template, go to the Issues tab. A quick key path mentioned in the source is G then I to reach Issues, and then H or the 3 key to move to the heading for the first lesson, usually titled something like Step 1.

Jamie: So the lesson content is not hidden in some custom widget. It’s just an issue.

Alex: Exactly. And Mona’s feedback usually arrives as issue comments. The source specifically reminds NVDA and JAWS users that pressing 9 can jump to the comments region, which is helpful when you want to hear Mona’s next instruction without hunting around the page.

Jamie: What about low-vision learners?

Alex: The nice thing is that GitHub Skills inherits the GitHub interface you already configured. Your existing theme, contrast, and font size settings carry over automatically because the course content is standard GitHub content. Step numbers show up as issue titles like Step 1, Step 2, and so on, so you can scan the Issues list for those numbered titles. And when you finish, Mona closes the final issue, so a visible closed badge is one of the completion cues.

Jamie: And for sighted users, the flow is just Start course, then Use this template, then Create a new repository, and wait for Mona to wake up?

Alex: That’s it. Mona generally activates within about 20 seconds. Then each step appears as a new issue or comment, and your open issues represent pending steps while closed issues represent completed ones.

Alex: Here’s the core pattern every GitHub Skills course follows. First, you navigate to the course URL and choose Start course. Second, GitHub copies that repository into your account. Third, Mona opens an issue with Step 1 instructions. Fourth, you complete whatever task the issue describes. That might be creating a branch, editing a file, or opening a pull request. Fifth, Mona detects what you did, validates it, and posts the next step either as a comment or as a new issue. Then you repeat until the final issue is closed with a completion message.

Jamie: So the teaching loop is: read, do, get checked, continue.

Alex: Perfectly said. It’s hands-on and interactive instead of passive. You’re learning by performing actual GitHub tasks in a real repository.

Jamie: And if someone wants deeper screen reader guidance for that interface, there’s a pointer to another appendix section, right?

Alex: Yes. The source points learners to a detailed screen reader navigation section in the resources appendix for more step-by-step GitHub Skills navigation help.

Alex: Now let’s anchor this in the workshop itself. Three GitHub Skills modules were used directly during Day 1, and the appendix says to finish these first if you didn’t complete them during the workshop.

Jamie: Which three?

Alex: Introduction to GitHub, which teaches branches, commits, pull requests, and merge. Communicate Using Markdown, which covers headings, emphasis, links, code blocks, task lists, and tables. And Review Pull Requests, which teaches assigning reviewers, leaving comments, suggesting changes, approving, and merging.

Jamie: So those line up with the workshop blocks, and they’re not optional review material. They’re the foundation for the rest.

Alex: Exactly. If you haven’t completed those, the appendix recommends doing that before moving into the broader learning paths.

Alex: After those workshop modules, the remaining courses are organized into six learning paths. You do not need to do every path. Choose based on your goals.

Jamie: Before we go path by path, how should learners navigate this appendix efficiently?

Alex: For screen reader users, the six paths are organized as level-3 headings with tables under them. You can jump between paths with the 3 key, then use T to enter the table for the current path. The course links are in the rightmost Link column, so once you’re in the table, move across to find the Start course link. The appendix also recommends copying the personal completion checklist into a GitHub issue or into your own notes so you can track progress in a format you already know how to access.

Jamie: And for low-vision users?

Alex: The tables have columns for order, module, duration, prerequisite, what you learn, and link. At high zoom, some columns may truncate, so widening the browser window can help. Also, durations range from about 30 minutes to 2 hours, so the duration column is there to help you plan realistic study sessions. And if you already know the course name you want, the appendix mentions a quick reference table listing all 36 courses alphabetically.

Jamie: And visually, the key idea is that each path is sequenced from introductory to advanced.

Alex: Yes. Start at order 1 within any path and work downward.

Alex: Let’s walk through the paths. The first path is Git fundamentals. This path deepens your understanding of Git version control beyond the basics covered in the workshop. Order one is Introduction to Git. It takes less than an hour, has no prerequisite, and teaches Git command-line and VS Code workflows for branches, commits, and merges.

Jamie: So that’s a major shift from doing everything in the GitHub web interface.

Alex: Exactly. It’s the bridge into local Git work. Then comes Resolve Merge Conflicts, a shorter course that builds on Introduction to GitHub and focuses on why conflicts happen, how to read conflict markers, and how to resolve them in the web editor. After that comes Change Commit History, which covers amending commits, interactive rebase, squashing, and reordering history.

Jamie: That last one feels advanced, but also really practical once you start cleaning up your work before sharing it.

Alex: Very practical. The appendix also ties this path back to the workshop by reminding learners that Day 1 introduced merge conflicts. This path gives you much deeper practice with both conflict resolution and history editing.

Alex: The second path is GitHub collaboration. This is about the features that make team workflows and open source projects run smoothly. Order one is Introduction to Repository Management. That course covers branch protection, issue templates, labels, milestones, and contributor-friendly settings.

Jamie: That sounds like the “make your repo welcoming and organized” course.

Alex: That’s a great description. Order two is Connect the Dots, which teaches cross-referencing issues and pull requests so related work is linked together inside a repository. Order three is GitHub Pages, where you deploy a site from your repository. Order four is Release-Based Workflow, which teaches creating releases, tagging versions, and managing work around releases.

Jamie: And that path connects back to the workshop section on labels, milestones, and notifications.

Alex: Yes. The appendix explicitly says this path extends those workshop skills into broader repository management and publishing workflows.

Alex: The third path is GitHub Actions and automation. This one is about building workflows that test, build, and deploy your projects automatically. It starts with Hello GitHub Actions, which introduces workflow files, triggers, jobs, steps, and your first automated run. Then Test with Actions builds on that and teaches continuous integration, meaning tests run automatically on every push and pull request.

Jamie: So learners get the mental model that Actions is event-driven automation living in the repository.

Alex: Exactly. After that comes Reusable Workflows, where you create shared workflows, call them from other repositories, and use matrix strategies. Then Write JavaScript Actions, which moves into building custom actions with JavaScript, including action metadata and inputs.

Jamie: The source we received was truncated there, but the checklist filled in the rest of the path, right?

Alex: Yes, and that matters for complete coverage. The personal checklist confirms the rest of Path 3 includes Publish Docker Images, Deploy to Azure, AI in Actions, and Create AI-Powered Actions.

Jamie: So the path grows from “what is a workflow” to testing, to reusing workflows, to writing custom actions, and then into packaging, deployment, and AI-enhanced automation.

Alex: That’s the right progression.

Alex: The fourth path is GitHub Copilot. This is a substantial path focused on AI-assisted development. The checklist gives us the full set of courses in that path: Getting Started with GitHub Copilot, Build Applications with Copilot Agent Mode, Copilot Code Review, Customize Your GitHub Copilot Experience, Expand Your Team with Copilot, Integrate MCP with Copilot, Scale Institutional Knowledge Using Copilot Spaces, Create Applications with the Copilot CLI, Your First Extension for GitHub Copilot, and Modernize Your Legacy Code with GitHub Copilot.

Jamie: That’s a broad range. It’s not just “get inline suggestions while typing.”

Alex: Not at all. The structure suggests a progression from initial use, to agent-style workflows, to review support, customization, team use, integrations, organizational knowledge, command-line use, extensions, and modernization. Even without every table row present in the excerpt, the appendix clearly intends this path to serve learners who want to use Copilot as part of individual, team, and institutional workflows.

Alex: The fifth path is security. This path is for learners who want to build secure habits into repository and code workflows. The checklist lists five courses: Secure Code Game, Introduction to Secret Scanning, Secure Repository Supply Chain, Introduction to CodeQL, and Configure CodeQL Language Matrix.

Jamie: So that likely moves from general security thinking, to finding exposed secrets, to supply-chain protection, and then into code scanning with CodeQL.

Alex: The sixth path is cloud and migration. The listed courses are Code with Codespaces, Migrate ADO Repository, and Idea to App with Spark.

Jamie: That’s an interesting trio: cloud development environment, migration from Azure DevOps repositories, and then building from idea to app with Spark.

Alex: Now, the appendix also includes a quick reference covering all 36 courses.

Jamie: And the point of that section is not a new learning sequence, but fast lookup?

Alex: Just as important as the catalog is the advice on how to integrate GitHub Skills into your actual learning journey.

After the workshop, the recommendation is to finish any incomplete workshop courses first, then choose one path that matches your goals rather than trying to tackle everything at once.

Jamie: So if someone wants stronger Git foundations, start with Path 1. If they care about contributing to projects and managing repositories, Path 2. If they want CI and deployment, Path 3. If they’re exploring AI-assisted workflows, Path 4. Security-minded learners take Path 5. Cloud environment or migration interests point to Path 6.

Jamie: What about progress tracking?

Alex: The source specifically includes guidance on tracking your progress and then gives a personal completion checklist. The practical takeaway is: keep a record of which courses you’ve started and completed. You can do that in notes, in a GitHub issue, or anywhere else accessible to you.
