72. Episode 50: Advanced Git Operations

Cherry-pick, rebase, revert, reset, tags, bisect, clean, and other Git recovery tools.

Based on: Appendix E: Advanced Git Operations

Download Episode 50 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 50: Advanced Git Operations

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. If you already know the everyday Git moves like clone, branch, commit, push, and pull, this lesson is about the next layer up: the commands people reach for when real work gets messy.

Jamie: So this is the part where Git starts feeling powerful and a little scary.

Alex: Exactly. We’re covering the operations that come up constantly in open source and team workflows: grabbing one commit without merging a whole branch, cleaning up history before a pull request, undoing mistakes safely, understanding detached HEAD, force pushing without causing trouble, finding the exact commit that introduced a bug, cleaning untracked files, and figuring out why a protected branch refuses your push.

Jamie: And the appendix this comes from is organized around three ways to do things, right?

Alex: Yes. Most sections show a VS Code path, a GitHub CLI path with gh when that makes sense, and the Git CLI path. Different tools, same underlying Git concepts.

Jamie: Let’s also keep the accessibility guidance in view, because this material is meant to work as a reference too.

Alex: Right. If you’re reading along with the markdown, each operation is its own numbered section. Screen reader users can jump by heading between operations, and then jump among the tool-specific subheadings. The table of contents links go directly to each operation. Low vision users get a very consistent layout: what the command is, when to use it, then the tool-specific steps. And there’s a quick reference table near the bottom for fast lookup.

Jamie: So the structure itself is part of the teaching.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Let’s start with cherry-pick. Cherry-pick means: take one specific commit from somewhere else and apply that commit onto the branch you’re on now.

Jamie: So not merge the branch. Not rebase the branch. Just copy one change.

Alex: That’s the idea. Think of it as surgically lifting one commit out of another branch. You’d use it when a bug fix exists on a feature branch and main needs that fix immediately, or when a teammate has one useful commit but you don’t want all their in-progress work, or when you committed to the wrong branch and need that commit somewhere else.

Jamie: Before you can cherry-pick, you need the commit identifier, the SHA.

Alex: Right. In VS Code, one path is the Timeline view. You can open the Timeline, move to the branch that contains the commit, inspect the history there, and copy the SHA from the details.

Jamie: And from the terminal?

Alex: A very direct command is to view another branch’s history without switching to it: git log, the branch name, and oneline output. That gives you short commit IDs followed by commit messages. So you might see something like a short SHA, then “Fix null pointer error in auth module,” then another SHA for “Add unit tests for login.” The short SHA is typically the first seven characters, and that’s often enough for local operations.

Jamie: That “without switching to it” part is nice. People often think they have to check out the other branch just to inspect it.

Alex: You usually don’t.

Jamie: Okay. Once I have the SHA, how do I actually do the cherry-pick?

Alex: In VS Code, open the Command Palette, type cherry, choose the Git cherry-pick command, paste or type the SHA, and VS Code applies it to your current branch.

Jamie: And gh?

Alex: GitHub CLI does not itself perform cherry-pick, because cherry-pick is a local Git operation. But gh can help you discover the commit SHA through the GitHub API. Then you still use regular git cherry-pick locally.

Jamie: So gh helps find; git helps apply.

Alex: Exactly. At the Git CLI, you can cherry-pick a single commit. You can also cherry-pick a range of commits using the older-dot-dot-newer syntax, where the first endpoint is exclusive. And you can use no-commit if you want Git to apply the changes without creating the commit immediately, which gives you a chance to review or modify the result first.

Jamie: That no-commit option sounds useful if I’m not totally sure the commit belongs exactly as-is.

Alex: Yes. It gives you a checkpoint before the final commit is created.

Jamie: What about conflicts?

Alex: Cherry-pick can conflict for the same reason merges do: the target branch and that commit both touched overlapping code. Git pauses, marks the conflicting files, and you resolve them. In VS Code you can use the conflict editor. After resolving, stage the fixed files. Then continue the cherry-pick. If you decide this was a mistake, abort and Git returns you to where you started.

Jamie: And for screen reader users, the appendix had a practical tip here.

Alex: Yes: if a cherry-pick stops because of a conflict, run git status. It tells you which files need attention. The conflict markers in the files are plain text, so they read line by line in a straightforward way.

Jamie: There was also a Copilot angle.

Alex: Right. If you’re unsure whether a commit is the right one to cherry-pick, you can inspect it with git show and paste that output into Copilot Chat with a question like, “What does this commit do, and should I cherry-pick it onto my branch?” And if a conflict appears, Copilot can help explain the conflict or suggest a resolution.

Alex: Now let’s move to interactive rebase, one of the most useful and most misunderstood Git tools.

Jamie: This is the one people use to make their branch history look less chaotic before opening a pull request.

Alex: Exactly. Interactive rebase lets you rewrite your local commit history before it becomes shared history. You can reorder commits, squash several tiny commits together, rewrite commit messages, drop a commit entirely, or pause to edit one.

Jamie: Give me the golden rule first.

Alex: Only rewrite commits that have not yet been pushed to a shared branch, unless you fully understand the consequences and are prepared to force push safely afterward. Rewriting public history can create problems for collaborators.

Jamie: So interactive rebase is ideal for cleaning up your own branch before the branch becomes everybody else’s problem.

Alex: Well said.

Jamie: How do you start one?

Alex: In VS Code, you’ll generally open the integrated terminal because full interactive rebase is really a terminal workflow. A common command is rebase interactively on HEAD tilde 3, which means, “open the last three commits for editing.” Another common form is interactive rebase against main, meaning, “rewrite everything on my branch since I diverged from main.”

Jamie: And when that opens, what exactly am I looking at?

Alex: A list of commits, one per line. Each line begins with a command word such as pick. Pick means keep the commit as-is. Squash means combine this commit into the one above it. Fixup also combines it into the one above but discards this commit’s message. Reword keeps the commit but asks you to edit the message. Drop removes the commit entirely. Edit pauses at that commit so you can amend it.

Jamie: So the rebase file is really a little instruction sheet to Git.

Alex: That’s a great mental model.

Jamie: What’s a common cleanup example?

Alex: Suppose you made one real commit and then two typo-fix commits. You can leave the first as pick and change the next two to squash. Save and close the file. Git then opens another editor asking for the final combined commit message. You write one clean message, save, and now those three commits become one tidy commit.

Jamie: And reword is for when the code is fine but the message is vague.

Alex: Exactly. Change pick to reword for that commit, save, and Git prompts you to edit the message.

Jamie: The appendix also included an important editor tip.

Alex: Yes. If rebase opens in vim and that’s not comfortable, especially for accessibility, set your Git editor to VS Code with core.editor set to code wait. Then future interactive rebases open in VS Code, which is often much more screen-reader-friendly.

Jamie: What if I get nervous halfway through?

Alex: Abort the rebase, and Git returns to the pre-rebase state. If you hit a conflict mid-rebase, resolve the conflict, stage the files, and continue the rebase. The pattern is similar to cherry-pick and merge: fix, stage, continue. If needed, abort.

Alex: Next is git reset, which is all about undoing, but at different depths.

Jamie: This is the one where the modes matter a lot.

Alex: Very much. Reset can move HEAD and optionally change the staging area and working tree. The three classic modes are soft, mixed, and hard.

Jamie: Let’s translate that into plain language.

Alex: Soft reset moves the branch pointer back but keeps your changes staged. Mixed reset, which is the default, moves the branch pointer back and unstages the changes, but keeps them in your files. Hard reset moves the branch pointer back and discards the changes from both staging and working tree.

Jamie: So soft is the gentlest undo, mixed is a deeper undo but keeps the work, and hard is destructive.

Alex: Exactly. Hard reset is the dangerous one. The appendix explicitly warns that discarding changes with hard reset may be impossible to recover without reflog, and even then you’re depending on local history that may not last forever.

Jamie: How might someone do this in VS Code?

Alex: The appendix includes VS Code routes for undoing the last commit through the Source Control panel and through the Command Palette. Those are friendly entry points when you want to undo a recent commit without memorizing flags.

Jamie: And at the CLI?

Alex: There are several common patterns. Undo the last commit but keep changes staged: soft reset to HEAD tilde 1. Undo the last commit but keep changes unstaged: mixed reset to HEAD tilde 1, or simply reset HEAD tilde 1 since mixed is the default. Undo the last three commits but keep all changes unstaged: reset mixed to HEAD tilde 3. Undo the last commit and discard the changes entirely: hard reset to HEAD tilde 1. You can also reset to a specific commit SHA if you want to move directly to some earlier point.

Jamie: There’s a separate but related task here too: unstaging.

Alex: Yes. Sometimes you do not want to undo a commit at all. You simply staged the wrong file. In VS Code, you can unstage from the Source Control interface. In Git CLI, you can unstage a specific file by resetting that file, or unstage everything by resetting with no path. That removes content from the staging area but leaves the working tree unchanged.

Jamie: That distinction is huge: unstaging is not deleting.

Alex: Exactly. It just says, “don’t include this in the next commit yet.”

Alex: Now let’s compare reset with revert, because people mix them up constantly.

Jamie: Revert is the safe undo for shared branches.

Alex: Right. Reset rewrites history. Revert preserves history by adding a new commit that undoes an earlier commit. That makes revert the safer choice when the branch is already shared, published, or protected.

Jamie: So if I accidentally broke main and the bad commit is already on the remote, I should usually revert, not reset.

Alex: Correct. In VS Code, there are interface-based ways to revert a commit. In the Git CLI, the standard form is revert followed by the commit SHA. By default that opens an editor so you can confirm or edit the revert commit message. If you want the default message without opening the editor, there’s a no-edit form. And if you want Git to apply the revert changes without committing yet, there’s a no-commit form so you can review or change the message yourself.

Jamie: The appendix also mentions reverting a merge commit, which is a special case.

Alex: Yes. Reverting a merge commit requires specifying which parent should be treated as the mainline. That’s because a merge has more than one parent, so Git needs to know which side you want to preserve when constructing the inverse change.

Jamie: So when do I use revert versus reset in one sentence?

Alex: Use reset for local history cleanup before sharing; use revert when history is already shared and you need a safe, auditable undo.

Alex: Let’s talk about tags.

Jamie: These are the labels you attach to important moments in history, like releases.

Alex: Exactly. A tag marks a specific commit with a memorable name. There are two main kinds here: lightweight tags and annotated tags.

Jamie: What’s the difference?

Alex: A lightweight tag is basically just a named pointer to a commit. An annotated tag stores extra metadata like tagger, date, and a message, which is why annotated tags are generally recommended for releases.

Jamie: How do you create them?

Alex: In VS Code, the Command Palette can help create tags. With GitHub CLI, one convenient path is to create a release through GitHub’s API or release tooling, which can create both the underlying tag and a GitHub Release in one step.

Jamie: That’s an important distinction: a Git tag and a GitHub Release are related but not identical.

Alex: Right. The release is a GitHub platform object; the tag is a Git object. Some GitHub workflows create both together.

Jamie: And the plain Git CLI options?

Alex: Create a lightweight tag at the current commit with just the tag name. Create an annotated tag with the a flag and a message. Tag a specific older commit by giving the tag name and the commit SHA. You can list all tags, list tags matching a pattern, and show the details of an annotated tag.

Jamie: Creating the tag locally doesn’t automatically publish it, though.

Alex: Exactly. You then push either one specific tag or all local tags to GitHub. And if you need to delete a tag, there are two separate steps to think about: delete the local tag, and if it was already published, delete the remote tag on the GitHub remote as well.

Alex: Now for detached HEAD.

Jamie: This phrase sounds mysterious the first time you hear it.

Alex: It does, but the core idea is simple: normally HEAD points to a branch name, and that branch name points to a commit. In detached HEAD, HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch. You can inspect history there, but if you make new commits and then move away without saving them onto a branch, they become easy to lose track of.

Jamie: How do people end up there?

Alex: Usually by checking out a specific commit SHA or sometimes a tag, instead of checking out a branch.

Jamie: If I just want to get back to normal, what do I do?

Alex: If you didn’t make any commits you care about, simply switch back to a real branch, often the branch you were on before.

Jamie: And if I did make commits while detached?

Alex: Then create a new branch at the current detached position. That anchors those commits to a branch, making them safe. After that, you’re on a real branch again and the work is no longer floating.

Jamie: And VS Code can help show this state too.

Alex: Yes. VS Code’s branch and source control indicators can reveal that you’re detached, and you can create or switch branches from the UI.

Alex: Let’s tackle force pushing safely, because this is where good intentions can become team problems.

Jamie: We need the difference between force and force-with-lease.

Alex: Absolutely. Force push overwrites the remote branch with your local branch. Force-with-lease is the safer variant: it will refuse to overwrite the remote if someone else has pushed changes since your last fetch. So it acts like a seatbelt.

Jamie: When would I need any force push at all?

Alex: Most commonly after rewriting commit history on your own branch, especially after interactive rebase. Your local branch now has a different history than the remote branch, so a normal push is rejected. Force-with-lease is then the typical way to update the remote copy of your branch.

Jamie: But not usually on shared branches like main.

Alex: Correct. This is usually for your own feature branch, not protected shared branches.

Jamie: How do the tools fit here?

Alex: VS Code offers push flows, but for force pushing, the appendix explicitly says to use git directly. GitHub CLI likewise is not the place for the actual force-push flag; use Git CLI.

Jamie: And the key commands?

Alex: Safe force push is push with force-with-lease. There’s also a way to inspect what will happen before pushing, and there is unconditional force, plain force, which the appendix says to avoid unless you know exactly what you’re doing.

Jamie: Can you walk through the common rebase-plus-force-push sequence?

Alex: Sure. One: you’re on your feature branch and rebase it onto main to pick up the latest changes. Two: resolve any conflicts and continue the rebase. Three: because the remote still has the old pre-rebase history, you push your branch with force-with-lease so the remote branch is updated safely.

Jamie: So the safe pattern is: rewrite locally, verify, then force-with-lease, not plain force.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Now let’s look at git bisect, which is one of Git’s most brilliant debugging tools.

Jamie: This is the “find the exact bad commit” feature by binary search.

Alex: Yes. Instead of checking every commit one by one, bisect repeatedly chooses a midpoint between a known bad commit and a known good commit. You test that midpoint and tell Git whether it’s good or bad. Each answer cuts the search space roughly in half.

Jamie: How do you start?

Alex: First, start bisect mode. Then mark the current broken state as bad. Then tell Git a commit you know was good, maybe by SHA, tag, or branch name from before the bug appeared.

Jamie: After that, Git checks out a midpoint and asks me to judge it.

Alex: Exactly. If the bug is present at that midpoint, mark it bad. If the bug is not present, mark it good. Git moves again. You keep repeating until Git identifies the first bad commit.

Jamie: And when I’m done?

Alex: End the bisect session to return to your original branch.

Jamie: The appendix also mentions automation.

Alex: Yes. If you have a reliable test script that exits successfully when things are good and fails when things are bad, you can ask Git to run that script automatically at each step. That turns bisect into a mostly hands-off search.

Jamie: And there was a note later about Copilot helping if the bisect itself becomes confusing.

Alex: Right. Copilot can help interpret odd outputs or help debug why your test script isn’t behaving consistently during bisect.

Alex: Next up is git clean, which sounds mild but can be destructive.

Jamie: This is for deleting untracked files, not tracked changes.

Alex: Correct. Clean removes files Git is not tracking. That often means build artifacts, generated files, or scratch files cluttering your working directory. The big rule here is: always dry-run first.

Jamie: Because otherwise you might delete something you forgot wasn’t tracked.

Alex: Exactly. The dry-run form shows what would be deleted without actually deleting it. The appendix even notes an equivalent dry-run spelling, so learners recognize both forms.

Jamie: What are the common variations?

Alex: You can remove untracked files only, remove untracked files and directories, remove untracked plus ignored files—which is especially dangerous because that includes things listed in gitignore, like build outputs—and use interactive mode so Git prompts you before deleting items.

Jamie: And the option meanings matter.

Alex: Yes. The appendix explicitly explains the common flags: n for dry run, f for force, because Git usually requires force before deleting, d for directories, and x for ignored files too.

Jamie: Is there a VS Code angle?

Alex: There is mention of VS Code, but git clean is fundamentally more of a command-line task. The key teaching point is understanding what counts as untracked and using dry-run before any destructive clean.

Alex: Now let’s talk about branch protection, because sometimes Git isn’t rejecting you due to a mistake in your command. Sometimes the repository rules are doing their job.

Jamie: This is the “why can’t I push to main?” lesson.

Alex: Exactly. Branch protection can block direct pushes, block merges until reviews pass, require status checks or CI, require up-to-date branches, and enforce other repository policies.

Jamie: So if a push or merge is blocked, it may be policy, not a broken workflow.

Alex: Right. And the correct flow for protected branches is very consistent. Never work directly on main. Create a branch. Make your changes and commit them. Push your branch, not main. Open a pull request on GitHub. Then wait for reviews and automated checks to pass, and merge through the pull request.

Jamie: That line from the appendix is subtle but important: protection rules often apply to the merge into the protected branch, not to your ability to push your own feature branch.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What if my branch is out of date with main and GitHub says it must be updated?

Alex: You usually have two options. Option A is merge main into your branch. That creates a merge commit and is often straightforward. Option B is rebase your branch onto main. That gives a cleaner history, but because it rewrites your branch history, it usually requires a force-with-lease push afterward.

Jamie: And those can be done in VS Code, plain Git CLI, or in some cases via GitHub tooling.

Alex: Yes. The appendix includes VS Code and CLI approaches, and also notes GitHub CLI routes for updating a pull request branch from the GitHub side when that workflow is available.

Jamie: How do I check what branch protection rules are actually active?

Alex: Through GitHub CLI, you can query branch protection information for a branch like main. And on GitHub.com, repository settings expose the rules in the branch protection or ruleset interface.

Jamie: So the real skill isn’t just knowing Git commands. It’s recognizing when repository governance is part of the workflow.

Alex: Precisely.

Alex: The appendix also includes a quick reference table of advanced commands.

Jamie: Which is not new content so much as a compact lookup.

Alex: Right. It gives one-row-per-operation summaries so you can quickly remind yourself which command family fits which problem: cherry-pick for transplanting a commit, interactive rebase for cleaning history, reset for local undo, revert for shared-history undo, tags for marking commits, bisect for bug hunting, clean for untracked files, and so on.

Alex: Before we finish, there’s a modern companion topic: using GitHub Copilot for Git operations.

Jamie: I like that this section is not “let Copilot do magic,” but “use Copilot to understand and choose better.”

Alex: Exactly. Copilot can be especially helpful in a few focused situations. One is resolving merge conflicts. You can show it the conflict markers and ask it to explain the competing changes or draft a merged version.

Jamie: Another is writing better commit messages.

Alex: Yes. If your commit message is vague, Copilot can turn a diff or a staged-changes summary into a clearer message that explains intent and outcome.

Jamie: And confusing Git output is a huge one.

Alex: Absolutely. Git error messages are often precise but not beginner-friendly. You can paste the terminal output into Copilot and ask, “What does this mean?” That includes things like rebase conflicts, non-fast-forward push errors, detached HEAD warnings, branch protection messages, and bisect output.

Jamie: The appendix also highlights using Copilot to choose the right command in the first place.

Alex: Right. You can describe your goal in plain language—something like, “I accidentally committed to the wrong branch but haven’t pushed yet; what command should I use?”—and Copilot can suggest likely commands, which you should then verify before running.

Jamie: There’s also a section about debugging a failing bisect and getting help with branch protection errors.

Alex: Yes. Those are great examples of Copilot as an interpreter and workflow coach rather than an autopilot. It can help you reason through what state Git thinks you’re in.

Jamie: And we should distinguish Copilot in Terminal from Copilot Chat.

Alex: Good point. Copilot Chat is conversational and better for explanations, pasted output, and back-and-forth questions. Copilot in the terminal or Copilot CLI is good for command suggestions. The appendix specifically notes that you can ask Copilot to suggest a Git command for what you want to do.

Jamie: So the safe pattern is: ask for explanation or suggestion, inspect the proposed command, understand it, then run it.

Alex: Exactly. Especially with destructive commands like reset hard, clean force, or force push.

Jamie: Before we close, can we do a rapid decision guide?

Alex: Sure. Need one specific commit from another branch? Cherry-pick. Need to tidy your own unpublished history? Interactive rebase. Need to undo local commits at varying depths? Reset. Need to safely undo something already shared? Revert. Need to mark a release point? Tag. Stuck on a commit instead of a branch? You’re probably in detached HEAD—switch back or create a branch. Rewrote history on your own branch? Force-with-lease, not plain force. Need to find which commit introduced a bug? Bisect. Want to remove untracked clutter? Clean, but dry-run first. Push to main blocked? You’re probably dealing with branch protection; work through a branch and pull request.

Jamie: And if the terminal starts sounding cryptic, use git status, read the repository rules, and ask Copilot to explain the output—not to replace your judgment, but to support it.

Alex: Well said. One last note: this appendix points back to earlier material on how Git works and to the Pro Git book and GitHub Docs as authoritative sources. That matters because advanced Git is easiest to learn when you keep connecting commands back to Git’s model of commits, branches, HEAD, and history.

Jamie: So the commands stop feeling random once you understand what they’re moving: pointers, snapshots, and recorded history.

Alex: Exactly. That’s the real upgrade from basic Git to confident Git.

Alex: Thanks for learning with us.

Jamie: See you next time.

73. Episode 51: Git Security for Contributors

Secrets, .gitignore, environment variables, push protection, and safe contributor habits.

Based on: Appendix F: Git Security for Contributors

Download Episode 51 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 51: Git Security for Contributors

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're talking about one of the most practical parts of working with Git and GitHub: keeping secrets out of your repository.

Jamie: And by secrets, we mean things like API keys, passwords, tokens, private keys, database URLs, all the stuff that absolutely should not end up in a commit.

Alex: Exactly. This lesson is for anyone who commits code or documentation. You do not need to be a security expert. In fact, most contributor security problems are not dramatic hacks. They're accidents. A token pasted into a config file. A .env file committed by mistake. A credential file that slipped into staging.

Jamie: So the reassuring part is that this is mostly about habits.

Alex: Yes. A few good habits prevent most of these problems.

Alex: A quick accessibility note before we dive in. This reference is structured from understanding the risk, to prevention, to recovery, to daily habits. If you're using a screen reader, the code blocks include exact terminal commands and gitignore patterns, so it can help to switch to a focused reading mode before copying. If you have low vision, the most important warnings in the original reference are emphasized, and the checklist at the end is designed to be used as a repeatable routine.

Jamie: So this is both a lesson and a reference workflow.

Alex: Right. You can listen straight through, or come back to the prevention steps, the recovery steps, and the checklist later.

Alex: Let's start with why this matters. If a secret is committed to a public GitHub repository, even for a few seconds, you should treat it as compromised.

Jamie: Even if you notice immediately and delete it?

Alex: Even then. There are continuous bots scanning public repositories for secrets. They can harvest exposed credentials within seconds. Also, deleting the file from the latest version of the project does not remove it from Git history. And if the repository has already been forked, that history may exist elsewhere too. Search engines may also have indexed content before you removed it.

Jamie: So the phrase to remember is: deleting the visible file is not the same as removing the leak.

Alex: Perfectly said. And the consequences can be expensive or damaging very quickly. A cloud key can rack up charges. A GitHub personal access token could allow access to repositories or let someone act as you. A payment platform key could be abused for fraudulent activity.

Jamie: Is there any good news here?

Alex: There is. GitHub can automatically revoke some of its own tokens when it detects them in a commit, like certain GitHub personal access tokens or app tokens. But for many third-party services, like AWS or Stripe, you must rotate the secret yourself, and fast.

Alex: The first major prevention tool is the .gitignore file.

Jamie: This is the file that tells Git what not to track.

Alex: Yes. If a file is listed in .gitignore and Git is not already tracking it, that file won't show up in git status, won't be staged by normal add commands, and won't be committed.

Jamie: What kinds of things belong there?

Alex: Three big categories. First, secrets and credentials. That includes environment files like .env, .env.local, environment-specific local files, generic star-dot-env patterns, key files like .pem, .key, .p12, .pfx, and SSH private key names like id_rsa or id_ed25519. Also credential files such as credentials.json, secrets.json, config slash secrets.yml, or cloud credential files.

Jamie: So if a file stores a secret, it is a strong candidate for .gitignore.

Alex: Exactly. Second category: editor and operating system clutter. On macOS that might be .DS_Store or .AppleDouble. On Windows, Thumbs.db or desktop.ini. For editors, JetBrains projects often ignore .idea slash. VS Code is nuanced: some teams commit selected settings, and some do not. So .vscode settings may be optional depending on team practice.

Jamie: That nuance matters, because learners sometimes assume every editor-generated file should always be ignored.

Alex: Right. Some workspace settings are intentionally shared. Third category: build output and dependencies. For Node projects that often means node_modules, dist, and build. For Python it might be __pycache__, .pyc files, .venv, or venv. And then general clutter like logs, temp files, and caches.

Jamie: But .gitignore has an important limitation, right?

Alex: It does. .gitignore only stops untracked files from being added. If Git is already tracking a file, adding it to .gitignore does not magically untrack it.

Jamie: So how do you check?

Alex: You can ask Git directly whether a file is tracked. For example, to check .env, run git ls-files space .env. If Git returns that filename, it's already tracked.

Jamie: And then you need to untrack it without deleting your local copy.

Alex: Exactly. The usual command is git rm --cached space .env. That removes it from Git's tracking index but leaves the file on your machine. Then add .env to .gitignore and commit that change.

Jamie: That's such an important distinction: remove from Git tracking, not from your disk.

Alex: Yes.

Alex: You can also create a global gitignore file for patterns you never want in any repository on your computer.

Jamie: Like OS junk files or personal editor clutter.

Alex: Exactly. One approach is to create a file such as tilde slash .gitignore_global, then tell Git to use it with a global config setting: core.excludesfile pointed at that file.

Jamie: So project-specific ignores stay in the repository's .gitignore, and machine-specific noise can live in the global ignore.

Alex: That's the clean mental model.

Jamie: And if someone doesn't want to write all these patterns from scratch?

Alex: GitHub maintains .gitignore templates for many languages and frameworks. You can choose one when creating a repository on GitHub, or download one for an existing project, such as the Node template, and append it to your .gitignore.

Alex: Now let's talk about the right way to store secrets: environment variables.

Jamie: Meaning the secret lives outside your repository, and your code reads it in when it runs.

Alex: Exactly. The anti-pattern is hardcoding a secret directly into source code. For example, writing an API key as a literal string in Python or JavaScript. The safer pattern is to read that value from the environment instead, using something like os.environ.get in Python or process.env in JavaScript.

Jamie: So the code can be committed, but the secret value stays outside the repo.

Alex: Right. Locally, many projects use a .env file to store those environment variables. That's convenient and common, but that file must never be committed. It belongs in .gitignore.

Jamie: And the values inside might include a GitHub token, a database URL, or a payment secret key.

Alex: Exactly. The code that loads the .env file can be in the repository. The actual .env file stays on your machine.

Jamie: How should teams share secrets, then, if not by email or chat?

Alex: Never through Slack, email, or GitHub comments. Safer options include GitHub Actions Secrets for automation, a password manager with secure sharing for team credentials, or a dedicated secrets manager for production systems.

Jamie: Can you give the GitHub Actions version in plain language?

Alex: Sure. In a GitHub Actions workflow, you define an environment variable from a stored GitHub secret, like secrets dot API_KEY, and then the workflow can use it during deployment without placing the actual secret in the workflow file.

Jamie: So the workflow references the secret by name, but the value lives in repository or organization settings.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Next habit: review before you commit.

Jamie: This sounds simple, but it's probably the most powerful routine in the whole lesson.

Alex: I think so too. Before committing, inspect exactly what you've staged. The key command is git diff --staged. That shows the content that is actually going into the commit.

Jamie: And you can also review a specific staged file the same way.

Alex: Yes. Use git diff --staged followed by a path if you want a narrower review. As you scan the diff, look for hardcoded passwords, tokens, API keys, .env files, credential files, or even TODO comments that mention sensitive details.

Jamie: That last one is sneaky. Sometimes the leak is not the credential itself, but a note about where the credential lives.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: And this is where the warning against git add dot comes in.

Alex: Yes. git add . stages everything it sees in the working tree. That is fast, but risky. A safer habit is to stage only known-clean files, like git add followed by specific paths. Or use git add -p, patch mode, which lets you review changes hunk by hunk and decide what to stage.

Jamie: Patch mode can feel slower at first, but it's a wonderful guardrail.

Alex: It is. And after staging, check git status to see what's staged and what isn't, then use git diff --staged for the actual content review.

Jamie: The source also mentions an AI-assisted review step.

Alex: Yes. After staging changes, you can use a tool like GitHub Copilot Chat and ask it to review your staged diff for accidentally included secrets, API keys, or credentials. That is not a replacement for your own review, but it can be an extra check.

Alex: Now let's add automation with pre-commit hooks.

Jamie: A pre-commit hook is a script that runs automatically when you try to commit, and it can block the commit if it finds a problem.

Alex: Exactly. Think of it as a safety net. The appendix presents three options.

Jamie: Let's do the practical overview.

Alex: Option A is detect-secrets, recommended in the source and Python-based. The workflow is: install the tool, create a baseline scan of your existing code, review that baseline so known non-secrets are marked safe, install the pre-commit hook, and test it manually.

Jamie: Why the baseline step?

Alex: Because many repositories already contain strings that look secret-like but are harmless examples, test values, or false positives. The baseline gives the tool a starting point so it can focus on new problems.

Jamie: So baseline first, then hook, then test.

Alex: Right.

Jamie: What about Option B?

Alex: Option B is gitleaks. It's Go-based and known for being easy to run with minimal dependencies. The source calls out installation on macOS and Windows, then two useful scan modes: scanning the entire repository history for secrets, and scanning only staged changes, meaning what you're about to commit.

Jamie: That distinction matters. One mode is for a deep audit. The other is for day-to-day protection.

Alex: Exactly. The source also describes adding gitleaks as a manual pre-commit hook by creating a script in .git slash hooks slash pre-commit.

Jamie: So that's a more hands-on setup.

Alex: Yes.

Jamie: And Option C?

Alex: Option C is the pre-commit framework, which manages multiple hooks for you. The workflow is: install pre-commit, create a .pre-commit-config.yaml file in the repository root, define the hooks you want there, install the hooks, and optionally run them manually against all files.

Jamie: So instead of wiring each hook by hand, you use a framework to manage them consistently.

Alex: Exactly. For contributors working across multiple repos, that can be especially nice.

Jamie: If a learner is choosing, what's the simplest advice?

Alex: Pick one automated secret scanning approach and actually use it. The perfect tool is less important than having a hook that runs before secrets leave your machine.

Jamie: Okay, let's tackle the stressful scenario. I accidentally committed a secret. What now?

Alex: Step one: rotate the secret immediately.

Jamie: Before anything else.

Alex: Before anything else. Assume the old secret is compromised. Generate a new token, key, or password with the provider, and revoke the old one if possible.

Jamie: Step two is asking whether it was pushed publicly.

Alex: Exactly. If the secret was committed locally but not pushed yet, you're in a much better position. One safe pattern is to undo the last commit while keeping your changes staged, remove the secret from the file, then re-add and recommit.

Jamie: So you fix the content before it ever reaches a public remote.

Alex: Right. Edit the file, remove the secret, stage the cleaned version, and create a new commit.

Jamie: But if it was pushed, deleting the line in a new commit is not enough because the secret still exists in history.

Alex: Exactly. That's step three: remove the secret from Git history.

Alex: The recommended modern tool in the appendix is git-filter-repo. You install git-filter-repo, then either remove a specific file from all history or replace a specific secret string throughout all history.

Jamie: So if the problem is, say, an accidentally committed .env file, you can strip that file from every historical commit. And if the problem is a literal token pasted in several places, you can replace that string across history.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And there's an alternative.

Alex: Yes, BFG Repo-Cleaner, which is fast and Java-based. The appendix notes downloading it from the BFG project site. With BFG, you can remove a file from all history or replace secret strings. For string replacement, the source calls out creating a passwords.txt file with one secret per line.

Jamie: So both tools are about rewriting history to eliminate the old secret traces.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: Then comes the part people are often nervous about: force push.

Alex: Yes. Step four is force pushing the cleaned history to the remote. Because you've rewritten commit history, a normal push won't work.

Jamie: And that can affect collaborators.

Alex: It can. Rewriting history is disruptive, which is another reason prevention matters so much. After that, step five is to tell GitHub to rescan, so its secret scanning systems can reassess the repository state.

Jamie: Can we summarize the decision flow in plain language?

Alex: Yes. First: rotate the secret immediately. Second: if it was never pushed, clean it locally and recommit. Third: if it was pushed, remove it from history, then force push the cleaned history, and follow up with GitHub rescanning and any provider-specific cleanup.

Alex: Now, GitHub also has built-in push protection.

Jamie: This is the feature that can stop you from pushing certain detected secrets.

Alex: Exactly. Push protection checks for supported secret patterns and can block the push before the secret lands in the remote repository.

Jamie: That sounds great, but I want learners to hear this clearly: it's helpful, not magical.

Alex: Precisely. Push protection covers many common secret types, but not every possible secret. You still need .gitignore, environment variables, review habits, and ideally hooks.

Jamie: What if push protection blocks you?

Alex: Treat that as a serious warning. Stop, inspect the file or diff, and determine whether the detected string is a real secret. If it is, remove it and store it properly. If it's a false positive, follow your project's and GitHub's guidance carefully before bypassing anything.

Jamie: And can you check whether a repository has push protection enabled?

Alex: Yes. The appendix includes checking your repository's push protection status through GitHub's security settings and secret scanning features. For learners, the main concept is: know whether your repo has that guardrail, but don't rely on it as the only one.

Alex: Let's talk about secure credential storage more broadly.

Jamie: Meaning not just secrets in code, but where your Git and development tools store credentials.

Alex: Exactly. The big rule is never store credentials in plaintext. Not in a plain text file, not hardcoded in a script, and not casually embedded in git config in a way that exposes the secret.

Jamie: So where should they go instead?

Alex: Use your operating system's secure credential store when possible. On macOS, that's Keychain. On Windows, Git for Windows typically integrates with Credential Manager. On Linux, a common approach is the libsecret store, though it may require installation.

Jamie: And a password manager?

Alex: Also a good option, especially for personal organization and for teams that need secure sharing. The appendix specifically points learners toward using a password manager rather than leaving tokens in notes or loose files.

Jamie: How do you check what Git is currently using?

Alex: You can inspect which credential helper is set in Git configuration. The practical point is to verify that Git is using a secure helper instead of relying on insecure plaintext storage.

Alex: Let's turn all of this into a repeatable checklist.

Jamie: Yes, because daily routines are what actually keep repos safe.

Alex: Before committing: make sure secrets are in environment variables, not code. Confirm .env and credential files are ignored. Stage carefully, not blindly. Review staged changes with git diff --staged. If you use patch mode or a pre-commit hook, this is where they help most.

Jamie: Before pushing: double-check what is about to leave your machine, make sure no secret warnings are appearing, and pay attention if push protection or a hook blocks you.

Alex: Repository setup, one time: create a strong .gitignore, consider a global gitignore for OS and editor noise, set up a pre-commit secret scanner, and use secure credential helpers on your machine.

Jamie: And if you're a maintainer?

Alex: Encourage or require these habits project-wide. Provide a good .gitignore. Document how contributors should handle .env files and local configuration. Consider pre-commit tooling, secret scanning, and push protection. Make the safe path the easy path.

Jamie: Before we wrap up, I want to return to the teaching structure for accessibility. This appendix was designed so learners can approach it in multiple ways: start with why leaks matter, jump to prevention if that's your immediate need, or revisit the checklist before every push.

Alex: Yes. And the authoritative guidance behind this material comes from GitHub's code security and secret scanning documentation, along with related GitHub security feature references and changelog updates.

Jamie: So this isn't just folklore. It's grounded in the platform's actual security guidance.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can you give us one final compact version?

Alex: Sure. Don't commit secrets. Ignore the right files. Store secrets in environment variables. Review staged changes before every commit. Use automated detection with hooks. If a secret leaks, rotate it immediately and clean history if needed. Use GitHub push protection when available, but don't depend on it alone. And store credentials in secure system stores, not plaintext.

Jamie: That's the habit loop.

Alex: It is. And it's one of the best ways to protect both your own work and every project you contribute to.

74. Episode 52: GitHub Desktop

Using GitHub Desktop as an accessible alternative for cloning, branching, committing, and syncing.

Based on: Appendix H: GitHub Desktop

Download Episode 52 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 52: GitHub Desktop

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we're exploring GitHub Desktop, which is GitHub's free, open-source visual Git client for Windows and macOS.

Jamie: So this is for someone who wants Git as its own app, separate from the code editor?

Alex: Exactly. If VS Code's Source Control view feels too tucked inside the editor, GitHub Desktop gives you a dedicated space for cloning repositories, creating branches, reviewing changes, committing, syncing with GitHub, and handling a lot of the day-to-day Git work.

Jamie: And it's worth saying: this appendix sits alongside the larger tool-choosing and Git-in-practice material, right?

Alex: Yes. Think of this as a practical companion. If you're deciding between tools, or trying to build an accessible contribution workflow, GitHub Desktop is one strong option. And because this lesson is for blind and low-vision learners too, we'll keep noting what works well, what doesn't, and when another tool may be the better fit.

Alex: Let's orient to the full journey. We'll cover what GitHub Desktop can and cannot do, how to install it, how sign-in works, what the interface looks like, cloning, branching, staging and committing, pushing and pulling, syncing a fork, resolving conflicts, viewing history, cherry-picking, stashing, undoing changes, accessibility notes, and then when to use Desktop versus VS Code versus the Git command line.

Jamie: So not just a sales pitch for the app.

Alex: Not at all. More like: here is the tool, here are its boundaries, and here is how to use it wisely.

Alex: A good place to start is scope. GitHub Desktop supports the everyday workflow most contributors use most days.

Jamie: What counts as everyday workflow here?

Alex: Cloning repositories from GitHub. Creating, switching, and deleting branches. Staging files, and even staging individual lines or hunks inside a file. Writing commit messages and committing. Pushing and pulling. Opening a pull request, though that part sends you to GitHub.com in your browser. It also supports merge conflict resolution with a visual editor, viewing commit history and diffs, cherry-picking commits from one branch to another, stashing and restoring uncommitted changes, undoing commits, and discarding changes.

Jamie: That is a lot. For many people, that really is the whole routine.

Alex: It is. But there are important limits. GitHub Desktop does not expose everything Git can do.

Jamie: Such as the scary advanced stuff?

Alex: Some of the advanced, powerful, and sometimes risky operations, yes. In the Desktop user interface, you do not get interactive rebase, so no visual equivalent of git rebase dash i. You also do not get git bisect, git clean, creating annotated tags, or commit signing with GPG or SSH from the UI.

Jamie: So if I need those, I leave GitHub Desktop?

Alex: You use the terminal, or sometimes VS Code's terminal. And GitHub Desktop helps with that by offering Repository, then Open in Terminal, or on Windows Open in Command Prompt, so you land in the correct repository folder immediately.

Jamie: That's a nice bridge. You're not trapped in the GUI.

Alex: Right. And for accessibility, that's significant. For screen reader users, Desktop handles a lot of core tasks through keyboard-friendly controls and standard text inputs, especially the commit message fields. For low-vision users, system zoom, display scaling, and high-contrast operating system themes matter a lot. And if the diff colors are hard to distinguish, opening the repository or diff in VS Code can give you more theme control.

Jamie: And for sighted users, the three-panel layout gives a quick snapshot: files on one side, diff on the other, commit area below.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Okay, let's install it.

Alex: On Windows, the recommended command-line install is winget install GitHub.GitHubDesktop.

Jamie: So if someone already uses Winget, that's quick.

Alex: Yes. The direct-download option is also simple: go to desktop dot github dot com, choose Download for Windows, run the installer, and it installs and launches automatically.

Jamie: And on a Mac?

Alex: If you use Homebrew, brew install dash dash cask github. Or go to the same website, choose Download for macOS, open the downloaded zip file, and drag GitHub Desktop into your Applications folder.

Jamie: And Linux?

Alex: No official Linux support for GitHub Desktop. Linux users should generally use VS Code's Source Control panel or the Git CLI.

Jamie: That's important not to gloss over.

Alex: Absolutely.

Jamie: Once it's installed, what does sign-in look like? Do we need to manage personal access tokens or SSH keys?

Alex: For normal GitHub.com use, no. GitHub Desktop uses browser-based OAuth sign-in. On first launch, you open GitHub Desktop, choose Sign in to GitHub.com, your browser opens to GitHub's authorization page, you sign in if needed, authorize GitHub Desktop, then return to the app.

Jamie: And after that?

Alex: The app stores credentials securely in the system keychain, so you usually won't be prompted for your password again.

Jamie: What if someone uses GitHub Enterprise or an organization-hosted server?

Alex: Then they choose Sign in to GitHub Enterprise Server and enter the server URL for that organization.

Alex: Now let's build a mental model of the interface. GitHub Desktop has three main visual areas, plus a commit area.

Jamie: Talk me through it as if I can't see the screen clearly.

Alex: At the top is the toolbar. On the left is the Current Repository control, which lets you switch among local repositories you've opened in GitHub Desktop. Near the middle is Current Branch, which opens the branch selector. On the right is the sync control, usually labeled Fetch origin, Pull origin, or Push origin depending on state.

Jamie: So the top bar answers three questions: which repo, which branch, and what's my sync status?

Alex: Perfectly said. Then in the left panel you'll usually see either the Changes tab or the History tab. Changes lists uncommitted work. History lists past commits. The larger main area to the right shows either file diffs or commit details depending on what you've selected. And near the bottom left is the commit area with a Summary field, optional Description field, and a commit button that usually says something like Commit to main or Commit to feature slash name.

Jamie: That sounds fairly structured.

Alex: It is. For keyboard users and screen reader users, that structure matters. You can tab among the major regions. The branch selector behaves like a searchable dropdown: type to filter, use arrow keys to move, press Enter to select. The commit button is announced with the target branch name.

Jamie: And for low-vision users?

Alex: The toolbar stays fixed at the top, which helps. Increasing operating-system display scaling enlarges the interface proportionally. And the Changes and History tabs are clearly separated in the left panel. For sighted users, one useful cue is that the sync button changes icon or label to show whether you're fetching, pushing, or pulling.

Jamie: Let's clone a repository. What's the easiest path?

Alex: Often from GitHub.com. On a repository page, use the Code button and choose Open with GitHub Desktop. That launches the app with the repository URL already filled in. You choose the local folder where the repository should live, then activate Clone.

Jamie: And if I want to stay inside the app?

Alex: Use the clone shortcut: Control Shift O on Windows, Command Shift O on macOS. Then choose either the GitHub.com tab to browse repositories connected to your account, or the URL tab to paste any repository URL. Pick the local path and choose Clone.

Jamie: The source also mentioned a GitHub CLI alternative.

Alex: Yes. If you're comfortable in the terminal, you can run gh repo clone owner slash repo-name, and after that open the repository in GitHub Desktop with the github command followed by the path to the repo.

Jamie: So Desktop can be the main tool or just one tool in a mixed workflow.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Now we've got a cloned repository. Branches are next, right?

Alex: Yes. Branching is one of the most common tasks. To create a new branch, open the Current Branch menu, choose the option to create a new branch, type the branch name, and confirm. GitHub Desktop will create it based on your current branch and switch you to it.

Jamie: So I'm not just naming it. I'm also choosing the branch I branch from, whether explicitly or implicitly.

Alex: Right. Usually it's based on whatever branch you're currently on, often main. To switch to an existing branch, open the same branch selector, type to filter if needed, move to the desired branch, and select it.

Jamie: What if I have uncommitted changes and try to switch?

Alex: GitHub Desktop may prompt you depending on whether the changes can safely move with you. In practice, if you're unsure, commit your work or stash it before switching branches. We'll talk about stashing later.

Jamie: And deleting a branch?

Alex: You generally switch away from the branch first, then use the branch menu to delete it. Deleting a branch removes the branch reference, not the commits themselves if they still exist elsewhere, but it's still something to do thoughtfully.

Alex: Now let's get into the heart of daily Git work: staging and committing.

Jamie: This is where people often blur concepts together. What does GitHub Desktop help us see clearly?

Alex: It makes the review step very concrete. In the Changes tab, the left side lists modified, added, and deleted files. Selecting a file shows its diff in the main pane, so you can inspect exactly what changed before committing.

Jamie: So reviewing changes is not optional busywork. It's how you confirm what you're about to record.

Alex: Exactly. Then comes staging. In GitHub Desktop, files in the Changes list usually have checkboxes. Checked means staged for the next commit. Unchecked means leave it out.

Jamie: That's a very approachable model.

Alex: It is. And it gets better: you can often stage individual lines or hunks within a file. That means if one file contains two unrelated edits, you may be able to commit only the part relevant to your current task.

Jamie: Can you explain hunk in plain language?

Alex: A hunk is a chunk of nearby changed lines shown together in a diff. It's larger than a single line, smaller than the whole file. GitHub Desktop can let you include only certain chunks, or sometimes individual lines, to keep commits focused.

Jamie: That helps create cleaner history.

Alex: Exactly. Once staged, you write the commit message. The Summary field is the short title of the commit. The Description field is optional extra detail. Then you activate the commit button.

Jamie: Any guidance on writing that summary?

Alex: Make it specific and useful. For example, not update stuff, but fix broken heading navigation in README. The summary should help your future self and collaborators understand intent quickly.

Jamie: And the source specifically notes that these fields are standard editable text inputs, which is good for screen reader support.

Alex: Yes, that's an important accessibility detail.

Jamie: After committing locally, we need to sync with GitHub.

Alex: Right. GitHub Desktop combines several related actions into the sync area at the top right. Fetch checks the remote for updates without changing your local branch. Pull fetches and then brings remote changes into your local branch. Push sends your local commits to GitHub.

Jamie: Let's separate those carefully. What does fetch do for a cautious learner?

Alex: Fetch is the safe look-before-you-touch option. It checks whether the remote has new commits and updates GitHub Desktop's awareness of that state, but it does not merge those commits into your current branch.

Jamie: So if I just want to know whether anything changed upstream, fetch first.

Alex: Exactly. If there are commits on GitHub that your local branch doesn't have, the app may then offer Pull origin. If you have local commits not yet on GitHub, it offers Push origin.

Jamie: And if both sides changed?

Alex: You may fetch, then pull, possibly followed later by push if you also have local work. The exact label can vary, but the conceptual model stays the same.

Jamie: The source also calls out keyboard shortcuts here.

Alex: Yes. The important lesson is not memorizing every shortcut, but knowing that the app supports keyboard access for clone and other common actions, and that sync operations are available through both toolbar controls and menus. If you're a keyboard-first user, it's worth exploring the menu bar on your platform to learn the exact commands GitHub Desktop exposes.

Jamie: Fork workflows are really common in open source. How does syncing your fork fit into GitHub Desktop?

Alex: If you've forked a repository, you usually have two remotes conceptually: your fork on GitHub, commonly called origin, and the original project repository, often called upstream. Syncing your fork means bringing changes from upstream into your local copy, and often later into your fork as well.

Jamie: And if upstream isn't set yet?

Alex: You need to configure the upstream remote. The appendix specifically notes setting up the upstream remote if it isn't already there. GitHub Desktop can help with common fork workflows, but there are times when checking or adding remotes may be clearer in the CLI.

Jamie: So the conceptual requirement is: know where your branch is pulling from and where it's pushing to.

Alex: Exactly. Without that, fork syncing becomes confusing fast.

Jamie: Now let's visit the part people dread: merge conflicts.

Alex: Yes, but they become less scary once you understand them. A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically reconcile competing changes, often because the same lines were changed in different ways on different branches.

Jamie: What does GitHub Desktop do when that happens?

Alex: It will tell you there are conflicts and guide you into resolving them, often by opening the conflicted files in your editor or a visual resolution flow. The step-by-step idea is: identify the conflicted files, open and inspect them, choose which content to keep or combine, remove the conflict markers if you're editing manually, save the file, and mark the conflict as resolved.

Jamie: Then what?

Alex: After resolving in your editor, return to GitHub Desktop. Review the now-resolved changes, commit the merge or conflict resolution, and continue syncing as needed.

Jamie: So Desktop is part coordinator, part visual assistant, but the actual text editing may happen in VS Code or another editor.

Alex: Precisely. And for blind users in particular, editing conflict markers in a familiar text editor like VS Code may be much more accessible than relying on a highly visual merge interface.

Alex: Once you've worked for a while, history becomes important.

Jamie: Not just what changed, but when and why.

Alex: Exactly. In the History tab, GitHub Desktop shows the commit timeline for the current repository or branch context. You can navigate through commits, select one, and inspect its details and diff.

Jamie: What about filtering commits?

Alex: Filtering helps narrow history, often by searching commit messages, authors, or relevant content exposed by the interface. The key skill is using search or filtering to avoid reading an entire history when you're really looking for one fix or one person's work.

Jamie: And a specific file's history?

Alex: You can view the history related to a particular file, which is very useful when you want to know who changed one document, script, or configuration file over time.

Jamie: Comparing branches is another big one.

Alex: Yes. Comparing branches lets you inspect how one branch differs from another before merging, cherry-picking, or opening a pull request. It's a way to answer, what is unique here relative to there?

Jamie: Speaking of moving work across branches, let's talk about cherry-pick.

Alex: Cherry-pick means taking a specific commit from one branch and applying it onto another branch, without merging the entire branch.

Jamie: So if a bug fix exists on one branch and I need that exact fix on another, cherry-pick is the targeted move.

Alex: Exactly. In GitHub Desktop, you typically find the commit in history, use the context menu or available command to cherry-pick it onto your current branch, and let Desktop apply it.

Jamie: And if the commit doesn't apply cleanly?

Alex: Then you get a conflict, just as you might during a merge. Resolve the conflicting files, save them, return to GitHub Desktop, and complete the process.

Jamie: So cherry-pick is powerful, but it can still require careful conflict resolution.

Alex: Yes.

Jamie: Now, stashing. This is one of those features people hear about before they really understand when to use it.

Alex: A stash is a temporary shelf for uncommitted changes. You use it when you're in the middle of work but need a clean working tree, often to switch branches or handle an urgent task.

Jamie: So it's like saying, hold this for me, I don't want to commit it yet.

Alex: Exactly. In GitHub Desktop, you can stash your current changes, which removes them from the working view and returns the repository to a cleaner state. Later, you restore the stash to bring those changes back.

Jamie: Any caution here?

Alex: Yes. A stash is convenient, but it is easier to forget than a commit. If the work is meaningful and coherent, a real commit on a branch is often safer. Use stash for short-term interruption management, not as long-term storage.

Jamie: Let's do undoing changes, because everyone eventually needs that.

Alex: Absolutely. GitHub Desktop supports a few kinds of undo. One is undoing the last commit. That generally removes the commit while keeping the changed content available locally, so you can adjust it and recommit.

Jamie: Useful if the message was wrong or the commit included something extra.

Alex: Exactly. Another option is discarding changes to a file. That throws away the uncommitted edits in that file and restores it to its last committed state.

Jamie: So that is destructive for uncommitted work.

Alex: Yes, and learners should pause before using it. There's also discarding all changes, which wipes all current uncommitted modifications in the repository working tree. That's even more destructive.

Jamie: So the rule is: understand whether you're undoing a commit or discarding uncommitted edits. Those are very different things.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Now let's spend real time on accessibility and screen reader notes, because this appendix explicitly includes them.

Jamie: Good. Start with what works well.

Alex: GitHub Desktop does many core tasks through standard controls: buttons, text fields, lists, checkboxes, dropdowns. Keyboard navigation across major regions is generally workable. Commit message fields are standard edit fields. Cloning, branching, staging, committing, and pushing are all possible without depending purely on a mouse.

Jamie: So for basic workflows, many users can absolutely use it.

Alex: Yes. But there are limitations. Dense diff views can be harder to parse with a screen reader than a plain-text diff in an editor or terminal. Some visual branch comparisons or conflict-resolution flows may be less comfortable nonvisually. And if you're trying to perform something Desktop doesn't support, you'll need another tool anyway.

Jamie: Let's make the Windows and macOS notes concrete.

Alex: On Windows with NVDA or JAWS, tabbing through controls and interacting with standard input fields generally works well. The branch selector, commit fields, file list, and top toolbar are usually manageable. But reading complex diffs line by line may be slower than opening the file in VS Code, where screen reader navigation can be more granular.

Jamie: And VoiceOver on macOS?

Alex: Similar story. VoiceOver users can navigate the application's controls, but richly visual diff presentation may be less efficient than reviewing changed files in an editor with strong text navigation commands. The app is usable, but not always optimal for every task.

Jamie: That leads naturally to the source's recommendation that VS Code may be a better accessible alternative in some cases.

Alex: Exactly. VS Code often gives blind users better file editing, better direct text access to diffs and conflict markers, and a single environment for coding plus Git tasks. GitHub Desktop can still be helpful for branch switching, a visual overview, or quick commit workflows, but if accessibility friction rises, opening the repository in VS Code is often the better path.

Jamie: And for low-vision users?

Alex: Use system zoom, scaling, and high-contrast themes. Be aware that additions and deletions in diffs use green and red backgrounds, so if color distinction is hard, increase text size or open the same work in VS Code with a theme that gives you better contrast. On both platforms, operating-system display settings do a lot of the accessibility heavy lifting.

Jamie: Can we summarize the learning-card style takeaways?

Alex: Sure. For screen reader users: GitHub Desktop handles core workflows with keyboard-accessible controls, and you can jump to the terminal for unsupported operations. For low-vision users: system scaling and themes matter, and VS Code may offer better diff customization. For sighted users: the layout provides fast visual status awareness, especially the file status icons and sync indicators.

Jamie: So when should someone use GitHub Desktop instead of VS Code or the Git CLI?

Alex: Use GitHub Desktop when you want a dedicated Git application with a clear visual workflow for cloning, branching, reviewing changes, and syncing. It's great when separating Git from coding helps reduce cognitive load.

Jamie: Use VS Code when?

Alex: When your work is tightly tied to editing files, reviewing text changes in context, resolving conflicts directly in source files, or when accessibility is better in your editor than in a standalone GUI. It's often the best all-in-one option.

Jamie: And Git CLI?

Alex: Use the Git command line when you need the full power of Git: interactive rebase, bisect, clean, advanced remote configuration, commit signing setups, scripts, automation, or simply the precision that comes from explicit commands.

Jamie: So this isn't a competition with one winner.

Alex: No. It's a toolkit. Many strong workflows combine all three. For example: clone and branch in GitHub Desktop, edit and resolve conflicts in VS Code, do advanced history surgery in the terminal.

Jamie: Before we close, let's mention sources.

Alex: The authoritative reference for this appendix is GitHub Desktop documentation from GitHub, along with broader GitHub Docs and related Git guidance. For accessibility framing, standard web accessibility guidance like WCAG is also relevant. If behavior changes in the app over time, always trust the current official GitHub Desktop docs over an older walkthrough.

Jamie: That's a good reminder, especially because UI labels and workflows can evolve.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: So the big takeaway?

Alex: GitHub Desktop covers a wide, practical slice of everyday Git work. It makes cloning, branching, staging, committing, syncing, history review, cherry-picking, stashing, and some conflict workflows approachable. It does not replace the terminal for advanced Git, and it does not always beat VS Code for accessibility or text-heavy tasks. But for many learners, especially those who want a purpose-built Git app, it's an excellent part of an accessible contribution workflow.

Jamie: And the best way to learn it is probably to use it on a real repository.

Alex: Yes. Clone something small, create a branch, make one change, review the diff, commit it, push it, and explore history. A calm, repeatable practice loop will teach you far more than memorizing buttons.

Jamie: Perfect. That's GitHub Desktop.

Alex: And we'll see you next time.

GitHub CLI reference and usage

Based on: GitHub CLI Reference

Download Episode 53 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 53: GitHub CLI Reference

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back to Git Going with GitHub. This is episode 53: GitHub CLI Reference. I am Alex, and today we are turning GitHub CLI Reference from a list of instructions into a working mental model that actually feels alive.

Alex: Using the GitHub CLI for issues, pull requests, authentication, and automation-friendly workflows. That is the surface description. Underneath it, we are building judgment: where to focus, what to ignore, and how to verify the result.

Alex: The next layer is this. Here is the learner-facing version. Or download the installer from cli.github.com. A good GitHub workflow is like a well-run meeting: everyone knows the topic, the next action, and who has the floor.

Jamie: What is the safe way to learn from that example?

Alex: For a learner, the useful signals are concrete. Where do you use GitHub? → GitHub.com (or Enterprise). Preferred protocol? → HTTPS (or SSH). Authenticate with browser? → Yes -- your browser opens for OAuth sign-in.

Alex: Treat examples as spoken recipes, not decorations. You may hear something like gh auth login. Check your auth status at any time; gh auth status; Log out; gh auth logout; Refresh credentials / add new scopes; gh auth refresh. Read the command, understand what it changes, then run it only when the repository state matches the lesson.

Jamie: What does someone need before they touch the keyboard?

Alex: Learning Cards: Getting Started with gh has three jobs: name the idea, give the learner a move, and show what counts as evidence.

Alex: The parts worth keeping in working memory are these. gh auth login uses plain-text arrow-key prompts -- every option is announced as you arrow through the list. After authentication, gh auth status confirms your login in a single readable line -- no browser needed. All gh output is plain text with no hidden elements, making it one of the most screen-reader-friendly GitHub interfaces. Use a high-contrast terminal theme (light text on dark background, or vice versa) for comfortable reading of command output. gh output is plain text with no color-dependent meaning -- colors are supplementary labels, not the only indicator.

Alex: The useful habit is simple: orient, act, verify, then continue. That pause between action and trust is part of the work.

Jamie: How do you keep commands from becoming magic words?

Read the command, understand what it changes, then run it only when the repository state matches the lesson.

Read the command, understand what it changes, then run it only when the repository state matches the lesson.

Alex: A solid issue habit is to read the title, the body, and the timeline before acting. You are listening for the requested action, the missing evidence, and the person who needs a response.

Jamie: Let's pause on Listing and filtering issues. What should a learner take away from it?
