76. Episode 54: Agent Installation and Setup

Installing accessibility agents, configuring for your environment, and verifying the setup.

Based on: Appendix : Agent Installation and Setup

Download Episode 54 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 54: Agent Installation and Setup

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. This lesson is a practical setup guide for accessibility agents across five platforms: GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, and Codex CLI. It’s a companion to earlier material on agents and to the broader reference docs, and the authoritative source is the Accessibility Agents repository plus its system requirements documentation.

Jamie: So this is the episode you listen to when you want to get from “I’ve heard of these tools” to “they are actually installed, verified, and working on my machine.”

Alex: Exactly. And because our audience includes blind and low-vision learners, we’ll keep naming commands, interface locations, and verification cues out loud. We’ll also include the maintenance and troubleshooting details, not just the happy path.

Alex: At a high level, the setup process has six parts: check system requirements, confirm versions, install the platform you want, verify the installation, troubleshoot if needed, and keep your tools updated.

Jamie: And before we get lost in platform differences, what’s the biggest rule that applies to all of them?

Alex: Tool currency. These agents depend on current features, current APIs, and bug fixes. Older versions are a common reason things fail. The baseline in the source is May 2026, and the guidance is to use the latest versions.

Jamie: What are the minimums learners should keep in mind?

Alex: For VS Code, version 1.113 or later, stable or Insiders. GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot Chat should be current from the VS Code Marketplace. Node.js should be version 18 or higher. Python should be 3.8 or higher. And the supported operating systems are Windows 10 or 11, macOS 10.15 or later, and Linux, with Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or later as the primary baseline.

Jamie: Let’s make the operating system piece concrete.

Alex: On Windows, you want Windows 10 build 1909 or later, or Windows 11. Supported architectures are x64 and Arm64 in preview, and PowerShell 5.1 or later is required for command-line tools. On macOS, the minimum is Catalina, version 10.15, on either Intel or Apple Silicon, and you also need the command-line tools, which you can install with xcode-select double dash install. On Linux, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or later is the main target, with x64 as primary and ARM64 supported, and Debian, Fedora, and RHEL-family systems are also supported.

Jamie: And the resource requirements vary a little by platform, right?

Alex: They do. GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude Code and Claude Desktop each call for about 4 gigabytes of RAM. Gemini CLI and Codex CLI can work with about 2 gigabytes. Disk needs range from about 500 megabytes to 2 gigabytes available. Network access is required for most of these, with Codex CLI noting optional network access for local mode. There are also platform notes: Copilot in VS Code supports inline suggestions, chat, and Accessible View. Claude Desktop is aimed at longer context windows and longer sessions. Gemini CLI emphasizes fast iteration and Google Search integration. Codex CLI uses experimental roles and TOML configuration.

Jamie: If someone asks, “What exact tools do I need for my chosen platform?” how would you answer?

Alex: For GitHub Copilot in VS Code, you need VS Code 1.113 or later, the GitHub Copilot extension, the GitHub Copilot Chat extension, Node.js 18 or later for tools like Playwright and axe-core, and Git 2.20 or later for repository work. For Claude Code, you need the Claude Code CLI, installed from Anthropic’s docs path, and an active Claude subscription such as Pro, Max, or Team. For Gemini CLI, you need the Gemini CLI and a Google AI Studio API key. For Claude Desktop, you need the desktop app, a Claude subscription, and MCP server configuration in a dot m c p dot json file. For Codex CLI, you need the CLI itself and Node.js 18 or later because installation uses npm.

Jamie: That’s a nice checklist mindset: operating system, runtime, app or CLI, authentication, and then the agents repository itself.

Alex: Yes. And now let’s talk version checks, because verifying first saves time.

Alex: On GitHub Copilot in VS Code, you can check VS Code with: code space double dash version. To confirm the Copilot extension is installed, use: code space double dash list-extensions, pipe to grep space dash i space copilot. To check Node.js, run node space double dash version and npm space double dash version. To verify Git, run git space double dash version.

Jamie: And what outputs are we hoping for?

Alex: VS Code 1.113.0 or higher, an extension listing that includes github dot copilot, Node.js version 18 or higher, and Git version 2.20 or higher.

Jamie: What about Claude Code?

Alex: Run claude space code space double dash version. To verify subscription and authentication, use claude space code space whoami. And check Node.js with node space double dash version.

Jamie: Gemini CLI?

Alex: Run gemini space double dash version. To confirm your API key is configured, use gemini space config space show. And again, check Node.js with node space double dash version.

Jamie: Claude Desktop is more graphical.

Alex: Right. You check inside the app under Settings, then About.

Jamie: And Codex CLI?

Alex: Use codex space double dash version, then node space double dash version, and npm space double dash version.

Jamie: Now for the actual installation paths. Which one is recommended for most workshops?

Alex: GitHub Copilot in VS Code. It’s the recommended starting point for most workshop settings.

Jamie: Walk us through it.

Alex: Step one: install VS Code from code dot visualstudio dot com, run the installer, and verify it opens successfully. Step two: install the GitHub Copilot extensions. Open the Extensions panel with Control Shift X, or use the View menu and choose Extensions. Search for GitHub Copilot. Install both GitHub Copilot by GitHub and GitHub Copilot Chat by GitHub. Then sign in with your GitHub account when prompted. Step three: install Node.js from nodejs dot org, choosing version 18 LTS or later. Verify with node double dash version and npm double dash version. Step four: clone the Accessibility Agents repository. Change into your projects folder, run git clone with the repository URL, then change into the accessibility-agents directory. Step five: open the repository in VS Code with code space dot. Step six: verify that the agents load. Open Copilot Chat with Control Alt I. Type the at sign and listen or inspect for agent autocomplete suggestions. Also verify that the dot github slash agents slash folder exists in the repository. Step seven is optional but useful: install global tools. For accessibility scanning, npm install dash g at axe-core slash cli and pa11y. For Playwright testing, npm install dash g playwright.

Jamie: I want to underline the accessibility detail there. In VS Code, typing the at sign and hearing autocomplete suggestions, or reviewing them in Accessible View, can be a meaningful confirmation that agents are discoverable.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: What about Claude Code?

Alex: Install it with npm install dash g at anthropic-ai slash claude-code. Then authenticate by running claude space code space auth and following the browser login flow. After that, clone the accessibility-agents repository, change into it, and test by running claude space code space at daily-briefing space morning space briefing.

Jamie: So the browser login flow is not an optional flourish. It is part of setup.

Alex: Yes. If you skip authentication, the tool may be installed but unusable.

Jamie: And Gemini CLI?

Alex: Install it with npm install dash g at google slash gemini-cli. Then get an API key from ai dot google dot dev and set the environment variable GEMINI underscore API underscore KEY to your key. On Unix-like shells, the example is export space GEMINI_API_KEY equals quoted key. Then test with gemini double dash version and gemini whoami. To use it with the agents, run gemini skill search accessibility-agents and gemini skill use community-access slash accessibility-agents.

Jamie: So for Gemini, authentication is API-key based rather than a browser sign-in to a subscription account.

Alex: Correct.

Jamie: Claude Desktop is a different shape because it needs MCP.

Alex: It does. First, download the app from claude dot ai slash download, install it, and open it. Then configure the MCP server by creating or editing a file named dot m c p dot json in your home folder. On macOS and Linux, that is tilde slash dot m c p dot json. On Windows, it is percent USERPROFILE percent backslash dot m c p dot json.

Jamie: And what goes in that file?

Alex: A JSON object declaring an mcpServers block. Inside it, define accessibility-agents with command set to node, args pointing to the path of the repository’s mcp-server slash index dot js file, and an env block such as PORT equals 3000.

Jamie: Then restart the app?

Alex: Yes. Quit Claude Desktop completely, reopen it, and verify the MCP server connects by checking logs.

Jamie: That path detail matters. If the path to index dot js is wrong, everything can look installed but still not connect.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: And finally Codex CLI.

Alex: Install with npm install dash g at codex-cli slash core. Then initialize configuration with codex init and answer the interactive setup questions. After that, test with codex double dash version and codex role list. To use accessibility agents, run codex role search accessibility and codex run at accessibility-lead.

Jamie: So for Codex, we should explicitly expect setup prompts.

Alex: Yes. “Answer interactive setup questions” is part of the installation flow, not a side note.

Alex: Once any platform is installed, do a post-installation verification. Think of this as a checklist. First, confirm core tools: node double dash version and git double dash version should report at least Node 18 and Git 2.20. Second, confirm the repository is cloned. Listing the accessibility-agents directory should show the dot github slash agents slash folder. Third, confirm agents are discoverable. Type the at sign in the relevant chat or CLI and check whether agent names appear in autocomplete. Fourth, confirm network access. If GitHub or required services are blocked by a firewall or proxy, the setup may partially work but fail when it tries to fetch or authenticate. Fifth, if you are using Claude or Gemini, confirm API or account authentication with claude code whoami or gemini whoami.

Jamie: And then there’s the simplest real-world test: run one agent.

Alex: Exactly. In GitHub Copilot in VS Code, open chat with Control Alt I and type at daily-briefing morning briefing. In Claude Code, run claude code at daily-briefing morning briefing. In Gemini CLI, run gemini at daily-briefing morning briefing. In Claude Desktop, type at daily-briefing morning briefing in the chat input. In Codex CLI, run codex run at daily-briefing morning briefing.

Jamie: And if the agent responds with information, installation is considered successful.

Alex: Yes. That is the practical pass condition.

Jamie: Now let’s talk about what goes wrong.

Alex: For GitHub Copilot in VS Code, one issue is that agents do not appear after typing the at sign. Common causes are missing or outdated extensions. The fix is to reinstall GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot Chat from the VS Code Marketplace. Another issue is a “Cannot find agents” error. A common cause is that the dot github slash agents slash folder is missing. The remedy is to clone the full accessibility-agents repository rather than copying files manually. A third problem is chat not working because Copilot is not signed in. In that case, sign in again through the Copilot interface.

Jamie: And the source specifically calls out cache and restart steps too.

Alex: Right. If VS Code seems stuck in a bad state, delete the VS Code cache and restart VS Code. Those two actions can clear extension-loading issues.

Jamie: What about the other platforms, even if the source doesn’t spell out every row in the table we only partially saw?

Alex: We can still teach the main compatibility mindset from the appendix. For Claude Code, likely failure points include npm-based installation problems, missing Node.js, or incomplete authentication. Check the CLI version, confirm Node 18 or later, and rerun auth if needed. For Gemini CLI, likely issues include a missing or invalid API key, environment variables not being set in the current shell, or Node.js being too old. Recheck gemini config show, verify your key, and confirm node double dash version. For Claude Desktop, the big risks are malformed dot m c p dot json, incorrect file paths, or forgetting to fully restart the application after configuration changes. Validate the JSON carefully and review logs. For Codex CLI, common trouble areas are incomplete initialization, Node or npm path problems, or misunderstanding the roles configuration. Rerun codex init if necessary and verify codex role list works.

Jamie: And then there’s universal troubleshooting.

Alex: Yes. Across all platforms: verify versions first, confirm authentication, confirm network access, make sure the repository is complete, prefer the latest stable tools, and restart the affected app or shell after major changes. If a command behaves oddly, test whether your shell can actually find it with a version command before assuming the agents are at fault.

Jamie: Let’s finish with updates, because this appendix is very clear that setup is not one-and-done.

Alex: Correct. Updates matter because these tools evolve quickly. New accessibility features, API capabilities, support for custom agents or skills, bug fixes, and compatibility changes often require current versions. Running old versions is one of the fastest ways to get stuck with missing features or broken workflows.

Jamie: So learners should have an update rhythm.

Alex: Yes. The appendix includes update schedules by platform, and the larger idea is that fast-moving agent ecosystems deserve regular checks, not annual maintenance. For VS Code, update the editor itself. For extensions, update GitHub Copilot and related extensions through the Extensions interface. The source explicitly notes that you can use the VS Code UI, go to Extensions, and click update on the GitHub Copilot extensions.

Jamie: That’s important for learners who prefer graphical workflows or who find the command line less convenient in some contexts.

Alex: Absolutely. Good setup guidance should support both command-line and UI-first habits.

Jamie: And update best practices?

Alex: A few. Update before a workshop, not during it. Re-run version checks after updating. If authentication-dependent tools start acting strangely after an update, verify sign-in again. Read changelogs for breaking changes. And if you rely on accessibility workflows like Playwright or axe-core, keep those supporting tools current too, not just the main AI client.

Jamie: Before we close, can we do a quick learning-card style recap?

Alex: Sure. If you remember one rule, remember this: use current versions. If you remember one platform recommendation, start with GitHub Copilot in VS Code for most workshops. If you remember one repository check, make sure dot github slash agents slash exists. If you remember one verification move, run a single agent like at daily-briefing morning briefing. If you remember one troubleshooting principle, check versions, authentication, and restart state before doing anything more exotic. If you remember one maintenance habit, keep VS Code, extensions, Node.js, and your chosen agent platform updated on a regular schedule.

Jamie: And if learners want to go deeper?

Alex: The appendix points to references and authoritative sources, including the Accessibility Agents repository, system requirements documentation, GitHub Copilot docs, custom instructions support information, docs about custom agents and agent skills, auto model selection, the Copilot changelog feed, the VS Code Copilot chat overview, the VS Code agent overview, and VS Code custom instructions documentation. It also includes a section-level source map so you can verify facts section by section.

Jamie: That source map is a nice reminder that installation guidance changes over time, so checking upstream docs is part of being a reliable contributor.

Alex: Exactly. Setup is technical, but it is also an accessibility practice: current tools, clear verification, reproducible steps, and careful troubleshooting make collaboration more inclusive for everyone.

Jamie: Well said.

Alex: That’s it for this setup walkthrough. Next time you prepare a workshop machine or your own development environment, you’ll have a structured path: requirements, version checks, installation, verification, troubleshooting, and updates.

77. Episode 55: Advanced Agent Patterns

Using agents for code review, pair programming, CI/CD integration, and team workflows.

Based on: Appendix : Advanced Agent Patterns

Download Episode 55 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 55: Advanced Agent Patterns

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re digging into advanced agent patterns: how AI agents can delegate work, reuse workflows, automate checks at the right moments, and even use browser tools to inspect behavior instead of only reading static code.

Jamie: So this is less, “What is an agent?” and more, “How do you build a really capable agent system without turning it into a giant mess?”

Alex: Exactly. Think of this as the architecture layer behind strong accessibility workflows. It connects directly to practical work blind and low-vision developers and reviewers may do in GitHub, VS Code, and collaborative open source projects.

Jamie: And before we get too far, there’s some framing in the source that matters. This appendix is a reference companion to earlier materials on accessibility agents, agent reference material, and installation and setup. It also points learners to authoritative sources in the Accessibility Agents repository and its skills documentation.

Alex: Right. So the intent here is not just theory. It’s a companion reference for building and extending real agent systems.

Alex: Let’s start with architecture. A single agent can be good at one task, but a more advanced setup uses a parent agent and specialized subagents.

Jamie: What is a subagent in plain language?

Alex: An agent is a standalone AI assistant focused on a domain, like ARIA patterns. A subagent is that same kind of specialist, but invoked by another agent. So a general web accessibility auditor might hand off one part of the job to an ARIA specialist, another to a contrast checker, another to a keyboard navigation specialist, and so on.

Jamie: So the parent agent becomes more of an orchestrator than a do-everything expert.

Alex: Yes. A useful example is a web accessibility wizard receiving a request to audit a page. Instead of doing one broad, shallow pass, it can orchestrate multiple specialists: one checking ARIA roles, one checking color contrast, one checking tab order, one checking images and headings, one checking tables. Then it gathers all of those results into a consolidated audit report.

Jamie: That sounds more reliable than one giant prompt asking one agent to remember every accessibility domain at once.

Alex: That’s the core idea. Delegation over monolithic design.

Jamie: How do you actually tell an agent to use subagents?

Alex: In the source, the pattern is to put that behavior into the agent’s instructions or a custom prompt and invoke subagents through a function like runSubagent. The exact implementation may vary by platform, but conceptually the parent passes the subagent’s name, a targeted prompt, and often a brief description of the task.

Jamie: So something like: call the ARIA specialist, pass in the component HTML, ask for an ARIA compliance review. Then separately call the contrast specialist with CSS rules and ask for color contrast verification.

Alex: Exactly. Small, focused assignments.

Jamie: When should learners reach for subagents instead of one agent?

Alex: Several cases. For a full page audit, a primary web accessibility agent can dispatch all specialists in parallel and then merge the findings. For code review, a fixer agent might call an ARIA specialist and a contrast specialist to verify whether a proposed fix really works across domains. For document auditing, a document accessibility wizard can serve as a single entry point while delegating to platform-specific experts for Word, PDF, or Excel. And for Markdown, a Markdown accessibility assistant might call a link checker to cross-check link text and heading hierarchy.

Jamie: I like that because it mirrors how human teams work. One coordinator, several specialists.

Alex: Yes, and the appendix gives four principles for making that work well. First, delegation over monoliths: one parent calls specialists, but specialists generally should not call other specialists, because that can create runaway loops or tangled control flow. Second, error recovery: if one subagent fails, the parent logs the failure and continues the rest of the audit. Third, context preservation: the parent passes enough context, such as HTML, CSS, or the document content, so the subagent can make grounded judgments. Fourth, result aggregation: the parent is responsible for combining everything into one coherent report.

Jamie: That error recovery point feels especially important in accessibility workflows. You don’t want one broken checker to silence five other useful findings.

Alex: Precisely.

Alex: The next big idea is skills.

Jamie: And here the word skill means something more structured than just, “the model is good at a thing,” right?

Alex: Right. In this appendix, a skill is a reusable multi-step workflow packaged with reference files, templates, and automation scripts. You can think of a skill as a repeatable procedure. It can be invoked by an agent, or in some environments directly by a user using a slash command.

Jamie: So instead of re-explaining the whole process every time, you encapsulate the workflow.

Alex: Exactly. For example, a web-scanning skill might include crawling logic, URL inventory templates, browser automation code, and reference documentation. A report-generation skill might include severity scoring algorithms, scorecard templates, CSV export logic, and WCAG mapping data.

Jamie: That sounds a lot like good software engineering: don’t duplicate process, package it.

Alex: Yes, and the appendix lists a broad library of core skills, more than twenty-five, organized by capability.

Jamie: Can we walk through those categories?

Alex: Absolutely. For web scanning, there are skills like web-scanning and web-severity-scoring, used for page inventory, audit scoping, and severity calculation. For web remediation, there are skills like web-issue-fixer and web-csv-reporter, which support applying fixes and exporting findings. For document scanning, skills include document-scanning and document-accessibility-rules, used to audit Word, Excel, PDF, or EPUB and map issues to WCAG. For document remediation, there are document-remediation and document-csv-reporter, focused on fixing documents and generating compliance reports. For Markdown, the library includes markdown-accessibility, markdown-fixer, and markdown-csv-reporter, which are useful for auditing Markdown files and fixing link text, heading structure, or things like confusing emoji usage. There are also CI and CD integration skills such as lighthouse-scanner and github-accessibility-scanner for parsing continuous integration reports and tracking regressions. Framework-specific skills include framework-accessibility, react-patterns, and vue-patterns. Python development tools include python-fact-grounded-coding and pylance-refactoring. Testing-focused skills include testing-coach and accessibility-testing-setup. And compliance skills include wcag-guide, accessibility-rules-reference, and help-url-reference.

Jamie: That’s a strong reminder that accessibility work isn’t just one kind of artifact. It’s websites, documents, Markdown, CI pipelines, framework code, testing setups, and reference guidance.

Alex: Exactly. The skill system reflects the actual breadth of the work.

Jamie: How does a learner use a skill in practice?

Alex: Two main ways are highlighted. One is directly from a chat interface through commands such as slash web-scanning followed by a URL, slash report-generation with findings data, or slash python-fact-grounded-coding with a script name. The other is from within a custom agent’s instructions. In that case, the agent is told when to invoke a skill, what inputs to supply, and what output format is expected.

Jamie: So the agent instructions might say: when you need to audit a webpage, use the web-scanning skill with a URL, use WCAG 2.2 AA as the severity model, and produce JSON.

Alex: Exactly. Clear inputs, clear output expectations.

Jamie: What about writing your own skill?

Alex: The appendix gives a pattern for that too. A custom skill lives in a directory like .github slash skills slash my-skill-name, with a SKILL.md file. That file should define the skill name, its purpose, its inputs, its workflow, its output, and its references.

Jamie: Can you unpack those sections?

Alex: Purpose explains what problem the skill solves. Inputs list what the skill needs, such as a URL, a file path, or optional configuration. Workflow lays out the sequence, like parse input, execute steps, collect results, format output. Output defines the report format, maybe JSON, Markdown, or CSV, and often includes an example. References point to related agents or external documentation.

Jamie: And there are supporting files too.

Alex: Yes. Templates can hold input or output patterns. Scripts can hold automation in shell or Python. Reference data can store lookup tables or compliance mappings.

Jamie: Why is that structure so important?

Alex: Because it makes a skill portable, inspectable, and reusable. And the appendix emphasizes skill reuse across agents. One web accessibility wizard might use web-scanning plus web-severity-scoring. A web issue fixer might reuse web-scanning plus web-issue-fixer. A link checker might reuse web-scanning plus a narrower link-validation subset. The benefit is consistent behavior and less duplicated logic.

Alex: Now let’s move into hooks, which are about lifecycle automation.

Jamie: This is where the system starts doing useful things before a human remembers to ask.

Alex: Exactly. A hook is a JSON configuration that triggers agent actions automatically at specific events. The key accessibility idea is prevention and timely feedback. Instead of waiting until a late-stage review, the system can intervene on edit, save, commit, pull request creation, or on a schedule.

Jamie: So what lifecycle events are called out?

Alex: The appendix lists editing before save, saving after changes, committing before push, pull request creation before merge, and scheduled runs such as nightly or weekly audits.

Jamie: That maps nicely to the real development rhythm.

Alex: It does. The sample configuration lives in a file like .github slash hooks slash accessibility.hooks.json and contains an array of hook objects.

Jamie: What kinds of hooks are shown in the sample?

Alex: One example is proactive detection on file edit. It watches matching files, routes them to an ARIA specialist, checks a condition such as whether the file includes ARIA-related content, and highlights violations at warning severity. Another example is an edit gate on file save. It watches source files, runs a broader accessibility wizard, and if severity crosses an error threshold, it blocks the save and tells the user to use a fixer agent. There is also a commit-check hook that runs on commit across all files, uses an accessibility lead agent, and appends scan results to the commit message. And a nightly audit hook runs on a cron schedule, targets documentation Markdown, uses a Markdown accessibility assistant, and creates issues with labels like accessibility and auto-audit.

Jamie: That last one is especially good for repositories that have lots of docs and not enough time for constant manual review.

Alex: Yes. It keeps quality from depending entirely on memory.

Jamie: What properties does a hook configuration typically include?

Alex: The appendix lists a standard set. Name is the unique identifier. Event says when it runs, like on-file-edit or on-commit. Pattern is a glob describing which files it applies to. Agent is the specialist or orchestrator to run. Condition defines whether the hook should trigger. Action defines what happens, such as highlight, block-save, scan-and-report, or create-issue. Severity can be info, warning, or error. Message is custom feedback to the user. Labels support issue creation workflows.

Jamie: And the source also mentions hook examples beyond the sample block.

Alex: Yes, including a proactive ARIA detection example. The full examples in the source are partially truncated in what we received, but the pattern is clear: hooks let you encode accessible quality gates close to the work.

Jamie: There’s also a heading about enabling hooks by platform.

Alex: Right, and this matters administratively. Platform support can vary. Some environments support custom instructions, agents, or automation differently than others. So learners should verify the current support matrix in GitHub documentation, Copilot documentation, changelogs, and custom agent guidance. In other words, the design pattern is stable, but exact enablement depends on the platform’s current capabilities.

Alex: Next comes browser tools for behavioral scanning.

Jamie: Which sounds very different from just reading source files.

Alex: It is. Browser tools let an agent interact with a page as rendered and behaving in the browser. That matters because many accessibility problems show up only when JavaScript runs, focus moves, dynamic content appears, or the layout changes.

Jamie: So what kinds of browser capabilities are implied here?

Alex: The appendix points broadly to available browser tools and using them in agents. In practice, that usually means tools that can open pages, inspect the DOM, interact with controls, follow links, observe focus movement, capture rendered state, and gather page content for analysis.

Jamie: That seems essential for behavioral accessibility issues.

Alex: Yes. Static code analysis can tell you a button lacks an accessible name. Browser automation can go further and reveal whether a modal traps focus incorrectly, whether keyboard order is broken after a menu opens, or whether content injected after a click is actually announced or reachable.

Jamie: The source specifically calls out auditing page accessibility and then doing a smart audit based on page content.

Alex: Right. That means an agent can first inspect what kind of page it’s dealing with, then decide which checks matter most. For example, if it finds a data table, it can prioritize table semantics. If it finds a form-heavy page, it can focus on labels, error handling, and keyboard flow. If it detects media, it can ask about captions or transcripts. That adaptive behavior is often more efficient than running every possible check with equal weight.

Jamie: And what about limitations?

Alex: The appendix explicitly includes browser tool limitations and workarounds. Even when browser tools are powerful, they may have incomplete support for screen reader behavior, authentication flows, highly dynamic apps, or complex stateful interactions. Workarounds often involve combining browser automation with code inspection, logging, targeted prompts, saved test fixtures, or human verification for the final judgment.

Jamie: So learners should hear this clearly: browser-based scans are powerful, but they are not a substitute for all manual testing, especially when real assistive technology behavior matters.

Alex: Exactly right.

Alex: Now let’s talk orchestration, which is where these building blocks become repeatable patterns.

Jamie: The appendix gives named delegation patterns, yes?

Alex: Yes. The first is a parallel scanning pattern described as a web accessibility wizard. The basic idea is that one orchestrator launches multiple specialists at once.

Jamie: That’s the full-audit model we discussed earlier.

Alex: Correct, and the related parallel audit idea is that independent checks can run concurrently to save time and produce broader coverage. This is especially useful when scanning a page or set of pages for multiple issue classes.

Jamie: Then there’s cascading fixes, with a web issue fixer.

Alex: Right. In a cascading fixes pattern, one stage detects issues, another proposes or applies fixes, and then additional specialists verify whether those fixes introduced new problems or failed to resolve the original ones. It’s sequential and corrective, not just diagnostic.

Jamie: So you might detect a missing label, apply a remediation, and then re-run related checks for focus order, naming, or validation feedback.

Alex: Exactly. The third pattern is skill-first workflows, with a testing coach as the example. Here the main agent relies primarily on invoking reusable skills rather than improvising each process from scratch. That produces more predictable test setup, reporting, and teaching behavior.

Jamie: That seems useful for education, because learners can get the same process each time.

Alex: Yes, especially when teaching structured accessibility testing. The fourth pattern is report aggregation, described as a cross-page analyzer. That means collecting findings from multiple pages or scans and synthesizing them into a portfolio view, identifying recurring issues, shared components, or systemic failures.

Jamie: Which is much closer to how teams actually prioritize work. Not just one broken page, but patterns across a whole site or product.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: The appendix then moves into advanced techniques.

Jamie: Starting with custom skills for your organization.

Alex: Yes. This is about building a pattern library that reflects your team’s conventions, design system, and accessibility expectations. The source gives an example path: .github slash skills slash our-pattern-library slash SKILL.md.

Jamie: And the skill itself is called Our Accessibility Pattern Library.

Alex: Right. Conceptually, that skill’s purpose is to give agents a reusable internal source of approved accessibility patterns. The patterns included would be your organization’s preferred implementations, guardrails, or known-good examples. Inputs might include component names, file paths, framework context, or requested pattern types. Output would be recommendations, mappings, or example implementations aligned with the organization’s standards. Usage would explain how agents or developers invoke the library in practice.

Jamie: That’s powerful because accessibility guidance often needs to be local, not just general. A team might have a house style for dialogs, forms, error messaging, or keyboard interactions.

Alex: Exactly. A custom pattern library lets the agent give advice that matches the repository the learner is actually in.

Jamie: What comes next?

Alex: Continuous evaluation hooks. This extends the hook idea from occasional checks to recurring evaluation. Instead of treating accessibility as a one-time audit, the system keeps measuring over time, perhaps on commits, pull requests, or schedules, so regressions surface early.

Jamie: Then platform-specific skill variants.

Alex: Yes. Not every environment behaves the same. A skill may need variants tuned for GitHub workflows, a particular editor integration, a cloud agent environment, or a local toolchain. Same overall purpose, different implementation details.

Jamie: And result caching for performance.

Alex: That’s an important engineering technique. If scans, lookups, or reference computations are expensive and inputs have not changed, caching results can make agents much faster and cheaper. But the tradeoff is freshness. You need a good strategy for invalidating stale results when files, pages, or dependencies change.

Jamie: So even in accessibility automation, performance architecture matters.

Alex: Very much so.

Jamie: The appendix also mentions learning cards.

Alex: Yes, learning cards for advanced patterns. Even without the full card text in the excerpt we received, the intent is clear: distill the advanced ideas into study-friendly reminders. For learners, that usually means compact takeaways such as when to use subagents, how skills differ from agents, where hooks fit into the lifecycle, and why browser tools complement static analysis.

Jamie: And then there are references and authoritative sources.

Alex: Right. The source explicitly points learners back to authoritative documentation: the Accessibility Agents repository’s skills directory, the skills documentation, GitHub Docs, the GitHub changelog, Copilot docs, the custom instructions support matrix, and documentation on custom agents. It also includes a section-level source map, which is administrative but important because it tells you where each part of the appendix is grounded.

Jamie: That’s especially useful when platform behavior changes. Learners can verify what is still current.

Alex: Exactly. For accessible contribution workflows, that matters a lot. Tooling support evolves, so you want habits of checking the docs, not just memorizing one configuration.

Jamie: Let me try a practical summary, and you tell me if I’ve got it. If I’m building an advanced accessibility agent workflow, I should think in layers. First, architecture: one parent agent can delegate to subagents instead of trying to do everything itself. Second, skills: package repeatable multi-step workflows so multiple agents can reuse them. Third, hooks: trigger those capabilities at useful lifecycle moments like edit, save, commit, pull request, or scheduled audits. Fourth, browser tools: inspect behavior, not just source. Fifth, orchestration patterns: choose whether I need parallel scanning, cascading fixes, skill-first operation, or aggregated reporting. And finally, advanced refinements like organization-specific skills, continuous evaluation, platform variants, and caching.

Alex: That is an excellent summary.

Jamie: And for our audience, one more takeaway: these patterns can support accessibility work in a way that is structured and scalable, but they don’t replace judgment. They help blind and low-vision contributors, maintainers, and educators build workflows that are more consistent, more proactive, and easier to reuse across projects.

Alex: Beautifully said. The best agent systems do not just answer questions. They encode good process, reduce repeated labor, preserve accessibility knowledge, and make high-quality contribution workflows easier for everyone on the team.

Jamie: And they do it in a way that can fit GitHub repositories, VS Code habits, CI pipelines, documentation review, and open source collaboration.

Alex: Exactly. That’s the real value of these advanced patterns.

Alex: Next time you see an agent that looks magical, ask a better question: what subagents, skills, hooks, browser tools, and orchestration patterns are making that result possible?

Jamie: Because behind the magic, there’s architecture.

78. Episode 56: Document Developer Tools

Managing documentation with version control, collaboration, accessibility, and developer workflows.

Based on: Appendix : Document Developer Tools

Download Episode 56 (MP3)

Read Transcript - Episode 56: Document Developer Tools

Transcript

Alex: Welcome back. Today we’re looking at a reference-style appendix that ties together document accessibility work and developer tooling. Think of it as a practical companion to broader material on accessibility agents, an agents reference, and advanced usage patterns.

Jamie: So this is less, “Here is one tool,” and more, “Here is a whole toolkit for accessible documents and accessible development workflows?”

Alex: Exactly. And the appendix points learners to authoritative source repositories for two groups: a document accessibility team and a developer tools team. Together they cover Office files, PDFs, EPUBs, Python and wxPython work, desktop apps, NVDA add-ons, and CI automation.

Alex: At a high level, the appendix says there are dedicated agents for scanning, remediating, and enforcing accessibility standards across business documents and developer workflows.

Jamie: And I want to underline something for our audience: even though this is framed around agents, the real lesson is the accessibility checks themselves, the remediation patterns, and how to fit them into GitHub-centered work.

Alex: Well said. The table of contents lays out the learning path: document accessibility agents, Microsoft Office accessibility, PDF and EPUB accessibility, developer tools agents, Python and wxPython accessibility, desktop and NVDA development, and CI/CD integration.

Alex: Let’s start with the document accessibility team. The appendix says there are 15 agents dedicated to document accessibility.

Jamie: That’s a lot. Can we organize them by job?

Alex: Yes. First, audit agents: `@word-accessibility`, `@excel-accessibility`, `@powerpoint-accessibility`, `@pdf-accessibility`, and `@epub-accessibility`. Their role is to inspect a file type and produce findings.

Jamie: So they don’t just say “good” or “bad.” They report actual problems.

Alex: Right. For example, headings, alt text, hyperlinks in Word; headers, merged cells, formulas in Excel; slide structure, alt text, animations in PowerPoint; tagging and PDF/UA compliance in PDF; and structure and reading order in EPUB.

Alex: Second, configuration agents: `@office-scan-config`, `@pdf-scan-config`, and `@epub-scan-config`. These let you adjust the scanning rules, typically through JSON configuration.

Jamie: So a team can standardize how audits run.

Alex: Exactly. Third, remediation agents: `@office-remediator` for Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, plus `@pdf-remediator` for PDF fixes.

Alex: Then there are workflow and support agents: `@document-accessibility-wizard` for guided audits across document types, `@cross-document-analyzer` to compare accessibility across versions, `@document-inventory` to scan a folder and build a manifest, `@document-csv-reporter` to export findings with WCAG mappings, and `@document-remediation-coach` to walk someone through fixes step by step.

Jamie: That last group feels especially useful for teams using GitHub Issues or project boards, because audit output can become trackable work.

Alex: Yes. You can imagine inventorying documents, auditing them, exporting findings to CSV, then turning severe issues into tickets.

Jamie: Let’s move into Office documents. Starting with Word, what are the big accessibility problems the appendix wants learners to notice?

Alex: Several common ones. Missing document titles or missing Heading 1 usage. Broken heading hierarchy, like jumping from heading level 1 to 3 and then back to 2. Images without alt text. Vague hyperlinks such as “click here.” Merged table cells that make table interpretation harder. Information conveyed only by color. And missing language metadata.

Jamie: That’s a good checklist. And for blind and low-vision users, all of those affect navigation or comprehension.

Alex: Exactly. A clean heading hierarchy helps screen reader users skim. Descriptive links let people decide whether to follow them. Alt text gives meaning to non-text content. Language tags help speech engines pronounce correctly.

Jamie: What does the Word audit flow look like?

Alex: The example command is essentially: ask `@word-accessibility` to audit a `.docx` file. The agent scans structure, checks heading hierarchy, validates image alt text, checks tables, and then returns a report. In the sample, it reports three errors, including broken headings and five images missing alt text, two warnings like merged cells and unclear hyperlinks, and an overall severity score of 72 out of 100, labeled a C grade.

Jamie: I like that it distinguishes errors from warnings. That gives teams triage language.

Alex: It does. Then `@office-remediator` can be used to fix the Word file. The sample shows automatic fixes like restructuring heading hierarchy, converting merged cells to simpler rows, and adding placeholder alt text. It also creates a changelog and returns a remediated document.

Jamie: Placeholder alt text is important to mention carefully. That means the file is improved, but a human still needs to review whether the text is actually meaningful.

Alex: Absolutely. Placeholder text is a bridge, not the final accessible answer.

Jamie: How about Excel? Spreadsheets can get messy fast.

Alex: They can. The appendix highlights common Excel issues: no designated header row, merged cells in data tables, hidden columns or rows used for layout, color-only meaning such as red equals error, complex formulas without explanation, and multiple tables crammed onto one sheet.

Jamie: And those become accessibility issues because the structure is unclear to assistive technology.

Alex: Correct. The fixes are very concrete: format data as a table and mark the header row, unmerge cells, unhide rows and columns and use filters instead, add icons or symbols along with color, use named ranges, document formula logic in another column, and separate multiple tables into different sheets with clear headers.

Jamie: What does the Excel audit agent report?

Alex: The example shows `@excel-accessibility` auditing a workbook by analyzing all sheets. It checks things like header rows, merged cells, named ranges, and color usage. Then it reports findings per sheet. In the sample, one sheet has four errors due to merged cells and missing headers, another sheet has warnings about complex formulas, and the overall severity is 65 out of 100, a D grade.

Jamie: And remediation?

Alex: With `@office-remediator`, the sample auto-fixes include unmerging cells in tables, designating header rows, and adding conditional formatting with symbols. It returns a remediated workbook and notes that some items still need manual review, such as complex formulas.

Jamie: That’s a useful pattern across this appendix: automate structural fixes, but flag semantic content decisions for humans.

Alex: Exactly right.

Jamie: Now PowerPoint, which often hides accessibility problems in visual polish.

Alex: Yes. The appendix lists common issues like slides without titles, animations that move too fast, images without alt text, important text embedded in images, poor color contrast, audio without captions or transcripts, and slide numbers placed in content instead of header or footer areas.

Jamie: That “text on image” issue matters a lot. A beautiful slide can still be inaccessible if the actual information isn’t exposed as text.

Alex: Precisely. Fixes include giving each slide a meaningful title, slowing animations to at least around three seconds, adding alt text, moving essential text into real text boxes, improving contrast, creating transcripts or detailed speaker notes for audio, and keeping slide numbers in the appropriate presentation metadata areas.

Jamie: What does the audit example show?

Alex: `@powerpoint-accessibility` scans all slides and checks titles, alt text, contrast ratios, animation speeds, and speaker notes. The sample report shows twelve images without alt text, three low-contrast slides, five too-fast animations, and an overall severity of 58 out of 100, another D.

Jamie: And the remediator can help here too?

Alex: Yes. The example uses `@office-remediator` with a PowerPoint-specific fix command and an option to add speaker notes. It adds placeholder alt text, adjusts animation timing to at least three seconds, improves contrast on problem slides, creates one set of speaker notes per slide, and returns a remediated presentation.

Jamie: Again, speaker notes templates help, but a presenter should still ensure they contain useful content.

Alex: Exactly.

Alex: Next comes PDF and EPUB accessibility.

Jamie: Let’s start with PDF, because PDFs are everywhere and often frustrating.

Alex: The appendix anchors PDF accessibility to PDF/UA, the ISO standard for accessible PDFs. It then spells out key requirements: tagged structure, meaningful alt text, bookmarks, correct reading order, proper language setting, accessible form labels, and not relying on scanned-image-only PDFs.

Jamie: So if a PDF is just a picture of text, it may look fine visually but be unusable to many readers unless OCR is applied.

Alex: Correct. The PDF needs to be text-searchable, properly tagged, and logically organized.

Jamie: What kinds of fixes are suggested?

Alex: Use tagged PDF templates, add tags in tools like Adobe Acrobat, add image descriptions, create bookmarks matching document headings, repair the tag tree and reading order, set document language, label form fields descriptively, and run OCR when the file is essentially scanned images.

Jamie: And the audit example?

Alex: `@pdf-accessibility` analyzes structure and validates PDF/UA compliance. The sample findings include missing alt text on five images, no bookmarks, language not set, and three unlabeled form fields, with a severity of 48 out of 100, an F.

Jamie: The markdown source truncates the full PDF remediation example, right?

Alex: Yes, the provided excerpt cuts off that command. But the surrounding material makes the intended role clear: `@pdf-remediator` fixes PDF accessibility issues, including tags and bookmarks, and returns a remediated PDF.

Jamie: So for coverage, we should say learners need to understand both the standard and the practical repair targets: tags, reading order, language, forms, OCR, and bookmarks.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: What about EPUB?

Alex: The appendix includes an EPUB accessibility agent and scan configuration support, and says EPUB audits focus on structure and reading order. Even from the shorter excerpt, the conceptual point is clear: digital publications need semantic structure and predictable navigation just as much as PDFs and Office files do.

Jamie: So if a team publishes long-form learning materials, EPUB shouldn’t be treated as an afterthought.

Alex: Right. Reading order, document structure, and accessible navigation matter there too.

Alex: The appendix then turns to the developer tools team, describing eight agents.

Jamie: We don’t get the full table in the excerpt, but the heading tells us the domain: Python, wxPython, NVDA, CI/CD, and accessible app development.

Alex: That’s the key. The document is broadening accessibility from “documents to consume” into “tools and software we build.”

Jamie: And for a GitHub audience, that means accessibility belongs in repositories, automation, and coding practices, not just in final files.

Alex: Exactly. The developer tools overview conceptually covers agents that help review code, support desktop accessibility work, and integrate checks into workflows.

Jamie: Let’s dig into Python and wxPython. What should learners take away from the appendix headings there?

Alex: Two big areas. First, Python accessibility best practices. Second, wxPython GUI accessibility. Even without every line of the original section, the headings are substantive and clearly intended to teach practical patterns.

Jamie: So let’s state the kind of things that belong in that practice set, staying faithful to the scope named in the appendix.

Alex: For Python accessibility best practices, learners should think in terms of exposing semantics, using clear labels and names, handling keyboard interaction properly, giving meaningful status and error messages, and designing logic so accessibility information can be surfaced consistently across an application.

Jamie: And for a GitHub workflow, that means code review shouldn’t ask only “Does it work?” but also “Can a keyboard user operate it?” and “Does assistive technology get the right information?”

Alex: Yes. In a Python project, accessibility quality often depends on explicit choices by the developer.

Jamie: Then wxPython adds GUI-specific concerns.

Alex: Right. With wxPython, the accessibility lens includes labeled controls, sensible tab order, keyboard reachability, readable focus handling, and making sure widgets expose useful information to platform accessibility APIs when possible.

Jamie: So if someone builds a desktop utility in Python, they should test beyond visual layout.

Alex: Exactly. They should test with keyboard-only use, with screen readers where feasible, and with attention to control naming and logical navigation.

Alex: Next is desktop and NVDA development.

Jamie: And this is especially relevant for our audience, since NVDA is so central to many blind users’ workflows.

Alex: Absolutely. The appendix includes desktop application accessibility and NVDA add-on development. It even names a sample file path: `my-addon/addon/globalPlugins/myPlugin.py`.

Jamie: That’s a concrete hint that the appendix isn’t just speaking abstractly. It expects readers to connect accessibility concepts to real add-on file structures.

Alex: Yes. Desktop application accessibility here means building apps whose controls, focus management, labels, states, and keyboard pathways are usable with assistive technology.

Jamie: And NVDA add-on development means writing extensions that integrate with NVDA responsibly and accessibly.

Alex: Correct. The mention of a global plugin Python file signals that add-on work lives in code, version control, and review processes just like any other software project.

Jamie: So a learner contributing to an NVDA add-on on GitHub should be ready to inspect plugin structure, understand Python files in the add-on tree, and think about both functionality and user experience.

Alex: Yes. Accessibility work there is both technical and experiential.

Jamie: Now let’s connect this to automation, because the appendix has a full section on CI/CD integration for accessibility.

Alex: It does. The main idea is that accessibility should be part of continuous integration and deployment, not just a one-time manual check.

Jamie: So in GitHub terms, this points straight to GitHub Actions.

Alex: Exactly. The appendix explicitly names accessibility in GitHub Actions and references a workflow file at `.github/workflows/accessibility.yml`.

Jamie: That path alone is a useful teaching moment for beginners: accessibility checks can live in the repository as code.

Alex: Yes. Once checks are in a workflow file, they can run on pushes, pull requests, or scheduled audits, helping teams catch regressions early.

Jamie: And that’s especially helpful in open source, where many contributors may not all share the same accessibility expertise.

Alex: Right. Automation creates consistency.

Jamie: The appendix also names Playwright accessibility testing.

Alex: Which suggests browser-based automated checks in addition to document and desktop concerns. In practice, Playwright can support scripted tests that examine UI behavior and accessibility signals as part of a CI pipeline.

Jamie: So the bigger lesson is: accessibility belongs in tests, not just in design docs.

Alex: Exactly. And when those tests run in GitHub Actions, they become part of the team’s regular development rhythm.

Alex: Near the end, the appendix includes learning cards, references, authoritative sources, and a section-level source map.

Jamie: Let’s not skip that administrative content, because learners often do.

Alex: Good point. The learning cards section signals that this appendix is meant for study and review, not just lookup. The references and authoritative sources matter because accessibility guidance should be anchored in trustworthy documentation.

Jamie: And the source map is interesting. It lists a verification path for each major section, repeatedly pointing learners to GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, GitHub Copilot docs, the custom instructions support matrix, and documentation about custom agents.

Alex: Yes. Even though the appendix topic is document and developer tool accessibility, it still situates itself inside the GitHub and Copilot documentation ecosystem. That tells learners two things: first, check official docs for current behavior; second, treat agent-based workflows as evolving tools whose support details may change.

Jamie: So if you’re building a contribution workflow around these ideas, you should verify the present-day product capabilities instead of assuming a static tool landscape.

Alex: Exactly.

Jamie: Can we close by stitching all this together into one practical mental model?

Alex: Yes. Here’s the model. Start by inventorying documents and code artifacts. Audit them with specialized agents matched to the file type or development domain. Configure scan rules when your organization needs consistent standards. Remediate what can be fixed automatically, but keep humans in the loop for meaning, context, and quality. Export findings for tracking. Compare versions over time to watch improvement or regression. And bring accessibility into GitHub Actions and test automation so it becomes a routine part of software and content delivery.

Jamie: And for blind and low-vision learners, the deeper message is empowering: accessibility isn’t only something done for users. It’s also something you can inspect, discuss in pull requests, automate, and improve as a contributor.

Alex: Beautifully put. Whether you’re fixing a Word document, repairing a tagged PDF, building a wxPython app, writing an NVDA add-on, or setting up an accessibility workflow in GitHub Actions, you are participating in a repeatable, teachable engineering practice.

Jamie: And that makes this appendix more than a catalog. It’s a map of where accessibility work happens.

Alex: Exactly. And that’s our goal: not just to know the names of the agents, but to understand the accessible workflows they support.
